Know the internals. Design the system. Debug the failure. Defend the trade-off. This handbook is for the senior (L5-equivalent) data engineering loop — the rounds where knowing what a watermark is gets you nothing, and explaining why yours is set to 90 seconds, what it costs, and what you'd see on the dashboard when it's wrong gets you the offer.

It is not meant to be read cover-to-cover before every interview. It is 20 parts and several hundred sections, because the job is that wide. Nobody interviews on all of it. Pick a mode, pick a path, and use the rest as a reference you trust.

How this handbook works

Every topic is organised around one progression. If you can move through it smoothly for a topic, you are ready for that topic. If you stall at any step, that is where to study.

StepWhat the interviewer is testingWhere it's trained
ExplainCan you state the mechanism at three depths and stop at the right one?“Answer depths” blocks (30 sec / 2 min / deep dive) throughout; the 30-second and 2-minute answers on every Interview Card
CalculateDo you size before you draw?Part 18 capacity toolkit; “Numbers that matter” on every card
DesignRequirements → numbers → model → architecture → failure → trade-off → ops → evolutionPart 18 framework; design scenarios in Part 08; transcripts in Part 09
DebugDo you diagnose before prescribing?Part 19 Debugging Lab; “Drill” blocks with hidden answers
DefendCan you hold a position under pushback — and drop it when the requirement changes?“Interviewer pushes back” blocks; Part 18 attack-mode catalogue
OperateWho gets paged, how you roll back, how you know it's right“Failure-first” tables; Parts 12, 14; Staff+ follow-ups

The recurring features

  • L5 Interview Card — ends every technical part. Must know, must explain, must draw, must code, must debug, numbers, traps, a 30-second and a 2-minute answer, and two follow-ups (deep-dive and Staff+). If you only have an evening, read the cards.
  • Answer depths — the same question answered in 30 seconds, 2 minutes and as a deep dive, with a note on where to stop. Senior candidates fail more often from answers with no shape than from answers with no content.
  • Interviewer pushes back — your claim, the follow-up that tests it, a strong answer and the tempting weak one.
  • Drill — a symptom, then “STOP. Answer before revealing.” The diagnosis is hidden until you click. Say your answer out loud first; recognition is not recall.
  • Failure-first — for each architecture: what fails, how you detect it, how you recover, how you stop it recurring.
  • 2026 Interview Note — separates the timeless concept from version-specific behaviour. Knowing which is which is itself a senior signal.
  • Code labels — every code block states engine, dialect and whether it runs as written (Yes), needs adapting (Illustrative) or is Pseudocode. Cross-engine SQL never runs unchanged; don't pretend it does in the room either.

Three ways to read it

A single “read time” for a handbook this size would be fiction. Each part shows three honest estimates under its title, derived from the page itself: Quick refresh (the lede, notes and Interview Card), Interview study (the full text at study pace) and Deep practice (drills, pushback rounds and the card's code/draw/debug prompts done for real). The contents below list all three per part.

Quick refresh · 15–30 min

The night before, or between rounds. Read the Interview Card of each part in your loop, then the matching cheat sheet in Part 20. Say every 30-second answer out loud. Don't open anything new.

Interview study · 60–120 min per part

One part per sitting. Read the sections the card points at, attempt each answer-depth question before reading it, and close by answering the card's “Must be able to explain” questions from memory.

Deep practice · open-ended

Drills with the answer hidden, the card's coding problems in a real editor, a whiteboard design from Part 18 against a timer, and a mock with someone who will push back. This is where offers are won.

The quality gate: twenty things you should be able to do

This is the bar the handbook is written to. If you can do all twenty convincingly — out loud, with numbers, under pushback — you are ready. Each links to where it's trained.

  1. Design a pipeline ingesting 100K events/sec — with numbers before boxes. → Part 18 §4 · capacity toolkit
  2. Explain why one Spark task takes 20× longer than the others — and what you'd measure to tell skew from a bad node. → Debugging Lab · Part 04 skew
  3. Explain Kafka's ordering guarantees, and what silently breaks them. → Part 13 ordering · Part 03 Kafka internals
  4. Design idempotent batch processing that is safe to rerun. → Part 18 §5 · Part 02 idempotency
  5. Explain watermark trade-offs: latency against completeness, and what happens to late events. → Part 03 watermarks · late data
  6. Design CDC from Postgres into a lakehouse. → Part 15 §8 · replication slots
  7. Choose a partition strategy — and defend it when one key is 20% of traffic. → Part 13 partitioning · Part 02 partition math
  8. Explain SCD Type 2 without memorised jargon. → Part 01 SCD
  9. Diagnose duplicate records in a streaming pipeline. → Debugging Lab · delivery semantics
  10. Estimate storage and compute for a stated workload. → Part 18 capacity toolkit
  11. Choose between Snowflake, BigQuery and a lakehouse for a stated workload. → Part 16 §11 · same model, different behaviour
  12. Secure sensitive customer data — design the control plane, not just “encrypt it”. → Part 14 SSN scenario · exfiltration scenario
  13. Design CI/CD for data pipelines. → Part 14 CI/CD · dbt slim CI
  14. Explain data contracts — and who is on the hook when one breaks. → Part 15 contracts · the 14-consumer incident
  15. Handle an incompatible schema change without breaking consumers. → Part 15 drill · compatibility
  16. Design a serving layer with sub-100-ms latency. → Part 16 §8
  17. Explain how AI/RAG changes data pipelines. → Part 17
  18. Recover from a bad production deployment. → Part 14 data release & rollback · failure drill
  19. Explain an architecture trade-off under interviewer pushback. → Part 18 §8 · attack-mode catalogue
  20. Describe a disagreement with a senior engineer without making either person sound foolish. → Part 09 Staff-signal behavioral

What changed in the 2026 edition

The earlier edition explained things. This one is organised around what you have to do with them in the room. Every part was audited against current official documentation; wrong or engine-specific claims were corrected or qualified; duplicate sections were merged; every code block now says where it runs. Eight parts are new: distributed systems, cloud, security & release engineering, CDC, contracts & dbt, serving systems & warehouse architecture, DE for AI systems, system design & capacity planning, the Debugging Lab and self-assessment & cheat sheets.

What “deep” means here

For every topic: the mechanism, the failure mode, how you'd notice it, how you'd debug it, and how you'd defend your choice when someone smart disagrees. Where a behaviour depends on the engine or version, the text says which. Where a number is a vendor default, it's labelled as one — defaults change; the reasoning behind them doesn't.

If your answer starts with a technology name before you've asked about scale, you've already skipped a step. That's the bar.

Known implementation differences The modeling concepts are engine-neutral. Hash functions, NULL handling in string concatenation, timestamp types and MERGE syntax all differ by engine, so every code block is labelled.

A modeling interview tests whether you can turn a vague business process into tables whose numbers are still right a year later. You declare the grain, choose history per attribute, join late data to the right version, and defend star vs wide table vs vault under pushback. Most "the number is wrong" incidents are modeling bugs, and this chapter is built around finding them.

1. Bounded vs Unbounded Data at Rest

Bounded data is finite: a snapshot, an archive, a reference table. You can scan it, sort it and re-derive it. Unbounded data is an append-only log that grows forever. The mechanics are in Part 02 §1. For modeling, one rule follows: it must be impossible to query an unbounded table without a time bound. Partition it by event date. Make retention (drop or cold-tier old partitions) and compaction part of the design. Guard the query path: a COUNT(DISTINCT user_id) with no dt filter works in month one and is unrunnable by year two.

BigQuery enforces the guard in DDL (require_partition_filter). Snowflake has no equivalent, so use STATEMENT_TIMEOUT_IN_SECONDS, resource monitors, and views that force a date predicate.

Engine: BigQueryDialect: GoogleSQLExecutable: Yes — BigQuery only
-- BigQuery: reject queries that don't filter on the partition column
CREATE TABLE playback.events_daily (
  event_ts      TIMESTAMP,
  user_id       STRING,
  title_id      STRING,
  watch_ms      INT64,
  dt            DATE
)
PARTITION BY dt
OPTIONS (
  require_partition_filter = TRUE,
  partition_expiration_days = 730   -- auto-drop after 2 years
);

The unbounded nature also affects backfills. For a bounded dimension, "regenerate from source" is a few GB; for an unbounded fact, it's years of events.

2. OLTP vs OLAP — The Physical Reality

The choice between row-oriented and column-oriented storage isn't philosophical — it's dictated by what the hardware does with your queries.

Row-oriented storage (Postgres, MySQL, Oracle)

A row is laid out contiguously on disk. Reading row 42 = one random I/O + parse the row. Fast for "give me all columns of one row by primary key." Slow for "give me the average of column X across 100M rows" because every row must be loaded even though only one column is needed.

Column-oriented storage (Parquet, ORC, Snowflake FDN, Redshift, BigQuery Capacitor)

Each column stored separately, with its own compression. Reading column X = read just X's bytes, skipping everything else. Compression ratios of 5–20× are routine because a single column has low cardinality locally.

A Parquet file is laid out as row groups, then column chunks, then pages. A footer holds the schema and per-chunk stats: min/max/null_count (distinct_count exists in the spec but is rarely written), plus optional page indexes. Those stats drive row-group skipping. That's why WHERE dt = '2026-04-16' AND country = 'US' is cheap on a table partitioned by dt and sorted by country. Dictionary and run-length encoding make repeated low-cardinality values nearly free. The format internals are in Part 02 §7.

The column-oriented nature has a direct modeling implication: adding a column is nearly free at read time (you only pay for it if you select it). Wide tables (OBT) aren't the disaster they'd be in a row store.

OLTP modeling implications

  • Normalize: each update touches one row, so redundancy is expensive.
  • B-tree indexes on everything queried. Covering indexes for hot queries.
  • FK constraints enforced at write.
  • Partitioning is a tool for manageability (vacuum, detach old partitions) more than performance.

OLAP modeling implications

  • Denormalize within reason. Joins are expensive in distributed systems; repeated string values cost almost nothing with dictionary encoding.
  • Sort / cluster by the most common filter key (usually date).
  • FK constraints are declared but not enforced (Snowflake, BigQuery, Databricks). Declare them anyway, with RELY where supported: optimizers use them for join elimination and BI tools read them. Integrity is enforced by pipeline tests.
  • Partitioning is the #1 physical layout decision. Get it wrong and queries scan entire years.

HTAP blur

Some engines (TiDB with TiFlash, SingleStore, Snowflake Hybrid Tables) keep a row store and a column store for the same logical table. Writes go to the rows and analytics read the columns. That's useful for mid-size mixed workloads. Check each product's consistency and scale limits before you promise them in a design.

3. Normalization Derived From Functional Dependencies

Normalization is taught as a set of rules. It's actually a consequence of functional dependencies — statements of the form "column set X determines column set Y" (written X → Y).

Given dependencies:

  • order_id → customer_id, order_date, status
  • customer_id → customer_name, country

The relation Orders(order_id, customer_id, order_date, status, customer_name, country) violates 3NF because customer_id (non-key) determines customer_name, country — a transitive dependency. Decomposition:

  • Orders(order_id, customer_id, order_date, status)
  • Customers(customer_id, customer_name, country)

1NF — atomic values

No arrays, no comma-separated strings, no nested structures that the DB can't query. tags = "red,blue,green" forces LIKE '%blue%' queries that can't use indexes. Decompose into a child table order_tags(order_id, tag).

Arrays (Postgres text[], BigQuery ARRAY<STRING>) bend strict 1NF. That's acceptable when the engine's array functions support the queries you need.

2NF — full functional dependency on the key

Only relevant for composite keys. If PK is (order_id, line_number) and order_date depends on order_id alone, order_date doesn't belong in the line-item table. Move it.

3NF — no transitive dependencies

Shown above. In practice, 3NF is the ceiling for OLTP — further decomposition rarely helps.

BCNF (3.5NF) — every determinant is a candidate key

The textbook case is Enrollment(student, course, instructor) with key (student, course), where (student, course) → instructor and instructor → course. It is in 3NF, because course is prime. It is not in BCNF, because instructor is a determinant but not a candidate key. Decompose into (student, instructor) and (instructor, course). These cases are rare in real data.

4NF & 5NF — multi-valued & join dependencies

These split independent multi-valued facts: a teacher teaches several courses and speaks several languages, and every combination gets stored. Name them if asked. You will almost never apply them consciously.

Practical heuristic

Normalize to 3NF. Denormalize deliberately, with a comment explaining why. A typical OLTP schema has 90% 3NF + 10% intentional denormalization (caching displayed values, storing denormalized totals for performance).

4. Dimensional Modeling — Kimball in Full

Kimball's dimensional model is a theory of analytic queries. It says: most analytics look like "a measure, broken down by attributes, filtered by other attributes." If your storage matches that shape, queries are trivial and fast.

The four-step process (and what each step actually means)

1 — Business process. One process, such as orders, shipments or playback sessions, not "the whole business". Each process is a candidate fact table. Get the list from business users, not from source-system tables.

2 — Grain. Declare exactly what one fact row represents, e.g. "one row per playback session". Prefer the atomic grain. The test: any two rows must be genuinely distinct events.

3 — Dimensions. Who, what, where, when, why, how. Dimensions are denormalized: category, subcategory and brand all sit in dim_product even though they form a hierarchy.

4 — Facts. The numeric measures at the declared grain. Prefer additive measures, and document which are semi-additive and which are non-additive (see additivity).

Full star schema — playback analytics

Engine: PostgreSQL 12+Dialect: PostgreSQLExecutable: Yes — PostgreSQL 12+ only
-- -----------------------------------------------------
-- Date dimension (discussed more in §8)
-- -----------------------------------------------------
CREATE TABLE dim_date (
    date_key           INT PRIMARY KEY,             -- 20260419
    full_date          DATE NOT NULL,
    day_of_week        SMALLINT NOT NULL,           -- 1=Monday
    day_name           VARCHAR(10) NOT NULL,
    day_of_month       SMALLINT NOT NULL,
    day_of_year        SMALLINT NOT NULL,
    week_of_year       SMALLINT NOT NULL,           -- ISO week
    month_num          SMALLINT NOT NULL,
    month_name         VARCHAR(10) NOT NULL,
    quarter            SMALLINT NOT NULL,
    year               SMALLINT NOT NULL,
    fiscal_year        SMALLINT NOT NULL,
    fiscal_quarter     SMALLINT NOT NULL,
    fiscal_period      SMALLINT NOT NULL,
    is_weekend         BOOLEAN NOT NULL,
    is_holiday         BOOLEAN NOT NULL,
    holiday_name       VARCHAR(50),
    is_business_day    BOOLEAN NOT NULL
);

-- -----------------------------------------------------
-- User dimension — SCD Type 2
-- -----------------------------------------------------
CREATE TABLE dim_user (
    user_key           BIGINT PRIMARY KEY,          -- surrogate
    user_id            VARCHAR(36) NOT NULL,        -- natural/durable
    email              VARCHAR(320),
    country_code       CHAR(2),
    subscription_tier  VARCHAR(20),                 -- basic/standard/premium
    household_size     SMALLINT,
    profile_language   VARCHAR(10),
    signup_date        DATE,
    churn_date         DATE,
    valid_from         TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL,
    valid_to           TIMESTAMPTZ,
    is_current         BOOLEAN NOT NULL,
    hash_diff          CHAR(32) NOT NULL            -- MD5 hex of tracked attrs (see §7)
);
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX dim_user_natural ON dim_user(user_id, valid_from);
CREATE INDEX dim_user_current ON dim_user(user_id) WHERE is_current;

-- -----------------------------------------------------
-- Title dimension — mostly Type 1, some Type 2 (rating)
-- -----------------------------------------------------
CREATE TABLE dim_title (
    title_key          BIGINT PRIMARY KEY,
    title_id           VARCHAR(36) NOT NULL,
    title              VARCHAR(500),
    title_type         VARCHAR(20),                 -- movie/series/documentary
    genre_primary      VARCHAR(50),
    content_rating     VARCHAR(20),                 -- MA, PG-13, etc.
    is_original        BOOLEAN,
    valid_from         TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL,
    valid_to           TIMESTAMPTZ,
    is_current         BOOLEAN NOT NULL
);

-- -----------------------------------------------------
-- Device dimension — Type 1 (device facts don't "change" per user)
-- -----------------------------------------------------
CREATE TABLE dim_device (
    device_key         BIGINT PRIMARY KEY,
    device_id          VARCHAR(64) NOT NULL,
    device_type        VARCHAR(20),                 -- tv/mobile/tablet/web
    os                 VARCHAR(50),
    app_version        VARCHAR(20)
);

-- -----------------------------------------------------
-- Playback session fact — transaction grain
-- One row per playback session (session starts and ends)
-- -----------------------------------------------------
CREATE TABLE fact_playback_session (
    session_key        BIGINT NOT NULL,             -- surrogate; PK is (session_key, dt): PG requires the partition key
    session_id         VARCHAR(64) NOT NULL,        -- natural, from client
    user_key           BIGINT NOT NULL REFERENCES dim_user,
    title_key          BIGINT NOT NULL REFERENCES dim_title,
    device_key         BIGINT NOT NULL REFERENCES dim_device,
    start_date_key     INT NOT NULL REFERENCES dim_date,
    end_date_key       INT NOT NULL REFERENCES dim_date,
    start_ts           TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL,
    end_ts             TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL,
    -- Measures (all numeric, additive where possible)
    watch_ms           BIGINT NOT NULL,             -- additive
    buffer_ms          BIGINT NOT NULL,             -- additive
    seeks              INT NOT NULL,                -- additive
    pauses             INT NOT NULL,                -- additive
    max_bitrate_kbps   INT,                         -- non-additive (roll up with MAX)
    avg_bitrate_kbps   INT,                         -- non-additive (store components, see below)
    completion_ratio   NUMERIC(4,3),                -- non-additive ratio
    -- Degenerate dimension (ended_reason) + non-additive measure (qoe_score)
    ended_reason       VARCHAR(20),                 -- user/credits/error
    qoe_score          NUMERIC(3,2),
    -- Partition
    dt                 DATE NOT NULL,
    PRIMARY KEY (session_key, dt)
)
PARTITION BY RANGE (dt);

Key details people miss:

  • Every FK is a surrogate _key, not a natural _id. The natural IDs are attributes, preserved for lookup.
  • start_date_key and end_date_key both reference dim_date — same table, role-playing.
  • session_id is stored as a degenerate dimension (an attribute on the fact with no corresponding dim table) because there's no other data to put in a dim_session.
  • max_bitrate_kbps rolls up with MAX. avg_bitrate_kbps can't be rolled up at all. To roll up a weighted average bitrate, also store the additive components (e.g. bitrate_kbps_x_ms and watch_ms) and divide at query time. days_from_today is deliberately missing from dim_date: stored, it goes stale every midnight, so compute it in a view.

The query this shape makes easy

Engine: PostgreSQL / SnowflakeDialect: ANSI-style SQLExecutable: Yes — PostgreSQL / Snowflake only
-- Total watch hours by country and content rating, last 7 days, weekdays only
SELECT
    u.country_code,
    t.content_rating,
    SUM(f.watch_ms) / 3600.0 / 1000 AS watch_hours
FROM fact_playback_session f
JOIN dim_user  u ON u.user_key  = f.user_key
JOIN dim_title t ON t.title_key = f.title_key
JOIN dim_date  d ON d.date_key  = f.start_date_key
WHERE d.full_date >= CURRENT_DATE - 7
  AND d.is_weekend = FALSE
GROUP BY u.country_code, t.content_rating
ORDER BY watch_hours DESC;

No CASE statements, no date arithmetic, no EXTRACT — just filter and group. This is why Kimball wins.

Surrogate keys: why, which kind, how to hash

Why not use natural keys? Four reasons. Source systems renumber and reassign IDs during migrations. SCD2 needs several rows per natural ID, so something must tell the versions apart. Two sources can have customer_id namespaces that collide. And integer keys are cheaper to join (in columnar stores this matters less than it used to).

RequirementSequence / identityHash (128-bit+)UUIDv4UUIDv7
Generate in any system without coordinationNoYesYesYes
Same key on re-run (idempotent)No (re-assigns)YesNoNo
Clustering / min-max pruningBestPoor (random)Poor (random)Good (time-ordered)
Size4–8 bytes16 bytes (32 hex chars)16 bytes16 bytes

A sequence needs a round-trip to one issuer. If facts load in Spark and dimensions in Snowflake, that round-trip is slow and fragile. That's why deterministic hashes are the lakehouse default. For an SCD2 version key, include the version's valid_from in the hashed input. Never use a 64-bit hash for keys. Snowflake HASH() and Spark xxhash64() give about a 2.7% chance of at least one collision at 109 keys, and Spark hash() is 32-bit Murmur3, so collisions are certain at warehouse scale. Because hash keys are random, cluster the table on date, not on the key.

Engine: SnowflakeDialect: Snowflake SQLExecutable: Yes — Snowflake only
-- The key spec IS the input spec: normalize, NULL-token, format explicitly.
SELECT
  MD5(
       COALESCE(LOWER(TRIM(source_system)), '~N~')             || '|' ||
       COALESCE(TRIM(source_id), '~N~')                        || '|' ||
       COALESCE(TO_VARCHAR(effective_date, 'YYYY-MM-DD'), '~N~')
  ) AS customer_sk,             -- 32-char hex
  source_system, source_id, effective_date
FROM staging_customer;

-- Spark SQL:  md5(concat_ws('|', coalesce(lower(trim(source_system)), '~N~'),
--               ..., coalesce(date_format(effective_date, 'yyyy-MM-dd'), '~N~')))
-- BigQuery:   TO_HEX(MD5(ARRAY_TO_STRING([...same COALESCEd parts...], '|')))
--             with FORMAT_DATE('%Y-%m-%d', effective_date)

Why every part gets an explicit NULL token: Snowflake || and CONCAT_WS return NULL if any argument is NULL, while Spark's concat_ws skips NULLs, so ('a', NULL, 'b') and ('a', 'b', NULL) hash the same. CAST(ts AS STRING) also formats differently per engine. Put this expression in one shared macro and test it on golden rows in every engine that computes keys.

Interviewer pushes back

You: “I'll use hash surrogate keys everywhere, the MD5 of the natural key. They're deterministic and need no coordination.”

Interviewer: “Spark and Snowflake compute the key for the same customer and get different values. And how often will MD5 collide?”

Strong answer: “Different keys mean different input strings, not a bad hash. Snowflake's CONCAT_WS returns NULL on any NULL argument, Spark's skips NULLs, and timestamp-to-string formats differ. So the key spec is really an input spec: trimmed, lower-cased text, an explicit NULL token, explicit date formats and a fixed delimiter. It lives in one macro and is tested across engines on golden rows. Collisions aren't the risk at 128 bits. At 1010 keys the birthday bound is about 10-19. The risk is 64-bit hashes, which reach about 3% at 109 keys.”

Weak answer: “MD5 is broken, switch to SHA-256.” MD5's weakness is adversarial collisions, which don't matter here. SHA-256 over the same inconsistent input string gives the same mismatch.

2026 Interview Note

What doesn't change: a key must be deterministic, wide enough, and computed from a canonical input. What does change: function names and return types differ by engine (BigQuery MD5 returns BYTES, Snowflake returns hex). UUIDv7 (RFC 9562, 2024) is time-ordered, which fixes UUIDv4's clustering problem. PostgreSQL 18 generates it natively with uuidv7(). Check your engine's support.

5. Fact Table Grain (The Most Important Decision)

Grain is where every modeling interview should start. The failure mode is a fact table where some rows are at one grain and others at another. The bug is invisible until a sum is 2× too large.

“What is the grain of this fact table, and why does it matter?”
30 sec

Grain is the sentence “one row = one ___”. For fact_playback_session it's one row per playback session. It matters because every SUM, COUNT and join assumes it. Mix two grains, or join to something finer, and totals get multiplied silently, with no error anywhere.

2 min

I declare the grain before choosing any columns, because it decides everything after it. It decides which dimensions can attach: a session row can't carry a per-heartbeat bitrate. It decides which measures are additive, and what the uniqueness test is (session_id unique, enforced as a test). It also tells you which joins are safe. Joining to anything finer, such as line items, a bridge, or an SCD2 dimension without an as-of predicate, fans rows out. I prefer the most atomic grain the source supports, because you can always aggregate up but you can never split a row back down.

Deep dive

Time is part of a periodic snapshot's grain (entity × day). That's why its measures are semi-additive. An accumulating snapshot is one row per process instance, and the row changes as milestones arrive. Grain is not partitioning, which is physical layout. Changing the grain is a breaking contract change, so it gets a new table or a major version, never an in-place edit. For streaming tables, the grain includes the window: one row per key per 5-minute window, with a rule for late updates.

Where to stop: the grain sentence, the uniqueness test, and one concrete fan-out example.

Three transactional fact patterns

Transaction fact — one row per event. Most common. Fully additive. Example: fact_playback_session above.

Periodic snapshot fact — one row per entity per period. Measures describe the state at period end. Semi-additive.

Engine: ANSI SQLDialect: ANSI DDLExecutable: Yes
CREATE TABLE fact_subscription_daily (
    snapshot_date_key  INT,
    user_key           BIGINT,
    -- Semi-additive: summable across users, NOT across days
    mrr_cents          BIGINT,       -- monthly recurring revenue
    status             VARCHAR(20),
    days_until_renewal SMALLINT,
    -- Additive within the day
    payments_made      INT,
    refunds_issued     INT,
    PRIMARY KEY (snapshot_date_key, user_key)
);

The MRR column is the classic semi-additive trap. Someone totals mrr_cents across two days and reports twice the real revenue. Fixes: label the column in the catalog and the semantic layer. Across time, aggregate with the period-end value (or AVG when the question really is "average balance"), and use SUM only across entities. A suffix such as _point_in_time helps humans notice.

Accumulating snapshot fact — one row per process instance, updated as it progresses through milestones.

Engine: ANSI SQLDialect: ANSI DDLExecutable: Yes
CREATE TABLE fact_order_fulfillment (
    order_key         BIGINT PRIMARY KEY,
    customer_key      BIGINT,
    -- Milestones (date keys; NULL until reached)
    order_date_key    INT NOT NULL,
    paid_date_key     INT,
    packed_date_key   INT,
    shipped_date_key  INT,
    delivered_date_key INT,
    returned_date_key INT,
    -- Durations, derived at each update
    hours_to_pay      INT,
    hours_to_pack     INT,
    hours_to_ship     INT,
    hours_to_deliver  INT,
    -- Measures
    order_total_cents BIGINT,
    items_count       INT
);

Use it when the process has a bounded, well-defined set of milestones. Lead-time questions ("how long from paid to shipped?") become AVG(hours_to_ship) instead of a self-join over millions of events. The cost is updates, which columnar engines dislike, and one correctness problem: milestone events arrive out of order and get replayed. The MERGE must be order-independent and idempotent, so each milestone keeps its earliest value however many times, and in whatever order, events are applied:

Engine: Snowflake / Databricks (Delta) / Postgres 15+Dialect: ANSI MERGEExecutable: Yes — Snowflake / Databricks / PostgreSQL 15+ only
MERGE INTO fact_order_fulfillment t
USING stg_order_milestones s                 -- deduplicated: one row per order_key
  ON t.order_key = s.order_key
WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET                 -- earliest wins, NULL-safe, replay-safe
  paid_date_key      = COALESCE(LEAST(t.paid_date_key, s.paid_date_key),
                                t.paid_date_key, s.paid_date_key),
  shipped_date_key   = COALESCE(LEAST(t.shipped_date_key, s.shipped_date_key),
                                t.shipped_date_key, s.shipped_date_key),
  delivered_date_key = COALESCE(LEAST(t.delivered_date_key, s.delivered_date_key),
                                t.delivered_date_key, s.delivered_date_key)
WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT
  (order_key, customer_key, order_date_key, paid_date_key,
   shipped_date_key, delivered_date_key, order_total_cents, items_count)
VALUES
  (s.order_key, s.customer_key, s.order_date_key, s.paid_date_key,
   s.shipped_date_key, s.delivered_date_key, s.order_total_cents, s.items_count);

The LEAST-inside-COALESCE form exists because LEAST returns NULL if any argument is NULL in Snowflake and most engines (Postgres ignores NULLs). Derive the hours_to_* durations from the milestone columns in the same statement or in a view, so they can never disagree with them. On Iceberg or Delta, pick merge-on-read for frequent milestone updates (see Part 07 §6).

Additivity

Additivity is the attribute a fact table most often gets wrong, and when it's wrong, every dashboard built on it is silently lying. There are three buckets:

Additivity Sum across any dim? Representative measures Warehouse pattern
AdditiveYesrevenue, quantity, watch_ms, clicks, impressions, bytes, kWhSUM() everywhere
Semi-additiveSome dims onlyaccount_balance, inventory_on_hand, headcount, MRR/ARR snapshot, queue_depth, open_ticketsSUM() across entities; across time, the period-end value (or AVG() for "average balance")
Non-additiveNeverunit_price, margin_pct, conversion_rate, CTR, churn_rate, NPS, p99 latency, exchange_rateStore numerator + denominator (or a sketch); compute in SELECT. Never pre-aggregate the ratio.

Measures that look additive but aren't

The following look like counts — they are not safely sum-able without context. Each has a specific remediation.

Misleading measureWhy it breaksFix
distinct_users per daySumming two days double-counts users active in bothStore users_active_hll (HyperLogLog sketch); merge sketches, then cardinality
avg_session_duration per dayAverage of averages weights each day equally regardless of trafficStore sum_duration_ms + session_count; divide at query time
median_order_valueMedians don't aggregate linearlyStore a t-digest or KLL sketch per day; merge sketches, then query percentiles
max_concurrent_streamsSumming daily maxes ≠ global max; daily max can coincide or notStore interval-level counts; compute max over intersection in SELECT
churn_rate (pre-computed)Churn % cannot be averaged across cohorts of different sizesStore churned_count + cohort_size; compute ratio in SELECT
weighted_avg_priceRe-weighted averages don't composeStore sum_price_times_qty + sum_qty; divide in SELECT
latency_p99 per minutePercentiles don't average — p99 of (p99s) is not the global p99Store histogram buckets or a sketch; query-time merge

The shape is always the same: store the components (sum and count, numerator and denominator, or a mergeable sketch) and derive the ratio on read. An AVG(avg_price) over seven days is an average of averages, not the weighted average anyone wanted.

Factless fact tables

A fact table with only FKs — no measures. Models events or eligibility:

Engine: ANSI SQLDialect: ANSI DDLExecutable: Yes
-- "Which users had access to which titles on which day"
CREATE TABLE fact_title_availability_daily (
    date_key  INT,
    user_key  BIGINT,
    title_key BIGINT,
    -- no measures
    PRIMARY KEY (date_key, user_key, title_key)
);

The "measure" is COUNT(*) — "how many users had access to Stranger Things in France on 2026-04-01."

These get huge fast (N_users × N_titles × N_days). Sparse-encode where possible (don't emit rows for absent combinations).

Multi-grain fact: how to avoid it

The canonical multi-grain bug: an orders fact table where some rows are "one per order" and some are "one per line item." Summing order_total sums header rows plus line rows — each order's total appears many times.

Rules:

  1. One fact table per declared grain.
  2. If you need both grains, build two fact tables: fact_order_header and fact_order_line. They roll up via shared dimensions.
  3. Never introduce an "aggregation type" column to disambiguate rows of different grains. That's a band-aid on a severed arm.
Drill · Modeling

Tuesday's release "added customer history" to dim_customer. Since then, the revenue dashboard shows exactly 2× Finance's number for some regions and the right number for the others. No pipeline failed. Which shapes produce an exact 2×, and how do you tell which one you have in ten minutes?

STOP. Answer before revealing.

Reveal the diagnosis
  1. Observe Exactly 2×, not 1.07×, means a row multiplier, not late or missing data. "Only some regions" means only some keys are multiplied. It started with a dimension change, so suspect the join, not the fact.
  2. Hypothesize (a) The fact now joins the SCD2 dimension on the natural key (customer_id) with no as-of predicate, so every customer with two versions is counted twice. (b) A duplicate stage row or a re-run left two is_current rows for some customers. (c) A many-to-many relationship was joined without allocation weights, e.g. customer ↔ region or account ↔ owner through a bridge.
  3. Measure Compare COUNT(*) of the fact with COUNT(*) of the fact joined to the dimension. Then list the multiplying keys: GROUP BY customer_id HAVING COUNT(*) > 1, once on all rows and once on current rows only.
  4. Isolate Take one doubled order and look at its joined rows. Two rows with different valid_from is (a). Two rows that are both is_current is (b). Two rows with different bridge keys is (c).
  5. Fix (a) Join facts on the version key stamped at load, or add event_ts >= valid_from AND event_ts < valid_to (see late-arriving facts). (b) Close the extra current rows, then make the load atomic and dedupe the stage (see SCD Type 2). (c) Use SUM(amount * weight), or publish the unweighted number explicitly as an "impact" figure (see bridge tables).
  6. Prevent Add a fan-out test on every model (the fact's row count is unchanged after each dimension join), uniqueness tests on the dimension's grain (customer_id, valid_from) and on "one current row per key", and a weight-sum test on every bridge.

6. Dimensions — Conformed, Junk, Degenerate, Mini, Role-Playing

Conformed dimensions

A dimension is conformed when multiple fact tables share it. This is how you answer "return rate by customer segment" — fact_returns.customer_key and fact_orders.customer_key must reference the same dim_customer.

Conforming is an organizational commitment as much as a technical one. A marketing dim_customer alongside a separate billing dim_customer is a failure. Build one, with every stakeholder as a consumer.

The enterprise bus matrix (Kimball's term) is a table of business processes × dimensions, with an X where they intersect. Use it to plan which dimensions must be conformed:

Junk dimensions

When you have a handful of low-cardinality flags and indicators that don't belong together but don't warrant their own dimensions: combine them into a junk dimension.

Engine: ANSI SQLDialect: ANSI DDLExecutable: Yes
-- Instead of: is_trial BOOLEAN, is_promo BOOLEAN, device_is_new BOOLEAN on every fact row...
CREATE TABLE dim_session_flags (
    flags_key   INT PRIMARY KEY,
    is_trial    BOOLEAN,
    is_promo    BOOLEAN,
    is_new_device BOOLEAN,
    signal_source VARCHAR(20)
);
-- At most 2 x 2 x 2 x (distinct signal_source values) rows: 24 with 3 sources.

Then the fact has one flags_key FK and you get clean reporting.

Degenerate dimensions

An attribute on the fact with no corresponding dim table — like session_id above. Reason: there's no other data about a session beyond what's already in the fact row. Creating dim_session would just be a table with one column.

Mini-dimensions

When a dimension has a subset of frequently-changing attributes that would inflate SCD2 storage: split them off.

Engine: n/aDialect: column listsExecutable: Pseudocode
-- dim_user (stable attrs)
user_key, user_id, email, country_code, signup_date, ...

-- dim_user_demographics (mini-dim; snapshots of volatile attrs)
demographics_key, age_bracket, income_bracket, household_size, interest_segment, snapshot_ts

The fact has FKs to both: user_key (as-current) and demographics_key (as-at-event-time). Saves SCD2 storage when the volatile attributes change often and the stable ones don't.

Role-playing dimensions

One physical dimension, multiple roles in the fact. dim_date plays order_date, ship_date, delivered_date. Implement as views aliasing the base dim so query joins read naturally:

Engine: ANSI SQLDialect: ANSI SQLExecutable: Yes
CREATE VIEW dim_order_date    AS SELECT * FROM dim_date;
CREATE VIEW dim_ship_date     AS SELECT * FROM dim_date;
CREATE VIEW dim_delivered_date AS SELECT * FROM dim_date;

SELECT
    od.year, od.month_num,
    sd.day_name AS ship_day,
    dd.week_of_year AS delivered_week,
    SUM(f.order_total_cents)
FROM fact_order_fulfillment f
JOIN dim_order_date      od ON od.date_key = f.order_date_key
JOIN dim_ship_date       sd ON sd.date_key = f.shipped_date_key
JOIN dim_delivered_date  dd ON dd.date_key = f.delivered_date_key
GROUP BY od.year, od.month_num, sd.day_name, dd.week_of_year;

The physical storage is one table; the logical model has three.

A semantic layer (LookML, dbt Semantic Layer, Cube and similar) usually declares roles as aliased joins instead of views. The principle is the same: one physical table, several named roles.

Swappable / outrigger

When a dimension attribute has its own attributes worth rolling up: a small normalized "outrigger" joined to the main dim. dim_product.category_id → dim_category.name, parent_category. Violates pure star; sometimes necessary.

7. Slowly Changing Dimensions — All Seven Types, with Code

Type 0 — Retain original

Never update. Fields like date_of_birth, signup_date, birth_country. No code needed beyond rejecting updates.

Type 1 — Overwrite

Just update, with no history. Use it for typo corrections. For GDPR erasure, Type 1 alone isn't enough. You have to purge every version row, then expire snapshots and time travel (Delta VACUUM, Iceberg expire_snapshots, Snowflake Time Travel and Fail-safe windows), and remove the bronze copies too.

Engine: Snowflake / ANSI MERGEDialect: ANSI SQLExecutable: Illustrative — adapt to your dialect
-- Stage has latest values; merge overwrites
MERGE INTO dim_user AS tgt
USING stg_user AS src
  ON tgt.user_id = src.user_id
WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET
    email         = src.email,
    country_code  = src.country_code,
    updated_at    = CURRENT_TIMESTAMP
WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT (...) VALUES (...);

The INSERT (...) is elided. Note that on an SCD2 table this MERGE overwrites every version of the user. That is Type 1 semantics applied to history, which is sometimes exactly what you want (a typo fix) and sometimes a silent history rewrite.

Type 2 — Add new row, track history

The standard. Full history. Every change creates a new row; old row closed with valid_to.

“Explain SCD Type 2 without the jargon.”
30 sec

When a customer moves from Austin to Denver, we don't overwrite Austin. We stamp the Austin row with the date it stopped being true. Then we add a new Denver row that starts on that date, and give each row its own ID. Every sale points at the row that was true on the day of the sale, so last year's report still says Austin and this year's says Denver.

2 min

Each version gets its own surrogate key. All versions share the durable natural key (user_id). Each covers a half-open interval [valid_from, valid_to), and a convenience is_current flag marks the open one. To detect changes, hash the tracked columns and compare hashes. To apply them, one atomic MERGE closes the old version and opens the new one. At load time, each fact is stamped with the version key that was valid at its event time, so later reads are a plain equi-join. It's a per-attribute choice: tier and region get history, typo fixes don't. The cost is row growth proportional to change frequency, which is why volatile attributes go to a mini-dimension or a snapshot fact.

Deep dive

The hard part is correctness under failure and disorder. Dedupe the stage. Take valid_from from the source's change time, not load time. A change that arrives out of order has to split an existing interval, not append one. Late facts need an as-of lookup. There are two invariant tests: exactly one current row per key, and no overlapping intervals. A snapshot (dbt or a nightly diff) sees only the state at run time and loses changes between runs. CDC sees every change. GDPR erasure has to reach every version and every table snapshot.

Where to stop: don't list Types 3–7 unless asked. Mention Type 6/7 only if they ask for "historical and current" reporting on the same facts.

The single-MERGE pattern (Snowflake)

This is a staged-union MERGE: dedupe the stage, find the rows that are new or changed, and send each changed key through twice. The copy with a real key matches the current row and closes it. The copy with a NULL key can never match, so it inserts the new version. That's one statement and one transaction. The stage carries changed_at, the source's change timestamp (for example a CDC commit time), which becomes the interval boundary.

Engine: SnowflakeDialect: Snowflake SQLExecutable: Yes — Snowflake only
-- user_key is not listed: the column has DEFAULT dim_user_seq.NEXTVAL
MERGE INTO dim_user t
USING (
  WITH src AS (                                    -- 1. one row per user_id
    SELECT s.*,
           MD5(COALESCE(email, '~N~')                     || '|' ||
               COALESCE(country_code, '~N~')              || '|' ||
               COALESCE(subscription_tier, '~N~')         || '|' ||
               COALESCE(TO_VARCHAR(household_size), '~N~') || '|' ||
               COALESCE(profile_language, '~N~')) AS hash_diff
    FROM stg_user s
    QUALIFY ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id
                               ORDER BY changed_at DESC) = 1
  ),
  changed AS (                                     -- 2. new or changed users
    SELECT src.*
    FROM src
    LEFT JOIN dim_user d
      ON d.user_id = src.user_id AND d.is_current
    WHERE d.user_id IS NULL OR d.hash_diff <> src.hash_diff
  )
  SELECT user_id AS merge_key, c.* FROM changed c  -- closes the old version
  UNION ALL
  SELECT NULL AS merge_key, c.* FROM changed c     -- inserts the new version
  WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM dim_user d
                WHERE d.user_id = c.user_id AND d.is_current)
) s
ON t.user_id = s.merge_key AND t.is_current
WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET
  valid_to   = s.changed_at,
  is_current = FALSE
WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT
  (user_id, email, country_code, subscription_tier, household_size,
   profile_language, signup_date, churn_date,
   valid_from, valid_to, is_current, hash_diff)
VALUES
  (s.user_id, s.email, s.country_code, s.subscription_tier, s.household_size,
   s.profile_language, s.signup_date, s.churn_date,
   s.changed_at, NULL, TRUE, s.hash_diff);

Why hash_diff: comparing a dozen nullable columns one by one is verbose and easy to get wrong. A hash of the tracked columns reduces change detection to one <>. MD5 is enough here, because the comparison is per key and nobody is attacking it. SHA-256 is fine if it's your platform standard. Hash an explicit NULL token, not '', so that NULL and the empty string differ.

Why one statement: an UPDATE-then-INSERT pair is clearer to read. But if the job fails between the two, users are left with no current row and inner joins silently drop their facts. If you keep two statements, wrap them in one transaction. The NULL-key trick is also why a single MERGE can close and insert for the same logical record, despite the common claim that it can't.

Failure-first: what can fail in an SCD2 load?
FailureDetectRecoverPrevent recurrence
Duplicate stage rows for one key → two current versions, doubled joins"One current row per key" testClose the extra rows; re-run for those keysROW_NUMBER() dedup by source change time before the MERGE
NULL vs '' hash collision → a real change goes undetectedSample audit: compare the raw columns where the hashes are equalRecompute hash_diff with the new token; re-detect changes from the source logExplicit NULL token; one shared hash macro
valid_from = load time → facts land on the wrong version; a backfill stamps everything "today"Intervals cluster at load timestamps; as-of results disagree with the sourceRebuild intervals from the CDC or bronze change logUse the source change timestamp (CDC commit time, updated_at)
Non-atomic close + insert fails halfway → users with no current row"One current row" test; fact row count drops after the joinRe-insert the current versions from the stageA single MERGE, or both statements in one transaction
Out-of-order changes → overlapping or gapped intervalsInterval test (below)Re-slice that key's intervals from the change logApply changes in source order; a late change splits an interval
Engine: ANSI SQLDialect: ANSI SQLExecutable: Yes
-- Invariant 1: exactly one current row per user (returns violators)
SELECT user_id
FROM dim_user
GROUP BY user_id
HAVING SUM(CASE WHEN is_current THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) <> 1;

-- Invariant 2: no overlaps, no gaps (returns violating versions)
SELECT user_id, valid_from, valid_to, next_from
FROM (
  SELECT user_id, valid_from, valid_to,
         LEAD(valid_from) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY valid_from) AS next_from
  FROM dim_user
) x
WHERE next_from IS NOT NULL
  AND (valid_to IS NULL OR valid_to <> next_from);

PySpark / Delta Lake version

The same staged-union MERGE runs on Delta Lake (SQL, or DeltaTable.merge in PySpark); Delta's docs use this shape for SCD2. On Databricks, Lakeflow Spark Declarative Pipelines (formerly DLT) generate it from AUTO CDC … STORED AS SCD TYPE 2, which succeeds APPLY CHANGES INTO. Apache Spark 4.2's open-source pipelines add Auto CDC for SCD Type 1. Check current docs for the syntax. Don't build keys from monotonically_increasing_id() plus an offset: they change on every re-run.

dbt snapshot (the declarative way)

Engine: dbt Core 1.9+ (dbt 2.x may differ — check docs)Language: YAMLExecutable: Yes — dbt Core 1.9+ only
# snapshots/dim_user.yml
snapshots:
  - name: dim_user_snapshot
    relation: source('raw', 'users')
    config:
      schema: snapshots
      unique_key: user_id
      strategy: check                 # prefer 'timestamp' + updated_at if trustworthy
      check_cols: [email, country_code, subscription_tier,
                   household_size, profile_language]
      hard_deletes: invalidate        # ignore (default) | invalidate | new_record

dbt adds dbt_valid_from, dbt_valid_to and dbt_scd_id, and does the close-and-insert for you. Know its limits:

  • A snapshot sees only the state at run time, so two changes between runs collapse into one. Use CDC if every change matters.
  • The check strategy compares every row on every run. Prefer timestamp when the source has a trustworthy updated_at.
  • Deletes are ignored unless you set hard_deletes.
2026 Interview Note

What doesn't change: a snapshot is a periodic diff of source state into SCD2 rows. What's version-specific: dbt Core 1.9 moved snapshot config to YAML (relation, and schema replacing target_schema). It also added hard_deletes, which replaces invalidate_hard_deletes, and dbt_valid_to_current. The legacy {% snapshot %} Jinja block still runs on 1.x. dbt v2 (September 2026) turns deprecations into errors, so read its upgrade guide before assuming legacy snapshot syntax survives.

Type 3 — Add new column (previous + current)

Tracks exactly one prior value. Niche — useful only when business cares about "previous region" specifically.

Engine: PostgreSQLDialect: PostgreSQLExecutable: Yes — PostgreSQL only
ALTER TABLE dim_user
  ADD COLUMN previous_country_code CHAR(2),
  ADD COLUMN country_changed_at TIMESTAMPTZ;

On update: UPDATE ... SET previous_country_code = country_code, country_code = new, country_changed_at = now().

Type 4 — History in a side table

Current row in the main dim (Type 1 semantics for ease of query); history in a separate table.

Engine: n/aDialect: pseudo-DDL (untyped columns)Executable: Pseudocode
-- Main dim (current-state only)
CREATE TABLE dim_user_current (
    user_key BIGINT PRIMARY KEY,
    user_id VARCHAR(36) UNIQUE,
    email, country_code, ...
);

-- History (append-only, every change)
CREATE TABLE dim_user_history (
    user_id VARCHAR(36),
    email, country_code, ...,
    valid_from TIMESTAMPTZ,
    valid_to TIMESTAMPTZ,
    change_reason VARCHAR(50)
);

Good when the main dim is hit constantly by dashboards and you want a narrow table. Point-in-time joins use the history table.

Type 6 — 1 + 2 + 3

A Type 2 dim where every historical row also carries the current value of select attributes. Lets you report "sales by the customer's current segment" even on old facts.

Engine: n/aDialect: pseudo-DDL (untyped columns)Executable: Pseudocode
CREATE TABLE dim_user (
    user_key BIGINT PRIMARY KEY,
    user_id  VARCHAR(36) NOT NULL,
    -- Historical values (Type 2 — different per version)
    email, country_code, subscription_tier,
    -- Current values (Type 1 — same across all versions of same user_id)
    current_email, current_country_code, current_subscription_tier,
    -- History metadata
    valid_from, valid_to, is_current,
    hash_diff
);

The Type 1 columns are updated across all rows with the same user_id whenever the current state changes — an expensive broadcast update, but query-time simplicity worth it.

Query patterns:

  • "Watch hours by historical segment": join on user_key, group by subscription_tier.
  • "Watch hours by current segment": join on user_key, group by current_subscription_tier.

Type 7 — Dual keys

The fact carries both the surrogate (user_key — version at event time) and the durable natural key (user_id). Consumers pick which to join on. Rare but powerful for complex reporting platforms.

Engine: ANSI SQLDialect: SQL fragmentsExecutable: Illustrative — adapt to your dialect
ALTER TABLE fact_playback_session ADD COLUMN user_id VARCHAR(36);  -- durable

-- Historical view
JOIN dim_user d ON d.user_key = f.user_key

-- Current view (resolve through natural key)
JOIN dim_user_current d ON d.user_id = f.user_id

Picking a type per attribute

Attributes within one dimension almost always use different types. The skill is choosing per attribute. A representative set:

AttributeTypeWhy
date_of_birth, signup_date0Facts of origin; a correction is a data fix
email (typo fix)1A correction shouldn't create a history row
display_name1 (or 6)The UI wants the current value everywhere
subscription_tier, plan_name2Revenue is attributed to the tier at event time
country_code, physical_address2Tax jurisdiction and regional reports are historical
list_price, cost_of_goods2Margin needs the price and COGS at order time
reporting_manager, owner_account_exec2"Who owned it when the deal closed?"
legal_name6Legal history for compliance; the display uses the current name
referred_by_user_id3Only "previous" is ever asked for
current_inventory, LTV, engagement score— (not a dim attribute)Computed or volatile: move it to a periodic snapshot fact

Write each decision down in the catalog. A newcomer should be able to predict whether an update to country_code creates a new row in dim_user.

The red-flag shapes

Three attribute categories warrant extra suspicion when choosing an SCD type:

  • Anything regulatory. Legal name, address, tax ID, consent flags — treat as Type 2 minimum, plus a separate audit trail, regardless of analytical need. Compliance trumps modeling elegance.
  • Anything that drives financial attribution. Tier, plan, price, territory assignment, account executive ownership — always Type 2. A future auditor will ask "who owned this account when the deal closed." Type 1 cannot answer that.
  • Anything computed. Lifetime value, segment classification, engagement score — don't SCD these; move them to a periodic snapshot fact. Dimensions should hold identity and attributes; computed aggregates belong with the facts.
Interviewer pushes back

You: “I'd make every attribute on dim_customer Type 2. That way we never lose history.”

Interviewer: “It's 200M customers, and last_login_at changes daily. What happens?”

Strong answer: “That one column could add up to 200M versions a day. The dimension outgrows the fact, every as-of join slows down, and change detection scans everything. History is a per-attribute decision, driven by a question someone will actually ask. Tier and region need values as of the event for revenue attribution, so they're Type 2. Typo fixes and display names are Type 1. Volatile or computed attributes (last login, engagement score) go into a periodic snapshot fact or a mini-dimension. If we want insurance, the full change log already sits in bronze or CDC, and we can rebuild a Type 2 from it later. We can't easily shrink a bloated dimension that every dashboard joins to.”

Weak answer: “Storage is cheap.” Storage isn't the cost. Join fan-in, change-detection work, and ambiguity about which version a fact should use are.

8. Date & Time Dimensions Done Right

A real date dimension turns fiscal, holiday and weekend logic into a filter instead of a CASE expression. Generate it once for a wide range (the example uses 2010–2040). Only the holiday and fiscal attributes need maintenance.

Generating dim_date (Postgres)

Engine: PostgreSQLDialect: PostgreSQLExecutable: Yes — PostgreSQL only
INSERT INTO dim_date (
    date_key, full_date, day_of_week, day_name,
    day_of_month, day_of_year, week_of_year,
    month_num, month_name, quarter, year,
    fiscal_year, fiscal_quarter, fiscal_period,
    is_weekend, is_holiday, holiday_name, is_business_day
)
SELECT
    TO_CHAR(d, 'YYYYMMDD')::INT                       AS date_key,
    d                                                 AS full_date,
    EXTRACT(ISODOW FROM d)                            AS day_of_week,
    TO_CHAR(d, 'FMDay')                               AS day_name,
    EXTRACT(DAY FROM d)                               AS day_of_month,
    EXTRACT(DOY FROM d)                               AS day_of_year,
    EXTRACT(WEEK FROM d)                              AS week_of_year,
    EXTRACT(MONTH FROM d)                             AS month_num,
    TO_CHAR(d, 'FMMonth')                             AS month_name,
    EXTRACT(QUARTER FROM d)                           AS quarter,
    EXTRACT(YEAR FROM d)                              AS year,
    -- Fiscal year = calendar year here; substitute your rules
    EXTRACT(YEAR FROM d)                              AS fiscal_year,
    EXTRACT(QUARTER FROM d)                           AS fiscal_quarter,
    EXTRACT(MONTH FROM d)                             AS fiscal_period,
    (EXTRACT(ISODOW FROM d) IN (6,7))                 AS is_weekend,
    FALSE                                             AS is_holiday,
    NULL                                              AS holiday_name,
    (EXTRACT(ISODOW FROM d) BETWEEN 1 AND 5)          AS is_business_day
FROM generate_series(DATE '2010-01-01', DATE '2040-12-31', INTERVAL '1 day') d;

-- Holidays (join a separate table, mark is_holiday)
UPDATE dim_date d SET is_holiday = TRUE, holiday_name = h.name, is_business_day = FALSE
FROM holidays h WHERE h.observed_date = d.full_date;

Trap: EXTRACT(WEEK) is the ISO week, and it has to be paired with the ISO year (EXTRACT(ISOYEAR FROM d)), not the calendar year. 2024-12-30 is ISO week 1 of 2025. Paired with calendar year 2024, it lands in the wrong week. Add an iso_year column next to week_of_year.

Time-of-day dimension (separate)

Never combine date + time into one dimension — cardinality explodes (30 years × 86400 seconds = ~1 billion rows).

Engine: ANSI SQLDialect: ANSI DDLExecutable: Yes
CREATE TABLE dim_time (
    time_key     SMALLINT PRIMARY KEY,         -- 0..1439 (minute-of-day)
    hour         SMALLINT,
    minute       SMALLINT,
    period       VARCHAR(2),                   -- AM/PM
    hour_12      SMALLINT,
    time_of_day_segment VARCHAR(20),           -- 'morning', 'evening'
    is_peak_hours BOOLEAN
);
-- 1440 rows total.

Facts reference both: start_date_key + start_time_key from start_ts.

Timezone handling — the ironclad rule

Store everything in UTC. Convert for display at presentation.

  • Source systems emit timestamps; normalize to UTC in the first transform (bronze → silver).
  • In Postgres/Redshift use TIMESTAMPTZ (it stores a UTC instant, not the zone). In BigQuery use TIMESTAMP, which is an absolute instant; DATETIME is the naive type. In Snowflake, TIMESTAMP defaults to TIMESTAMP_NTZ (see TIMESTAMP_TYPE_MAPPING), so declare TIMESTAMP_TZ/_LTZ, or store UTC in NTZ by documented convention. None of these store the original zone. If you need it, keep it in a separate column.
  • For local-time analytics ("plays during 8pm local per user"), precompute the local date and time at ingest, using the user's timezone as of the event. A user's timezone is itself a slowly changing attribute. Someone who moves from New York to London shouldn't have old plays re-bucketed.
Engine: PostgreSQLDialect: PostgreSQLExecutable: Yes — PostgreSQL only
-- event_ts is TIMESTAMPTZ (a UTC instant): one AT TIME ZONE gives local wall-clock.
-- (If event_ts were a naive UTC timestamp you'd need
--  event_ts AT TIME ZONE 'UTC' AT TIME ZONE u.timezone.)
-- u.timezone should come from the user's version valid at event_ts, not the current one.
SELECT
    e.event_ts AT TIME ZONE u.timezone          AS local_ts,
    (e.event_ts AT TIME ZONE u.timezone)::DATE  AS local_date
FROM raw_events e
JOIN dim_user u ON u.user_id = e.user_id AND u.is_current;   -- simplification

DST is the silent bug. Be ready for 2026-03-08 02:30 US/Eastern, which doesn't exist. Library defaults silently shift it. Java ZonedDateTime.of moves gap times forward; use ZonedDateTime.ofStrict if you want it to throw. Python zoneinfo never raises, so check a round-trip or fold. pytz raises only with is_dst=None. Validate explicitly.

9. Data Vault 2.0 — When and Why

Data Vault is a modeling methodology for enterprises with many source systems, strong auditability requirements, and the need to evolve quickly without reshaping downstream.

Core structures

Hub — unique list of business keys.

Engine: PostgreSQLDialect: PostgreSQLExecutable: Yes — PostgreSQL only
CREATE TABLE hub_customer (
    customer_hk    CHAR(64) PRIMARY KEY,       -- hash of business key
    customer_bk    VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL,       -- natural / business key
    load_dts       TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL,
    record_source  VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL
);

Link — relationships between hubs.

Engine: PostgreSQLDialect: PostgreSQLExecutable: Yes — PostgreSQL only
CREATE TABLE link_order (
    order_hk       CHAR(64) PRIMARY KEY,        -- hash(customer_bk, product_bk, order_bk)
    customer_hk    CHAR(64) NOT NULL,   -- no REFERENCES: hubs/links/sats load in parallel
    product_hk     CHAR(64) NOT NULL,
    order_bk       VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL,
    load_dts       TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL,
    record_source  VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL
);

Satellite — descriptive attributes, with full history built in.

Engine: PostgreSQLDialect: PostgreSQLExecutable: Yes — PostgreSQL only
CREATE TABLE sat_customer_details (
    customer_hk    CHAR(64) NOT NULL,
    load_dts       TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL,
    load_end_dts   TIMESTAMPTZ,
    hash_diff      CHAR(64) NOT NULL,
    -- Attributes
    email          VARCHAR(320),
    country_code   CHAR(2),
    subscription_tier VARCHAR(20),
    record_source  VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL,
    PRIMARY KEY (customer_hk, load_dts)
);

Loading pattern

Loads are parallel. Hash keys are computed from business keys, not looked up, so hubs, links and satellites need no load order (keep FKs unenforced). Two rules keep that safe. Normalize business keys before hashing, or 'abc ' and 'ABC' become two customers. And make hub inserts idempotent under concurrency, with an insert-only MERGE or a dedup step instead of a check-then-insert race.

Engine: Snowflake / Spark SQLDialect: Snowflake SQLExecutable: Yes — Snowflake only
-- Load pattern (per source, per hub): normalize the BK, then hash
INSERT INTO hub_customer (customer_hk, customer_bk, load_dts, record_source)
SELECT DISTINCT
    SHA2(UPPER(TRIM(s.customer_id)), 256) AS customer_hk,
    UPPER(TRIM(s.customer_id))            AS customer_bk,
    CURRENT_TIMESTAMP,
    'billing_system'
FROM stage_billing s
LEFT JOIN hub_customer h
  ON h.customer_hk = SHA2(UPPER(TRIM(s.customer_id)), 256)
WHERE h.customer_hk IS NULL;

Trade-offs and when to use it

QuestionData Vault fitsStar / lakehouse direct fits
How many sources feed one business entity?Many, overlapping and changing. New sources are absorbed additively as new satellites and links, not by reshaping tablesFew, with one system of record each
Audit / regulatory lineage?Every attribute needs load_dts + record_source and insert-only historyStandard tests plus bronze retention are enough
Who queries it?It's awkward to query directly. PIT and bridge tables help, but BI reads an information mart (a star) on topAnalysts query the star
TeamCan staff two layers and generate the vault with automationA small team that needs one layer

A 2.1 revision of the methodology exists. The hub/link/satellite core above is unchanged, but check the specifics before citing them.

10. One Big Table & the Columnar Revolution

Columnar compression changes the math. With dictionary encoding, 100M repetitions of "premium" cost about one small code per row plus one dictionary entry, and run-length encoding shrinks sorted runs to a few bytes each.

This means denormalizing a dimension into a fact table adds almost no storage. The join-elimination benefit is real. Hence OBT.

What OBT looks like

Engine: Databricks SQLDialect: Databricks SQL (Delta, liquid clustering)Executable: Yes — Databricks only
-- A wide, denormalized table. Real ones run to ~200 columns.
CREATE TABLE gold.playback_sessions_enriched (
  session_id              STRING,
  -- user attributes, as of session start (from dim_user)
  user_id                 STRING,
  user_country_code       STRING,
  user_subscription_tier  STRING,
  user_segment            STRING,
  -- title and device attributes
  title_id                STRING,
  title_type              STRING,
  title_genre_primary     STRING,
  title_is_original       BOOLEAN,
  device_type             STRING,
  -- measures: additive components, not ratios
  watch_ms                BIGINT,
  buffer_ms               BIGINT,
  seeks                   INT,
  -- derived flags that don't exist in the star
  watched_in_peak_hours   BOOLEAN,
  was_binge_session       BOOLEAN,
  start_ts                TIMESTAMP,          -- UTC instant
  dt                      DATE
)
CLUSTER BY (dt, user_country_code, title_genre_primary);
-- Liquid clustering can't be combined with PARTITIONED BY.
-- BigQuery equivalent: PARTITION BY dt CLUSTER BY user_country_code, title_genre_primary

Consumer queries have zero joins:

Engine: Databricks SQLDialect: Spark SQLExecutable: Yes — Databricks only
SELECT
    user_country_code, title_genre_primary,
    SUM(watch_ms) / 3600e3 AS watch_hours
FROM gold.playback_sessions_enriched
WHERE dt BETWEEN '2026-04-12' AND '2026-04-18'
GROUP BY user_country_code, title_genre_primary;

Zone maps + clustering make this scan a tiny fraction of the table.

OBT trade-offs

Pros:

  • One join-less table.
  • Dashboards fly.
  • Simple mental model for analysts.
  • Compressed storage overhead compared with the star is usually modest, because repeated dimension values dictionary- and RLE-encode well within each column chunk. It is usually larger than the star, not smaller.

Cons:

  • History: each attribute is pinned to one temporal choice (as of the event, or current).
  • Change cost: new user_segment logic means rewriting every historical row.
  • Contracts and governance: 200 columns for many consumers, with email copied onto billions of rows, so GDPR deletes touch all of them.

The same question as an interview judgement call: Part 08, star schema vs OBT.

Interviewer pushes back

You: “I'd model this as a star: conformed dimensions, one fact table per process.”

Interviewer: “Why not just one big table? Storage is cheap, and columnar compression makes the repeated values nearly free.”

Strong answer: “Storage isn't the cost. Correctness and change are. An OBT pins each dimension attribute to one temporal choice, as of the event or current, not both. When the user_segment logic changes, billions of rows get rewritten. PII like email spreads into every fact row, so GDPR erasure becomes a full-table rewrite. I'd keep the conformed star as the source of truth and materialize OBTs per consumption pattern from it, so they're disposable. If the use case really is one dashboard with no history requirement, I'd go straight to an OBT.”

Weak answer: “Stars are best practice” or “joins are slow.” The first defends a brand, not a requirement. The second is false for small dimensions on modern engines, and it concedes the argument anyway.

Hybrid: Kimball silver + OBT gold

The pragmatic pattern most serious teams end up with:

  • Silver = cleansed, conformed entities. Some teams put the Kimball star here; others build it in gold.
  • Gold = one OBT per consumption pattern, materialized from silver.

Regenerate gold cheaply when dimensions change. Silver provides the single source of truth. BI reads gold for speed.

11. Medallion Architecture (Bronze/Silver/Gold)

The lakehouse convention. Each layer has a distinct purpose:

Bronze — raw, append-only, preserved

No business logic is applied. The schema is preserved (or promoted, with all fields retained). Ingest is replay-safe: sink commits are checkpointed. Producer duplicates are kept along with a stable dedup key (the event ID, or Kafka topic/partition/offset) and removed in silver.

Engine: Spark Structured Streaming 3.5 / 4.x + IcebergLanguage: Python (PySpark)Executable: Illustrative — adapt to your dialect
# Ingest Kafka events to a bronze Iceberg table (append-only)
(spark.readStream.format("kafka")
    .option("kafka.bootstrap.servers", BROKERS)
    .option("subscribe", "playback-events")
    .load()
    .selectExpr("CAST(key AS STRING) AS event_key", "value AS payload",
                "topic", "partition", "offset",          # dedup key for silver
                "timestamp AS kafka_ts", "current_date() AS ingest_date")
    .writeStream
    .format("iceberg")
    .outputMode("append")
    .option("checkpointLocation", "s3://lake/checkpoints/bronze_events/")
    .trigger(processingTime="5 minutes")
    .toTable("lake.bronze.events"))   # partition spec lives on the table, not here

Bronze is the replay layer. If silver or gold gets corrupted, you rebuild from it, but only within its retention. Replay reaches back only as far as bronze files and table snapshots are kept, so set bronze retention and snapshot expiry deliberately rather than leaving the defaults.

Silver — cleaned, conformed, typed, deduped

Business entities emerge here: cleansed, typed, conformed, and deduplicated by the key that bronze preserved. SCD handling usually lives here. Whether the Kimball star sits in silver or gold varies by organization. Either works if it's written down.

Gold — consumption-ready, OBT per use case

One gold table per dashboard domain. Materialized from silver. Rebuilt cheaply.

The implicit contract

  • Bronze is owned by the ingestion team. Contract: "we will deliver every source event at least once with a stable dedup key, preserve schema, and never backfill by overwrite."
  • Silver is owned by the platform team. Contract: "conformed dimensions, typed, documented, stable schema."
  • Gold is owned by the consumer team. Contract: "you build it, you own it; break it quietly and it's on you."

Medallion + streaming

It works the same way. Bronze is an append stream. Silver does streaming dedup, sessionization and enrichment, written as upserts; in Spark Structured Streaming that means foreachBatch + MERGE. Gold is periodic or streaming rollups. Row-level deletes (Iceberg v2 delete files, v3 deletion vectors, Delta deletion vectors) make frequent upserts feasible, as long as you run compaction. Every streaming upsert leaves small files and delete files behind.

2026 Interview Note

What doesn't change: merge-on-read trades cheaper writes for read-time merging plus compaction. What's version-specific: Iceberg format v3 adds deletion vectors (at most one per data file, replacing v2 position-delete files), row lineage, default values and a variant type. Engine support varies. Snowflake announced v3 GA in May 2026, for example. Check your engine's support matrix before you design around v3.

12. NULL Semantics — The Silent Source of Bugs

NULL in SQL is three-valued logic. NULL = NULL is NULL (not TRUE). x = NULL always yields NULL. This is the source of countless quiet bugs.

This section covers what NULL does to a model. SQL-level detail is in Part 02 §18, and the NOT IN trap is in Part 05 §12.6.

NULL in joins

a.x = b.x never matches when either side is NULL. If you want NULL to equal NULL, use:

  • a.x IS NOT DISTINCT FROM b.x (Postgres, Snowflake, BigQuery, Spark; Spark also has <=>). Postgres can't use it as a hash or merge join key, so large joins fall back to nested loops.
  • COALESCE(a.x, '') = COALESCE(b.x, '') (universal but ugly; only works if '' isn't a valid value)
  • EQUAL_NULL(a.x, b.x) (Snowflake; equal_null in Spark 3.4+)

NULL in aggregations

COUNT(*) counts rows. COUNT(x), SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX and COUNT(DISTINCT x) ignore NULLs, so AVG(x) divides by the non-NULL count. That surprises anyone who expected NULL to mean zero.

NULL in filters

WHERE x <> 5 excludes rows where x is 5 AND rows where x is NULL. If you want nulls too: WHERE x IS NULL OR x <> 5. Forgetting this is a dominant source of silent data loss.

NULL ordering

  • Postgres: NULLs sort LAST by default in ASC, FIRST in DESC. Override with NULLS FIRST / NULLS LAST.
  • MySQL, Spark, BigQuery: NULLs sort FIRST in ASC. Snowflake: like Postgres by default (DEFAULT_NULL_ORDERING).
  • Be explicit. Always.

NULL in GROUP BY

NULLs form their own group. GROUP BY country returns one row with country = NULL for all rows missing country. Surface this explicitly in reports or filter before aggregation.

NULLs in window functions

LAG(x) returns NULL before the first row. Use LAG(x, 1, default_value) or COALESCE. For "last known value", LAG(x) IGNORE NULLS works in Snowflake, Spark 3.2+ and Oracle and returns the previous non-NULL value. BigQuery's LAG has no IGNORE NULLS, so use LAST_VALUE(x IGNORE NULLS) over a frame, as below.

Engine: BigQueryDialect: GoogleSQLExecutable: Yes — BigQuery only
-- Last non-null country (for users with intermittent country updates)
SELECT user_id, event_ts,
       LAST_VALUE(country IGNORE NULLS) OVER (
           PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY event_ts
           ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
       ) AS country_known
FROM events;

Rule: every NULL should be documented

Either NULL means "not yet known" (e.g., churn_date) or "not applicable" (e.g., return_reason on non-returned orders). Document which. Consider sentinel values (unknown codes instead of NULL) when the latter — they force explicit handling downstream.

Engine: ANSI SQLDialect: column-definition fragmentExecutable: Illustrative — adapt to your dialect
-- Instead of NULL for "unknown country":
country_code CHAR(2) NOT NULL DEFAULT 'ZZ',   -- ZZ = unknown
-- Reports naturally include "ZZ" as a group rather than silently dropping.

13. Data Contracts & Schema Evolution

A data contract is a guarantee between a producer and consumers about a dataset's schema, semantics, freshness, and quality. Without it, consumers build on sand.

Two formats are worth naming in 2026. The Open Data Contract Standard (ODCS, from the Linux Foundation's Bitol project) is YAML for producer–consumer contracts; check the current version before citing fields. dbt model contracts (contract: {enforced: true}, dbt 1.5+) fail the build if a model's columns or types drift from its YAML. The example below is a simplified custom format that shows what any contract has to say.

What a contract specifies

Engine: n/aLanguage: YAML (custom format, not ODCS)Executable: Illustrative — adapt to your dialect
# data_contracts/playback_sessions.yaml
id: bronze.playback_sessions
version: 3.1.0
owner: playback-platform@co
schema:
  event_id:        { type: string, required: true, unique: true }
  session_id:      { type: string, required: true }
  user_id:         { type: string, required: true, pii: true }
  title_id:        { type: string, required: true }
  event_ts:        { type: timestamp, required: true, timezone: UTC }
  event_type:      { type: string, required: true, enum: [start, heartbeat, end, error] }
  watch_ms:        { type: long, required: false, constraints: "value >= 0" }
sla:
  freshness: "p99 < 15 minutes after event_ts"
  completeness: ">= 99.5% of upstream client emissions"
  uniqueness: "100% on event_id within 7 days"
breaking_changes_require:
  - major_version_bump
  - 30_day_deprecation_notice
  - consumer_acknowledgment_from: [analytics, ml-platform, product-insights]

Schema evolution rules

Say which direction you mean. BACKWARD compatible means readers on the new schema can read data written with the old one. FORWARD means readers still on the old schema can read data written with the new one. FULL means both. These are Schema Registry's definitions. For warehouse tables, the practical question is: do existing queries and dashboards still run?

Change Compatibility Action
Add optional column Full (backward + forward) if it has a default Minor version
Add required column Breaking Major version, default-fill historical rows
Drop column Breaking Deprecate (write-null for N versions, then drop)
Rename column Breaking Add new, deprecate old, drop after transition
Widen type (INT → BIGINT) Backward only: old readers may break Minor version
Narrow type Breaking Major version, data validation
Change semantics without renaming Catastrophic Never. Rename + deprecate.
Interviewer pushes back

You: “Renaming the column is safe. Iceberg tracks columns by ID, so it's metadata-only.”

Interviewer: “Then why did three dashboards and a dbt model break the next morning?”

Strong answer: “Metadata-only means no file rewrite. It doesn't mean no consumer impact. SQL, BI tools and dbt models bind by name, so every reader of qoe_score now fails. The table format made the rename cheap, but the contract has to make it safe. So I treat a rename as a breaking change: add the new name (or a view alias), publish both, deprecate the old one with a date, and drop it after consumers acknowledge.”

Weak answer: “Consumers should have used SELECT *.” That moves the breakage somewhere else and makes it harder to find.

Enforcing contracts

In CI, compare the declared schema with what the producer actually emits, and fail the merge on a breaking diff. dbt contracts do this for models. For files and topics, a small check against the Parquet or Avro schema, or Schema Registry compatibility checks, does the same job.

Pair with runtime data quality tests (Great Expectations, Soda, dbt tests) that run on each pipeline execution and block promotion on failure.

Lakehouse-native schema evolution

Iceberg tracks columns by ID, so it supports all of these natively. Delta supports rename and drop only with column mapping enabled (delta.columnMapping.mode = 'name'), and type widening through the newer type-widening table feature. The Iceberg rules:

  • Iceberg tracks columns by unique ID, not name. Rename is metadata-only, no rewrite.
  • Add column: metadata-only; existing rows treated as NULL.
  • Drop column: metadata-only (writes stop emitting it; old files untouched).
  • Reorder: metadata-only.
  • Type promotion (INT → LONG, FLOAT → DOUBLE): metadata-only, allowed.
  • Type narrowing: not allowed.
Engine: Spark SQL on IcebergDialect: Spark SQLExecutable: Yes — Spark 3.5+ / 4.x with Iceberg only
-- Iceberg
ALTER TABLE silver.playback_sessions ADD COLUMN engagement_score DOUBLE;
ALTER TABLE silver.playback_sessions RENAME COLUMN qoe_score TO quality_score;

Internals and the Delta specifics are in Part 07 §9.

14. Modeling Checklist & Anti-Patterns

Before shipping a model, check the following. They are also the questions a design review, or an interviewer, will ask you to defend:

  1. Grain declared and documented? If two engineers could disagree about what a row represents, the model is broken.
  2. Are all keys surrogate? Natural keys are attributes, not PKs on dims.
  3. Is every measure's additivity documented? Labels in the data catalog; column naming conventions (_point_in_time, _ratio).
  4. Is history handled deliberately? SCD type per attribute, not per dim.
  5. Are dimensions conformed across facts? Single dim_customer, multiple FKs.
  6. Is the date dimension a real table? Not a function call.
  7. Are rapidly-changing dimension attributes split into mini-dimensions? So SCD2 doesn't explode.
  8. Are all NULLs meaningful and documented? Sentinel values where applicable.
  9. Are timestamps UTC with explicit timezone storage? Local times precomputed for user-local analytics.
