  10. Does the table have a partition/cluster strategy that prunes typical queries? Default: partition by date, cluster by most-filtered high-cardinality column.
  11. Are contracts published and enforced? Schema + SLA + tests in version control, blocked by CI.
  12. Can the table be rebuilt from bronze in a reasonable window? If not, you have single-source fragility.

Anti-patterns

  • Mixed-grain fact tables. Invisible bug, impossible to audit.
  • Natural keys as PKs. Breaks the first time source-system renumbering happens.
  • FLOAT for money. Accumulation errors. Use BIGINT cents or DECIMAL(18,2).
  • Naive local timestamps. Ambiguous across DST. Store UTC (typed, or by documented convention) plus the source zone.
  • "Latest" table that's actually mutable. A view over SCD2 with WHERE is_current is safe; an actual table that gets UPDATE'd is a mutation-ordering bug farm.
  • Soft-delete flags consumers must remember. Expose a view that filters is_deleted. In OLTP, back it with a partial index.
  • EAV (entity-attribute-value) inside a warehouse. (entity_id, attr_name, attr_value) — looks flexible, makes every query a pivot, kills indexability.
  • Copying source tables verbatim into the warehouse as "the model." Source schema serves source transactions; warehouse schema should serve analytics.
  • Dimensions that aren't dimensions. Low-cardinality flags scattered across facts are junk-dimension candidates. In columnar stores, keeping them inline is also acceptable.

15. Bridge Tables and Many-to-Many Dimensions

Not every dimension attaches to a fact with a clean foreign key. A policy can have multiple beneficiaries. An insurance claim can have multiple diagnosis codes. A marketing touch can belong to multiple campaigns. These require bridge tables — and bridge tables are where naive data modelers get caught.

The problem with denormalizing

The tempting shortcut is diagnosis_code_1 … diagnosis_code_N columns on the fact. It works until a claim has 12 codes. Then you drop data, add columns, or reshape the fact and break every consumer.

The bridge table pattern

Three tables: the fact (fct_claim), the dimension (dim_diagnosis), and the bridge (bridge_claim_diagnosis). The bridge stores one row per (claim_sk, diagnosis_sk) with an allocation weight.

Engine: ANSI SQLDialect: ANSI DDLExecutable: Yes
CREATE TABLE bridge_claim_diagnosis (
  claim_sk      BIGINT       NOT NULL,
  diagnosis_sk  BIGINT       NOT NULL,
  is_primary    BOOLEAN      NOT NULL,
  weight        DECIMAL(9,8) NOT NULL,   -- allocation; must SUM to 1 per claim_sk
  PRIMARY KEY (claim_sk, diagnosis_sk)
);

The weight column is what makes the dollars add up. Without it, ten codes on a claim attribute the same dollars ten times. There are two legitimate answers, and you should name both. The allocated view (SUM(amount * weight)) reconciles to finance. The impact view is unweighted ("total dollars on claims that mention diabetes"). It correctly answers a different question, and it must never be summed across codes. Interviewers probe for exactly this distinction.

Aggregation safely across a bridge

Engine: ANSI SQLDialect: ANSI SQLExecutable: Yes
-- Allocated: reconciles to finance
SELECT
  d.diagnosis_category,
  SUM(f.claim_amount * b.weight) AS allocated_amount
FROM fct_claim f
JOIN bridge_claim_diagnosis b ON b.claim_sk = f.claim_sk
JOIN dim_diagnosis d           ON d.diagnosis_sk = b.diagnosis_sk
GROUP BY d.diagnosis_category;

-- Test: weights sum to 1 per claim (returns violating claims)
SELECT claim_sk, SUM(weight) AS total_weight
FROM bridge_claim_diagnosis
GROUP BY claim_sk
HAVING ABS(SUM(weight) - 1) > 0.0001;

Wrong: SUM(f.claim_amount) over the same join. Each claim is counted once per code, and nothing errors.

16. Late-Arriving Facts and Dimensions

"Late-arriving" data is the term of art for rows whose business timestamp is in the past but whose arrival timestamp is now. Two distinct cases, each with its own playbook.

Late-arriving facts

A mobile app emits an event on Tuesday but the SDK holds it in local cache due to offline mode, and uploads it Thursday. The fact has a business date of Tuesday. You must decide: does Tuesday's daily aggregate get corrected retroactively, or is the late record attributed to Thursday?

Decide, per consumer, which date owns the row. Finance usually wants the business date: Tuesday gets restated, so its partition must be reprocessable and the report must say that its numbers can change. Operations often wants the arrival date: Tuesday stays closed. Publishing both, or business date with a stated restatement window, is fine. Conflating them silently is the bug. See also Part 03 (watermarks) and the Part 08 incident.

The dimension lookup is where late facts go wrong. A Tuesday event loaded on Thursday must get Tuesday's customer version. Joining on is_current gives Thursday's version, and joining on the natural key alone fans out across all versions. Look up the version as of the event time on the half-open interval, and stamp its key onto the fact:

Engine: ANSI SQLDialect: ANSI SQLExecutable: Yes
-- As-of lookup at load time; facts then join on user_key alone
SELECT e.event_id,
       e.event_ts,
       COALESCE(d.user_key, -1) AS user_key       -- -1 = reserved 'Unknown' member
FROM stg_events e
LEFT JOIN dim_user d
  ON  d.user_id   = e.user_id
  AND e.event_ts >= d.valid_from
  AND e.event_ts <  COALESCE(d.valid_to, TIMESTAMP '9999-12-31 00:00:00');

An event older than the user's first version also falls through to -1. Set the first version's valid_from to the entity's creation time (or a low sentinel) so that doesn't happen by accident.

Late-arriving dimensions

A fact arrives referencing a new customer_id that doesn't exist in dim_customer yet. Three strategies:

  1. Inferred member. Insert a placeholder row into dim_customer with the known natural key and NULL (or "Unknown") attributes, so the fact joins. When the full dimension row arrives, overwrite the inferred row in place, even in an SCD2 dimension, so earlier facts pick up the attributes. Later changes create new versions as normal. Best default.
  2. Quarantine. Hold the fact in a quarantine table until the dim row appears. Replay when it does. Use when joining with missing context would be meaningless.
  3. Orphan facts. Letting the fact land with a NULL dimension key means inner joins silently drop it. If you can't infer a member, point at a reserved -1 'Unknown' member and reprocess later.
L5 Interview CardData Modeling
Must know
  • Grain first: “one row = one ___”, enforced by a uniqueness test.
  • Additivity: additive / semi-additive (period-end across time) / non-additive (store components or sketches).
  • SCD2: a key per version, a durable natural key, half-open [valid_from, valid_to), exactly one current row. Choose the type per attribute.
  • Facts attach to the dimension version valid at event time, stamped at load by an as-of lookup, never via is_current.
  • Late dimensions: an inferred member overwritten in place, or a -1 Unknown member. Never NULL foreign keys.
  • Hash keys: 128-bit+ over a normalized, NULL-tokened, explicitly formatted input. 64-bit hashes collide at warehouse scale.
  • Bridges need allocation weights that sum to 1. Know allocated vs impact.
  • The star is the source of truth. OBTs are disposable per-consumer materializations.
Must be able to explain
  1. SCD Type 2, without jargon.
  2. What the grain of this fact table is, and what breaks if it's mixed.
  3. When you'd choose an OBT or a Data Vault over a star, and what would change your mind.
Must be able to draw

A star with conformed dimensions, plus one customer's SCD2 timeline with a late fact landing on the right version:

dim_user(SCD2)  dim_title  dim_date
        ╲          │          ╱
      fact_playback_session
      grain: 1 row per session

 ├─101 Austin─┼─102 Denver─┼─103 Boston─▶
                   ▲ late fact → 102
Must be able to code
  • A single-statement SCD2 MERGE with stage dedup and a NULL-safe hash_diff.
  • An as-of join of late facts to an SCD2 dimension, with an Unknown-member fallback.
  • Invariant tests: one current row per key, no overlapping intervals, fan-out (row count unchanged by joins), bridge weights sum to 1.
Must be able to debug
  • The dashboard is exactly 2× Finance's number after a dimension change: a natural-key join to SCD2, duplicate current rows, or an unweighted bridge.
  • Users vanish from current-state reports after a failed SCD2 run: the close committed, the insert didn't, and inner joins dropped their facts.
Numbers that matter
  • Collision odds ≈ n² / 2b+1: at 109 keys, a 64-bit hash gives ≈ 2.7%; at 1010 keys, a 128-bit hash gives ≈ 10-19.
  • Date dimension: ~365 rows per year, ≈ 11k for 30 years. Minute-of-day: 1,440. Date × second combined: ≈ 109 rows, which is why they're separate.
  • SCD2 rows ≈ entities × (1 + changes per entity). One daily-changing attribute on 100M entities is up to 100M rows a day.
  • A dense coverage fact of users × titles × days explodes fast (hypothetical 10M × 10k × 365 ≈ 3.6×1013), so store sparse rows only.
  • Junk dimension size = the product of flag cardinalities (2 × 2 × 2 × 3 = 24).
Classic traps
  • Joining facts to an SCD2 dimension on the natural key or on is_current.
  • Summing a semi-additive snapshot (MRR, balances) across days.
  • Hash keys built with concat_ws or COALESCE(x, ''), or a 64-bit hash. And promising “exactly once” in bronze.
30-second answer

How would you model this business process? I name the process and declare the grain, “one row = one ___”, before any columns. Next come the dimensions that describe it, deciding per attribute whether history matters, and the measures, each checked for additivity. It's built as a star with conformed dimensions as the source of truth. Wide tables for specific dashboards are materialized from it and are disposable.

2-minute answer

First I ask who consumes it, what questions they ask, how fresh it must be, and whether they need history as of the event or current values. Then I pick one business process and its atomic grain, and back the grain with a uniqueness test. I choose the fact type: transaction, periodic snapshot (semi-additive), or accumulating snapshot (idempotent milestone MERGE). Dimensions are conformed across processes, with the SCD type chosen per attribute. Facts get the version key through an as-of lookup at load, late dimensions get inferred or Unknown members, and many-to-many relationships get a weighted bridge. Measures are stored as additive components. Physically: partition by date, cluster by the common filter, and use deterministic 128-bit keys. Then contracts and tests: grain uniqueness, one current row, no interval overlaps, fan-out, and weight sums. What would change my mind: a single dashboard with no history requirement means an OBT directly. Dozens of overlapping sources plus audit requirements mean a Data Vault under the star.

Deep-dive follow-up

A customer's region change arrives today, but it's effective from last month. What happens to your SCD2 intervals, to facts already stamped with the old version key, and to last month's published revenue by region?

Staff+ follow-up

Three teams each maintain their own dim_customer with different definitions of “active customer”. How do you get to one conformed dimension without a six-month freeze, and who owns it afterwards?

Part 02

Batch Processing

Quick refresh15 minInterview study55 minDeep practice60 min
Last technically reviewed September 2026
Covers completeness, job anatomy, write-audit-publish, idempotency, MERGE, incremental loads, backfills, file formats, partitioning, compaction, CDC basics, DQ gates, orchestration, critical path, cost, restart semantics
Versions referenced Spark 3.5 / 4.x, Iceberg 1.10–1.11 (format v2/v3), Delta Lake 3.3 / 4.x, Airflow 2.x and 3.x (3.3 current), dbt 1.8+, Debezium 3.x
Primary references Iceberg Spark writes · Delta Lake docs · Upgrading to Airflow 3 · Parquet docs · Spark SQL tuning
Known implementation differences Overwrite semantics differ by engine: Iceberg uses overwritePartitions() or dynamic INSERT OVERWRITE, Delta uses replaceWhere, and a v1 mode("overwrite") can replace the whole table.

A batch question is rarely about Spark syntax. The interviewer wants to know whether you can build a pipeline that is safe to rerun. Can you say when the input is complete? Can you rerun yesterday without doubling it? Can you backfill two years without paging anyone? Can you estimate the bill before you run it? Most of this chapter comes back to one property: the same logical date and the same input must always produce the same output.

1. Mental Model: Bounded vs Unbounded Data (Deep)

A batch job processes bounded data, so it can sort globally, total, and wait for everything before emitting. But most "bounded" inputs are a window cut from an unbounded stream. "Yesterday's events" is only sealed if you can say when late data stops arriving.

The completeness contract: "how do you know yesterday is complete?"

Three honest answers, strongest first:

  • An explicit completion signal: a _SUCCESS file, a manifest listing files and row counts, or a published asset/dataset event from the producer.
  • Reconciliation: compare your row count and control totals with the upstream system's audit counts.
  • A grace window: "day D is sealed 2 hours after midnight UTC", plus a scheduled re-run that picks up stragglers.

A sealed drop allows strict checks and a full-refresh fallback. A late-arriving source needs a safety window (reprocess event_time ≥ D − 7 days) or a scheduled restatement. Either way, the rule is part of the table's contract.

Watermark-as-promise, applied to batch

"Process yesterday with a 2-hour buffer" is an implicit watermark. Make the promise explicit:

Engine: Python 3.11+ (stdlib)Language: PythonExecutable: Yes
from datetime import date, datetime, time, timedelta, timezone

def run_daily(dt: date, safety_hours: int = 2) -> None:
    sealed_at = datetime.combine(dt + timedelta(days=1), time.min, tzinfo=timezone.utc) \
                + timedelta(hours=safety_hours)
    if datetime.now(timezone.utc) < sealed_at:      # explicit raise: `assert` vanishes under python -O
        raise RuntimeError(f"Not safe to process {dt} before {sealed_at.isoformat()}")
    ...

Bounded storage, unbounded log

Lakehouse formats expose each table's change log: time travel to a snapshot, or increments since the last run. What an increment contains is engine-specific:

Engine: Spark + IcebergLanguage: PythonExecutable: Yes — appended rows only
# Iceberg incremental read: rows from APPEND snapshots between the two ids.
# It does not return updates or deletes; use the create_changelog_view procedure for those.
df = (spark.read
      .format("iceberg")
      .option("start-snapshot-id", last_processed_snapshot)   # exclusive
      .option("end-snapshot-id",   current_snapshot)          # inclusive
      .load("warehouse.bronze.events"))

2. Anatomy of a Batch Job

Stages, in order. Each can fail; each must be recoverable.

  1. Bind logical_date, never current_date.
  2. Check completeness. Fail fast; an empty "success" is worse than a failure.
  3. Read pinned at a snapshot/version id, and log it.
  4. Dedupe → conform → enrich (as-of) → transform.
  5. Write staged: branch, WAP id or staging table.
  6. Audit counts, uniqueness, control totals vs the previous run.
  7. Publish atomically, then emit the asset event.
  8. Log rows in/out, source snapshot ids, code version, runtime.

The validation gate

The airbag, and the step most often skipped. One aggregate pass; three separate .count() calls are three full scans.

Engine: PySpark 3.x/4.xLanguage: PythonExecutable: Illustrative — thresholds are examples
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

def validate(df, expected_min_rows: int, prior_rows: int | None) -> dict:
    m = df.agg(
        F.count("*").alias("rows"),
        F.countDistinct("event_id").alias("keys"),
        *[F.sum(F.col(c).isNull().cast("int")).alias(f"null_{c}")
          for c in ("user_id", "title_id", "watch_ms")],
    ).first().asDict()

    if m["rows"] < expected_min_rows:
        raise ValueError(f"row count {m['rows']} below floor {expected_min_rows}")
    if m["keys"] != m["rows"]:
        raise ValueError(f"{m['rows'] - m['keys']} duplicate event_id values")
    if prior_rows and abs(m["rows"] / prior_rows - 1) > 0.5:
        raise ValueError(f"row count moved >50% vs prior run ({prior_rows})")   # catches 2x reruns
    m["warnings"] = [c for c in ("user_id", "title_id", "watch_ms")
                     if m[f"null_{c}"] / m["rows"] > 0.005]
    return m

Keep audit records in a permanent table; it answers "what changed overnight?"

Write-audit-publish (WAP)

"Stage, validate, then swap." Iceberg: write to an audit branch (spark.wap.branch) or with spark.wap.id on a write.wap.enabled=true table, then fast-forward or cherry-pick into main. Delta and most warehouses: staging table plus atomic swap or INSERT OVERWRITE. Snowflake: zero-copy clone plus ALTER TABLE … SWAP WITH. Check current docs for exact procedure names. The idea is timeless: consumers never read unaudited data.

Failure-first: what can fail in a daily batch pipeline?
FailureDetectRecoverPrevent recurrence
Source unavailable or incompleteNo completion marker by the deadline; row count far below the source's audit countHold the run and alert the producer. Don't publish an empty partitionSensor or asset trigger instead of cron; a freshness SLO on the source; a completeness check against the producer's control totals
Partial write (job died mid-commit)Orphan files with no committed snapshot; _SUCCESS missing on Hive-style pathsRerun. A table-format commit is atomic, so the half-written files were never visible. Clean up orphans laterWrite only through a table format or WAP. Never write in place on raw object-store paths
Duplicate input (producer retry, replayed file)Distinct keys < rows in the audit; a control total well above the sourceDedupe by business key and overwrite the affected partitionDedupe before transform; key-scoped MERGE or partition overwrite, never a blind append
Schema drift (renamed, retyped or new column)Schema check at read time; null-rate spike on a mapped columnQuarantine the run and patch the mapping, then rerun the datesA data contract plus registry compatibility rules; fail on breaking changes, allow additive ones
Late partition (data for D lands after D was sealed)Rows with event_date < D arriving in today's bronze; the reconciliation job flags a diffRe-run the affected dates. That's only safe if the job is idempotentA grace window, a scheduled N-day restatement, and a "last restated at" field consumers can see
Storage or catalog unavailable (throttling, 503s, commit conflicts)Retries exhausted; commit-conflict exceptions; 503 SlowDown throttling responsesRetry with backoff. The commit is atomic, so a retry can't double-writeFewer, larger files; spread prefixes; serialize writers to the same table or use the engine's conflict-retry settings

3. Idempotency — Proofs and Patterns

Definition: running the job again for the same logical_date leaves the target in the same state as running it once. Formally, if f is the job bound to a logical date and a pinned input, and S_0 is the starting state, then f(f(S_0)) = f(S_0).

Idempotent is not deterministic. A version-guarded MERGE is idempotent, but can pick a different winner on each run if updated_at ties. Reproducibility also needs a pinned input: log the source snapshot id and have reruns read that snapshot.

It matters because orchestrators retry, backfills re-run history, and people press the button twice.

Pattern 1 — Partition overwrite

For outputs partitioned by the job parameter. Syntax is engine-specific, and getting it wrong can replace the whole table:

Engine: Spark 3.x/4.x + Iceberg · Delta LakeLanguage: PythonExecutable: Yes — each statement on its own engine
# Iceberg (DataFrameWriterV2): replace exactly the partitions present in df
df.writeTo("warehouse.silver.playback_sessions").overwritePartitions()

# Delta: replace rows matching the predicate; by default the write fails
# if df contains rows outside it
(df.write.format("delta")
   .mode("overwrite")
   .option("replaceWhere", f"dt = '{ctx.logical_date}'")
   .saveAsTable("silver.playback_sessions"))
Engine: Spark SQL (Iceberg or Hive-format tables)Dialect: Spark SQLExecutable: Yes
SET spark.sql.sources.partitionOverwriteMode = dynamic;   -- Spark's default is static
INSERT OVERWRITE silver.playback_sessions
SELECT * FROM stg_playback WHERE dt = DATE '2026-04-19';
-- dynamic: replaces only partitions present in the SELECT
-- static, no PARTITION clause: replaces the WHOLE table

All three scope the overwrite to the partitions written; the commit is atomic. Guard the scope before writing:

Engine: PySparkLanguage: PythonExecutable: Yes
if df.filter(F.col("dt") != F.lit(ctx.logical_date)).limit(1).count():
    raise ValueError("output contains rows outside the target partition")

Pattern 2 — MERGE by key

Engine: Generic (Spark SQL + Delta/Iceberg, Snowflake, BigQuery, PostgreSQL 15+)Dialect: ANSI-style MERGEExecutable: Illustrative — adapt to your dialect
MERGE INTO silver.dim_user AS t
USING stg_user AS s
  ON t.user_id = s.user_id
WHEN MATCHED AND t.updated_at < s.updated_at THEN UPDATE SET ...
WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT (...) VALUES (...);

A second run finds no t.updated_at < s.updated_at rows. Only as good as the version column (see the pushback in §4).

Pattern 3 — Hash + upsert

Engine: Spark SQL / Databricks (SHA2, CONCAT_WS)Dialect: Spark SQLExecutable: Illustrative — adapt to your dialect
MERGE INTO silver.events AS t
USING (
    SELECT *, SHA2(CONCAT_WS('||', event_id, event_ts, payload), 256) AS row_hash
    FROM stg_events
) AS s
  ON t.event_id = s.event_id
WHEN MATCHED AND t.row_hash <> s.row_hash THEN UPDATE SET ...
WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT (...) VALUES (...);

Trap: CONCAT_WS skips NULLs, so ('a', NULL) and (NULL, 'a') hash alike. Coalesce columns first.

Anti-pattern: INSERT ... SELECT without dedup

Engine: GenericDialect: ANSI SQLExecutable: Yes
-- BAD: second run doubles the data
INSERT INTO silver.events SELECT * FROM stg_events;

The most common idempotency bug. Use MERGE or a scoped overwrite; "delete then insert" only works as one atomic commit.

Anti-pattern: now() in transform

Engine: GenericDialect: ANSI SQLExecutable: Yes
-- BAD: second run produces different output because now() changes
SELECT *, NOW() AS processed_at FROM stg_events;

Fix: derive from logical_date or a per-run constant. Same for "current" dimension lookups.

Anti-pattern: keys that differ across runs

Engine: PySparkLanguage: PythonExecutable: Yes
# BAD: Spark's monotonically_increasing_id() isn't stable across runs
df.withColumn("key", F.monotonically_increasing_id())

Fix: a deterministic hash of the natural key.

Engine: PySparkLanguage: PythonExecutable: Yes
df.withColumn("key", F.sha2(F.concat_ws("||", *natural_key_cols), 256))

Testing idempotency

Engine: PySpark + pytestLanguage: PythonExecutable: Illustrative — fixtures elided
def test_idempotent_run(tmp_table, test_data):
    run(RunContext(logical_date=date(2026,4,10), ...))
    snapshot1 = spark.table(tmp_table).collect()
    run(RunContext(logical_date=date(2026,4,10), ...))
    snapshot2 = spark.table(tmp_table).collect()
    assert snapshot1 == snapshot2, "Output differs between runs — not idempotent"

Catches now() leaks, appends and unstable keys. Sort first or use exceptAll both ways; collect() order isn't guaranteed.

“How do you make a batch job idempotent?”
30 sec

Make the output a pure function of the logical date and a pinned input. Then write it with a scoped replace: overwrite the partition for that date, or MERGE on the business key with a version guard. Never a blind append. Rerunning date D then replaces D with identical content.

2 min

There are three ways to lose idempotency. Write mode: an append doubles the data, and a static overwrite can wipe the table. Non-deterministic input: now(), reading a table that changed overnight, "current" dimension rows, generated ids. Side effects: emails, API calls and downstream events fired on every run. My fixes: pin and log the source snapshot, dedupe by key before writing, scope the overwrite to the partitions I produce, route side effects through a publish step that runs once per logical date, and prove all of it with a CI test that runs the job twice and diffs the output.

Deep dive

Idempotent is not the same as deterministic. A MERGE can be idempotent and still pick different winners when updated_at ties, so add a tiebreaker. For streaming foreachBatch, a batch can be replayed after a failure, so either guard on a source version (LSN) or use Delta's idempotent writes (txnAppId/txnVersion). With WAP, a failed audit never reaches consumers. Exactly-once is a property of the pipeline's boundaries, not of any one product.

Where to stop: name the write mode, the pinned input and the test. Only list engine configs if they ask.

Interviewer pushes back

You: “If it fails, I'll just rerun the job.”

Interviewer: “The write is mode("append"), and the upstream table was compacted and corrected overnight. What does the rerun produce?”

Strong answer: “Two separate bugs. The append means the partition now holds the first run's rows plus the second run's, so revenue roughly doubles. The unpinned read means the second run's rows aren't even the same as the first run's, so dedupe by business key can't fully save me. I'd switch to overwritePartitions() or replaceWhere for that date, read the source at the snapshot id logged by the original run (or deliberately at the new one, if the correction is the point), and add an audit gate that fails when the row count for a logical date jumps against its previous run.”

Weak answer: “Reruns are safe because Spark is fault-tolerant.” Spark retries tasks inside a job. It does nothing to stop a second job from appending.

Drill · Idempotency

A rerun of yesterday's job was triggered after a transient failure. Finance now reports yesterday's revenue at 1.97× the usual figure. Nothing else changed.

STOP. Diagnose before you fix. Is this an append, a non-deterministic input, or both?

Reveal the diagnosis
  1. Observe: about 2× for one date only; other dates are normal. Check which runs committed: the Iceberg snapshots metadata table (operation) or Delta DESCRIBE HISTORY. Two commits for the same logical date, both append, is the smoking gun.
  2. Hypothesize: (a) append write mode, so run 1 and run 2 both persisted, even if run 1 "failed" after its commit; (b) a scoped overwrite whose predicate didn't match (for example dt string vs date); (c) the input moved between runs, so rows differ.
  3. Measure: COUNT(*) vs COUNT(DISTINCT order_id) for the date. Exactly 2× with every key duplicated means pure append. About 1.97× means some keys appear once, so the second run read a different input (late rows arrived, or the source was corrected). Compare the source snapshot ids in the audit log for both runs.
  4. Isolate: here, the rows ratio is 1.97 and ~3% of keys are singletons. So it's an append and an unpinned read. Also check downstream: which aggregates, extracts and dashboards already consumed the doubled partition?
  5. Fix: roll the table back to the snapshot before the rerun (rollback_to_snapshot / RESTORE), or overwrite date D from a clean run at a pinned input. Then re-trigger every downstream job that consumed D, and tell finance which figure was wrong and for how long.
  6. Prevent: make the write a scoped overwrite or a key-based MERGE; pin and log the input snapshot; add an audit gate on the row-count delta against the previous run of the same logical date; add a run-twice test in CI.

4. MERGE Under the Hood

Where many batch correctness and cost incidents start.

The logical model

Engine: Generic — NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE in Delta/Databricks, BigQuery, SQL Server, PostgreSQL 17+; not SnowflakeDialect: ANSI-style MERGEExecutable: Pseudocode
MERGE INTO target t
USING source s
  ON t.key = s.key
WHEN MATCHED AND <cond> THEN UPDATE SET ...
WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT ...
WHEN MATCHED AND <cond2> THEN DELETE
WHEN NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE THEN DELETE;   -- supported by some engines

Each matched pair takes the first WHEN MATCHED clause whose condition holds; unmatched source rows go to NOT MATCHED; unmatched target rows to NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE where supported.

The multi-match rule

One target row matching several source rows is ambiguous; most engines error:

Engine: Delta Lake / Spark (error text)Dialect: n/aExecutable: Illustrative — message wording varies by engine
ERROR: Cannot perform MERGE as multiple source rows matched and attempted to modify
       the same target row.

Fix: dedupe the source to one row per join key before the MERGE.

Engine: PostgreSQL 15+ (MERGE)Dialect: PostgreSQLExecutable: Illustrative — clauses elided
MERGE INTO target t
USING (
    SELECT DISTINCT ON (user_id) *           -- Postgres
    FROM stg_user
    ORDER BY user_id, updated_at DESC
) s
ON t.user_id = s.user_id
...

Portable form; add a deterministic tiebreaker (updated_at DESC, source_lsn DESC):

Engine: GenericDialect: ANSI SQL (fragment)Executable: Illustrative — adapt to your dialect
USING (
    SELECT * FROM (
        SELECT *, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY updated_at DESC) rn
        FROM stg_user
    ) WHERE rn = 1
) s

Execution on lakehouse (Iceberg/Delta)

Files are immutable: MERGE rewrites the files holding matched keys (or records deletes) and commits a new snapshot. Cost is files touched, not rows changed: 1% of rows scattered over 1,000 files of 512 MB can rewrite ~500 GB. Internals: Part 07 §6 and Part 07 §18.

Copy-on-write vs merge-on-read

Copy-on-writeMerge-on-read
WhereIceberg's default write.{delete,update,merge}.mode; Delta without deletion vectorsIceberg with write.*.mode=merge-on-read (v2: position/equality delete files; v3: deletion vectors); Delta with deletion vectors
WriteRewrite every touched fileWrite small delete markers plus new rows
ReadFastApplies deletes at read time; slows down until you compact
FitsUpdate-light: daily overwrites, SCD2Update-heavy: CDC, frequent upserts
2026 Interview Note

Timeless: immutable files force a choice between paying at write time and paying at read time. Version-specific: Iceberg format v3 replaces v2 position-delete files with deletion vectors (at most one per data file). Recent Databricks runtimes enable deletion vectors by default on new Delta tables, while OSS Delta leaves them off unless you set the table property. Check your engine's defaults before you claim either one.

Partition-aware MERGE

Engine: Spark SQL + Delta/IcebergDialect: Spark SQLExecutable: Illustrative — clauses elided
MERGE INTO target t
USING source s
ON  t.user_id = s.user_id
AND t.dt = s.dt                      -- prunes only via runtime/dynamic filtering
AND t.dt >= DATE '2026-04-01'        -- literal bound: guaranteed static pruning
...

Without a pruning predicate the engine may scan every target file.

Why is my MERGE slow?

In order: no pruning predicate; source not deduped; skewed key; thousands of small target files; copy-on-write rewriting big files for tiny changes. In Delta, compare numTargetRowsCopied with numTargetRowsUpdated (DESCRIBE HISTORY); 100× more copied than updated is write amplification.

Interviewer pushes back

You: “The nightly MERGE is idempotent because of WHEN MATCHED AND t.updated_at < s.updated_at.”

Interviewer: “Upstream reprocessed and re-sent yesterday's rows with new updated_at values but identical content. What happens?”

Strong answer: “Every row wins, so the MERGE rewrites every file it touches. Correctness is fine, but it's a cost spike, and anyone reading the change feed sees a flood of fake updates. I'd add a content-hash guard (AND t.row_hash <> s.row_hash) so only real changes update. And if upstream can re-send older content with a newer timestamp, updated_at isn't a version at all. I'd ask for a monotonic source version (LSN or sequence) in the contract.”

Weak answer: “It's idempotent, so nothing happens.”

5. Incremental Processing Patterns

Full refresh is simple and expensive; incremental is cheap and full of traps.

Pattern 1 — High watermark incremental

Pull everything past the last processed ingestion position, with an overlap. Overlap means the write must be a MERGE; an append duplicates the overlap.

Engine: PySpark + Delta LakeLanguage: PythonExecutable: Illustrative — transform and the target table assumed
from datetime import timedelta
from delta.tables import DeltaTable
from pyspark.sql import functions as F, Window

OVERLAP = timedelta(hours=6)

def run_incremental():
    # HWM derived from committed output, driven by a SERVER-assigned ingest time
    hwm = spark.table("silver.events").agg(F.max("ingested_at")).first()[0]
    src = spark.table("bronze.events")
    if hwm is not None:
        src = src.where(F.col("ingested_at") > F.lit(hwm - OVERLAP))
    w = Window.partitionBy("event_id").orderBy(F.col("ingested_at").desc())
    batch = transform(src.withColumn("rn", F.row_number().over(w)).where("rn = 1").drop("rn"))
    (DeltaTable.forName(spark, "silver.events").alias("t")
        .merge(batch.alias("s"), "t.event_id = s.event_id")
        .whenNotMatchedInsertAll()
        .execute())

HWM failure modes:

  1. Late commits: a long transaction commits later with an earlier updated_at. Overlap must exceed the longest transaction.
  2. Boundary ties: > hwm drops rows sharing the value; >= re-reads them (fine with MERGE).
  3. Clock skew: one device with a future clock pushes an event_ts HWM ahead and everyone else is skipped. Use a server-assigned ingest time or offset.
  4. HWM stored apart from data: derive it from committed output, or commit both together.

Pattern 2 — Partition-based incremental

One source partition in, the matching target partition overwritten (§3 Pattern 1):

Engine: PySpark + IcebergLanguage: PythonExecutable: Yes — transform assumed
def run_incremental(dt):
    day = spark.table("bronze.events").where(F.col("dt") == F.lit(dt))
    transform(day).writeTo("silver.events").overwritePartitions()

Cleaner than a HWM: reruns are safe and a backfill is a loop over dates.

Pattern 3 — Snapshot-diff incremental (Iceberg / Delta)

Read what changed since the last snapshot. Iceberg's incremental read returns appended rows only (use create_changelog_view for updates/deletes); Delta CDF returns all change types, but only for versions written after delta.enableChangeDataFeed was set.

Engine: Spark + Iceberg · Spark + Delta Lake (CDF enabled)Language: PythonExecutable: Yes — each block on its own engine
# Iceberg: appended rows only
df_new = (spark.read.format("iceberg")
    .option("start-snapshot-id", last_snapshot)
    .option("end-snapshot-id",   current_snapshot)
    .load("warehouse.bronze.events"))

# Delta: Change Data Feed (table property delta.enableChangeDataFeed = true)
df_changes = (spark.read.format("delta")
    .option("readChangeFeed", "true")
    .option("startingVersion", last_version)
    .option("endingVersion",   current_version)
    .table("bronze.events"))
# _change_type: insert | update_preimage | update_postimage | delete

Pattern 4 — Merge-on-arrival (streaming batch)

A streaming query on a batch schedule (Trigger.AvailableNow, Spark 3.3+):

Engine: Spark 3.3+ Structured Streaming + IcebergLanguage: PythonExecutable: Yes — paths elided
(spark.readStream.format("iceberg")
    .load("warehouse.bronze.events")
    .writeStream.format("iceberg")
    .option("checkpointLocation", "s3://…/ckpt/silver_events/")
    .trigger(availableNow=True)          # process what's there, then stop
    .toTable("warehouse.silver.events")
    .awaitTermination())

Exactly-once here holds only because the source is replayable and the sink transactional.

6. Backfills — Design, Safety, and Throttling

Prerequisites: a date-parameterized, idempotent job; a concurrency cap; isolated compute; per-date progress tracking.

Orchestrated backfill

Skip the home-grown thread-pool driver; the orchestrator already has retries, caps and per-date state. Airflow 3 backfills are scheduler-managed (airflow backfill create --dag-id … --from-date … --to-date …, with a max-active-runs cap and a reprocess policy; check current docs for flags). On Airflow 2.x, a triggered DAG with dynamic task mapping:

Engine: Airflow 2.4+ (TaskFlow); on Airflow 3 import from airflow.sdkLanguage: PythonExecutable: Illustrative — run_daily_for assumed
from datetime import date, datetime, timedelta
from airflow.decorators import dag, task          # Airflow 3: from airflow.sdk import dag, task

@dag(schedule=None, start_date=datetime(2026, 1, 1), catchup=False,
     max_active_tasks=8,                           # the throttle
     params={"start": "2026-01-01", "end": "2026-02-01"})
def backfill_playback():
    @task
    def list_dates(start: str, end: str) -> list[str]:
        s, e = date.fromisoformat(start), date.fromisoformat(end)
        return [(s + timedelta(days=i)).isoformat() for i in range((e - s).days + 1)]

    @task(retries=2)
    def run_one(dt: str):
        run_daily_for(dt)

    run_one.expand(dt=list_dates("{{ params.start }}", "{{ params.end }}"))

backfill_playback()

Trigger it with airflow dags trigger backfill_playback --conf '{"start":"2026-01-01","end":"2026-02-01"}'.

2026 Interview Note

Airflow 3 is current (3.0 GA April 2025; 3.3 at time of writing), so check current docs. What changed:

  • execution_date is gone; use logical_date, which can be None for manual or asset-triggered runs.
  • Datasets are now Assets.
  • Task-level sla and sla_miss_callback were removed; Deadline Alerts arrived in 3.1.
  • DAGs import from airflow.sdk.
  • Backfill is scheduler-managed.
  • catchup defaults to False.

Timeless: parameterize on the logical date, cap concurrency, and keep backfills from starving daily runs. Label any Airflow code you write in an interview with the version it targets.

Backfill correctness

  • Code version: new code restates history. Tag output with the version; announce it.
  • Historical shapes: handle old schemas, or backfill from a normalized bronze.
  • As-of dims: join the dim version valid at event time (event_ts >= valid_from AND event_ts < valid_to), not the current row.
  • Downstream events: 730 partitions must not fire 730 asset events. Suppress, publish once.
  • Deletes: rebuilding from raw can resurrect GDPR-deleted rows. Re-apply the deletion ledger.

Cost-aware backfills

Estimate first: run one representative week, measure vCPU-hours and bytes scanned, multiply. Backfill coarse rollups first if that is all the consumer needs.

“How do you backfill two years of data safely?”
30 sec

Only backfill a job that's already idempotent and parameterized by date. Run it as throttled, per-partition reruns on isolated compute. Write to a shadow table or branch, reconcile against what's there now, and publish once, without firing downstream triggers 730 times.

2 min

Scope and cost first. Run one week and extrapolate ×104. Freeze the code version and tag the output with it. Check the inputs still exist: raw retention, expired snapshots, historical schemas. Order: newest-first delivers value quickly; oldest-first is required for anything stateful. Throttle with the orchestrator's max-active-runs and pools so daily SLAs hold. Join dims as-of event time. Validate each partition against the current one (counts, control totals, a diff sample) before you swap. Communicate the restatement to consumers.

Deep dive

Stateful jobs (running balances, SCD2 builds, sessions that cross midnight) can't be parallelized per day. Run them in sequence, or recompute from a state checkpoint. Rebuilding from raw can resurrect GDPR-deleted rows, so re-apply deletions. Backfilled data must not re-trigger prod consumers or reverse-ETL syncs. Watch storage too: the old snapshots stay until expiry, so a two-year rewrite can briefly double the table's footprint.

Where to stop: cost estimate, isolation, validation before swap, downstream suppression. Only go into orchestrator flags if they ask.

7. File Format Internals — Parquet, ORC, Avro

Interview yield: "why is SELECT * slow?" and "why doesn't my filter prune?" Both are answered by the Parquet read path.

Parquet (columnar, analytic)

Structure
  • File
    • Magic bytes "PAR1"
    • Row Group 1
      • Column Chunk: col_a
        • Page 1 (data + RLE/dict encoding)
        • Page 2
        • ...
      • Column Chunk: col_b
      • ...
    • Row Group 2
    • ...
    • File Metadata (schema, row group locations, column stats)
    • Magic bytes "PAR1"
  • Row group: unit of parallelism and stats skipping; 128 MB default in parquet-java/Spark (parquet.block.size); pyarrow and DuckDB size by row count.
  • Page: unit of decompression (~1 MB in parquet-java). Dictionary encoding falls back to plain when the dictionary outgrows its limit.
  • Stats: min, max and null count per column chunk. The page index (ColumnIndex/OffsetIndex) adds per-page min/max. Bloom filters are optional and opt-in: parquet-java 1.12+ writes them when parquet.bloom.filter.enabled is set.
  • Encodings: PLAIN (values stored unencoded, though the page codec still compresses them), RLE_DICTIONARY (the usual default), DELTA_BINARY_PACKED (sorted ints and timestamps), DELTA_BYTE_ARRAY (strings with shared prefixes).
  • Codecs: Spark defaults to SNAPPY. ZSTD is typically smaller for a little more CPU and is a common 2026 choice. Use LZ4_RAW, not the legacy LZ4 codec, whose Hadoop framing is deprecated.

Read path: footer → skip row groups by min/max → dictionary filtering → page index skips pages → decode only projected columns. So SELECT * pays for every column, and a filter prunes only if data is sorted or clustered on it; random order makes every min/max span everything.

ORC (columnar, Hive-era)

Same idea (stripes ≈ row groups, richer indexes); common in Hive-heritage stacks. New lakehouse tables are overwhelmingly Parquet.

Avro (row-oriented, streaming)

Poor for analytics, strong in flight: Kafka plus a schema registry, because Avro resolves a writer schema against a reader schema.

Format choice

Analytic tables: Parquet under Iceberg/Delta. Kafka payloads: Avro or Protobuf with a registry. Row lookups: a row store (Part 16).

8. Partition Design Math

Partitioning is for pruning and lifecycle; clustering is for selectivity inside a partition. Most bad layouts use partitions for the second job.

The sizing rule (one rule, used everywhere in this chapter)

Partitions needn't be small; files must be 128 MB–1 GB. Daily works from ~1 GB/day to multiple TB/day if files are right-sized and clustered. Go hourly only for hour-bounded queries. Under ~1 TB total, prefer no partitioning plus clustering. Ten years daily is 3,650 partitions (fine); 10M user_id partitions of a few KB is a disaster.

Partition evolution

Iceberg changes the spec without rewriting data; old files keep the old spec (Hive would need a full rewrite).

Engine: Spark SQL + Iceberg SQL extensionsDialect: Spark SQL (Iceberg DDL)Executable: Yes — Iceberg Spark only
-- add a bucket field going forward
ALTER TABLE silver.events ADD PARTITION FIELD bucket(16, user_id);
-- or move from daily to hourly for new data
ALTER TABLE silver.events REPLACE PARTITION FIELD days(event_ts) WITH hours(event_ts);
-- Trino equivalent: ALTER TABLE ... SET PROPERTIES partitioning = ARRAY[...]

Partition pruning — what actually happens

Query (Iceberg, spec days(event_ts)): WHERE event_ts >= '2026-04-19' AND event_ts < '2026-04-20' AND country = 'US'.

The planner converts the range to day partitions, reads only their manifests, prunes files by the per-file min/max of country, and schedules tasks on the survivors.

What breaks pruning:

  • WHERE DATE(event_ts) = …: may not become a partition filter (engine/version-dependent); never prunes a Hive dt table. Use half-open ranges.
  • Type mismatch (dt = '20260419' against a DATE column); opaque UDFs.
  • BETWEEN on timestamps: inclusive, so it catches next-day midnight. The classic double-count.

Hidden partitioning (Iceberg's killer feature)

Users filter on event_ts, not a dt column, and pruning still happens. More in Part 07 §5.

Engine: Spark SQL + IcebergDialect: Spark SQLExecutable: Illustrative — column list elided
CREATE TABLE silver.events (event_id STRING, event_ts TIMESTAMP, user_id STRING, ...)
USING iceberg
PARTITIONED BY (days(event_ts), bucket(16, user_id));

SELECT COUNT(*) FROM silver.events
WHERE event_ts >= '2026-04-19' AND event_ts < '2026-04-20'   -- half-open: one day
  AND user_id = 'abc';                                         -- one of 16 buckets

Clustering (sort within partition)

Engine: Iceberg (Spark SQL) · Delta Lake · SnowflakeDialect: Mixed — one statement per engineExecutable: Yes — each line on its own engine
-- Iceberg: write new data sorted by user_id within each partition
ALTER TABLE silver.events WRITE ORDERED BY user_id;

-- Delta: z-order after writes (multi-column space-filling curve)
OPTIMIZE silver.events ZORDER BY (user_id, country);

-- Snowflake: clustering key (automatic maintenance)
ALTER TABLE silver.events CLUSTER BY (user_id);
2026 Interview Note

Timeless: partition coarsely for pruning and lifecycle, then cluster for selectivity. Version-specific:

  • Delta: Liquid Clustering (GA since Delta 3.2) replaces partitioning plus Z-order for new tables, and Databricks advises against partitioning tables under about 1 TB.
  • BigQuery: partition plus cluster, with a per-table partition cap.
  • Snowflake: no user-defined partitions, only micro-partitions and optional clustering keys.
  • Iceberg: sort orders, plus storage-partitioned joins in Spark 3.3+.

Check current docs for the limits.

Bucket partitioning

bucket(N, key) gives predictable file counts and one-bucket pruning on equality. Shuffle-free joins need a storage-partitioned join (Spark 3.3+, spark.sql.sources.v2.bucketing.enabled) with identical bucket specs; Iceberg buckets are not Hive/Spark buckets.

Engine: Spark SQL + IcebergDialect: Spark SQLExecutable: Illustrative — column list elided
CREATE TABLE silver.events ( ... )
USING iceberg
PARTITIONED BY (days(event_ts), bucket(32, user_id));

32 × 365 = 11,680 partitions a year. Worth it only at ≳4 GB/day, so each bucket-day still fills a 128 MB file.

9. Small Files and Compaction

Each file has a fixed open/footer/planning cost, and manifests grow with file count.

Causes: high write parallelism on low volume (200 tasks × 24 runs = 4,800 files/day); short streaming triggers (1-minute = ~525,000 commits/year); over-partitioning.

Prevention at write time

  • coalesce(N) avoids a shuffle but also shrinks the upstream stage to N tasks; use repartition after heavy work (Part 04 §10).
  • Iceberg write.distribution-mode=hash groups rows by partition before writing.
  • AQE's advisoryPartitionSizeInBytes (default 64 MB) shapes files only when a shuffle precedes the write.
  • Target file size: Iceberg write.target-file-size-bytes defaults to 512 MB.
Engine: PySpark + Iceberg (DataFrameWriterV2)Language: PythonExecutable: Yes
(df.writeTo("silver.events")
   .option("target-file-size-bytes", str(512 * 1024 * 1024))
   .append())

Compaction (post-write): the maintenance quartet

Maintenance is part of the pipeline, not housekeeping:

JobIcebergDeltaIncident when missing
Compact data filesrewrite_data_filesOPTIMIZE"Reads got 10× slower over three months"
Compact deletesrewrite_position_delete_filesOPTIMIZE / purge DVsMOR table reads slow down daily
Rewrite manifestsrewrite_manifestscheckpoints (automatic)Query planning takes longer than execution
Expire snapshots and orphansexpire_snapshots, remove_orphan_filesVACUUMStorage bill grows while table size stays flat
Engine: Spark SQL + Iceberg procedures · Delta LakeDialect: Spark SQLExecutable: Yes — prefix procedures with your catalog name
-- Iceberg: compact files under 100 MB toward ~512 MB
CALL cat.system.rewrite_data_files(
  table   => 'silver.events',
  options => map('target-file-size-bytes', '536870912',
                 'min-file-size-bytes',    '104857600'));
CALL cat.system.rewrite_manifests('silver.events');

-- Delta
OPTIMIZE silver.events;

Garbage collection (expiring snapshots)

Engine: Spark SQL + Iceberg procedures · Delta LakeDialect: Spark SQLExecutable: Yes — prefix procedures with your catalog name
-- Iceberg: expire snapshots older than 7 days, keep at least 5
CALL cat.system.expire_snapshots(
  table => 'silver.events',
  older_than => TIMESTAMP '2026-04-12 00:00:00',
  retain_last => 5);
CALL cat.system.remove_orphan_files(table => 'silver.events');

-- Delta (7 days is the default minimum retention)
VACUUM silver.events RETAIN 168 HOURS;

Don't use time travel as retention; for long-term audit use Iceberg tags or an immutable export. More in Part 07 §7.

Interviewer pushes back

You: “I'll partition by hour so queries are fast.”

Interviewer: “The table grows 20 GB a day, written hourly by a 200-task job. What does it look like after a year?”

Strong answer: “Do the math. That's 200 files × 24 hours = 4,800 files a day, about 1.75M files a year, averaging ~4 MB each. A one-day query opens 4,800 files instead of about 40 files of 512 MB, and planning cost grows with manifest size. Queries here are day-bounded, so I'd partition by day, set a hash distribution so each hourly write produces a handful of files, cluster by the hot filter column, and run daily compaction. I'd only go hourly if queries filter by hour and each hour holds hundreds of MB.”

Weak answer: “More partitions means more pruning.” Pruning helps only if the surviving files are worth opening.

10. CDC (Change Data Capture) Patterns

Full treatment in Part 15

This section is the batch-side primer. Part 15: CDC, Data Contracts & Transformation Engineering covers CDC end to end, including:

  • log-based vs polling
  • snapshots and bootstrap handoff
  • tombstones
  • per-key ordering by LSN
  • transaction boundaries
  • replication-slot risk
  • a full Postgres-to-lakehouse design

Go there for depth.

Full snapshot (baseline)

Engine: PySpark JDBC → IcebergLanguage: PythonExecutable: Illustrative — connection details elided
# JDBC to Iceberg (full reload)
(spark.read
    .format("jdbc")
    .option("url", "jdbc:postgresql://...")
    .option("dbtable", "public.orders")
    .option("partitionColumn", "order_id")
    .option("numPartitions", 20)
    .option("lowerBound", "1")
    .option("upperBound", "100000000")
    .load()
    .write
    .format("iceberg")
    .mode("overwrite")
    .saveAsTable("bronze.orders"))

Captures hard deletes, no CDC state; expensive, one run of lag. Twenty parallel JDBC connections are not one consistent snapshot unless you read a replica or snapshot.

Incremental snapshot (changed-rows-only)

Engine: PySpark JDBC → Delta LakeLanguage: PythonExecutable: Illustrative — options elided
hwm = get_high_watermark("bronze.orders", "updated_at")
(spark.read
    .format("jdbc")
    .option("dbtable", f"(SELECT * FROM orders WHERE updated_at > '{hwm}') AS t")
    ...
    .write
    .format("delta")
    .mode("append")
    .saveAsTable("bronze.orders_changes"))

# Upsert into bronze.orders using MERGE

Cheaper; misses hard deletes and inherits every HWM trap from §5.

Log-based CDC (Debezium, Fivetran, AWS DMS)

Reads the change log (Postgres WAL via logical decoding, MySQL row binlog, SQL Server CDC tables, Oracle redo via LogMiner), one event per row change:

Engine: Debezium (Postgres connector), JSON converterDialect: JSONExecutable: Illustrative — trimmed envelope
{
  "before": {"order_id": 42, "status": "paid",    "total": 100},
  "after":  {"order_id": 42, "status": "shipped", "total": 100},
  "op": "u",
  "ts_ms": 1713567890000,
  "source": {"schema": "public", "table": "orders",
             "lsn": 3187640, "ts_ms": 1713567889950}
}

Ops: c, u, d, r (snapshot read), t (truncate). A delete is followed by a tombstone (key, null value) by default, so skip nulls. Top-level ts_ms is when Debezium processed the event; order by source.lsn (or binlog file + position).

Seconds of lag, hard deletes, full history. It is not zero-touch: no query load, but it needs wal_level=logical plus a replication slot (Postgres), binlog_format=ROW (MySQL) or per-table CDC (SQL Server), and a stalled consumer makes the source retain WAL until the primary's disk fills.

Upserting CDC into a lakehouse

Four rules: (1) dedupe each micro-batch to one row per key, or the first key changed twice in 30 s raises a multi-match error; (2) join on the key only, since an OR in ON defeats the equi-join; (3) guard every branch on the source log position, since foreachBatch is at-least-once; (4) map envelope fields to target columns explicitly (UpdateAll on an envelope fails).

Engine: Spark 3.5/4.x Structured Streaming + Delta LakeLanguage: PythonExecutable: Illustrative — envelope_schema, BOOTSTRAP and a target with src_lsn assumed
from pyspark.sql import functions as F, Window
from delta.tables import DeltaTable

changes = (spark.readStream.format("kafka")
    .option("kafka.bootstrap.servers", BOOTSTRAP)
    .option("subscribe", "cdc.public.orders")
    .load()
    .where(F.col("value").isNotNull())                        # skip tombstones
    .select(F.from_json(F.col("value").cast("string"), envelope_schema).alias("e"))
    .where(F.col("e.op").isin("c", "u", "d", "r"))           # truncates handled separately
    .select(
        F.col("e.op").alias("op"),
        F.coalesce("e.after.order_id", "e.before.order_id").alias("order_id"),
        F.col("e.after.status").alias("status"),
        F.col("e.after.total").alias("total"),
        F.col("e.source.lsn").alias("src_lsn")))               # ordering key, not ts_ms

def merge_batch(batch_df, batch_id):
    w = Window.partitionBy("order_id").orderBy(F.col("src_lsn").desc())
    latest = batch_df.withColumn("rn", F.row_number().over(w)).where("rn = 1").drop("rn")
    cols = {c: f"s.{c}" for c in ("order_id", "status", "total", "src_lsn")}
    (DeltaTable.forName(spark, "silver.orders").alias("t")
        .merge(latest.alias("s"), "t.order_id = s.order_id")  # key-only equi-join
        .whenMatchedDelete(condition="s.op = 'd' AND s.src_lsn > t.src_lsn")
        .whenMatchedUpdate(condition="s.op != 'd' AND s.src_lsn > t.src_lsn", set=cols)
        .whenNotMatchedInsert(condition="s.op != 'd'", values=cols)
        .execute())

(changes.writeStream
    .foreachBatch(merge_batch)
    .option("checkpointLocation", "s3://…/ckpt/orders_cdc/")
    .trigger(processingTime="30 seconds")
    .start())

The LSN guard on updates and deletes makes replays no-ops. One gap: a hard delete takes its LSN with it, so a replayed older change could resurrect the row. Strict pipelines soft-delete (is_deleted + src_lsn) and purge later; see Part 15. Managed options (Lakeflow AUTO CDC / APPLY CHANGES, Snowflake Streams) handle this sequencing.

CDC + SCD2

Each update closes the current row and opens a new one; each delete closes it. Worked design: Part 08: SCD Type 2 ingestion from Kafka CDC.

11. Data Quality in Batch Pipelines

Checks are the AUDIT step of WAP, not a later dashboard. This section covers which ones block; tooling (Great Expectations, Soda, reconciliation, SLOs) is in Part 12.

Taxonomy of checks

Check typeExamplePolicy
Schemacolumns exist with expected typesBlock
UniquenessPK is uniqueBlock
Row count and volume> 0; within ±20% of the 7-day average; ±5% of upstreamBlock on zero or >50% moves; warn on drift
Control totalssum(amount) matches sourceBlock for finance tables
ReferentialFKs resolveWarn, with an unresolved-rate threshold
Null rate and range< 1% null; values physically plausibleWarn
Freshnessmax(event_ts) within the SLOAlert (check on a schedule, not only when the job runs)

Block on what makes the number wrong; warn on what makes it suspicious. Blocking checks that fire weekly get disabled, which is worse than none.

dbt tests (declarative)

Engine: dbt 1.8+ with dbt_utils (dbt v2 shipped Sept 2026, so check current docs)Language: YAMLExecutable: Yes — needs the dbt_utils package
# models/silver/playback_sessions.yml
version: 2
models:
  - name: playback_sessions
    columns:
      - name: session_id
        data_tests: [unique, not_null]       # `tests:` before dbt 1.8
      - name: user_id
        data_tests:
          - not_null
          - relationships: {to: ref('dim_user'), field: user_id}
      - name: watch_ms
        data_tests:
          - dbt_utils.accepted_range: {min_value: 0, max_value: 86400000}
    data_tests:
      - dbt_utils.recency: {datepart: hour, field: max_end_ts, interval: 2}

Designing "what to check"

Every PK not null and unique; every FK resolves; every measure in a plausible range; every timestamp in window (catches 1970-01-01); every enum in its set; every table's volume against its own history.

12. Orchestration Patterns for Batch

The simple scheduled DAG

Asset-based orchestration (Dagster, Airflow Assets)

Declare tables and their producers; the orchestrator derives the graph. Dagster adds partitioned assets (natural backfills) and asset checks.

Engine: Dagster 1.xLanguage: PythonExecutable: Illustrative — helpers undefined
from dagster import asset

@asset
def bronze_events(context):
    return pull_from_kafka(context)

@asset
def silver_events(bronze_events):
    return transform(bronze_events)

@asset
def gold_daily_plays(silver_events):
    return aggregate(silver_events)

Sensor-based triggering

Trigger on arrival, not the clock. Default poke mode holds a worker slot for the whole wait; use deferrable=True or mode="reschedule".

Engine: Airflow 2.x/3.x + Amazon providerLanguage: PythonExecutable: Yes — provider version dependent
from airflow.providers.amazon.aws.sensors.s3 import S3KeySensor

wait = S3KeySensor(
    task_id="wait_for_upstream",
    bucket_key="s3://upstream/events/{{ ds }}/_SUCCESS",
    timeout=4 * 60 * 60,
    poke_interval=300,
    deferrable=True,          # frees the worker slot while waiting
)

Data-aware scheduling (Datasets in Airflow 2.4+, Assets in Airflow 3) runs the consumer when the producer publishes. Emit the event after the audit, never after the raw write.

Backfill separation

Keep backfills from starving daily runs: Airflow 3 runs them through the scheduler with their own max-active-runs cap; otherwise use a separate DAG or pool. Dedicated compute, lower priority, no 3 a.m. pages for backfill failures.

SLA management

Every table should have three SLOs, exposed as metrics with an on-call owner (see Part 12 §3):

  • Freshness: updated within 1 hour of upstream sealing.
  • Completeness: at least 99% of expected rows.
  • Correctness: blocking checks green.
Engine: Airflow 2.x onlyLanguage: PythonExecutable: Yes — Airflow 2.x only (removed in Airflow 3.0)
# Airflow SLA miss callback
def sla_miss_callback(dag, task_list, blocking_task_list, slas, blocking_tis):
    notify_on_call(...)

default_args = {
    "sla": timedelta(hours=1),
    "sla_miss_callback": sla_miss_callback,
}

On Airflow 3 use Deadline Alerts (3.1+; check current docs). More portable: measure freshness at the table (now() − max(committed_at)) with an external monitor. Late data is the incident; the task is only where you notice it.

13. Dependency Graphs and Critical Path Analysis

At scale a pipeline is a DAG of hundreds of tasks. When does it finish, and which node's slip delays everything?

Modeling the graph

Nodes are tasks with durations; edges are "B waits for A". The longest path is the critical path: its tasks have zero slack, everything else has some.

Why this matters for interviews

Common prompt: "finishes at 6am, business wants 4am." Weak: "optimize the slowest job." Strong: shorten the critical path by speeding up tasks on it, removing false dependencies, starting on data readiness instead of fixed cron, or splitting long tasks. Then recompute, because a different path often becomes critical.

The Airflow / Dagster reality

Take durations from orchestrator metadata; longest path via topological sort plus DP over an adjacency list, O(V+E):

Engine: Python 3 (stdlib)Language: PythonExecutable: Yes
from collections import defaultdict, deque

def critical_path(nodes, edges, duration):
    succ, indeg = defaultdict(list), {n: 0 for n in nodes}
    for a, b in edges:
        succ[a].append(b); indeg[b] += 1
    finish = {n: duration[n] for n in nodes}          # earliest finish time
    q = deque(n for n in nodes if indeg[n] == 0)
    while q:
        n = q.popleft()
        for b in succ[n]:
            finish[b] = max(finish[b], finish[n] + duration[b])
            indeg[b] -= 1
            if indeg[b] == 0:
                q.append(b)
    return max(finish.values())

14. The Batch Cost Model

Estimate from first principles: vCPU-hours × rate, a platform multiplier, bytes stored, bytes crossing a boundary. Prices below are illustrative round numbers for the arithmetic, not vendor quotes; say so in the interview. Vendor levers: Part 11.

The four costs (plus the one people forget)

  1. Compute: vCPU-hours × rate. Illustrative rate: $0.05 per vCPU-hour, all-in.
  2. Platform premium: the managed-service surcharge (Databricks DBUs, EMR fees, warehouse credits). Illustrative: +50% on compute.
  3. Storage: illustrative $0.02/GB-month hot; archive tiers are several times cheaper but add retrieval fees and minimum durations. Request charges bite at millions of small files.
  4. Shuffle: local disk, so it costs time; usually smaller than input after projection and filtering.
  5. Data transfer: illustrative $0.02/GB inter-region, $0.09/GB to the internet, same-region typically free. The one people forget.

Worked estimate — 10 TB daily batch

10 TB in, 3-way join, 2 TB out, ~3 TB shuffle. ~1.5 h on 400 vCPUs (~1.9 GB/s aggregate scan, unremarkable).

TermArithmeticIllustrative $
Compute400 vCPU × 1.5 h × $0.05$30
Platform premium+50%$15
Shuffle3 TB on local disk≈ $0 (runtime)
Output storage2,000 GB × $0.02, per month, per day retained$40 per month per day kept → ~$1,200/month after 30 days
Write output cross-region2,000 GB × $0.02$40
Read input cross-region10,000 GB × $0.02$200
Ship input to the internet10,000 GB × $0.09$900

Defensible answer: "About $45 a run same-region. Compute in another region adds ~$200 a run to read the input, more than 4× the compute. Retained output becomes the biggest line within a month." Egress here ranges from ~1× to ~20× compute depending on which boundary the bytes cross, so name the boundary. That is why "move compute to another region" is so often wrong, and why retention is a cost decision.

15. Parallelism Math and the Skew Tax

Speedup is capped by the sequential fraction (Amdahl) and by the largest partition. The second bites in data work.

The skew tax, quantified

1 TB as 100 × 10 GB finishes in one worker's 10 GB time. Make one piece 500 GB and the rest ~5 GB: the stage takes one worker's 500 GB time, 50× slower for the same work. Detect it with max vs median partition size or task duration (10× is skew).

Mitigations (details in Part 04)

  • AQE skew join is on by default with AQE (Spark 3.2+). It splits sort-merge join partitions larger than both skewedPartitionFactor × median and skewedPartitionThresholdInBytes. It doesn't fix aggregations.
  • Salting: add CAST(FLOOR(RAND() * 10) AS INT) as a salt on the big side, and replicate the other side across salts 0–9 with explode(sequence(0, 9)).
  • Broadcast the small side.
  • Isolate hot keys into a separate path.

Full treatment: Part 04 §7.

16. Checkpoint and Restart Semantics

Fail at hour 4 of 6: resume or restart? Decide before the failure.

Three restart strategies

  1. Idempotent restart from zero: simple; wastes compute per failure.
  2. Task-level: resume at the failed task; each task's output commits atomically.
  3. Intra-task: persist a cursor; hard to get right, worth it past ~2 h.

The atomic-write discipline

Stage, validate, then commit atomically (table-format snapshot commit or metadata pointer swap). An S3/GCS "rename" is copy plus delete and not atomic. Hive-style tables need _SUCCESS markers and readers that respect them.

The "restart at noon" drill

A common prompt: "Yesterday's job failed at 11pm. You rerun it at noon today. What happens downstream?" A senior answer lists:

  1. Which tables get rewritten.
  2. Which downstream jobs already ran on missing or partial input. They must be re-triggered, and if they append, deduped.
  3. Which caches and extracts are now stale.
  4. Which SLAs tripped.
  5. Who you tell, and what you tell them.

If you can't answer this for your pipelines, you don't own them operationally.

17. Partition Key Decisions by Domain

Sizing rule: §8. Pattern: partition on the date the business reports by, cluster on the entity, never partition on a skewed or high-cardinality id.

TablePartitionCluster / sortCommon wrong pick
App/web eventsevent_dateuser_id, event_nameuser_id: cardinality explosion
Ordersorder_datecustomer_idorder_id: one row per partition
Payments / ledgerposting_date (the close runs on it)account_idmerchant_id: power-law skew
CDC change logchange_datesource_table, PKsource_table: one giant partition
IoT telemetry (very high volume)ingest_date (+ hour only if queries are hour-bounded)device_id bucketraw device_id
Catalog (~100K rows)nonetitle_idgenre: rarely prunes
Daily snapshotssnapshot_dateskusku: millions of partitions
ML featuresfeature_dateentity_id bucketraw entity_id

For the interview framing, see Part 08: partition by user_id or by date?.

18. NULL Semantics — Examples by Domain

Every nullable column's contract should say which NULL it means. Mechanics (joins, aggregates, windows): Part 01 §12. The batch-relevant cases:

MeaningExampleHandling
Unknowncustomer_dobLeave NULL, and document it
Pendingshipped_ts in an accumulating snapshotNULL is the signal; test with IS NULL
Not scored / unassignedfraud_score, segment_idEnums: sentinel 'UNASSIGNED'. Numerics: keep NULL plus a reason column (score_status='declined'); a -1 sentinel silently corrupts AVG and MIN
Open interval endvalid_toNULL or 9999-12-31, whichever makes range joins simple
Zero vs NULLrefund_amount0 when you know there was no refund; NULL only when you don't know

The aggregation trap

SUM(col) / COUNT(*) counts NULL rows in the denominator; AVG(col) doesn't. A common "numbers are off" ticket.

The NULL-vs-zero revenue bug

Missing or NULL "no sales" rows make MoM show NULL instead of "down 100%". Build a dense calendar (the sparse-months question in Part 09's SQL bank), then COALESCE to 0.

L5 Interview CardBatch Processing
Must know
  • Idempotency contract: output = f(logical_date, pinned input), written with a scoped overwrite or a version-guarded MERGE.
  • Engine-specific overwrite: Iceberg overwritePartitions() / dynamic INSERT OVERWRITE, Delta replaceWhere. A static overwrite can replace the whole table.
  • MERGE: dedupe the source to one row per key, add a deterministic tiebreaker, and a pruning predicate. Cost = files touched.
  • HWM traps: late commits, boundary ties, client clock skew, HWM stored apart from the data. Overlap + MERGE, not overlap + append.
  • Write-audit-publish: consumers never see unaudited data; asset events fire after the audit.
  • Layout: partition for pruning and lifecycle, cluster for selectivity, right-size files (128 MB–1 GB); maintenance is part of the pipeline.
  • Log-based CDC isn't zero-touch; order by source LSN, not ts_ms (Part 15).
Must be able to explain
  1. Why is INSERT INTO … SELECT not idempotent, and what are the three fixes?
  2. How do you know yesterday's data is complete?
  3. Why can a MERGE that touches 1% of rows rewrite most of the table?
Must be able to draw

The WAP batch pipeline:

SOURCE → BRONZE → VALIDATE → TRANSFORM
  → WRITE(stage) → AUDIT → PUBLISH → SERVE

Mark where a failure stops, and what a rerun replaces.

Must be able to code
  • Dedupe to the latest row per key with ROW_NUMBER() and a tiebreaker.
  • A MERGE with a version guard and a content-hash guard.
  • A critical-path longest-path DP over a task DAG.
Must be able to debug
  • A rerun doubled yesterday's revenue: an append plus an unpinned input. Roll back, re-trigger consumers, add a row-delta gate.
  • Reads 10× slower after three months: small files and delete files piling up. Run the maintenance quartet.
Numbers that matter
  • Target file size: 128 MB–1 GB. Daily partitions are fine from ~1 GB/day to TBs/day.
  • 200 tasks × 24 hourly writes = 4,800 files a day, about 1.75M a year.
  • Skew: one 500 GB partition among 5 GB ones is ~50× wall-clock.
  • Cross-region reads can cost several times the compute (method: bytes × $/GB). Quote real prices only from current docs.
  • Two-year backfill = 730 partitions. Estimate from one week × 104.
Classic traps
  • BETWEEN on timestamps double-counts midnight.
  • "Partition by user_id for fast lookups."
  • "Reruns are safe because Spark is fault-tolerant."
30-second answer

How do you design a batch pipeline that is safe to rerun? Parameterize every job on a logical date and a pinned input snapshot. Make the write a scoped replace: partition overwrite, or a MERGE on the business key with a version guard. Stage, audit, then publish atomically, so a failed run leaves prod untouched and a rerun replaces the same slice with the same content.

2-minute answer

I start with the completeness contract (marker, reconciliation or grace window), so a run never publishes a partial day. Inside the job: dedupe by key, conform, join dims as-of event time, and ban now() and generated ids. The write is engine-explicit (Iceberg overwritePartitions(), Delta replaceWhere, or a MERGE with a deterministic tiebreaker), and it goes to a WAP branch or staging table. The audit checks PK uniqueness, control totals, and the row count against the previous run of the same date, which catches the classic doubled rerun. Publishing commits atomically, then emits one asset event. Side effects run once per logical date. A run-twice diff test in CI proves idempotency, and the audit log records the input snapshot, so a rerun can reproduce the original or deliberately pick up a corrected input. Backfills are the same job, throttled on isolated compute, with downstream triggers suppressed.

Deep-dive follow-up

Your upstream re-sends corrected rows for the last 30 days, with new updated_at values but mostly identical content. Walk through what your MERGE, your change-feed consumers and your cost look like, and what you would change in the contract.

Staff+ follow-up

Forty teams each own dozens of batch pipelines with inconsistent rerun behavior. What platform guarantees (WAP by default, a logical-date contract, restatement announcements, a backfill service) would you standardize, and how would you migrate without a freeze?

Versions referenced Kafka 4.x (KRaft-only; 4.3 current), Flink 2.x (2.3 current) with code on 1.20 LTS APIs, Spark Structured Streaming 3.5 / 4.x, Amazon Kinesis and Amazon Data Firehose
Primary references Kafka docs · Flink docs · Spark Structured Streaming guide · Kinesis Data Streams docs
Known implementation differences Flink keeps a watermark per source split and combines them continuously, while Spark keeps one watermark per query and advances it between micro-batches; Spark's Kafka sink is at-least-once, while Flink's KafkaSink and Kafka Streams can write transactionally.

The interviewer is testing whether you can reason about time and failure, not whether you know an API. Can you say why a window result is or is not final? What happens to an event that arrives late, out of order, or twice? Where exactly does "exactly-once" stop? Flink code here uses the 1.x DataStream API (1.20 LTS) unless labelled. The concepts carry to 2.x unchanged.

1. Unbounded Data — What Actually Changes

An unbounded source has four properties that break batch intuitions:

  1. No sealed state. You never "have all the data"; every result is "as of now".
  2. Arbitrary lateness. Events arrive minutes to days after they happened (mobile reconnects, buffering clients).
  3. Out-of-order arrival. 10:05 can arrive after 10:07 because it took a different route.
  4. Continuous state. Windows, joins and aggregations hold state that grows until you expire it.

Consequence 1: "correct" becomes "correct as of watermark W"

A batch SELECT SUM(watch_ms) GROUP BY dt has one answer. The streaming equivalent keeps updating as late data arrives. At any moment it means "the sum of everything observed up to watermark W, with events older than W treated as closed."

Consequence 2: computations have four dimensions, not one

Beam's influential model:

  • What are you computing? (the aggregation function)
  • Where in event time? (the windowing scheme)
  • When in processing time? (the trigger — when to emit a result)
  • How do refinements relate? (accumulating, discarding, accumulating-with-retractions)

Consequence 3: state is load-bearing

A batch job's state is transient. A streaming job's state is the product: lose it and you lose correctness. Checkpointing it, bounding it (TTL) and restoring it make up most of streaming engineering.

Consequence 4: time is a first-class citizen

In batch, time is a parameter. In streaming it drives the dataflow: watermarks advance, triggers fire, windows close, state expires.

2. The Three Times (Event, Processing, Ingestion)

  • Event time (ET) — when the event happened, stamped by the producer (client, sensor, database transaction). Business metrics are defined on it: "watch hours on 2026-04-18" means event_time falls on that date.
  • Ingestion time (IT) — when the event was received by the messaging system (e.g., the time Kafka assigned on append).
  • Processing time (PT) — when the stream processor is evaluating the event.

Relationships:

  • Causally ET ≤ IT ≤ PT — but the recorded timestamps violate it routinely (client clock skew; Kafka CreateTime is set by the producer, LogAppendTime by the broker). Validate and clamp future event times: one device with its clock set to 2031 can drag a max-based watermark years ahead and make everything else "late".
  • IT - ET is the producer delay — how long the event took to reach the log.
  • PT - IT is the processing lag — how far behind the consumer is.
  • PT - ET is the end-to-end latency consumers experience.

None of these is what a watermark bounds. A watermark bounds out-of-orderness; see Choosing B.

Distribution of ET → IT lag

Heavily right-skewed. An example distribution for a mobile app (hypothetical; measure your own):

  • p50: milliseconds to seconds.
  • p99: tens of seconds to minutes.
  • p99.9: hours (mobile reconnects, app-in-background).
  • p99.99: days (offline clients syncing weeks later).

Lesson: tune to the distribution, not the average. Measure your own tail before choosing a tolerance. Mobile datasets commonly have a long tail of minutes to days.

When does processing time ever make sense?

For system-health metrics ("events/sec arriving now"), wall-clock behaviour (alarms, heartbeats) and stateless transforms. For any business metric, use event time.

3. Watermarks — Math and Mechanics

A watermark is an assertion: "no more events with event_time ≤ W are expected." Operators use it to decide when a window is complete and to fire event-time timers. This is not the batch "high watermark" of Part 02, which is a bookmark of what you have already loaded.

Perfect vs heuristic watermarks

  • Perfect watermark: actually correct. Only achievable when the source has complete knowledge of its input (e.g., ingestion-time ordered logs, a finite set of files, a DB log with commit order). Rare.
  • Heuristic watermark: a guess, usually max(event_time seen) − B. Wrong sometimes; that is what late-data handling is for.

Bounded out-of-orderness watermark

The common practical watermark is computed per source split (per Kafka partition): W(t) = max(event_time seen before t) − B, where B is the bounded out-of-orderness. Flink actually emits max − B − 1 ms, so an event exactly B behind is still on time.

Example with B = 5 seconds:

  • Stream sees events {ET: 10:00:00, ET: 10:00:02, ET: 10:00:01, ET: 10:00:04, ET: 10:00:03, ...}.
  • After ET: 10:00:04 is observed, watermark ≈ 10:00:04 - 5s = 09:59:59.
  • ET: 10:00:03 arrives next: 10:00:03 > 09:59:59, so it is on time.
  • After ET: 10:00:10 is observed, watermark ≈ 10:00:05. Events with ET < 10:00:05 are now late.

Choosing B (bounded out-of-orderness)

B bounds out-of-orderness: how far an arriving event trails the newest event already seen, max_event_time_seen − event_time, measured per partition. It does not bound end-to-end delay (processing_time − event_time). The difference shows up exactly when it hurts. During a two-hour backlog replay, PT − ET is two hours for every event, yet out-of-orderness stays at seconds and nothing is late. Size B from delay and you hold every window open for hours after an outage.

  1. Measure out-of-orderness per partition (below).
  2. Compute p50 / p99 / p99.9.
  3. Pick B at the tail you are willing to route to late handling.

Math: if B = p99 of out-of-orderness, roughly 1% of events arrive behind the watermark. They are dropped only if their window has already fired (window end + allowed lateness ≤ watermark).

Higher BLower B
Late eventsFewerMore (correctness ↓)
Emission latencyHigherLower
Active stateLarger (windows open longer)Smaller

Orders of magnitude (measure yours): web/mobile analytics, seconds to a few minutes; well-clocked sensors, about a second; file-drop sources, hours.

Measuring out-of-orderness (not delay)

Track two metrics and never confuse them. Delay (ingest_ts − event_ts) drives freshness SLOs. Out-of-orderness (running max(event_ts) − event_ts in partition/offset order) sizes B. You can compute both offline from landed bronze data that kept the Kafka partition and offset:

Engine: Spark SQL / DataFrame (batch)Language: PythonExecutable: Yes — Spark 3.1+ only
from pyspark.sql import Window, functions as F

# bronze = landed Kafka records that kept partition, offset and ingest time
w = (Window.partitionBy("kafka_partition")
           .orderBy("kafka_offset")
           .rowsBetween(Window.unboundedPreceding, Window.currentRow))

m = (bronze
     .withColumn("delay_ms",                      # freshness, NOT the watermark bound
                 F.unix_millis("ingest_ts") - F.unix_millis("event_ts"))
     .withColumn("ooo_ms",                        # out-of-orderness: sizes B
                 F.unix_millis(F.max("event_ts").over(w)) - F.unix_millis("event_ts")))

m.select(F.percentile_approx("ooo_ms",   [0.5, 0.99, 0.999]).alias("ooo_p50_p99_p999"),
         F.percentile_approx("delay_ms", [0.5, 0.99, 0.999]).alias("delay_p50_p99_p999")
        ).show(truncate=False)

In the running job, alert on watermark lag (wall clock − current watermark) and on the late-record rate. Flink's window operator exposes numLateRecordsDropped.

Watermark propagation in a dataflow graph

Each operator tracks its own watermark. With several inputs it takes the minimum:

The practical consequence: one slow or empty input stalls the whole pipeline. Watch per-operator watermarks in the Flink UI. Fixes:

  • Idleness (withIdleness): a split with no data for the timeout is excluded from the min. Idleness is not progress. The watermark still does not advance without data. Idleness only stops a silent split from holding the others back.
