  • Use watermark alignment (WatermarkStrategy.withWatermarkAlignment(group, maxDrift), Flink 1.15+) so fast sources/splits pause instead of racing ahead and bloating state.
  • Heartbeat events from producers, when the business can supply them.
Engine: Flink DataStream APILanguage: JavaExecutable: Yes
WatermarkStrategy<Event> strategy = WatermarkStrategy
    .<Event>forBoundedOutOfOrderness(Duration.ofSeconds(5))
    .withIdleness(Duration.ofMinutes(1))
    .withTimestampAssigner((ev, ts) -> ev.eventTime);

Watermarks across Kafka partitions

FLIP-27 sources (KafkaSource) keep one watermark per partition and take the min, so everything above applies per partition. Avoid a partitioning key that leaves partitions empty for long stretches.

The "punctuated" variant

Instead of heuristics, the producer emits explicit marker records: "I am at event time T; nothing earlier will come from me." Flink supports this via a WatermarkGenerator that calls output.emitWatermark(...) directly inside onEvent when it sees a marker (leaving onPeriodicEmit empty). It fits sources with explicit sequencing, such as a CDC stream.

“What is a watermark?”
30 sec

A watermark is the stream's event-time clock. It asserts that no more events with timestamp ≤ W are expected. Operators use it to close windows and fire event-time timers. In practice it is a heuristic: max event time seen minus an out-of-orderness bound. Events behind it are "late". They are re-fired under allowed lateness, sent to a side output, or dropped.

2 min

It is generated per source split as max ET − B and emitted periodically. It propagates as the min across inputs, so one slow or empty partition holds back the whole job. Use idleness detection for silent splits and watermark alignment for fast ones. Size B from observed out-of-orderness (maxET − ET), not end-to-end delay. The trade-off: a larger B means fewer late events but more latency and more state. Late data has three outlets: allowedLateness (re-fire, needs an upsert sink), a side output for reconciliation, or a drop. In Spark, withWatermark also bounds state for aggregations and stream-stream joins.

Deep dive

Perfect vs heuristic watermarks (the Dataflow model). Periodic vs punctuated generators: a punctuated one emits inside onEvent. Watermarks are not restored from checkpoints. After a restore they re-advance as data replays. Event-time results are deterministic on replay; processing-time triggers are not. Spark keeps one global watermark per query (min across inputs by default; spark.sql.streaming.multipleWatermarkPolicy=max to change it) and advances it between micro-batches. Failure modes: idle partitions, a clock-skewed future timestamp that pushes W ahead (clamp it), and backfilling through a live job.

Where to stop: finish the 2-minute answer, then stop unless they ask about replay, Spark vs Flink, or "what goes wrong in production?"

4. Windows — Types, State, and Trade-offs

A window groups events by time (or session). Each window maintains state (the aggregating values) and emits a result when it's ready.

2026 Interview Note

Flink 1.x vs 2.x APIs. The Flink code in this part uses the 1.x DataStream API; 1.20 is the 1.x LTS line. Flink 2.0 (March 2025) removed or changed several of those APIs. Time.minutes(...) became Duration.ofMinutes(...). SourceFunction/addSource and SinkFunction/addSink gave way to the Source and Sink V2 APIs (fromSource, sinkTo). open(Configuration) became open(OpenContext). TwoPhaseCommitSinkFunction gave way to Sink V2 committers. Blocks that depend on the old APIs are labelled "Yes — Flink 1.x (1.20 LTS) only". The concepts are unchanged: windows, watermarks, keyed state, checkpoints. In an interview, say so and name the API you would use on 2.x.

Tumbling window

Fixed size, non-overlapping. Each event belongs to exactly one window.

State: O(1) per key per active window. Simplest.

Engine: Spark Structured Streaming (PySpark)Language: PythonExecutable: Yes
# PySpark Structured Streaming — 1-minute tumbling window
(events
    .withWatermark("event_ts", "5 seconds")
    .groupBy(F.window("event_ts", "1 minute"), "title_id")
    .agg(F.sum("watch_ms").alias("watch_ms")))
Engine: Flink DataStream APILanguage: JavaExecutable: Yes — Flink 1.x (1.20 LTS) only
// Flink
events
    .keyBy(e -> e.titleId)
    .window(TumblingEventTimeWindows.of(Time.minutes(1)))
    .aggregate(new SumAggregator());

Sliding (hopping) window

Fixed size, slides forward by a step smaller than the size. Each event belongs to size/slide windows: with size 10 min and slide 1 min, every event lands in 10 overlapping windows. State: O(size/slide) × keys. That gets expensive quickly.

Use when: you need rolling metrics ("watch hours in the trailing 10 minutes, updated every minute").

Tip: sliding windows can often be emulated by a tumbling window at the fine granularity + downstream rollup, which is cheaper.

Session window

Dynamic size, closes when there's a gap of inactivity longer than the session timeout.

State: O(events per active session) with apply/process, because events are buffered. With aggregate/reduce it is O(1) per session, because they fold incrementally.

Engine: Flink DataStream APILanguage: JavaExecutable: Yes — Flink 1.x (1.20 LTS) only
events
    .keyBy(e -> e.userId)
    .window(EventTimeSessionWindows.withGap(Time.minutes(30)))
    .aggregate(new SessionBuilder());

Challenge: a single "always-active" user (a bot, a scraper, a stuck client) holds a session open forever, preventing emission. Solutions:

  • Maximum session length (cap at e.g. 4 hours).
  • Bot filtering at ingestion.
  • Late "ejection" if max latency exceeded.

Global window

One window per key for the whole stream; a custom trigger decides when to emit. It is rarely right unless you want something like a counter that never resets.

Custom windows (e.g., calendar-aligned)

Windows aligned to calendar boundaries ("this day in the user's local timezone", "this business week"). In Flink, write a WindowAssigner whose assignWindows maps each event to [local midnight, next local midnight) in the user's zone, plus the default trigger and serializer. Test DST days, which are 23 or 25 hours long.

Window state size

For N keys: tumbling O(N); sliding O(N × size/slide); session O(active sessions), multiplied by events per session when buffering. High cardinality + long windows + fine slides make state explode. Mitigations:

  • RocksDB backend (disk-backed state, not memory-bound).
  • Pre-aggregate (use aggregate not apply — maintains incremental state, not buffered events).
  • TTL on state (Flink's StateTtlConfig).

5. Triggers and Emission Policy

A trigger decides when a window's current result is emitted. Default: on watermark (once per window, when watermark passes end-of-window). But you can do much more.

When to use custom triggers

Speculative early results (latency over accuracy), every N events, every 10 s of processing time for live dashboards, or on a data condition ("count exceeds threshold").

Example: early + on-watermark + late

Built-ins cover the common cases. ContinuousEventTimeTrigger and ContinuousProcessingTimeTrigger fire periodically. CountTrigger fires every N elements. PurgingTrigger wraps any of them to turn accumulating into discarding. For "speculative every 10 s, then final on watermark, then once per late event", write your own Trigger<Object, TimeWindow>. You cannot extend EventTimeTrigger, because its constructor is private:

Engine: Flink DataStream APILanguage: JavaExecutable: Yes — Flink 1.19+ (incl. 2.x) only
public class EarlyFiringTrigger extends Trigger<Object, TimeWindow> {
    private final long intervalMs;
    public EarlyFiringTrigger(long intervalMs) { this.intervalMs = intervalMs; }

    @Override
    public TriggerResult onElement(Object el, long ts, TimeWindow w, TriggerContext ctx) {
        if (w.maxTimestamp() <= ctx.getCurrentWatermark()) {
            return TriggerResult.FIRE;                  // late, within allowedLateness: re-fire
        }
        ctx.registerEventTimeTimer(w.maxTimestamp());   // final, on-watermark firing
        long now = ctx.getCurrentProcessingTime();
        ctx.registerProcessingTimeTimer(now - (now % intervalMs) + intervalMs);  // next early firing
        return TriggerResult.CONTINUE;
    }

    @Override
    public TriggerResult onProcessingTime(long time, TimeWindow w, TriggerContext ctx) {
        return w.maxTimestamp() <= ctx.getCurrentWatermark()
            ? TriggerResult.CONTINUE                    // already final: stop speculating
            : TriggerResult.FIRE;                       // speculative result, state kept
    }

    @Override
    public TriggerResult onEventTime(long time, TimeWindow w, TriggerContext ctx) {
        return time == w.maxTimestamp() ? TriggerResult.FIRE : TriggerResult.CONTINUE;
    }

    @Override
    public void clear(TimeWindow w, TriggerContext ctx) {
        ctx.deleteEventTimeTimer(w.maxTimestamp());
        // a leftover processing-time timer fires on a purged window and emits nothing
    }
}

// usage (imports omitted)
events.keyBy(e -> e.titleId)
      .window(TumblingEventTimeWindows.of(Duration.ofMinutes(1)))
      .trigger(new EarlyFiringTrigger(10_000))
      .aggregate(new ViewerCountAgg());

Other engines expose the same idea differently. Spark has no per-window triggers; its output modes play that role. append emits once, when the watermark closes the window. update emits changed rows every micro-batch. complete emits the whole result table. Flink SQL has experimental early/late-fire options (table.exec.emit.early-fire.*) and otherwise emits a changelog.

Accumulation mode

When you emit multiple times for the same window, what do the downstream consumers see?

  • Accumulating: each emission is the latest running total (count=42 replaces count=37). Needs an upsert sink keyed by (key, window_start), e.g. a compacted topic.
  • Discarding: each emission carries only the events since the last one. Downstream must sum emissions. Smaller messages, but harder downstream.
  • Accumulating + retracting: each emission retracts the previous value and adds the new one. Most expressive and most expensive; it suits changelog consumers.

6. Late Data Strategies

An event is "late" if it arrives after its window's watermark has passed.

Strategy 1: Drop (default in Spark)

Late events are silently discarded. Fast, simple, incorrect for audit-sensitive workloads.

Spark nuance: data within the watermark delay is guaranteed to be aggregated; data beyond it may be dropped (not guaranteed) — don't rely on either for audit counts.

Strategy 2: Allowed lateness (extend window life)

Hold the window open past watermark by some duration; late events that arrive within this grace period update the window and trigger re-emission.

Engine: Flink DataStream APILanguage: JavaExecutable: Yes — Flink 1.x (1.20 LTS) only
events
    .keyBy(e -> e.userId)
    .window(TumblingEventTimeWindows.of(Time.minutes(1)))
    .allowedLateness(Time.minutes(10))     // 10 extra minutes
    .aggregate(new Counter());

State cost: windows held for window_size + allowed_lateness. For a 1-minute window with 10-minute lateness, state is held 11 minutes per window.

Downstream must handle re-emissions — sink must be upsert-capable.

Strategy 3: Side output (recommended)

Route late events to a separate "late" stream for reconciliation downstream.

Engine: Flink DataStream APILanguage: JavaExecutable: Yes — Flink 1.x (1.20 LTS) only
OutputTag<Event> lateTag = new OutputTag<>("late"){};

SingleOutputStreamOperator<Result> result = events
    .keyBy(e -> e.userId)
    .window(TumblingEventTimeWindows.of(Time.minutes(1)))
    .sideOutputLateData(lateTag)
    .aggregate(new Counter());

DataStream<Event> lateEvents = result.getSideOutput(lateTag);
lateEvents.addSink(new LateEventSink());  // write to separate topic/table

A batch job then re-processes the affected windows from the late table. That is the streaming-plus-audit pattern in §13.

Strategy 4: Retractions

Emit a retraction for the previous result and a new result reflecting the late event. Downstream must support retractions (a log of changes, not a snapshot).

Supported natively in Flink Table API with Retract mode. Upsert sinks handle retractions by deletion+insertion.

How to measure lateness, and why "delay" is the wrong number, is covered in §3.

Drill · Streaming

An hourly dashboard reads a Flink job's output table. The row for window 02:00–03:00 was first written at 03:01. It changed again at 03:40, 05:10 and 09:25, each time with a higher count. Finance wants to know when the number is final.

STOP. Answer before revealing.

Reveal the diagnosis
  1. Observe Updates arrive hours after the window closed and only ever increase the count. Line up each write time with the job's restart history.
  2. Hypothesize (a) Allowed lateness is set to hours, and each late event re-fires the window in accumulating mode. (b) A processing-time or continuous trigger keeps firing. (c) The job restarted and replayed from a checkpoint into an append sink, so re-emissions look like changes. (d) A backfill or bulk client sync is pushing old events through the live job.
  3. Measure Read the configured allowedLateness and trigger. For the records behind each update, compare event time with arrival time. Check numLateRecordsDropped, the side-output volume, and the checkpoint/restart timeline.
  4. Isolate Updates that line up with restarts point to replay into a non-idempotent sink. Updates that follow late arrivals point to the lateness policy. Rising counts with no late arrivals point to a trigger.
  5. Fix Decide the finality contract explicitly. Allowed lateness should be sized to a business need (say 10 minutes), with a side output beyond it. Write to an upsert sink keyed by (key, window_start). Publish a status column: provisional until watermark ≥ window end + lateness, then final. A daily batch reconciles the long tail.
  6. Prevent Alert on any write to a window after it is marked final. Document the lateness SLA next to the metric definition, so "final" means one thing everywhere.

7. Delivery Semantics Proved

"Exactly-once" is often said without precision. Exactly-once is a property of a pipeline, not of a product. Name the boundaries or don't say it.

Definitions

Define them by effect (a row written, a counter incremented, a record published), not by delivery. At-most-once: each message's effect happens 0 or 1 times. At-least-once: 1 or more. Exactly-once: exactly 1.

The impossibility footnote

With crashes and timeouts, delivery cannot be exactly-once: a request that got no response may or may not have arrived. The effect can be, if retries are paired with deduplication or idempotent writes. That is what "effectively exactly-once" means.

The three conditions (the third comes in two forms)

Effectively-once needs all three:

  1. Replayable source. After a failure the system re-reads from a precisely recorded position: Kafka offsets, Kinesis sequence numbers, a table snapshot. A fire-and-forget HTTP push source is not replayable.
  2. Deterministic or checkpointed processing. Re-processing the same input produces the same output. Alternatively, any non-determinism (random IDs, wall-clock reads, lookups against a mutable table) is captured in checkpointed state before it affects output, so replay reuses it instead of recomputing it.
  3. A sink that is either:
    • transactional: output is committed atomically with the source position, tied to the checkpoint or micro-batch. Examples: Flink two-phase-commit sinks, Kafka transactions, a Delta/Iceberg commit keyed by batch id. Or
    • idempotent: writing a record twice has the same effect as writing it once. This means a keyed upsert or overwrite: MERGE or ON CONFLICT on a deterministic key, or overwriting a deterministic partition.

Miss any condition and you have at-least-once, or worse. Pick one form of the sink, not both. An idempotent sink under at-least-once delivery is exactly-once in effect, with no distributed transaction. Part 13 unifies delivery semantics and ordering across the whole stack: clients, brokers and databases.

Spark Structured Streaming's exactly-once

Mechanism: a micro-batch's planned offsets go to the offsets/ log before it runs; after the sink commits, its id goes to commits/. On restart Spark re-runs the planned-but-uncommitted batch with the same offsets, which is harmless only if the query is deterministic and the sink tolerates the re-run:

  • File / table sinks: write files, then commit idempotently keyed by batchId (_spark_metadata log for the plain file sink; Delta txnAppId/txnVersion; Iceberg snapshot metadata) — so a re-executed batch is not committed twice.
  • Kafka sink: at-least-once only — Spark does not use Kafka transactions; a re-executed micro-batch can re-publish. Dedupe downstream (key + idempotent consumer) or use Flink / Kafka Streams for transactional output.
  • foreachBatch: at-least-once unless you make the write idempotent yourself. Use a MERGE on a business key, or Delta's txnAppId/txnVersion write options with the batchId.

Where it breaks: non-deterministic queries (rand(), current_timestamp(), a mutable lookup table), non-idempotent sinks (HTTP POST, a keyless JDBC insert), Kafka as a sink (at-least-once by design), and a lost checkpoint directory.

Engine: Spark Structured Streaming + IcebergLanguage: PythonExecutable: Yes — Spark 3.1+ with the Iceberg runtime only
(stream
    .writeStream
    .format("iceberg")
    .option("checkpointLocation", "s3://ckpt/events/")
    .trigger(processingTime="30 seconds")
    .toTable("lake.silver.events"))

Flink's exactly-once via 2PC and checkpoints

Flink uses asynchronous barrier snapshotting (a Chandy-Lamport variant) for checkpoints. When barriers are aligned it records no in-flight channel state. Transactional sinks add two-phase commit on top.

Barriers are injected at source tasks, not by the JobManager into the stream. Every task, not only the sinks, acknowledges its snapshot to the CheckpointCoordinator (JobManager). When all tasks have acked, checkpoint C is complete and notifyCheckpointComplete lets sinks commit.

Aligned vs unaligned: aligned barriers block any input whose barrier arrived first. That is clean, but slow under backpressure. Unaligned checkpoints (Flink 1.11+) let barriers overtake in-flight records and persist those records in the snapshot. They are less sensitive to backpressure but produce bigger snapshots. Tuning is in §12.

Two-phase commit at sinks: on the barrier, the sink pre-commits: it flushes into an open transaction or staging files and records the pending transaction in its checkpointed state. On checkpoint-complete it commits. On restore it commits pending transactions from the restored checkpoint and aborts anything newer. The consequence: read_committed readers see output once per checkpoint, so your checkpoint interval is now a latency floor. The Kafka side of this is in §15.

What EO does NOT guarantee

  • Ordering across keys or partitions: EO is about effects, not order.
  • No revisions: updates to already-committed results still reach downstream as new records.
  • Cross-system atomicity: the guarantee covers one job plus the systems its sources and sinks can commit with. An HTTP call, an email, or a second database outside the checkpoint is not covered.
  • Business-level dedup: if the producer sent an event twice, EO faithfully processes both copies. Dedupe on a business key.

Idempotent sink as an alternative to 2PC

This is often simpler than 2PC: at-least-once delivery into a sink that is idempotent by key. It comes in two shapes: insert-if-absent for events, overwrite for aggregates.

Engine: PostgreSQLDialect: PostgreSQL (prepared statement)Executable: Yes — PostgreSQL 9.5+ only
-- events: insert once
INSERT INTO fact_event (event_id, user_id, watch_ms)
VALUES ($1, $2, $3)
ON CONFLICT (event_id) DO NOTHING;

-- window aggregates: overwrite with the recomputed value
INSERT INTO agg_watch_1m (title_id, window_start, watch_ms)
VALUES ($1, $2, $3)
ON CONFLICT (title_id, window_start)
DO UPDATE SET watch_ms = EXCLUDED.watch_ms;

There is no coordination with the checkpoint, and output is visible immediately. Requirements: a deterministic key (an event id from the producer, or (key, window_start)). For the overwrite form, the value must be deterministic too, so replay recomputes the same total. It does not work on sinks that cannot enforce uniqueness, such as plain append-only files or most HTTP APIs without an idempotency key.

When exactly-once is worth its cost

Transactional exactly-once costs latency, because output is visible once per checkpoint. It also costs operational surface: transaction timeouts, fencing, stalled read_committed readers. Pay for it where a duplicate is both invisible downstream and expensive.

SituationTransactional EO?Why
Stateful aggregates (counts, sums) into an append-only sinkYesA replayed increment cannot be recognised downstream
Upsert by a deterministic key, e.g. (key, window_start)Usually noReplays overwrite with the same value; at-least-once is enough
Money, billing, inventoryYes, plus business-key dedupCorrectness beats latency; EO does not catch upstream duplicates
External side effects (email, SMS, payment API)Not available from the engineIdempotency keys at the receiver, or a "sent" ledger checked before calling
Low-latency alerts and dashboardsOften noPer-checkpoint visibility adds latency; at-least-once + dedup key is faster
Upstream already duplicates eventsNot by itselfEO processes duplicates faithfully; dedupe on a business key
Non-deterministic logicNot until fixedReplay produces different output; make it deterministic or checkpoint the result
Interviewer pushes back

You: “We get exactly-once end to end: Flink checkpoints plus a transactional sink.”

Interviewer: “Your final sink is a partner's HTTP API. What happens on a restart?”

Strong answer: “Then it isn't end to end. Flink replays from the last completed checkpoint, and every POST made after that checkpoint is sent again. An HTTP call cannot join the checkpoint's transaction. So I stop claiming exactly-once at that boundary and make the effect idempotent. Each request carries a deterministic idempotency key, the event_id or a hash of key and window, and the API dedupes on it. If it can't, I keep a sent-ledger keyed by that id and check it before calling. If neither is possible, I state the guarantee plainly: at-least-once, with duplicates bounded by the records in one checkpoint interval, plus a reconciliation job against the partner's records.”

Weak answer: “Flink's two-phase commit covers it.” Or wrapping the call in a custom two-phase-commit sink that has no way to roll back a POST.

8. Flink Internals — Dataflow, Barriers, State

Architecture

  • JobManager (process): the coordinator. It hosts a Dispatcher, a ResourceManager and one JobMaster per job.
  • Dispatcher: receives job submissions and starts a JobMaster per job.
  • JobMaster: owns one job's ExecutionGraph, schedules its tasks and runs its CheckpointCoordinator.
  • ResourceManager: acquires TaskManagers and slots (Kubernetes, YARN, standalone).
  • TaskManagers: workers; each offers N slots, and each slot runs subtasks.

Tasks, subtasks, and chains

A job is a DAG of operators; each runs as parallelism subtasks in TaskManager slots. Operators connected 1:1 with no shuffle are chained into one thread, which means no serialization and no network hop. keyBy and rebalance break the chain.

Engine: Flink DataStream APILanguage: JavaExecutable: Illustrative — adapt to your dialect
DataStream<Event> events = env.fromSource(kafkaSource, wm, "kafka"); // FLIP-27 source
DataStream<Event> filtered = events.filter(ev -> ev.valid);    // chained with source
KeyedStream<Event, String> keyed = filtered.keyBy(ev -> ev.userId);  // NOT chained (keyBy shuffles)
DataStream<Result> windowed = keyed.window(...).aggregate(...); // new chain

Keyed state vs operator state

  • Keyed state: scoped to the current key after keyBy (ValueState, ListState, MapState, ReducingState, AggregatingState). This is how Flink scales stateful work.
  • Operator state: per subtask, not per key. Sources use it for offsets; broadcast state is a variant.

Keyed state is accessed through a handle registered once per task (getRuntimeContext().getState(descriptor) in open()), optionally with a TTL. Flink scopes every read and write to the current key automatically, so the code never looks up the key itself.

State backends

  • HashMapStateBackend: in-JVM-memory. Fastest. State bounded by heap. Asynchronous full snapshots (no incremental; GC pressure grows with state). Use for small-to-moderate state.
  • EmbeddedRocksDBStateBackend: on-disk key-value store (RocksDB). State bounded by local disk. Asynchronous and incremental checkpoints. Use for state > a few GB.

RocksDB is an LSM tree. Writes go to an in-memory memtable, which flushes to immutable SST files, and background compaction merges levels. Every access serialises the key and value. That is why it is slower than heap state, and also why it is not bounded by heap.

Incremental checkpoints

With RocksDB, Flink checkpoints only the SSTables that changed since the last checkpoint. New SSTables uploaded; unchanged ones referenced by manifest. Reduces checkpoint time from "full state" to "delta state."

Savepoints vs checkpoints

  • Checkpoints: system-owned, periodic, optimized for fast recovery. May be incremental.
  • Savepoints: user-triggered, versioned, portable across Flink versions (with caveats). Use for explicit restarts (deploys, cluster migrations, schema changes).
Engine: Flink CLILanguage: bashExecutable: Yes
flink savepoint <job_id> s3://savepoints/myjob/

flink run -s s3://savepoints/myjob/savepoint-xxx <new-jar>.jar

State migration

When you change the shape of state (add a field, change types), you need a migration. Flink supports:

  • Schema evolution: automatic for POJO and Avro state types (add/remove fields); Kryo-serialized state cannot evolve — avoid it for long-lived state.
  • State Processor API: read a savepoint as a DataStream (DataSet in older releases), transform it (change types, re-key, bootstrap), write a new savepoint.
2026 Interview Note

Flink 2.x deltas. Flink 2.0 (March 2025; 2.3 is current at time of writing) removed the DataSet API, the Scala APIs and SourceFunction/SinkFunction. It added disaggregated state: the ForSt backend keeps primary state on remote storage such as S3. Configuration moves from environment setters to config keys (state.backend.type, execution.checkpointing.*). The timeless parts are keyed state, barriers, snapshots and savepoints. Backend names, setter APIs and state-on-object-store are version-specific.

9. Kafka Internals — ISR, Controllers, Exactly-Once

Topic, partition, offset

A topic is a named append-only log split into partitions. Each partition is an ordered sequence of records with increasing offsets. Producers pick the partition (hash of the key, or explicitly); consumers read sequentially and track offsets.

Read parallelism = number of partitions. In a consumer group (classic or KIP-848 protocol) each partition goes to at most one consumer; consumers beyond the partition count sit idle. Separate groups read independently, each with its own offsets. (Share groups (KIP-932, production-ready in Kafka 4.2) let many consumers share a partition with per-record acknowledgement, at the cost of ordering.)

“What ordering guarantees does Kafka give you?”
30 sec

Order within a partition only. Records with the same key go to the same partition (hash of the key mod the partition count), so you get per-key order. There is no order across partitions or topics. Global order needs a single partition, which caps you at one consumer.

2 min

Four things break per-key order. (1) Retries without idempotence: with several requests in flight, a failed batch retried after a later one lands behind it. Idempotence (the default since Kafka 3.0) fixes this for up to 5 in-flight requests. (2) Partition count changes: adding partitions remaps keys, so a key's old records sit in one partition and its new ones in another. (3) Multiple producers writing the same key: the log orders by arrival at the leader, not by event time. (4) Consumer parallelism within a partition: handing records to a thread pool or to async calls reorders them unless you re-partition by key inside the consumer. Rebalances and replays can also redeliver older records after newer ones.

Deep dive

The durable fix is to stop depending on arrival order. Carry a version or event timestamp and apply "highest version wins" at the sink. In Flink, keyBy preserves per-key order only between two operators, and a parallel sink can reorder again. Kinesis has the same model per shard. The cross-system view of ordering is in Part 13.

Where to stop: "per partition, per key via hashing, and here is what breaks it". Go deeper only if they probe partition expansion or consumer threading.

Replication

Each partition has N replicas (typically 3):

  • Leader: handles all writes and, by default, reads (consumers may fetch from a nearby follower since Kafka 2.4 — KIP-392).
  • Followers: fetch from the leader.
  • ISR (in-sync replicas): replicas caught up within replica.lag.time.max.ms. The partition's high watermark is the offset replicated to the whole ISR, and consumers see only records below it.

Durability, precisely:

  • acks=0: fire-and-forget.
  • acks=1: wait for the leader to append (page cache, not fsync). The record is lost if the leader dies before followers copy it.
  • acks=all (producer default since Kafka 3.0, with enable.idempotence=true): wait for every replica currently in the ISR. Durable only with min.insync.replicas >= 2 and unclean leader election disabled; otherwise the ISR can shrink to the leader alone.
  • "Has the record" means in memory on several brokers, not fsynced. Durability comes from replicas in separate failure domains (racks, AZs), so a correlated power loss can still lose acknowledged writes.

Controller and leader election (KRaft)

The active controller is the Raft leader of the KRaft controller quorum (Kafka 4.x is KRaft-only; ZooKeeper-elected controllers exist only in ≤3.9 clusters). The quorum is either dedicated controller nodes or, in small clusters, combined broker+controller nodes. Cluster metadata (topics, partition leaders, ISRs) lives in a replicated metadata log that every broker replays.

On broker failure:

  1. Controller detects failure (missed broker heartbeats / session timeout to the KRaft quorum).
  2. It removes the failed broker from the ISR of the affected partitions.
  3. Controller elects a new leader: the first replica in the partition's assignment order that is alive and in the ISR (Kafka 4.x adds Eligible Leader Replicas, KIP-966).
  4. Controller publishes the change to brokers via the metadata log; producers/consumers learn it by refreshing metadata after a NOT_LEADER_OR_FOLLOWER error.

With unclean election disabled (the default), the new leader has every committed record. unclean.leader.election.enable=true lets an out-of-sync replica lead: you buy availability with data loss.

KRaft and the ZooKeeper legacy

KRaft (production-ready since 3.3) runs cluster metadata in an internal Raft log; Kafka 4.0 (2025) removed ZooKeeper entirely — ZK→KRaft migration must be done on 3.x before upgrading. General coordination and fencing: Part 13.

2026 Interview Note

Kafka 4.x. If you learned Kafka from pre-2025 material, update three answers. (1) "One broker is the controller, elected through ZooKeeper" becomes "a Raft quorum of controllers, with metadata as a log". (2) "Rebalances stop the world" becomes "the KIP-848 protocol (GA in 4.0, opt-in via group.protocol=consumer) makes them incremental and broker-driven". (3) "Consumers ≤ partitions" is still true for consumer groups but not for share groups (4.2). The timeless parts are partitions, ISR, offsets and per-partition order. At time of writing the current release line is 4.3; check current docs.

Kafka exactly-once

Idempotent producers, transactions, read_committed and sendOffsetsToTransaction are covered in one place: §15.

Consumer rebalance protocol

When members join, leave or time out, partitions move:

  • Eager (classic protocol, legacy assignors): every consumer revokes everything, then the group re-syncs. Stop-the-world; minutes for large groups.
  • Cooperative sticky (classic protocol, CooperativeStickyAssignor, Kafka 2.4+): only the partitions that move are revoked, over two rounds, and everyone else keeps processing.
  • Next-gen consumer protocol (KIP-848, GA in 4.0; opt-in via group.protocol=consumer): the broker computes assignments incrementally, with no group-wide sync barrier. partition.assignment.strategy is ignored in favour of the server-side group.remote.assignor.

Static membership (group.instance.id): a consumer that restarts within session.timeout.ms gets its partitions back without a rebalance. This is the fix for rolling deploys.

Rebalance storms: a poll loop slower than max.poll.interval.ms (big batches × slow processing) gets the member evicted. Another member redoes its uncommitted work: duplicates plus churn. Lower max.poll.records or move work off the poll thread, and commit in onPartitionsRevoked.

Trap: Flink's KafkaSource does not use group rebalancing. Its split enumerator assigns partitions. group.id only receives offset commits, which happen on checkpoint, so lag dashboards trail by up to one checkpoint interval.

Log compaction

For changelog topics keyed by entity ID, compaction keeps only the latest record per key; a tombstone (null value) deletes the key after a grace period.

A compacted topic is a durable key-value store you can read as a stream: materialised CDC state, Kafka Streams state changelogs, configuration.

10. Streaming Joins

Stream-stream window join

Join two streams within a time window: match pairs (a, b) where a.timestamp and b.timestamp fall within a common window and the join key matches.

Engine: Flink DataStream APILanguage: JavaExecutable: Yes — Flink 1.x (1.20 LTS) only
clicks.join(impressions)
    .where(c -> c.userId).equalTo(i -> i.userId)
    .window(TumblingEventTimeWindows.of(Time.minutes(5)))
    .apply(new JoinFn());

State: O(|clicks| + |impressions|) within the window. Grows linearly with window size and rate.

Stream-stream interval join

Match event pairs within a relative time interval: for each a, find b where a.ts - X ≤ b.ts ≤ a.ts + Y.

Engine: Flink DataStream APILanguage: JavaExecutable: Yes — Flink 1.x (1.20 LTS) only
clicks.keyBy(c -> c.userId)
    .intervalJoin(impressions.keyBy(i -> i.userId))
    .between(Time.minutes(-1), Time.minutes(5))
    .process(new IntervalJoinFn());

Used for causal analysis (impressions preceding clicks) where window alignment would be wrong.

Stream-table (temporal) join

Join events against a slowly changing table, such as a dimension or a compacted topic. Implementation patterns:

  • Broadcast state: broadcast the table updates to all parallel instances of the join operator. Each instance keeps the table in local state. Great when the table is small (< 1 GB).
  • Keyed state + async lookup: each event does an async DB lookup, keeping a cache in keyed state.
  • Versioned table joins (Flink Table API): FOR SYSTEM_TIME AS OF syntax.
Engine: Flink SQLDialect: Flink SQL (event-time temporal join)Executable: Yes — Flink SQL only
-- Flink SQL: temporal join
SELECT o.*, c.country, c.subscription_tier
FROM orders o
JOIN user_dim FOR SYSTEM_TIME AS OF o.event_ts AS c
  ON o.user_id = c.user_id;

The engine maintains the history of user_dim; the join picks the version of each user that was current at event_ts. That requires a versioned table (primary key plus its own watermark, typically a changelog/CDC source) and an event-time attribute on o.event_ts.

  • Temporal vs lookup join: FOR SYSTEM_TIME AS OF o.proc_time against a JDBC/HBase-style table is a lookup join. It queries the external table's current value at processing time and is not replayable. AS OF o.event_ts against a versioned table is the deterministic, event-time join.
  • Regular (unwindowed) joins in Flink SQL keep both sides in state forever unless you set state TTL (table.exec.state.ttl). This is a common cause of "state grew for weeks, then checkpoints failed".

Stream enrichment via async I/O

When the dimension is too large for broadcast state but must be looked up per event:

Engine: Flink DataStream APILanguage: JavaExecutable: Yes
AsyncDataStream.unorderedWait(
    events,
    new AsyncDatabaseLookup(),
    30, TimeUnit.SECONDS,     // timeout
    1000                       // capacity (max concurrent lookups)
).map(enriched -> process(enriched));

Concurrent async lookups keep the pipeline fed while external systems respond. Critical: use unorderedWait if order doesn't matter (higher throughput); orderedWait otherwise.

11. State Management at Scale

State TTL

Per-state configurable time-to-live. Flink's StateTtlConfig:

Engine: Flink DataStream APILanguage: JavaExecutable: Yes — Flink 1.x (1.20 LTS) only
StateTtlConfig ttlConfig = StateTtlConfig
    .newBuilder(Time.hours(24))
    .setUpdateType(StateTtlConfig.UpdateType.OnCreateAndWrite)
    .setStateVisibility(StateTtlConfig.StateVisibility.NeverReturnExpired)
    .cleanupInRocksdbCompactFilter(1000)
    .build();

Cleanup strategies:

  • In-access: expired state is removed on read (cheap but delays cleanup).
  • Full-snapshot: expired entries are filtered out of full snapshots only — local state is not shrunk; not effective with incremental RocksDB checkpoints.
  • RocksDB compaction filter: cleanup during RocksDB's background compaction. Preferred for large state.

Bounded session windows via custom expiration

Session windows without an explicit maximum length can grow without bound. The hand-rolled fix is a KeyedProcessFunction. It keeps a session summary in ValueState and registers an event-time timer at lastEventTs + gap. On each event it closes and re-opens the session if the gap was exceeded or the duration passed the maximum. When the timer fires it emits the summary and clears state. Two details trip people up: delete the superseded timer when you register a new one, and handle out-of-order events by comparing against the session's min/max times rather than assuming arrival order.

State partitioning evolution

Changing the key you partition on means migrating state. Take a savepoint, re-key the state with the State Processor API, write a new savepoint, and start the new job from it. The alternative is to start fresh and rebuild history from a replay. Both are painful, so plan keys up front.

State size budgeting

state_size = num_keys × bytes_per_key_state × num_windows_active_per_key. Example: 100M users × 1 KB (a few counters, last-event-ts) × 1 active session = 100 GB.

RocksDB backend + local SSD + incremental checkpoints handle this fine. HashMap backend could only hold this spread across many TaskManagers, and GC pauses plus full (non-incremental) snapshots make it impractical.

At 1 TB (1B users) RocksDB on fast SSDs still works. Beyond that, split the job or move state to an external store with async lookup.

12. Backpressure and Flow Control

Backpressure: a slow stage forces faster stages upstream to slow down. Without it you get unbounded buffers, OOM, or data loss.

How Flink signals backpressure

Flink uses credit-based flow control. Each receiving task advertises its free buffers (credit), and senders send only against credit. A slow operator stops granting credit, so upstream blocks, and the block propagates back to the source. A Kafka source then simply stops fetching.

The chain: producer → broker → consumer → sink

Inside Flink, backpressure is end to end. Kafka breaks the chain on purpose: it is the shock absorber between producers and consumers. A slow consumer does not slow the producer down; it builds lag.

StageWhat pushes backSymptom at saturationFirst knob
Producerbuffer.memory fills; send() blocks up to max.block.msRising send latency, timeouts, lost events if the app fires and forgetslinger.ms/batch.size, compression, more partitions
BrokerClient quotas throttle; request queues fill; disk or network saturation shrinks the ISRThrottle-time metrics, produce latency, under-replicated partitionsQuotas, more brokers, partition reassignment
ConsumerNothing upstream; it just falls behindLag grows; past retention, data is deleted unreadMore partitions + consumers, max.poll.records, Spark maxOffsetsPerTrigger
SinkRate limits, warehouse/JDBC throttling, slow commitsBackpressure inside the job; checkpoint duration climbsBatching, an async sink with rate limiting, idempotent bulk writes

The point to make in an interview: consumer lag beyond topic retention is silent data loss. Retention deletes segments by time or size whether or not anyone has read them. The consumer's next fetch asks for an offset that no longer exists, and auto.offset.reset quietly moves it. Alert on lag in time (seconds behind) against retention, not only in record counts. Part 13 walks the full chain, including how it collapses.

Diagnosing backpressure

The Flink UI shows backpressure per task (OK / LOW / HIGH). A backpressured task is a victim, not the culprit. Walk downstream to the first operator that is not backpressured but has high busyTimeMsPerSecond — that one is the bottleneck.

Metrics to check:

  • backPressuredTimeMsPerSecond, busyTimeMsPerSecond, idleTimeMsPerSecond: where each task spends its time.
  • inPoolUsage / outPoolUsage (and outputQueueLength): buffer saturation on each side of a network edge.
  • numRecordsInPerSecond vs numRecordsOutPerSecond: a disparity means buffering or filtering.

Fixing backpressure

  • Increase downstream parallelism for the slow operator. It helps only if the load is spread across keys.
  • Optimize the slow operator: the usual culprits are Python UDFs, synchronous external calls and state-backend misuse.
  • Use async I/O for external lookups.
  • Spread hot keys: salt the key and aggregate in two stages, the same principle as Spark skew salting.

Backpressure and checkpoints

Aligned checkpoints need barriers to reach every operator. Under backpressure, barriers queue behind records. Snapshots stall, checkpoints time out, the job restarts and reprocesses, and the whole cycle repeats.

Unaligned checkpoints (Flink 1.11+) let barriers overtake in-flight records and store those records as channel state.

Engine: Flink DataStream APILanguage: JavaExecutable: Yes — Flink 1.x (1.20 LTS) only
env.getCheckpointConfig().enableUnalignedCheckpoints();

Prefer aligned checkpoints with execution.checkpointing.aligned-checkpoint-timeout (switch to unaligned only when alignment stalls) plus buffer debloating (Flink 1.14+); unaligned checkpoints persist in-flight data, enlarging snapshots and restores. Then fix the bottleneck; checkpoint tuning only treats the symptom.

13. Lambda vs Kappa Revisited

Lambda architecture

Lambda has a batch layer (complete, slow), a speed layer (fresh, approximate) and a serving layer that merges them. The problem is two codebases for one business rule. Drift is inevitable, and every wrong number starts with "which layer produced this?"

Kappa architecture

Kappa uses one streaming codebase, and reprocessing means replaying the log through the same code. Its real cost is replay. You need the history: long Kafka retention, tiered storage (KIP-405), or a lakehouse table you can stream from. You also need enough throughput to replay days of data without starving the live job. The usual approach is to run a second copy of the job and cut over.

The pragmatic middle: streaming + batch audit

This is the common production pattern. The streaming job serves "hot" answers and routes late events to a side output (§6). A scheduled batch job over bronze produces "certified" results for the affected windows. The gap between hot and certified is monitored, and a large gap is an incident. The streaming code is the product. The batch path is a reference check, not a second implementation of every rule. For the "is Lambda dead?" framing, see Part 08.

14. Streaming Pipeline Example End-to-End

A full example: video playback sessionization.

Data flow

Flink sessionization job

Engine: Flink DataStream API + Kafka and Iceberg connectorsLanguage: JavaExecutable: Illustrative — adapt to your dialect
// Flink 1.20 DataStream API. KafkaSource / KafkaSink are the FLIP-27 / Sink V2 connectors.
DataStream<PlaybackEvent> events = env.fromSource(
    KafkaSource.<PlaybackEvent>builder()
        .setBootstrapServers("kafka:9092")
        .setTopics("playback.events")
        .setGroupId("sessionizer")      // offsets committed on checkpoint, for monitoring only
        .setStartingOffsets(OffsetsInitializer.committedOffsets(OffsetResetStrategy.LATEST))
        .setValueOnlyDeserializer(new PlaybackEventDeserializer())
        .build(),
    WatermarkStrategy.<PlaybackEvent>forBoundedOutOfOrderness(Duration.ofSeconds(30))
        .withIdleness(Duration.ofMinutes(1))
        .withTimestampAssigner((ev, ts) -> ev.eventTime),
    "kafka-playback");

DataStream<PlaybackEvent> validated = events.filter(PlaybackEvent::isValid).name("validate");

// Sessionize by sessionId with a 30-minute event-time gap
OutputTag<PlaybackEvent> lateTag = new OutputTag<>("late-events") {};
SingleOutputStreamOperator<PlaybackSession> sessions = validated
    .keyBy(ev -> ev.sessionId)
    .window(EventTimeSessionWindows.withGap(Time.minutes(30)))  // 2.x: Duration.ofMinutes(30)
    .allowedLateness(Time.minutes(15))
    .sideOutputLateData(lateTag)
    .aggregate(new SessionAggregator(), new SessionEmitter())    // O(1) state per session
    .name("sessionize");

// Sink 1: Kafka, transactional. read_committed consumers see output once per checkpoint.
Properties txProps = new Properties();
txProps.setProperty("transaction.timeout.ms", "900000"); // > checkpoint interval + recovery, <= broker max
sessions.sinkTo(KafkaSink.<PlaybackSession>builder()
        .setBootstrapServers("kafka:9092")
        .setRecordSerializer(new SessionSerializer())
        .setDeliveryGuarantee(DeliveryGuarantee.EXACTLY_ONCE)
        .setTransactionalIdPrefix("session-sink-")         // stable across restarts
        .setKafkaProducerConfig(txProps)
        .build()).name("sink-sessions");

// Sink 2: Iceberg. The Flink sink writes RowData and commits on checkpoint.
DataStream<RowData> sessionRows = sessions.map(SessionRows::toRowData);
FlinkSink.forRowData(sessionRows)
    .tableLoader(TableLoader.fromCatalog(catalogLoader,
        TableIdentifier.of("silver", "fact_playback_session")))
    .writeParallelism(8)
    .distributionMode(DistributionMode.HASH)  // cluster by table partition: fewer small files
    .append();

// Sink 3: late events to a reconciliation topic. At-least-once; the consumer dedupes by event_id.
sessions.getSideOutput(lateTag).sinkTo(KafkaSink.<PlaybackEvent>builder()
        .setBootstrapServers("kafka:9092")
        .setRecordSerializer(new EventSerializer("playback.events.late"))
        .setDeliveryGuarantee(DeliveryGuarantee.AT_LEAST_ONCE)
        .build()).name("sink-late");

// Checkpointing: 1.x setters; 2.x prefers execution.checkpointing.* and state.backend.* config keys
env.enableCheckpointing(60_000, CheckpointingMode.EXACTLY_ONCE);
env.getCheckpointConfig().setMinPauseBetweenCheckpoints(30_000);
env.setStateBackend(new EmbeddedRocksDBStateBackend(true));   // incremental
env.getCheckpointConfig().setCheckpointStorage("s3://checkpoints/sessionizer/");
env.execute("playback-sessionizer");

SessionAggregator: incremental state

Engine: Flink DataStream APILanguage: JavaExecutable: Yes
public class SessionAggregator
    implements AggregateFunction<PlaybackEvent, SessionAccumulator, PlaybackSession> {

    public SessionAccumulator createAccumulator() { return new SessionAccumulator(); }

    public SessionAccumulator add(PlaybackEvent ev, SessionAccumulator acc) {
        // min/max, not first/last: events arrive out of order
        acc.startTs = acc.startTs == 0 ? ev.eventTime : Math.min(acc.startTs, ev.eventTime);
        acc.endTs   = Math.max(acc.endTs, ev.eventTime);
        switch (ev.type) {
            case HEARTBEAT: acc.watchMs  += ev.watchDeltaMs;  break;
            case BUFFERING: acc.bufferMs += ev.bufferDeltaMs; break;
            case SEEK:      acc.seeks    += 1;                break;
            case ENDED:     acc.endedReason = ev.endedReason; break;
        }
        acc.userId = ev.userId; acc.titleId = ev.titleId;
        return acc;
    }

    public PlaybackSession getResult(SessionAccumulator acc) { return PlaybackSession.from(acc); }

    public SessionAccumulator merge(SessionAccumulator a, SessionAccumulator b) {
        // session windows merge when a late event bridges two sessions
        a.startTs = Math.min(a.startTs, b.startTs);
        a.endTs   = Math.max(a.endTs, b.endTs);
        a.watchMs += b.watchMs; a.bufferMs += b.bufferMs; a.seeks += b.seeks;
        if (a.endedReason == null) a.endedReason = b.endedReason;
        return a;
    }
}

What makes this production-grade

  • Event time, idleness, and a late-data side output: disorder is handled and nothing is silently dropped.
  • Incremental aggregation (AggregateFunction): state per session is O(1), not O(events).
  • Transactional Kafka sink with a stable transactional-id prefix.
  • Iceberg DistributionMode.HASH: shuffles by table partition key so each partition is written by few writers (fewer small files) — watch for skew on hot partitions.
  • RocksDB + incremental checkpoints: state can grow to hundreds of GB.

Exactly-once sink config traps:

  • transaction.timeout.ms must exceed the checkpoint interval plus worst-case recovery time, and must stay ≤ the broker's transaction.max.timeout.ms (15 minutes by default at time of writing; check current docs). If it is too short, the broker aborts pre-committed transactions during a slow restart, and output the job considered committed is silently lost.
  • read_committed consumers see output only when the checkpoint completes. A 60 s interval adds up to about 60 s of latency.
  • An open transaction pins the partition's last stable offset (LSO). Every read_committed consumer stalls behind it until it commits or times out.

What to monitor

  • End-to-end latency: p50/p95/p99 of now() - eventTime at the sink.
  • Source lag: Flink commits offsets only on checkpoint, so consumer-group lag tools trail the job. Prefer the source's pendingRecords metric or lag in seconds.
  • Kafka sink transaction commit/abort rate: a rising abort rate means something is wrong.
Failure-first: what can fail?
FailureDetectRecoverPrevent recurrence
Watermark stuck (idle or empty partition)Watermark lag vs wall clock; no window outputwithIdleness; fix producer keyingIdleness by default; watermark-lag alert
Checkpoints time out under backpressureCheckpoint duration and failure count; backPressuredTimeMsPerSecondFix the bottleneck; aligned-checkpoint timeoutCapacity headroom; alert on the duration trend
EO sink loses output after a long restartGaps in the sessions topic; aborted transactionsReplay from the last good checkpoint or savepointtransaction.timeout.ms > interval + recovery
Consumer lag exceeds retentionLag in seconds vs retention.msBackfill from bronze / lakehouse; reset offsets deliberatelyAlert at 50% of retention; tiered storage
State grows without boundCheckpoint size trend, RocksDB disk usageSavepoint + State Processor API cleanupTTL on every keyed state; max session length

15. Idempotent Producers and Exactly-Once in Kafka

Kafka's exactly-once mechanics live here; §7 and §9 point here. It is three mechanisms composed: the idempotent producer, transactions, and offsets inside the transaction. They cover Kafka → process → Kafka, and nothing outside Kafka.

Layer 1 — Idempotent producer

The broker assigns a producer id (PID), and the producer numbers its records per partition. The broker drops a retried batch whose sequence it has already written and rejects gaps. So retries neither duplicate nor reorder (up to 5 in-flight requests). On by default since Kafka 3.0. The limits: it covers one producer session and one partition. A restarted producer without a transactional.id gets a new PID and no protection.

Layer 2 — Producer transactions

Set a transactional.id, call initTransactions() once, and bracket writes with beginTransaction() / commitTransaction(). On commit/abort, the transaction coordinator (the broker owning the __transaction_state partition for this transactional.id) writes a COMMIT/ABORT control marker into every partition the transaction touched. read_committed consumers read only up to the last stable offset (LSO). Aborted data stays in the log behind an ABORT control marker and is skipped by read_committed consumers. It is not a "tombstone"; that word means a null-value compaction record.

Layer 3 — Offsets inside the transaction

For consume → process → produce, the consumed offsets must commit atomically with the output. sendOffsetsToTransaction(offsets, consumer.groupMetadata()) writes them to __consumer_offsets inside the same transaction. The older String groupId overload is deprecated. Kafka Streams (processing.guarantee=exactly_once_v2) uses exactly this. Flink instead stores source offsets in its checkpoint and commits pre-committed Kafka transactions when the checkpoint completes (KafkaSink with DeliveryGuarantee.EXACTLY_ONCE). Spark's Kafka sink uses neither and is at-least-once (§7).

Engine: Kafka Java client (2.5+, incl. 4.x)Language: JavaExecutable: Illustrative — adapt to your dialect
// consumer: enable.auto.commit=false, isolation.level=read_committed
producer.initTransactions();                   // fences older instances of this transactional.id
while (running) {
    ConsumerRecords<String, String> recs = consumer.poll(Duration.ofMillis(500));
    if (recs.isEmpty()) continue;
    try {
        producer.beginTransaction();
        for (ConsumerRecord<String, String> r : recs)
            producer.send(new ProducerRecord<>("out_topic", r.key(), transform(r.value())));
        producer.sendOffsetsToTransaction(nextOffsets(recs), consumer.groupMetadata());
        producer.commitTransaction();
    } catch (ProducerFencedException | OutOfOrderSequenceException | AuthorizationException e) {
        producer.close();                      // fatal: another instance owns this id
        throw e;
    } catch (KafkaException e) {
        producer.abortTransaction();           // abortable: retry from last committed offsets
        rewindToCommitted(consumer);
    }
}

What can still go wrong

  • Zombie producers. Re-initialising the same transactional.id bumps its epoch and fences the old instance; generating a random id per restart disables fencing entirely. Two live pods that share an id fence each other, and you see ProducerFencedException churn.
  • Hanging transactions. A transaction left open (crashed producer, lost marker) pins the LSO. Every read_committed consumer of that partition stops advancing until transaction.timeout.ms expires. Transactions v2 (KIP-890, Kafka 4.x with transaction.version=2) bumps the epoch on every transaction and closes most of these cases on the server side.
  • Timeouts vs checkpoints. For Flink, transaction.timeout.ms must outlive the checkpoint interval plus recovery time (§14).
  • External side effects. A REST call inside the loop is outside the transaction and can happen twice.
  • read_uncommitted consumers. This is the consumer default. It sees aborted and in-flight records. EOS is a configured guarantee, end to end.

16. Complex Event Processing and MATCH_RECOGNIZE

"Find users who did X, then Y, then Z within 10 minutes" is a Complex Event Processing (CEP) problem. There are three ways to implement it.

Path 1 — Flink CEP library

Pattern.begin("a").where(...).next("b").where(...).within(...) compiles to an NFA (non-deterministic finite automaton), matched per key in event-time order. within takes Time in 1.x and Duration in 2.x.

Path 2 — SQL MATCH_RECOGNIZE

MATCH_RECOGNIZE is SQL:2016 row-pattern matching, supported by Flink SQL, Oracle, Snowflake and others, with differing syntax and limits. In Flink, ORDER BY must be the event-time attribute, and WITHIN bounds the pattern so that state can be pruned:

Engine: Flink SQLDialect: Flink SQL (MATCH_RECOGNIZE)Executable: Yes — Flink SQL only
SELECT *
FROM events
MATCH_RECOGNIZE (
  PARTITION BY user_id
  ORDER BY event_ts                    -- must be the event-time attribute
  MEASURES A.event_ts AS start_ts, C.event_ts AS end_ts
  ONE ROW PER MATCH
  AFTER MATCH SKIP PAST LAST ROW
  PATTERN (A B* C) WITHIN INTERVAL '10' MINUTE
  DEFINE
    A AS A.event_name = 'view_plan',
    B AS B.event_name IN ('hesitate', 'back', 'scroll'),
    C AS C.event_name = 'purchase'
);

Path 3 — Hand-rolled stateful operator

For simple patterns (A then B), a stateful operator keyed by user_id is often cleanest. Store the last-seen-A timestamp per key, and on each B check whether it falls within the window. It is simpler than CEP but does not generalise to longer patterns.

Interview probe

"How would you detect account-takeover patterns in real time?" Strong answer: pattern-match on [login-success, IP-change, password-change, payment-added] within N minutes; use MATCH_RECOGNIZE on Flink SQL with WITHIN INTERVAL '30' MINUTE and a watermark delay sized to out-of-orderness (seconds, not the pattern window); emit to an alert topic; tune false positives with thresholds and an allow-list.

17. Stream-Table Duality in Depth

A table is the latest state of a stream of changes, and a stream is the change log of a table. Table → stream: CDC from the database log (Debezium; see Part 15) or a compacted topic (§9). Stream → table: replay the stream with upsert semantics, as a Kafka Streams KTable or a Flink GROUP BY result. Flink SQL makes the change kinds explicit: +I insert, -U/+U update before/after, -D delete. A sink must accept the kinds the query produces (append-only, upsert by key, or retract).

Join behaviour follows from this (details in §10). A stream-table join enriches each event with the table's current value, or with its as-of value in a temporal join. For stream-stream joins, late rows are dropped by window/interval joins; regular (unwindowed) outer joins emit retractions and keep unbounded state without TTL.

18. Stateful Functions and Application-Level Patterns

Flink's KeyedProcessFunction and the Kafka Streams Processor API blur the line between stream processing and event-driven applications. Three patterns are worth recognising.

Pattern A — Stateful session accumulation

Keyed by user. State is an incremental summary (counters, first and last event time), not a list of events. A timer closes the session after 30 minutes of inactivity and emits one record. §14 builds it out; §11 covers bounding it.

Pattern B — The operator-as-state-machine

Keyed by order_id. State is the current lifecycle phase (placed, paid, shipped, delivered), and milestone events drive the transitions: (placed, payment_received) → paid. Invalid transitions go to a dead-letter side output. You get an accumulating snapshot in streaming form, with explicit invariants.

Pattern C — Distributed cache with TTL

Keyed by feature_id. State is a cached value plus its expiry, and a periodic timer refreshes entries before they expire. This works as a small online feature store living inside the pipeline. Use it when the feature set fits in state and latency matters more than scale.

19. Amazon Kinesis — Architecture and Trade-offs

Three different products. Kinesis Data Streams (KDS) is a durable log like Kafka. Amazon Data Firehose (formerly Kinesis Data Firehose) is a fully managed delivery conveyor belt. Amazon Managed Service for Apache Flink (formerly Kinesis Data Analytics) is a serverless Flink runner.

Kinesis Data Streams — internals

A stream consists of one or more shards. Each shard accepts up to 1 MB/s or 1,000 records/s of writes and serves 2 MB/s of reads. Records carry a partition key (MD5-hashed to a 128-bit shard boundary), a sequence number (monotonically increasing per shard), and a data blob (1 MiB maximum historically; AWS has raised the limit since, so check current docs).

Retention is 24 hours by default, extendable to 365 days (at cost). Reads don't delete records; each consumer tracks its own position (KCL checkpoints), so independent consumers read at their own pace, as with Kafka consumer groups.

Capacity mode: provisioned (you size the shards) or on-demand (AWS scales shards and bills by throughput). On-demand suits spiky or unknown traffic and is usually dearer at steady high volume.

DimensionKinesis Data StreamsKafka (self-managed)
Partitioning unitShard (1 MB/s write)Partition (no enforced throughput)
ScalingShard split/merge (minutes, not instant); or on-demand modeOnline, throttled partition reassignment (kafka-reassign-partitions / Cruise Control); adding partitions changes key→partition mapping
Consumer modelStandard (2 MB/s total) or enhanced fan-out (2 MB/s per consumer)Consumer group offset commits
OrderingPer-shard, by sequence numberPer-partition, by offset
Ops burdenZero infra; pay per shard-hour + data volumeBrokers, KRaft controllers, replication, monitoring (or managed: MSK, Confluent Cloud)
EcosystemNative AWS (Lambda, Glue, MSF)Kafka Connect, Streams, Flink, Spark

Enhanced fan-out vs standard

Standard consumers share each shard's 2 MB/s of reads. The shard allows only 5 GetRecords calls/s shared by all consumers — five consumers polling every 200 ms already need 25 calls/s and get throttled. Enhanced fan-out (SubscribeToShard) gives each registered consumer its own 2 MB/s push channel, with read latency around 70 ms in AWS's documentation. Beyond ~2 consumers per shard, or when read latency matters, enhanced fan-out is usually worth its extra per-consumer-shard-hour and per-GB charges.

Amazon Data Firehose

Firehose is a zero-code delivery pipeline: ingest → optional Lambda transform → S3 / Redshift / OpenSearch / Splunk. It handles batching, compression and JSON→Parquet conversion. Delivery is at-least-once. Buffer size and buffer interval trade file size against latency. At time of writing the interval can go as low as 0 s (zero buffering), so check current docs for bounds. Not suitable when you need replay or consumer-controlled offsets.

Amazon Managed Service for Apache Flink

Standard Flink (DataStream or Table API) with checkpointing, scaling and version upgrades managed for you. It saves a lot of operational work, but for continuous high-throughput jobs it is expensive compared with self-managed Flink on EMR or Kubernetes.

Interview probes on Kinesis

  • "Our Lambda consumer is falling behind on KDS." Diagnosis: check iterator age in CloudWatch (GetRecords.IteratorAgeMilliseconds). Root causes: Lambda concurrency limit throttling, shard count too low, processing time per record too high. Fix: split hot shards, raise the event source mapping's ParallelizationFactor (up to 10 concurrent batches per shard, with per-key order kept), increase Lambda concurrency, or switch to EFO for dedicated bandwidth.
Interviewer pushes back

You: “I would use Kafka for the event bus.”

Interviewer: “Why not Kinesis? We're all-in on AWS.”

Strong answer: “It depends on four things. Fan-out: how many independent consumers per stream? Kinesis standard consumers share 5 GetRecords calls/s and 2 MB/s per shard, so more than two usually means paying for enhanced fan-out. Semantics: do we need transactional writes into the bus, or Kafka Connect/Debezium CDC? Kinesis has neither. Replay: Kinesis keeps up to 365 days; Kafka with tiered storage can keep far more. Ops and cost at our volume. If we're at a few MB/s with three consumers, AWS-native sinks and no team to run Kafka, Kinesis on-demand is the right call. If we need CDC, exactly-once into the bus, many consumers or multi-cloud, I'd pick managed Kafka (MSK or Confluent), not self-hosted.”

Weak answer: “Kafka is the industry standard,” or “Kafka is faster.” That is brand loyalty, not requirements.

20. Event-Driven Architecture Patterns

In an event-driven architecture, services publish and consume events instead of calling each other. Streaming pipelines sit on top of that substrate, and its design mistakes surface as data-quality bugs.

Choreography vs Orchestration

Choreography: services react to events on a shared bus with no coordinator (OrderPlaced → inventory emits StockReserved → payment emits PaymentCharged). You get loose coupling. You pay in debugging distributed causality and "who handles X?" confusion.

Orchestration: a central orchestrator sends commands and waits for replies. It is the state machine. The flow is explicit, but the orchestrator can become a bottleneck.

The senior signal: choreography fails silently (an event nobody consumes), orchestration fails loudly (the orchestrator backs up).

The Saga Pattern

Distributed transactions without a two-phase commit. A saga is a sequence of local transactions, each publishing an event that triggers the next step. If a step fails, compensating transactions roll back the prior steps.

A choreography-based saga emits compensating events: simple, but hard to trace in long chains. An orchestration-based saga sends compensating commands explicitly: easier to audit, and its state must be durable.

For data pipelines: a job that updates three tables per event makes three local transactions. If the third fails, compensation must undo or flag the first two, or downstream readers see partial state.

The Transactional Outbox Pattern

Problem: a service writes to its database and publishes an event. If the service crashes between the DB commit and the Kafka publish, the event is lost — DB is updated, downstream is not notified. Solution: write the event to an outbox table in the same DB transaction as the business write. A separate relay publishes outbox rows to Kafka. It is either a poller that marks rows as sent, or log-based CDC (Debezium's outbox event router) that tails the WAL. With CDC, rows can be deleted right after insert and sent_at is unnecessary. CDC depth is in Part 15.

Engine: PostgreSQLDialect: PostgreSQLExecutable: Illustrative — adapt to your dialect
-- Outbox table schema (gen_random_uuid() is built in from PostgreSQL 13)
CREATE TABLE event_outbox (
  id           UUID PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
  created_at   TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  event_type   TEXT NOT NULL,          -- 'OrderPlaced', 'PaymentCharged'
  aggregate_id TEXT NOT NULL,          -- the business entity ID
  payload      JSONB NOT NULL,
  sent_at      TIMESTAMPTZ             -- NULL = not yet relayed
);

-- Business logic transaction (atomic):
BEGIN;
  INSERT INTO orders (...) VALUES (...);
  INSERT INTO event_outbox (event_type, aggregate_id, payload)
    VALUES ('OrderPlaced', $order_id, $payload);
COMMIT;

Guarantees: at-least-once delivery (the relay may re-publish on crash); idempotency must be handled by consumers. The outbox is the standard way to couple a relational write with an event publish without a distributed coordinator (alternatives: CDC directly on the business table, or event sourcing).

CQRS and the Read Model

CQRS splits the write model (an append-only, authoritative event log) from read models (derived, eventually consistent views shaped for queries).

For data pipelines, the event log is your bronze table and every silver or gold dataset is a read model. "Why doesn't the KPI match the source?" is answered by tracing log → transform → read model.

Interview probes on EDA

  • "An upstream service changed its event schema and broke your pipeline." Strong answer: a schema registry with compatibility rules enforced at publish time, and versioned event types. The root fix is a data contract enforced before the event is written, not after it's read (Part 15).
  • "How do you test an event-driven pipeline end to end?" Strong answer: contract tests at each schema boundary using Pact or Avro schema registry; integration tests against a real broker in a container (e.g., Testcontainers); replay from the event log to validate transform correctness after code changes.
L5 Interview CardStreaming Processing
Must know
  • A watermark is max ET − B per split, min across inputs. B bounds out-of-orderness, not end-to-end delay. Idleness is not progress.
  • Exactly-once needs a replayable source, deterministic-or-checkpointed processing, and a sink that is transactional or idempotent. It costs latency, because output is visible per checkpoint.
  • Spark's Kafka sink is at-least-once. Flink's KafkaSink and Kafka Streams can be transactional.
  • Kafka orders records per partition only. Key → partition; changing the partition count breaks per-key order.
  • Durability is acks=all + min.insync.replicas ≥ 2 + unclean election off. It relies on replication, not fsync.
  • Kafka 4.x is KRaft-only. KIP-848 rebalancing is GA but opt-in (group.protocol=consumer).
  • Checkpoints: barriers at sources → align → async snapshot → all tasks ack → sinks commit.
  • Backpressure turns into lag at Kafka, and lag beyond retention is silent data loss.
Must be able to explain
  1. Why is B sized from out-of-orderness and not delay? What happens after a two-hour outage?
  2. Walk through a Flink checkpoint. Where does a transactional sink commit, and what does that do to latency?
  3. When does at-least-once plus an idempotent sink beat transactional exactly-once?
Must be able to draw

The sessionization pipeline: clients → keyed Kafka topic → Flink (event time, RocksDB state, checkpoints) → transactional Kafka sink + Iceberg + late-event topic, with the guarantee named on every arrow.

clients → Kafka → Flink ─┬→ Kafka (EO)
                         ├→ Iceberg
                         └→ late topic → reconcile
Must be able to code
  • An event-time windowed aggregation with a watermark and a late-data side output (Flink or Spark).
  • An idempotent upsert sink keyed by (key, window_start).
  • Dedup by event_id in keyed state with a TTL.
Must be able to debug
  • Frozen dashboard: after a producer re-keyed, 3 of 48 partitions went empty. The min-over-splits watermark stuck, state grew for hours and checkpoints ballooned. Fix: withIdleness plus a watermark-lag alert.
  • EO sink lost output: a 20-minute restart outlived transaction.timeout.ms, so the broker aborted the pre-committed transactions. Fix: set the timeout above interval + recovery, within the broker maximum, and alert on checkpoint duration.
Numbers that matter
  • At-least-once replay after a failure ≈ records since the last commit. At 10k events/s with a 60 s interval, that is up to ~600k re-sent records.
  • Transactional output latency ≥ the checkpoint interval (plus checkpoint duration).
  • State: 100M keys × 1 KB ≈ 100 GB. That needs RocksDB + incremental checkpoints, spread across TaskManagers.
  • Lag budget: at 50 MB/s ingest and 7-day retention, a consumer can fall ~30 TB behind before data is deleted. Measure lag in time.
  • A Kinesis shard takes ~1 MB/s or 1,000 records/s in and 2 MB/s out, shared by standard consumers (check current docs).
Classic traps
  • "We set B to p99 of end-to-end latency." The first replay then holds every window open for hours.
  • "Spark gives us exactly-once into Kafka." It is at-least-once.
  • "Exactly-once covers the SMS / HTTP call." Side effects need idempotency keys.
30-second answer

How do you guarantee correct results from a streaming pipeline when events arrive late, out of order, or twice? I compute on event time, with watermarks sized to the out-of-orderness I actually measure, so disorder within that bound doesn't matter. I decide explicitly what happens past the bound: allowed lateness into an upsert sink, or a side output plus reconciliation. I make duplicates harmless with a replayable source, deterministic processing, and a sink that is either transactional on checkpoints or idempotent by key. On top of that, I dedupe on a business key, because exactly-once won't catch duplicates the producer created.

2-minute answer

Late: the watermark is max ET − B per partition, min across inputs, with idleness for empty partitions. B comes from measured maxET − ET. Windows fire at the watermark. Allowed lateness re-fires them into a sink keyed by (key, window_start). Anything later goes to a side output, and a batch audit certifies the affected windows; the output table marks rows provisional until final. Out of order: event-time windows make arrival order irrelevant within B. Kafka only orders per partition, so anything order-sensitive is keyed and carries a version, and the sink applies the highest version. Twice: Kafka offsets make the source replayable; Flink checkpoints state and offsets together; the sink either commits transactionally on checkpoint (visible once per interval) or upserts idempotently (visible immediately). I choose per consumer: transactions for append-only aggregates and money, idempotent upserts for dashboards. Side effects outside the job get idempotency keys.

Deep-dive follow-up

Your job restores from a checkpoint taken 10 minutes before the crash. Exactly which records are replayed? Which outputs become visible twice with a transactional sink, and which with an idempotent one? Why does the watermark start from scratch?

Staff+ follow-up

Billing, real-time dashboards and ML features all consume this topic, with different correctness needs. How do you set one platform contract for lateness, finality and duplicates, and who pays for exactly-once?
