Part 04

Spark Internals

Quick refresh15 minInterview study55 minDeep practice60 min
Last technically reviewed September 2026
Covers Catalyst, AQE, shuffle, join selection, skew, Tungsten & memory, partitioning, Python boundary, plan reading, configs, dynamic allocation, native engines, Spark 4.x changes
Versions referenced Apache Spark 3.5 (extended LTS, security fixes only) and 4.0 / 4.1 / 4.2 (4.2.0 released July 2026)
Primary references Spark SQL performance tuning · Spark configuration · SQL migration guide · ANSI compliance · Spark 4.0 release notes
Known implementation differences Defaults quoted are open-source Spark; Databricks (Photon, DBR), EMR and other distributions change several of them.

The interviewer is testing whether you can read Spark as a compiler plus a distributed memory manager: say what the plan will be before you run it, name the stage boundary where time goes, and explain why one task out of a thousand is the whole job. Config names are the least of it. What matters is knowing which layer owns the problem.

"Spark is a distributed compiler and memory manager that happens to execute SQL." If you can hold that sentence and defend it, you're at L5.

1. The layered architecture you must carry in your head

A query passes through five layers. Know which one owns the problem:

  1. Parser / DataFrame API: produces an unresolved logical plan.
  2. Analyzer: resolves tables, columns, types and functions against the catalog.
  3. Optimizer (Catalyst): rule-based rewrites. Output: optimized logical plan.
  4. Planner: picks physical operators (join and aggregate strategies). Output: physical plan.
  5. Execution: the DAG scheduler cuts the plan into stages at every shuffle; tasks run whole-stage-generated code on executors; AQE re-plans at each stage boundary.

Debugging rule: if EXPLAIN FORMATTED is wrong at layer N, don't look at layer N+1. A filter that didn't push down is an optimizer problem, not a shuffle problem.

Engine: Apache Spark 3.x / 4.xLanguage: Python (PySpark)Executable: Yes
df.explain(mode="formatted")  # full plan
df.explain(mode="cost")       # optimized logical plan + size/row stats (pre-execution; AQE final plan only after an action)

For deeper diagnosis, log every rule that fires:

Engine: Apache Spark 3.x / 4.xLanguage: Python (PySpark)Executable: Yes
spark.conf.set("spark.sql.planChangeLog.level", "WARN")
# prints every rule that fires during optimization

2. Catalyst: logical plan → optimized plan → physical plan

2.1 The tree

A logical plan is an immutable tree of nodes (Project, Filter, Join, Aggregate, leaf Relations). Rules are functions LogicalPlan → LogicalPlan that pattern-match subtrees and return a rewritten tree.

Engine: Apache Spark (Catalyst internals)Language: ScalaExecutable: Illustrative — adapt to your dialect
// Simplified Catalyst rule idea
object PushDownFilter extends Rule[LogicalPlan] {
  def apply(plan: LogicalPlan): LogicalPlan = plan transform {
    case Filter(cond, Project(fields, child)) if cond.references.subsetOf(child.outputSet) =>
      Project(fields, Filter(cond, child))  // push Filter under Project
  }
}

2.2 The rule batches (greatest hits)

Batches of rules, many run to a fixed point. Know a handful:

BatchKey rulesWhat it does
Finish AnalysisEliminateSubqueryAliases, ComputeCurrentTime, ReplaceExpressionsfinal clean-up after analysis (name/type resolution already happened in the Analyzer)
SubqueryRewritePredicateSubqueryIN/EXISTS subquery → semi/anti join
Infer FiltersInferFiltersFromConstraintsa = b AND a = 5 infers b = 5
Operator OptimizationsPushDownPredicates, ColumnPruning, CombineFilters, ConstantFolding, BooleanSimplification, NullPropagation, EliminateOuterJointhe heart of Catalyst
Join ReorderReorderJoin, CostBasedJoinReorderheuristic reorder; cost-based only with CBO on

Two rules do most of the work: predicate push-down (through Project, Join, Aggregate and into the file scan so Parquet reads the minimum bytes) and ColumnPruning (whole column chunks never leave storage).

2.3 Analyzing the optimized plan

Engine: Apache Spark 3.x / 4.xLanguage: Python (PySpark)Executable: Yes
df = (spark.table("bronze.playback_events")
      .filter("event_date = '2026-04-15'")
      .filter("user_id = 1234")
      .select("title_id", "watch_ms"))

df.explain(mode="formatted")
Engine: Apache Spark 3.5 / 4.xLanguage: EXPLAIN outputExecutable: Illustrative — adapt to your dialect
== Optimized Logical Plan ==
Project [title_id#1, watch_ms#2]
+- Filter (isnotnull(user_id) AND (event_date = 2026-04-15) AND (user_id = 1234))
   +- Relation bronze.playback_events[...] parquet

== Physical Plan ==
*(1) Project [title_id#1, watch_ms#2]
+- *(1) Filter (isnotnull(user_id#3) AND (user_id#3 = 1234))
   +- *(1) ColumnarToRow
      +- FileScan parquet bronze.playback_events
            PartitionFilters: [event_date = 2026-04-15]
            PushedFilters: [IsNotNull(user_id), EqualTo(user_id,1234)]
            ReadSchema: struct<title_id:bigint,watch_ms:bigint>

*(1) = codegen stage 1. PartitionFilters = directory pruning. PushedFilters = handed to the Parquet reader to skip row groups by min/max; Spark re-applies the filter above the scan.

2.4 When plans go wrong: the "why didn't it push down" checklist

  1. A Python/Scala UDF touched the column (opaque to Catalyst).
  2. The filter sits above a Window on a non-partition column, or is non-deterministic.
  3. The predicate isn't a simple comparison the source understands (COALESCE(col, 0) = 5): Spark filters, but Parquet can't skip row groups.
  4. The files have no usable statistics.
  5. Type mismatch (string column vs int literal) → an implicit cast wraps the column and pushdown is lost. Under ANSI mode (default in 4.x) a bad value in that cast can also fail the query.
  6. You cache()d above the filter; the filter now runs against the cached relation, not the files.

2.5 Runtime pruning: DPP and bloom-filter joins

Dynamic partition pruning (Spark 3.0+, on by default). In a star join where the fact table is partitioned on the join key, Spark turns the filtered dimension into a runtime subquery and prunes fact partitions before scanning them. You see it as dynamicpruningexpression(...) in the fact scan's PartitionFilters. No partition-column join key, no DPP.

Runtime bloom-filter joins (added in 3.3; on by default in 4.x source, check your 3.x minor). For a shuffle join where one side is selectively filtered, Spark builds a bloom filter from that side and applies it to the other side's scan, shrinking the shuffle. It is a heuristic, gated by size thresholds; it shows up as might_contain in the plan. Neither feature fixes a bad join; both quietly make good star joins cheaper.

3. The cost model (such as it is) and why it's wrong

Spark's cost-based optimizer (CBO) uses statistics from ANALYZE TABLE: row count, size, and per-column min/max/nullCount/distinctCount (approximate), optionally histograms. It is off by default in open-source Spark (spark.sql.cbo.enabled=false, and spark.sql.cbo.joinReorder.enabled=false).

3.1 Why the CBO is a paper tiger

Stats go stale (nobody re-runs ANALYZE after every write), selectivity estimates assume uniform data while real keys are Zipfian, and AQE's real shuffle sizes beat any plan-time estimate anyway.

3.2 The two cases where CBO actually earns its keep

  1. Star-schema join reordering across many dimensions.
  2. Sharper broadcast decisions: the planner picks BHJ from size stats alone (no CBO needed); CBO column stats sharpen the post-filter estimate, so a filtered 2 GB dimension can be seen as 20 MB.

3.3 What to run

Engine: Apache Spark 3.x / 4.xDialect: Spark SQLExecutable: Yes
ANALYZE TABLE silver.dim_title COMPUTE STATISTICS;
ANALYZE TABLE silver.dim_title COMPUTE STATISTICS FOR COLUMNS title_id, genre;
ANALYZE TABLE silver.dim_title COMPUTE STATISTICS FOR ALL COLUMNS;

For partitioned tables: ANALYZE TABLE t PARTITION (event_date='2026-04-15') COMPUTE STATISTICS.

4. Adaptive Query Execution (AQE): the runtime re-planner

AQE is the most important Spark performance feature of recent releases. It turns "compile once" into "re-plan at every stage boundary with real shuffle statistics". On by default since 3.2 (spark.sql.adaptive.enabled).

4.1 What AQE actually does

RuleWhat it doesKey config (OSS names)
Coalesce shuffle partitionsmerges contiguous small post-shuffle partitions into fewer tasksspark.sql.adaptive.coalescePartitions.enabled, advisoryPartitionSizeInBytes (64 MB), coalescePartitions.parallelismFirst
Skew joinsplits oversized partitions of a shuffle join into several tasksspark.sql.adaptive.skewJoin.enabled, skewedPartitionFactor (5.0), skewedPartitionThresholdInBytes (256 MB)
Join strategy switchSMJ → BHJ when a side turns out small; SMJ → SHJ when all partitions are small enoughspark.sql.adaptive.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold (3.2+, falls back to spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold); localShuffleReader.enabled=true then skips the reduce-side fetch; maxShuffledHashJoinLocalMapThreshold (0 = off)

4.2 The coalesce algorithm

Without AQE, every shuffle gets spark.sql.shuffle.partitions (200) tasks, however small. AQE merges them (simplified):

Engine: Apache Spark (AQE)Language: Python-likeExecutable: Pseudocode
target = advisoryPartitionSizeInBytes   # 64 MB default
partitions = shuffle_map_output  # in partition-id order; only contiguous ranges merge
groups, current, size = [], [], 0
for p in partitions:
    if size + p.size > target and current:
        groups.append(current); current, size = [], 0
    current.append(p); size += p.size
if current: groups.append(current)
# each group = one reduce task reading a contiguous range of partition ids

Result: fewer, bigger tasks. Trap: spark.sql.adaptive.coalescePartitions.parallelismFirst=true (OSS default since 3.2) ignores the advisory size and computes a smaller target from the cluster's default parallelism, bounded below only by minPartitionSize (1 MB). Set it false to actually get ~64 MB partitions; the config's own documentation recommends false on busy clusters.

4.3 The skew handling algorithm

Engine: Apache Spark (AQE)Language: Python-likeExecutable: Pseudocode
median_size = median(partition_sizes)
is_skewed(p) = p.size > median_size * skewedPartitionFactor
               AND p.size > skewedPartitionThresholdInBytes

Split: the skewed partition is read as several sub-partitions of roughly advisory size; each sub-task joins against a copy of the matching partition from the other side. The other side is therefore read once per sub-task, which is cheap only when that partition is small. If splitting would force an extra shuffle, AQE skips it unless spark.sql.adaptive.forceOptimizeSkewedJoin=true.

4.4 Dynamic join strategy conversion

The plan said SMJ, but after filter and aggregation one side's shuffle output is 8 MB (under the 10 MB default, or spark.sql.adaptive.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold). AQE converts to a broadcast hash join, building the hash table from the already-materialized shuffle output instead of re-reading the source.

4.5 Verifying AQE fired

explain() before an action shows only the initial plan (isFinalPlan=false). After the action, the SQL tab in the Spark UI shows the final plan: look for AQEShuffleRead (called CustomShuffleReader before 3.2) with coalesced or skewed, and join nodes that changed.

Engine: Apache Spark 3.x / 4.xLanguage: Python (PySpark)Executable: Yes
df.explain(mode="formatted")
# post-execution to see AQE's final plan:
spark.sparkContext.uiWebUrl  # browse to SQL tab

4.6 When to turn AQE off (rare)

Plan-stability tests, or code that (wrongly) depends on the number of output partitions. AQE does not apply to Structured Streaming micro-batches anyway. Otherwise: leave it on.

4.7 What AQE can't do

  • Un-broadcast: a BHJ planned from stale stats still broadcasts, then OOMs or times out.
  • Fix skew before the first shuffle: one huge unsplittable input file is still one task.
  • Split skew outside shuffle joins: GROUP BY with non-partial aggregates, windows, and full outer joins are not split by the skew-join rule.
  • Undo a bad plan shape: it re-plans only what is downstream of a finished stage.
Interviewer pushes back

You: “I'd set spark.sql.shuffle.partitions to 2000.”

Interviewer: “Why 2000? The input is 20 GB on Sundays and 2 TB at month end.”

Strong answer: Do the arithmetic. Aim for roughly 100–200 MB per task. At 2 TB, 2000 partitions is ~1 GB each: spills and long tails. At 20 GB it is ~10 MB each: task-scheduling overhead, 2000 × M shuffle blocks to fetch, and 2000 small output files. So I'd set the initial count for the largest day and let AQE coalesce, with parallelismFirst=false so coalescing targets bytes, not core count. Then I'd check the final plan and the output file sizes.

Weak answer: A magic number from a blog post, applied to every job, never revisited when data volume changes.

5. Shuffle: the disk-and-network truth

Every shuffled byte is serialized, written to local disk, fetched over the network and deserialized. It is usually the biggest cost in the job.

5.1 The shuffle lifecycle

Each map task sorts records by target partition, spills as needed, and merges into ONE data file plus ONE index file of N (offset, length) entries.

5.2 The External Shuffle Service (ESS)

Map outputs live on executor-local disk; lose the executor and the map stage re-runs. The External Shuffle Service is a long-running process per node (YARN aux-service or standalone Worker; OSS Spark has no supported ESS on Kubernetes — there use shuffle tracking, decommissioning with shuffle-block migration, or a remote shuffle service) that serves shuffle files after the executor is gone.

Engine: Apache Spark (YARN / standalone)Language: Spark configExecutable: Yes
spark.shuffle.service.enabled = true    # ESS serves shuffle files
spark.dynamicAllocation.enabled = true  # executors can now be released safely

5.3 Push-based shuffle (Magnet — Spark 3.2+, YARN only, requires ESS)

Map tasks push blocks to merger nodes so reducers read one pre-merged block per partition instead of M small random reads. spark.shuffle.push.enabled (default false) plus ESS server config. Benefit: fewer, larger sequential reads and better locality (LinkedIn reported large shuffle-fetch wins; measure yours).

5.4 Shuffle size math

With M map tasks, N reduce partitions and D bytes shuffled (after compression): disk write ≈ D, network ≈ D (minus local blocks), disk read ≈ D, and M × N block fetches. D = 10 GB, N = 1000 → 10 MB per partition, fine. N = 10000 → 1 MB each, and with 5000 mappers that is 50 million block fetches. Target roughly 64–200 MB per post-shuffle partition.

5.5 Shuffle when executors are ephemeral

On Kubernetes and spot capacity, executors disappear. Options:

  • Remote shuffle services: Apache Celeborn (from Alibaba's RSS), Apache Uniffle (from Tencent's Firestorm); Uber built its own RSS. Shuffle lives on a separate worker cluster, so executors can come and go. Common at very large shops, especially on Kubernetes.
  • Object-store fallback (e.g. Spark's decommission fallback storage spark.storage.decommission.fallbackStorage.path, or vendor S3 shuffle plugins): slower per byte, but survives node loss.

6. Join algorithms: BHJ, SMJ, SHJ, BNLJ

6.1 Decision tree (simplified)

Engine: Apache Spark 3.x / 4.x plannerLanguage: Python-likeExecutable: Pseudocode
if hint:  BROADCAST > MERGE > SHUFFLE_HASH > SHUFFLE_REPLICATE_NL
          (first hint valid for this join type wins)
elif equi-join keys exist:
    if a buildable side < spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold (10 MB):
        → BroadcastHashJoin
    elif preferSortMergeJoin=false and build side small enough per
         partition and ≥3× smaller than the other:
        → ShuffledHashJoin
    elif keys sortable:
        → SortMergeJoin
    else:
        → ShuffledHashJoin
else (no equi-join keys):
    → BroadcastNestedLoopJoin if a side is broadcastable,
      else CartesianProduct (inner) / BNLJ
# at runtime AQE may turn SMJ into BHJ, or into SHJ via
# maxShuffledHashJoinLocalMapThreshold

6.2 Broadcast Hash Join (BHJ)

How it works (OSS): the small side is collected to the driver, built into a HashedRelation, and shipped as a TorrentBroadcast (executors fetch ~4 MB pieces from the driver and each other). Each executor keeps one copy; tasks probe it for their slice of the large side. The large side never shuffles.

Math: driver and every executor hold the in-memory table, often several times its Parquet size; network ≈ |small| × #executors. Hard limits: 8 GB or ~512 million rows.

Why 10 MB: size estimates can be badly wrong, and a wrong broadcast kills the driver. 10 MB is safe everywhere, optimal nowhere.

Raising it: only with driver and executor headroom, and raise spark.driver.maxResultSize (1g) with it. Prefer a hint on the one join you measured:

Engine: Apache Spark 3.x / 4.xLanguage: Python (PySpark)Executable: Yes
spark.conf.set("spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold", "100MB")  # raise with care
# Or hint:
from pyspark.sql.functions import broadcast
large.join(broadcast(small), "user_id")
Engine: Apache Spark 3.x / 4.xLanguage: Python (PySpark)Executable: Yes
spark.conf.set("spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold", "200MB")
Engine: Apache Spark 3.x / 4.xLanguage: Python (PySpark)Executable: Yes
from pyspark.sql.functions import broadcast
fact.join(broadcast(dim), "key")

When it breaks:

  • Stale stats: a dimension grew from 8 MB to 3 GB after a backfill, stats still say 8 MB. AQE does NOT demote a BHJ planned from stale scan stats — it still broadcasts, then OOMs or times out. Refresh stats, lower the threshold or hint. AQE only helps in the SMJ→BHJ direction.
  • Timeout: spark.sql.broadcastTimeout (default 300 s) covers building the small side too, so a slow upstream query can trip it.
  • Join type: a broadcast hint on a side that join type can't build is ignored (6.6).
“Broadcast hash join vs sort-merge join — how does Spark pick?”
30 sec

For an equi-join, if the side Spark is allowed to build is estimated under spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold (10 MB in open-source Spark), it broadcasts it: no shuffle of the big side. Otherwise it shuffles both sides and sort-merges. Hints override the size rule, and AQE can switch a planned SMJ to BHJ once it sees the real shuffle size.

2 min

Order of decisions: hints first (BROADCAST, MERGE, SHUFFLE_HASH, SHUFFLE_REPLICATE_NL). Then the join type limits which side can be built: left outer can only broadcast the right, full outer can never broadcast. The size comes from catalog or file-size statistics; CBO is not required but sharpens post-filter estimates. SMJ is the default for large × large because its memory is bounded and it spills gracefully; SHJ only if preferSortMergeJoin=false or hinted. At runtime AQE sees materialized shuffle sizes and can convert SMJ to BHJ (spark.sql.adaptive.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold) or to SHJ.

Deep dive

The dangerous direction is the other one: a BHJ planned from stale stats. AQE will not demote it; the driver collects gigabytes and dies or the broadcast times out. Estimates are of in-memory size while files are compressed, so a "40 MB" Parquet table can be several hundred MB as a hash relation. Hard ceiling 8 GB. I'd show the plan node (BroadcastHashJoin … BuildRight vs SortMergeJoin), then the SQL tab's final plan to prove what actually ran.

Where to stop: once you've named the stale-stats failure and how you'd see it in the plan; don't recite every threshold.

6.3 Sort-Merge Join (SMJ)

Shuffle both sides by key, sort each partition, walk two cursors. Cost: network |L| + |R|, sort O(n log n) per partition (spills as needed), merge O(|L| + |R|). Memory is bounded except for a long run of one key on the buffered side, which is where skew hurts. Bounded memory is why it's the large × large default.

6.4 Shuffled Hash Join (SHJ)

Shuffle both sides; hash the smaller side per partition; no sort. Faster when the build side fits. Chosen when preferSortMergeJoin=false (default true from 2.0 through 4.x) and size conditions hold, by SHUFFLE_HASH hint, or by AQE. Risk: a skewed build partition that doesn't fit.

6.5 Broadcast Nested-Loop Join (BNLJ)

No equi-join keys (ON a.x < b.y): O(|L| × |R|). Unintended BNLJ or CartesianProduct means fix the query: add an equality (e.g. a bucketed range key) or pre-filter.

6.6 Join types × strategies — what's supported

FULL OUTER: SMJ, SHJ (3.1+) or BNLJ — never BHJ. LEFT OUTER can broadcast only the right side, RIGHT OUTER only the left. INNER can build either side. LEFT SEMI / LEFT ANTI build the right. The plan tells you which side was built:

Engine: Apache Spark 3.x / 4.xLanguage: EXPLAIN outputExecutable: Illustrative — adapt to your dialect
*(3) BroadcastHashJoin [user_id#1], [user_id#10], Inner, BuildRight
*(4) SortMergeJoin [user_id#1], [user_id#10], Inner
*(5) ShuffledHashJoin [user_id#1], [user_id#10], Inner, BuildLeft

6.7 Storage-partitioned join (SPJ)

If both tables are DataSource V2 tables (Iceberg, for example) partitioned compatibly on the join keys, Spark 3.3+ can join partition-to-partition with no shuffle at all. It is off by default in open-source Spark (spark.sql.sources.v2.bucketing.enabled=false in 3.5/4.x), later releases added knobs for mismatched partitions, and Iceberg needs its own preserve-data-grouping setting. Check current Spark and Iceberg docs before promising it; when it works, it removes the biggest shuffle in a large × large join.

7. Skew: detection, splitting, salting, AQE handling

7.1 Detecting skew

Spark UI, Stage page → Summary Metrics: max vs median for duration, Shuffle Read Size/Records, Spill, GC. A slow task with a matching read-size outlier is skew; with a normal read size it's a node or a pathological record. Programmatic check:

Engine: Apache Spark 3.x / 4.xLanguage: Python (PySpark)Executable: Yes
from pyspark.sql.functions import col, count, percentile_approx

skew_check = (df.groupBy("join_key")
              .count()
              .selectExpr("percentile_approx(count, 0.50) as p50",
                          "percentile_approx(count, 0.99) as p99",
                          "max(count) as max"))
skew_check.show()

If p99 / p50 > 5 or a handful of keys hold a large share of rows, plan for skew.

“Why does one Spark task take 20× longer than the others?”
30 sec

Usually skew: one partition holds far more data, from a hot key after a shuffle or one huge unsplittable input file before it. I'd confirm in the Stage page: if the slow task's shuffle-read size is also ~20× the median, it's data; if its size is normal, it's the node or one pathological record.

2 min

Five causes, each with a tell. (1) Key skew: huge read size and records, same partition id every run. (2) Input skew: stage 0, one enormous gzip file or row group. (3) Spill/GC spiral: big spill and GC time on that task. (4) Straggler node: normal size, slow host, different host each run. (5) Pathological value: normal size, but a UDF or regex on a 10 MB string. Fix to match: AQE skew join or salting for joins, two-stage aggregation for non-partial aggregates, a splittable layout for input skew, speculation for bad nodes.

Deep dive

AQE's skew-join rule splits a shuffle-join partition when it is over 5× the median and over 256 MB (OSS defaults); the final plan shows AQEShuffleRead … skewed. It does nothing for windows, full outer joins or skew before the first shuffle. Plain GROUP BY with sum/count is rarely the problem: map-side partial aggregation sends one row per key per map task. collect_list, exact distinct counts and windows over a hot key are where two-stage aggregation pays.

Where to stop: when you've said how you'd tell skew from a bad node. Don't reach for salting before you've shown the evidence.

The full drill (999 tasks finish in 40 seconds, one runs 21 minutes) is in the Debugging Lab.

7.2 AQE skew handling (the easy fix)

With spark.sql.adaptive.skewJoin.enabled=true (default), AQE splits any shuffle-join partition that is > skewedPartitionFactor × median (5.0) AND > skewedPartitionThresholdInBytes (256 MB). Lower the threshold if your partitions are small but still lopsided. It does not help pre-shuffle skew, window or non-partial-aggregate skew, or full outer joins (see 4.7).

7.3 Salting

For a hot join key AQE won't split: spread the large side over N salts, replicate the small side N times.

Engine: Apache Spark 3.x / 4.xLanguage: Python (PySpark)Executable: Yes
from pyspark.sql.functions import col, concat, lit, pmod, xxhash64

# Step 1: deterministic salt on the large side (hash of a unique column, not rand())
salt_factor = 100
salted = df.withColumn("salt", pmod(xxhash64("event_id"), lit(salt_factor))) \
           .withColumn("key_salted", concat(col("user_id"), lit("_"), col("salt")))

# Step 2: explode the small side (cross join with salts)
small_exploded = small_df.crossJoin(
    spark.range(salt_factor).toDF("salt")
).withColumn("key_salted", concat(col("user_id"), lit("_"), col("salt")))

# Step 3: join on the salted key
joined = salted.join(small_exploded, "key_salted")

Cost: the small side grows N×. Use a deterministic salt: rand() can assign different salts when a task is retried after a lost shuffle, risking duplicated or dropped rows. Salt only known hot keys to keep replication small.

7.4 Two-stage aggregation (for GROUP BY skew)

For aggregates that can't be combined map-side:

Engine: Apache Spark 3.x / 4.xLanguage: Python (PySpark)Executable: Yes
from pyspark.sql import functions as F
# Stage 1: pre-aggregate with a deterministic salt
stage1 = (df.withColumn("salt", F.pmod(F.xxhash64("event_id"), F.lit(100)))
          .groupBy("user_id", "salt")
          .agg(F.sum("amount").alias("sum_amt")))

# Stage 2: final aggregate without salt
stage2 = stage1.groupBy("user_id").agg(F.sum("sum_amt").alias("total"))

Stage 2 combines at most 100 rows per key. For sum/count Spark's own partial aggregation usually makes this unnecessary; the shape matters for collect_list-style aggregates.

7.5 Isolating the heavy hitters

When one key holds most rows: process heavy keys separately (often broadcasting just their matches), join the rest normally, union.

Engine: Apache Spark 3.x / 4.xLanguage: Python (PySpark)Executable: Illustrative — adapt to your dialect
heavy = df.filter(col("user_id") == "netflix_test_account")   # process separately
normal = df.filter(col("user_id") != "netflix_test_account")  # normal join
# union at the end
Interviewer pushes back

You: “The join is skewed, so I'd just salt the key.”

Interviewer: “AQE already handles skew. Why salt, and what does it cost you?”

Strong answer: First I'd check whether AQE already split it: the final plan shows AQEShuffleRead … skewed on a sort-merge join, and it only fires above 5× median and 256 MB by default. If it did, I'm done; maybe lower the threshold. Salting costs an N× copy of the other side, an extra column, an extra shuffle shape to maintain, and correctness risk if the salt is rand() and a task retries. I'd salt only when AQE can't help: full outer joins, windows, skew in a non-partial aggregate, or a hot key known in advance. Even then I'd salt only the hot keys, or split them out and broadcast their matches.

Weak answer: Salting every key with N=100 by reflex, without checking the plan, then being surprised the small side is now 100× bigger.

8. Tungsten: binary memory, UnsafeRow, codegen

Tungsten made Spark behave more like a database engine than a JVM app full of objects. Phase 1 (1.4–1.6): binary memory and UnsafeRow; phase 2 (2.0): whole-stage codegen.

  1. Explicit binary memory management via sun.misc.Unsafe — pages are on-heap long[] by default, off-heap only with spark.memory.offHeap.enabled=true (Spark 4 on Java 17/21 still uses Unsafe via --add-opens).
  2. UnsafeRow: a binary row format with fixed offsets; no Java object per field, far less GC.
  3. Whole-stage codegen: fuse a chain of operators into one generated Java method.

8.1 UnsafeRow layout

Null bitset, then one 8-byte slot per field, then a variable-length region (strings store offset + length in their slot). A 10-field fixed-width row is ~88 bytes (8-byte null bitset + 10 × 8-byte slots), versus a few hundred bytes as boxed Java objects. Cache-friendly; SIMD gains come from columnar/vectorized readers, not UnsafeRow.

8.2 Whole-stage codegen

For SELECT col1 + col2 FROM t WHERE col3 > 10, Catalyst generates code equivalent to:

Engine: Apache Spark (whole-stage codegen output)Language: Java (generated)Executable: Illustrative — adapt to your dialect
while (iter.hasNext()) {
  UnsafeRow row = iter.next();
  int col3 = row.getInt(2);
  if (col3 > 10) {
    int col1 = row.getInt(0);
    int col2 = row.getInt(1);
    int result = col1 + col2;
    outputBuffer.putInt(result);
  }
}

One JIT-friendly loop instead of a virtual call per row per operator. Databricks' 2016 microbenchmarks showed up to ~10× on specific operators; end-to-end gains are smaller. Codegen operators show as *(n) in EXPLAIN.

8.3 When codegen doesn't kick in

  • The operator doesn't support it (Python UDFs, some generators and window operators). Missing stars = that operator runs interpreted; it splits the stage rather than disabling it — measure before blaming it.
  • Generated method exceeds spark.sql.codegen.hugeMethodLimit (65535 bytecode bytes) or the schema exceeds spark.sql.codegen.maxFields (100). Separately, HotSpot won't JIT methods > 8000 bytecode bytes, so near-limit stages can run interpreted.

9. Memory model: execution, storage, user, reserved

Spark's unified memory model (since 1.6). Inside each executor heap:

Execution can evict cached blocks, but only until storage shrinks to the storageFraction floor; cache inside that floor is immune. Storage borrows only free execution memory and never evicts it.

9.1 Off-heap memory

Engine: Apache Spark 3.x / 4.xLanguage: Spark configExecutable: Yes
spark.memory.offHeap.enabled = true
spark.memory.offHeap.size = 4g

Less GC pressure; since 3.0 the size is added to the container request on top of overhead. Worth it when GC dominates and the cause isn't skew.

9.2 The OOM debugging flowchart

  1. Container killed (exit 137, "exceeding memory limits"): native memory (Python, Arrow, native libs) over the limit. Raise spark.executor.memoryOverhead or set spark.executor.pyspark.memory.
  2. Java heap OOM: a large broadcast, a skewed hash-table partition, or over-caching. Fix the cause before adding heap.
  3. GC overhead / thrash: fix the skew/over-caching first; then add heap or move Tungsten off-heap. Raising spark.memory.fraction shrinks user memory and can worsen old-gen pressure — change it only with GC logs in hand.
  4. Heavy spill: a task's data exceeds its execution-memory share. Either raise memory or INCREASE shuffle partitions (smaller per-task hash maps).

memoryOverhead gotcha: 10% suits a JVM, not a JVM plus Python workers holding Arrow batches. For Pandas-UDF jobs budget it explicitly (20–30% of heap is a common starting point) and check container metrics.

10. Partitioning, coalesce, repartition — when each is wrong

  • repartition(n): full round-robin shuffle; more parallelism or an even rebalance.
  • repartition(n, col): hash shuffle on col; only when the keys aren't skewed.
  • coalesce(n): no shuffle; merges existing partitions, only downward.
  • repartitionByRange(n, col): sampled range partitioning for sorted output.
  • REBALANCE hint (3.2+): a shuffle that AQE sizes and de-skews; the usual right answer before a write.

10.1 The classic mistake

Engine: Apache Spark 3.x / 4.xLanguage: Python (PySpark)Executable: Illustrative — adapt to your dialect
df.filter("event_date = '2026-04-15'").coalesce(1).write.parquet(...)

You wanted one file. You got the entire read + filter as one task: coalesce adds no shuffle boundary, so it collapses the upstream stage. A 10-node job becomes a 1-core job.

Correct:

Engine: Apache Spark 3.x / 4.xLanguage: Python (PySpark)Executable: Illustrative — adapt to your dialect
df.filter("event_date = '2026-04-15'").repartition(1).write.parquet(...)
# OR: df.hint("rebalance") (REBALANCE, 3.2+) lets AQE size output files; maxRecordsPerFile only CAPS rows per file (splits, never merges)
df.filter(...).write.option("maxRecordsPerFile", 1_000_000).parquet(...)

10.2 Writing files — controlling output count

Engine: Apache Spark 3.x / 4.xLanguage: Python (PySpark)Executable: Yes
(df.repartition(200, "event_date")
   .sortWithinPartitions("event_date", "user_id")
   .write
   .partitionBy("event_date")
   .option("maxRecordsPerFile", 5_000_000)
   .parquet(path))
  • repartition(200, "event_date"): co-locates all records for a given date in the same task — so one task writes each date (1 date = 1 busy task + 199 empty). Prefer REBALANCE(event_date) or repartition on (event_date, salt).
  • sortWithinPartitions: tighter Parquet min/max stats, better row-group skipping.
  • partitionBy: one directory per date. maxRecordsPerFile: caps file size (splits, never merges).

Small-file economics and compaction are covered in Part 02 §9.

11. Pandas UDFs, Arrow, and the JVM↔Python boundary

A regular Python UDF pickles rows in small batches and calls your function once per row in a Python worker — per-row interpreter overhead dominates. Arrow-optimized Python UDFs arrived in 3.4 (spark.sql.execution.pythonUDF.arrow.enabled) and 3.5 (@udf(useArrow=True)); default false through 4.1; the 4.2 release notes list it as on by default — check current docs).

Pandas UDFs (vectorized) use Apache Arrow columnar record batches (10,000 rows by default) streamed over a local socket — one Python call per batch. Not zero-copy across the boundary, but orders of magnitude less overhead.

11.1 Types of Pandas UDFs

Engine: Apache Spark 3.5 / 4.xLanguage: Python (PySpark, pandas)Executable: Illustrative — adapt to your dialect
from pyspark.sql.functions import pandas_udf
from pyspark.sql.types import DoubleType
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
from typing import Iterator

# 1. Series → Series (scalar)
@pandas_udf(DoubleType())
def log1p_udf(s: pd.Series) -> pd.Series:
    return np.log1p(s)  # vectorized; no per-element .map()

# 2. Iterator[Series] → Iterator[Series] (expensive setup once per task)
@pandas_udf(DoubleType())
def model_score(iterator: Iterator[pd.Series]) -> Iterator[pd.Series]:
    model = load_model_once()  # loaded once per task (partition), not per batch
    for s in iterator:
        yield pd.Series(model.predict(s.values))

# 3. Grouped Map (applyInPandas)
def normalize(pdf: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
    pdf["z"] = (pdf["x"] - pdf["x"].mean()) / pdf["x"].std()
    return pdf

df.groupBy("user_id").applyInPandas(normalize, schema="user_id long, x double, z double")

11.2 The Arrow boundary

Engine: Apache Spark 3.5 / 4.x (OSS)Language: Spark configExecutable: Yes
spark.sql.execution.arrow.pyspark.enabled = true  # toPandas()/createDataFrame only; default false in OSS
spark.sql.execution.arrow.maxRecordsPerBatch = 10000  # rows per Arrow batch; tune for memory

Pandas UDFs always use Arrow; that first flag governs only toPandas() and createDataFrame(pandas_df). Databricks turns it on by default.

11.3 Pandas UDF gotchas

  • Memory: 10,000 rows × 1 KB = 10 MB per batch per Python worker, times cores, plus your model, all in overhead, not heap (§9).
  • Per-element Python: Series.map() or apply() inside a Pandas UDF reverts to a Python loop and throws away the vectorization.
  • Schema: for applyInPandas, returned columns are matched to the schema by NAME when labels are strings (default), by position only when they aren't — a misnamed column fails at runtime, a positional one silently mis-assigns.

Arrow and pandas/Polars interop outside Spark: Part 06 §5.

12. Reading the plan: a query walkthrough

A representative prompt: "For the last 7 days, top 10 titles per country by completions."

Engine: Apache Spark 3.x / 4.xLanguage: Python (PySpark)Executable: Yes
completions = (spark.table("silver.fact_playback_completion")
               .filter("event_date >= current_date() - INTERVAL 7 DAYS"))

dim_title = spark.table("silver.dim_title")
dim_country = spark.table("silver.dim_country")

joined = (completions
          .join(dim_title, "title_id")
          .join(dim_country, "country_id"))

from pyspark.sql import Window
from pyspark.sql.functions import count, row_number, col

w = Window.partitionBy("country_name").orderBy(col("completions").desc())

top10 = (joined
         .groupBy("country_name", "title_id", "title_name")
         .agg(count("*").alias("completions"))
         .withColumn("rn", row_number().over(w))
         .filter("rn <= 10"))

top10.explain(mode="formatted")

Physical plan with AQE, after execution (illustrative; Spark 3.5+/4.x, ids and codegen markers trimmed):

Engine: Apache Spark 3.5+ / 4.xLanguage: EXPLAIN outputExecutable: Illustrative — adapt to your dialect
AdaptiveSparkPlan isFinalPlan=true
+- Filter (rn <= 10)
   +- Window [row_number() ... AS rn]
      +- WindowGroupLimit [country_name], [completions DESC], row_number(), 10, Final
         +- Sort [country_name ASC, completions DESC]
            +- AQEShuffleRead coalesced
               +- ShuffleQueryStage 2
                  +- Exchange hashpartitioning(country_name, 200)
                     +- WindowGroupLimit [country_name], [completions DESC], row_number(), 10, Partial
                        +- Sort [country_name ASC, completions DESC]
                           +- HashAggregate(keys=[country_name, title_id, title_name], functions=[count(1)])
                              +- AQEShuffleRead coalesced
                                 +- ShuffleQueryStage 1
                                    +- Exchange hashpartitioning(country_name, title_id, title_name, 200)
                                       +- HashAggregate(keys=[...], functions=[partial_count(1)])
                                          +- BroadcastHashJoin [country_id], [country_id], Inner, BuildRight
                                             :- BroadcastHashJoin [title_id], [title_id], Inner, BuildRight
                                             :  :- Filter isnotnull(title_id)
                                             :  :  +- FileScan silver.fact_playback_completion
                                             :  :       PartitionFilters: [event_date >= 2026-04-12]
                                             :  +- BroadcastQueryStage 0 (dim_title)
                                             +- BroadcastQueryStage (dim_country)

Read it bottom to top:

  1. FileScan with PartitionFilters: only 7 date directories are read.
  2. Two broadcast joins: the fact table never shuffles for the joins.
  3. Partial aggregate → Exchange → AQEShuffleRead coalesced: 200 planned partitions merged into fewer tasks, then the final aggregate.
  4. WindowGroupLimit (3.5+): top 10 per country kept before the second shuffle, then sort, window, filter.

Failure modes to know:

  • dim_title outgrows the threshold → SMJ, and the fact table shuffles. Worse: stale stats keep the BHJ and the driver dies (§6.2).
  • Built-in functions on a partition column still prune (any deterministic predicate over only partition columns is evaluated against partition values). A Python/Scala UDF, or a predicate mixing partition and data columns, disables pruning and you scan every partition.
  • A few countries dominate → a long tail in the window stage, which AQE's skew rule won't split.

13. Configuration cheat sheet — what each knob actually does

Values are the open-source Spark default (3.5/4.x) — Databricks and other distributions may differ.

ConfigOSS default (3.5 / 4.x)What it does / when to touch
spark.sql.shuffle.partitions200Initial post-shuffle partitions. Size for your largest input; let AQE coalesce.
spark.sql.adaptive.advisoryPartitionSizeInBytes64MBCoalesce/split target. Often raised to 128–256 MB.
spark.sql.adaptive.coalescePartitions.parallelismFirsttrueIgnores the advisory size (keeps parallelism). Set false for size-based coalescing.
spark.sql.adaptive.skewJoin.*enabled; factor 5.0; threshold 256MBSkew-join split conditions (both must hold).
spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold10MBPlan-time broadcast cutoff. -1 disables.
spark.sql.adaptive.autoBroadcastJoinThresholdunset → global valueRuntime (AQE) broadcast cutoff, 3.2+.
spark.sql.ansi.enabledfalse (3.5) / true (4.x)Bad casts, overflow, divide-by-zero raise instead of returning NULL.
spark.sql.optimizer.dynamicPartitionPruning.enabledtrueDPP (3.0+).
spark.sql.optimizer.runtime.bloomFilter.enabledtrue in 4.x; check your 3.x minorRuntime bloom-filter joins (3.3+).

spark.sql.files.maxPartitionBytes / openCostInBytes128MB / 4MBInput split size; small-file packing.
spark.executor.memoryOverheadmax(384MB, 10% of heap)Native/Python memory. Raise for PySpark, Arrow, RocksDB.
spark.memory.offHeap.enabledfalseTungsten pages off-heap; size added to the container.

spark.sql.execution.pythonUDF.arrow.enabledfalse (3.5–4.1)Arrow-optimized regular Python UDFs; 4.2 notes say on by default — check.
spark.dynamicAllocation.shuffleTracking.enabledtrueKeeps executors that hold live shuffle data; enables DA without ESS.
spark.shuffle.service.enabledfalseNeeded for DA unless shuffle tracking or decommissioning with shuffle migration is used. Push-based shuffle requires it.

14. Dynamic allocation and elastic clusters

Dynamic allocation adds executors when tasks back up and releases idle ones. Done right, it's the cheapest way to run bursty batch; done wrong, intermittent slowness.

14.1 The shuffle-data-loss trap

Release an executor and its local shuffle files go with it; a later stage that needs them re-runs the upstream stage. Fix: on YARN, the external shuffle service. On Kubernetes, spark.dynamicAllocation.shuffleTracking.enabled (default true — executors holding live shuffle data aren't released, so scale-down is slower), plus spark.decommission.enabled with shuffle-block migration or a remote shuffle service (Celeborn).

14.2 When it's the wrong choice

  • Jobs of a couple of minutes: executor start-up dominates.
  • Streaming: classic DA reacts to task backlog, which micro-batches express poorly.
  • Hard per-job budgets: cap maxExecutors or cost becomes unpredictable.

15. Photon and native accelerators

Photon (Databricks) and similar native engines (Velox under Presto C++/Prestissimo and Apache Gluten for Spark, Apache DataFusion Comet for Spark, NVIDIA RAPIDS for GPU) replace JVM operators with vectorized C++, Rust or CUDA kernels. On the right workloads, often 2–3× faster (vendor-reported); Photon compute carries a higher DBU rate, so net cost must be measured per workload.

15.1 What they accelerate, and what they don't

  • Good: columnar scans with filters, hash aggregations and joins on primitive types.
  • Neutral: shuffle-bound jobs, and anything that falls back (Python UDFs, unsupported types or functions); each fallback adds a row/column conversion. Check the plan for what ran natively.

15.2 The interview question

"You enabled Photon, cost dropped 40%, one dashboard broke. Why?" A native engine is a second implementation: casts, overflow, NULL handling or floating-point aggregation order can differ at the edges. Regression-test results on both engines before flipping production.

16. PySpark vs Scala — where the performance actually goes

The lore says "Scala is faster." For DataFrame and SQL code it isn't: the Python client builds plans that run in the JVM — via Py4J (classic) or, with Spark Connect (3.4+, GA in 4.0), as unresolved plans sent over gRPC. Python is not on the hot path.

16.1 Where Python actually costs you

  1. Row-at-a-time Python UDFs: per-row serialization and interpreter calls, often an order of magnitude slower than a built-in. Use built-ins first.
  2. Pandas / Arrow UDFs: batch-at-a-time; the pragmatic choice when you need Python libraries.
  3. Driver-side loops: a thousand small actions each pay planning and scheduling. Build one query, run it once.

Spark Connect changes the operational story: the client is a thin gRPC process with no JVM and no SparkContext/RDD API, so driver-side debugging and some libraries that reach into the JVM behave differently. Ask which mode a platform runs before assuming classic PySpark.

16.2 Decision guidance

DataFrame/SQL only: the language your team writes best. Python libraries needed: PySpark with Pandas UDFs. Tight custom per-row logic at TB scale: Scala/Java UDFs win, modestly.

17. Spark 3.5 LTS vs 4.x — what changes in an interview

2026 Interview Note

The execution model in this chapter (Catalyst, stages, shuffle, AQE) is timeless across 3.5 and 4.x. What changed is behaviour at the edges. Spark 3.5 is on extended support (security fixes only, until November 2027 per the Apache versioning policy); 4.0, 4.1 and 4.2 are the maintained feature lines at time of writing (2026) — check current docs.

Area3.54.xWhy an interviewer cares
ANSI modeoff: bad cast → NULL, overflow wrapson by default: invalid cast, overflow, divide-by-zero raiseOld jobs fail; use try_cast, try_divide, try_add
Spark Connectavailable (3.4+)GA, broader API; spark.api.mode switchThin client; no RDD/SparkContext in Connect sessions
VARIANT—new type; parse_json, variant_getSemi-structured data without string JSON re-parsing
JVM / ScalaJava 8/11/17, Scala 2.12/2.13Java 17/21, Scala 2.13 onlyEvery 2.12 jar and connector must be rebuilt
PythonArrow Python UDFs opt-inPython Data Source API (4.0); Arrow UDFs on by default in 4.2 per its notesUDF performance and type-coercion behaviour shift
Other—SQL pipe syntax, collations, session variables; Spark Declarative Pipelines (4.1)Know they exist; don't over-claim details
Drill · Spark 4 upgrade

A nightly job ran unchanged on Spark 3.5 for two years. After the platform moved to Spark 4.0 it fails every night with [CAST_INVALID_INPUT] The value 'N/A' of the type "STRING" cannot be cast to "INT". The owner wants to set spark.sql.ansi.enabled=false and move on.

STOP. Answer before revealing.

Reveal the diagnosis
  1. Observe The error class and the query context name the expression and column. Nothing in the code changed; the engine default did.
  2. Hypothesize ANSI mode is on by default in 4.x. On 3.5 the same cast returned NULL, silently, so the job has been writing NULLs for every 'N/A' row all along.
  3. Measure On yesterday's input, count rows where col IS NOT NULL AND try_cast(col AS INT) IS NULL. That number is how much data 3.5 was quietly nulling out.
  4. Isolate Re-run once with ANSI off in a sandbox to confirm it's the only failure; run the whole job with ANSI on to find the next one (overflow, divide-by-zero).
  5. Fix Make the intent explicit: try_cast where bad input is expected, and route failed rows to a quarantine table with a count metric. Don't turn ANSI off globally; that hides the next bug too.
  6. Prevent Upgrade canaries: run critical jobs on the new runtime against a production sample with ANSI on before cut-over, and add a data-quality check on cast-failure rates.

A related incident, a job that OOMs only on Mondays, is worked through in Part 08.

18. Closing framework

Spark problems almost always sit in one of six buckets:

  1. Plan is wrong: filter didn't push down, wrong join strategy. → Fix the query, hint, refresh stats.
  2. Partition count is wrong: too many tiny tasks or too few giant ones. → Size for the largest input; AQE coalescing with parallelismFirst=false.
  3. Skew: one task is the long tail. → AQE skew join, salting, isolate heavy hitters.
  4. Shuffle is too big: eliminate it (broadcast, SPJ), shrink it (pre-aggregate, runtime filters), or move it (RSS, push-based shuffle on YARN).
  5. Memory: OOM, spill, GC. → Tell container kill from heap OOM; fix the cause, then overhead, off-heap, partition count.
  6. Driver: collecting too much. → maxResultSize, no big collect(), watch broadcasts.

That framing survives most interview questions and most 3am pages.

L5 Interview CardSpark Internals
Must know
  • Plan layers: parser → analyzer → optimizer → planner → stages; read EXPLAIN FORMATTED for PartitionFilters, PushedFilters, *(n) and the join node.
  • Stages end at shuffles; one task per partition; the AQE final plan exists only after an action.
  • AQE's three levers (coalesce, join switch, skew split) and its limits: can't un-broadcast, can't fix pre-shuffle, window or full-outer skew; watch parallelismFirst.
  • Join choice: hints first; BHJ below the threshold (10 MB OSS, 8 GB hard ceiling), never for full outer; SMJ default for large × large; no equi-key → BNLJ/Cartesian.
  • Sort-based shuffle: 1 data + 1 index file per map task; M × N block fetches.
  • Memory: 300 MB reserved, 0.6 unified, 0.5 storage floor, overhead max(384 MB, 10%); exit 137 = container kill, not heap.
  • Spark 4.x: ANSI on by default, Spark Connect, VARIANT, Java 17/21 + Scala 2.13; 3.5 on extended support.
Must be able to explain
  1. Why one task takes 20× longer than the rest, and how you'd tell skew from a bad node.
  2. How Spark picks BHJ vs SMJ, and why a stale-stats broadcast is worse than a missed one.
  3. Why coalesce(1) before a write made the whole job single-threaded.
Must be able to draw

The execution path with its stage boundaries:

SQL → logical → optimized → physical
  → stages cut at Exchange
  → tasks per partition → shuffle
  → AQE re-plan → next stage
Must be able to code
  • Two-stage (salted) aggregation with a deterministic salt.
  • A broadcast-hinted join plus the explain that proves it ran.
  • A Pandas UDF (iterator form) that loads a model once per task.
Must be able to debug
  • Dimension grew from 8 MB to 3 GB after a backfill; stale stats kept the broadcast; driver OOM at 02:00. AQE didn't help.
  • Job moved to Kubernetes with dynamic allocation and shuffle tracking disabled by a copied conf; executors reclaimed, FetchFailed, stages recomputed, 3× wall-clock.
Numbers that matter
  • Aim for ~100–200 MB per post-shuffle partition; 1 MB partitions mean overhead dominates.
  • M × N block fetches: 5,000 mappers × 10,000 reducers = 50 million.
  • A broadcast table's in-memory size is often several times its Parquet size.
  • Default skew trigger (OSS): > 5× median AND > 256 MB. Check your distribution.
Classic traps
  • coalesce(1) collapses upstream parallelism; use repartition(1) or REBALANCE.
  • A rand() salt plus a task retry can duplicate or drop rows; salt with a hash of a stable column.
  • arrow.pyspark.enabled doesn't govern Pandas UDFs; applyInPandas matches columns by name.
30-second answer

“Walk me through what Spark does with your query, and where it goes wrong at scale.” The driver parses and resolves the query, Catalyst rewrites it (push filters down, prune columns), and the planner picks join and aggregate strategies. The DAG scheduler cuts that plan into stages at every shuffle and runs one task per partition on executors. AQE re-plans at each stage boundary using real sizes. At scale it goes wrong in three places: the shuffle (too big, too many tiny blocks), skew (one task holds the job), and memory (a broadcast or a hot partition that doesn't fit).

2-minute answer

Add the evidence for each step. The plan: EXPLAIN FORMATTED shows whether partition filters and pushed filters landed, and which join node was chosen: BHJ under the broadcast threshold, SMJ otherwise, with hints and join type able to override. Execution: every Exchange is a stage boundary; map tasks write one sorted data file plus an index, and reducers fetch M × N blocks, so partition count matters in both directions. AQE coalesces contiguous small partitions (watch parallelismFirst), switches SMJ to BHJ when a side turns out small, and splits skewed join partitions, but it can't un-broadcast or fix skew outside shuffle joins. Failure diagnosis lives in the Stage page's max vs median metrics and the SQL tab's final plan. Memory failures split into container kills (overhead, Python) and heap OOMs (broadcast, skew, cache). On 4.x, add ANSI: bad data that used to become NULL now fails the job.

Deep-dive follow-up

“AQE converted your sort-merge join to a broadcast join at runtime. What work did it save, and what had already been paid for?”

Staff+ follow-up

“You run 4,000 Spark jobs on Kubernetes with spot nodes. How do you design shuffle, dynamic allocation and the Spark 3.5 → 4.x upgrade so that one platform change doesn't silently break a hundred pipelines?”
