Part 05

SQL Deep Dive

Quick refresh15 minInterview study50 minDeep practice70 min
Last technically reviewed September 2026
Covers logical vs physical order, join algorithms, pruning, subqueries, window frames, gaps & islands, sessionization, as-of joins, sketches, anti-patterns, tuning, CTEs, materialized views, hints
Versions referenced PostgreSQL 12+ (CTE inlining), 13+ (WITH TIES), 18 current; Apache Spark 3.5 / 4.x (ANSI on by default since 4.0); Snowflake, BigQuery, DuckDB as of 2026
Primary references PostgreSQL docs · Spark SQL reference · Spark ANSI compliance · Snowflake SQL reference · BigQuery query syntax · DuckDB docs
Known implementation differences NULL ordering, integer division, alias visibility, QUALIFY, frame support, CTE materialization, hints and sketch APIs all differ by engine — every code block below names its dialect.

The interviewer is testing whether you can see through the SQL to the engine: predict the plan, say what gets scanned, shuffled and sorted, spot the query that is fast but wrong, and name which parts of your answer are ANSI and which are one vendor's dialect. Correctness first, then cost.

1. The mental model: SQL is declarative; engines are procedural

You write what you want; the planner picks join order and strategy, storage layout decides which bytes are read, and the execution engine (row-at-a-time vs vectorized) decides how fast rows flow. At L5 you predict the plan, the cost, and what happens when data doubles. Three questions, always:

  1. Which side builds, which probes? ("Driving table" means the selective outer input in OLTP, the fact table in a star schema — say which.)
  2. Where do filters apply? At scan time (push-down), or after?
  3. Where do shuffles happen? Between which operators, on which key?

2. Logical plan processing order (the one the spec promises)

The logical order of a SELECT determines name visibility and semantics:

Consequences you must carry:

  • A SELECT alias is not visible in WHERE in portable SQL. Snowflake and DuckDB allow it; Postgres and BigQuery don't; Spark 3.4+ allows lateral aliases only within the SELECT list.
  • HAVING filters aggregates. Window results exist only after HAVING: filter them with QUALIFY (Snowflake, BigQuery, Databricks, DuckDB) or a wrapping subquery (Postgres; OSS Spark 3.x — check current docs for 4.x).
Engine: AnyDialect: ANSI SQLExecutable: Yes (the first query errors by design)
-- Wrong (portable):
SELECT user_id, COUNT(*) AS cnt
FROM events
WHERE cnt > 5                 -- ERROR: cnt doesn't exist yet at WHERE
GROUP BY user_id;

-- Right:
SELECT user_id, COUNT(*) AS cnt
FROM events
GROUP BY user_id
HAVING COUNT(*) > 5;

2.1 The quiet reorderings

The logical order is what the query means, not what the engine does. The optimizer reorders anything that preserves semantics — pushing predicates below a join is the everyday case.

2026 Interview Note

The same SQL is not the same query across engines. Timeless concept: SQL semantics are only as portable as the features you touch. Version- and vendor-specific behavior that bites in interviews and migrations:

  • NULL ordering: Postgres, Oracle and Snowflake sort NULLs as largest (last on ASC); Spark, BigQuery and MySQL put them first on ASC. Write NULLS FIRST/LAST when it matters.
  • Integer division: 7/2 is 3 in Postgres and SQL Server, 3.5 in Snowflake, BigQuery, Spark and DuckDB.
  • QUALIFY: present in Snowflake, BigQuery, Databricks, DuckDB; absent in Postgres.
  • Spark 4.0 ANSI mode (spark.sql.ansi.enabled=true by default): invalid casts, overflow and divide-by-zero now fail instead of returning NULL. Jobs written for 3.x can break on upgrade; use try_cast/try_divide deliberately.
  • Date functions: DATEDIFF argument order and units differ (Snowflake DATEDIFF(day, start, end), Spark datediff(end, start), BigQuery DATE_DIFF(end, start, DAY)).

3. Physical plan processing order (what actually happens)

Engine: AnyDialect: ANSI SQLExecutable: Yes
SELECT u.country, COUNT(*) AS plays
FROM fact_plays p
JOIN dim_user u ON p.user_id = u.user_id
WHERE p.event_date = '2026-04-15'
  AND u.signup_country_id = 42
GROUP BY u.country
HAVING COUNT(*) > 100
ORDER BY plays DESC
LIMIT 10;

A plausible Postgres plan, paraphrased (real EXPLAIN output is a tree read bottom-up):

3.1 Reading EXPLAIN from any engine

  • Postgres: EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS). Compare estimated vs actual rows; shared hit vs read is cache vs disk.
  • Snowflake: EXPLAIN USING TEXT for the plan; Query Profile for partitions scanned vs total, spill and the most expensive operator.
  • BigQuery: execution graph in the console; a dry run reports bytes processed (the on-demand billing basis) before execution.
  • Spark: df.explain("formatted") and the SQL tab of the UI (see Part 04 §2).

Every engine shows the same operators under different names: scan, filter, join, aggregate, sort, exchange.

4. Join algorithms with complexity math

Engine-neutral view. For Spark's specific strategies (BHJ, SMJ, SHJ, BNLJ) and their thresholds see Part 04 §6.

AlgorithmPreconditionsTotal costMemory
Nested Loopany conditionO(N·M)O(1)
Index Nested Loopindex on inner join keyO(M · log N)O(1)
Hash JoinequijoinO(N + M): build N, probe MO(N) — build side
Sort-Merge Joinequijoin, sortable keys (sorted by the algorithm unless already ordered)O(N log N + M log M) sort + O(N+M) mergeO(largest duplicate-key run) buffered
Runtime filter / dynamic pruningnot a join algorithm — prunes the probe-side scan using build-side keysshrinks M before the joinsmall (bloom filter / key set)

4.1 Nested Loop Join

Scan the inner per outer row. Fine when the inner is tiny, the condition is non-equi, or an index makes it an Index Nested Loop. Spark uses BroadcastNestedLoopJoin only when there is no equi-key.

4.2 Hash Join

Hash the smaller input, stream the larger through it. Memory ≈ 50–200 bytes/row: 10M build rows is 0.5–2 GB. If it doesn't fit: Grace (partition both sides by hash, spill, join pairs) or Hybrid (keep one partition in memory).

4.3 Sort-Merge Join

Sort both sides, walk two cursors. Scales and spills gracefully; buffers duplicate-key runs, which is where skew hurts. The sort is skipped only with a real ordering guarantee — a clustered index in OLTP; bucketing or storage-partitioned joins (3.3+) in Spark. Z-ORDER and Snowflake clustering prune files but guarantee no order.

4.4 Choosing a strategy (mental shortcut)

Engine: AnyLanguage: Planner heuristicExecutable: Pseudocode
if no equi-join key:                       nested loop (beware Cartesian)
elif index on inner.join_key and outer small: index nested loop
elif small.rows × row_size < memory_budget: hash join (build on small)
else:                                      sort-merge (or grace hash)

5. Indexes, zone maps, Bloom filters: what prunes and when

5.1 B-tree indexes (OLTP default)

O(log N); fanout in the hundreds means ~4 levels cover ~108 rows. A covering index holds every column the query needs, so the table is never touched.

Engine: PostgreSQL 11+ (also SQL Server)Dialect: PostgreSQLExecutable: Yes — PostgreSQL 11+ only (INCLUDE)
CREATE INDEX idx_plays_user_date ON fact_plays (user_id, event_date)
INCLUDE (watch_ms);
-- SELECT watch_ms FROM fact_plays WHERE user_id = 1234 AND event_date = '2026-04-15'
-- satisfied entirely from index.

5.2 Hash indexes (in-memory dbs, Postgres for exact match)

O(1) exact lookup, no range scans. Rarely the first choice.

5.3 Bitmap indexes (low-cardinality)

One bitmap per value, one bit per row; AND/OR is nearly free. Persistent in Oracle; built at runtime from B-trees in Postgres (Bitmap Heap Scan); approximated in columnar engines by dictionary encoding plus zone maps.

5.4 GIN / GiST / BRIN indexes

  • GIN: inverted index for JSONB, arrays, full-text.
  • GiST: generalized search tree for geospatial and range types.
  • BRIN: min/max per block range — a zone map inside Postgres, for large time-ordered tables.

5.5 Zone maps / min-max statistics (columnar warehouses)

Parquet row groups, Snowflake micro-partitions, Delta and Iceberg file stats all keep per-column min/max; the engine skips any unit whose range excludes the filter value. This only works on clustered data — random write order gives every file the full range. Fix with layout: Snowflake CLUSTER BY, Iceberg sort order, Delta Z-ORDER or liquid clustering.

Interviewer pushes back

You: “The lookup by customer_id is slow, so I'd add an index.”

Interviewer: “This is Snowflake. There's no CREATE INDEX on a standard table.”

Strong answer: In a columnar warehouse the equivalent of an index is data layout: pruning via min/max stats. I'd check the profile for partitions scanned vs total. If it's scanning most of the table, the column isn't clustered — options are a clustering key (cost: background reclustering credits), Search Optimization for point lookups on a high-cardinality key, or a narrower table sorted by customer_id if this access path dominates. Then I'd confirm the win in the profile, not assume it.

Weak answer: Insisting on an index, or throwing warehouse size at a scan that should have pruned 99% of files.

5.6 Bloom filters

Probabilistic set membership: tunable false-positive rate, no false negatives. For n elements and FP rate p: bits m = −n·ln(p) / (ln 2)², hashes k = (m/n)·ln 2. 10M elements at 1% FP ≈ 96 Mbit ≈ 12 MB.

Parquet stores them per row group (parquet-mr 1.12+); Iceberg sets them per column:

Engine: Apache Spark + Apache IcebergDialect: Spark SQLExecutable: Yes — Spark with Iceberg catalog
ALTER TABLE silver.fact_playback_session
  SET TBLPROPERTIES ('write.parquet.bloom-filter-enabled.column.user_id' = 'true');

"Definitely not" skips the file — the win for selective lookups on an unclustered key, where zone maps can't help.

5.7 The pruning checklist

Partitioned and clustered, still slow — what pruned?

  1. Partitions: filter on the partition column itself, not a function of another? Check PartitionFilters.
  2. Zone maps: clustered on the filter column?
  3. Bloom filters: configured for the column?
  4. Runtime pruning: did the dimension filter reach the fact scan (Spark DPP 3.0+, Snowflake join filters)?
  5. Columns: only the needed ones read?

Each is multiplicative.

6. Subquery types and how they translate to joins

6.1 Scalar subquery (one row, one column)

Engine: AnyDialect: ANSI SQLExecutable: Yes
SELECT user_id, (SELECT MAX(event_ts) FROM sessions WHERE user_id = u.user_id) AS last_seen
FROM dim_user u;

Naively, per outer row. Modern optimizers decorrelate it into a left join against an aggregate:

Engine: AnyDialect: ANSI SQLExecutable: Yes
SELECT u.user_id, s.last_seen
FROM dim_user u
LEFT JOIN (SELECT user_id, MAX(event_ts) AS last_seen FROM sessions GROUP BY user_id) s
  ON u.user_id = s.user_id;

The COUNT bug: decorrelating (SELECT COUNT(*) …) this way turns 0 into NULL; hand-written rewrites need COALESCE(cnt, 0) (12.8).

6.2 IN / EXISTS (existence)

Engine: Apache Spark / Databricks (first query: any)Dialect: Spark SQLExecutable: Yes — Spark SQL / Databricks only (LEFT SEMI JOIN)
SELECT * FROM dim_user WHERE user_id IN (SELECT user_id FROM sessions WHERE event_date >= '2026-04-01');
-- The optimizer plans this as a semi join. Spark SQL lets you write it directly:
SELECT u.*
FROM dim_user u
LEFT SEMI JOIN sessions s
  ON u.user_id = s.user_id AND s.event_date >= '2026-04-01';
-- DuckDB spells it SEMI JOIN. Postgres/Snowflake/BigQuery have no syntax: write IN / EXISTS.

A semi join returns each matching left row once and no right columns — no DISTINCT needed, no fan-out possible.

6.3 NOT IN / NOT EXISTS (anti)

Critical NULL pitfall:

Engine: AnyDialect: ANSI SQLExecutable: Yes
SELECT * FROM dim_user WHERE user_id NOT IN (SELECT user_id FROM blocked_users);

One NULL in blocked_users.user_id and this returns zero rows: x NOT IN (…, NULL) is never TRUE. Engines must honor that (Spark plans a null-aware anti join), so fix the SQL — prefer NOT EXISTS:

Engine: AnyDialect: ANSI SQLExecutable: Yes
SELECT u.* FROM dim_user u
WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM blocked_users b WHERE b.user_id = u.user_id);

6.4 Lateral / CROSS APPLY (correlated row-returning)

Engine: PostgreSQL (DuckDB similar; SQL Server uses CROSS APPLY)Dialect: PostgreSQLExecutable: Yes — PostgreSQL; support for LATERAL + LIMIT varies elsewhere
SELECT u.user_id, top3.title_id
FROM dim_user u,
LATERAL (
  SELECT title_id
  FROM fact_plays p
  WHERE p.user_id = u.user_id
  ORDER BY play_count DESC
  LIMIT 3
) top3;

Good in OLTP with an index on (user_id, play_count); in a warehouse, ROW_NUMBER() … <= 3 parallelizes better.

7. Window functions: frames, partitions, and performance

Anatomy:

Engine: AnyDialect: ANSI SQL grammarExecutable: Pseudocode
function(args) OVER (
  [PARTITION BY partition_cols]
  [ORDER BY order_cols]
  [ROWS | RANGE | GROUPS frame_spec]
)

7.1 Frame types

  • ROWS: physical rows. ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW is exactly 3 rows.
  • RANGE: bounded by the ORDER BY value; rows tied on it are peers and move together. RANGE BETWEEN INTERVAL '7 days' PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW scopes by value, not count.
  • GROUPS: counts peer groups. Postgres 11+, SQLite and DuckDB only — not Spark, Snowflake or BigQuery.

7.2 Function families

  • Ranking: ROW_NUMBER, RANK, DENSE_RANK, NTILE, PERCENT_RANK, CUME_DIST.
  • Offset / value: LAG, LEAD, FIRST_VALUE, LAST_VALUE, NTH_VALUE.
  • Aggregates over windows: SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX, COUNT.

7.3 The default frame trap

With ORDER BY and no frame, the standard default is RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW — ending at the current row and its peers. The trap is ties:

Engine: PostgreSQL / Spark SQL / BigQuery / DuckDBDialect: ANSI SQLExecutable: Yes (check Snowflake's documented default frame per function)
SELECT user_id, event_ts, amount,
  SUM(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY event_ts) AS running_range,
  SUM(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY event_ts, charge_id
                    ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS running_rows
FROM fact_charges;
-- Two charges at the same event_ts, 10 then 5:
--   running_range = 15, 15   (each row's frame includes its peer)
--   running_rows  = 10, 15   (deterministic thanks to the charge_id tiebreaker)

(Without ORDER BY the frame is the whole partition.) A batch load stamping many rows with one timestamp turns a running balance into a staircase. Fix: ROWS plus a unique tiebreaker.

7.4 Window performance model

Shuffle by PARTITION BY, sort by ORDER BY, walk the frame. Cost = shuffle + sort; frame evaluation is near O(n).

  • Always PARTITION BY in a distributed engine — otherwise everything goes to one task.
  • Windows sharing a PARTITION/ORDER BY share one sort.
  • Top-k per group: ROW_NUMBER() … <= k lets engines keep k rows per partition instead of a full sort — Spark 3.5+ WindowGroupLimit (k ≤ spark.sql.optimizer.windowGroupLimitThreshold, default 1000).
  • QUALIFY ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY ts DESC) = 1 where supported; elsewhere a subquery.

7.5 Running totals pattern

Engine: AnyDialect: ANSI SQLExecutable: Yes
SELECT
  user_id, event_ts, amount,
  SUM(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY event_ts
                    ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS running_total,
  AVG(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY event_ts
                    ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS trailing_7_avg
FROM fact_charges;

6 PRECEDING is the last 7 rows, not 7 days. For calendar intent see the intent table.

7.6 First/last value pattern

Engine: AnyDialect: ANSI SQLExecutable: Yes
SELECT
  user_id, session_id, event_ts,
  FIRST_VALUE(event_type) OVER (PARTITION BY session_id ORDER BY event_ts
                                ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING) AS first_event,
  LAST_VALUE(event_type) OVER (PARTITION BY session_id ORDER BY event_ts
                               ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING) AS last_event
FROM session_events;

The LAST_VALUE trap: the default frame ends at the current row and its peers, so LAST_VALUE without an explicit frame returns the current row's value, not the partition's last. The UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING frame fixes it. FIRST_VALUE is correct under the default frame. Often clearer: FIRST_VALUE(x) OVER (… ORDER BY event_ts DESC).

“Explain window frames: ROWS vs RANGE.”
30 sec

ROWS counts physical rows around the current row. RANGE bounds by the ORDER BY value, so rows tied on that value are peers and move together. With ORDER BY and no frame, the default is RANGE from the partition start to the current row's last peer.

2 min

Two consequences. Ties: a running SUM gives tied rows the same total, and LAST_VALUE returns the current row — so for anything row-by-row I write ROWS and add a unique tiebreaker. Calendar windows: ROWS 6 PRECEDING is 7 rows, which spans more than 7 days when days are missing; RANGE BETWEEN INTERVAL 6 DAYS PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW is 7 calendar days, or I densify with a date spine first. I pick by the business definition, then check determinism.

Deep dive

Support differs: GROUPS frames exist only in Postgres 11+, SQLite and DuckDB; interval RANGE offsets need a date/timestamp or numeric ORDER BY key (BigQuery wants numeric — order by UNIX_DATE(d) with RANGE 6 PRECEDING). Implementation: invertible aggregates (SUM, COUNT) slide by add/subtract; MIN/MAX need a deque or segment tree. In distributed engines the frame is cheap; the shuffle and sort on PARTITION BY dominate, and a hot partition key becomes one straggler task.

Where to stop: frame mechanics and the ties example; go into segment trees only if asked about implementation.

8. Gaps and islands — the four canonical variants

Find runs where a property holds, or the holes between them. More in Part 09 §4.

8.1 Variant 1: consecutive identical values

Engine: AnyDialect: ANSI SQLExecutable: Yes
-- Find streaks of same status per user
WITH marked AS (
  SELECT user_id, event_ts, status,
    ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY event_ts) AS rn_all,
    ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id, status ORDER BY event_ts) AS rn_status
  FROM fact_events
)
SELECT user_id, status,
  MIN(event_ts) AS streak_start,
  MAX(event_ts) AS streak_end,
  COUNT(*) AS streak_len
FROM marked
GROUP BY user_id, status, (rn_all - rn_status);

Why it works: rn_all − rn_status is constant within a streak and changes with the status.

8.2 Variant 2: consecutive integers (gap detection)

Engine: AnyDialect: ANSI SQLExecutable: Yes
-- Find missing invoice numbers
SELECT invoice_num + 1 AS gap_start,
       next_num - 1    AS gap_end
FROM (
  SELECT invoice_num,
         LEAD(invoice_num) OVER (ORDER BY invoice_num) AS next_num
  FROM invoices
) t
WHERE next_num - invoice_num > 1;

No PARTITION BY: fine in Postgres, a single task in Spark. Partition by a coarse key at scale.

8.3 Variant 3: date gaps (missing daily data)

Engine: PostgreSQL (DuckDB similar)Dialect: PostgreSQLExecutable: Yes — PostgreSQL only (generate_series, ::date)
WITH calendar AS (
  SELECT generate_series(DATE '2026-01-01', DATE '2026-04-15', INTERVAL '1 day')::date AS d
)
SELECT d FROM calendar
LEFT JOIN daily_metrics m ON m.metric_date = calendar.d
WHERE m.metric_date IS NULL;

Spines elsewhere: Spark explode(sequence(start, end, INTERVAL 1 DAY)), BigQuery UNNEST(GENERATE_DATE_ARRAY(…)), Snowflake GENERATOR + DATEADD — or just keep a dim_date.

8.4 Variant 4: consecutive timestamp "islands" (session gaps)

See Sessionization below.

9. Sessionization with LAG + running SUM

Definition: a session is a run of events from one user with no gap larger than 30 minutes.

Engine: PostgreSQLDialect: PostgreSQLExecutable: Yes — PostgreSQL (INTERVAL '30 minutes', EXTRACT(EPOCH …)); adapt elsewhere
WITH events AS (
  SELECT user_id, event_ts
  FROM fact_events
  WHERE event_date BETWEEN '2026-04-15' AND '2026-04-15'
),
with_prev AS (
  SELECT user_id, event_ts,
    LAG(event_ts) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY event_ts) AS prev_ts
  FROM events
),
flagged AS (
  SELECT user_id, event_ts,
    CASE WHEN prev_ts IS NULL OR event_ts - prev_ts > INTERVAL '30 minutes'
         THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS session_start
  FROM with_prev
),
numbered AS (
  SELECT user_id, event_ts,
    SUM(session_start) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY event_ts) AS session_num
  FROM flagged
)
SELECT user_id, session_num,
  MIN(event_ts) AS session_start_ts,
  MAX(event_ts) AS session_end_ts,
  COUNT(*) AS event_count,
  EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM MAX(event_ts) - MIN(event_ts)) AS duration_seconds
FROM numbered
GROUP BY user_id, session_num;

LAG gets the previous event; flag a gap over 30 minutes; a running SUM of flags numbers the sessions; group by it.

The midnight bug: filtering to one event_date splits every session spanning midnight. Read a lookback margin of at least the gap, sessionize, keep sessions that start on the target day.

This is the batch equivalent of a session window; Flink instead merges per-event windows in state (Part 03).

10. As-of joins / point-in-time joins

"What was user X's subscription tier at the moment they made this play?"

The dimension has history (SCD2); you want the row valid at each fact's timestamp. Get it wrong and future information leaks into training data.

10.1 Approach 1: BETWEEN join (supported natively in many engines)

Engine: AnyDialect: ANSI SQLExecutable: Yes
SELECT p.*, d.plan_name, d.plan_price
FROM fact_playback p
JOIN dim_subscription_history d
  ON p.user_id = d.user_id
 AND p.event_ts >= d.valid_from
 AND p.event_ts <  d.valid_to;

Use half-open [valid_from, valid_to) and a far-future valid_to for current rows, not NULL, or they silently drop. With the user_id equality present, Spark does SMJ/BHJ on user_id and applies the range as a post-join filter — users with many versions multiply rows first. BNLJ is only for pure range joins; Databricks adds a RANGE_JOIN hint. Postgres hash-joins and filters, or nested-loops on a (user_id, valid_from) index.

10.2 Approach 2: LATERAL correlated subquery

Engine: PostgreSQLDialect: PostgreSQLExecutable: Yes — PostgreSQL (LATERAL + LIMIT); not BigQuery
SELECT p.*, d.plan_name
FROM fact_playback p,
LATERAL (
  SELECT plan_name
  FROM dim_subscription_history d
  WHERE d.user_id = p.user_id
    AND d.valid_from <= p.event_ts
  ORDER BY d.valid_from DESC
  LIMIT 1
) d;

Needs only valid_from. Excellent in OLTP with a (user_id, valid_from) index; a per-row probe at warehouse scale.

10.3 Approach 3: Spark SQL — union and carry the last value forward

OSS Spark SQL has no ASOF JOIN. The scalable pattern skips the join: put dimension changes and facts on one timeline per key, then fill forward.

Engine: Apache Spark 3.x / 4.x (Databricks too)Dialect: Spark SQLExecutable: Yes — Spark SQL
WITH timeline AS (
  SELECT user_id, event_ts AS ts, 1 AS is_fact, play_id, CAST(NULL AS STRING) AS plan_name
  FROM fact_playback
  UNION ALL
  SELECT user_id, valid_from AS ts, 0 AS is_fact, NULL AS play_id, plan_name
  FROM dim_subscription_history
),
filled AS (
  SELECT *,
    last(plan_name, true) OVER (             -- true = ignore NULLs
      PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY ts, is_fact   -- dim row sorts first on a tie
      ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS plan_asof
  FROM timeline
)
SELECT play_id, user_id, ts AS event_ts, plan_asof AS plan_name
FROM filled
WHERE is_fact = 1;

One shuffle and sort, no row explosion, >= semantics via the is_fact tiebreak. Caveats: a hot user is one partition; a real NULL plan_name is skipped — use a sentinel.

Native as-of syntax exists elsewhere: Snowflake ASOF JOIN … MATCH_CONDITION(p.event_ts >= d.valid_from) ON p.user_id = d.user_id, and DuckDB, ClickHouse and kdb+:

Engine: DuckDB (ClickHouse similar)Dialect: DuckDBExecutable: Yes — DuckDB only
-- DuckDB / ClickHouse ASOF JOIN
SELECT p.*, d.plan_name
FROM fact_playback p
ASOF LEFT JOIN dim_subscription_history d
  ON p.user_id = d.user_id AND p.event_ts >= d.valid_from;

10.4 Approach 4: "expand-and-join" (batch feature stores)

Precompute a daily snapshot per user and equi-join on (user_id, date): storage traded for a plain hash join.

11. Sketches: HyperLogLog, Theta, Bloom, t-digest, Count-Min

Exact COUNT(DISTINCT) shuffles every row. Sketches trade a bounded error (≈0.5–2% typical) for KB-sized, mergeable state: rollups combine sketches, not raw rows.

11.1 HyperLogLog (HLL) — approximate distinct count

Hash each element; per bucket, keep the longest run of leading zeros. Error ≈ 1.04/√m: m = 214 gives ≈0.8%. Defaults differ — Spark's approx_count_distinct uses 5% relative SD unless told otherwise. Trap: APPROX_COUNT_DISTINCT returns a number, and daily numbers don't add up to a monthly distinct count. Store and merge the sketch:

Engine: Snowflake (other engines in comments)Dialect: Snowflake SQLExecutable: Yes — Snowflake only
SELECT HLL(user_id) FROM fact_plays;                             -- approx distinct, one shot
CREATE TABLE daily_user_hll AS
  SELECT event_date, HLL_ACCUMULATE(user_id) AS hll_state       -- storable sketch
  FROM fact_plays GROUP BY event_date;
SELECT HLL_ESTIMATE(HLL_COMBINE(hll_state))                     -- month from daily sketches
FROM daily_user_hll
WHERE event_date BETWEEN '2026-04-01' AND '2026-04-30';

-- BigQuery:   HLL_COUNT.INIT per day, HLL_COUNT.MERGE across days
-- Spark 3.5+: hll_sketch_agg / hll_union_agg / hll_sketch_estimate
-- Trino:      approx_set / merge / cardinality

11.2 Theta sketch — distinct with set operations

HLL unions cleanly; Theta also intersects and subtracts — "watched X and Y" without raw data. Native in Apache Druid; elsewhere via Apache DataSketches libraries. Snowflake and BigQuery have no native Theta at time of writing (check current docs), and HLL intersection by inclusion–exclusion is very noisy for small overlaps.

11.3 Bloom filters — set membership

See 5.6.

11.4 t-digest / KLL / GK — approximate quantiles

One summary answers p50/p95/p99. Names and algorithms differ: Snowflake APPROX_PERCENTILE (t-digest; mergeable via _ACCUMULATE/_COMBINE), Trino approx_percentile, Spark percentile_approx (GK-family, accuracy 10000), BigQuery APPROX_QUANTILES.

Engine: Snowflake / TrinoDialect: Snowflake SQL, Trino SQLExecutable: Yes — each line on its own engine
-- Snowflake
SELECT APPROX_PERCENTILE(latency_ms, 0.99) FROM fact_requests;
-- Trino
SELECT approx_percentile(latency_ms, 0.99) FROM fact_requests;

11.5 Count-Min, and when (not) to reach for sketches

Count-Min estimates per-item frequency for heavy hitters (Snowflake APPROX_TOP_K, BigQuery APPROX_TOP_COUNT). Use sketches for rollups over billions of rows and batch+stream partials. Not for finance or regulatory numbers, small data, or decisions a 1–2% error would flip.

12. Anti-patterns that kill query plans

12.1 Function on the indexed column

Engine: Any (DATE() is MySQL/BigQuery/Spark; Postgres uses event_ts::date)Dialect: GenericExecutable: Illustrative — adapt to your dialect
-- Bad: index on event_ts not used
SELECT * FROM fact_plays WHERE DATE(event_ts) = '2026-04-15';
-- Good:
SELECT * FROM fact_plays
WHERE event_ts >= '2026-04-15' AND event_ts < '2026-04-16';

Same for partitions and zone maps: range-filter the stored column.

12.2 Implicit casts

Engine: Any (coercion rules differ per engine)Dialect: GenericExecutable: Illustrative — adapt to your dialect
-- Bad: the COLUMN side gets cast. account_code is VARCHAR.
SELECT * FROM fact_plays WHERE account_code = 1234;
--   Many engines cast account_code to a number on every row: index / zone-map
--   pruning is lost, and under Spark 4.0 ANSI mode a value like 'A-17'
--   makes the whole query fail instead of quietly not matching.
-- Good: compare like with like.
SELECT * FROM fact_plays WHERE account_code = '1234';
-- The reverse (user_id BIGINT = '1234') is usually harmless: the literal is coerced once.

12.3 SELECT *

Columnar I/O scales with columns read; SELECT * reads all 200 and breaks on schema change. Name columns.

12.4 DISTINCT as a bug fix

A query that "needs" DISTINCT usually has a join fan-out. Fix the join.

Interviewer pushes back

You: “Revenue is double-counted? I'll add DISTINCT and the duplicates go away.”

Interviewer: “Two different orders can have the same amount on the same day. And why are there duplicates at all?”

Strong answer: DISTINCT hides the bug, drops legitimate identical rows, and costs a full shuffle or sort. I check the grain: COUNT(*) vs COUNT(DISTINCT key) on each join input. Usually a dimension isn't unique on the join key — an SCD2 table joined without valid_from <= ts < valid_to, or a many-to-many bridge. I fix the join (add the validity predicate, or dedupe the dimension with ROW_NUMBER() = 1, or aggregate the many side before joining), then add a uniqueness test on the dimension key so it can't regress.

Weak answer: DISTINCT or GROUP BY every column — the number looks plausible and is still wrong.

12.5 OR across tables in a JOIN

Engine: AnyDialect: ANSI SQLExecutable: Yes (Postgres, Snowflake, BigQuery, Spark, DuckDB)
-- Slow: no single equi-key, so many engines fall back to a nested loop.
SELECT a.id AS a_id, b.id AS b_id
FROM a JOIN b ON a.x = b.x OR a.y = b.y;

-- Rewrite: one hash join per branch. Branch 2 excludes the pairs branch 1
-- already produced. UNION ALL keeps legitimate duplicates (UNION would drop them).
SELECT a.id AS a_id, b.id AS b_id FROM a JOIN b ON a.x = b.x
UNION ALL
SELECT a.id AS a_id, b.id AS b_id FROM a JOIN b ON a.y = b.y
WHERE NOT COALESCE(a.x = b.x, FALSE);   -- NULL-safe exclusion

The exclusion must mean exactly "branch 1 did not match". a.x <> b.x drops pairs where either x is NULL; IS DISTINCT FROM still drops pairs where both are NULL (never matched by =). Check the plan first — some optimizers do this expansion themselves.

12.6 NOT IN with nullable subquery

See 6.3. Use NOT EXISTS.

12.8 Correlated subquery in SELECT

Engine: AnyDialect: ANSI SQL (USING not in SQL Server)Executable: Yes
-- Bad only if the optimizer can't decorrelate (non-equality correlation, LIMIT);
-- Postgres/Spark/Snowflake usually rewrite this to the LEFT JOIN below.
SELECT user_id,
  (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM sessions s WHERE s.user_id = u.user_id) AS cnt
FROM dim_user u;

-- Explicit: one GROUP BY; COALESCE fixes the COUNT bug (0, not NULL)
SELECT u.user_id, COALESCE(s.cnt, 0) AS cnt
FROM dim_user u
LEFT JOIN (SELECT user_id, COUNT(*) AS cnt FROM sessions GROUP BY user_id) s
  USING (user_id);
Drill · Fix this broken SQL

The spec: "every user, with their order count since 1 Aug — including users with zero." dim_user has 3.4M rows. The report returns 1.2M rows and not one of them has orders_since = 0.

Engine: AnyDialect: ANSI SQLExecutable: Yes (and wrong)
SELECT u.user_id, COUNT(o.order_id) AS orders_since
FROM dim_user u
LEFT JOIN fact_orders o ON o.user_id = u.user_id
WHERE o.order_date >= DATE '2026-08-01'
GROUP BY u.user_id;

STOP. Answer before revealing.

Reveal the diagnosis
  1. Observe Row count equals the number of users with orders; zero-order users are missing entirely.
  2. Hypothesize Something is discarding NULL-extended rows from the LEFT JOIN.
  3. Measure The WHERE predicate is on the right table. For users with no orders, o.order_date is NULL, NULL >= date is unknown, and WHERE drops the row. Optimizers see this and literally plan an inner join.
  4. Isolate Remove the WHERE: 3.4M rows come back.
  5. Fix Move the right-table predicate into the join: LEFT JOIN fact_orders o ON o.user_id = u.user_id AND o.order_date >= DATE '2026-08-01'. COUNT(o.order_id) then yields 0 for unmatched users.
  6. Prevent A test that the output row count equals dim_user's; a lint rule flagging WHERE predicates on the nullable side of an outer join. Sibling bug: NOT IN over a nullable column returning zero rows (6.3).
Failure-first: what can fail in "correct-looking" SQL?
FailureDetectRecoverPrevent recurrence
Join fan-out (dimension not unique on key)Output grain check; totals exceed source reconciliationFix join predicate or dedupe dimension; restate affected outputsUniqueness test on every join key
NOT IN over a nullable columnSudden zero-row output; volume alertRewrite to NOT EXISTSLint rule; NOT NULL constraint or filter in subquery
OR-join rewrite drops rowsRow-count / sum parity vs the original queryUNION ALL + NULL-safe exclusionParity test required for every performance rewrite
Running total wrong on tied timestampsBalances "jump"; two runs disagreeROWS frame + unique tiebreakerDeterminism test: rerun, diff outputs
Implicit cast kills pruning, or fails under Spark 4 ANSIPartitions scanned jumps; cast errors after upgradeFix types at the source; try_cast where bad data is expectedTyped contracts and schema tests upstream

13. Query tuning workflow

  1. Confirm it's the query — not queueing, a cold cache or a busy warehouse.
  2. Read the plan with runtime stats and find the dominant operator.
  3. Scan? Pruning (5.7), functions or casts on filter columns, columns read.
  4. Join? Strategy, build side, estimated vs actual rows (stale stats), fan-out, skew (Part 04 §7).
  5. Sort / window / shuffle? PARTITION BY key, needless final ORDER BY, broadcastable side.
  6. I/O? Small files and spill; codecs matter less than pruning (Spark 4.0: Parquet snappy, ORC zstd).
  7. Change one thing, re-measure.

13.1 "When in doubt, measure" checklist

  • SELECT COUNT(*), COUNT(DISTINCT key) on each input: size, and whether the key is unique.
  • SELECT key, COUNT(*) FROM t GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 2 DESC LIMIT 20: hot keys, including NULL and 'unknown'.
  • SHOW CREATE TABLE / SHOW TBLPROPERTIES: partitioning, clustering, sort order.

13.2 A 3-minute triage

“How do you tune a slow query?”
30 sec

I don't guess. I confirm it's the query and not queueing or a cold cache, read the plan with runtime stats, find the one operator that dominates — scan, join, shuffle/sort, or spill — make the smallest change that removes that cost, and re-measure with the same profile.

2 min

How big are the inputs, and how many bytes and partitions were scanned vs expected? If the scan dominates, it's pruning: filter on the partition column, remove functions and casts on filter columns, fix clustering. If a join dominates: estimated vs actual rows, strategy and build side, fan-out, skew visible as one straggler task. If sort or window: the PARTITION BY key. I prefer changing the query shape or data layout over hints — pre-aggregate before the join, filter early, broadcast the small side — and I finish with a regression guard: bytes-scanned or runtime alert.

Deep dive

Engine specifics: Postgres EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS), misestimates from correlated columns (extended statistics), index-only scans. Snowflake Query Profile: partitions scanned vs total, spill to local vs remote storage, "exploding join", clustering depth. BigQuery: slot-ms, shuffle bytes, max vs average stage time for skew. Spark: task-time distribution per stage, AQE's final plan vs initial plan, PartitionFilters, spill. And the Staff-level move: sometimes it isn't a query problem — the table has the wrong grain or layout for its dominant access path, and the fix is a model change.

Where to stop: the loop plus one concrete fix per bottleneck type. Don't recite configuration keys.

Drill · Inspect this EXPLAIN plan

fact_plays is partitioned by event_date (three years, ~1,100 partitions). A one-day country report that should take a minute runs for 40. Here is the plan, trimmed.

Engine: Apache Spark 3.5 / 4.xLanguage: EXPLAIN output (trimmed)Executable: Illustrative — plan output, not code
AdaptiveSparkPlan isFinalPlan=false
+- HashAggregate(keys=[country], functions=[count(1)])
   +- Exchange hashpartitioning(country, 200)
      +- HashAggregate(keys=[country], functions=[partial_count(1)])
         +- SortMergeJoin [user_id], [user_id], Inner
            :- Sort [user_id ASC NULLS FIRST]
            :  +- Exchange hashpartitioning(user_id, 200)
            :     +- Filter (cast(event_ts as date) = 2026-04-15)
            :        +- FileScan parquet silver.fact_plays
            :             PartitionFilters: []
            :             PushedFilters: [IsNotNull(event_ts)]
            +- Sort [user_id ASC NULLS FIRST]
               +- Exchange hashpartitioning(user_id, 200)
                  +- Filter (signup_country_id = 42)
                     +- FileScan parquet silver.dim_user
                          PushedFilters: [EqualTo(signup_country_id,42)]

STOP. Answer before revealing.

Reveal the diagnosis
  1. Observe PartitionFilters: [] on a partitioned table. The date predicate sits in a Filter above the scan, on cast(event_ts as date), and was not pushed down.
  2. Hypothesize The query filters on a function of event_ts instead of the partition column, so all ~1,100 partitions are listed and read; the day's filter runs after the full scan.
  3. Measure SQL tab: files and bytes read for the fact scan vs one day's partition size.
  4. Isolate Add event_date = DATE'2026-04-15'; re-explain: PartitionFilters now lists it.
  5. Fix Filter on the partition column (keep an event_ts range if you need sub-day precision). Second finding: both sides are shuffled for a SortMergeJoin although dim_user filtered to one country is small. isFinalPlan=false means this is the pre-execution plan — check whether AQE switched to a broadcast at runtime; if not, fix stats or add /*+ BROADCAST(u) */.
  6. Prevent CI plan check that fails on PartitionFilters: [] for partitioned tables; on BigQuery, the table option require_partition_filter does this for you.

For the production variant — "same query went from 20 seconds to 11 minutes with no code change" — see the Debugging Lab, Part 19.

14. CTE Materialization — Inlined vs Cached

Some engines inline CTEs like views (referenced twice, run twice); some compute once and reuse.

Engine-by-engine behavior

EngineDefault behaviorOverride
Postgres ≤ 11Always materialized — an optimization fence; predicates don't push inRewrite as a subquery
Postgres ≥ 12Inlined if referenced once (and side-effect free); materialized if referenced more than onceAS MATERIALIZED / AS NOT MATERIALIZED
SnowflakeOptimizer decides; a multiply-referenced CTE can be computed once and reused (WithClause / WithReference in Query Profile)Temporary table to force it
BigQueryNon-recursive CTEs are not materialized: executed once per referenceCREATE TEMP TABLE in a script
Spark SQLInlined; identical shuffle subtrees can be deduplicated via ReusedExchange, but scans and filters before the shuffle may run twiceCACHE TABLE name AS SELECT …

The performance trap

If the expensive subtree appears twice in the plan, materialize it.

Engine: Snowflake / BigQuery / Postgres (temp-table syntax varies)Dialect: GenericExecutable: Illustrative — adapt to your dialect
-- Risky where CTEs are inlined: the heavy aggregate may run twice
WITH heavy AS (
  SELECT user_id, SUM(amount) AS amt FROM fact_orders WHERE ... GROUP BY user_id
)
SELECT ... FROM heavy h1 JOIN heavy h2 ON ...;

-- Deterministic: compute once, read twice
CREATE TEMP TABLE heavy AS
  SELECT user_id, SUM(amount) AS amt FROM fact_orders WHERE ... GROUP BY user_id;
SELECT ... FROM heavy h1 JOIN heavy h2 ON ...;
2026 Interview Note

Timeless concept: a CTE is a naming device, not a caching instruction. Version-specific: "CTEs are optimization fences" was true of Postgres through 11 and stopped being true in 12 (2019). Answers that still say it about Postgres date the candidate; answers that assume every engine materializes CTEs over-promise.

15. Materialized Views and Incremental Refresh

A cached result; the question is how it stays fresh and what that costs.

Full refresh

Recompute from scratch: always correct, cost scales with the base tables.

Incremental refresh

Apply only the delta — for restricted query shapes; outside them engines fall back to full refresh, often silently.

  • Snowflake: MVs are single-table, no joins; Dynamic Tables (GA 2024) handle joins, incrementally when the shape allows.
  • BigQuery: incremental for filters and aggregations; joins with restrictions — check current docs.
  • Databricks: MVs maintained by Lakeflow Spark Declarative Pipelines (formerly DLT), incremental when the shape allows.
  • Postgres: full refresh only (CONCURRENTLY avoids blocking readers); incremental via pg_ivm or triggers.

Lakehouse MERGE-based patterns

Compute the delta, MERGE INTO the output: a materialized view you own, schedule, and keep one-row-per-key (Part 07 §6).

16. Query Hints — Per-Engine Grammar

Use a hint only after measuring that the optimizer is wrong and the cause (stats, shape, layout) can't be fixed upstream.

Snowflake

No optimizer-hint syntax. USE_CACHED_RESULT and QUERY_TAG are session parameters, CLUSTER BY is DDL. Levers: query shape, clustering, Search Optimization, warehouse size.

BigQuery

Essentially no user-facing optimizer or join hints at time of writing (check current docs); GROUP BY ROLLUP is grouping syntax, not a hint. Levers: partition and cluster keys, early filters, pre-aggregation, temp tables, BI Engine, search indexes.

Spark SQL

OSS join hints: BROADCAST (aliases BROADCASTJOIN, MAPJOIN), MERGE (SHUFFLE_MERGE, MERGEJOIN), SHUFFLE_HASH, SHUFFLE_REPLICATE_NL — precedence in that order when both sides are hinted. Partition hints: COALESCE, REPARTITION, REPARTITION_BY_RANGE, REBALANCE (3.2+). SKEW and RANGE_JOIN are Databricks-only; AQE handles most skew (Part 04 §4). Most common legitimate use: BROADCAST on a dimension with stale stats.

Postgres

No hints by design — they rot as data changes; pg_hint_plan adds them. Prefer ANALYZE, extended statistics and indexes.

The meta-lesson

A hint is a smell. Fresh stats, an optimizer-friendly shape and a read plan come first; a hint as the first tuning move worries interviewers.

17. Window Function Choice — Examples by Intent

The wrong choice gives a plausible, wrong answer nothing will flag.

You want to…UseCommon wrong pickWhy it matters
Exactly N rows per group, ties broken arbitrarilyROW_NUMBER() + a tiebreaker in ORDER BYRANK()RANK can exceed N on ties; ROW_NUMBER needs a tiebreaker to be deterministic
Top-N including everything tied at NRANK() <= N (or FETCH FIRST N ROWS WITH TIES, Postgres 13+/Oracle, whole result only)DENSE_RANK() <= NDENSE_RANK returns every row of the top N distinct values
Rank labels without gapsDENSE_RANK()RANK()RANK gives 1,1,3; DENSE_RANK gives 1,1,2
Previous / next row per groupLAG(col, n) / LEAD(col, n)self-joinOne pass vs a join
Running totalSUM(col) OVER (… ORDER BY ts, id ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING)no frame + non-unique ORDER BYDefault RANGE frame gives tied rows the same total (7.3)
Trailing 7 calendar daysRANGE BETWEEN INTERVAL 6 DAYS PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW (Postgres 11+, DuckDB, Spark on date/timestamp keys — check version); BigQuery: RANGE 6 PRECEDING over UNIX_DATE(d); or densify firstROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROWWith missing days, 7 rows span more than 7 days
First / last value per groupFIRST_VALUE, or LAST_VALUE with an explicit frameLAST_VALUE with no frameSee 7.6
Percentile rank within groupPERCENT_RANK() / CUME_DIST() (tie-aware)NTILE(100), ROW_NUMBER()/COUNT(*)NTILE splits ties across buckets
Session number per userSUM(new_session_flag) OVER (PARTITION BY user ORDER BY ts)recursive CTERecursive is row-by-row (§9)
Nth most recent per groupROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY grp ORDER BY ts DESC) = NORDER BY ts DESC LIMIT NLIMIT applies to the whole result, not per group
Cumulative distinct countFirst-seen flag ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY key ORDER BY ts) = 1, then a running SUM of the flagCOUNT(DISTINCT col) OVER (…)Exact, one pass; Spark and Postgres reject DISTINCT window aggregates
Percent of total per groupcol / SUM(col) OVER (PARTITION BY grp)join to a grouped subqueryOne pass; watch integer division (§2 note)
L5 Interview CardSQL Deep Dive
Must know
  • Logical order FROM → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → WINDOW → QUALIFY → SELECT → DISTINCT → ORDER BY → LIMIT; the optimizer may reorder anything that preserves meaning.
  • Hash join O(N+M) with memory on the build side; sort-merge buffers duplicate-key runs; nested loop only without an equi-key or with an index.
  • Pruning (partitions, zone maps, Bloom, runtime filters) usually matters more than join choice, and needs layout plus a filter on the stored column.
  • NULL semantics: NOT IN with a NULL returns nothing; <> drops NULL rows; WHERE on the right side of a LEFT JOIN makes it inner.
  • Default frame with ORDER BY is RANGE to the current row and its peers; LAST_VALUE needs an explicit frame; ROWS ≠ calendar days.
  • RANK() <= N for top-N with ties; DENSE_RANK() <= N returns N distinct values.
  • Sketches: store mergeable state, not APPROX_COUNT_DISTINCT numbers.
  • Dialect literacy: what is not portable (QUALIFY, SEMI JOIN, GROUPS, LATERAL+LIMIT, ASOF JOIN, hints, sketch APIs, NULL ordering, integer division, Spark 4 ANSI).
Must be able to explain
  1. Why can't WHERE reference a window function, and what do you do instead?
  2. Why does a running total "jump" on tied timestamps?
  3. Why is DISTINCT the wrong fix for duplicated revenue?
Must be able to draw

A two-table join plan bottom-up — scans with pruning, the exchange, build vs probe, aggregate, sort, limit — and mark where filters were pushed.

Limit ← Sort ← Aggregate ← HashJoin
                          ├ probe: fact scan (pruned)
                          └ build: dim scan (filtered)
Must be able to code
  • Sessionization with LAG + running SUM, including the midnight boundary.
  • Gaps and islands via ROW_NUMBER difference.
  • A point-in-time (as-of) join three ways: range join, LATERAL, union + fill-forward.
Must be able to debug
  • A performance rewrite of an OR join under-reports revenue: UNION dropped identical rows and <> dropped NULLs. Fix with UNION ALL + NULL-safe exclusion and a parity test.
  • A one-day query scans three years: PartitionFilters: [] because the filter wraps event_ts in a cast instead of using event_date.
Numbers that matter
  • Hash build side: ~50–200 bytes/row, so 10M rows ≈ 0.5–2 GB.
  • Bloom filter: ~10 bits per element for 1% FP (10M keys ≈ 12 MB).
  • HLL: error ≈ 1.04/√m; 214 registers ≈ 0.8%, state in KB.
  • B-tree: fanout in the hundreds → ~4 levels for 108 rows.
  • Pruning is multiplicative: 1 day of 1,100 partitions is ~0.1% of the bytes.
Classic traps
  • A CTE referenced twice runs twice where CTEs are inlined (BigQuery; partly Spark).
  • ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING sold as "7 days".
  • "I'd add an index" in a columnar warehouse with no indexes.
30-second answer

How does a SQL engine execute your query, and how do you make it fast and correct? The engine turns declarative SQL into a physical plan: scans with pruning, joins chosen by size and key (hash, sort-merge, nested loop), exchanges, aggregates and sorts. I make it correct first — grain, NULL semantics, deterministic ordering — then fast by reading the plan and removing the dominant cost: usually bytes scanned, then the biggest join or shuffle.

2-minute answer

Correctness: I check each join's grain so nothing fans out, use NOT EXISTS over NOT IN, keep right-table predicates of a LEFT JOIN in the ON clause, and give window functions explicit ROWS frames and unique tiebreakers. Execution: the logical order defines meaning, but the optimizer pushes filters into scans, picks build and probe sides, and in distributed engines shuffles by join and group keys. Speed: I confirm it's not queueing or cache, read the plan with runtime stats, and classify the bottleneck. A scan problem is pruning — filter the partition column, no functions on filter columns, cluster on the access path. A join problem is strategy, stats, fan-out or skew. A sort or window problem is the partition key. I change one thing, re-measure, and add a regression guard. I also say which parts are dialect-specific — QUALIFY, hints, NULL ordering, Spark 4's ANSI casts — because the same SQL is not the same query across engines.

Deep-dive follow-up

“Your as-of join between 5B plays and a 50M-row subscription history is the slowest stage. Walk me through three implementations and pick one for Spark.”

Staff+ follow-up

“Analysts across three engines keep reinventing the same metrics with subtly different SQL. How do you make 'active users' mean one thing — and prove it — without freezing everyone's velocity?”
