Part 06

Python for Data Engineering

Quick refresh10 minInterview study35 minDeep practice60 min
Last technically reviewed September 2026
Covers GIL and concurrency, memory, pandas / Polars / DuckDB / PySpark, Arrow, generators, asyncio, multiprocessing, validation, testing, packaging, profiling
Versions referenced CPython 3.12–3.14 (3.14 current; 3.15 due Oct 2026), pandas 3.0, Polars 1.x, DuckDB 1.x, Pydantic 2.x, PySpark 4.x, Airflow 3.x, uv
Primary references Python free-threading · PEP 779 · pandas Copy-on-Write · Polars · DuckDB · uv
Known implementation differences GIL, GC, default multiprocessing start method and pandas copy semantics all changed between 3.12 and 3.14 / pandas 2 and 3 — say which version you mean.

Not CPython trivia. The interviewer is testing whether you can tell I/O-bound from CPU-bound, keep memory bounded on inputs bigger than RAM, pick the smallest engine that meets the SLA, and ship tested, reproducible code.

1. The Python execution model that matters for DE

Three layers matter: the interpreter (bytecode, one eval loop), refcounting plus a cyclic GC, and the C/Rust extension layer (NumPy, PyArrow, Polars, DuckDB) where the heavy work runs, usually without the GIL. You don't make data code fast by writing better Python loops. You make it fast by getting the loop out of Python.

2026 Interview Note

3.11's specializing interpreter (PEP 659) sped up pure-Python loops; 3.13 added an experimental JIT, off by default. The timeless point stands: a per-row Python loop is still orders of magnitude slower than a vectorized engine.

2. The GIL — what it actually locks

The Global Interpreter Lock lets only one thread execute Python bytecode at a time. It protects interpreter state (chiefly refcounts), not your data.

2.1 What it blocks — and what it doesn't

  • Pure-Python CPU work on threads: no speedup. Threads take turns (switch interval 5 ms).
  • I/O on threads: real speedup. Socket reads, file I/O and time.sleep release the GIL while blocked.
  • C/Rust extensions: depends. Polars, DuckDB, PyArrow and most NumPy kernels release it and run multi-threaded. pandas releases it only in some Cython kernels; much of a merge or groupby holds it, so thread scaling is modest.

2.2 Free-threaded Python (PEP 703 → PEP 779)

The free-threaded build replaces the GIL with atomic/biased refcounting and per-object locks. 3.13 shipped it as experimental; 3.14 made it officially supported but optional (PEP 779): a separate python3.14t, while the default build keeps the GIL.

2026 Interview Note

Timeless: threads don't speed up pure-Python CPU work on a GIL build. Version-specific: on 3.14t they can, at a single-thread cost the 3.14 docs put at roughly 5–10%. Importing a C extension not marked free-threading-safe re-enables the GIL (check sys._is_gil_enabled()), so check cp314t wheels for every native dependency. It is not the default in 3.14 or 3.15, and it exposes races the GIL used to hide. 3.14 also adds subinterpreters (InterpreterPoolExecutor).

2.3 The shortcut: concurrent.futures

Engine: CPython stdlibLanguage: Python 3.8+Executable: Illustrative — fetch_url / crunch are yours
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor, ProcessPoolExecutor

with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=32) as ex:     # I/O-bound: GIL released while waiting
    pages = list(ex.map(fetch_url, urls))

with ProcessPoolExecutor(max_workers=8) as ex:     # pure-Python CPU-bound: one GIL per process
    results = list(ex.map(crunch, chunks, chunksize=16))
“Does the GIL matter for data engineering?”
30 sec

Less than people think. It serializes Python bytecode, not I/O and not the C/Rust engines doing the work. Most pipeline time is network waits or Polars/DuckDB/Arrow/Spark compute. It bites on per-row Python CPU loops: parsing, custom transforms, Python UDFs.

2 min

Classify first. I/O-bound: threads or asyncio. Vectorized: already multi-core. Pure-Python CPU: vectorize, else processes (paying for pickling), else pilot 3.14t. PySpark Python UDFs run in separate worker processes, so their limit is JVM↔Python serialization, not the GIL; built-ins or Arrow pandas UDFs fix it (Part 04).

Deep dive

3.13t experimental → 3.14t supported, optional (PEP 779). One unsafe extension re-enables the GIL, so assert sys._is_gil_enabled() in production; shared dicts and counters stop being accidentally safe.

Where to stop: don't recite the switch interval or bytecode unless asked. The signal is classifying the workload.

Interviewer pushes back

You: “I'd use multiprocessing to speed up downloading these 20,000 S3 objects.”

Interviewer: “Why processes?”

Strong answer: “Actually, I wouldn't: it's I/O-bound, and threads release the GIL on sockets. Processes add memory, pickling and fork-safety problems for nothing. A thread pool sharing one boto3 client (clients are thread-safe; sessions aren't), or asyncio with a semaphore, tuned against the real ceilings: NIC bandwidth, S3 per-prefix request rates, throttling. Processes only if each object then needs CPU-heavy parsing.”

Weak answer: “Python has a GIL, so parallelism always means processes.”

3. Memory: refcounting, GC, and the bytes you don't see

What a candidate needs: every Python object carries a 16-byte header (refcount + type pointer), so a column of Python objects costs an 8-byte pointer plus ~30–60 bytes per value, while Arrow costs the payload plus 4–8 bytes of offsets. 10M short strings: roughly 0.6 GB against ~100 MB. That order-of-magnitude gap is the argument for columnar.

3.1 Refcounting and the cyclic GC

An object is freed the moment its refcount hits zero; only reference cycles wait for the cyclic GC. If memory keeps growing, the cause is almost always a reference you still hold, not the GC.

2026 Interview Note

Through 3.13 the cyclic GC has three generations (gc.set_threshold; defaults changed across versions). 3.14 made it incremental with young/old generations, shortening pauses, and threshold semantics changed, so re-check any gc tuning on upgrade. gc.disable()/gc.freeze() can help allocation-heavy batch jobs; measure first.

3.2 Memory profiling

Engine: CPython stdlib tracemallocLanguage: Python 3.4+Executable: Yes
import tracemalloc
tracemalloc.start()
before = tracemalloc.take_snapshot()
run_one_batch()                                   # your code
after = tracemalloc.take_snapshot()
for stat in after.compare_to(before, "lineno")[:10]:
    print(stat)                                   # which lines grew, and by how much

Diffing snapshots over time is the leak-hunting move. tracemalloc sees Python allocations only; use memray for native memory (Arrow, NumPy) (§12).

3.3 The __slots__ lever

__slots__ (or @dataclass(slots=True)) drops the per-instance __dict__ (lazily materialized since 3.11) and still shrinks small objects noticeably. Holding 10M small objects? The better fix is an Arrow table.

Drill · Python memory

A Python ingestion job (API pages → transform → Parquet) grows in memory until the container is OOM-killed after ~6 hours (exit 137). A restart "fixes" it for another 6.

STOP. Answer before revealing.

Reveal the diagnosis
  1. Observe Plot RSS against records processed. A monotonic slope means accumulation. Does it steepen when the sink is slow? Then suspect retry buffering.
  2. Hypothesize (1) Unbounded accumulation: results.append or a list where a generator belongs; a "seen ids" set that never expires. (2) pandas copies: df = pd.concat([df, chunk]) in a loop. (3) Leaked references: lru_cache without maxsize, a module-level response dict, stored exceptions pinning frames. (4) Retries buffering: failed pages parked in memory, an unbounded asyncio.Queue, gather over every page. (5) Allocator fragmentation.
  3. Measure tracemalloc snapshot diffs every 15 min; memray on a replayed hour; queue, cache and retry-list lengths as metrics.
  4. Isolate Replay fixed input locally, disabling stages one at a time. Flat Python heap but growing RSS means native memory or fragmentation.
  5. Fix Stream end to end (generators, batched, write and drop each batch). Bound everything: Queue(maxsize=…), lru_cache(maxsize=…), windowed or external dedup state, a capped retry buffer that spills to a DLQ. Append Parquet files instead of concatenating. Fragmentation: MALLOC_ARENA_MAX=2 or jemalloc.
  6. Prevent A CI peak-memory budget on a fixed fixture, an alert on RSS slope, and checkpoints so a restart resumes instead of reprocessing six hours.

4. Pandas vs Polars vs DuckDB vs PySpark — the trade math

4.1 The honest comparison

Dimensionpandas 3PolarsDuckDBPySpark
EngineNumPy + Arrow (strings Arrow-backed by default)Rust on ArrowC++ vectorized SQL, in-processJVM cluster; Arrow at the Python boundary
ExecutionEagerLazy (scan_*) or eagerLazy SQL plansLazy, distributed
ParallelismMostly one coreAll coresAll coresMany nodes
Bigger than RAMNo (chunk by hand)Streaming engine (not every op)Spills to diskSpills and distributes
Sweet spotSmall data, ecosystem glueSingle-node DataFrame pipelinesSingle-node SQL, CI data checksBeyond one node, shuffle-heavy joins
Python UDFsSlow (per row)Slow; expressions are fastSlow; SQL is fastUse built-ins or Arrow pandas UDFs

4.2 Speed math (orders of magnitude, hypothetical)

10 GB CSV → group by → Parquet on a laptop: pandas, minutes if it fits at all; Polars streaming or DuckDB, tens of seconds; PySpark local, a minute or two of mostly JVM and task overhead. Rule of thumb: if it fits on one machine, including out-of-core via Polars streaming or DuckDB spilling, single-node wins. Reach for Spark when data volume, concurrency or SLAs exceed one node, or when the platform already runs Spark.

“When would you use Polars or DuckDB instead of Spark?”
30 sec

When the job fits one machine, including out-of-core, and doesn't need a cluster's fault tolerance: a big node handles hundreds of GB with no JVM, shuffle or cluster to run. Spark when data or SLA outgrow one node, or for shuffle-heavy joins of two very large tables.

2 min

Numbers first: bytes scanned after projection and pruning, peak working set of the largest join or aggregation, the SLA. If one node reads the pruned input in minutes and join state fits or spills, single-node is cheaper, simpler, and runs in CI. DuckDB for SQL-shaped work and checks; Polars for DataFrame pipelines. Name the costs: a single-node job fails as a unit (no per-task retry, no spot tolerance), and scale-out moves across jobs (one partition per orchestrator task).

Deep dive

Out-of-core isn't free: Polars streaming doesn't cover every operation (unsupported parts run in memory; inspect the plan), and spill-heavy DuckDB runs slow sharply. Both read Iceberg/Delta well; commit and maintenance support depends on library and version, so check before making them the writer. Common hybrid: Spark for heavy bronze→silver, DuckDB/Polars for gold marts and tests.

Where to stop: sizing logic and the failure-mode trade-off, not benchmark war stories.

Interviewer pushes back

You: “pandas is fine here, it's only 40 GB.”

Interviewer: “How much RAM will that take?”

Strong answer: “40 GB of what? Compressed Parquet expands several times when decoded, CSV in pandas takes a multiple of file size, and merge/groupby add intermediates, so peak could be several times 40 GB. I'd shrink the problem first (needed columns only, filters in the scan, Arrow dtypes), then use Polars scan_parquet with streaming or DuckDB, which push down and spill. If the pruned working set still exceeds one node, that's Spark.”

Weak answer: “We'll get a bigger machine” with no estimate, or “switch to Spark” by reflex.

4.3 pandas traps: copies and chained assignment

Engine: pandas 3.xLanguage: Python 3.11+Executable: Yes
df2 = df[df["x"] > 0]          # boolean mask: always a new object
df2["y"] = 1                   # changes df2 only, never df
df[df["x"] > 0]["y"] = 2       # chained assignment: never writes through (warns)
df.loc[df["x"] > 0, "y"] = 3   # the one correct way to update df in place
2026 Interview Note

pandas 2.x offered Copy-on-Write as an opt-in; pandas 3.0 makes it mandatory (the mode.copy_on_write option is a deprecated no-op), so chained assignment never writes through and defensive .copy() is mostly dead weight. 3.0 also defaults strings to the Arrow-backed str dtype. On pandas <3, SettingWithCopyWarning ambiguity is still real.

4.4 Polars: lazy plans

Engine: Polars 1.25+Language: Python 3.9+Executable: Yes — needs S3 credentials, or point it at a local path
import polars as pl

top = (pl.scan_parquet("s3://bucket/events/*.parquet")   # lazy: nothing read yet
         .filter(pl.col("event_date") == pl.date(2026, 4, 15))  # Date, not a string
         .group_by("country")
         .agg(pl.col("watch_ms").sum().alias("total_ms"))
         .sort("total_ms", descending=True)
         .head(10))
result = top.collect(engine="streaming")   # out-of-core where supported

The filter and projection are pushed into the Parquet scan. Comparing a Date column to a string raises InvalidOperationError; Polars doesn't guess types.

2026 Interview Note

collect(streaming=True) was deprecated in Polars 1.25 for collect(engine="streaming") on a new streaming engine. Concept unchanged: a lazy plan executed in batches, memory bounded by batch, not input.

4.5 PySpark

Never iterate row by row in Python over a Spark DataFrame. Use built-in functions first, Arrow-backed pandas UDFs second, and toPandas() only for small results. The JVM↔Python mechanics are in Part 04 §12.

5. The Arrow boundary: zero-copy between worlds

Arrow is a columnar in-memory format with a stable C ABI. Inside one process, Arrow libraries share buffers with no copy (C Data Interface / PyCapsule). Across processes (Spark JVM → Python worker) it is Arrow IPC: bytes are copied, but no per-cell objects.

5.1 Why it matters

5.2 Who speaks Arrow

PyArrow, Polars, DuckDB, DataFusion, pandas (Arrow dtypes), Spark (pandas UDFs, toPandas, Spark Connect), Snowpark, BigQuery Storage API; PyIceberg and delta-rs return Arrow. Parquet/ORC readers decode into Arrow: fast, but not zero-copy.

5.3 The composition pattern

Engine: DuckDB 1.x + Polars 1.xLanguage: Python 3.9+Executable: Illustrative — needs S3 credentials (DuckDB httpfs / secret) and your regions frame
import duckdb, polars as pl

revenue = duckdb.sql("""
    SELECT region, SUM(amount) AS rev
    FROM read_parquet('s3://bucket/orders/*.parquet')
    WHERE order_ts >= CURRENT_DATE - INTERVAL 30 DAY
    GROUP BY region
""").pl()                                   # result materialized once, handed over as Arrow

top = revenue.join(regions, on="region").sort("rev", descending=True)
check = duckdb.sql("SELECT count(*) FROM top WHERE rev < 0")   # DuckDB scans the Polars frame in place

DuckDB scans a Polars, Arrow or pandas frame in place by variable name; .pl()/.arrow() build the result once as Arrow. SQL where SQL is clearer, expressions where DataFrames are, no serialization between them.

5.4 The strings caveat

Arrow strings are an offsets array plus one character buffer; object-dtype str columns convert one value at a time, never zero-copy. pandas 3.0's Arrow-backed default removes most of this (on 2.x, dtype_backend="pyarrow"). NumPy-backed numerics may still copy.

6. Generators, iterators, and chunked I/O

Bounded memory is a design property: each stage pulls one item or batch at a time; nothing collects "all of it".

6.1 Generator pipelines

Engine: CPython stdlibLanguage: Python 3.12+ (itertools.batched)Executable: Yes — write_batch is yours
import json
from itertools import batched            # 3.12+; strict= added in 3.13

def read_lines(path):
    with open(path) as f:
        yield from f

def parse(lines):
    for line in lines:
        yield json.loads(line)

def recent(records, since):
    return (r for r in records if r["ts"] >= since)

records = recent(parse(read_lines("events.jsonl")), since=1_767_225_600)
for batch in batched(records, 5_000):    # one batch in memory at a time
    write_batch(batch)                   # e.g. a Parquet row group

Memory is O(batch), whatever the file size. Pre-3.12, write batched with islice. Same shape: pd.read_csv(chunksize=), ParquetFile.iter_batches().

6.2 itertools — the standard toolbelt

batched, islice, chain; groupby groups adjacent keys only, so sort first.

6.3 Async generators

async def + yield, consumed with async for, fits a paginated API: fetch the next page only when the consumer asks. Pages within one cursor are inherently sequential.

7. Async/await for I/O-bound DE work

7.1 The mental model

One thread runs an event loop; coroutines yield at await, so others run while one waits on a socket. A coroutine costs ~1–2 KB; an OS thread reserves a multi-MB virtual stack (8 MB default on Linux) plus scheduler cost. So asyncio scales to thousands of concurrent requests more cheaply than threads, and far more cheaply than processes. Below a few hundred connections a thread pool is about as fast and simpler.

7.2 Bounded, retrying, cancellable

Engine: CPython asyncioLanguage: Python 3.11+ (TaskGroup, asyncio.timeout)Executable: Yes — with any async client (httpx.AsyncClient, aiohttp) and your TransientError
import asyncio, random

async def fetch_with_retry(client, url, sem, attempts=5):
    for attempt in range(attempts):
        async with sem:                              # bound in-flight requests
            try:
                async with asyncio.timeout(10):
                    return await client.get(url)
            except (TransientError, TimeoutError):
                if attempt == attempts - 1:
                    raise
        await asyncio.sleep(min(30, 0.5 * 2**attempt) * random.random())  # jittered backoff, outside the semaphore

async def fetch_all(client, urls, concurrency=20):
    sem = asyncio.Semaphore(concurrency)
    async with asyncio.TaskGroup() as tg:            # one failure cancels the siblings
        tasks = [tg.create_task(fetch_with_retry(client, u, sem)) for u in urls]
    return [t.result() for t in tasks]

Bare gather(*10_000 coroutines) has no backpressure and one failure doesn't cancel the rest. Retries need an idempotent sink (keyed upsert, or a deterministic path per page) or they double-count. For millions of URLs, feed a bounded asyncio.Queue(maxsize=…) to N workers instead of one task per URL.

S3 inventory, corrected. The tempting version creates an S3 client per task, has no semaphore, and claims "~80 ms total". Share one client (aioboto3), bound concurrency with the same semaphore pattern, and do the maths honestly: pages within a prefix are sequential (each needs the previous continuation token), so total time ≈ the slowest prefix's page count × per-call latency. Parallelism comes only from spreading across prefixes.

7.3 The mistake: blocking the loop

time.sleep, requests.get, sync boto3 or psycopg2 inside a coroutine freezes every coroutine: p99 jumps to seconds, Kafka consumers miss heartbeats. Use httpx.AsyncClient/aiohttp, aioboto3, asyncpg; asyncio debug mode logs slow callbacks.

7.4 Running blocking code from async

await asyncio.to_thread(fn, arg) (3.9+) for blocking I/O; loop.run_in_executor(process_pool, fn, arg) for CPU work.

7.5 When NOT to use async

CPU-bound work (it holds the loop hostage), code with no concurrency need, Spark transformations, or when a key dependency has no async client.

8. Multiprocessing patterns that work in production

8.1 ProcessPoolExecutor

For pure-Python CPU work you can't vectorize. chunksize: too small pays IPC per item, too large makes stragglers; start near items / (workers × 4). Arguments and results are pickled, so send paths or keys, not DataFrames.

8.2 Shared memory (Python 3.8+)

multiprocessing.shared_memory lets workers attach to one NumPy/Arrow buffer by name instead of pickling it. Workers close() after dropping their array views; the creator also unlink()s in a finally, or the segment leaks in /dev/shm (small by default in containers). Often simpler: write Parquet/Arrow IPC to local disk and memory-map it.

8.3 The fork vs spawn gotcha

fork copies the parent, including locks held by other threads, so a parent with a boto3 client, logging handler or DB pool can fork a child that deadlocks intermittently. Create clients after the fork, or pass mp_context=get_context("spawn"|"forkserver") explicitly so laptop and production match.

2026 Interview Note

Linux defaulted to fork through 3.13; from 3.14 the default is forkserver. Safer, but workers and arguments must now be picklable and importable (as on macOS/Windows), and code relying on fork-inherited globals can break on upgrade. 3.12+ warns when forking a multi-threaded process.

9. Type hints, dataclasses, and runtime data validation

9.1 Dataclasses: structure, not validation

Engine: CPython stdlibLanguage: Python 3.10+ (slots=True)Executable: Yes
from dataclasses import dataclass, field
from datetime import datetime, timezone

@dataclass(frozen=True, slots=True)
class PlaybackEvent:
    user_id: int
    title_id: int
    event_ts: datetime
    watch_ms: int = 0
    metadata: dict = field(default_factory=dict)

ev = PlaybackEvent(1, 42, datetime.now(timezone.utc))
ev.metadata["k"] = "v"    # allowed: frozen is shallow
hash(ev)                  # TypeError: unhashable type: 'dict'

frozen=True is shallow: it blocks reassignment, but the dict stays mutable and makes hash() raise. Use tuple/frozenset fields for a truly immutable record. And dataclasses don't validate: PlaybackEvent("x", …) is accepted.

9.2 Pydantic for runtime validation

Engine: Pydantic 2.xLanguage: Python 3.9+Executable: Yes — raw / raw_rows are your input
from datetime import datetime, timezone
from pydantic import AwareDatetime, BaseModel, Field, TypeAdapter, field_validator

class PlaybackEvent(BaseModel):
    user_id: int = Field(gt=0)
    title_id: int = Field(gt=0)
    event_ts: AwareDatetime                          # naive timestamps rejected
    watch_ms: int = Field(ge=0, le=24 * 3600 * 1000)

    @field_validator("event_ts")
    @classmethod
    def not_future(cls, v: datetime) -> datetime:
        if v > datetime.now(timezone.utc):           # not utcnow(): deprecated, naive
            raise ValueError("event_ts in the future")
        return v

ev = PlaybackEvent.model_validate(raw)               # raises ValidationError with the field path
rows = TypeAdapter(list[PlaybackEvent]).validate_python(raw_rows)   # a whole batch

datetime.utcnow() (deprecated in 3.12) is naive: comparing it with an aware value raises TypeError, and mixing them silently shifts by the UTC offset. Pydantic v2's Rust core handles per-record ingestion; at millions of rows a second, validate batches or the Arrow schema instead.

9.3 Three levels of contract

LevelToolUse for
1. Static shapedataclass / attrs + mypyInternal structures you control
2. Runtime validationPydantic BaseModel / TypeAdapterAPI ingestion, config, DLQ replays: anything from outside
3. Cross-service contractAvro/Protobuf + schema registryProducers and consumers in different languages; the source of truth lives outside Python (Part 15)

9.4 Type-checking pipelines

mypy (or pyright) and ruff in pre-commit and CI, blocking merges. They catch the str-vs-date bug before a 3 a.m. backfill does.

10. Testing strategy for data pipelines

Test logic on tiny hand-written data; test data on real data, every run. Different jobs.

10.1 The pyramid

10.2 Pure-function units and property tests

Engine: pytest + Hypothesis 6.xLanguage: Python 3.10+Executable: Yes — and the property test fails, on purpose
from hypothesis import given, strategies as st

def normalize_country(raw: str | None) -> str:
    if raw is None:
        return "UNK"
    return raw.strip().upper()[:3]

def test_normalize_country_examples():
    assert normalize_country(" gb ") == "GB"
    assert normalize_country(None) == "UNK"

@given(st.text(max_size=20))
def test_normalize_country_idempotent(s):
    once = normalize_country(s)
    assert normalize_country(once) == once

The examples pass; the property fails. Hypothesis shrinks to something like "a b" → "A " → "A": truncating after strip() leaves trailing whitespace. Fix: raw.strip().upper()[:3].rstrip(), and the property passes. That is the point of property tests: they find what examples miss, and idempotence is exactly the property reruns depend on.

10.3 PySpark step tests

Engine: PySpark 3.5+ / 4.xLanguage: Python 3.10+Executable: Yes — with your dedupe_events
import pytest
from pyspark.sql import SparkSession
from pyspark.testing import assertDataFrameEqual     # built in since Spark 3.5
from my_pipeline.silver import dedupe_events

@pytest.fixture(scope="session")
def spark():
    return SparkSession.builder.master("local[2]").getOrCreate()

def test_dedupe_keeps_latest(spark):
    cols = ["user_id", "event_id", "event_ts", "value"]
    df = spark.createDataFrame([
        ("u1", "e1", "2026-01-01T10:00:00", 100),
        ("u1", "e1", "2026-01-01T10:00:01", 200),   # later wins
        ("u2", "e2", "2026-01-01T10:00:00", 50)], cols)
    expected = spark.createDataFrame([
        ("u1", "e1", "2026-01-01T10:00:01", 200),
        ("u2", "e2", "2026-01-01T10:00:00", 50)], cols)
    assertDataFrameEqual(dedupe_events(df), expected)   # row order ignored by default

chispa does the same on older Spark. Session-scope the fixture: JVM startup dominates test time.

10.4 dbt data tests

Engine: dbt 1.8+Language: YAMLExecutable: Yes — dbt ≥1.8 (data_tests:; older versions use tests:)
models:
  - name: silver_playback_session
    columns:
      - name: session_id
        data_tests: [unique, not_null]
      - name: user_id
        data_tests:
          - not_null
          - relationships:
              to: ref('dim_user')
              field: user_id

10.5 Data tests vs code tests

Code tests prevent regressions in your logic; data tests (dbt, Great Expectations, Soda) catch changes in their data. You need both (Part 12).

11. Packaging and deploying to Spark / Lambda / Airflow

11.1 Project layout, tooling and lockfiles

src/my_pipeline/ (bronze/silver/gold), tests/, thin dags/; all logic in the tested package.

Engine: PEP 621 build (hatchling)Language: TOMLExecutable: Yes
[project]
name = "my-pipeline"
version = "0.4.2"
requires-python = ">=3.12"
dependencies = ["pyarrow>=17", "pandas>=2.2", "pydantic>=2.6"]

[project.optional-dependencies]
dev = ["pyspark>=4.0,<5", "pytest", "hypothesis", "mypy", "ruff"]   # the cluster provides pyspark

[build-system]
requires = ["hatchling"]
build-backend = "hatchling.build"

Tooling: pip has a real resolver but no native lock workflow (pip-tools, or the experimental pip lock → PEP 751 pylock.toml); fine for scripts, drifts in teams. Poetry: lockfile, well understood, slower on big graphs; stay if it works. uv: fast, uv.lock, manages Python versions; the common default for new projects, though moving from Poetry is a migration, not a drop-in. Whatever the tool, dependencies go in one image layer and code in the next. A common broken version runs uv sync before the source exists and then runs the system Python instead of the venv:

Engine: Docker + uvLanguage: DockerfileExecutable: Yes — needs a src-layout project with uv.lock
FROM python:3.13-slim
RUN pip install uv
WORKDIR /app
COPY pyproject.toml uv.lock ./
RUN uv sync --frozen --no-dev --no-install-project   # layer 1: deps only (changes rarely)
COPY src/ ./src/
RUN uv sync --frozen --no-dev                        # layer 2: install the project itself
ENV PATH="/app/.venv/bin:$PATH"                      # run the venv's python, not the system one
CMD ["python", "-m", "my_pipeline.main"]

11.2 Distributing to Spark

Every executor needs the same environment. Three approaches: (1) bake it into the image (most reproducible); (2) --py-files with a .zip/.whl, pure Python only; (3) a packed env (venv-pack/conda-pack) via --archives. Spark Connect can add artifacts at runtime (addArtifacts).

Engine: spark-submit (YARN / Kubernetes)Language: bashExecutable: Yes — cluster deploy mode
venv-pack -o env.tar.gz
spark-submit --deploy-mode cluster \
  --archives env.tar.gz#environment \
  --conf spark.pyspark.python=./environment/bin/python \
  app.py
# client mode: ./environment exists only on executors — don't point the driver at it

11.3 Airflow

The DAG orchestrates; it doesn't compute. Operators call Spark, dbt or a container; logic stays in the tested library.

Engine: Airflow 3.xLanguage: Python 3 (versions per the Airflow 3.x support matrix)Executable: Yes — Airflow 3.x only (2.x: from airflow import DAG, airflow.operators.python)
from datetime import datetime
from airflow.sdk import DAG
from airflow.providers.standard.operators.python import PythonOperator
from my_pipeline.jobs import submit_bronze            # logic lives in the library

with DAG("playback_pipeline", start_date=datetime(2026, 1, 1), schedule="@daily"):
    PythonOperator(task_id="bronze", python_callable=submit_bronze)

11.4 Lambda / serverless

For event-driven enrichment and fan-out. At time of writing (2026) AWS limits zip packages (with layers) to 250 MB unzipped and container images to 10 GB; check current docs. Import time is cold-start time, and pandas + PyArrow are heavy. SnapStart now covers Python 3.12+; beware state restored from the snapshot (random seeds, connections, credentials).

12. Performance debugging toolkit

12.1 Profilers

Engine: cProfile, py-spy, memray, line_profilerLanguage: bashExecutable: Yes — Linux; py-spy on a live PID may need CAP_SYS_PTRACE / sudo
python -m cProfile -s cumulative job.py | head -40   # deterministic, per function
py-spy record -o profile.svg --pid <PID>             # sampling flamegraph, no code change
py-spy dump --pid <PID>                              # what is every thread doing right now?
memray run -o out.bin job.py && memray flamegraph out.bin   # native + Python allocations
kernprof -lv job.py                                  # line-level; decorate with @profile

py-spy reads the target's memory from outside the process, so it is safe on a stuck production job, but it sees Python frames only: in PySpark, the Python driver process and workers. For the JVM use jstack, async-profiler, the Spark UI.

12.2 DataFrame performance checklist

  • Object dtype where Arrow belongs? Check .dtypes.
  • Row-wise .apply()? Replace it with vectorized expressions, .map(dict) or a join.
  • On pandas <3, defensive .copy()? pandas ≥3 is always Copy-on-Write.
  • Reading unneeded columns or rows? Use projection (columns=) and predicate pushdown (scan_parquet, filters=).

12.3 Where is the time?

Five buckets: I/O wait, serialization (JSON, pickle, Python↔JVM), pure-Python loops, native compute, and rarely GC (gc.get_stats()). Profile, classify, fix the biggest. Each has a different fix, so guessing is expensive.

13. Closing principle

The best DE Python is mostly not Python: Arrow, Polars, DuckDB and Spark calls held together by a thin, tested, bounded-memory orchestration layer. Move data between fast engines with the least overhead, and prove with tests that it arrived correct.

L5 Interview CardPython for Data Engineering
Must know
  • GIL in 2026: default CPython still has one; 3.14t is supported but optional (PEP 779), and an unsafe C extension re-enables it.
  • Threads/asyncio for I/O; vectorized engines for compute; processes only for unvectorizable Python CPU work.
  • Zero-copy Arrow holds inside one process. Spark↔Python is Arrow IPC, a cheap copy.
  • pandas 3: Copy-on-Write always on, Arrow strings by default. Polars: lazy, collect(engine="streaming").
  • Bounded memory by design: generators, batched, bounded queues; async with Semaphore, TaskGroup, timeouts, jittered retries, no blocking calls.
  • Lockfile; deps layer before code; the cluster provides pyspark; 3.14 on Linux defaults to forkserver.
Must be able to explain
  1. Does the GIL matter for data engineering?
  2. When would you use Polars or DuckDB instead of Spark?
  3. Why is a Polars→DuckDB handoff zero-copy but a Spark→pandas one is not?
Must be able to draw

A bounded-memory ingestion pipeline:

API pages ─(async, sem=N, retry)─▶ parse
   ▼
batched(5k) ─▶ write Parquet part
   ▼
commit checkpoint (page cursor)
Must be able to code
  • Chunked streaming dedup of a 50 GB file in bounded memory: generator reader, batches, dedup state bounded by hash-partitioning the key or a time window (or pushed into DuckDB).
  • An idempotent retrying API ingester: bounded concurrency, jittered exponential backoff, deterministic output per page so a retry overwrites, not duplicates.
  • A pytest for a transformation: examples plus a Hypothesis idempotence property, f(f(x)) == f(x).
Must be able to debug
  • Memory grows to an OOM kill after ~6 hours: accumulation, concat-in-a-loop, leaked references, retry buffering (§3 drill).
  • An async service's p99 goes from 200 ms to 30 s and Kafka consumers rebalance: py-spy dump shows the loop thread in socket.recv under a sync requests.get.
Numbers that matter
  • Python object ≈ 30–60 B/value vs Arrow payload + 4–8 B: ~10× memory.
  • Coroutine ≈ 1–2 KB; OS thread reserves MBs of virtual stack.
  • "40 GB of input" can be several times that in RAM once decoded and joined.
  • Free-threaded 3.14: ~5–10% single-thread cost per the Python docs; benchmark yours.
Classic traps
  • @dataclass(frozen=True) with a dict field: neither immutable nor hashable.
  • datetime.utcnow(): deprecated and naive; comparing it with aware timestamps raises or shifts.
  • gather over 10,000 coroutines: no backpressure, and one failure doesn't cancel the rest.
30-second answer

How do you write Python data pipelines that are correct, testable, and fast enough? Python orchestrates; Arrow-native engines compute, the smallest one that meets the SLA. Stream with bounded memory. Logic lives in pure functions tested with examples and properties. Every write is idempotent, so retries are safe.

2-minute answer

Correct: validate at the boundary (Pydantic; a schema registry across services), aware timestamps, idempotent writes via keyed upserts or deterministic paths so reruns can't double-count. Testable: transforms as pure functions; millisecond unit and property tests, local Spark/Polars step tests, one small end-to-end fixture, plus production data tests for upstream drift. Fast enough: classify the bottleneck (I/O, serialization, Python loop, native compute) with py-spy or memray, then fix it: asyncio/threads for I/O, Polars/DuckDB for single-node compute, Spark beyond one node, processes only for unvectorizable Python. Reproducible: lockfile, layered images, pinned runtime with versions stated.

Deep-dive follow-up

“Your ingester timed out after the sink accepted the page, then retried. Walk me through why the table isn't double-counted, and what breaks that guarantee.”

Staff+ follow-up

“You have 200 Python pipelines across three packaging styles and Python 3.10–3.14 (3.10 reaches end of life in October 2026). What platform standards do you set, and how do you migrate without a freeze?”
