Part 07

Lakehouse: Iceberg & Delta

Quick refresh15 minInterview study45 minDeep practice70 min
Last technically reviewed September 2026
Covers Iceberg and Delta on-disk layout, the commit protocol, isolation and conflicts, hidden partitioning, COW vs MOR, deletion vectors, compaction and clustering, time travel, schema evolution, catalogs (REST, Polaris, Unity, Glue, S3 Tables), table maintenance, multi-table publishing
Versions referenced Iceberg 1.10 / 1.11 (format v2 and v3), Delta Lake 3.3 / 4.x (4.4 at time of writing), Spark 3.5 / 4.x
Primary references Iceberg spec · Iceberg docs · Delta Lake docs · Delta protocol · Apache Polaris · Unity Catalog OSS
Known implementation differences Isolation defaults, deletion-vector support, S3 commit mechanics and v3 reader support differ by engine and version; the concepts below are stable, the flags are not.

The interviewer is testing whether you understand a table format as a commit protocol over immutable files: what makes a commit atomic, when two writers conflict, what merge-on-read defers and who pays for it later, and which maintenance jobs keep the table alive. Feature lists don't count. Mechanism, cost and failure modes do.

"A lakehouse table is a directory of immutable files plus a manifest that says which of those files are 'now'. Everything else — ACID, time travel, schema evolution, hidden partitioning — is a side effect of how that manifest is structured."

1. Why open table formats exist

Warehouses gave you ACID over proprietary storage other tools couldn't reach. Data lakes (Parquet on S3 plus a Hive Metastore) were cheap and open, but a "table" was a directory listing: no transactions, no safe concurrent writes. Iceberg (Netflix → Apache), Delta Lake (Databricks) and Hudi (Uber) add a metadata layer that, not the directory, defines which files are in the table. That buys atomic commits, snapshot isolation, time travel, ID-based schema evolution and (in Iceberg) hidden partitioning, while engines still read plain Parquet.

What it costs you: every write becomes a small distributed transaction with retries, and the table needs maintenance jobs (compaction, snapshot expiry, orphan cleanup) that a warehouse runs for you. That trade is the whole chapter.

2026 reality. The formats are converging: Delta UniForm writes Iceberg metadata, Apache XTable translates between formats, Iceberg v3 adopted Delta-style deletion vectors, and Databricks bought Tabular in 2024. Lock-in now lives in the catalog (§12), not the format.

2026 Interview Note — what's version-specific in this chapter

The concepts (immutable files, one atomic pointer swap, optimistic retries, COW vs MOR) have not changed since 2020. The table below is what has. At time of writing: Iceberg 1.11 (May 2026) and 1.10 (September 2025); Delta Lake 4.4 (August 2026), with 3.3.x still patched for Spark 3.5. Check current docs before quoting a version.

AreaTimeless conceptVersion-specific (2026)
Row-level deletesMOR marks rows deleted and defers the rewriteIceberg v2: position/equality delete files. Iceberg v3: deletion vectors (Puffin bitmaps, at most one per data file). Delta: deletion vectors (2.4+, extended through 3.x).
Format v3 extrasMetadata evolves; readers must understand itIceberg v3 adds column default values (initial-default/write-default), variant, row lineage (_row_id), nanosecond timestamps and geo types. Reader support differs by engine and version. A v3 table is unreadable to a v2-only reader, so check every consumer before upgrading.
Commit coordinationOne atomic compare-and-swap per commitIceberg REST catalogs do the CAS server-side. Delta 4.0 added catalog-managed tables (preview), which have since grown through the Unity Catalog Delta API. The catalog brokers every commit instead of put-if-absent on storage.
ClusteringCo-locate rows that are filtered togetherDelta liquid clustering (GA since 3.2) replaces partitioning plus Z-order. Iceberg uses sort orders and zorder() rewrites.
InteropOne copy of data, many enginesDelta UniForm publishes Iceberg metadata. Using deletion vectors with UniForm needs IcebergCompatV3, which is experimental at time of writing.
CatalogsThe catalog owns the "current" pointerThe Iceberg REST spec is the common API. Apache Polaris became a top-level project in February 2026. Unity Catalog has an OSS version (LF AI & Data). AWS offers S3 Tables and a Glue Iceberg REST endpoint.

2. Iceberg on disk: the layered metadata

Iceberg is a tree of immutable metadata files. Every write produces new ones, and a single atomic swap of the catalog's "current metadata" pointer commits the write.

Structure
  • Catalog (HMS / Glue / JDBC / REST: Polaris, Unity, S3 Tables…):
  • table: silver.fact_playback
  • current_metadata_pointer: s3://.../metadata/00042-<uuid>.metadata.json
  • s3://bucket/warehouse/silver/fact_playback/
    • data/ # immutable Parquet/ORC files
      • event_date=2026-04-15/
        • 00000-1234-5678.parquet
        • 00001-1234-5678.parquet
        • delete files (v2 position/equality) or deletion vectors (v3, Puffin)
      • event_date=2026-04-14/
      • ...
    • metadata/
    • 00041-<uuid>.metadata.json # previous table state
    • 00042-<uuid>.metadata.json # current — what catalog points to
      • schemas, partition specs, sort orders, snapshots[], refs (branches/tags)
      • each snapshot has manifest_list pointer
    • snap-7843290023-1-...avro # manifest list for snapshot 7843290023
      • rows: each is (manifest_file_path, partitions_summary)
    • 8743-1-...avro # manifest file
      • rows: each is (data_file_path, partition, lower_bounds, upper_bounds, record_count)
    • 8744-1-...avro

Read it top-down: catalog pointer → metadata.json → snapshot → manifest list → manifests → data and delete files. Nothing below the pointer is modified in place.

2.1 The four metadata levels (top to bottom)

  1. Table metadata (metadata.json): format-version, schemas, partition specs, sort orders, snapshots[], refs (branches/tags), current-snapshot-id, properties. Format v2 is the safe default. v3 is available in Iceberg 1.10+, but check every reader first.
  2. Snapshot: id, parent id, sequence-number, timestamp, a summary of added/removed files and records, and the manifest-list pointer.
  3. Manifest list (snap-…avro): one row per manifest, with per-partition summaries. This enables manifest-level pruning before any manifest is opened.
  4. Manifest (Avro): one row per data or delete file, with per-column lower/upper bounds and null, value and NaN counts. File-level pruning happens here.

2.2 What a query does

For SELECT ... WHERE event_date = '2026-04-15' AND user_id = 1234:

  1. Catalog → current metadata file → current snapshot's manifest list.
  2. Drop manifests whose partition summaries exclude 2026-04-15.
  3. In the remaining manifests, drop data files whose event_date/user_id bounds can't match.
  4. Scan surviving Parquet files. Row-group stats and Bloom filters prune further.

Each level prunes multiplicatively. Delta does the same file skipping with log stats. Iceberg's extra lever is manifest-level pruning on partition summaries. Either way, planning cost scales with metadata size (§7.4).

2.3 The atomic commit

  1. Write new data files to data/.
  2. Write new manifest files referring to them. Unchanged manifests are reused, not copied.
  3. Write a new manifest list.
  4. Write a new metadata.json containing the new snapshot.
  5. Atomic compare-and-swap of the catalog pointer: "set it to v43 only if it is still v42".

Only step 5 needs coordination. HMS uses a lock plus conditional update, Glue a table-version check, JDBC a conditional UPDATE. REST catalogs (Polaris, Unity, Glue REST, S3 Tables) do the CAS server-side against commit requirements such as assert-ref-snapshot-id. The "Hadoop" catalog relies on atomic rename, which object stores lack. Don't use it on S3.

“Walk me through an Iceberg commit end-to-end.”
30 sec

The writer reads the current metadata from the catalog, writes immutable data files, then writes new manifests, a manifest list and a new metadata.json. Finally it asks the catalog for an atomic compare-and-swap of the table pointer from the version it read to the new one. Nothing is visible until the swap. If another writer won, it refreshes, re-validates and retries.

2 min

The data files are the expensive part, and they are never redone on retry. Only the metadata is rebuilt on top of the winner's snapshot. Whether a retry is allowed depends on the operation. An append re-applies cleanly, because new files can't conflict. An overwrite or row-level delete checks whether files it read or deleted were changed since its starting snapshot, at the configured isolation level. Retries are bounded client-side (commit.retry.*). The CAS itself is catalog-specific: an HMS lock, a Glue version check, a JDBC conditional update, or REST commit requirements. Readers are unaffected throughout, because they pin whichever snapshot was current when they planned.

Deep dive

Failure cases are the interesting part. If the writer crashes before the CAS, the table is untouched and the files it wrote become orphans for cleanup. If the CAS times out, the client can't know whether it succeeded (Iceberg raises CommitStateUnknownException). It must not delete its files, because they may now be live. Sequence numbers decide which delete files apply to which data files: a delete applies only to data with a lower sequence number. That is how MOR stays correct under concurrent commits. Each commit also appends to metadata.json, so tune write.metadata.previous-versions-max and expire snapshots or the file grows without bound. In v3, row lineage IDs are assigned at commit.

Where to stop: after the CAS, one retry case and the commit-state-unknown case. Don't recite manifest Avro schemas.

3. Delta on disk: the transaction log

Delta keeps an ordered log of JSON commit files (plus periodic Parquet checkpoints). Table state at version V is the replay of add/remove actions up to V.

Structure
  • s3://bucket/warehouse/silver/fact_playback/
    • _delta_log/
      • 00000000000000000000.json # initial commit
      • 00000000000000000001.json # next commit, etc.
      • ...
      • 00000000000000000010.checkpoint.parquet # Parquet checkpoint of state
      • 00000000000000000010.json
      • _last_checkpoint # pointer to most recent checkpoint
    • (data files, optionally partition-prefixed)
    • part-00000-abc.snappy.parquet
    • ...

3.1 What's in a JSON commit

Engine: Delta Lake transaction log (any writer)Language: JSON (newline-delimited actions)Executable: Pseudocode
{"commitInfo": {...}}
{"protocol": {"minReaderVersion": 1, "minWriterVersion": 4}}
{"metaData": {...schema, partitionColumns, format, properties...}}
{"add": {"path": "part-...parquet", "partitionValues": {...}, "size": 1234567, "stats": "{json}", ...}}
{"add": {"path": "...", ...}}
{"remove": {"path": "old-file.parquet", "deletionTimestamp": ..., ...}}

Each add carries stats (numRecords, minValues, maxValues, nullCount). These serve the same purpose as Iceberg's manifest stats.

3.2 Checkpoints

Delta periodically writes a Parquet checkpoint of the full state (every 10 commits by default in delta-spark), and readers replay forward from _last_checkpoint. V2 checkpoints and log compaction keep this fast on huge tables.

3.3 Atomic commit

Version N+1 is a put-if-absent of N+1.json. If it already exists, the writer lost: it reads the winner's actions, runs a conflict check and retries as N+2, or fails. No catalog is involved, except for Delta 4.x catalog-managed tables.

S3 only added conditional writes in 2024. Before that, multi-cluster S3 writers needed a DynamoDB-backed log store. It is engine-dependent now: delta-rs 1.0+ uses S3 conditional puts, while delta-spark has documented S3DynamoDBLogStore for multi-cluster writes. Check your version before removing it.

4. Snapshot isolation: how ACID is achieved on object storage

ACID comes from immutable files plus one atomic swap point. Readers get snapshot isolation. Writers are optimistic: Iceberg's write.{delete,update,merge}.isolation-level defaults to serializable (snapshot is looser). Delta defaults to the weaker WriteSerializable, and Serializable is opt-in.

4.1 The protocol

  1. Read your start snapshot: S0 = current_snapshot().
  2. Write data files and new metadata without touching the pointer.
  3. Swap atomically from S0. If the pointer moved, re-validate against the intervening commits: rebuild metadata and retry, or fail.

4.2 Conflict resolution rules

Conflicts come from read-then-rewrite operations on the same files, not from "the same partition".

Writer AWriter BConflict?
Blind appendBlind append (even the same partition)No
AppendMERGE / UPDATE / DELETEDepends: under serializable/Serializable, new files matching the MERGE's filter conflict; under snapshot/WriteSerializable usually not
MERGE / UPDATE / DELETESame, overlapping filesYes: one wins, the other fails validation
CompactionStreaming MERGE on the same partitionsYes, the classic one: compact cold partitions
AnySchema/protocol changeUsually yes

Databricks' row-level concurrency (DVs plus row tracking) narrows conflicts from files to rows. It is platform-dependent.

Interviewer pushes back

You: “Iceberg gives us ACID, so running the hourly MERGE and the CDC MERGE concurrently is fine.”

Interviewer: “Both jobs update the last 3 days of fact_orders. What happens at 02:00 when both run?”

Strong answer: ACID means neither job corrupts the table. It doesn't mean both succeed. Concurrency is optimistic. Both MERGEs read overlapping files, one CAS wins, and the other re-validates, finds its input files rewritten, and fails. It then redoes the whole scan-and-rewrite, not just the metadata step. With a streaming writer committing every minute, the batch job can lose every race: a retry storm burning compute without progress. The fix is to shrink the conflict surface. Give each partition one writer (route CDC and batch through one MERGE job), keep the MERGE predicate tight so it reads few files, use MOR so rewrites touch less, and schedule compaction away from hot partitions. Retry budgets (commit.retry.*) are the last knob, not the first.

Weak answer: "Add more retries" or "the format handles concurrency". Both treat a design problem as a tuning problem.

4.3 Read-your-writes semantics

A reader sees exactly its pinned snapshot. Caveat: expiry can delete files an old snapshot needs, so long queries or streaming readers resuming from old snapshots fail. Keep retention above your longest reader.

5. Hidden partitioning: Iceberg's killer feature

Fundamentals are in Part 02. In Hive-style tables the partition column is separate, and queries must filter on it literally:

Engine: Hive / Spark SQL (Hive-style table)Dialect: HiveQLExecutable: Illustrative — adapt to your dialect
-- Old Hive trap
SELECT * FROM events WHERE DATE(event_ts) = '2026-04-15';
-- DATE(event_ts) doesn't match the event_date partition column → full scan

Iceberg stores the transform (days(event_ts)) in the partition spec and derives partition values itself:

Engine: Spark SQL + IcebergDialect: Spark SQLExecutable: Illustrative — adapt to your dialect
CREATE TABLE silver.events (
  event_ts TIMESTAMP,
  user_id BIGINT,
  ...
)
PARTITIONED BY (days(event_ts), bucket(16, user_id));
Engine: Spark SQL or Trino + IcebergDialect: ANSI-style SQLExecutable: Yes
SELECT * FROM silver.events WHERE event_ts >= '2026-04-15' AND event_ts < '2026-04-16';

The planner maps the event_ts range onto days(event_ts) and prunes. Users never see or filter a partition column.

5.1 Available transforms

  • identity(col): the raw value (Hive-style).
  • bucket(N, col): hash into N buckets. It spreads writes and bounds partition count on high-cardinality keys.
  • truncate(W, col): the first W characters for strings. For ints and decimals it is v - (v % W), which floors to a multiple of W. It is not mod.
  • years / months / days / hours(ts): time-based.

5.2 Partition spec evolution

Change partitioning without rewriting data: each file keeps the spec it was written under. Say volume grew 20× and daily partitions are too big:

Engine: Spark SQL + Iceberg SQL extensionsDialect: Spark SQLExecutable: Yes — Iceberg Spark runtime with extensions enabled
ALTER TABLE silver.events REPLACE PARTITION FIELD days(event_ts) WITH hours(event_ts);
-- also: ADD PARTITION FIELD ... / DROP PARTITION FIELD ...

Old files keep day partitions and prune at day granularity until rewritten. New files get hour.

6. MERGE under the hood: COW vs MOR

Both strategies first scan to find matching rows. They differ in what they write.

6.1 Copy-on-Write (COW) — the original

COW rewrites every data file containing a changed row and removes the old files in the new snapshot. Reads stay clean.

Write amplification depends on scatter. 1% of rows in a 1 GB file means rewriting 1 GB (100×). A MERGE touching 0.1% of a 1 TB partition rewrites nearly the whole terabyte (~1000×) if keys are scattered, or a handful of files if the table is clustered on the merge key. Cluster on the merge key before switching to MOR.

6.2 Merge-on-Read (MOR) — the streaming-friendly mode

MOR writes new or updated rows to new files and records deletions separately (an update is delete plus insert), as position deletes, equality deletes or deletion vectors (§10).

Write: still scans to locate matches (except equality deletes), then writes only new rows plus a small delete file or DV. Near 1× bytes, because the rewrite is deferred to compaction, not avoided. Read: every query applies the deletes until compaction absorbs them.

6.3 Choosing COW vs MOR

Workload COW MOR
GDPR deletes (rare, scattered) expensive, but bytes are gone after expiry cheap write; row still on disk until compaction + expiry (see note)
Daily SCD2 merge (5% changed) OK if clustered on the key good
Minutely/hourly streaming upsert bad good, with a compaction SLO
Read-heavy, infrequent writes good OK, pays a read tax
Append-only time series n/a: no row-level changes
2026 Interview Note — deletion is not erasure

Under MOR (and with deletion vectors on any format), DELETE FROM users WHERE id = 42 is logical. The row's bytes stay in the Parquet file, and in every older snapshot, until you (1) rewrite the affected files, (2) expire the snapshots that reference the old files and (3) let the file cleanup run (expire_snapshots deletes unreferenced files in Iceberg, VACUUM in Delta). Only then is it physically gone. For a GDPR right-to-erasure request, state this chain and its deadline explicitly.

Configuration is per table, and in Iceberg per operation:

Engine: Spark SQL + Iceberg / Delta LakeDialect: Spark SQLExecutable: Yes
-- Iceberg
ALTER TABLE silver.fact_playback SET TBLPROPERTIES (
  'write.delete.mode' = 'merge-on-read',
  'write.update.mode' = 'merge-on-read',
  'write.merge.mode'  = 'merge-on-read'
);

-- Delta (deletion vectors are roughly equivalent to position deletes)
ALTER TABLE silver.fact_playback SET TBLPROPERTIES (
  'delta.enableDeletionVectors' = 'true'
);

6.4 Delta deletion vectors (the equivalent of MOR)

A RoaringBitmap per data file marks deleted rows, so writers touch only the bitmap. Support arrived in stages (DELETE in 2.4, UPDATE/MERGE through 3.x). Databricks enables DVs by default on new tables, while the OSS default depends on version. Iceberg v3 uses the same idea (one Puffin DV per data file).

“Copy-on-write vs merge-on-read — which and when?”
30 sec

COW rewrites every file containing a changed row at write time, so reads stay clean. MOR writes only new rows plus delete markers (delete files or deletion vectors), and every reader applies them until compaction. COW suits read-heavy tables with infrequent changes. MOR suits frequent upserts, but only with a compaction budget.

2 min

Decide with three numbers: how many files each write touches, how often you write, and how often you read. A table merged every minute and read hourly wants MOR. A table merged daily and read 500 times a day probably wants COW, clustered on the merge key so each merge touches few files. MOR's hidden costs: it still scans to find matches, reads pay per delete file until compaction, the compaction job becomes a hard dependency, and deletes are logical until files are rewritten and snapshots expire. In Iceberg you can choose per operation (write.delete/update/merge.mode). In Delta the lever is deletion vectors.

Deep dive

Position deletes and DVs are cheap to apply (a bitmap per file). Equality deletes are expensive, because every row is compared against key sets, but they let Flink upsert without reading the target. Sequence numbers make deletes apply only to older data. v2 tables can accumulate many small position-delete files per data file, which v3's one-DV-per-file rule fixes. Compaction and streaming MERGE conflict on the same partitions, so run compaction on cold partitions or use partial-progress commits. Set an SLO such as "delete bytes under 5–10% of data bytes per partition" and alert on it.

Where to stop: once you've named the read-frequency vs write-frequency trade and the compaction dependency. Go to sequence numbers only if asked.

Drill · Iceberg MOR

Two weeks ago the team switched fact_orders (Iceberg v2, CDC upserts every 5 minutes) from copy-on-write to merge-on-read. The CDC job now finishes in 40 seconds instead of 6 minutes. Dashboard queries on the table have gone from 4 seconds to 40, and they get slower every day.

STOP. Answer before revealing.

Reveal the diagnosis
  1. Observe The slowdown is gradual, not a step, and data volume hasn't grown. That points to something accumulating. The obvious candidate is delete files.
  2. Hypothesize Each 5-minute commit adds position (or equality) delete files, and nothing compacts them. Every scan task now opens dozens of delete files per data file.
  3. Measure SELECT content, count(*), sum(file_size_in_bytes) FROM cat.db.fact_orders.files GROUP BY content (0 = data, 1 = position deletes, 2 = equality deletes). Check snapshot summaries for total-delete-files. Here: 290K delete files against 18K data files.
  4. Isolate Run the same query FOR VERSION AS OF the last COW snapshot. It is fast, so the data isn't the problem, the deletes are. Equality deletes from the CDC sink are the worst offenders, because they are checked row by row.
  5. Fix rewrite_position_delete_files, then rewrite_data_files with delete-file-threshold on the hot partitions, off-peak so it doesn't fight the CDC writer. Then expire_snapshots.
  6. Prevent Schedule compaction as part of the MOR decision, not after it. Alert when delete files per data file exceed a threshold or delete bytes pass ~5–10% of data bytes. On v3 or Delta, deletion vectors cap the per-file count.

6.5 MERGE example

Engine: Spark SQL + Iceberg or Delta LakeDialect: Spark SQLExecutable: Yes
MERGE INTO silver.dim_user t
USING staging.user_updates s
  ON t.user_id = s.user_id
WHEN MATCHED AND s.is_deleted THEN DELETE
WHEN MATCHED AND s.hash_diff <> t.hash_diff THEN UPDATE SET
    plan = s.plan,
    country_id = s.country_id,
    updated_ts = current_timestamp()
WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT (user_id, plan, country_id, updated_ts)
                     VALUES (s.user_id, s.plan, s.country_id, current_timestamp());

If one target row matches several source rows, the SQL standard requires an error, and Spark with Iceberg or Delta raises one. Deduplicate the source first.

7. Compaction: bin-packing, sorting, Z-ORDER

Small files and delete files degrade reads and inflate metadata. Causes and sizing are in Part 02 §9. Here are the format tools.

2026 Interview Note — procedure calls

The Iceberg CALL system.… procedures below are Spark with the Iceberg SQL extensions. Qualify them with your catalog name (CALL my_catalog.system.rewrite_data_files(…)) if it isn't the session's current catalog. Trino exposes the equivalents as ALTER TABLE … EXECUTE optimize / expire_snapshots / remove_orphan_files. Managed services (S3 Tables, Glue table optimizers, Databricks predictive optimization) can run these for you.

7.1 Bin-packing (size compaction)

Engine: Spark + Iceberg procedures / Delta LakeDialect: Spark SQLExecutable: Yes
-- Iceberg
CALL system.rewrite_data_files(
  table => 'silver.fact_playback',
  options => map('target-file-size-bytes', '536870912')  -- 512 MB
);

-- Delta
OPTIMIZE silver.fact_playback;

Compaction groups small files per partition into target-sized outputs in one commit, so it can conflict with concurrent MERGEs (§4.2). It absorbs deletes only for the files it rewrites.

7.2 Sort compaction

Engine: Spark + Iceberg proceduresDialect: Spark SQLExecutable: Yes
-- Iceberg
CALL system.rewrite_data_files(
  table => 'silver.fact_playback',
  strategy => 'sort',
  sort_order => 'event_ts ASC, user_id ASC'
);

The rewrite range-sorts across the file group, not just within each file, so output files cover non-overlapping key ranges. Tight file-level min/max skips whole files. It costs a shuffle.

7.3 Z-ORDER (Delta + others)

Z-order interleaves column bits so rows close in N dimensions sit close on disk. Use it when queries filter on any of a few columns.

Engine: Delta Lake (Spark / Databricks)Dialect: Spark SQLExecutable: Yes — not on liquid-clustered tables
-- Delta
OPTIMIZE silver.fact_playback ZORDER BY (user_id, title_id);

Rough math: with F files and N Z-ordered columns, each column is cut into ~F1/N ranges, so a one-column filter reads ~F−1/N of files. At F = 10,000: N = 2 reads ~1%, N = 4 reads ~10%. A linear sort reads ~1/F for the lead column and nearly everything for the rest. Beyond 2–3 columns the benefit fades.

Engine: Spark + Iceberg / Delta Lake 3.2+Dialect: Spark SQLExecutable: Yes — Iceberg Spark procedures; Delta 3.2+ on a liquid-clustered table
-- Iceberg: Z-order is a sort strategy
CALL system.rewrite_data_files(
  table => 'silver.fact_playback',
  strategy => 'sort',
  sort_order => 'zorder(user_id, title_id)'
);

-- Delta liquid clustering (replaces partitioning + ZORDER)
ALTER TABLE silver.fact_playback_lc CLUSTER BY (user_id, title_id);
OPTIMIZE silver.fact_playback_lc;  -- clusters incrementally

Liquid clustering (Delta, GA since 3.2) clusters incrementally and lets you change keys without rewriting history. It excludes partitioning and ZORDER, and is the default choice for new Delta tables.

7.4 Manifest compaction

Many small commits leave many small manifests and slow planning. rewrite_manifests is cheap, so run it regularly on high-commit tables.

Engine: Spark + Iceberg proceduresDialect: Spark SQLExecutable: Yes
CALL system.rewrite_manifests('silver.fact_playback');

7.5 Equality / position delete compaction

Engine: Spark + Iceberg procedures (v2 delete files)Dialect: Spark SQLExecutable: Yes
-- Iceberg
CALL system.rewrite_position_delete_files('silver.fact_playback');

-- For more aggressive compaction that absorbs deletes into data files:
CALL system.rewrite_data_files(
  table => 'silver.fact_playback',
  options => map('delete-file-threshold', '1')   -- rewrite any data file with >=1 delete
);

Only the second call (followed by expiry) removes deleted rows from disk.

7.6 Maintenance pattern

Order: compaction, expiry, then orphan cleanup (least often).

Engine: Spark + Iceberg proceduresDialect: Spark SQLExecutable: Yes
-- Compact small files, absorb deletes
CALL system.rewrite_data_files('silver.fact_playback');

-- Compact manifests
CALL system.rewrite_manifests('silver.fact_playback');

-- Expire old snapshots (default keeps 5 days)
CALL system.expire_snapshots(
  table => 'silver.fact_playback',
  older_than => TIMESTAMP '2026-04-09 00:00:00'
);

-- Remove orphan files (never referenced by any snapshot); default older_than = 3 days — keep it above your longest write
CALL system.remove_orphan_files('silver.fact_playback');

Rule of thumb: reads slowing while data doesn't grow means compaction debt. Compact when delete bytes pass ~5–10% of data bytes (a starting point; tune to your read SLO). On Delta: OPTIMIZE/liquid clustering, VACUUM, and REORG … APPLY (PURGE) for erasure.

8. Time travel and snapshot expiration

Old snapshots stay queryable until you expire them.

Engine: Spark 3.3+ with Iceberg / Delta LakeDialect: Spark SQLExecutable: Yes
-- Iceberg: query by snapshot ID or timestamp
SELECT * FROM silver.fact_playback FOR VERSION AS OF 7843290023;
SELECT * FROM silver.fact_playback FOR TIMESTAMP AS OF '2026-04-15 12:00:00';

-- Delta
SELECT * FROM silver.fact_playback VERSION AS OF 42;
SELECT * FROM silver.fact_playback TIMESTAMP AS OF '2026-04-15 12:00:00';

8.1 Practical uses

  • Audit, debugging, reproducibility: the table before last night's bad merge; ML training pinned to a snapshot or tag.
  • Rollback (§8.3) and incremental reads (Iceberg changelog scans, Delta Change Data Feed).
  • Write-audit-publish: Iceberg branches/tags live in table metadata (since 1.2, any catalog). Write to an audit branch (write.wap.enabled + spark.wap.branch), validate, then fast_forward main. Delta has no branches; use shallow clones or staging tables.

8.2 Expiration trade-off

Retention costs storage only for churned files (replaced by compaction, MERGE or overwrite). Append-only tables keep almost nothing extra; a table rewritten daily keeps a full copy per retained day. Short retention limits recovery and breaks long readers (§4.3). Typical: 5–7 days. Delta defaults at time of writing: log retention 30 days, deleted-file retention 7 days (what VACUUM honours). Time travel past the VACUUM horizon fails.

Engine: Spark SQL + IcebergDialect: Spark SQLExecutable: Yes
ALTER TABLE silver.fact_playback SET TBLPROPERTIES (
  'history.expire.min-snapshots-to-keep' = '20',
  'history.expire.max-snapshot-age-ms'   = '604800000'  -- 7 days
);

8.3 Rollback

Engine: Spark + Iceberg procedures / Delta LakeDialect: Spark SQLExecutable: Yes
-- Iceberg
CALL system.rollback_to_snapshot('silver.fact_playback', 7843290023);

-- Delta
RESTORE TABLE silver.fact_playback TO VERSION AS OF 42;

Iceberg moves the current-snapshot pointer back. Delta RESTORE writes a new commit that re-adds the old files, visible in history. Both need the old files un-expired. Neither fixes downstream consumers that already read the bad data.

9. Schema evolution: column-id semantics

Iceberg tracks every column by an immutable field ID. Names and positions are labels.

9.1 What's safe

  • Add: new ID, reads as NULL from older files (v3 adds initial-default/write-default).
  • Drop: the ID is retired, so a later same-named column can't resurrect old data.
  • Rename, reorder: metadata-only.
  • Promote: int → long, float → double, decimal precision up (same scale).

9.2 What's not safe (requires rewrite or fails)

  • Incompatible type changes (string → int, decimal scale): rewrite.
  • Tightening to NOT NULL when NULLs exist.
  • Renames under a consumer that maps by name (view, dbt model, raw Parquet reader): the table is fine, the consumer breaks.

9.3 Why Parquet "just works"

Iceberg writers store field IDs in the Parquet schema. Files written without IDs (migrated via migrate/add_files) are read through schema.name-mapping.default. Get it wrong and columns silently read as NULL.

Engine: Spark SQL + Iceberg SQL extensionsDialect: Spark SQLExecutable: Yes — decimal promotion must keep the scale
ALTER TABLE silver.events ADD COLUMN device_class STRING;
ALTER TABLE silver.events RENAME COLUMN device_class TO device_type;
ALTER TABLE silver.events DROP COLUMN device_type;
ALTER TABLE silver.events ALTER COLUMN price TYPE decimal(18, 4);  -- promotion

All four are metadata-only. No data file is rewritten.

9.4 Delta schema evolution

Delta maps by name unless column mapping is on ('delta.columnMapping.mode' = 'name'; reader v2 / writer v5), which rename and drop require. Delta 4.0 made type widening GA. Protocol upgrades can lock out older readers.

10. Delete files: position vs equality

Format v2 has two delete-file kinds. v3 adds a third representation.

10.1 Position deletes

"Row N of file F is deleted." Cheap to apply as a per-file bitmap.

10.2 Equality deletes

"Any row with these key values is deleted." No target read needed.

10.3 When each is used

  • Position deletes: batch MERGE, UPDATE and DELETE (Spark, Trino).
  • Equality deletes: Flink upsert and CDC sinks. Compact them into position deletes, or rewrite data, quickly.
  • Deletion vectors (v3): replace position delete files with at most one Puffin bitmap per data file, fixing v2's pile-up of small position deletes. Equality deletes remain.

11. Iceberg vs Delta vs Hudi — the trade table

At time of writing (2026); engine support moves quarterly.

CapabilityIcebergDelta LakeHudi
Commit mechanismCatalog CAS on metadata pointerPut-if-absent of N.json (or catalog-managed commit)Timeline of instants + file groups
Hidden partitioning / clusteringYes (transforms, spec evolution); sort / zorder rewritesNo hidden partitioning; liquid clustering (3.2+)Partial; clustering service
Schema evolutionField IDs: add, drop, rename, reorder, promoteRename/drop need column mapping; type widening (4.0)Add; more via schema-on-read
Row-level changesCOW or MOR per operation (row-level deletes need v2+); v3 uses deletion vectorsCOW, or MOR via deletion vectors (DELETE 2.4+, UPDATE/MERGE through 3.x)COW or MOR tables (MOR with log files)
Branches / tagsYes: table-level refs since 1.2, any catalog; Nessie adds multi-table branchesNo (shallow clone is the nearest)Savepoints
v3 / 4.x extrasVariant, row lineage, default values, nanosecond timestamps, geoVariant, row tracking, catalog-managed tables, V2 checkpointsRecord-level index, metadata table
EnginesSpark, Flink, Trino, Snowflake, BigQuery, Athena, DuckDB, PyIcebergSpark, Trino (read/write incl. MERGE), Flink, delta-rs, DuckDB, PolarsSpark, Flink, Trino (read)
CatalogsREST (Polaris, Unity, Glue, S3 Tables…), HMS, Glue, JDBC, NessieUnity, HMS, Glue; path-based tables need noneHMS, Glue, sync tools
Streaming upsertsFlink equality deletes; needs scheduled compactionStructured Streaming MERGE; DVs; UniForm for Iceberg readersDesigned for it (MOR, indexes, table services)

The honest take: Iceberg is the broadest multi-engine standard. Delta is strongest on Databricks and increasingly open via Delta Kernel and OSS Unity. Hudi is fine for upsert-heavy CDC if you're already on it. The catalog decision now matters more than the format.

11.1 How to pick — the decision heuristic

  • Several engines writing? Iceberg with a REST catalog.
  • Databricks-centred? Delta with Unity; UniForm or UC's Iceberg endpoints for outside readers.
  • Heavy CDC upserts? Already on Hudi, stay. Fresh, Iceberg or Delta with MOR/DVs and a compaction SLO.
  • Analytics with occasional updates? Either; follow your engines and catalog.
Interviewer pushes back

You: “We'll standardise on Delta and use UniForm, so Snowflake and Trino can use the same tables as Iceberg.”

Interviewer: “So Trino can write to them as Iceberg too?”

Strong answer: No. UniForm is one-directional. Delta stays the source of truth, and after each Delta commit it generates Iceberg metadata pointing at the same Parquet files, so Iceberg clients get read access. Writes must go through Delta. An Iceberg writer committing to that table would fork the metadata. It also has constraints. The Iceberg view can lag the Delta commit, because metadata generation is asynchronous. It needs column mapping. Historically it couldn't be combined with deletion vectors, and IcebergCompatV3, which allows both, is experimental at time of writing. So: "one Delta table, readable as Iceberg" is supported. "Delta and Iceberg as co-equal writers" is not. If several engines must write, pick Iceberg with a REST catalog, or route all writes through one engine.

Weak answer: "UniForm makes Delta and Iceberg the same thing." That treats a metadata mirror as a two-way sync.

12. Catalog choices: Hive Metastore, Glue, Nessie, Polaris, Unity

The catalog stores table → current metadata and performs the commit CAS. It is the control plane (who can write, access control, multi-table commits) and the biggest lock-in risk: the files are open, the pointer may not be.

12.1 The Iceberg REST catalog spec

An open HTTP API any engine can speak. The server does the CAS against client-supplied requirements (assert-ref-snapshot-id), vends short-lived table-scoped storage credentials, and can offer a multi-table commit endpoint and server-side scan planning. Optional endpoints vary by server.

CatalogWhat it isCommit / notes (2026 — check current docs)
Hive MetastoreThrift service over MySQL/Postgres; universal legacyLock + conditional update; coarse ACLs. Legacy.
AWS Glue Data CatalogManaged HMS-compatible catalog; regional (replicate for DR)Version check. Iceberg branches work (they're in table metadata). Iceberg REST endpoint; Lake Formation governance.
AWS S3 TablesAWS-managed "table buckets" storing Iceberg tablesAWS product, not OSS. Built-in compaction and snapshot management; check features per region.
Apache PolarisOpen-source Iceberg REST catalog (originated at Snowflake)Apache TLP since Feb 2026. RBAC, credential vending. Managed as Snowflake Open Catalog.
Unity CatalogDatabricks governance catalog, plus an OSS project under LF AI & DataDatabricks: managed Delta and Iceberg tables, catalog commits, lineage. OSS: Iceberg REST reads, UC Delta API. Not feature-equal.
Project NessieGit-like catalogCatalog-level branches across tables; a merge publishes many at once.
OthersJDBC catalog, Lakekeeper, Apache GravitinoJDBC: conditional UPDATE. Others: REST implementations.

12.2 The pragmatic choice

Default to a REST catalog: Glue or S3 Tables on AWS, Polaris for engine neutrality, Unity on Databricks, Nessie when cross-table branching is a real requirement, HMS for legacy. Ask any catalog two questions: can every engine I need write through it? and how do I get my tables out?

12.3 The migration trap

Switching catalogs sounds metadata-only and isn't. Every engine's config moves, every table is re-registered at its exact current metadata location, and access policies and maintenance settings are rebuilt. Writers must freeze during cut-over, or two catalogs both accept commits and the table forks.

13. Operating a lakehouse: gotchas and patterns

13.1 The small-files killer

A 30-second checkpoint with 100 active partitions is ~200 files a minute, ~288K a day, plus one snapshot per commit. The full incident (20K files to 8 million) is a drill in Part 19. Mitigations:

  • Checkpoints of 1–5 minutes.
  • write.distribution-mode=hash (Iceberg), so each partition is written by one task.
  • Scheduled compaction plus rewrite_manifests. OSS Iceberg has no write-side auto-compaction: use managed compaction (S3 Tables, Glue optimizers, Databricks predictive optimization), or Delta's optimizeWrite/autoCompact where your version supports them.

13.2 The expiration trap

  • expire_snapshots removes snapshots and files only they reference. Too aggressive and long queries, streaming restarts and time travel fail. Retain above your longest reader and recovery window.
  • remove_orphan_files deletes files no snapshot references, including files a writer has written but not yet committed: a backfill longer than older_than loses its files, then commits metadata pointing at them. A path-scheme mismatch (s3a:// listing vs s3:// metadata) makes every live file look orphaned. Use older_than in days, dry_run first, and explicit equal_schemes/prefix_mismatch_mode.
Engine: Spark + Iceberg proceduresDialect: Spark SQLExecutable: Yes — parameter availability varies by Iceberg version
-- 1. Look before deleting
CALL system.remove_orphan_files(
  table      => 'silver.fact_playback',
  older_than => TIMESTAMP '2026-04-12 00:00:00',   -- >= 3 days ago
  dry_run    => true
);
-- 2. If the list is sane, re-run with dry_run => false.
--    Mixed schemes? equal_schemes => map('s3a,s3n','s3')
Drill · Iceberg maintenance

At 09:10 every query on silver.sessions starts failing with FileNotFoundException on files under data/event_date=2026-03-*. Those files belong to a backfill whose commit succeeded at 08:55. Nobody ran a DELETE. The nightly maintenance job ran at 08:00.

STOP. Answer before revealing.

Reveal the diagnosis
  1. Observe The missing files are all from one commit, and that commit is the latest snapshot. The table's metadata is consistent. The storage underneath it isn't.
  2. Hypothesize Something deleted the files between their write and the commit. The 08:00 maintenance job is the suspect, since orphan cleanup deletes files no snapshot references, and uncommitted files qualify.
  3. Measure Maintenance logs show remove_orphan_files(older_than => now() - interval 1 hour). The backfill started at 05:40 and wrote the March files between 05:45 and 06:50. At 08:00 they were more than an hour old and unreferenced. S3 access logs or CloudTrail confirm DELETEs from the maintenance role at 08:03.
  4. Isolate Check the second classic cause too: does the job list s3a:// while metadata stores s3://? Here, no. It is purely the short older_than.
  5. Fix Restore the objects if bucket versioning is on (delete markers are removable). Otherwise roll back to the pre-backfill snapshot and re-run the backfill.
  6. Prevent Set older_than to at least 3 days and above the longest writer. Dry-run and alert when the delete count spikes. Enable bucket versioning with a short noncurrent-version lifecycle. Don't let maintenance run while a table's long writers are active.

13.3 Concurrent writers conflict spiral

A stream commits every minute; a 20-minute batch MERGE over the same partitions loses the CAS, redoes everything and loses again. Fixes, in order: disjoint partitions (pure appends never conflict, §4.2); a single writer (staging table, then one MERGE); only then client retries (commit.retry.*), which help short commits but can't save a job that always loses.

13.4 Cross-region reads

Remote reads cost data egress, not metadata. For DR, S3 cross-region replication is not enough: Iceberg metadata stores absolute paths, so the replica still points at the source bucket. Rewrite paths (rewrite_table_path, Iceberg 1.8+; check your version) or use multi-region access points, then register the copy in the DR catalog. Delta logs usually use relative paths inside the table directory, but shallow clones and absolute paths still bite.

13.5 Auditing / data contracts

Both record when and what changed. Delta's commitInfo can carry the user (on Databricks). Iceberg summaries record operation and engine, not user; for "who", use the catalog's audit log.

Engine: Spark SQL + Iceberg metadata tablesDialect: Spark SQL (Trino: "fact_playback$snapshots")Executable: Yes
SELECT *
FROM silver.fact_playback.snapshots
ORDER BY committed_at DESC
LIMIT 10;

Metadata tables (.snapshots, .files, .partitions, .manifests) are the basis for monitoring, e.g. alerting on commits that remove far more records than usual.

13.6 Cost monitoring

Small-file request costs and planning time are real bills. Track per table: files per partition, average file size (alert below ~64 MB; healthy is ~128 MB–1 GB), manifest count, delete-file ratio, snapshot count.

Failure-first: what can fail in lakehouse commits and maintenance?
FailureDetectRecoverPrevent recurrence
Concurrent writer conflict / retry stormCommitFailedException / ConcurrentModificationException rates; job runtime ≫ workRe-run the losing job after the winner; serialize via the orchestratorOne writer per partition; tight MERGE predicates; compaction off hot partitions; bounded retries
Partial write (writer dies before commit)Failed job, table unchanged; unreferenced files in storageNothing to roll back; rerun the idempotent jobIdempotent writes; periodic safe orphan cleanup
Commit state unknown (CAS timed out)CommitStateUnknownException in logsRe-read the table: if the snapshot exists, done; else retry. Never delete that job's files blindlyIdempotent job keys (e.g. snapshot summary property) so a rerun can detect a prior success
Orphan cleanup deletes live or in-flight filesFileNotFoundException on recent files; delete spike in S3 logsRestore versioned objects, or roll back and re-runolder_than ≥ longest write (days); dry run; explicit scheme/prefix handling; bucket versioning
Snapshot expiry breaks time travel / long readers"snapshot not found" / missing files in long queries or streaming restartsRe-run the reader from current state or a tagged snapshotRetention > longest reader and recovery window; tag snapshots that must survive
Catalog unavailableCatalog errors / timeouts on every commit and planWriters fail (data files become orphans); readers with cached metadata may continue brieflyHA catalog deployment; alert on commit latency; don't point engines at raw metadata paths as a workaround
Compaction races with writesCompaction commits failing validation; rising file counts despite "running" compactionRe-run on cold partitions; partial-progress commitsSchedule by partition age; partial-progress.enabled; alert on compaction failures, not just runtimes

14. Multi-table transactions: publishing across tables

Commits are atomic per table. Cross-table atomicity is your problem unless the catalog explicitly supports it.

14.1 The problem, stated precisely

If fct_order commits and dim_customer fails, readers see orders with unknown customer keys. Readers between two successful commits see the same.

14.2 Mitigation strategies, most common first

  1. Order the commits. Dimensions before facts. When facts must land first, insert inferred placeholder members and backfill. Each step idempotent.
  2. Write-audit-publish per table. Iceberg WAP branch, validate, fast_forward each main. Still separate commits: the window shrinks, it doesn't close.
  3. Consumer-side publish marker. Consumers read only snapshots recorded in a small "published" table updated after all tables commit. Atomic from the reader's view, on any catalog.
  4. Catalog-level atomicity. A Nessie multi-table branch merge; or the Iceberg REST multi-table commit (POST …/transactions/commit) via the Java catalog API. No Spark SQL syntax; server support varies.

External two-phase commit is rarely worth it: table formats expose no "prepare" phase.

14.3 What to say in an interview

"Atomic per table. I'd commit dims first, keep steps idempotent and gate consumers on a publish marker; with Nessie or a REST server that implements multi-table commit, I'd use that."

Closing principle

Iceberg and Delta made object storage behave like a database. The price: you operate it like one. Conflicts, compaction, expiry, orphan cleanup and schema discipline are your job, or a managed service's that you still verify. Get maintenance right and the lakehouse is boring. Skip it and you'll be paged at 3am within a quarter.

L5 Interview CardLakehouse: Iceberg & Delta
Must know
  • A commit writes immutable data and metadata, then does one atomic swap: catalog CAS (Iceberg) or put-if-absent of N.json (Delta). Losers re-validate and retry.
  • Readers get snapshot isolation. Writers get optimistic concurrency. Delta defaults to WriteSerializable, Iceberg to serializable for row-level ops. Blind appends never conflict.
  • COW rewrites touched files. MOR writes delete files or deletion vectors and taxes reads until compaction.
  • A MOR delete is logical. Erasure needs rewrite plus snapshot expiry (plus VACUUM on Delta).
  • The maintenance quartet: compaction, manifest/log compaction, snapshot expiry, safe orphan cleanup.
  • Schema evolution by field ID (Iceberg) or column mapping (Delta). Hidden partitioning with spec evolution.
  • The catalog is the control plane: REST spec, Polaris, Unity, Glue/S3 Tables. Atomicity is per table unless the catalog says otherwise.
Must be able to explain
  1. Walk through an Iceberg commit, including what happens when the CAS loses or times out.
  2. When two writers conflict, and why two appends to the same partition don't.
  3. COW vs MOR for a given read/write ratio, and what MOR does to GDPR deletes.
Must be able to draw

The Iceberg hierarchy with the commit path:

catalog ─CAS─▶ metadata.json
                 ↓ current snapshot
               manifest list
                 ↓ (partition summaries)
               manifests
                 ↓ (column stats)
               data files + deletes/DVs
Must be able to code
  • A MERGE with delete/update/insert branches and a deduplicated source.
  • A maintenance job: rewrite_data_files → rewrite_manifests → expire_snapshots → remove_orphan_files (dry run, safe older_than).
  • A partition evolution with REPLACE PARTITION FIELD, and a time-travel query plus rollback.
Must be able to debug
  • Reads 10× slower after switching to MOR: delete-file accumulation with no compaction.
  • FileNotFoundException on a fresh commit: orphan cleanup with a short older_than, or an s3a/s3 scheme mismatch.
Numbers that matter
  • Target files ~128 MB–1 GB. Alert when the average falls below ~64 MB.
  • COW write amplification ≈ file size ÷ changed bytes per touched file: 1% of a 1 GB file means 100×.
  • 30-second checkpoints × 100 partitions ≈ 288K files a day.
  • Z-order on N columns over F files reads ~F−1/N per single-column filter.
  • Compact when delete bytes reach ~5–10% of data bytes. That is a starting point, not a constant.
Classic traps
  • "MOR makes GDPR deletes cheap." The bytes are still there until rewrite plus expiry.
  • "Two jobs appending to one partition will conflict." They won't. Read-then-rewrite operations conflict.
  • "Cross-region replication gives us DR." Absolute paths in metadata say otherwise.
30-second answer

Why do open table formats exist and what do they cost you? They make a pile of immutable Parquet files in cheap object storage behave like a table: atomic commits, snapshot isolation, time travel and safe schema evolution, readable by many engines. They do it with a metadata layer and one atomic pointer swap per commit. The cost is that every write becomes an optimistic transaction that can conflict, and the table needs maintenance a warehouse would do for you: compaction, snapshot expiry, orphan cleanup, and a catalog you must choose and operate.

2-minute answer

Plain data lakes had no transactions. A "table" was a directory listing, so concurrent writes and partial failures corrupted it. Iceberg and Delta put a metadata layer on top, a manifest tree or a transaction log, and make the new version visible with one atomic step: a catalog compare-and-swap or a put-if-absent log entry. Everything else follows from that. Readers pin a snapshot, so you get isolation and time travel. Field IDs make renames safe. Hidden partitioning lets queries prune without knowing the layout. The costs are concrete. Concurrent MERGEs on the same files conflict and retry. MOR makes writes cheap but taxes every read until compaction, and its deletes aren't physical until rewrite plus expiry. Small files and metadata bloat need scheduled jobs. Expiry and orphan cleanup can break readers or delete live data if misconfigured. And the catalog becomes your control plane and your lock-in point. I'd choose the format by engines and catalog, then budget the maintenance explicitly.

Deep-dive follow-up

“Your Iceberg commit call timed out. Did the write happen, what do you do with the files you wrote, and how do you make the job safe to rerun?”

Staff+ follow-up

“Three engines (Spark, Flink, Snowflake) must write to the same tables across two clouds. Design the catalog, commit ownership, maintenance ownership and exit strategy, and say what you would refuse to support.”

Part 08

Interview Scenarios — Incidents, Designs, Internals, Judgment

Quick refresh20 minInterview study45 minDeep practice80 min
Last technically reviewed September 2026
Covers incident triage, pipeline and streaming design, Spark / Flink / Kafka / Iceberg internals, modeling judgment, quality engineering, trade-offs, behavioural
Versions referenced Spark 3.5 / 4.x, Flink 1.20 LTS / 2.x, Kafka 3.x / 4.x, Iceberg 1.10–1.11 (spec v2 / v3), Delta Lake 4.x, BigQuery Editions, Snowflake (2026)
Primary references Spark performance tuning (AQE) · Flink event time · Iceberg Spark procedures · Kafka docs · BigQuery Editions
