  • The "single thing we'd regret most" question is a generally powerful frame for reducing scope without giving up value.

11.7 — "A feature you built caused a production incident. Walk me through it."

The scenario

You shipped a new incremental loader for fct_order_line. It processed only the last 24 hours of orders each run, merging into the target table. Friday afternoon deploy. Saturday morning the CFO's weekend revenue dashboard showed revenue down 40% week-over-week. It wasn't. The bug: your incremental filter used order_updated_at >= now() - interval '24 hours', but the source system updates the updated_at field on status changes (cancellations, refunds). The loader was picking up cancellations and treating them as the whole truth for those orders, overwriting the full-truth rows from the previous day's full-scan load. The effect: order totals got replaced by their cancellation deltas, which are negative or zero.

The answer

"[Owning it in the first sentence] I shipped a loader that overwrote correct revenue rows with cancellation-only updates because I used the wrong incremental column. The CFO saw a 40% revenue drop on a Saturday morning before anyone was awake to catch it. That's the top line.

[The pager-to-fix timeline] Saturday 8:47am our on-call got paged by the dashboard owner, who got a Slack from the CFO. On-call pinged me, I was at my laptop by 9:10. Diagnosis by 9:35 — the merge query was trivially wrong once I read it with fresh eyes. Rollback by 9:50 via the previous day's snapshot. Full table refresh by 11:20. Incident resolved before noon.

[The specific decision that failed] My mistake wasn't 'we needed more tests.' The specific decision was: I trusted the column name order_updated_at without asking what event types trigger an update. I assumed 'updated' meant 'updated once, at creation.' It didn't. If I'd asked the ops team what writes to that column, I'd have known. I didn't ask.

[The prevention, systemic not personal] Two fixes shipped the next week. First, the loader now re-reads the full current row for every changed order_id, not the delta, before the MERGE, and the source contract documents which events bump updated_at. Second, I added a pre-commit data-diff that compares the target table's revenue sum before and after the merge, with a 5% guardrail. If it would drop revenue by more than 5%, the merge aborts and pages on-call. Those two changes shipped as a PR, with tests, in the next sprint. The diff guardrail has since caught two unrelated issues on other tables.

[What I'd do differently] Beyond the specific fix: I now treat 'the column name is clear' as a yellow flag, not a green one. Every column I pull into a critical transform, I ask the producer about write semantics before I ship. It's a 10-minute conversation that would have saved a Saturday morning."

What the interviewer hears

  • Owning it in one blunt sentence — no warm-up, no hedging.
  • Timeline specificity (8:47, 9:10, 9:35, 9:50, 11:20) signals that the candidate owned the incident.

11.8 — "A junior engineer is blocked and frustrated. How do you mentor them out of it?"

The scenario

A junior data engineer on your team is building their first streaming pipeline — a Flink job consuming Kafka into Iceberg. They've been stuck for four days on a watermark issue: records are being dropped as "late" even though they look on-time. They're working late, increasingly defensive in standup, and two days ago said "I don't think streaming is for me." You know exactly what the bug is within 30 seconds of reading their code. Do you just tell them?

The answer

"[The question to ask yourself first] 'Do I just tell them' is the wrong frame. The right frame is: 'what's the most valuable thing they can learn in the next hour?' If I tell them the answer, they save four days on this bug and learn one fact. If I walk them to the answer, they save four days on this bug and learn a debugging pattern they'll use for every streaming bug for the next decade. The second payoff is worth the extra 45 minutes.

[The move — Socratic debug] I booked 90 minutes with them, not a drive-by. I asked them to walk me through their mental model of watermarks before we looked at any code. Within two minutes it was clear they thought watermarks were a global clock, not a per-source boundary. That was the actual misconception under the bug. The code issue was just the symptom.

[Teaching the model, not the fix] We spent 20 minutes on a whiteboard sketching how watermarks propagate through operators, including the specific case where a slow partition on one side of a union stalls the whole watermark. Then I asked them to re-read their code with that model. They found the bug themselves — they'd assigned the watermark after the source with zero out-of-orderness, so records from a partition running 8 seconds behind the others arrived behind the watermark. Moving the WatermarkStrategy onto the Kafka source, so watermarks are tracked per partition, fixed it.

[The frustration piece] The 'streaming is not for me' comment was the one I addressed directly, but carefully. Not 'don't say that' — that lands as dismissive. Instead: 'You've done four days of work that you're about to learn didn't need to take four days. That's frustrating. What made the difference just now — do you think?' They said 'having someone to walk through it with.' That was the teach moment — asking for help earlier isn't weakness, it's pipeline engineering at senior scale because the cost of a day of stuck-ness is higher than the cost of a 30-minute pair session.

[The durable change] I set up a weekly 30-minute standing 1:1 with them specifically for 'what are you stuck on this week.' Not status, not progress — just stuck-ness. Three months later they were running streaming incident reviews for the whole team. Not because of any heroics on my part — because they now knew when to ask for help and when to work through something alone.

[What I'd do differently] I'd have caught their frustration earlier. Four days of stuckness is four days too many. The signal was in standup two days before — they stopped volunteering details. I should have pulled them aside then, not waited until they were already saying 'this isn't for me.'"

What the interviewer hears

  • The candidate understands that teaching the model pays off more than teaching the fix — classic senior-to-staff transition thinking.
  • Addressing the "streaming isn't for me" comment directly but gently shows emotional intelligence under pressure.

11.9 — The Meta-Pattern Across These Scenarios

Five behaviors show up in every senior-level answer above. Memorize them as the questions to ask yourself when preparing your own DE stories:

  1. Did you do the other person's homework before expecting them to do yours? Reading the migration plan, pulling the Spark UI, sketching the per-column DQ tiers. Work-before-ask is the scarcest behavior in senior rounds.
  2. Did you separate the decidable from the philosophical? Tests-redundancy is falsifiable; vendor-lock is judgment. Addressing each with the right tool (data vs. explicit acceptance) is what senior engineers do that mid engineers don't.
  3. Did you invite the skeptic or opponent to co-own the next step? Asking them to design the pilot kill criteria, write the counter-case, or audit your DQ tier assignments. Co-ownership converts opposition into investment.
  4. Did your answer include at least one specific thing you got wrong? Not as performance — as operational learning. "I was going to push for the full contract; the reframe was better." "I should have pulled them aside two days earlier."
  5. Did your fix extend beyond the specific problem to the class? The data-diff guardrail that now catches bugs on other tables. The standing 1:1 for stuck-ness. The "attack unknowns first" principle. Systemic fixes are the Staff+ signal that transactional fixes cannot replace.

Every DE behavioral story you prepare should be audited against these five. If any three are missing, the story reads as mid-level regardless of how technically impressive the situation was.

12. Staff-Signal Behavioral Scenarios

Section 11 tells eight stories in full. This section is the compact bank: fourteen prompts that senior and staff behavioral rounds lean on, each reduced to what the interviewer is probing, the shape of an L5 answer, the failure that sinks it, and the extension that reads as Staff+. Where §11 already has a worked transcript, the card links to it instead of repeating it.

Two conventions. Numbers in the answer shapes are hypothetical examples; use your own, and have them ready. Level names are shorthand (L5 = senior, L6 = staff); your target company's ladder may label them differently.

The one question every Staff+ extension ends on

An L5 story ends when the problem is solved. A Staff+ story ends when the fix outlives you: a default changed, a review step added, a person grown, a team that now makes the call without you. Every card below closes on the same follow-up, because staff interviewers ask it in some form: "How did this improve the organization after you left the project?" If your only answer is "the pipeline got faster," the story is L5.

12.1 — Disagreeing with a Staff engineer

Prompt: "Tell me about a time you disagreed with a more senior engineer on a technical decision."

Probing: can you disagree on evidence rather than status, and can you tell the story so both people sound competent? Interviewers are listening for how you describe the other person. Contempt is disqualifying even when you were right.

L5 answer shape (a modelled answer; the numbers are illustrative):

  • S: "Our nightly orders job was missing its 6am SLA about once a week. The staff engineer who built it wanted to keep the full nightly rebuild and add compute. I wanted to switch to an incremental MERGE."
  • Name both positions fairly: "His priority was correctness: a full rebuild has no state to corrupt, and he'd been burned by incremental drift before. Mine was cost and runtime: we were rebuilding three years of data to pick up one day of changes. Both were legitimate. We were assuming different late-arrival rates."
  • A: "So I proposed we measure the thing we disagreed about. I pulled 30 days of updated_at distributions: about 99.6% of changes touched the last 7 days. I brought it to him 1:1 before the design review and asked him to find holes in it."
  • Resolution: "He found one: refunds could land 60 days late. We shipped a hybrid: an incremental MERGE over a 7-day window every night, plus a weekly full rebuild that reconciles and alerts on drift. His safety net, my runtime."
  • R: "Runtime went from roughly 3 hours to 25 minutes; the weekly reconcile has caught drift twice. What I'd do differently: open with the data question, not my solution."

Common failure: the story is about being right. "He was stuck in his ways" makes you sound like someone who'll be difficult in the next disagreement, and it makes the interviewer wonder how you'd describe them.

Staff+ extension: turn the disagreement into a decision rule. "We wrote down when this team uses incremental versus full rebuild, based on measured late-arrival rates, and added a drift check to our pipeline template. Two later pipelines picked the pattern without a debate." Then answer: "How did this improve the organization after you left the project?"

"Tell me about a disagreement with a senior engineer."
30 sec

"A staff engineer and I disagreed on full rebuild versus incremental for a job missing its SLA. We were assuming different late-arrival rates, so I measured them, and he found the case my data missed: late refunds. We shipped a hybrid, incremental nightly plus a weekly reconcile. It met the SLA and kept his correctness guarantee."

2 min

The five beats above. Spend a full sentence stating his reasoning at its strongest before you state yours. Name the hidden assumption you disagreed on, the evidence you gathered, the flaw he found, the combined decision, one number, and one thing you'd do differently.

Deep dive

Be ready for the mechanics: how the MERGE was keyed, why 7 days, what the reconcile compares (row counts and sums per partition, then a key-level diff on mismatch), what happens when the weekly job finds drift, and who gets paged. Then the org layer: the written decision rule, and how the next team used it.

Where to stop: when the interviewer knows what the assumption was, who contributed what, and what changed afterwards. Don't relitigate the argument.

Interviewer pushes back

You: "…and he found the late-refund case my analysis had missed."

Interviewer: "So you were wrong?"

Strong answer: "Partly, yes. My proposal alone would have silently dropped late refunds. His alone would have kept missing the SLA. The decision was better than either of our starting positions, and that only happened because I brought him the data before the meeting instead of trying to win in it. I'd rather be partly wrong in a 1:1 than fully wrong in production."

Weak answer: "Not really. It was an edge case, and my approach was basically right." Minimising the other person's contribution is exactly what the question was testing for.

12.2 — Influencing without authority

Prompt: "Tell me about getting another team to do something they didn't plan to do."

Probing: do you move people by making the ask cheap and aligned with their goals, or by escalating?

L5 answer shape:

  • S/T: you needed a producer team to add an event field or stop a breaking change; it wasn't on their roadmap.
  • A: you learned their priorities first and framed the ask in their terms ("this removes 2 of your 5 weekly support tickets").
  • A: you cut the cost to them: you wrote the PR, the test and the rollout note yourself.
  • R: shipped in their next sprint; one example number, such as a downstream incident class that no longer occurs.

Common failure: "I escalated to my manager, who talked to their manager." That's authority, borrowed.

Staff+ extension: you changed the path so the next ask is cheap: a documented contract-change process, a shared schema repo, a standing sync. Worked transcript: §11.1. "How did this improve the organization after you left the project?"

12.3 — Migration strategy

Prompt: "Walk me through a migration you led. How did you sequence it?"

Probing: reversibility, consumer empathy, and whether you knew when you were finished.

L5 answer shape:

  • S: an example is 40 consumers on a legacy table or orchestrator, with a hard deadline such as a license end.
  • A: you took an inventory (consumers, engines, criticality) before touching anything.
  • A: parallel run with a reconciliation check, pilot on low-risk consumers, then cohorts with explicit sign-off.
  • A: a written rollback for every phase and exit criteria for each cohort.
  • R: finished on time with the old path decommissioned. Say "decommissioned"; half-migrations are the default outcome.

Common failure: technical steps only, with no consumer plan and no end state. The legacy system is still running two years later.

Staff+ extension: the playbook became reusable (inventory template, reconcile job, comms cadence), and you deleted the old system instead of leaving it for someone else. Technical version: §5 Scenario C. "How did this improve the organization after you left the project?"

12.4 — Stopping a bad architecture

Prompt: "Tell me about a time you stopped a design you believed was wrong."

Probing: can you block something without blocking someone, and did you offer a path forward?

L5 answer shape:

  • S: a proposal to, for example, dual-write from the application to both the warehouse and a cache, with no reconciliation.
  • A: you raised it in review as a failure scenario ("if write two fails after write one succeeds, which is the truth?"), not as a verdict.
  • A: you proposed an alternative with its own costs stated (CDC from the source of truth, plus ~1 minute of lag).
  • A: you offered to prototype it, so rejecting the first design didn't cost the author their timeline.
  • R: the team adopted the alternative, or kept the original with a mitigation. Either is a fine result if you say why.

Common failure: "I told them it wouldn't work." Nobody hears a design being stopped; they hear a person being overruled.

Staff+ extension: the failure scenario became a standing review question or a checklist item, so the next dual-write gets caught without you in the room. "How did this improve the organization after you left the project?"

12.5 — Changing direction mid-project

Prompt: "Tell me about a time you realised mid-project that the plan wouldn't work."

Probing: do you quantify before escalating, and escalate with options instead of alarm?

L5 answer shape:

  • S: in week 4 of 7, a benchmark showed the read path was an order of magnitude off target.
  • A: you proved it wasn't tunable (tuning moved it 20%, not 10×).
  • A: you sent a one-pager the same day with three options, each with cost, time and risk, plus a recommendation.
  • R: the decision was made in days; you shipped a week late instead of a quarter late.

Common failure: sitting on bad news for two more weeks of tuning because escalating feels like failing.

Staff+ extension: "riskiest unknown first" became a project-kickoff step, with a latency spike in week 1. Worked transcript: §11.4. "How did this improve the organization after you left the project?"

12.6 — Platform adoption

Prompt: "Tell me about introducing a tool or platform your team resisted."

Probing: do you treat skeptics as reviewers or as obstacles?

L5 answer shape:

  • A: you restated the objections in the skeptics' own words and confirmed them.
  • A: you split the objections into testable ones (answered with data) and judgment calls (acknowledged, not argued).
  • A: a small pilot with success and kill criteria written by the lead skeptic.
  • R: an expansion decision at the review date, and the skeptic's concern turned out to be real and got handled.

Common failure: a finished proposal defended in a team meeting, with adoption measured by mandate.

Staff+ extension: adoption measured by pull, not push (other teams asked for it), plus the paved-road docs that made that possible. Worked transcript: §11.3. "How did this improve the organization after you left the project?"

12.7 — Communicating an outage

Prompt: "A key dataset is wrong and executives are looking at it. How do you communicate?"

Probing: do you manage the trust impact as well as the technical one?

L5 answer shape:

  • A: within minutes, a first note to consumers: what's affected, what not to use, when the next update comes. Send it before you know the cause.
  • A: updates on a fixed cadence (for example every 30 minutes), even when the update is "no change."
  • A: separate channels: technical detail in the incident channel, impact and ETA for stakeholders.
  • R: the corrected number went out with the delta explained, followed by a short written post-incident summary: impact, cause, fix, prevention.

Common failure: silence until the fix is done. Stakeholders fill the silence with their own theories, and the CFO repeats the wrong number.

Staff+ extension: a comms template and a data-incident severity scale, plus "certified" markers on dashboards so consumers know which numbers are trustworthy. Related: §5 Scenario B, Part 12 §6. "How did this improve the organization after you left the project?"

12.8 — Prioritizing technical debt

Prompt: "How did you get time for technical debt when the roadmap was full?"

Probing: can you translate debt into business cost, instead of calling it "cleanup"?

L5 answer shape:

  • S: a fragile pipeline consuming, for example, about 30% of on-call pages.
  • A: you quantified the cost: pages per month, engineer-hours, delayed features, SLA misses.
  • A: you ranked debt items by cost of keeping them against cost of fixing them, and proposed the top two, not a rewrite.
  • A: you negotiated a fixed allocation (say one sprint in five) or bundled a fix with a feature that touched the same code.
  • R: pages dropped measurably, with the before and after numbers.

Common failure: "The code was messy so we rewrote it." With no cost, no ranking and no result, it sounds like a hobby.

Staff+ extension: a debt register reviewed each quarter alongside the roadmap, with the ranking method adopted by other teams. "How did this improve the organization after you left the project?"

12.9 — Saying no to product

Prompt: "Tell me about declining a request from product."

Probing: is your "no" principled, cheaper than the ask, and followed by a "here's what we can do"?

L5 answer shape:

  • S: a request for sub-second freshness on a dashboard read twice a day.
  • A: you asked what decision the data drives and how quickly someone acts on it.
  • A: you priced both options: always-on streaming, a serving store and on-call, against a 15-minute micro-batch.
  • A: you offered the cheaper option plus a trigger for revisiting it ("if ops starts acting within minutes, we upgrade").
  • R: product agreed, and the trigger never fired, or it did and you upgraded on schedule.

Common failure: "no" based on effort alone ("that's hard"), with no alternative offered.

Staff+ extension: a published freshness tier menu with prices, so future requests start from a tier instead of a negotiation. Related: Part 08, §11.6. "How did this improve the organization after you left the project?"

12.10 — Mentorship

Prompt: "Tell me about someone you helped grow."

Probing: do you teach models or hand out answers, and can you point to evidence the person grew?

L5 answer shape:

  • S: a junior stuck for days on a streaming bug and losing confidence.
  • A: you diagnosed the misconception, not just the bug, by asking them to explain their mental model first.
  • A: you let them find the fix, then addressed the confidence issue directly.
  • R: evidence of growth, such as running reviews or on-call alone within a quarter.

Common failure: "I paired with them and fixed it." That's help, not mentorship.

Staff+ extension: the mentoring scaled: an onboarding path, a debugging guide, and the person now mentoring others. Worked transcript: §11.8. "How did this improve the organization after you left the project?"

12.11 — Cross-team ownership

Prompt: "Tell me about a problem that sat between teams and nobody owned it."

Probing: do you step into ownership gaps, and do you close them structurally rather than heroically?

L5 answer shape:

  • S: an orphaned pipeline whose author had left. Three teams consumed it, none owned it, and it failed about monthly.
  • A: you stabilised it first: runbook, alerting, one fix.
  • A: you mapped the consumers and costs and proposed an owner, with a clear handover.
  • A: if no team would take it, you proposed deprecation with a date instead of adopting it silently.
  • R: an owner named in the catalog, failures down, or the pipeline deleted.

Common failure: heroic fixes every month for a year. You've become the unacknowledged owner, and it will leave with you.

Staff+ extension: a rule that nothing ships without an owner field in the catalog, and a quarterly orphan sweep. "How did this improve the organization after you left the project?"

12.12 — Architecture review

Prompt: "Tell me about a design review you ran or contributed to that changed the outcome."

Probing: can you review for failure modes and trade-offs rather than taste, and make review cheap for the author?

L5 answer shape:

  • S: a design doc for a new ingestion service.
  • A: you read it asynchronously and left comments ranked as blocking, should-fix or nit.
  • A: your blocking comment was a concrete scenario (for example "what happens on replay after a schema change?") with a suggested fix.
  • A: in the meeting you spent the time on the one or two decisions that were hard to reverse.
  • R: the design changed on the irreversible point; nits were resolved in comments.

Common failure: fifty unranked comments, or style debates in the meeting while the irreversible decision goes unexamined.

Staff+ extension: the review template, covering requirements, numbers, data model, failure modes, rollback and cost, became the team's standard. Reviews got shorter and caught more. Design framework: Part 18. "How did this improve the organization after you left the project?"

12.13 — Incident leadership

Prompt: "Tell me about leading an incident that crossed several teams."

Probing: can you coordinate rather than debug alone, and run a blameless review that produces real fixes?

L5 answer shape:

  • S: an upstream schema change broke three pipelines and a finance report.
  • A: you took the incident-commander role explicitly and assigned roles: investigator, comms, scribe.
  • A: mitigation before root cause: pause the downstream publish and serve the last good snapshot.
  • A: you ran the review blamelessly. Actions had owners and dates, and at least one was systemic.
  • R: time to mitigate and time to resolve (example: 40 minutes and 5 hours), with the actions closed.

Common failure: the IC is also the lead debugger, so comms stall and nobody sees the whole picture. Or the review names a person.

Staff+ extension: contract checks in the producer's CI so this class of change is blocked before merge, plus a cross-team on-call handoff. Related: Part 12 §6, Part 19. "How did this improve the organization after you left the project?"

12.14 — Balancing delivery vs reliability

Prompt: "Tell me about a time speed and reliability pulled in opposite directions."

Probing: do you make the risk explicit and bounded, or pick a side on principle?

L5 answer shape:

  • S: a launch date against a missing guardrail (DQ gates, backfill tooling, a contract).
  • A: you separated what is dangerous to skip from what is only nice to have.
  • A: you shipped with the dangerous items covered and the rest time-boxed, with a named owner and date.
  • A: an escape hatch, such as a manual override with logging, so the safety mechanism can't hold the launch hostage.
  • R: launched on time, the deferred items landed, and there was one near-miss the guardrail caught.

Common failure: "Reliability always comes first." Nobody believes it, and it signals you can't ship.

Staff+ extension: an error-budget-style policy: when the pipeline is within its SLO, the team ships; when it isn't, reliability work jumps the queue. The trade-off becomes a rule instead of an argument. Worked transcripts: §11.5–11.6. "How did this improve the organization after you left the project?"

Behavioral answer checklist: run every story through it
CheckPass looks like
First sentenceThe stakes or the failure, not the backstory
"I" with verbsYour decisions are distinguishable from the team's
The other personTheir position stated at its strongest; they sound competent
EvidenceData or a prototype settled it, not seniority or volume
A numberAt least one before/after, and you know where it came from
What you got wrongOne specific, operational miss
LengthUnder 4 minutes spoken; a 30-second version ready
Staff+ closeA concrete answer to "How did this improve the organization after you left the project?"

13. Closing Note

Interviews reward a specific kind of preparation — the kind that produces fluent speech under pressure, not encyclopedic knowledge in silence. Everything in this part is aimed at the first, not the second.

If you do the four-week roadmap, run three mocks, prepare one story per frame (with a 30-second version of each), and can say the first 30 seconds of your answer to each scenario in §5 — you will walk into the loop fluent rather than merely informed. That's the bar to aim for.

Good luck.

Part 10

Data Governance & Compliance

Quick refresh10 minInterview study40 minDeep practice55 min
Last technically reviewed September 2026
Covers GDPR engineering obligations, right to erasure in an immutable lakehouse, crypto-shredding, CCPA/CPRA opt-out and consent, SOX ITGCs, retention enforcement, column-level lineage and OpenLineage, catalogs, PII discovery and classification, auditability
Versions referenced Delta Lake 3.x/4.x (deletion vectors, REORG … APPLY (PURGE)), Apache Iceberg 1.x (format v2/v3), Snowflake Enterprise Edition, Airflow 2.7+/3.x OpenLineage provider
Primary references GDPR text (EUR-Lex) · UK ICO — right to erasure · EDPB guidelines · CPPA regulations (CCPA) · Delta deletion vectors · Iceberg Spark procedures · OpenLineage · Snowflake ACCESS_HISTORY
Known implementation differences Every engine can delete a row; they differ in when the bytes are physically gone (deletion vectors, delete files, Time Travel, Fail-safe), and that gap is where compliance bugs live.

The interviewer is not testing whether you can recite GDPR articles. They are testing whether you can turn a legal obligation into a mechanism a pipeline enforces, and prove afterwards that it ran. Can you delete one person from a petabyte of immutable files? Can you say which dashboards break if a column changes, or who read a sensitive column last Tuesday? And can you do it without locking analysts out? This chapter stays at the level of engineering obligations. It is not legal advice: your privacy counsel decides what "erased", "anonymous" and "necessary" mean. How access control is implemented (IAM, RBAC/ABAC, KMS, masking and row policies, tokenization, exfiltration controls) is in Part 14.

2026 Interview Note

Timeless: logical delete is not physical delete; identifiers should be isolated so erasure is cheap; policies attach to classifications, not to tables; lineage makes impact analysis and erasure scoping possible; audit evidence must live somewhere its subject cannot edit. Version-specific: the command that makes bytes disappear (REORG … PURGE, rewrite_data_files, VACUUM), retention defaults, which edition includes access history, and product names in the catalog market. Say which you are describing.

1. GDPR — Engineering Obligations

The General Data Protection Regulation (EU 2016/679) applies in two cases (Art. 3). The first is controllers and processors established in the EU. The second is non-EU organisations that offer goods or services to people in the EU, or monitor their behaviour. What counts is where the data subject is, not their citizenship or residency. For a data engineer, the useful framing is that each principle becomes a mechanism you can point to.

The Article 5 principles (six in 5(1), plus accountability in 5(2))

PrincipleEngineering mechanism
Lawfulness, fairness, transparencyLegal basis recorded per purpose; consent as events (§3)
Purpose limitationPurpose tags on datasets; access granted per purpose, not "all of gold"
Data minimisationIngest an allow-list of fields, not SELECT *; tokenize identifiers at bronze
AccuracyCorrections propagate like erasures (same lineage, same rewrite)
Storage limitationA retention policy stored as data and enforced by a job (§5)
Integrity and confidentialityClassification-driven masking, row policies and encryption (Part 14)
Accountability (5(2))You must demonstrate compliance: lineage, access logs, erasure proofs, records of processing, DPIAs

Accountability is the one engineers forget. A control with no evidence that it ran is, to an auditor, a control you do not have (§10).

Right to Erasure (Article 17) — the obligation

A data subject may ask you to delete their personal data. You must respond within one month, extendable by two further months for complex or numerous requests (Art. 12(3)). The GDPR text says nothing about backups. Regulator guidance (for example the UK ICO) accepts putting backed-up data "beyond use" until the backup rotates out, provided any restore re-applies the erasure queue first. Document that policy. The mechanics get their own section: §2.

Pseudonymization and Anonymization

Pseudonymization (Art. 4(5)) replaces direct identifiers with a token, and the means of re-linking are kept separately under strict control. It is still personal data: pseudonymization reduces risk, not obligations. Anonymization takes data out of scope only when re-identification is no longer "reasonably likely" by any party (Recital 26). No numeric threshold exists in law. k-anonymity alone rarely meets the bar because of linkage and homogeneity attacks (WP29 Opinion 05/2014). Differential privacy with a tracked budget (ε) is stronger and costs utility. Most "anonymized" analytics tables are really pseudonymized. Label them that way.

Interviewer pushes back

You: “We anonymize the events table by replacing email with SHA-256(email).”

Interviewer: “Is that table still in GDPR scope?”

Strong answer: “Yes. An unsalted hash of an email is a dictionary lookup: hash a list of emails (a CRM export, a breach dump) and join. It is also a stable key that singles a person out across tables. That is pseudonymization at best. For a joinable key I use an HMAC with a KMS-held key analysts cannot read, or better a random surrogate from a mapping table, so erasure can delete the mapping. The table stays classified as personal data. If I need anonymous output, I publish aggregates with minimum group sizes or DP results and get the assessment signed off.”

Weak answer: “SHA-256 is irreversible, so it's anonymous.” Irreversible functions are not the threat model. Guessable inputs are.

Data Residency and Transfers

GDPR does not require EU storage. It restricts transfers outside the EEA (Chapter V: adequacy decisions such as the 2023 EU–US Data Privacy Framework, SCCs, BCRs). Hard residency usually comes from sector or national law or customer contracts. The pattern is the same either way: per-region storage and compute, with only aggregates or pseudonymized data crossing. Watch the subtle transfers. A federated query whose coordinator runs outside the region pulls EU rows out, even if storage never moved. So do replicated logs. Cross-region replication of personal data is a legal decision, not a tuning knob.

2. Right to Erasure in an Immutable Lakehouse

Immutable files and retained history are what make time travel work, and what make erasure hard. A DELETE commits a new version; the old bytes stay in storage, reachable by time travel and often still inside the current files. Erasure is a chain, complete only when the last link has run.

Step 1 — Locate: you cannot delete what you cannot find

Two indexes: a PII index (which columns hold which identifier types, from classification, §9) and column-level lineage (where they flowed, §6). The danger is what lineage misses: free text, JSON blobs, SELECT * extracts, training snapshots, notebook uploads. Every in-scope table needs a subject key; an email buried in JSON keyed by event_id means a full scan on every request.

Design for erasure: isolate identifiers

Do the numbers first. A 1 PB event table in 1 GB files is about a million files. Partitioned by date, with active users present on most days, a weekly batch of 10,000 erasures touches nearly every file: you rewrite the petabyte weekly. Clustering by user_id helps within a partition, not across 1,000 of them. The durable fix is to keep direct identifiers out of the big tables:

  • Identity vault / mapping table. At ingest, replace email, phone and account ID with a random subject_sk. Direct identifiers live only in the small subject_sk → identity table and a few PII dimensions, which is where erasure deletes and purges.
  • Facts carry only the surrogate. Once the mapping is gone, fact rows no longer link to a person through the key. Whether they are still personal data is a legal judgement: quasi-identifiers (precise location, device ID) can re-identify. Get it signed off, and generalize or delete those too.
  • Where facts must be erased batch requests, cluster by the subject key so DELETE prunes files, and schedule the physical purge to fit inside the deadline.

Steps 2–5 — Delete, purge, expire, remove

Engine: Delta Lake 3.x/4.x on Spark or DatabricksDialect: Spark SQLExecutable: Yes — Delta with deletion vectors enabled; adapt table names
-- 2. Logical delete: new table version; with deletion vectors (DVs) on,
--    the data files are NOT rewritten, only marked
DELETE FROM silver.user_profile
WHERE subject_sk IN (SELECT subject_sk FROM gov.erasure_queue
                     WHERE status = 'PENDING');

-- 3. Purge: rewrite every file that carries soft-deleted rows
REORG TABLE silver.user_profile APPLY (PURGE);

-- 4+5. Delete files no longer referenced by any version inside the
--      retention window (default 7 days, delta.deletedFileRetentionDuration)
VACUUM silver.user_profile;          -- after the window has elapsed
Engine: Apache Iceberg 1.x on Spark 3.5/4.xDialect: Spark SQL (Iceberg procedures)Executable: Illustrative — adapt catalog, table and timestamps
-- 2. Logical delete (copy-on-write rewrites files now;
--    merge-on-read writes position/equality deletes or v3 DVs)
DELETE FROM lake.silver.user_profile
WHERE subject_sk IN (SELECT subject_sk FROM lake.gov.erasure_queue
                     WHERE status = 'PENDING');

-- 3. Purge: rewrite any data file that has at least one delete applied
CALL lake.system.rewrite_data_files(
  table   => 'silver.user_profile',
  options => map('delete-file-threshold', '1'));

-- Tags and branches pin snapshots: check before expiring
SELECT name, type, snapshot_id FROM lake.silver.user_profile.refs;

-- 4. Expire old snapshots (this also deletes files they alone referenced)
CALL lake.system.expire_snapshots(
  table => 'silver.user_profile',
  older_than => TIMESTAMP '2026-09-17 00:00:00', retain_last => 1);

-- 5. Remove files no snapshot ever referenced (failed/aborted writes)
CALL lake.system.remove_orphan_files(
  table => 'silver.user_profile',
  older_than => TIMESTAMP '2026-09-21 00:00:00');

Three details separate a senior answer from a textbook one:

  • The erasure deadline bounds your time-travel window. Snapshot retention + purge cadence + VACUUM soft-delete window must be less than the SLA. A 90-day time-travel policy on a PII table is a compliance decision, whether or not anyone made it. Managed warehouses have the same shape: Snowflake Time Travel (up to 90 days on Enterprise Edition) then 7 days of Fail-safe for permanent tables; BigQuery's time-travel window plus fail-safe. You cannot query fail-safe, but it exists. Check current docs.
  • Metadata leaks values. Min/max column stats live in the Delta log and Iceberg manifests, so an email can outlive its data file. Turn stats off for identifier columns (Iceberg write.metadata.metrics.column.<col>=none; Delta delta.dataSkippingStatsColumns — check current docs).
  • Concurrency. An erasure DELETE conflicts with compaction and streaming MERGE on the same files under optimistic concurrency (Part 7 §4). Retry on conflict; the queue makes it idempotent.
Interviewer pushes back

You: “We have deletion vectors on, so the DELETE is cheap and the user is gone.”

Interviewer: “Gone from where?”

Strong answer: “From query results on the current version, and that's all. A deletion vector is a bitmap saying ‘skip row 4,812 of this file’. The file still holds the email, and a time-travel query to the prior version returns it. DVs make the delete cheap, not complete. I purge (Delta REORG … APPLY (PURGE), Iceberg rewrite_data_files) so no live file holds the row, then expire snapshots and VACUUM so no old file does. The request stays open until a verification scan comes back empty.”

Weak answer: “Time travel is only 7 days, so it's fine.” That is 7 days after the purge. Without the purge, the current files hold the data forever.

Step 6 — Beyond the table

CopyWhy it survives a table deleteMechanism
Delta Change Data Feed_change_data holds pre-imagesRemoved by VACUUM; include in SLA math
Kafka topicsKept until retention expiresShort retention; or compacted topics keyed by subject plus tombstones. A topic keyed by event_id cannot be erased by key
Raw / bronze landingA replay or backfill resurrects the userErasure list as a suppression filter in ingest and every backfill
Deep clones, extracts, BI caches, replicasPhysical copies with their own TTLs; lineage often stops at the exportRegister every copy in the catalog with an erasure handler or a TTL under the SLA
Derived aggregatesFine if truly aggregated; not at group size 1Minimum group sizes; recompute small groups
Feature stores, vector indexesEmbeddings of a user's text are derived personal datasubject_sk metadata on every vector; delete by filter
Trained modelsWeights may memorise training rowsLegal and ML question; usually retrain next cycle on erased data, documented (Part 17)

Step 8 — Prove it

Keep an append-only erasure log, one row per request per table per step: request_id, subject_ref, table, step, table_version_before/after, rows_affected, completed_at, job_run_id. Do not put the email in it. Use a keyed hash or the request ID, or the log becomes the PII you just deleted. Close the request only after a verification scan of current and still-retained versions returns zero hits.

Alternative — crypto-shredding

Encrypt each subject's PII fields with a per-subject data key, wrapped by a KMS key. To erase, destroy the key: every copy (old snapshots, backups, CDF, replicas) becomes unreadable without rewriting a file. KMS mechanics are in Part 14.

GainCost
Erasure is O(1) and reaches immutable copies and backupsMillions of keys. The key store must support real deletion, so it cannot be a lakehouse table with time travel or backed up forever
No petabyte rewrites; history stays intactEncrypted columns cannot be filtered, joined, grouped or min/max-pruned. Randomized ciphertext also compresses poorly
Also limits blast radius of a leaked fileDecrypt on read adds cost and a hard dependency on the key service. Lose the key store and you have shredded everyone

Whether ciphertext under a destroyed key counts as erased is a legal judgement; get it signed off. The common hybrid: crypto-shred identifier columns in wide, long-retained facts; physically delete from small PII dimensions.

“How do you delete one user's data from a petabyte lakehouse?”
30 sec

You design so you rarely have to. Direct identifiers live in a small identity table, facts carry a surrogate key, and erasure deletes the mapping and the PII dimensions. Where rows must go, it is a chain, not a statement: locate through the PII index and lineage, DELETE, purge files that still hold the row, expire snapshots, vacuum, then clear copies outside the table. It is only done when a verification scan finds nothing.

2 min

Requests land in a queue with a deadline. A weekly batch runs DELETE/MERGE by subject key on every table in the PII index, clustered by that key so pruning works. Deletion vectors make that cheap but logical, so it follows with REORG PURGE or rewrite_data_files, snapshot expiry and VACUUM, with retention set so the chain fits the deadline. The same list suppresses the user at ingest (no resurrection by backfill) and drives Kafka tombstones, feature-store and vector deletes. Every step writes to an append-only erasure log. Backups go "beyond use"; restores re-apply the queue.

Deep dive

Cost: scattered users mean a rewrite per touched file, so batching and identifier isolation are cost decisions. Leaks: column stats in the Delta log and Iceberg manifests, snapshots pinned by Iceberg tags, warehouse fail-safe, CDF pre-images. Crypto-shredding for long-retention facts, with its key-store and query-cost trade-offs. Legal edges you escalate rather than decide: residual quasi-identifiers, trained models, legal holds.

Where to stop: once you have named "logical vs physical", the SLA-bounds-retention rule and the verification scan, go deeper only if they ask about cost or crypto-shredding.

Drill · Erasure

An erasure request was marked COMPLETED 12 days ago. An analyst runs SELECT … FROM silver.user_profile TIMESTAMP AS OF '2026-08-20' and the user's email is in the result.

STOP. Answer before revealing.

Reveal the diagnosis
  1. Observe Current version clean, historical version not: the logical delete worked; purge/expire/vacuum did not cover this version.
  2. Hypothesize (a) The job set COMPLETED after DELETE, and nothing purged or expired. (b) Snapshot or time-travel retention is longer than the erasure SLA. (c) An Iceberg tag or branch pins that snapshot. (d) VACUUM or expiry is scheduled but failing, or disabled on this table. (e) The query hit a deep clone or extract, not the table.
  3. Measure Delta: DESCRIBE HISTORY (DELETE, REORG, VACUUM?) and retention properties. Iceberg: snapshots and refs tables, expiry job logs. Resolve the analyst's table name to a storage path.
  4. Isolate If 2026-08-20 sits inside a 60-day retention window with no purge step, this is design, not a flaky job: every user erased in 60 days is exposed.
  5. Fix Reopen affected requests; purge, expire and VACUUM every PII table; drop pinning tags (after checking for legal holds); re-run the verification scan.
  6. Prevent State machine DELETED → PURGED → EXPIRED → VERIFIED; only VERIFIED is complete. CI check: PII-tagged tables have retention ≤ SLA − purge cadence. Daily canary: erase a synthetic subject and alert if it is still found after the SLA.
Failure-first: what can fail in the erasure pipeline?
FailureDetectRecoverPrevent recurrence
Request closed after logical delete onlyVerification scan across retained versions finds the subjectReopen; run purge, expire, vacuumState machine; close only on VERIFIED
A table holding PII is not in the indexPeriodic classifier scan finds an untagged PII columnAdd it to the index; re-run erasures for the SLA windowClassification runs on schema-change events; PRs fail without tags
Backfill or stream replay resurrects erased usersSuppression-list anti-join count > 0 in bronzeRe-run erasure on affected tablesSuppression filter in every ingest and backfill path
DELETE loses optimistic-concurrency races with compaction or MERGEJob retries exhausted; queue age growsRetry off-peak; pause the conflicting job for that tableIdempotent queue; alert on queue age vs deadline
VACUUM or expiry silently disabled or failingOldest reachable version age > policyRun manually; fix the scheduleMonitor "oldest version age" per PII table
Copies outside the table (Kafka, CDF, vectors, extracts)Verification scan covers only tablesPer-store delete; rebuild indexEvery store registered with an erasure handler, or it cannot hold PII

3. CCPA / CPRA — Opt-out, Limit, Consent

The CCPA took effect on 1 January 2020. The CPRA amendments, operative 1 January 2023, created the California Privacy Protection Agency and added rights to correct, to opt out of "sharing", and to limit use of sensitive personal information. What changes pipelines:

  • "Sale" and "sharing" (for cross-context behavioural advertising) are defined broadly. Sending identifiable data to a third-party ad or analytics partner can qualify.
  • Opt-outs must be honoured within 15 business days under the CPPA regulations, and a browser Global Privacy Control signal counts as an opt-out of sale and sharing, so opt-outs arrive as events from the web edge, not only from a settings page.
  • Sensitive personal information (precise geolocation, financial account, health, government ID and others) carries a separate "Limit the Use of My Sensitive Personal Information" right.
  • Access and deletion requests get 45 days, extendable once by 45.

The design error is a per-regime boolean table (consent_gdpr, consent_ccpa). Consent is per purpose, changes over time and must be provable. Model it as an event log, derive current state, and join it into every export or restricted-purpose job:

Engine: PostgreSQL 14+ (any ANSI window-function engine with small changes)Dialect: PostgreSQL SQLExecutable: Yes — PostgreSQL
CREATE TABLE consent_event (
  subject_sk      bigint      NOT NULL,
  purpose         text        NOT NULL,  -- 'ads_sharing','analytics','sale',...
  status          text        NOT NULL CHECK (status IN ('granted','denied','withdrawn')),
  source          text        NOT NULL,  -- 'gpc_header','settings_page','cmp_banner'
  policy_version  text        NOT NULL,
  effective_at    timestamptz NOT NULL
);

-- Current state per subject and purpose; downstream exports anti-join on this
CREATE VIEW consent_current AS
SELECT subject_sk, purpose, status, source, effective_at
FROM (
  SELECT c.*, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY subject_sk, purpose
                                 ORDER BY effective_at DESC) AS rn
  FROM consent_event c
) x
WHERE rn = 1;

Make the join fail closed: a missing row means "not permitted" for sale, sharing or restricted purposes. The log doubles as evidence of which policy version the user saw, when, and through which channel.

4. SOX — IT General Controls for Data Systems

SOX requires internal control over financial reporting (ICFR). Pipelines feeding financial statements are tested as IT general controls (ITGCs):

  • Change management. Reviewed, approved, traceable to a deployed commit. SOX prescribes no tickets, but an unapproved production change is an ITGC exception reported as a control deficiency (which can escalate to a material weakness). Keep a documented emergency-change path with after-the-fact approval.
  • Logical access. Least privilege, periodic access reviews, and segregation of duties: authors don't approve their own changes or hold standing write access to production financial tables.
  • Operations. Monitoring, and evidence that failures were resolved.
  • Data integrity. Reconciliation is the key control: counts and control totals (amounts by entity and period) between ledger and warehouse, breaks escalated, evidence kept.
  • Audit trails. Shipped to write-once storage (§10). Delta DESCRIBE HISTORY is operational history bounded by delta.logRetentionDuration, not an audit log.

5. Data Retention Engineering

Periods come from legal and the records schedule; the engineering job is to enforce them mechanically and prove it. The periods below are illustrative, not legal defaults.

Data categoryIllustrative retentionEngineering mechanism
Raw event logs with identifiersWeeks to a few monthsS3 lifecycle: Standard → delete at expiry. Don't transition short-lived data to Glacier: 90-day minimum-duration charges and per-object transition fees (Part 11)
Aggregated analyticsYearsGlacier Instant Retrieval if still queried (Athena reads it directly). Deep Archive only for data you will restore before querying (hours)
PII-containing recordsAccount lifetime + a documented grace periodRetention job keyed on account_closed_at; same purge chain as erasure
Audit logsCommonly 7 years for financial-control evidence (SOX §802 / SEC Rule 2-06 practice). GDPR sets no fixed period: justify and document oneSeparate account; S3 Object Lock in compliance mode
Financial transactionsPer records schedule (often multi-year)Cold storage plus retained reconciliation checksums

Keep the policy as data: a retention_policy table (dataset, basis_column, retain_days, action, legal_hold) joined to classification tags, from which a nightly job generates deletes and logs each run. On Delta and Iceberg, ALTER TABLE … DROP PARTITION is Hive syntax and is not supported; use a DELETE aligned to partition boundaries:

Engine: Delta Lake or Apache Iceberg on SparkDialect: Spark SQLExecutable: Yes — adapt table name and date
-- Metadata-only when the predicate matches whole partitions:
-- files are dropped from the snapshot, not rewritten.
DELETE FROM lake.bronze.events WHERE event_date < DATE '2026-06-26';
-- Bytes are physically removed only after snapshot expiry / VACUUM.

Legal hold beats retention. Litigation can freeze deletion for a dataset or subject; the job checks legal_hold first, and an S3 Object Lock legal hold blocks deletion regardless of lifecycle rules. When a hold collides with an erasure request, you don't choose: escalate, record the decision, resume when it lifts.

2026 Interview Note

Retention for the table and retention for its history are different knobs. Expiring rows older than 90 days does nothing if the table keeps 180 days of snapshots. The timeless rule: history retention ≤ data retention. The version-specific part is the knob names: Delta delta.deletedFileRetentionDuration and delta.logRetentionDuration, Iceberg history.expire.max-snapshot-age-ms, Snowflake DATA_RETENTION_TIME_IN_DAYS. On Databricks, predictive optimization may run VACUUM for you. Check what it is configured to do before you rely on it.

6. Data Lineage

Lineage earns its place through three uses: impact analysis (what breaks if I change this column?), root cause (where did this bad number come from?) and compliance scoping (where did this PII flow? step 1 of erasure).

Table-level lineage

Captured from dbt's manifest.json, from Airflow via the OpenLineage provider (apache-airflow-providers-openlineage, Airflow 2.7+, operator-dependent), or from warehouse query logs. Enough for coarse impact; not for PII: gold.orders depends on silver.users, but does it carry the email?

Column-level lineage

Two capture methods, with opposite failure modes:

Parse the SQL (static)Runtime events (dynamic)
HowParse model or query text into an AST, resolve against schemas (sqlglot's lineage, dbt's compiled SQL)The engine reports what it actually read and wrote from its analyzed plan (OpenLineage Spark integration, Snowflake ACCESS_HISTORY objects_modified, Unity Catalog lineage system tables)
StrengthsAvailable before the job runs, so it works in CI for "this PR breaks 14 dashboards"Sees what really ran: dynamic SQL, generated queries, notebooks
Breaks onSELECT * without a schema, dynamic SQL, UDFs, Python/DataFrame transforms, macrosJobs that never ran in the window, opaque UDFs and Python, engines without an integration

Use both: static for pre-merge impact checks, runtime for the truth graph. A missing edge is a known gap, never evidence of "clean".

Once lineage lives in a table of edges, impact analysis is a graph walk:

Engine: PostgreSQL 14+Dialect: PostgreSQL SQLExecutable: Yes — PostgreSQL (the CYCLE clause needs 14+)
-- lineage_edge(src_dataset, src_column, dst_dataset, dst_column, job)
WITH RECURSIVE downstream AS (
  SELECT dst_dataset, dst_column, 1 AS depth
  FROM lineage_edge
  WHERE src_dataset = 'crm.users' AND src_column = 'country'
  UNION ALL
  SELECT e.dst_dataset, e.dst_column, d.depth + 1
  FROM lineage_edge e
  JOIN downstream d
    ON e.src_dataset = d.dst_dataset AND e.src_column = d.dst_column
  WHERE d.depth < 20
) CYCLE dst_dataset, dst_column SET is_cycle USING path
SELECT dst_dataset, dst_column, MIN(depth) AS hops
FROM downstream
GROUP BY dst_dataset, dst_column
ORDER BY hops;

OpenLineage standard

OpenLineage is an open standard (an LF AI & Data project) for lineage events. A run emits START and COMPLETE (or FAIL) events carrying the job, the run ID, and input and output datasets. Facets add detail such as schema, data-quality metrics and a columnLineage facet. The integrations are the Spark listener (column lineage derived from the logical plan), the Airflow provider, dbt (openlineage-dbt, run through the dbt-ol wrapper) and Flink. Events go to any compatible backend: Marquez (the reference implementation), DataHub, OpenMetadata, or commercial catalogs. Producers emit once to a standard, so changing catalogs doesn't mean re-instrumenting every job (see also Part 8).

7. Metadata Management and Data Catalogs

A catalog holds technical metadata (schema, partitions, freshness, quality scores) and business metadata (meaning, owner, SLA, glossary, classification). For governance it is where tags live and policies attach. Its other role, the table-format catalog that brokers commits, is in Part 7 §12.

Data catalog tools

ToolStrengthsWatch for
Unity Catalog (Databricks; OSS since 2024)Tags, row filters, column masks, lineage and audit system tablesCheck OSS vs hosted parity
Snowflake HorizonTag-based masking, access history, classification inside the warehouseGoverns Snowflake objects; external lake assets need integration
DataHub / OpenMetadata (open source)Connectors, lineage graph, glossary, OpenLineage ingestSelf-run; enforcement stays in engines
Glue + DataZone / SageMaker Catalog (similarly: Dataplex, Purview)Zero ops on AWS; Iceberg REST endpoint; Lake Formation tag-based accessAWS-only; glossary and lineage need the layer on top

The L5 point is that a discovery catalog is not an enforcement point. A tag in DataHub protects nothing until an engine policy reads it.

8. PII Handling — Detection and Protection

Detection

  • Column-name heuristics (email, ssn, dob, ip_address): cheap, and a good prior.
  • Value rules: email regex, national-ID patterns, card numbers with a Luhn check, E.164 phones. High precision; they miss odd formats.
  • NER models (spaCy, Presidio's analyzers) for names and addresses in free text. Better recall, slower and noisier.

Tools: AWS Macie (S3 only), Google Cloud Sensitive Data Protection (formerly Cloud DLP), Microsoft Presidio (open source), and classifiers built into Snowflake and Databricks. Scan incrementally on new tables, schema changes and new partitions. Sampling has a blind spot: a column with 0.1% pasted emails passes a 1,000-row sample about a third of the time.

Protection strategies

StrategyReversible?Joinable?Use case
Static masking (redact at write)NoNoNon-prod copies, extracts
Dynamic masking (policy at read)n/a (underlying data intact)For privileged rolesOne table, different views per role
Keyed hash (HMAC)NoYes (same key)Joinable pseudonymous keys for analytics
Mapping table / vault tokenizationYes (with vault)YesPayment data (PCI scope reduction); erasure by deleting the mapping
Deterministic encryption / FPEYes (with key)YesFormat-constrained legacy systems
Encryption at rest (SSE-KMS)Yesn/aDisk and snapshot theft only. Not a control against authorised query users
Per-subject envelope encryptionUntil key is destroyedNoCrypto-shredding (§2)
Generalization / DP noiseNoNoResearch datasets, published aggregates

How these are enforced (masking and row-access policy SQL, tokenization service architecture, KMS key hierarchy) is in Part 14.

9. Data Classification

Sensitivity labels drive access, retention and handling. A common model: Public; Internal (SSO-gated); Confidential (masked by default, access logged: revenue, customer PII); Restricted (need-to-know, time-bound grants: health, government IDs, M&A). Label columns, not tables: a table-level Restricted label either blocks analysts from 40 harmless columns or exempts the 2 dangerous ones.

Propagation is where claims outrun tooling: some catalogs propagate tags along lineage, many stacks don't. Where yours doesn't, enforce it in CI: a model reading a tagged column must tag its output or declare the transform that removes the tag (aggregate, HMAC, drop). A derived column inherits the strictest input classification unless a reviewed transform lowers it.

10. Auditability — Who Accessed What

An auditable platform can answer who read or changed which data, when, using which code, and under which approval. It can also show that the answer has not been edited.

Query and access logs

Snowflake: ACCOUNT_USAGE.ACCESS_HISTORY records the columns each query read (Enterprise Edition+, up to ~3h latency, 365-day retention, so copy it out). BigQuery: INFORMATION_SCHEMA.JOBS plus Cloud Audit Logs (data-access logs must be enabled). Redshift: SYS_QUERY_HISTORY (STL tables keep only days) plus audit logging to S3 or CloudWatch. Databricks: the system.access.audit system table. Figures at time of writing (2026); check current docs.

Engine: SnowflakeDialect: Snowflake SQLExecutable: Yes — Snowflake Enterprise Edition+; adapt object and column names
-- Who read CUSTOMERS.EMAIL in the last 7 days (base objects = underlying tables,
-- so reads through views are attributed to the source column)
SELECT ah.query_start_time,
       ah.user_name,
       ah.query_id
FROM snowflake.account_usage.access_history ah,
     LATERAL FLATTEN(input => ah.base_objects_accessed) obj,
     LATERAL FLATTEN(input => obj.value:"columns")       col
WHERE ah.query_start_time >= DATEADD(day, -7, CURRENT_TIMESTAMP())
  AND obj.value:"objectName"::string  = 'PROD.CRM.CUSTOMERS'
  AND col.value:"columnName"::string  = 'EMAIL'
ORDER BY ah.query_start_time DESC;

Land every engine's access log in one central audit table (principal, object, column, tag, time). Alert on Restricted reads outside the approved group and on volume anomalies (a service account that reads 10k rows suddenly reading 50M).

Pipeline change audit

Every pipeline run logs the job, run ID, code commit SHA, triggering principal, input datasets with snapshot IDs or versions, output version, and rows in and out. Then "which run produced this number?" is a lookup, and time travel can reproduce it: the evidence SOX, GDPR accountability and incident reviews all want. OpenLineage run events carry most of it.

Immutability

Tamper-evident means write-once storage (S3 Object Lock compliance mode, which even root cannot shorten), a separate account the platform team does not administer, and integrity validation (CloudTrail log-file validation, or a hash chain over daily batches). Table-format history is not an immutability control. Delta Change Data Feed and Iceberg snapshots are removed by VACUUM and expire_snapshots, and anyone with write access to the bucket can delete them. CDF also keeps pre-images of erased rows, which is why _change_data is in the erasure chain (§2). Audit logs holding query text or values can themselves contain PII: log references and column names, not results, and classify the audit store too.

11. Compliance Without Blocking Analysts

Governance that needs a ticket per query gets routed around, into a CSV on a laptop. Make the compliant path the easiest one.

  • Masked by default, not denied by default. All rows visible; identifiers masked or HMAC'd. Most analysis needs "same user", not "which user".
  • Policies on tags, not grants on tables. Tag once; the mask follows into every table and engine that honours the tag.
  • Purpose-based, time-bound elevation. Unmasked access is self-service with a stated purpose and an expiry, logged and reviewed, never a standing role.
  • Safe gold layer. Aggregates with minimum group sizes and pseudonymous facts are the default surface; restricted raw data stays in a zone few touch.
  • Controls in CI, not in meetings. The reviewer sees "this model exposes PII.EMAIL to tier Internal" before merge, not in an audit six months later.
L5 Interview CardData Governance & Compliance
Must know
  • GDPR scope follows the data subject's location (Art. 3). Seven Art. 5 principles, including accountability.
  • Erasure deadline: one month, extendable by two (Art. 12(3)). CCPA: 45 + 45 days, opt-outs within 15 business days, GPC is an opt-out.
  • Logical delete (DVs, delete files) ≠ physical delete. Purge → expire → vacuum.
  • Hashing an email is pseudonymization; GDPR restricts transfers, not storage location.
  • Column-level lineage: static parsing vs runtime events (OpenLineage).
  • Policies attach to column tags; table-format history is not an audit log.
Must be able to explain
  1. Why a DELETE on a Delta table with deletion vectors does not erase anything physically.
  2. Why consent should be an event log per purpose, not a boolean per regime.
  3. How crypto-shredding reaches backups, and what it costs you.
Must be able to draw

The erasure chain, with the SLA arithmetic under it, and a lineage graph with a column path traced to a dashboard.

queue → locate → DELETE → purge
 → expire → vacuum → beyond-table
 → backups → verify → log
Must be able to code
  • The erasure sequence on Delta (DELETE, REORG PURGE, VACUUM) or Iceberg (procedures).
  • A recursive-CTE impact query over a lineage edge table.
  • Current consent state from an event log with ROW_NUMBER.
Must be able to debug
  • An erased user reappears in a time-travel query (retention exceeds the SLA; no purge; a tag pins the snapshot).
  • An erased user reappears after a backfill (no suppression filter at ingest).
Numbers that matter
  • 1 PB / 1 GB files ≈ 1M files. Scattered erasures rewrite most of them, so isolate identifiers.
  • Snapshot retention + purge cadence + vacuum window < erasure SLA (for example 7 + 7 + 7 < 30 days).
  • Warehouse history exists beyond what you can query (Snowflake Fail-safe, BigQuery fail-safe), so include it in the SLA math. Check current docs.
  • A 1,000-row sample misses a PII rate of 0.1% in a column about 37% of the time ((0.999)^1000 ≈ 0.37).
Classic traps
  • Marking an erasure complete after the logical DELETE.
  • Calling SHA-256(email) "anonymized".
  • Relying on Delta history or CDF as an immutable audit trail, while CDF quietly keeps erased rows.
30-second answer

How do you make a data platform compliant without stopping analysts from working? You make the compliant path the default path. Classify columns automatically and attach masking, retention and erasure policies to the tags, not to tables. Give analysts masked-by-default access with pseudonymous join keys, and time-bound elevation for the rare unmasked case. Keep lineage and access logs so you can prove all of it afterwards.

2-minute answer

Turn each obligation into a mechanism. Minimisation: an ingest allow-list, identifiers swapped for surrogate keys at bronze. Storage limitation: a retention-policy table enforced nightly, history retention inside it. Erasure: a queue-driven chain (delete, purge, expire, vacuum, beyond-table copies), verified and logged, cheap because identifiers live in a small vault. Consent: a per-purpose event log that exports join to, failing closed. Access: scanner → tags → engine policies, so a new column is protected with no ticket. Accountability: column-level lineage plus access logs in write-once storage. Analysts get all rows with identifiers masked or HMAC'd, safe aggregates, and purpose-stated, expiring elevation. Checks run in CI, so problems surface on the PR, not in the audit.

Deep-dive follow-up

“Your events table is 1 PB, partitioned by day, and legal says the fact rows must be erased too. Walk me through the weekly cost, and what you change in the layout or the design to get it down by 100×.”

Staff+ follow-up

“Legal says erasure must also cover trained models and a vendor's copy of your data. What do you commit to, what do you push back on, and how does that change your contracts, your feature store and your retraining cadence?”
