Part 11

Cost Optimization

Quick refresh10 minInterview study35 minDeep practice55 min
Last technically reviewed September 2026
Covers cost anatomy, unit economics, Snowflake, Databricks, BigQuery, Redshift, S3 and data transfer, Spark cost levers, attribution, commitments, spot, bill-spike diagnosis
Versions referenced Snowflake Gen1/Gen2 standard warehouses; Databricks serverless (GA) and Lakeflow Spark Declarative Pipelines; BigQuery Editions (post-July 2023); Redshift RA3 and Serverless; Amazon S3 storage classes
Primary references Snowflake cost docs · Databricks billing system tables · BigQuery pricing · Redshift Serverless billing · S3 pricing
Known implementation differences Every platform meters a different unit (credits, DBUs + VMs, bytes or slot-hours, RPU-hours, requests + GB-months), so compare workloads by cost per unit of work, never by list rate.

The interviewer is not checking whether you memorised a price sheet. They want to see that you can say where the money goes, attribute it to an owner, estimate it before you build, diagnose a spike from evidence, and cut it without breaking an SLA. Senior engineers think in dollars per unit of work as naturally as in milliseconds.

2026 Interview Note

Vendor pricing is time-sensitive. Every dollar figure here is illustrative, at time of writing — check current pricing; rates vary by region, edition and contract. Mechanisms (what is metered, what spikes it, which lever moves it) change slowly. Answer with mechanisms and ratios.

1. Where the Money Goes

Every data platform bill decomposes into five buckets. Four appear on an invoice; the fifth is usually the largest and never does.

  • Compute is where the levers are: idle time, over-sizing and repeated work. Storage is cheap but grows quietly (time travel, unexpired snapshots, duplicate copies).
  • Surprises come from counts, not sizes. A 10× jump in file count or one cross-region read path can move the bill more than doubling the data.
  • People cost is part of the answer. A self-run cluster that saves 20% of compute but needs half an engineer may cost more. Saying so is a senior signal.

Cost model per platform

For architecture trade-offs (when to pick which warehouse), see Part 16. This table is only about the bill.

PlatformWhat you pay forWhat makes it spikeThe one lever that matters most
SnowflakeWarehouse credits per running second (60 s minimum per resume); serverless features; cloud services above 10%; storageWarehouses that never suspend; cache-defeating dashboards; clustering churnWarehouse per workload with the right size and auto-suspend, attributed by QUERY_TAG
Databricks (classic)Two bills: DBUs to Databricks (rate set by compute type and tier) plus VMs to your cloudIdle all-purpose clusters; production jobs on all-purpose computeJob compute plus cluster policies (auto-termination, max size, required tags)
Databricks (serverless)One bundled DBU rate, higher per unit, no VM billIdle tail until auto-stop; no budget ownerAuto-stop settings and budget policies on serverless usage
BigQuery on-demandBytes scanned per querySELECT *; missing partition filters; BI re-scansPartition + cluster, and require_partition_filter
BigQuery EditionsSlot-hours (baseline plus autoscaled slots), optional commitmentsAutoscaling max too high; runaway scheduled queriesBaseline sized to the steady floor, max as the budget cap
Redshift provisioned (RA3)Node-hours; managed storage; concurrency scaling beyond free credits; Spectrum bytesConcurrency scaling running all day; clusters sized for peakReserved nodes for the floor, pause/resize for the rest
Redshift ServerlessRPU-hours while queries runBase RPUs set high; no usage limitUsage limits plus a base capacity tied to the SLA
S3 / object storageGB-month by class; requests per 1,000; retrievals; transferSmall files (PUT/LIST); tiny-object transitions; cross-region or NAT-routed readsBigger files (compaction) and keeping compute next to the data

2. Estimating Cost: Unit Economics

"Our warehouse costs $80k a month" tells you nothing. "Cost per pipeline run went from 3 credits to 11 while input volume stayed flat" tells you where to look. Senior engineers turn the bill into unit costs:

  • Cost per TB processed: engine and query efficiency. Drifting up with flat volume means a regression (lost partition filter, dropped cluster key, spill).
  • Cost per pipeline run: what owners reason about. It catches runaway retries and backfills.
  • Cost per query / dashboard view: exposes auto-refresh and cache misses.
  • Cost per business unit (per order, per model trained): what finance uses to judge whether the spend is worth it.

Estimating before you build

The method is the same on every platform: work per execution × executions per period × price per unit of work, then add the idle tail and a retry factor. A hypothetical BI dashboard makes the point:

  • The dashboard has 8 tiles, and each tile scans one 2 TB fact table. Unpartitioned, that is 8 × 2 TB = 16 TB per refresh.
  • With auto-refresh every minute during 10 business hours: 600 refreshes × 16 TB = 9.6 PB scanned per day. On any bytes-scanned model that is ruinous. On a warehouse model it means a warehouse that never suspends.
  • Partition by day and filter to the last 7 days of a 2-year table: each scan drops to roughly 1% (7/730). A 15-minute refresh cuts executions 15×. Result caching removes most of the rest. The same dashboard now costs about three orders of magnitude less.

You found the multiplier (refresh frequency × bytes per refresh) before picking a technology. General capacity arithmetic is in Part 18.

Attribution: tags, showback, chargeback

You cannot compute unit cost without attribution. Cloud resource tags cover VMs and buckets. Platform spend needs platform tags: Snowflake QUERY_TAG and object tags, Databricks custom_tags on compute (surfaced in system.billing.usage), and BigQuery job labels (surfaced in INFORMATION_SCHEMA.JOBS). The minimum tag set is team, env, pipeline and cost_center. §9 covers enforcement.

Engine: SnowflakeDialect: Snowflake SQLExecutable: Yes — Snowflake only (ACCOUNT_USAGE access required)
-- Tag work at the session level so queries can be attributed
ALTER SESSION SET QUERY_TAG = 'team=growth;pipeline=daily_orders;env=prod';

-- Credits per warehouse per day (includes idle time; cloud services shown separately)
SELECT warehouse_name,
       DATE_TRUNC('day', start_time)       AS day,
       SUM(credits_used_compute)           AS compute_credits,
       SUM(credits_used_cloud_services)    AS cloud_services_credits
FROM snowflake.account_usage.warehouse_metering_history
WHERE start_time >= DATEADD('day', -30, CURRENT_TIMESTAMP())
GROUP BY 1, 2
ORDER BY compute_credits DESC;

-- Credits per query tag (excludes warehouse idle time by design)
SELECT query_tag, SUM(credits_attributed_compute) AS credits
FROM snowflake.account_usage.query_attribution_history
WHERE start_time >= DATEADD('day', -30, CURRENT_TIMESTAMP())
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY credits DESC;

Metered credits minus attributed query credits is roughly the idle cost. On BI warehouses it is often the biggest single waste.

3. Snowflake Cost Optimization

Snowflake bills warehouse compute in credits, serverless features in credits, and storage per TB-month. The levers are:

Virtual warehouse sizing

Each size step doubles credits per hour (standard Gen1 warehouses: XS=1, S=2, M=4, L=8, XL=16). Billing is per second, with a 60-second minimum each time a warehouse resumes. Gen2 and Snowpark-optimized warehouses bill at different per-hour rates (check current docs). A credit costs a few dollars depending on edition, region and contract (illustrative, at time of writing — check current pricing). Reason in credits, not dollars.

The arithmetic that matters: a query that takes 4 minutes on M uses 4 credits/h × 4/60 h ≈ 0.27 credits. If it scales linearly, it takes 2 minutes on L: 8 × 2/60 ≈ 0.27 credits. Same cost, half the wall time. So the rule is the opposite of "bigger costs more":

  • Upsize when the query parallelises (large scans, big joins and aggregations) or when it spills. Spill to local and especially to remote storage makes a small warehouse slower and more expensive. Removing spill can make the bigger warehouse strictly cheaper.
  • Don't upsize when the query doesn't speed up (a small table, a single-threaded step, or a query queued behind others). Then you pay 2× the rate for the same wall time. Queueing is a concurrency problem, and multi-cluster solves it, not size.
  • Measure first: spill bytes, queued_overload_time and partitions scanned vs total in QUERY_HISTORY.
2026 Interview Note

Timeless: size doubles rate, so linear scaling is cost-neutral. Version-specific: Gen2 standard warehouses (GA May 2025; default for new standard warehouses under bundle 2026_03) are faster at a higher per-hour rate, the same "speedup must beat the premium" test as Photon (§4).

Auto-suspend and multi-cluster

Auto-suspend is a trade-off: suspending drops the local disk cache, and every resume pays the 60-second minimum. Use ~60 seconds for ETL warehouses that run and go quiet; give BI warehouses queried every few minutes a longer suspend so the cache stays warm. Multi-cluster (Enterprise+) fixes queueing; choose the Economy scaling policy when cost beats latency. One warehouse per workload class isolates contention and makes attribution trivial.

Result cache and query reuse

Snowflake reuses a persisted result for 24 hours (the window resets on each reuse, up to 31 days) and uses no warehouse credits, but only when all of these hold:

  • the SQL text is identical,
  • the underlying data is unchanged,
  • the role has the required privileges, and
  • the query has no non-deterministic functions like CURRENT_TIMESTAMP().

The last condition is the classic trap: a BI tool that injects CURRENT_TIMESTAMP() or a moving literal misses every time and keeps the warehouse awake. Fix the SQL (a date parameter) rather than bolting on a cache. Use ALTER SESSION SET USE_CACHED_RESULT = FALSE only for benchmarks.

Clustering keys

Micro-partitions follow insertion order. If queries filter on event_date but data lands out of order, pruning fails and scans balloon. Automatic clustering rearranges data by the key in the background, and it bills serverless credits for as long as the table keeps changing.

  • Cluster only large (multi-TB) tables with selective, frequent filters that don't match load order.
  • Pick a key with enough distinct values to prune, but not raw high-cardinality columns. Coarsen them: TO_DATE(event_ts), not event_ts or user_id. Too few distinct values (a status flag) prunes nothing. Too many makes reclustering expensive and never-ending.
  • Check with SYSTEM$CLUSTERING_INFORMATION and watch AUTOMATIC_CLUSTERING_HISTORY. A clustered table with heavy update churn can cost more to keep clustered than it saves in scans.

Materialized views, dynamic tables, search optimization

Materialized views (Enterprise Edition+) are single-table (no joins) and maintained by a billed serverless service. The test: maintenance credits per day vs queries per day × credits saved per query. An MV on a table that changes every minute but is queried twice a day loses. For joins or pipelines, use Dynamic Tables: a longer target lag means fewer refreshes and fewer credits. Search Optimization (Enterprise+, serverless-billed) pays only for real needle-in-haystack lookups.

Guardrails: resource monitors and the cloud-services line

Engine: SnowflakeDialect: Snowflake SQLExecutable: Yes — Snowflake only (ACCOUNTADMIN to create monitors)
CREATE RESOURCE MONITOR bi_monthly
  WITH CREDIT_QUOTA = 500
       FREQUENCY = MONTHLY
       START_TIMESTAMP = IMMEDIATELY
  TRIGGERS ON 80 PERCENT DO NOTIFY
           ON 100 PERCENT DO SUSPEND;

ALTER WAREHOUSE bi_wh SET RESOURCE_MONITOR = bi_monthly;

Resource monitors cap warehouses only. Serverless features (clustering, MV maintenance, Snowpipe, search optimisation, serverless tasks) are separate line items. Cloud services (compilation, metadata) are billed only above 10% of daily warehouse compute. If that line grows, look for floods of tiny queries or metadata-heavy operations.

4. Databricks Cost Optimization

Compute types, the two bills, and autoscaling

Databricks bills DBUs. The price per DBU depends on compute type, tier and cloud: Jobs compute is the cheapest and All-purpose costs a multiple of it. The VM size sets DBUs per hour. Classic compute is two bills: DBUs to Databricks and VMs to your cloud account. Serverless bundles both into one higher DBU rate. List prices are illustrative and change, so check current pricing.

  • Production pipelines run on job compute, which starts for the run and terminates after. Running scheduled jobs on an all-purpose cluster pays the interactive rate for batch work.
  • Interactive clusters get auto-termination (tens of minutes idle), enforced by a cluster policy together with max size, allowed instance types and required custom_tags. Policies are the guardrail. A wiki page is not.
  • Autoscaling: classic autoscaling suits variable batch load, though it adds spin-up latency. For predictable batch, a right-sized fixed cluster is often cheaper. Databricks advises against classic autoscaling for Structured Streaming. Use enhanced autoscaling in Lakeflow Spark Declarative Pipelines (formerly DLT), or a fixed size.
Engine: DatabricksDialect: Databricks SQLExecutable: Yes — Databricks with Unity Catalog system tables enabled
-- List-price cost by team tag and product, last 30 days
SELECT u.custom_tags['team']     AS team,
       u.billing_origin_product  AS product,
       SUM(u.usage_quantity * lp.pricing.default) AS list_cost
FROM system.billing.usage u
JOIN system.billing.list_prices lp
  ON  u.sku_name   = lp.sku_name
  AND u.cloud      = lp.cloud
  AND u.usage_unit = lp.usage_unit
  AND u.usage_start_time >= lp.price_start_time
  AND (lp.price_end_time IS NULL OR u.usage_start_time < lp.price_end_time)
WHERE u.usage_date >= current_date() - INTERVAL 30 DAYS
GROUP BY ALL
ORDER BY list_cost DESC;

This is the DBU side at list price. On classic compute, join the VM bill from your cloud's cost tooling on the same tags.

Spot / preemptible instances

Spot is typically well over half off on-demand (illustrative; varies by instance and region). The pattern: on-demand driver, spot workers with on-demand fallback. Turn on graceful decommissioning (Spark 3.1+, supported on Databricks) so shuffle and cached blocks migrate off a node when the reclaim notice arrives: spark.decommission.enabled true, spark.storage.decommission.enabled true, spark.storage.decommission.shuffleBlocks.enabled true. It is best-effort, because the notice window is short.

Interviewer pushes back

You: "Batch workers go to spot with on-demand fallback."

Interviewer: "Why not move everything to spot? It's more than half off."

Strong answer: "The discount is on the rate; reclaims charge you in wall time and recompute. A lost driver kills the application. A lost worker takes its shuffle files with it, so upstream stages rerun, and on a wide shuffle that can cost more than the discount. Streaming pays in latency: every reclaim is a state restore and a lag spike against the freshness SLO. And spot dries up exactly when everyone scales. So: stateless batch workers on spot with graceful decommission and fallback; drivers, tight-SLO streaming and long non-restartable shuffles on-demand. Judge it by cost per run including retries."

Weak answer: "Spot is cheaper, and Spark retries failed tasks, so it's free money." That ignores driver loss, shuffle recompute and SLAs.

Photon, serverless and SQL warehouses

Photon is Databricks' C++ vectorized engine. It typically speeds SQL/DataFrame-heavy workloads 2–3×, more on some scans and aggregations, and nothing on Python UDFs (see Part 4, §19). Photon compute is billed at a higher DBU rate, so it saves money only when the speedup beats that premium. A 2.5× speedup on a job that is 80% Photon-eligible wins. A UDF-heavy job pays the premium for nothing. Measure cost per run with Photon on and off.

Serverless SQL warehouses start in seconds and auto-stop after a configurable idle period (minutes). You pay for running time including that idle tail, not "only for active query time". That is far cheaper than always-on classic for bursty BI. For all-day load, compare against a right-sized pro or classic warehouse.

2026 Interview Note

Serverless compute for notebooks, jobs and pipelines is GA and the default for new jobs, with Photon and autoscaling on automatically. The question becomes "who owns the serverless budget?" Timeless: serverless trades a higher unit rate for no idle clusters and no ops.

Disk cache vs Spark caching

The disk cache (formerly "Delta cache") keeps local-SSD copies of remote Parquet/Delta files for the cluster's lifetime. DataFrame.cache() persists at MEMORY_AND_DISK for one application only; use it for reuse within a job (§8).

5. BigQuery Cost Optimization

Two pricing models

  • On-demand bills bytes processed per query: the columns read, from the partitions not pruned. Compute time is irrelevant. A 3-second query that scans 5 TB costs more than a 10-minute query over 50 GB.
  • Editions (Standard, Enterprise, Enterprise Plus) bill slot-hours. You set a reservation baseline and an autoscaling max, and can add 1- or 3-year commitments on the baseline. Editions replaced flat-rate pricing: new flat-rate and flex commitments could not be bought after July 2023, so answers that mention "flex slots" are out of date. Under editions, bytes scanned stop being the bill directly, but they still drive slot time.

On-demand suits spiky, modest usage. Editions suit steady, heavy usage, and the autoscaling max is your budget cap. A max nobody reviews is a blank cheque.

Cutting bytes: partition, cluster, project

Engine: BigQueryDialect: GoogleSQLExecutable: Yes — BigQuery only
CREATE TABLE analytics.events (
  event_ts   TIMESTAMP,
  user_id    STRING,
  event_name STRING,
  payload    JSON
)
PARTITION BY DATE(event_ts)
CLUSTER BY event_name, user_id
OPTIONS (
  require_partition_filter = TRUE,   -- queries without a partition filter are rejected
  partition_expiration_days = 400
);
  • Partition by the date you filter on. require_partition_filter turns "someone forgot the WHERE clause" from a large bill into an error.
  • Cluster on the next most selective filter columns. Block pruning then cuts bytes further within each partition.
  • Project: storage is columnar, so SELECT * on a wide table pays for every column. LIMIT does not reduce bytes scanned on an unclustered table.

Guardrails: dry run, byte caps, reuse

Engine: BigQuery (bq CLI)Language: bashExecutable: Yes — Google Cloud SDK bq
# Estimate bytes before running (no charge for a dry run)
bq query --use_legacy_sql=false --dry_run \
  'SELECT user_id, COUNT(*) FROM analytics.events
   WHERE DATE(event_ts) = "2026-09-01" GROUP BY user_id'

# Fail the query instead of billing more than ~100 GB
bq query --use_legacy_sql=false --maximum_bytes_billed=100000000000 '...'
  • For clustered tables the dry-run figure is an upper bound, because block pruning happens at run time. Put maximum_bytes_billed in CI and in scheduled queries as a circuit breaker, and set custom query quotas per user or project.
  • Materialized views (incremental refresh, with automatic query rewrite) and BI Engine (an in-memory acceleration reservation) can make dashboard repetition cheap. Both are billed separately and are worth it only when the repetition is real (check current docs for limits). The query results cache is free for identical deterministic queries.
  • Attribute with job labels and INFORMATION_SCHEMA.JOBS:
Engine: BigQueryDialect: GoogleSQLExecutable: Yes — BigQuery only (adjust region qualifier)
SELECT (SELECT value FROM UNNEST(labels) WHERE key = 'team') AS team,
       COUNT(*)                                  AS jobs,
       SUM(total_bytes_billed) / POW(1024, 4)    AS tib_billed,
       SUM(total_slot_ms) / (1000 * 3600)        AS slot_hours
FROM `region-us`.INFORMATION_SCHEMA.JOBS
WHERE creation_time >= TIMESTAMP_SUB(CURRENT_TIMESTAMP(), INTERVAL 7 DAY)
  AND job_type = 'QUERY'
GROUP BY team
ORDER BY tib_billed DESC;

Storage: partitions unmodified for 90 days drop to a cheaper long-term rate automatically, and each dataset can bill logical or physical (compressed) bytes (check current pricing). Part 8 has the "slots exhausted" scenario.

6. Redshift Tuning

Distribution and sort keys

A skewed distribution key leaves one slice working while you pay for the rest to wait. Co-locate frequent joins on a shared key, use DISTSTYLE ALL for small dimensions, and let AUTO distribution and sort keys handle most tables. Prefer compound sort keys; interleaved keys are generally discouraged for their maintenance cost.

Workload management (WLM)

WLM routes queries (by user or query group) to queues with concurrency slots and memory shares, not CPU. Without it, one 60-minute exploratory query starves the dashboards. Prefer automatic WLM with query priorities plus query monitoring rules that log, hop or abort runaways. Short Query Acceleration is a separate feature that predicts runtime, not a queue with a timeout. Serverless has no WLM; it uses base capacity and usage limits.

VACUUM and ANALYZE

Dead rows persist until VACUUM. Auto vacuum and auto-analyze can lag heavy-churn tables, and stale statistics produce bad plans that burn node-hours. Run ANALYZE after large loads.

RA3, Serverless and concurrency scaling

  • RA3 bills compute (node-hours) and managed storage (GB-month) separately: size nodes for compute, reserve the always-on floor, pause dev clusters.
  • Serverless bills RPU-hours while queries run. Levers: base capacity (faster and pricier) and usage limits (RPU-hours per period, alert or turn off). A workgroup without a usage limit is a warehouse without a resource monitor.
  • Concurrency scaling adds transient clusters for read bursts. Free credits accrue (roughly an hour per day at time of writing — check current docs); beyond that it bills per second. Cap it, or it quietly becomes a second cluster.
  • Spectrum queries over S3 bill bytes scanned, so partitioned Parquet matters there exactly as it does in BigQuery.

7. S3 Cost Controls

Storage classes

The ratios matter more than the rates. Storage prices below are relative to Standard and illustrative (us-east-1, at time of writing — check current pricing).

ClassStorage vs StandardRetrievalMinimum durationMinimum object billingUse
Standard1×NoneNoneNoneActive data
Standard-IA~½Per-GB fee30 days128 KBAccessed about monthly
One Zone-IA~0.4×Per-GB fee30 days128 KBRe-creatable data only (single AZ)
Glacier Instant Retrieval~⅙Higher per-GB fee, milliseconds90 days128 KBArchive read about quarterly
Glacier Flexible Retrieval~⅙ or lessExpedited (1–5 min, priciest), Standard (3–5 h), Bulk (5–12 h, free at time of writing)90 days~40 KB metadata overhead per objectCompliance archive
Glacier Deep Archive~1/20 or lessStandard (within 12 h), Bulk (within 48 h)180 days~40 KB metadata overhead per objectMulti-year retention, legal hold

Early deletion bills the full minimum (a 60-day object in Glacier bills 90), and a 10 KB file in IA bills as 128 KB. Both penalties land hardest on small-file lakes.

Lifecycle policies

Engine: Amazon S3 (lifecycle configuration)Language: JSONExecutable: Yes — aws s3api put-bucket-lifecycle-configuration
{
  "Rules": [{
    "ID": "raw-tiering",
    "Status": "Enabled",
    "Filter": { "And": { "Prefix": "raw/", "ObjectSizeGreaterThan": 131072 } },
    "Transitions": [
      { "Days": 30,  "StorageClass": "STANDARD_IA" },
      { "Days": 90,  "StorageClass": "GLACIER_IR" },
      { "Days": 365, "StorageClass": "DEEP_ARCHIVE" }
    ],
    "Expiration": { "Days": 2555 }
  }]
}
  • Separate rules for raw/* (the replay source, longer) and processed/* (re-creatable, shorter). Retention itself comes from policy (Part 10).
  • Transitions bill per object: tiering a million 50 KB files can cost more than it saves. Hence ObjectSizeGreaterThan; newer configurations also skip sub-128 KB objects by default (check your bucket).
  • Don't transition data you will delete before the minimum duration. Just expire it.
  • Intelligent-Tiering charges a monthly monitoring fee per 1,000 objects; objects under 128 KB are not monitored and stay in the frequent tier.
  • Table formats: expire snapshots and vacuum orphans. Otherwise old versions accumulate as full-price Standard storage (see Part 7).

Request cost

Requests are billed per 1,000. PUT/COPY/POST/LIST cost roughly an order of magnitude more than GET (illustratively $0.005 vs $0.0004 per 1,000 in us-east-1 — check current pricing). A streaming job writing a file per partition per minute, across 200 partitions, makes about 290k PUTs a day before counting the LISTs that readers issue. Fix the file count first:

  • use bigger trigger intervals;
  • compact or OPTIMIZE on a schedule (Part 7);
  • let table-format manifests replace directory listing;
  • use S3 Inventory instead of repeated LIST crawls.

Data transfer: the surprise bill

  • NAT gateway: private compute reaching S3 through NAT pays a per-GB processing fee. A free S3 gateway endpoint removes it; this is one of the most common avoidable charges.
  • Cross-AZ traffic (Kafka replication, shuffles across zones, clients in another AZ) bills per GB in each direction.
  • Cross-region and internet egress cost most per GB. Keep compute in the bucket's region; a BI tool in another cloud reading the lake is a cost decision.

8. Spark Cost Levers

Spark tuning is covered in depth in Part 4. For cost, it reduces to four translations from runtime symptom to money:

  • Spill → bigger or more nodes, for longer. A wrong shuffle partition count (the old 200 default) either spills (huge partitions) or wastes scheduling on thousands of tiny tasks. Target on the order of 100–200 MB per post-shuffle partition and let AQE coalesce (Part 4, AQE).
  • Skew → idle executors you are still paying for. One 21-minute task holds a cluster of finished executors (Part 4, skew).
  • Tiny files → LIST calls and task overhead. Aim for files in the hundreds-of-MB range.
  • Unnecessary shuffle. Broadcasting a small dimension avoids shuffling the large fact side entirely. Multi-GB dimensions are not broadcast candidates: they blow driver or executor memory, and a sort-merge join (or bucketing) is safer (Part 4, broadcast). Cache a DataFrame only when it is reused and expensive to recompute, and unpersist it afterwards.

9. Cloud FinOps for Data Platforms

FinOps treats spend as a product metric with an owner, a budget and a trend line. For data teams, "owner" means a pipeline or a warehouse, not a cloud account.

Tagging strategy

Required tags: team, env, pipeline, cost_center. AWS Tag Policies standardise values but don't block untagged resources; add SCPs with aws:RequestTag conditions (or Azure Policy deny). Platform spend needs platform tags, enforced where compute is created (cluster policies, service-account session settings). Track the untagged share as a metric and drive it to zero.

Showback and chargeback

Showback reports each team's unit costs to them. Chargeback bills their budget and changes behaviour faster, but chargeback on untrusted attribution (§2) just starts arguments. Start with showback: a weekly unit-cost report per pipeline and a monthly review of the top 10 consumers.

Commitments: reserved capacity, savings plans, contracts

Every platform sells commitment discounts: Reserved Instances / Savings Plans (roughly 30–70% off, illustrative), Snowflake capacity, Databricks commit units, BigQuery edition commitments, Redshift reserved nodes. One formula covers them all: a commitment at discount d breaks even at utilisation 1 − d. Commit to the floor of a stable baseline; leave the peak on-demand.

Interviewer pushes back

You: "First I'd attribute spend and remove idle and repeated work."

Interviewer: "That's slow. Just buy reserved capacity and take 40% off tomorrow."

Strong answer: "A commitment discounts the rate, not the waste. Commit first and you lock today's waste in for one to three years, and when the cleanup lands, utilisation falls below break-even (60% at 40% off). I'd spend a few weeks removing idle and repeated work, measure the new floor, commit to that, and keep bursts on-demand. If finance needs a number now, commit a conservative slice of the current minimum, not the average."

Weak answer: "Yes, a reservation is the quickest win." It ignores utilisation risk and the fact that it prices today's inefficiency into a multi-year contract.

Cost anomaly detection

Cloud anomaly detection catches VM and transfer spikes. Warehouse spend needs platform-level alerts: resource monitors, BigQuery quotas, Redshift usage limits, Databricks budgets. Alert on unit cost too: cost per run up 30% on flat volume is a regression even if the monthly total looks normal.

Drill · Cost incident

Monday morning: the warehouse bill for the last 24 hours is double the trailing 30-day daily average. No new pipelines were deployed. Data volume is flat. Finance wants an answer by noon.

STOP. List what you would check, in order, before proposing a fix.

Reveal the diagnosis
  1. Observe Break the spike down by warehouse (or project/workgroup) and by hour from metering history. Is it one warehouse or all of them? Did it start at a specific hour? A step change points to a config change. A ramp points to growth or a leak.
  2. Hypothesize (a) a dashboard switched to 1-minute auto-refresh on an XL warehouse that now never suspends; (b) cache misses from CURRENT_TIMESTAMP() in the SQL; (c) a dropped cluster key or partition filter, so full scans; (d) a runaway backfill started Friday; (e) a failing job retrying a heavy step; (f) an incident upsize never reverted; (g) clustering or MV maintenance churning after a bulk update.
  3. Measure Group QUERY_HISTORY by query_parameterized_hash (or tag): executions, elapsed time, partitions scanned vs last week; cache-hit rate, failures by error code, spill, ALTER WAREHOUSE resizes; serverless line items separately.
  4. Isolate In this representative case, one parameterized hash ran 60 times an hour, all day, on BI_WH (XL), scanning 100% of partitions, with 0% cache hits. The dashboard owner had switched on 1-minute refresh on Friday. The query filters WHERE ts > DATEADD(day, -7, CURRENT_TIMESTAMP()), which defeats both the result cache and pruning on the date-clustered table.
  5. Fix Change the refresh to match how often the data actually lands (hourly loads mean hourly refresh). Rewrite the filter as a date predicate on the clustered column so results are reusable. Right-size the BI warehouse from spill and queue metrics. Leave its auto-suspend long enough to keep the cache warm.
  6. Prevent Resource monitors (notify 80%, suspend 100%) on every warehouse; alert on daily cost above a multiple of the trailing median; a refresh policy in the BI admin; mandatory QUERY_TAG so the next spike has a name on it.

10. Cutting 30% Without Hurting SLAs

"How would you cut this platform's cost by 30% without hurting SLAs?"
30 sec

Attribute first, then cut waste before touching anything SLA-bearing. On most platforms the top ten consumers are the majority of spend, and the first big wins are idle compute, repeated work (cache-defeating dashboards, full rescans) and work on the wrong compute type. I'd guard every change with the pipeline's freshness and latency SLOs, and commit to discounts last, on the new floor.

2 min

Week 1: tag coverage and a unit-cost baseline (cost per run, per TB, per dashboard view) with SLOs alongside, so every cut is checked against both. Then work through the levers roughly in order of savings per unit of risk:

  1. Idle: auto-suspend or auto-terminate, policies, killing orphaned clusters and dev warehouses.
  2. Repetition: dashboard refresh matched to data arrival, deterministic SQL so caches hit, MVs where they pay.
  3. Scan reduction: partition and cluster keys, require_partition_filter, projection, and incremental models instead of full rebuilds.
  4. Right-sizing from spill and queue metrics, sometimes up.
  5. Compute type: job vs all-purpose, spot workers for batch, serverless for spiky loads.
  6. Storage hygiene: snapshot expiry, lifecycle rules, dropping duplicate copies.
  7. Commitments on the new floor.

Each change ships behind its SLO dashboard and can be rolled back.

Deep dive

Rank candidates by (monthly cost × plausible reduction) ÷ engineering effort. Idle and repetition fixes are cheap and safe. Scan reduction needs backfills. Compute-type changes need retry and SLA testing. Watch for false savings: a smaller warehouse that spills, or spot that doubles runtime. Report results as unit cost so volume changes don't hide or fake them. Name what you won't cut: replay-source retention, the on-demand driver, month-end headroom.

Where to stop: once you've named attribution → waste → scans → sizing → commitments with an SLO guard, stop unless asked for a specific platform.

L5 Interview CardCost Optimization
Must know
  • The five buckets: storage, compute, transfer, API calls, people. Compute dominates, and transfer and requests cause the surprises.
  • Snowflake bills per second with a 60 s minimum per resume. Each size doubles the rate, so a linearly-scaling query costs the same at any size, and spill makes a small warehouse more expensive.
  • Databricks classic is two bills (DBU + VM). Jobs compute is far cheaper than all-purpose. Photon and serverless carry a higher unit rate.
  • BigQuery on-demand bills bytes scanned. Editions (which replaced flat-rate in 2023) bill slot-hours, with the autoscaling max as the budget cap.
  • S3: PUT/LIST cost about 10× GET, IA/Glacier IR bill a 128 KB minimum per object, and every class has a minimum duration. NAT-routed S3 traffic is avoidable.
  • A commitment at discount d breaks even at utilisation 1 − d. Commit to the floor, after optimising.
  • Attribution uses platform tags (QUERY_TAG, custom_tags, job labels). Report unit cost, not totals.
Must be able to explain
  1. Why can a bigger warehouse be cheaper?
  2. Why does a BI dashboard with CURRENT_TIMESTAMP() in its SQL cost more than one without?
  3. When is serverless more expensive than classic compute?
Must be able to draw

The cost anatomy of one pipeline, source to dashboard, with a meter on each hop:

S3 raw ─PUT/LIST─▶ Spark job ─DBU+VM─▶ lake
   │                                   │
 GB-month                     warehouse credits
                                       ▼
                      dashboard ×refresh/hr
Must be able to code
  • A query over metering/billing system tables that attributes cost per tag per day and flags days above 2× the trailing median.
  • A partitioned + clustered table DDL with a mandatory partition filter.
  • An S3 lifecycle rule that tiers only objects above 128 KB.
Must be able to debug
  • "The warehouse bill doubled overnight": auto-refresh plus cache-defeating SQL, a dropped cluster key, a runaway backfill, retries, or an upsize that was never reverted.
  • "S3 cost rose 5× after moving to 1-minute micro-batches": PUT/LIST explosion, plus lifecycle transitions of sub-128 KB objects.
Numbers that matter
  • Size +1 = rate ×2, so upsizing is cost-neutral only if runtime halves.
  • Break-even utilisation = 1 − discount (35% off → 65%).
  • A partition filter over 7 of 730 days scans about 1% of the table.
  • One file per partition per minute × 200 partitions ≈ 290k PUTs a day.
  • Refresh every minute vs every hour = 60× the executions.
Classic traps
  • "Bigger warehouse = more expensive". Not when it scales or stops spilling.
  • "Serverless and Photon are always cheaper". They carry a higher unit rate, and serverless has an idle tail.
  • "Buy reservations first". That locks in today's waste below break-even.
30-second answer

Where does the money go on a data platform, and how do you control it? Mostly into compute, much of it idle or repeated work. The surprises come from transfer and request counts, and the hidden cost is people. I control it by attributing every unit of spend to an owner with platform tags, tracking unit cost per run and per TB, removing idle and repeated work first, right-sizing from spill and queue metrics, and only then committing to discounts on the stable floor.

2-minute answer

Meters first: warehouses bill running time, BigQuery on-demand bills bytes, lakes bill GB-months plus per-object requests, networks bill bytes crossing boundaries. Attribute with per-workload compute and policy-enforced tags (QUERY_TAG, custom_tags, labels), and show teams their unit cost. Then pull levers in order of savings per unit of risk: idle, repetition (refresh cadence, cache-friendly SQL), scan volume (partition, cluster, mandatory filters), sizing (sometimes up, to stop spill), compute type (job vs all-purpose, spot for batch workers, serverless for spiky loads), storage hygiene (snapshot expiry, size-filtered lifecycle, S3 endpoints instead of NAT), and last, commitments on the new floor. Guardrails keep it fixed: resource monitors, byte caps, usage limits, unit-cost alerts, each change checked against its SLO.

Deep-dive follow-up

"Your team's Snowflake spend is 40% idle time on BI warehouses. Walk me through fixing it without making dashboards slower. What do you measure before and after?"

Staff+ follow-up

"Design a cost-governance model for 30 teams sharing one lakehouse: attribution, budgets, who can create compute, how commitments are split, and how you stop chargeback from becoming a political fight."

Part 12

Data Quality & Reliability

Quick refresh10 minInterview study35 minDeep practice55 min
Last technically reviewed September 2026
Covers the data-quality pipeline, expectations at a gate (GX Core 1.x, dbt tests), write-audit-publish, observability and anomaly detection, SLIs/SLOs and error budgets, reconciliation, testing layers, incident severity and comms
Versions referenced Great Expectations GX Core 1.x (1.23 at time of writing; 0.18 and earlier sunset Oct 2025), dbt 1.10+ (dbt 2.0 released Sep 2026), Apache Iceberg 1.4+ branches, Delta Lake 3.x/4.x, Snowflake
Primary references GX Core docs · dbt data tests · dbt model contracts · Iceberg branching · Snowflake ALTER TABLE … SWAP WITH · Google SRE workbook: SLOs
Known implementation differences The gate-then-publish idea is universal; how you stage and atomically publish (Iceberg branch, Delta staging table, Snowflake clone + swap, view swap) is engine-specific, and validation library APIs change between major versions.

The interviewer is not checking whether you know a validation library. They are checking whether you can say where bad data gets stopped, who finds out, how fast, and how you would prove to Finance that a number is right. "The DAG was green" is not an answer. A candidate who can name the gate, the owner of each check, the SLO, and the reconciliation that closes the loop sounds like someone who has been paged for this.

Senior (L5) interviews increasingly probe reliability engineering for data: not just "did the pipeline run" but "is the data correct, complete and on time, and how would you know?" The job succeeding is a statement about your orchestrator. It says nothing about your data.

1. The Data-Quality Pipeline — Where Bad Data Gets Stopped

Every quality system is the same loop: stop what you can predict at the boundaries, detect what you can't with monitors, and turn every incident into a new check. Draw this before naming any tool.

Three distinctions carry most of the interview:

  • Prevent vs detect. Contracts and gate expectations catch the failures you anticipated. Monitors catch the ones you didn't (a partner silently changes units). You need both.
  • Fail-closed vs warn. A blocking check keeps yesterday's good data in place and makes today's late. A warning publishes and files a ticket. Choose per check based on which is worse for the consumer: late data or wrong data. Billing: fail closed. A marketing dashboard's null rate on an optional column: warn.
  • Every check has an owner and an action. A check that fails and nobody looks at is worse than no check: it trains the team to ignore red.
“How do you know your data is correct?”
30 sec

I don't assume it; I check it at three points. Contracts at ingest reject malformed input. Expectations run on the output in staging and block publish if a critical one fails. After publish, monitors watch freshness, volume and distribution, and a daily reconciliation compares control totals against the system of record. Each check has an owner and a severity.

2 min

"Correct" needs a definition first: correct relative to what source, under which business definition, by when. Then layers. Code tests in CI catch logic bugs; contracts at the producer boundary catch shape drift. Write-audit-publish means consumers only ever see validated snapshots: the job writes to a branch or staging table, runs expectations (unique keys, row count vs a same-weekday baseline), and only then swaps. Observability catches the unknown unknowns. Reconciliation against the source ledger is the proof. All of it rolls up into SLOs for freshness, completeness and correctness, so "trustworthy" is a measured number, not a feeling.

Deep dive

Expect follow-ups on: which checks block versus warn and why; how WAP is implemented on your engine (Iceberg branch + fast-forward, Delta staging + single-commit overwrite, Snowflake clone + SWAP WITH); how the anomaly baseline handles weekly seasonality and launches; reconciliation tolerance and how you localise a mismatch; what the error budget does when it runs out; and how a post-mortem produces a new check rather than a slide.

Where to stop: don't list twenty expectation types. Name the gate, one blocking check, one monitor, the reconciliation, and who gets paged.

Failure-first: what can fail in the quality pipeline itself?
FailureDetectRecoverPrevent recurrence
Contract check too strict: a harmless additive column quarantines a whole feedQuarantine volume spikes; downstream freshness breachRelax the rule, replay the DLQ into the pipelineContracts allow additive changes; breaking-change rules reviewed with the producer
Quarantine becomes a landfill: rows land there and nobody replays themMonitor quarantine row count and age, not just existenceTriage, fix, replay with idempotent writesEvery quarantine table has an owner and an age SLO
Gate silently skipped (task marked skipped, trigger rule lets publish run anyway)Publish step asserts a passing validation result for this snapshot/run idRoll back to last validated snapshotPublish depends on the validation artifact, not on task ordering
Monitor blind spot: a table that never logs never alertsRegistry of expected tables/partitions, LEFT JOIN to observationsBackfill the missing loadFreshness driven from expectations, not from what showed up
Alert fatigue: real alert ignored among 40 noisy onesAlert-to-action ratio; pages acknowledged without actionSilence or delete the noisy checksEvery alert has an owner and a runbook; demote checks nobody acts on
Post-mortem actions never landSame root cause in a second post-mortemEscalate the action itemAction items tracked with owner and due date; review at the next incident review

2. Declarative Expectations at a Gate (Great Expectations GX Core 1.x)

Great Expectations (GX Core 1.x since August 2024 — the 0.x API still found in many codebases is incompatible) is a widely used open-source validation framework. dbt data tests, Soda Core and Deequ/PyDeequ solve the same problem, as do platform-native options (Databricks Lakeflow Spark Declarative Pipelines (formerly DLT) expectations, Snowflake Data Metric Functions — edition and version gates apply, check current docs).

Core concepts

  • Expectation: a falsifiable assertion about data, as a typed class. gx.expectations.ExpectColumnValuesToNotBeNull(column="user_id"), ExpectColumnValuesToBeBetween(column="age", min_value=0, max_value=130), ExpectTableRowCountToBeBetween(min_value=10000, max_value=50000000).
  • Expectation Suite: a named collection of expectations for one dataset or pipeline stage.
  • Data Source → Data Asset → Batch Definition (Fluent data sources, the only kind in 1.x): what data, and how to slice it into a batch (whole DataFrame, a partition).
  • Validation Definition / Checkpoint: a Validation Definition pairs a Batch Definition with a Suite; a Checkpoint runs one or more of them and fires Actions (Slack, Data Docs).

Production pattern: validate the output before publish

Engine: Great Expectations GX Core 1.x on PySparkLanguage: PythonExecutable: Yes — GX Core 1.x only (assumes an active SparkSession spark; verify names against current GX docs)
# GX Core 1.x. The 0.x API (run_checkpoint, Batch Requests, data connectors) was removed in 1.0.
import great_expectations as gx

context = gx.get_context()   # file-backed if a gx/ project dir exists, else ephemeral

ds = context.data_sources.add_spark(name="spark")
asset = ds.add_dataframe_asset(name="silver_fact_playback")
batch_def = asset.add_batch_definition_whole_dataframe("daily_partition")

suite = context.suites.add(gx.ExpectationSuite(name="fact_playback"))
suite.add_expectation(gx.expectations.ExpectColumnValuesToNotBeNull(column="user_id"))
suite.add_expectation(gx.expectations.ExpectColumnValuesToBeBetween(
    column="watch_ms", min_value=0, max_value=86_400_000))

vd = context.validation_definitions.add(
    gx.ValidationDefinition(name="fact_playback_vd", data=batch_def, suite=suite))
checkpoint = context.checkpoints.add(gx.Checkpoint(
    name="silver_fact_playback_checkpoint", validation_definitions=[vd],
    actions=[gx.checkpoint.UpdateDataDocsAction(name="update_docs")]))

# Validate the STAGED output, not the input and not prod
df = spark.table("staging.fact_playback").where("dt = date_sub(current_date(), 1)")
result = checkpoint.run(batch_parameters={"dataframe": df})

if not result.success:   # fail closed: do not publish staging into silver
    raise ValueError("Data quality validation failed — see Data Docs")

The .add() calls raise if the object already exists; in a scheduled job, define suites once (in code review) and load them with context.checkpoints.get(...). The placement matters more than the API: validate the silver output before it is published — write to a staging branch/table, validate, then publish (write-audit-publish). Validate bronze input only for contract checks; a quarantined input batch is cheaper than a bad gold table.

2026 Interview Note

The code above is GX Core 1.x. If a codebase you inherit says context.run_checkpoint(...) or validator.expect_column_values_to_not_be_null(...), it is 0.x, which was sunset in October 2025 — migrating is real work, not a rename. The tool changes; the concept does not: declarative expectations, versioned with the pipeline, run at a gate, with each one explicitly fail-closed or warn. In an interview, say that sentence first, then name whichever tool your team uses. dbt tests, Soda checks and Deequ constraints are the same idea in different syntax.

Expectation types to know

Check (GX 1.x class)What it catchesUsually
ExpectColumnValuesToNotBeNull / …ToBeUniqueBroken keys, fan-out from a bad join, replay duplicatesBlock (on keys)
ExpectColumnValuesToBeBetweenUnit bugs (ms vs s), negative amountsBlock on money; warn elsewhere
ExpectTableRowCountToBeBetweenTruncation, empty loads, double ingestionBlock if bounds come from a baseline, not a guess
ExpectColumnKLDivergenceToBeLessThanDistribution drift vs a reference (cents→dollars, a new default value)Warn; route to owner
Interviewer pushes back

You: “Quality is solid — we have about 2,000 dbt tests.”

Interviewer: “Which of them block publish? And when one fails at 3 a.m., who looks at it?”

Strong answer: “Test count is an input metric. What matters is coverage of the failure modes that have actually hurt us, and what happens on failure. We tier them: around fifty are blocking, on the gold tables consumers act on — key uniqueness, not-null on join keys, control totals, row count vs baseline. Those run before publish and page the owning team. The rest are warnings that open tickets routed by model owner, and we review the warn-level tests every quarter: anything that has failed repeatedly with no action gets fixed or deleted. I'd also report tests that never failed and never could — not_null on a column with a NOT NULL constraint is noise.”

Weak answer: “We run them all in CI and the failures show up in the dbt logs.” Nobody reads logs. A failure without an owner and an action is decoration.

3. Write-Audit-Publish (WAP)

WAP is the pattern that makes "consumers never see unvalidated data" true by construction rather than by hope.

  1. Write the new data somewhere consumers don't read: a branch, a staging table, a clone.
  2. Audit it there: expectations, row counts, reconciliation against the source.
  3. Publish with one atomic, metadata-only operation: fast-forward a branch, swap tables, repoint a view. If the audit fails, do nothing — consumers keep the last good version, and the failure is "late", not "wrong".

The timeless requirement is that publish is a pointer move, not a copy. If publishing means re-writing the data, you've re-opened the window where consumers can read a partial result.

EngineWrite / stagePublishWatch out for
Apache Iceberg (1.2+ branches; fast_forward in newer 1.x)Write to a branch (spark.wap.branch) on a table with write.wap.enabledCALL system.fast_forward('db.t', 'main', 'audit_…')Branches are per table; multi-table atomic publish needs a catalog-level mechanism (e.g. Nessie) or a view layer
Delta LakeNo table branches. Write to a staging table (or a SHALLOW CLONE of prod)One transaction into prod (INSERT OVERWRITE … REPLACE WHERE / MERGE) — each commit is atomicThe publish copies data (cost/time); keep it a single commit. RESTORE is the rollback
SnowflakeZero-copy CLONE of prod, or a separate staging tableALTER TABLE prod SWAP WITH stageGrants and dependent objects: check how they behave on swap in current docs
Any warehouseVersioned table revenue_v20260923CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW revenue AS SELECT * FROM revenue_v…Consumers must read the view, never the versioned tables
Engine: Apache Iceberg 1.4+ on Spark 3.5 (Iceberg SQL extensions enabled)Dialect: Spark SQLExecutable: Illustrative — adapt catalog, table and branch names
-- One-time: allow WAP on the table
ALTER TABLE prod.db.fact_playback SET TBLPROPERTIES ('write.wap.enabled' = 'true');

-- WRITE: create a branch for this run and direct session writes to it
ALTER TABLE prod.db.fact_playback CREATE BRANCH audit_20260923;
SET spark.wap.branch = audit_20260923;
INSERT OVERWRITE prod.db.fact_playback
SELECT * FROM staging_view WHERE dt = DATE '2026-09-23';   -- main is untouched

-- AUDIT: validators read the branch explicitly
SELECT COUNT(*), COUNT(DISTINCT playback_id)
FROM prod.db.fact_playback VERSION AS OF 'audit_20260923'
WHERE dt = DATE '2026-09-23';

-- PUBLISH (only if audit passed): metadata-only pointer move
CALL prod.system.fast_forward('db.fact_playback', 'main', 'audit_20260923');
Engine: SnowflakeDialect: Snowflake SQLExecutable: Illustrative — adapt to your schema
CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE gold.revenue_stage CLONE gold.revenue;  -- zero-copy
-- rebuild / merge today's data into gold.revenue_stage, then run checks against it
ALTER TABLE gold.revenue SWAP WITH gold.revenue_stage;          -- atomic publish
Interviewer pushes back

You: “I'd stage, validate, then swap.”

Interviewer: “Why not publish immediately, test afterwards, and time-travel back if something's wrong? Same safety, no extra step.”

Strong answer: “Rollback only undoes the table. It doesn't undo the dashboards that were read, the reverse-ETL sync that pushed bad values into the CRM, or the model that trained on it in the window. Test-after is acceptable for exploratory tables with no automated consumers. For anything that feeds another system, the audit has to happen before anyone can read. The cost of WAP is a few minutes of latency and some staging storage; I'd take that trade on any table with a money or customer-facing consumer.”

Weak answer: “Time travel makes it safe.” It makes the table recoverable, not the consequences.

4. Data Observability and Anomaly Detection

Gate checks catch what you predicted. Observability catches the rest. The common framing (popularised by Monte Carlo) is five signals: freshness (last load vs schedule), volume (drops from partial loads, spikes from double ingestion), schema (drift that bypassed the contract), distribution (null rate, cardinality, percentiles — a redacted field silently breaks a fraud model) and lineage (so an alert names the upstream cause and the downstream blast radius).

Observability tooling

OptionTypeTrade-off
Monte Carlo, Acceldata and similar observability productsCommercialFast coverage and ML baselines across many tables; cost and another system to trust
ElementaryOpen source (dbt-native)Anomaly tests run as dbt tests; only sees what dbt builds
Soda Core / platform-native (Snowflake Data Metric Functions, Databricks Lakehouse Monitoring)Open source / built-inChecks-as-code; native options avoid another vendor but tie you to the platform (edition gates apply)

Key metrics to instrument

Two monitors every candidate should be able to write. Note the design choices: freshness is driven from a registry of what should exist (a table that never logs must still alert), and volume compares yesterday's complete day against the same weekday, so it doesn't false-alarm every morning on a partial today or every Monday on weekly seasonality.

Engine: SnowflakeDialect: Snowflake SQLExecutable: Yes — Snowflake only (given the ops tables); DATEDIFF/DAYOFWEEK differ elsewhere
-- Freshness: registry-driven, so a table with no log rows at all still alerts
SELECT r.table_name,
       MAX(f.loaded_at) AS last_loaded,
       DATEDIFF('minute', MAX(f.loaded_at), CURRENT_TIMESTAMP()) AS minutes_stale
FROM ops.expected_tables r
LEFT JOIN ops.table_freshness_log f ON f.table_name = r.table_name
GROUP BY r.table_name, r.max_staleness_min
HAVING MAX(f.loaded_at) IS NULL
    OR DATEDIFF('minute', MAX(f.loaded_at), CURRENT_TIMESTAMP()) > r.max_staleness_min;

-- Volume: yesterday vs the same weekday over the prior 8 weeks (z-score)
WITH daily AS (
  SELECT dt, COUNT(*) AS n
  FROM silver.fact_playback
  WHERE dt BETWEEN CURRENT_DATE - 57 AND CURRENT_DATE - 1
  GROUP BY dt
),
baseline AS (
  SELECT AVG(n) AS mu, STDDEV(n) AS sigma
  FROM daily
  WHERE DAYOFWEEK(dt) = DAYOFWEEK(CURRENT_DATE - 1) AND dt < CURRENT_DATE - 1
)
SELECT t.dt, COALESCE(d.n, 0) AS n, b.mu,
       (COALESCE(d.n, 0) - b.mu) / NULLIF(b.sigma, 0) AS z
FROM (SELECT CURRENT_DATE - 1 AS dt) t            -- date spine: a missing day still returns a row
LEFT JOIN daily d ON d.dt = t.dt
CROSS JOIN baseline b
WHERE COALESCE(d.n, 0) = 0
   OR ABS(COALESCE(d.n, 0) - b.mu) / NULLIF(b.sigma, 0) > 3;

Eight same-weekday points is a small sample; the standard deviation is noisy, so pair the z-score with a floor (e.g. also require a >10% relative change) before paging.

Anomaly detection: static thresholds vs seasonal baselines vs ML

ApproachGood atBad atUse when
Static threshold (rows > 1M, stale > 2h)Explainable, zero setup, stable for hard invariantsGrowth, seasonality; thresholds rot silentlyFreshness deadlines, hard business limits, "zero rows"
Seasonal baseline (same weekday / hour, z-score or percentage band)Weekly/daily cycles; cheap SQL you can explain to on-callHolidays, launches, trend breaks; needs historyVolume and key-metric monitors on most tables
ML / vendor models (forecast bands, learned thresholds)Scale across thousands of tables with no per-table tuningOpaque ("why did this fire?"), learns the incident as the new normal, noisy on sparse tablesBroad low-cost coverage of the long tail, with severity set low

The honest summary: the detector matters less than the routing. Tier the tables (tier 1 = money and customer-facing) and let only tier-1 anomalies page.

Interviewer pushes back

You: “We'd turn on anomaly detection for every table and alert on every anomaly — better safe than sorry.”

Interviewer: “You have 3,000 tables. At a 1% daily false-positive rate, what does on-call look like in a month?”

Strong answer: “About 30 false alerts a day, roughly 900 a month — the team stops reading them by week two, and the one real incident drowns. So: alerts page only for tier-1 tables and only for signals tied to an SLO (freshness deadline, completeness, reconciliation). Everything else goes to a daily digest or a ticket for the owning team. I'd track alert precision — the share of alerts that led to an action — and delete or demote any monitor below a bar. Alerting on SLO burn rather than on each blip is the same idea SRE uses for services.”

Weak answer: “We'll tune the thresholds later.” Later never comes; people mute the channel.

5. SLIs, SLOs and Error Budgets for Data

Define the indicators first

An SLA is a promise to consumers with consequences; an SLO is your internal target, set tighter so you breach it before the SLA; an SLI is the measurement. For data, three SLIs cover almost everything:

SLIMeasured asExample SLO (hypothetical)
Freshness (batch)Did the partition publish by the deadline? One good/bad event per dayGold daily_revenue published by 06:30 UTC on 99% of days (rolling 90 days); the SLA to consumers says 07:00
Freshness (streaming)p99 lag from event time (or source commit) to queryable, per minutep99 lag ≤ 5 min in 99.5% of minutes over 28 days
CompletenessRows landed ÷ rows in source for the same window, after a settle period≥ 99.9% of source events present within 24h, on 99% of days
CorrectnessDid the daily reconciliation pass within tolerance?Control totals vs billing ledger within ±0.1% on 99.5% of days

Measure streaming latency from event time, not from ingestion: if you start the clock at ingestion, all upstream lag is invisible and your SLO is green while consumers wait. Freshness also has a dependency chain: a 07:00 gold SLA sets the upstream budget (silver by 06:30, bronze by 06:00), and whoever owns the slowest upstream owns most of the risk.

Error budgets — the unit matters

For batch, "43 minutes of downtime a month" is the wrong unit; a daily table is either on time or it isn't. Count days. Worked example (hypothetical):

  • SLO: 97% of daily loads on time over a rolling 90 days → budget = 0.03 × 90 = 2.7, so 2 late days per 90.
  • Streaming: 99.5% of minutes within lag target over 28 days → 40,320 × 0.005 ≈ 200 minutes of budget.
  • In August the pipeline was late twice (a source outage, a bad deploy). Budget spent. The agreed policy kicks in: schema migrations and non-urgent refactors of that pipeline pause, and the next sprint's work is the fix for the deploy-caused miss (a canary run on a sample, stricter pre-publish checks).

The budget turns "reliability vs velocity" from an argument into a rule both sides signed up to.

6. Reconciliation — Proving the Number

Reconciliation proves the warehouse matches the system of record. It is the only check that tests reality rather than plausibility: every row can pass not-null and range checks while revenue is off by 4%.

Reconciliation patterns

PatternWhat it checksImplementation
Row count by sliceSame number of recordsCOUNT(*) per day (and per source/region) on both sides, same window, same timezone
Control totalsNumeric sums matchSUM(amount) per day × currency vs the billing ledger
Hash-diffNo field-level corruptionHash of delimited, NULL-coalesced, type-normalised columns per key (e.g. MD5(CONCAT_WS('|', COALESCE(CAST(c1 AS VARCHAR),'∅'), …))); compare per-partition aggregates first, then drill to keys. Plain CONCAT returns NULL on any NULL input in several engines, and without delimiters 'ab'+'c' = 'a'+'bc'

Reconciliation design

  • Agree the definition before the query. Most "mismatches" are definition gaps: gross vs net of refunds, booking date vs event date, UTC vs local-day cutoff, FX rate at transaction vs at report date, test/internal accounts, tax included or not. Write the definition down with the source owner (for revenue, that means Finance) and version it.
  • Aggregate first, then drill. Compare counts and sums per day × slice (currency, region, source system). Only drill to row-level keys in the slices that disagree. Row-level diff of the whole table is expensive and buries the pattern.
  • Tolerance is explicit. Exact match for counts from the same ledger; a small band (say ±0.1%) where late-arriving events or FX rounding are expected, with a settle period (reconcile D-1 at D+1, re-check at D+3). A tolerance nobody can justify is a place for bugs to hide.
  • Slice until it breaks. When totals disagree, split by one dimension at a time — day, currency, country, product, source system, account type — and follow the slice where the gap concentrates. A uniform gap across every slice points at a definition (refunds, tax). A gap concentrated on a few days points at an event (duplicate replay, missed partition). A gap in one currency points at FX. Within three or four splits you usually have the cause.
  • Placement. Run it after the load, before publish, as part of the audit step. Failures write to an audit table and alert the owner. Don't auto-roll back data that is already live downstream — that needs a human decision — but do block the next publish until someone has looked.
Engine: generic warehouse SQLDialect: ANSI-ish SQLExecutable: Illustrative — adapt to your dialect
-- Control totals per day x currency; drill into only the slices that disagree
WITH src AS (
  SELECT txn_date, currency, COUNT(*) AS n, SUM(net_amount) AS amt
  FROM billing.ledger_snapshot
  WHERE txn_date = DATE '2026-09-22'
  GROUP BY txn_date, currency
), tgt AS (
  SELECT order_date AS txn_date, currency, COUNT(*) AS n, SUM(net_revenue) AS amt
  FROM gold.fact_revenue
  WHERE order_date = DATE '2026-09-22' AND is_test_account = FALSE
  GROUP BY order_date, currency
)
SELECT COALESCE(s.txn_date, t.txn_date) AS txn_date,
       COALESCE(s.currency, t.currency) AS currency,
       s.n AS src_n, t.n AS tgt_n, s.amt AS src_amt, t.amt AS tgt_amt,
       (t.amt - s.amt) / NULLIF(s.amt, 0) AS pct_diff
FROM src s
FULL OUTER JOIN tgt t ON s.txn_date = t.txn_date AND s.currency = t.currency
WHERE s.n IS NULL OR t.n IS NULL
   OR s.n <> t.n
   OR ABS((t.amt - s.amt) / NULLIF(s.amt, 0)) > 0.001;
Drill · Reconciliation

The CFO's deck says Q3 revenue is $41.2M. Your gold dashboard says $42.7M — 3.7% higher than Finance. Every pipeline is green and every dbt test passes. You have one afternoon. What do you check, in what order?

STOP. Answer before revealing.

Reveal the approach
  1. Observe Don't open the code yet. Get Finance's exact definition and source: which ledger, gross or net, which date field, which timezone, which FX rate, which accounts excluded.
  2. Hypothesize The usual suspects, cheapest first: (1) gross vs net — refunds, chargebacks, discounts or tax included on one side; (2) timezone cutoff — UTC day vs Finance's local business day moves revenue across period boundaries; (3) FX date — rate at transaction vs at month-end; (4) test/internal/employee accounts not filtered; (5) duplicates from an at-least-once replay or a fan-out join; (6) booking date vs recognised-revenue date.
  3. Measure Reconcile per day × currency (query above). Shape of the gap is the clue: uniform ~3.7% on every day and slice → a definition gap (refunds or tax); spikes on specific days → duplicates or a replayed partition; one currency only → FX; gap only on the first/last day of the quarter → timezone cutoff.
  4. Isolate Slice the offending slice until it breaks (country, product, account type), then drill to keys with an anti-join or a row count per order id > 1.
  5. Fix Correct the definition or the dedup; restate affected periods with a note to consumers stating old number, new number and why.
  6. Prevent A gold metric definition owned jointly with Finance; a daily control-total check vs the billing ledger that blocks publish outside tolerance; tests for the specific cause (uniqueness on order id, a test-account filter).

More diagnosis scenarios, including "Airflow succeeded but yesterday's partition is missing", are in the Debugging Lab (Part 19).

7. Testing Layers for Data Pipelines

The full treatment — pytest and chispa for PySpark, Hypothesis, dbt unit tests, data tests vs code tests — lives in Part 6 §10. The interview-ready version is a pyramid with the question each layer answers:

LayerAnswersRuns
Unit tests (small in-memory DataFrames, dbt unit tests)Is my logic right on known inputs? (dedup keeps latest, SCD2 closes rows)Every PR, seconds
Integration / CI build on a sampleDoes the pipeline build end to end, schemas line up, counts plausible?Every PR, minutes
Contracts at the boundaryDid the producer change shape or meaning?Producer CI + ingest
Data tests at the gateIs today's data valid?Every run, before publish
Monitors + reconciliationWhat didn't we think to test?Continuously / daily

Code tests catch bugs in your logic with fixed inputs; data tests catch surprises in their data with your fixed logic. Mention only one and you have described half a system.

Contracts

dbt model contracts (contract: {enforced: true}, dbt 1.5+) enforce shape at build time; data tests (dbt, GX, Soda) enforce values. Contract design — ownership, versioning, breaking vs additive changes — is covered in Part 1 §13, and producer-side enforcement with CDC and dbt in Part 15.

dbt testing patterns: blocking vs warning

Engine: dbt 1.10+ with dbt_utils 1.xLanguage: YAMLExecutable: Illustrative — partial; an enforced contract requires every column declared with a data_type
# models/silver/fact_playback.yml
version: 2
models:
  - name: fact_playback
    config:
      contract: {enforced: true}          # build fails if columns/types drift
    data_tests:
      - dbt_utils.recency:
          arguments: {datepart: hour, field: loaded_at, interval: 2}
          config: {severity: warn}        # stale = ticket, not a blocked build
    columns:
      - name: playback_id
        data_type: bigint
        constraints: [{type: not_null}]
        data_tests:
          - unique                        # blocking (severity: error is the default)
      - name: user_id
        data_type: bigint
        data_tests:
          - not_null
          - relationships:
              arguments: {to: ref('dim_user'), field: user_id}
      - name: watch_ms
        data_type: bigint
        data_tests:
          - dbt_utils.accepted_range:
              arguments: {min_value: 0, max_value: 86400000}   # max 24h in ms
              config: {severity: error, error_if: ">100", warn_if: ">0"}
2026 Interview Note

Syntax drift here is real: tests: became data_tests: in dbt 1.8 (the old key still works), dbt 1.10 moved generic-test arguments under arguments: (older projects get a deprecation warning), and dbt 2.0 shipped in September 2026 — check current docs before copying YAML. The durable idea is severity with warn_if/error_if: every test declares whether it blocks, which is the fail-closed-vs-warn decision made explicit and reviewable.

8. Data Incident Management

Severity tiers

Severity is set by consumer impact, not by how broken the pipeline looks. Response times below are illustrative; set them per organisation.

SeverityDefinitionResponseExamples
SEV-1Wrong or missing data in a money, regulatory or customer-facing pathPage nowBilling extract missing; dashboard shows $0 revenue; wrong data synced to customers
SEV-2Tier-1 SLO breached or about to be; reconciliation failedPage, business hours+Gold table 2h late; control totals off beyond tolerance
SEV-3Quality issue with limited or no current consumer impactSame/next day ticketNull-rate spike in a low-traffic dimension
SEV-4Cosmetic / informationalBacklogMissing description, stale docs

The first 15 minutes (data-specific)

  1. Stop the bleeding: freeze publishing for the affected tables (pause the DAG or the publish step) so the bad version doesn't get worse or spread to more downstream syncs.
  2. Scope via lineage: which downstream tables, dashboards, reverse-ETL syncs and models read it since the bad load?
  3. Tell consumers early, even before you know the cause. "We know, don't act on X" is worth more than a perfect root cause at noon.
  4. Preserve evidence: record snapshot/version ids, run ids and the bad input files before retention or compaction removes them.
  5. Restore the last good version if that is safe (time travel / restore / swap back), then fix forward.

Comms template

[SEV-2] daily_revenue overstated for 2026-09-20 → 09-22 — investigating
Impact: Revenue dashboards and the Finance daily extract show ~3–4% higher revenue for these dates. Other tables are unaffected.
What to do: Don't use these dates for reporting until resolved. The 09-19 figures and earlier are correct.
Status: Publishing paused. Suspected duplicate events from a replay. Next update by 14:00 UTC.
Owner: data-platform on-call (#data-incidents)

Impact first, in the consumer's words; what to do; what you know; when the next update comes. Send the "resolved" message with the restated numbers.

Runbook anatomy

Every tier-1 pipeline has a runbook: owner, where to look, known failure modes and fixes, how to re-run or backfill safely, escalation, who to notify. A runbook that lives only in someone's head is not a runbook.

Post-mortem: every incident becomes a check

Blameless post-mortems look for systemic causes: timeline, root cause, contributing factors, action items with owners and dates. The test of a data post-mortem is whether it closes the loop in the diagram above: which check would have caught this, and at which stage — the contract that should have rejected it, the gate expectation that should have blocked publish, the monitor that should have fired an hour earlier. If the answer is "none of them could have", the action item is to add one.

On-call and toil reduction

Alerts are actionable, runbooks current, rotations sized so nobody is primary too often. Track toil explicitly and drive it down (Google SRE caps toil at 50% of an engineer's time; good data teams aim far lower). If the same manual fix appears in three post-mortems, automate it.

L5 Interview CardData Quality & Reliability
Must know
  • Write-audit-publish: stage → validate output → atomic pointer-move publish; consumers never read unvalidated data.
  • Layers: code tests in CI, contracts at the boundary, data tests at the gate, monitors and reconciliation after publish.
  • Every check is explicitly blocking or warning, with an owner and an action.
  • Freshness is driven from what should exist; volume compares complete days to a same-weekday baseline.
  • Reconcile against the source's definition (gross/net, timezone, FX date, test accounts), aggregate first, slice until it breaks.
  • Batch SLOs count days on time; streaming SLOs measure p99 event-time lag; the error budget has an agreed policy.
  • GX Core 1.x replaced the 0.x API in Aug 2024; the concept (declarative expectations at a gate) outlives the syntax.
Must be able to explain
  1. Why "the DAG succeeded" says nothing about data correctness.
  2. How WAP is implemented on Iceberg vs Delta vs Snowflake, and why publish must be metadata-only.
  3. Why alerting on every anomaly makes you less reliable, not more.
Must be able to draw

The quality loop:

ingest → contract ─fail→ DLQ
  → transform → stage → gate ─fail→ block
  → publish → monitors → alert → incident
  → post-mortem → new check → gate
Must be able to code
  • A registry-driven freshness check that alerts on tables that never logged.
  • A same-weekday volume anomaly check on yesterday's complete partition.
  • A per-day × currency control-total reconciliation with FULL OUTER JOIN and a tolerance.
Must be able to debug
  • Revenue 3.7% higher than Finance with all tests green (definitions first, then slices).
  • Volume monitor firing every Monday / every morning (weekly seasonality, partial-day compare).
Numbers that matter
  • 97% on-time over 90 days ≈ 2 late days of budget; 99% over a year ≈ 3–4.
  • 99.5% of minutes over 28 days ≈ 200 minutes of streaming lag budget.
  • 3,000 tables × 1% false positives ≈ 30 bogus alerts a day.
  • Tolerance bands of order 0.1% for money, exact for counts from the same ledger (set per case, justified).
Classic traps
  • Writing GX 0.x run_checkpoint code in a 2026 answer.
  • Hash-diff with plain CONCAT: NULLs and missing delimiters make the hash lie.
  • Validating the input instead of the output, or testing after publish and calling time travel "safe".
30-second answer

How do you make data trustworthy — and prove it? Stop bad data at the boundaries, detect the rest, and measure the result. Contracts reject bad input; expectations on staged output block publish; monitors watch freshness, volume and distribution; a daily reconciliation against the system of record proves the numbers; SLOs make "trustworthy" a number.

2-minute answer

First agree what "correct" means with the owner of the number: source, definition, deadline. Then build the loop. Contracts at the producer boundary quarantine malformed data into an owned DLQ. Transforms write to a branch or staging table; blocking expectations (unique keys, not-null joins, row count vs a seasonal baseline, control totals) run there, and publish is an atomic swap only if they pass — so failure means late, not wrong. After publish, tier-1 monitors on freshness, volume and distribution page the owning team; everything else goes to tickets, so alerts stay trusted. Reconciliation per day and slice against the ledger is the proof. Freshness, completeness and correctness roll up into SLOs with an error budget and a policy for when it's spent. Every incident ends with a new check at the stage that should have caught it.

Deep-dive follow-up

“Your gold layer spans five tables that must be published together. Iceberg branches are per table. How do you make the publish atomic across all five, and what do consumers see if table three fails its audit?”

Staff+ follow-up

“You own quality for 3,000 tables across 40 producing teams and have no budget for a vendor. How do you decide which tables get blocking gates, who owns failures, and how you show leadership that trust is improving quarter over quarter?”
