Part 13

Distributed Systems for Data Engineers

Quick refresh10 minInterview study45 minDeep practice75 min
Last technically reviewed September 2026
Covers replication, replication lag, consistency models, CAP and PACELC, consensus and fencing, partitioning and consistent hashing, ordering, delivery semantics, end-to-end backpressure, clocks
Versions referenced Kafka 4.x (KRaft only), Apache Iceberg 1.x, Amazon S3 (strong read-after-write since December 2020)
Primary references Kafka docs · Iceberg docs · S3 consistency model · ZooKeeper docs · DynamoDB read consistency
Known implementation differences The concepts here are timeless; the knobs (acks, ISR rules, read consistency flags, cache invalidation, MV refresh) differ by product and version, so name the product before quoting a behavior.

This chapter tests whether you can reason about a pipeline as what it actually is: a set of machines that disagree about what has happened and when. The interviewer is not looking for Raft trivia. They want to hear you locate where data can be lost, duplicated, reordered or invisible, name the guarantee each boundary provides, and pick the trade-off on purpose. Part 03 has the Kafka and Flink mechanics; this part is the layer underneath that makes those mechanics make sense.

2026 Interview Note

Timeless: quorums, leader election, fencing, the latency-versus-consistency trade, idempotence, the impossibility of exactly-once delivery, and the fact that wall clocks lie. None of that has changed in decades and none of it will. Version-specific: Kafka 4.0 removed ZooKeeper mode entirely, so every current Kafka cluster runs KRaft; idempotent producers became the default in Kafka 3.0; Amazon S3 became strongly consistent for read-after-write (including overwrites, deletes and LIST) in December 2020, while other object stores and S3-compatible systems have their own rules. When you quote behavior, say which bucket it is in. "Kafka elects controllers through ZooKeeper" was true, and saying it in 2026 dates your experience. "Object stores are eventually consistent" is still true of some stores and false of S3. Precision here is the signal.

1. Why DE Interviews Test Distributed Systems

Every pipeline is a distributed system with a clock problem. A CDC stream reads a database replica, ships through a replicated log, lands in object storage, gets committed to a table format via a catalog, and is queried by a warehouse that caches results for a BI tool that caches extracts. That is six independent systems, each with its own notion of "done", and none of them shares a clock.

Most senior DE incidents are distributed-systems incidents wearing a data costume. Duplicate rows after a failover are a delivery-semantics problem. A dashboard showing yesterday's number after a successful load is a consistency problem. A job that runs fine for months then dies every Monday morning is a partitioning problem. Late totals that drift are a clock problem.

The interviewer is checking three things:

  • Vocabulary with precision. Can you say "at-least-once with an idempotent sink" instead of "exactly-once"? Can you distinguish replication lag from consumer lag?
  • Boundary thinking. Guarantees exist per hop. The end-to-end guarantee is the weakest hop. Name the hops.
  • Trade-off ownership. Strong consistency costs latency and availability. You should be able to say what you would pay, and why the business needs it.

If your answer to "why did the count double?" starts with "Kafka has exactly-once", you have skipped every step the interviewer cared about.

2. Replication: Leaders, Followers, Quorums and Lag

Replication keeps copies of the same data on several machines, for durability (survive a disk), availability (survive a node) and read scale. There are three shapes, and each fails differently.

Leader/follower (single-leader)

One node accepts writes; followers copy its log. Postgres and MySQL streaming replication, Kafka partitions, most metadata stores. Ordering is easy because one node decides it. The cost: the leader is a write bottleneck, and failover is the dangerous moment. If replication is asynchronous, a leader can acknowledge a write, die, and a follower that never received it becomes the new leader. The write is gone, and the client was told it succeeded.

Kafka's answer is the in-sync replica set: with acks=all and a minimum ISR of at least 2, a write is acknowledged only once every in-sync replica has it, and only an in-sync replica can be elected (unless unclean election is enabled). The mechanics are in Part 03 §9. The timeless point: durability is decided by what the acknowledgement waited for, not by the replication factor printed on the topic.

Multi-leader

Several nodes accept writes, typically one per region, and replicate to each other asynchronously. Good for multi-region write latency and offline clients. The price is write conflicts: two regions update the same row concurrently, and something must decide the winner. Last-writer-wins by timestamp is the common default and silently discards data whenever clocks disagree (see §10). For a DE, multi-leader matters mostly as a source: CDC from an active-active database can deliver two conflicting versions of a row, in different orders, from different regions. Your merge logic needs a conflict rule that matches the source's, or the lake and the database will disagree forever.

Leaderless and quorums

Any replica accepts reads and writes; the client (or a coordinator) talks to several. Dynamo-style stores such as Cassandra work this way. With N replicas, a write waits for W acknowledgements and a read queries R replicas. If R + W > N, every read set overlaps every write set in at least one replica, so a read can see the latest acknowledged write.

Say the caveats, because the interviewer will: overlap is necessary, not sufficient. Sloppy quorums and hinted handoff (writes accepted by a stand-in node during a partition) break the overlap. Concurrent writes still need a conflict rule. And a write that failed to reach W may still be sitting on one replica and resurface later. Quorums buy tunability, not linearizability.

Replication lag and what it does to pipelines

Asynchronous followers are behind the leader by some amount: milliseconds when healthy, minutes during a long transaction, a bulk load or a network hiccup. Every pipeline that reads a follower inherits that lag, and it causes three concrete bugs:

  • CDC or extracts from a replica. Your nightly extract runs at 00:05 against a read replica that is 12 minutes behind. The "yesterday" partition is missing the last minutes of yesterday, and nothing fails. Fix: extract by a watermark taken from the replica's own replay position (or the source's commit LSN), not by wall-clock time, and check replica lag before starting.
  • Read-after-load in the warehouse. The load job reports success; the validation query, run by a different session or routed to a different cluster, sees the old count. Whether this can happen depends on the product's commit visibility and caching, which is exactly why you should name the product.
  • Object storage. Amazon S3 has provided strong read-after-write consistency for PUTs, overwrites, DELETEs and LIST operations since December 2020. Older S3-era workarounds (S3Guard, "wait then list") exist because that was not always true. Other object stores and S3-compatible systems document their own guarantees; don't assume S3's apply. Note also that strong consistency of individual objects does not make a directory of files a transaction, which is why table formats commit through a single atomic metadata swap (Part 07).

3. Consistency Models, Practically

Consistency models describe what a reader is allowed to see relative to writes. You do not need the formal definitions. You need one sentence for each and one DE failure that it prevents.

ModelWhat it promisesDE failure when you don't have it
Linearizable (strong)Once a write is acknowledged, every later read anywhere sees it. The system behaves like one copy.Two schedulers both read "lock free" from a lagging store and both run the backfill. Leader election and locks need this.
EventualIf writes stop, replicas converge. No promise about when, or what you see before then.A dedup lookup against an eventually consistent key-value store misses a key written 50 ms earlier, and the duplicate gets through.
CausalIf write B depended on write A, nobody sees B without A.An order_item CDC event arrives in the lake before its order because they came from different partitions; the join drops it or produces an orphan.
Read-your-writesA client sees its own writes.An orchestrator task writes a manifest, the next task (same pipeline, different connection routed to a replica) reads the old manifest and processes the wrong file list.
Monotonic readsA client never sees time go backwards.A dashboard refresh hits replica 1 (count 1,040), then replica 2 (count 1,012). The stakeholder files a data-quality ticket.

The L5 move is to notice that most pipeline guarantees are session guarantees (read-your-writes, monotonic reads) that you get by pinning a pipeline's reads to the same node or the same snapshot. Table formats give you this cheaply: a reader that pins a snapshot id sees a consistent, unchanging view for the life of the query, no matter what commits land meanwhile.

A common prompt: "It was written, but downstream can't see it"

A common interview prompt: "Your pipeline wrote the record successfully, but the downstream consumer cannot see it yet. Where can consistency lag occur?" A weak answer names one cause. A strong answer walks the layers in order, because "successfully" meant something different at each one.

  1. Producer ack versus replication. With acks=1 the leader has it; followers may not. In Kafka, consumers only read up to the high watermark (the offset replicated to the ISR), so a record the producer considers written can be briefly invisible, or lost on failover.
  2. Consumer lag and transactional visibility. The record is committed in the log, but the consumer group is minutes behind. Or the consumer uses read_committed and the producer's transaction is still open, so the record sits behind the last stable offset.
  3. Processor staging. A streaming job writes output files but only makes them visible at checkpoint or micro-batch commit. Checkpoint interval is a visibility floor. A checkpoint that keeps failing means output never becomes visible, even though files are piling up in storage.
  4. Commit visibility and metadata caching. For Iceberg or Delta, data exists once the catalog pointer (or log entry) moves. Files written but not committed are invisible, correctly. Separately, some engines cache table metadata for a period, so a long-lived session can keep reading an older snapshot until it refreshes. Check your engine's catalog cache settings.
  5. Warehouse layer. Replicated or multi-cluster reads, materialized views and incremental tables that refresh on a schedule or a target lag. Many warehouse query-result caches invalidate automatically when the underlying table changes; views that refresh on a schedule do not, by design. Know which your product does at time of writing and check current docs.
  6. BI extracts and dashboard caches. The most common answer in practice and the one engineers forget: the dashboard is reading a scheduled extract from 06:00.

Close the answer with the diagnostic: compare the record's position at each layer (producer offset → consumer committed offset → table snapshot id and commit time → MV last refresh → extract timestamp). The first layer where it is missing is the culprit. Put a _loaded_at and source offset on every row so you can do this in minutes.

Drill · Consistency

The load job logs "inserted 2,400,118 rows, committed". The row-count check that runs 20 seconds later reports the previous day's count. Rerunning the check five minutes later passes. This happens on roughly one day in ten.

STOP. Answer before revealing.

Reveal the diagnosis
  1. Observe Data is correct eventually, so this is visibility lag, not loss. Intermittent, so it depends on timing or routing.
  2. Hypothesize (a) the check reads a replica or a different compute cluster with its own metadata cache; (b) the check queries a materialized view or incremental table on a refresh schedule; (c) the check's session pinned an older table snapshot or cached catalog metadata; (d) the load's commit is asynchronous and "committed" meant "submitted".
  3. Measure Log the snapshot id / commit id the load produced. Have the check log the snapshot id it read and the object it queried (base table or view). Compare timestamps on the bad days.
  4. Isolate In a representative case, the check hit a view with a refresh interval, and the bad days were the ones where the load finished just after a refresh.
  5. Fix Point correctness checks at the base table, or at an explicit snapshot id handed over by the load step. Never gate on a derived object whose freshness you don't control.
  6. Prevent Make the handoff explicit: the writer publishes "snapshot X is ready" and the reader reads snapshot X. Visibility becomes a contract, not a race.

4. CAP and PACELC, Practically

CAP says that during a network partition, a replicated system must choose between consistency (refuse or delay some operations so nobody sees stale data) and availability (answer everything, possibly with stale data). It is not "pick two of three". Partitions are not optional, so the only real choice is what you do when one happens.

CAP's weakness as an interview tool is that partitions are rare. PACELC fixes that: if there is a Partition, choose A or C; Else, in normal operation, choose Latency or Consistency. The "else" half is what you pay every single day, and it is the half that matters to a pipeline's SLA. Waiting for a quorum of replicas across availability zones costs a round trip on every write. Not waiting is faster and occasionally wrong.

SystemTypical configurationPartitionNormal caseWhat it means for you
Kafkaacks=all, min ISR 2, unclean election offLeans C: rejects writes if ISR shrinks below minimumLeans C: write latency includes follower fetchProducers see errors during broker loss instead of silent loss. Plan retries.
Kafkaacks=1Leans ALeans LFaster; a leader crash can drop acknowledged records.
Cassandra-style storesTunable per query (e.g. ONE vs QUORUM)A at low consistency levelsL at low levels, C-ish at QUORUMThe choice is per query. A pipeline writing at ONE and reading at ONE can miss its own writes.
DynamoDBDefault reads eventually consistent; strongly consistent reads optionalDepends on read modeEventual reads are cheaper and lower latencyDedup lookups need the strongly consistent read or a conditional write.
Spanner-style databasesConsensus-replicated, externally consistentCC, pays commit latencyCorrect by default, slower writes, cross-region commits cost real milliseconds.
Iceberg table + catalogAtomic pointer swap in catalogC: commit fails if catalog unreachableC for commits; readers pinned to snapshotsWriters retry on conflict; readers never see half a commit.

Treat that table as "typical configuration", not a classification. Most modern systems are tunable, which is the point: the system doesn't choose, you do, per workload.

“Explain CAP vs PACELC.”
30 sec

CAP: during a network partition a replicated system must choose between staying consistent and staying available. PACELC adds the part you pay daily: when there is no partition, you still choose between low latency and strong consistency, because consistency means waiting for other replicas.

2 min

CAP is often misread as "pick two". Partitions happen whether you like it or not, so the actual choice is C or A when they do. But partitions are rare, and CAP says nothing about the normal case. PACELC does: every synchronous replica acknowledgement is a round trip, and cross-zone or cross-region round trips dominate write latency. Kafka with acks=all chooses consistency in both cases; with acks=1 it chooses latency and availability. For a pipeline, the question becomes: what is the business cost of reading stale or losing an acknowledged write, versus the cost of slower writes and errors during failures? Payments and ledgers pay for C. Clickstream usually buys L.

Deep dive

The "C" in CAP is linearizability, which is stronger than what most data systems offer or need. Plenty of useful systems are neither CAP-consistent nor CAP-available in the strict sense, such as a single-leader database with async replicas. The practical frame is per-operation: which operations need linearizability (leader election, locks, catalog commits, idempotency checks) and which tolerate staleness (analytics reads, dashboards). Put the linearizable operations on a small consensus-backed component and keep the bulk data path coordination-free. That is exactly how a lakehouse is built: a strongly consistent catalog pointer over eventually-read, immutable data files.

Where to stop: once you have said "per operation, linearizable metadata over coordination-free data", stop unless asked for proofs.

5. Consensus and Coordination

Consensus is how a group of machines agrees on one value (who the leader is, what the next log entry is, which snapshot is current) despite some of them crashing or being slow. At interview depth you need four ideas, not the protocol.

The four ideas

  • Leader election. One node is designated to make decisions, so the rest don't need to agree on every operation, only on who the leader is.
  • Majority quorum. A decision needs a majority (3 of 5, 2 of 3). Two majorities always overlap, so two conflicting decisions can't both be made. This is why consensus clusters are odd-sized, and why 5 nodes tolerate 2 failures while 4 nodes still only tolerate 1.
  • Terms or epochs. Every election increments a number. Messages carry it. Anyone seeing a higher number knows the old leader is deposed.
  • Fencing tokens. The epoch, passed to the resource being protected, which rejects any request with an older token. This is the part DEs actually implement.

Why fencing is the part you must know

A leader (or lock holder, or job instance) can be paused by a long GC, a VM migration or a network stall, lose its lease, get replaced, and then wake up still believing it is in charge. It writes. Now two writers are active. Timeouts cannot prevent this, because the paused process doesn't know it was paused.

You have seen this pattern already. Kafka's transactional producers are fenced by epoch when a new instance registers the same transactional.id (Part 03 §16). Kafka partition leaders carry a leader epoch so followers can truncate divergent log suffixes after failover. An Iceberg commit that expects metadata version 41 fails if the catalog is already at 42. Same idea every time: the resource checks the token.

ZooKeeper vs KRaft

Kafka historically stored cluster metadata (controller identity, partition leaders, ISR) in ZooKeeper, a separate consensus service. KRaft moves that into Kafka itself: a quorum of controller nodes runs a Raft-based metadata log, and brokers replicate that log. Kafka 4.0 removed ZooKeeper mode entirely, so a 4.x cluster is KRaft-only and migration had to happen on 3.x. What to say in an interview: one fewer distributed system to operate, metadata is an event log that brokers replay instead of a store they poll, and controller failover is faster. What not to say: that KRaft makes the data path consensus-based. Partition data replication is still leader/follower with ISR; consensus is for metadata.

Why coordination is expensive, and how data systems avoid it

Every consensus decision costs at least one network round trip to a majority, a durable fsync on each of them, and the latency of the slowest member of the quorum you wait for. Tail latency compounds: if each replica has a 1% chance of a 50 ms stall, waiting for several replicas makes stalls common. Cross-region, the round trip alone is tens of milliseconds or more. You cannot do that per record at a million records a second.

So data systems use coordination for metadata and avoid it for data:

  • Partitioning. Split the data so each partition has one owner and needs no agreement with the others. Kafka partitions, Spark tasks, Flink key groups.
  • Single-writer per partition. One consumer per partition per group; one Flink subtask per key group. Ordering and state become local.
  • Immutable data plus one atomic pointer. Write any number of files without coordination, then commit by a single compare-and-swap. Iceberg's commit asks the catalog to move the table's metadata pointer from version N to N+1 only if it is still N. If another writer got there first, the commit fails and the writer re-reads, checks for conflicts, and retries. That is optimistic concurrency: no locks held while writing, one coordinated step at the end. It degrades under many concurrent writers to the same table, which is the conflict spiral in Part 07.
  • Batching coordination. Kafka commits offsets periodically, Flink checkpoints every N seconds, Spark commits per micro-batch. You coordinate once per batch, not per record, and pay for it in visibility latency.
Interviewer pushes back

You: “Two instances of the job must never write the same partition, so I'll take a distributed lock with a 30-second TTL before writing.”

Interviewer: “Your instance takes a 45-second GC pause while holding the lock. What happens?”

Strong answer: The lock expires, a second instance acquires it, and when the first wakes it writes anyway, because it has no way of knowing it paused. A lock with a TTL is a performance optimization, not a safety guarantee. For safety the storage must reject the stale writer: pass a monotonically increasing fencing token with each write, or make the write itself a conditional commit (Iceberg-style compare-and-swap on the table version, a conditional put on a version column). And make the write idempotent so if both do run, the result is the same.

Weak answer: “I'll make the TTL longer” or “I'll add a heartbeat.” Both shrink the window without closing it.

6. Partitioning and Sharding

Partitioning is how data systems scale writes and avoid coordination. Part 02 covers the arithmetic for choosing partition counts and file layouts (§8, §17); this section is about the distribution strategies and how they fail.

StrategyHow keys mapGood atFails when
Hashhash(key) mod PEven spread of many keys; point lookupsOne key is hot (hashing can't split a single key); range scans hit every partition; changing P remaps nearly every key
RangeSorted key ranges, e.g. by date or idRange scans, time-based pruning, ordered outputMonotonic keys (timestamps, auto-increment ids) send all new writes to the last range
Directory / lookupExplicit table: key → partitionMoving individual heavy tenants; flexible placementDirectory becomes a dependency on every request; must itself be consistent and available
Consistent hashingKeys and nodes on a ring; key goes to next node clockwiseAdding/removing nodes moves only about 1/N of keysWithout virtual nodes, load is uneven; still can't split one hot key

Consistent hashing and virtual nodes

With hash mod P, going from 10 to 11 partitions remaps roughly 10/11 of all keys, which for a stateful system means moving almost all state. Consistent hashing places nodes on a hash ring; each key belongs to the first node clockwise. Adding a node takes over only the arc between it and its predecessor, about 1/N of keys.

Why virtual nodes: with one position per physical node, arcs are random lengths, so one node may own 40% of the ring. And when a node dies, its whole arc lands on a single neighbour, which is how one failure turns into two. With many virtual positions per node (tens to hundreds is common), the arcs average out and a dead node's load spreads across all survivors. Cassandra-style stores and many caches use this. Kafka does not: its default partitioner hashes the key modulo the partition count, which is why adding partitions to a keyed topic breaks per-key ordering and co-location.

Worked example: a hot partition

Hypothetical numbers. An events topic has 64 partitions, keyed by user_id. Total throughput 200,000 events/s, so 3,125 events/s per partition on average. Each consumer handles about 8,000 events/s before falling behind (measured, not assumed).

One B2B tenant's integration account generates 20% of traffic: 40,000 events/s, all with the same user_id. Hashing sends all of it to one partition. That partition now receives 40,000 + ~2,500 = ~42,500 events/s against a consumer ceiling of 8,000. It falls behind by ~34,500 events per second, about 124 million events per hour. The other 63 partitions are 40% utilized. Adding partitions does nothing: the key still hashes to one place. Adding consumers does nothing: one partition is read by at most one consumer in a group.

Options, in order of how much they cost you:

  1. Check whether you need per-user ordering at all. If the consumer aggregates counts, order doesn't matter; key by (user_id, event_id % 16) and spread the hot user over 16 partitions. Aggregate twice (partial, then final), the same two-stage trick as Spark skew in Part 04.
  2. If per-user order matters, salt only the known heavy keys and reorder downstream by a per-key sequence number. You've traded broker-enforced order for application-enforced order; say that explicitly.
  3. Isolate the heavy hitter. Route that tenant to its own topic with its own partitions and consumers. A directory-based decision layered on hash partitioning.
  4. Make the consumer faster for that key (batching writes, async I/O), which buys headroom without changing semantics.
Interviewer pushes back

You: “I would partition by user_id.”

Interviewer: “What happens when one user generates 20% of traffic?”

Strong answer: Then one partition carries 20% of load and caps the whole pipeline, and neither more partitions nor more consumers help because a single key can't be split by hashing. First I'd ask what user_id is buying: if it's per-user ordering for sessionization, I keep it for normal users and salt only the heavy keys, restoring order downstream with a per-user sequence. If it's only for aggregation, I salt everyone and aggregate in two stages. I'd also detect heavy keys continuously (top-k per partition on the producer or from partition throughput metrics) rather than wait for lag to tell me.

Weak answer: “I'll increase the partition count.” The hot key still lands on exactly one partition, and on a keyed topic you've just remapped every other key.

Rebalancing costs

Moving partitions between nodes is never free. Moving data means copying bytes (a Kafka partition reassignment copies the full retained log to new replicas, competing with live traffic unless throttled). Moving ownership means pausing: a consumer-group rebalance stops some or all consumers while assignments change, and stateful processors must restore state for newly assigned partitions before resuming. Kafka's newer consumer rebalance protocol (KIP-848, generally available in Kafka 4.0) and cooperative assignors reduce the stop-the-world effect; check what your client version uses. The timeless rule: design for few, planned rebalances, over-provision partitions up front for keyed topics, and throttle data movement.

7. Ordering

"Is the data ordered?" has four different answers, and interviewers like to see if you know which one you're claiming.

KindMeaningCostWhere you get it
Global (total) orderEvery consumer sees every event in one agreed sequenceOne sequencer: throughput of a single partition or leaderSingle-partition topic; a consensus log
Per-partition orderOrder within a partition, none acrossScales with partitions; you choose the keyKafka, Kinesis shards
Causal orderEffects follow causes, unrelated events unorderedNeed to carry dependency info (version vectors, sequence numbers)Application design; co-locating related entities by key
Event-time orderOrder by when things happened, reconstructed laterBuffering and watermarks, bounded latenessStream processors (see Part 03 §3)

Global order is a throughput cap. A single ordered sequence means a single decider, so the whole system runs at one node's speed. If a requirement says "events must be processed in order", ask: in order per what? Almost always the answer is per account, per order, per device. Key by that, and you get the order that matters at the parallelism you need.

Ordering across retries

A producer sends batch 1 and batch 2 on the same connection. Batch 1 fails transiently; batch 2 succeeds; batch 1 is retried and lands after batch 2. Per-partition order is now broken, without any failure being reported. Historically the fix was max.in.flight.requests.per.connection=1, which kills throughput. With the idempotent producer (default since Kafka 3.0), the broker tracks sequence numbers per producer and partition and rejects out-of-sequence batches, so order is preserved with up to 5 in-flight requests. Mechanics in Part 03 §16. The timeless point: retries reorder unless something numbers the messages. Your own HTTP or database writers have the same bug and usually no broker to catch it.

Ordering across repartitioning

Order is a property of a path. Any time data is re-keyed (a shuffle, a keyBy, a topic with a different key, an increase in partition count), the new partition receives records from many upstream partitions, interleaved by arrival. Order by the new key is only guaranteed if all records for that key came from one upstream partition in order. Two cases to name:

  • Adding partitions to a keyed Kafka topic. Keys remap. For a while, old records for key K sit in partition 3 and new ones in partition 11, read by different consumers at different speeds. Consumers can see newer before older. Drain first, or create a new topic and migrate.
  • Re-keying in a stream job. Events keyed by device_id re-keyed to account_id: an account's events arrive from many devices' partitions in no particular order. If you need order by account, you need event time and a buffer, or a sequence number assigned at the source.

8. Delivery Semantics, Unified

Part 03 proves the definitions (§7) and walks Kafka's transactional machinery (§16). This section is the unifying rule: a delivery guarantee belongs to a boundary, and a pipeline's guarantee is the weakest boundary on the path. Exactly-once is a property of a pipeline, not of a product. Name the boundaries or don't say it.

GuaranteeSource mustProcessing mustSink mustTypical failure mode
At-most-onceNothing specialCommit position before processingNothing specialCrash after commit, before write: data lost silently
At-least-onceBe replayable from a positionCommit position after the sink write succeedsAccept duplicatesCrash after write, before commit: replay writes again
Effectively-onceBe replayableDeterministic, or carry a stable id per recordIdempotent: upsert/MERGE on a key, or dedup on idNon-deterministic ids (UUID at processing time) defeat the dedup
Exactly-once (transactional)Be replayable, positions committable in the same transactionDeterministic replayTransactional: output and source position commit atomicallySide effects outside the transaction (API calls, emails) still repeat

Two things to say out loud. First, delivery cannot be exactly-once over an unreliable network; a sender that got no response cannot know whether the message arrived. What can be exactly-once is the effect, by deduplication or atomic commit. Second, effectively-once via an idempotent sink is usually simpler, cheaper and more portable than a distributed transaction. Reach for transactions when the sink can't be made idempotent, or when the output is itself a log (Kafka to Kafka).

“What does exactly-once actually mean?”
30 sec

That each input's effect on the output is applied once, even though messages may be delivered and processed more than once. It requires a replayable source, deterministic processing, and a sink that is either idempotent or commits output and source position atomically. It holds only within those boundaries.

2 min

Physical delivery is at-least-once at best, because retries are the only answer to an ambiguous failure. Exactly-once is built on top by making retries harmless. Two routes: idempotence (the sink ignores a second write with the same key: MERGE on a natural key, a dedup table, Kafka's producer sequence numbers) or atomic commit (Kafka transactions with sendOffsetsToTransaction, Flink's two-phase commit sinks, Spark's commit log for file sinks). Then state the conditions: it's meaningful only if the source can replay from a committed position, processing gives the same output for the same input, every sink participates, and downstream readers only read committed data (read_committed, snapshot reads). Break any one and you are back to at-least-once.

Deep dive

The usual breakers: a UUID or now() generated during processing makes replay produce different keys; a lookup against a mutable table gives different enrichments on replay; a REST call or email inside the processor is outside every transaction; a consumer reading read_uncommitted sees aborted data; a sink with a dedup window shorter than the maximum replay distance lets old duplicates through after a long outage. And end-to-end means end-to-end: if the source system itself re-emits an event (a CDC connector re-snapshotting a table, a client retrying a checkout), that is a new input as far as the pipeline is concerned, so you need a business key to dedupe it.

Where to stop: after naming the three conditions and one concrete breaker. Only go into transaction coordinators if asked.

Drill · Kafka / Delivery

After a broker failover at 14:02, the orders table in the lake has about 3,000 duplicate rows, all with distinct surrogate keys but identical business content. The producer has idempotence enabled. The streaming job claims "exactly-once".

STOP. Answer before revealing.

Reveal the diagnosis
  1. Observe Duplicates cluster at the failover. Distinct surrogate keys means they were written as different rows, so the sink didn't recognize them as the same.
  2. Hypothesize (a) The producer's idempotence protects one producer session per partition; if the producer application restarted or timed out and resent from its own source, it's a new session and new records. (b) The stream job replayed from its last checkpoint after the failover-induced error, and the sink appends rather than merges. (c) Surrogate key generated at processing time (UUID), so replayed records got new keys and even a MERGE on that key wouldn't dedupe.
  3. Measure Compare Kafka offsets on the duplicate pairs (same offset twice = consumer-side replay; different offsets = producer-side resend). Check the job's restart and checkpoint logs around 14:02. Check how the surrogate key is generated.
  4. Isolate A representative finding: same source offsets appear twice; job restarted from a checkpoint 90 seconds old; sink is a plain append; key is a UUID created in the job.
  5. Fix Derive the row key deterministically from the input (topic, partition, offset, or the business key plus source version) and write with MERGE / upsert, or use a transactional sink whose commit is tied to the checkpoint. Deduplicate the affected window by business key.
  6. Prevent A test that kills the job mid-batch and asserts no duplicates; a daily uniqueness check on the business key; review any uuid() or now() in a streaming write path.
Interviewer pushes back

You: “We use Flink with exactly-once checkpointing, so there are no duplicates.”

Interviewer: “Your job also calls a fraud-scoring API per event and posts alerts to a webhook. Still exactly-once?”

Strong answer: Not for those. Checkpointing makes Flink's own state and a two-phase-commit sink exactly-once; the API call and the webhook are side effects outside the transaction and will repeat on every replay since the last checkpoint. For the scoring call, that's fine if it's a pure read. For the webhook I need idempotence on the receiving side: send a deterministic alert id (derived from the event id) and have the receiver dedupe, or write alerts to a transactional topic and let a separate at-least-once sender dedupe against a table. I'd state the guarantee as "exactly-once for the lake table, at-least-once with idempotency keys for alerts".

Weak answer: “Flink guarantees exactly-once end to end.” The framework guarantees what it controls. It doesn't control the webhook.

9. Backpressure End-to-End

Backpressure is what happens when a stage can't keep up: it must either slow its upstream, buffer, or drop. Part 03 covers the stream-processor mechanics (§12). The distributed-systems view is that a pipeline is a chain of queues, and every unbounded queue is a place where an overload hides until it becomes an outage.

Where queues accumulate, hop by hop:

  • Producer: a bounded client buffer. When it's full, sends block or fail. Good: that is backpressure reaching the application. Bad if the application then buffers in its own unbounded in-memory list.
  • Broker: the log is the queue, bounded by retention time or size, not by consumer progress. A slow consumer does not slow the producer. It just falls further behind until the oldest unread data ages out.
  • Consumer: fetch buffers and any internal work queue. If processing is handed to a thread pool with an unbounded queue, the consumer keeps polling and committing offsets for work that hasn't happened, which quietly turns at-least-once into at-most-once on a crash.
  • Sink: connection pools, write batches, and the sink's own admission control (rate limits, warehouse concurrency queues, database lock waits).

Recognizing collapse

Lag itself is not the alarm; lag that grows is. Healthy systems recover after a spike; collapsing ones go non-linear. Signals, roughly in the order they appear:

  • Lag growth rate positive and not recovering after the input spike has passed. Compute time-to-retention: current lag divided by net drain rate. If that number is smaller than retention, you are about to lose data.
  • Retry storms. The sink slows, clients time out and retry, and the retries add load to the sink that caused the timeouts. Throughput goes down while request count goes up. The fix is exponential backoff with jitter, retry budgets, and circuit breakers, not more retries.
  • GC pressure. Buffers grow, heap fills, GC pauses lengthen, processing slows further, buffers grow more.
  • Timeouts cascading upstream. A slow sink makes consumers slow, which makes synchronous callers time out, which makes their callers retry.
  • Rebalance storms. A consumer spends longer than the poll interval limit on one batch (because the sink is slow), is ejected from the group, triggers a rebalance, everyone pauses, lag jumps, the next batch is bigger, and it happens again. The group spends more time rebalancing than consuming. Smaller batches and faster per-batch work break the loop; a larger poll interval only hides it.

The design principle: bounded queues everywhere, so overload shows up as blocked producers or explicit rejection at a point you chose, plus load shedding or a dead-letter path for work you can defer. An overloaded system that says "no" early degrades; one that says "yes" to everything collapses.

10. Time and Clocks

Clocks on different machines disagree. NTP-synchronized servers are typically within milliseconds of each other, but a misconfigured host, a VM resumed from suspension, or a mobile device can be off by seconds, hours or years. Clocks can also jump backward when corrected. So:

  • Never order events across hosts by producer timestamp. Two events 3 ms apart on different machines can carry timestamps in either order. Within one partition, use the log offset. Within one entity, use a source-assigned sequence or version number (a database LSN, a per-entity version column).
  • Last-writer-wins by wall clock loses data. In multi-leader replication or in an upsert keyed on updated_at, a host with a fast clock wins every conflict, including against later writes. Prefer source versions or LSNs as the tiebreaker.
  • Event time plus watermarks is how streaming copes. You process by when things happened, accept they arrive out of order, and use a watermark as a declared estimate of "we've probably seen everything up to T". Lateness beyond it is handled by policy, not ignored. Mechanics in Part 03 §2 and §3.
  • Measure durations with monotonic clocks, not wall clocks, in your own code. A wall clock adjusting during a timeout calculation gives you negative latencies and surprising expiries.
  • Record several times. Event time (from the source), ingestion time (broker append), processing time (when you handled it). The gaps between them are your best freshness and skew diagnostics.

Some databases use tightly bounded clock uncertainty (specialized time infrastructure) to get consistent ordering across regions. That is the exception that proves the rule: they had to engineer the uncertainty down and then wait it out on every commit.

Failure-first: what can fail?
FailureDetectRecoverPrevent recurrence
Acknowledged writes lost on leader failover (async replication or acks=1)Source-vs-sink reconciliation by offset or id; gaps in per-key sequence numbersReplay from source for the affected windowacks=all with min ISR ≥ 2, unclean election off; durability requirement written down per topic
Replica-lag gap in extractsRow counts short for last minutes of the window; compare replica replay position with sourceRe-extract the window after replica catches upExtract by commit position/watermark, gate on replica lag
Duplicates after failover / replayUniqueness test on business key; same source offset appearing twiceDeduplicate by business key and latest source versionDeterministic keys, MERGE/upsert or transactional sink
Split brain: two writers after a pauseConflicting commits, fence exceptions, interleaved outputsStop one writer; rebuild affected partition from sourceFencing tokens or conditional commits at the storage layer
Hot partitionPer-partition lag and throughput skew; one consumer saturated, others idleTemporarily isolate the heavy keyHeavy-key detection, salting where order allows, per-tenant routing
Reordering after repartition or retryPer-key sequence regressions; state machines seeing impossible transitionsReprocess affected keys in event-time/sequence orderIdempotent producer; source sequence numbers; migrate topics instead of adding partitions
Lag exceeds retentionTime-to-retention alert (lag ÷ net drain rate)Backfill from source or archive; raise retention temporarilyAlert on lag growth rate, not lag level; bounded queues and load shedding
Stale reads after successful loadSnapshot id read ≠ snapshot id writtenRe-run the consumer against the committed snapshotExplicit snapshot handoff; checks against base tables, not refresh-based views
L5 Interview CardDistributed Systems for Data Engineers
Must know
  • Durability is what the ack waited for, not the replication factor.
  • R + W > N gives quorum overlap, not linearizability.
  • PACELC: the everyday trade is latency versus consistency, not just A versus C during partitions.
  • Fencing tokens, not TTL locks, stop zombie writers.
  • Coordinate metadata, not data: partitioning, single writer, atomic pointer swap.
  • Order is per key and per path; retries and re-keying break it.
  • Exactly-once = replayable source + deterministic processing + idempotent or transactional sink, per boundary.
  • Never order across hosts by wall-clock timestamp.
Must be able to explain
  1. The record was written; why can't downstream see it? Walk every layer.
  2. Why does adding partitions not fix a hot key, and what does?
  3. Under what conditions is exactly-once meaningful, and what breaks it?
Must be able to draw

Producer → broker (leader + ISR) → consumer group → idempotent sink → table commit via catalog CAS, marking where each guarantee is enforced and where queues accumulate.

P ─acks=all─▶ L ─▶ F,F   (durability)
              │ offsets
              ▼
          consumer ─MERGE on key─▶ table
                         │ CAS v41→v42
                         ▼
                      catalog
Must be able to code
  • An idempotent MERGE keyed on business key plus source version that tolerates replays and out-of-order versions.
  • A consumer loop that commits offsets only after the sink write succeeds, with bounded work queue.
  • A heavy-key salting scheme with two-stage aggregation.
Must be able to debug
  • Duplicate rows after a broker failover in a job that claims exactly-once.
  • A row-count check that intermittently reads stale data right after a successful load.
Numbers that matter
  • Majority quorum: 3 nodes tolerate 1 failure, 5 tolerate 2; 4 still tolerate only 1.
  • Hash mod P, P → P+1 remaps about P/(P+1) of keys; consistent hashing moves about 1/N.
  • Same-zone round trip: sub-millisecond; cross-region: tens to hundreds of ms. Each synchronous replica ack pays it.
  • Time-to-retention = lag ÷ (consume rate − produce rate).
  • A key with 20% of traffic caps throughput at about 5× one consumer's capacity for the whole keyed stream, if everything else is perfect.
Classic traps
  • "Kafka is exactly-once" with a webhook in the processor.
  • Adding partitions to a keyed topic to fix lag, breaking ordering.
  • Last-writer-wins by updated_at from multiple hosts.
30-second answer

Where can a pipeline lose, duplicate or hide data, and how do you stop it? At every boundary between systems. Loss comes from acknowledging before replication or committing before writing; duplicates come from replay into non-idempotent sinks; invisibility comes from lag at some layer. I make sources replayable, sinks idempotent or transactional, and handoffs explicit by position or snapshot id, then the end-to-end guarantee is the weakest boundary.

2-minute answer

Where can a pipeline lose, duplicate or hide data, and how do you stop it? Walk the path. Producer to broker: durability depends on acks and in-sync replicas, and retries can reorder unless messages are sequenced. Broker to consumer: commit offsets after the sink write, not before, or a crash loses data; consumer lag and open transactions delay visibility. Consumer to sink: replays will happen, so derive keys deterministically and MERGE, or tie the sink commit to the checkpoint. Sink to reader: table formats commit by an atomic catalog swap, so readers see all or nothing, but views, caches and BI extracts add their own lag, so gate consumers on the committed snapshot id. Across all of it: partition by the key that ordering actually needs, watch for heavy keys, fence writers with epochs rather than trusting locks, bound every queue, and never trust wall clocks across hosts.

Deep-dive follow-up

Your Iceberg table has twelve concurrent streaming writers and commits start failing with conflicts and retrying in a loop. Explain why optimistic concurrency degrades here and redesign the write path.

Staff+ follow-up

The company is going multi-region active-active for the order service. What does that do to the CDC feed, ordering, conflict resolution and the lake's source of truth, and which guarantees would you tell the business they are giving up?

Part 14

Production Data Platform — Cloud, Security & Release Engineering

Quick refresh15 minInterview study60 minDeep practice70 min
Last technically reviewed September 2026
Covers cloud reference architecture, cross-cloud map, IAM/RBAC/ABAC, workload identity federation, secrets & KMS, private networking & exfiltration, masking, row security, tokenization, multi-tenancy, Terraform, Kubernetes, CI/CD for data, write-audit-publish, blue/green, shadow runs, expand/contract
Versions referenced Terraform 1.x / OpenTofu 1.x, Snowflake Enterprise Edition policies, Databricks Unity Catalog, BigQuery policy tags & row access policies, GitHub Actions OIDC
Primary references AWS IAM · GCP Workload Identity Federation · Azure managed identities · Terraform · Snowflake column security · Unity Catalog · GitHub Actions OIDC
Known implementation differences Every cloud has the same primitives (identity, key, network boundary, policy) with different names, scopes and defaults — design with the primitive, then look up the product.

This chapter is where "Data Engineer" becomes "Senior Data Platform Engineer." The interviewer is not checking whether you can name forty cloud services. They are checking whether you can say who is allowed to read a column and prove it, how a credential gets into a job without living in a repo, what stops a table from leaving the network, and what you do at 9:40 a.m. when last night's deploy published wrong numbers to the CFO's dashboard. Security and release engineering are the same skill seen from two angles: controlling change and controlling access to a system other people depend on.

2026 Interview Note

Timeless: least privilege, short-lived credentials, envelope encryption, separating who can manage a key from who can use it, network boundaries, immutable artifacts, write-audit-publish, expand/contract migrations. Version-specific: every product name in this chapter. Managed services get renamed, merged and retired on a timescale shorter than a career — Kinesis Data Firehose became Amazon Data Firehose, Azure's analytics story moved from HDInsight to Synapse to Microsoft Fabric, and managed Airflow on Azure has changed names more than once. In an interview, lead with the primitive ("a short-lived federated identity") and follow with the product ("on AWS that's an IAM role assumed through OIDC"). Candidates who can only speak in product names sound like they memorized a certification; candidates who only speak in primitives sound like they have never shipped. Say both.

1. The Reference Cloud Data Platform

Every cloud data platform is built from seven kinds of thing. Learn the kinds; the logos change.

Building blockThe design question an L5 asks
Object storage (system of record)Who can write, who can read, and can any of it become public?
Compute (Spark/Flink/containers)What identity does the job run as, and what can that identity reach?
WarehouseIs access enforced in the warehouse, the storage, or both — and do they agree?
Streaming logTopic ACLs, TLS, and who can create a consumer group on PII topics?
OrchestrationIt holds connections to everything — the most privileged thing in the platform. What does it hold, and where?
Identity (IAM)Are there any long-lived credentials left? Where?
NetworkingWhat path does a byte take from storage to a laptop, and where can you cut it?

Three properties make this diagram "production" rather than "demo":

  • Identity is federated from one place. Humans get roles through SSO groups; machines get roles through workload identity. Nobody has a personal access key to production storage.
  • The network has an inside. Storage, warehouse, KMS and secrets are reached over private endpoints. The compute has no route to arbitrary internet destinations.
  • Audit leaves the blast radius. The account that runs pipelines cannot delete the logs that describe what pipelines did. This is the point of immutable audit from Part 10.

Account structure: separate accounts/projects/subscriptions per environment, plus a security/audit account. Account boundaries are the strongest isolation the cloud gives you for free; IAM inside one account is a weaker second line. "We separate prod and dev by naming convention" is an audit finding, not a design. Cost-side cloud scenarios live in Part 08.

2. Cross-Cloud Conceptual Map

Use this table to translate, not to memorize. It is a conceptual map at time of writing (2026) — names and product boundaries move, so check current vendor docs before you quote one in a design doc. Where a cell lists several products, it is because the cloud genuinely has several overlapping answers.
