Two differences that matter in design, not just naming: GCP VPCs are global while AWS VPCs and Azure VNets are regional; and data-access audit logging is often opt-in (S3 data events, many GCP Data Access logs) — if "who read this file?" depends on a log you never enabled, you have no answer.

Interviewer pushes back

You: “We'd use Glue for ETL, Redshift for the warehouse, and Kinesis for streaming.”

Interviewer: “Fine. Now tell me the same design without product names.”

Strong answer: “A durable ordered log for events with per-key ordering and 7 days of replay; a batch engine that can shuffle a few TB nightly and write an open table format; a SQL serving layer for 200 concurrent analysts with column-level policy. Every component runs as a distinct workload identity with no static keys, reaches storage over private endpoints, and uses customer-managed keys. On AWS that maps to Kinesis or MSK, EMR or Glue, and Redshift or Iceberg-plus-Athena.”

Weak answer: Repeating the product list louder. The test is whether product names stand on requirements or replace them.

3. Identity & Access: Design the Control Plane

A data platform has a data plane (bytes moving through jobs and queries) and a control plane (who can run what, as which identity, against which resources — and who can change those rules). Most candidates detail the data plane and wave at the control plane with "we'd use IAM." An L5 designs it explicitly: most breaches and compliance findings are control-plane failures.

Principals: humans, workloads, and the ones that should not exist

  • Humans authenticate through SSO with MFA and get access by group membership, never direct grants. Offboarding is one action.
  • Workloads get a workload identity (IAM role, service account, managed identity) — one per workload class, not one "etl-user" for everything, or the audit log says "etl-user read the SSN table" and nothing more.
  • Long-lived keys — access key pairs, service-account key files, storage account keys, passwords in config — should not exist. Each can be copied, committed, and used from anywhere until someone notices.

Workload identity federation: no keys to leak

The workload proves who it is with a token from something that already knows it (Kubernetes, GitHub Actions, another cloud) and exchanges it for short-lived cloud credentials. Nothing secret is stored.

The same shape covers Kubernetes pods, cross-cloud access, and warehouse storage integrations (the warehouse assumes a role you created; you never hand it a key). The interview tell: "where is the secret stored?" The right answer is "nowhere — credentials are minted per run."

RBAC vs ABAC

RBAC (role-based)ABAC (attribute/tag-based)
Rule shape"Role finance_analyst can SELECT on fin.transactions.""Anyone whose clearance ≥ the column's sensitivity tag, and whose region matches the row's region, can read it."
Scales withNumber of roles × number of objects. Grows quadratically in a big catalog.Number of tags and policies. A new table inherits controls the moment it is tagged.
Failure modeRole explosion; grants nobody can explain; new tables are wide open until someone remembers.A mis-tagged or untagged column is silently unprotected. Tagging becomes a critical pipeline.
Audit question it answers well"Who has access to table X?""Is every PII column protected by policy?"

The senior answer is both: RBAC for coarse entitlements, ABAC for sensitive columns and rows — with automated, enforced tagging: classification (Part 10) at ingest, CI failing any table whose PII-looking columns lack a tag, and untagged columns in restricted schemas defaulting to masked. Fail closed.

Least privilege that survives contact with reality

  • Scope by resource, not just action. s3:GetObject on arn:...:bucket/curated/finance/*, not on *. Wildcard resources are where least privilege goes to die.
  • Separate read, write, and admin identities per domain. The job that writes curated.orders should not be able to drop curated.payments.
  • Break-glass, not standing admin. Humans are read-only in prod; elevated access is requested, time-boxed (an hour, not a quarter), approved, logged.
  • Use access analyzers and last-used data. Every major cloud can report which permissions a role actually used. Remove what has not been used in 90 days. Permissions only ever get added unless something removes them.
  • Guardrails above accounts. Org policies enforce what no account admin can undo: no public buckets, no disabling audit logs, no unapproved regions.

Credential rotation

Rotation is the tax you pay for credentials you could not eliminate. Rank your credentials by how you would remove them, not by how you would rotate them:

  1. Eliminate — federation, managed identities, storage integrations. Nothing to rotate.
  2. Short-lived, auto-issued — dynamic database credentials from a secrets engine (issued per job, expire in hours). Rotation is automatic by construction.
  3. Long-lived but managed — a third-party API key stored in a secrets manager with scheduled rotation. The job reads it at runtime; nothing caches it on disk.
  4. Long-lived and manual — the vendor SFTP password. Document it, alarm on its age, and put it on a list someone reviews.

The rotation question that catches people is dual validity: rotate a password and jobs that started with the old one fail mid-run. Support two valid credentials during an overlap (create new → deploy consumers → verify → revoke old). Same for certificates and API tokens.

4. Secrets, Keys & Encryption

Secret management

Rules that hold on every platform:

  • Secrets live in a secrets manager and are fetched at runtime by an identity allowed to read that specific secret. Not in environment files in the repo, not in Airflow Variables in plain text, not in notebook cells, not baked into container images.
  • Secrets never appear in logs. Config dumps and JDBC URLs in exception messages are the usual leaks; redact in the logging layer.
  • Pre-commit and CI secret scanning on every repo. When one is found in history, the fix is rotation, not a force-push — assume anything that reached a remote has been cloned.

KMS and envelope encryption

Nobody sends petabytes to a KMS. Envelope encryption splits the problem:

Why it matters: the KMS unwrap is an authorization check independent of storage permissions. GetObject without decrypt permission returns ciphertext — two controls on one byte. It also gives you crypto-shredding: destroy a per-tenant or per-subject key and every copy, backups included, becomes unreadable — one of the few credible answers to erasure in immutable storage (Part 10).

Key management decisions an L5 names:

  • Customer-managed keys (CMK) for anything sensitive: you control the key policy, see usage, and can revoke.
  • Separation of duties. Key administrators and key users are disjoint. Policies can express this; defaults usually don't.
  • Rotation is not remediation. Automatic rotation adds new key material for new writes; it does not re-encrypt existing data. A compromised key needs re-encryption.
  • Key deletion is data deletion. Alarm on scheduled key deletions like you would on DROP DATABASE.

Encryption in transit, TLS and mTLS

  • TLS authenticates the server to the client and encrypts the channel. Required everywhere: JDBC connections to the warehouse, Kafka client connections, calls to storage APIs. Enforce it — bucket policies can deny non-TLS requests; warehouses and Kafka brokers can refuse plaintext listeners.
  • mTLS additionally authenticates the client with a certificate. Kafka commonly uses mTLS or SASL for client identity; service meshes use mTLS between pods. Automate issuance and rotation; hand-issued certs expire on holiday weekends.
  • Inside the VPC is not "trusted." A compromised pod can sniff or impersonate. Encrypt internal hops; for Spark, enable RPC authentication and encryption, and encrypt shuffle/spill for sensitive data.
Interviewer pushes back

You: “The PII table is sensitive, so I'd just encrypt it.”

Interviewer: “Encrypted with whose key, and who can decrypt?”

Strong answer: “A provider-managed key stops someone who steals a disk — not an over-privileged role, because storage decrypts transparently for anyone with read access. The real control is the key policy: a customer-managed key per sensitivity zone, decrypt granted only to the pipeline role that writes the zone and the tokenization service, no human decrypt, every decrypt logged. Analysts read a derived table with tokens or masks. Key administrators and key users are disjoint groups, so nobody can grant themselves decrypt.”

Weak answer: “AES-256 at rest and TLS in transit.” Every managed service does that by default; it answers a compliance checkbox, not the access question.

5. Private Networking & Exfiltration Controls

Identity decides who can read. Network decides where the bytes can go afterwards. You need both, because a valid identity running on an attacker's laptop — or a legitimate developer copying a table to a personal bucket — passes every identity check.

Private endpoints, conceptually

By default, a job inside a VPC reaches object storage or the warehouse over the provider's public endpoints — via a NAT gateway, across the public address space. A private endpoint puts an interface for that service inside your network so traffic never leaves the provider backbone, and — more importantly — lets you attach a policy to the endpoint. You can then say: "from this network, you may reach only buckets owned by our organization." That single condition closes the classic exfiltration path of a valid job writing to an attacker-owned bucket.

The exfiltration surface of a data platform

Path outControl
Job writes to an external bucketEndpoint policies / service perimeters restricting to org-owned resources; no general internet egress from compute subnets.
Job calls an arbitrary HTTPS endpoint (paste site, personal API)Egress through a proxy or firewall with an allow-list of domains (package mirror, vendor APIs); deny by default.
Bucket or object made publicAccount/org-level block-public-access settings enforced by org policy so no account admin can turn them off.
Warehouse unload to an external stageWarehouse-level settings that require pre-approved storage integrations for unloads (Snowflake has parameters for this — check current names); deny ad-hoc stages.
Notebook result download / "export to CSV"Workspace admin controls that disable or limit result downloads for restricted workspaces; row limits on exports.
BI tool extract / scheduled email of a full tableBI connects through masked views with a service identity; extract permissions restricted; export row caps.
Developer laptop with production credentialsNo long-lived keys; production data access only from managed environments inside the perimeter; conditional access on device posture.

The concept behind VPC Service Controls (GCP) and AWS data perimeters is the same: a boundary defined by identities, resources and networks together. A request succeeds only if a trusted identity accesses a trusted resource from an expected network. Any two of three is not enough. Say this sentence in an interview and you have described a data perimeter without naming a product.

6. Data-Layer Controls: Masking, Row Security, Tokenization, Tenancy

Part 10 covers what each protection technique is (masking, pseudonymization, tokenization, generalization). This section covers where to enforce them and how they fail in a real platform.

Dynamic column masking and row-level security

Dynamic masking returns the clear value to one role and a masked value to another at query time; row-level security appends a predicate the user cannot see or remove. Both beat one copy of every table per audience. What makes them production-grade:

  • Attach by tag, not by table. A masking policy bound to a pii=ssn tag protects every future column tagged ssn. A policy bound table-by-table protects the tables someone remembered.
  • Entitlements live in a mapping table, not in the policy body. The policy says "look up this role's allowed regions"; the mapping table is managed by an access-request workflow. Changing access is then a governed row change, not a DDL deploy.
  • Policies apply to the engine, not the bytes. A Snowflake masking policy protects queries through Snowflake. If the same data sits in an external Parquet file that a Spark cluster can read directly, the policy does not exist for Spark. Every engine that can read the storage must enforce equivalent policy, or must be denied the storage.
  • Watch for inference. Masked columns can still leak through GROUP BY, joins on the clear value, or WHERE ssn = '123-45-6789' probing. Masking hides display; it does not always hide predicates. Tokenizing the column in the analytics copy closes that gap.
Engine: SnowflakeDialect/Language: Snowflake SQLExecutable: Yes — requires Enterprise Edition or higher for masking/row access policies; adapt database, role and table names
-- 1. Masking policy: full SSN only for an approved role, last 4 otherwise.
CREATE OR REPLACE MASKING POLICY governance.policies.ssn_mask
  AS (val STRING) RETURNS STRING ->
  CASE
    WHEN IS_ROLE_IN_SESSION('PII_SSN_READER') THEN val
    WHEN val IS NULL THEN NULL
    ELSE '***-**-' || RIGHT(val, 4)
  END;

-- 2. Bind it to a tag so every column tagged pii_type='ssn' is covered.
CREATE TAG IF NOT EXISTS governance.tags.pii_type
  ALLOWED_VALUES 'ssn', 'email', 'phone';
ALTER TAG governance.tags.pii_type SET MASKING POLICY governance.policies.ssn_mask;
-- (One masking policy per data type per tag; values are distinguished by
--  the policy body or by separate tags. Check current tag-policy rules.)

ALTER TABLE fin.core.transactions
  MODIFY COLUMN customer_ssn SET TAG governance.tags.pii_type = 'ssn';

-- 3. Row access policy driven by an entitlement mapping table.
CREATE OR REPLACE ROW ACCESS POLICY governance.policies.region_rap
  AS (row_region STRING) RETURNS BOOLEAN ->
  IS_ROLE_IN_SESSION('FIN_GLOBAL_ANALYST')
  OR EXISTS (
    SELECT 1
    FROM governance.entitlements.role_region e
    WHERE IS_ROLE_IN_SESSION(e.role_name)
      AND e.region = row_region
  );

ALTER TABLE fin.core.transactions
  ADD ROW ACCESS POLICY governance.policies.region_rap ON (region);
Engine: Databricks Unity CatalogDialect/Language: Databricks SQLExecutable: Illustrative — syntax per Unity Catalog docs at time of writing; requires UC-enabled compute and appropriate privileges; adapt names
-- Column mask: a SQL UDF returning the column's type.
CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION governance.policies.ssn_mask(ssn STRING)
  RETURN CASE
    WHEN is_account_group_member('pii_ssn_readers') THEN ssn
    ELSE concat('***-**-', right(ssn, 4))
  END;

ALTER TABLE fin.core.transactions
  ALTER COLUMN customer_ssn SET MASK governance.policies.ssn_mask;

-- Row filter: a boolean UDF over the filter column(s).
CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION governance.policies.region_filter(region STRING)
  RETURN is_account_group_member('fin_global_analysts')
      OR (region = 'EU' AND is_account_group_member('fin_eu_analysts'))
      OR (region = 'US' AND is_account_group_member('fin_us_analysts'));

ALTER TABLE fin.core.transactions
  SET ROW FILTER governance.policies.region_filter ON (region);

-- BigQuery equivalent concepts (not this syntax): column-level access via
-- policy tags + data masking policies; row-level via
--   CREATE ROW ACCESS POLICY ... ON ds.t GRANT TO (...) FILTER USING (...);

The engines agree on the concept and on nothing else: Snowflake checks roles, Unity Catalog checks account groups, BigQuery grants row policies to principals. None of these statements runs elsewhere. The hard-coded regions in the Databricks filter are what a mapping table replaces at scale.

Tokenization in the platform: vault vs format-preserving

Part 10 defines tokenization (PII handling). The platform decisions:

Vault tokenizationFormat-preserving encryption (FPE) / vaultless
HowRandom token; mapping token↔value stored in a secured vault service.Deterministic keyed transform; token has the same format (9 digits in, 9 digits out). No mapping table.
DetokenizeVault lookup — an audited, rate-limitable API call.Decrypt with the key — anyone holding the key can reverse at any rate.
Joins across datasetsYes, if the same value always maps to the same token (deterministic vault).Yes, deterministic by construction.
Failure modeVault outage stops ingest; vault loss is data loss.Key leak reverses every token ever issued. Low-entropy fields (SSN has ~10⁹ values) are enumerable if the key leaks.

A defensible default for regulated identifiers: tokenize at the edge of the platform (ingest), so the lake and warehouse only ever hold tokens; keep detokenization behind a narrow service with its own identity, rate limits and audit; treat the small set of workflows that need clear values (fraud investigation, regulatory reporting) as named exceptions with their own zone.

PII isolation zones

Multi-tenant isolation

A common interview prompt: "You're building a data product for B2B customers. How do you keep tenant A from ever seeing tenant B's data?" The options sit on a spectrum:

ModelIsolationCost / opsWhen
Shared tables + row filter on tenant_idLogical. One missing predicate or policy bug leaks across tenants.Cheapest; one pipeline, one schema to migrate.Many small tenants, low sensitivity, strong central policy enforcement.
Schema (or database) per tenantGrant-level. Blast radius of a grant mistake is one tenant.Migrations × N tenants; catalog grows; per-tenant pipelines or fan-out.Tens to low thousands of tenants; contractual isolation requirements.
Account/project per tenant + per-tenant keyPhysical plus cryptographic. Crypto-shred a tenant on offboarding.Highest; fleet management becomes the product.Few large, regulated tenants; customer-managed-key (BYOK) demands.

The strong answer mixes them: row filters for the long tail, a per-tenant data key even in shared storage (offboarding by crypto-shred), dedicated deployments for the few tenants who pay for them — plus a cross-tenant leak test in CI that queries every tenant-facing view as tenant A and asserts zero rows of any other tenant_id.

7. Scenario: “Analysts Need Transactions but Must Never See SSNs”

A representative L5 security design prompt. The trap is answering "masking policy" in one breath. The interviewer wants the whole control plane, layer by layer, and wants you to find the holes in your own design before they do.

Requirements — ask before designing

  • "Never see" means what? Never displayed, never queryable (no WHERE ssn = …), or never present anywhere analysts can reach? Three different designs; regulated identifiers usually need the last.
  • Do analysts need to join on the person? Distinct customers and joins to a customer dimension need a stable identifier — just not the SSN.
  • Who needs the clear value, and which engines touch the data? Usually a small fraud team doing individual lookups; every engine is a separate enforcement point.
  • What proof is required? An auditor will ask "show me nobody outside fraud read an SSN last quarter." Design for that query.

Controls by layer

LayerControlWhy this layer
Data (primary)Tokenize SSN at ingest. The curated transactions table carries customer_token (deterministic, joinable) and no SSN column at all. Clear SSNs exist only in the restricted zone.You cannot leak a column that is not there. Masking hides; removal prevents.
Data (defence in depth)If an SSN column must exist in a shared table (legacy, migration period): tag-bound masking policy that fails closed, plus a policy that blocks predicates on it or a tokenized shadow column for filtering.Covers the gap while you migrate, and any future table where someone copies the column.
IdentityAnalysts get fin_analyst via SSO group. pii_ssn_reader is a separate role, granted only through a time-boxed access request approved by data owner + security. No role inherits it.Role hierarchies are how clear access leaks: someone grants pii_ssn_reader to fin_admin, and fin_admin to half the team.
StorageRestricted zone in a separate account/project, separate CMK; analyst and general ETL roles have no decrypt permission on that key.Even a misconfigured warehouse grant or direct Spark read hits ciphertext.
NetworkRestricted zone reachable only via private endpoints from the ingest and tokenization services. Analyst tooling cannot route there at all.A stolen analyst credential used from outside still fails.
Classification pipelinePII scanner runs on every new/changed table; CI fails a model that produces a column matching SSN patterns without a tag; nightly scan of curated zone for SSN-shaped values in free-text columns.The SSN will arrive in a notes column or a JSON blob eventually. Detect it.
AuditWarehouse access history (column-level where available) + KMS decrypt logs + detokenization API logs → append-only audit store in the security account. Alerts on any SSN-tagged column access or detokenize call outside the fraud team's role.Turns "we believe nobody saw it" into "here is the query that proves it."

Failure modes to name before the interviewer does

  • Copies escape the policy. A privileged CREATE TABLE … AS SELECT * materializes clear values into an untagged table. Tag propagation (check your platform), scanning, and fewer privileged roles.
  • Free text. An SSN pasted into a memo field. Scanners and redaction at ingest.
  • Low-entropy tokens. A deterministic keyed hash of a 9-digit SSN can be brute-forced in seconds if the key leaks (10⁹ candidates). Use a vault or a strong keyed construction, and treat the key as restricted-zone material.
  • Engines that bypass the warehouse by reading the underlying storage. See Scenario 2.
  • Dead-letter tables and logs capture the offending row, SSN included. They inherit the zone of the data they contain.

Trade-offs

  • Tokenize at ingest vs mask at query: tokenizing is stronger but adds an ingest dependency on the vault; masking is quick but relies on every engine enforcing it. Default: tokenize regulated identifiers, mask lower-risk PII.
  • Deterministic tokens enable joins — and cross-dataset linkage. Per-domain token keys limit linkage at the cost of cross-domain joins.
  • Access-request friction: if legitimate access takes three weeks, people find a copy. Keep approved time-to-access in hours.

8. Scenario: “Your Spark Cluster Can Read Production PII. How Do You Stop Developers Pulling It Locally?”

This is the exfiltration version of the previous prompt, and it is harder because the principal is trusted: developers legitimately run code on the cluster. The question is really "how do you let people compute on data without letting them carry it away?"

Requirements

  • Who needs to run code against production data, and why? Debugging a production job differs from exploration — and most development doesn't need production PII; the ask exists because staging data is bad.
  • What is "locally"? Download, personal bucket, paste site, screenshot. You can close the first three technically. The fourth you can only make slow and detectable.

Controls by layer

LayerControl
IdentityThe cluster's workload identity (not the developer's) reads data, and it is scoped to the job's inputs. Developers submit code; they do not hold storage credentials. Interactive clusters on PII run with per-user identity passthrough or catalog-enforced permissions so each human is individually authorized and audited — never a shared "notebook" role with s3:*.
DataDefault the development path to non-PII: tokenized curated data, masked views, or a sampled-and-scrubbed copy in a lower environment. Production PII access is an exception workflow. Enforce fine-grained policy in the catalog (Unity Catalog, Lake Formation, Ranger, or equivalent) so Spark respects column masks and row filters — raw path access to restricted storage is denied.
NetworkCluster in private subnets; no general internet egress; storage reached via private endpoints whose policies allow only org-owned buckets; package installs from an internal mirror. The laptop has no network path to the restricted storage at all.
PlatformDisable or cap notebook result downloads, display() export and file download from workspace storage for restricted workspaces; block writing to user-controlled locations; restrict cluster creation to approved policies (no attaching arbitrary init scripts or instance profiles).
EndpointAccess to the restricted workspace only from managed devices (conditional access), optionally via a virtual desktop so data renders but does not sync.
Audit & detectionStorage data-event logs, catalog audit logs, query history; alert on volume anomalies (a user reading 100× their baseline), reads of restricted tables from interactive clusters, new external locations, and egress attempts blocked by the proxy.

Failure modes

  • Instance-profile inheritance. Every notebook on a cluster inherits the cluster's cloud role. If the cluster role can read restricted storage, so can every user's arbitrary Python — including boto3 calls that bypass the catalog entirely. Catalog enforcement only works if the underlying role cannot reach the data directly.
  • The "temporary" debug bucket with a lax policy. Org guardrails and endpoint policies make it impossible, not discouraged.
  • Logs. df.show(1000) writes PII to driver logs with a different access model. Treat them as PII.
  • Slow drip. Row caps stop bulk export, not 1,000 rows a day. Per-user volume baselines detect it.

Trade-offs

Every control costs velocity: a package mirror to maintain, harder shared clusters, broken download workflows. The senior move is to make the safe path the fast path — a refreshed, scrubbed dataset in a lower environment removes most reasons to want production PII. Security that fights every workflow gets bypassed.

Drill · Security design

An audit finds that a service-account JSON key for the production ETL identity was committed to a public GitHub repo 11 days ago. The identity can read all curated tables. What do you do in the first hour, and what do you change so this cannot recur?

STOP. Answer before revealing.

Reveal the response
  1. Observe The key has been compromised since the push — public repos are scraped for credentials within minutes. Deleting the commit changes nothing.
  2. Contain Disable the key now and accept that jobs using it fail. Don't delay revocation to prepare a replacement.
  3. Measure Audit logs for that key id over 11 days: which calls, from which IPs, reading what. Anything outside known runners and schedules is an incident with notification obligations — bring in security and legal.
  4. Isolate What else could the identity do — write, grant, create keys? Look for new principals, keys, shares or buckets created in the window.
  5. Fix Replace the key with workload identity federation, scoped to the job's actual inputs rather than "all curated tables."
  6. Prevent Org policy forbidding service-account key creation; secret scanning with push protection; alert on any key creation; a report of remaining long-lived credentials trending to zero.

9. Infrastructure as Code: Terraform Without Fear

"How do you safely change a production data platform?" starts with: nobody changes it by clicking. Buckets, roles, key policies, warehouses, catalogs, grants and network rules are declared in code, reviewed, and applied by a pipeline. The console is for reading.

The concepts that come up

ConceptThe production concern
State (resource ↔ real id mapping)Often contains secrets. Remote, encrypted, access-restricted — never in git.
State lockingConcurrent applies can corrupt state. Remote backends lock; use it.
Plan / applyReview the plan, not just the code, and apply the saved plan so what runs is what was approved.
DriftScheduled plans alert on non-empty diffs. Drift in IAM or network rules is a security event.
ModulesHow the secure configuration becomes the default. Pin versions; a module upgrade is a change.
Blast radiusSplit state by environment and domain. One state for "all of prod" means one bad plan touches everything.

The line in a plan that should stop you cold is -/+ destroy and then create replacement on anything stateful: a bucket, a database, a KMS key, a catalog. Renaming a resource or changing an immutable attribute can trigger replacement. Protect stateful resources with lifecycle guards (prevent_destroy), deletion protection at the provider level, and a CI rule that fails any plan containing a destroy on a tagged-stateful resource without an explicit override.

Engine: Terraform (AWS provider)Dialect/Language: HCLExecutable: Illustrative — resource and argument names follow the AWS provider at time of writing; adapt and pin versions
terraform {
  backend "s3" {
    bucket       = "acme-tfstate-prod"
    key          = "data-platform/curated/terraform.tfstate"
    region       = "us-east-1"
    encrypt      = true
    use_lockfile = true   # state locking; older setups used a DynamoDB table
  }
}

resource "aws_kms_key" "curated" {
  description         = "CMK for curated zone"
  enable_key_rotation = true
  # key policy (omitted): admins can manage, only pipeline roles can decrypt
}

resource "aws_s3_bucket" "curated" {
  bucket = "acme-curated-prod"
  lifecycle { prevent_destroy = true }
}

resource "aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block" "curated" {
  bucket                  = aws_s3_bucket.curated.id
  block_public_acls       = true
  block_public_policy     = true
  ignore_public_acls      = true
  restrict_public_buckets = true
}

resource "aws_s3_bucket_server_side_encryption_configuration" "curated" {
  bucket = aws_s3_bucket.curated.id
  rule {
    apply_server_side_encryption_by_default {
      sse_algorithm     = "aws:kms"
      kms_master_key_id = aws_kms_key.curated.arn
    }
    bucket_key_enabled = true   # fewer KMS calls, lower cost
  }
}

# CI deploy role assumable only by one repo's main branch via OIDC.
data "aws_iam_policy_document" "ci_trust" {
  statement {
    actions = ["sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity"]
    principals {
      type        = "Federated"
      identifiers = [var.github_oidc_provider_arn]
    }
    condition {
      test     = "StringEquals"
      variable = "token.actions.githubusercontent.com:aud"
      values   = ["sts.amazonaws.com"]
    }
    condition {
      test     = "StringEquals"
      variable = "token.actions.githubusercontent.com:sub"
      values   = ["repo:acme/data-pipelines:environment:prod"]
    }
  }
}

resource "aws_iam_role" "ci_deploy_prod" {
  name                 = "ci-deploy-data-pipelines-prod"
  assume_role_policy   = data.aws_iam_policy_document.ci_trust.json
  max_session_duration = 3600
}

What to point at: remote, encrypted, locked state; a bucket a careless plan cannot destroy; public access blocked (also enforce at org level); a CI role trusting one repo in one environment — not repo:acme/*.

Interviewer pushes back

You: “All our infrastructure is in Terraform, so changes are safe.”

Interviewer: “Someone renames the bucket resource in a refactor PR. The code review looks fine. What happens?”

Strong answer: “Terraform sees one resource removed and one added: destroy-and-create on the lake bucket. Code review misses it because the diff is a rename; the plan shows it. Here the provider refuses to delete a non-empty bucket unless force_destroy is set — luck, not design, and a database or catalog may not be so forgiving. So: the plan is posted on the PR, a policy check fails any destroy on a resource tagged stateful, stateful resources carry prevent_destroy and deletion protection, and refactors use a moved block so state is updated instead of the resource replaced. IaC makes changes reviewable; it makes them safe only when the plan is what gets gated.”

Weak answer: “We'd restore from backup.” Name the backup, its age, and how long restoring a lake takes before offering it as the plan.

10. Kubernetes for Data: When and When Not

Kubernetes appears as the Spark operator (or native spark-submit to Kubernetes), the Flink Kubernetes operator, and the host for platform services (Airflow, Trino, schema registry).

When it earns its place: you already run a staffed Kubernetes platform and want one scheduling, identity and observability model; long-running streaming jobs benefit from operator-managed lifecycle (savepoint on upgrade, restore on failure, specs in git); many small Spark jobs where pod start beats cluster spin-up and bin-packing saves money.

When not: you have no platform team — Kubernetes moves node pools, autoscaling, upgrades, network plugins and shuffle-on-ephemeral-disk pain from the provider to you; or your workload is mostly SQL in a managed warehouse, where Kubernetes to run a scheduler that submits SQL is overhead with no return.

Security if you do run it: one namespace and service account per workload class; workload identity bound to the service account, not a node role every pod inherits; default-deny network policies; no privileged containers or host mounts. A Spark driver that can read restricted storage because the node can is Scenario 2's failure mode in a different uniform.

11. Environments, Promotion & Immutable Artifacts

Dev, staging, prod — and what "staging" must actually mean

EnvironmentDataWho deploysPurpose
DevSynthetic or scrubbed samples; per-developer schemas/branches.Developers, freely.Iteration.
StagingProduction-shaped: realistic volume and skew, tokenized/scrubbed, refreshed regularly.CI only.Prove the artifact that will go to prod works at production shape.
ProdReal.CI only, with approval gates; humans read-only by default.Serve.

Staging with 1% of production volume and no skew passes everything, then prod OOMs on the customer with 40% of events. Staging that doesn't reproduce production shape is a syntax checker with a budget. Zero-copy clones, table branches (Iceberg, Nessie, lakeFS) and scrubbed snapshots make it affordable. Security catch: a clone of prod is prod data and stays in prod's zone unless tokenized.

Build once, promote the same artifact

  • Immutable, versioned artifacts. A wheel, a JAR, a container image with a digest, a compiled dbt manifest — built once from a commit and identified by version and hash. Staging and prod run the byte-identical artifact. Rebuilding for prod means you tested something else. (Packaging mechanics are in Part 06 §11 and Part 06 §18.)
  • Environment differences are config, not code. Bucket names, warehouse sizes, catalog names come from per-environment config resolved at deploy time. No if env == "prod" branches that staging never exercises.
  • Lockfiles for everything. Python dependencies pinned with hashes, container base images pinned by digest, Terraform providers and modules pinned. "It worked yesterday" plus an unpinned transitive dependency is a common root cause for a Monday-morning failure that no code change explains.
  • Record provenance in every run. Each pipeline run logs artifact version, commit SHA, config hash and input snapshot ids to the run audit table (Part 10). When numbers change, you can answer "what changed" in one query.

Secrets and permissions in CI

CI authenticates via OIDC, scoped per environment; the prod role is assumable only from the protected branch and a deployment environment with required reviewers. Fork PRs never receive credentials. Pin third-party actions to a commit SHA — a compromised action runs with your deploy role.

12. CI/CD for Data Pipelines

Part 08 gives the short checklist for warehouse CI/CD and Part 12 covers test types. This section is about the part software CI/CD does not teach you: data pipelines have two inputs — code and data — and both change. A pipeline breaks with no code change (upstream drift, new skew), and a "correct" code change can move every number on a dashboard. CI has to test both.

“How would you design CI/CD for data pipelines?”
30 sec

Same skeleton as application CI/CD — lint, unit tests, build an immutable artifact, promote it through environments — plus two data-specific stages: a data diff that runs the new version against production-shaped data and compares outputs to the current version, and write-audit-publish in production so a bad run never becomes visible to consumers. Code gets reviewed; data gets gated.

2 min

On PR: lint, type-check, unit tests on small fixtures, contract tests against declared consumer schemas, and a compile/dry-run against the real catalog so references and permissions resolve. Then a data diff: build the changed models against a clone or branch of production and report row-count, key-level and column-level differences versus prod, posted on the PR — the reviewer approves the data change, not just the code. On merge: build the artifact once, run it in staging on production-shaped data, promote the same artifact to prod behind an approval. In prod every run writes, audits, then atomically publishes. Rollback is a snapshot restore plus the previous artifact.

Deep dive

Slim CI: build only changed models and their descendants (dbt state selection or orchestrator lineage) — full rebuilds of a 2,000-model project per PR are slow and expensive. Diffs must be key-aware: row counts can match while every value moved. Exact match for finance facts, tolerance bands for approximate metrics. Infrastructure runs a separate plan/apply pipeline with policy-as-code checks. Backfills are deployments: versioned, reviewed, dry-run on one partition, published through the same WAP gate.

Where to stop: once you've said "code gets reviewed, data gets gated" and shown the data diff plus WAP, stop unless asked about slim CI or backfills.

Engine: GitHub ActionsDialect/Language: YAMLExecutable: Illustrative — action versions, role ARNs and the make targets are placeholders; pin actions to commit SHAs in real use
name: data-pipelines
on:
  pull_request:
  push:
    branches: [main]

permissions:
  contents: read          # least privilege by default

jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: astral-sh/setup-uv@v5
      - run: uv sync --frozen            # fail if lockfile is stale
      - run: make lint typecheck unit-test contract-test

  data-diff:                             # PR only: diff vs prod-shaped clone
    if: github.event_name == 'pull_request'
    needs: test
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment: ci-dev                  # dev role, read-only on prod clone
    permissions: { contents: read, id-token: write, pull-requests: write }
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials@v4
        with:
          role-to-assume: ${{ vars.CI_DEV_ROLE_ARN }}
          aws-region: us-east-1
      - run: make build-changed TARGET=pr_${{ github.event.number }}
      - run: make data-diff BASE=prod TARGET=pr_${{ github.event.number }}
      - run: make post-diff-comment

  release:                               # main only: build once, promote
    if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'
    needs: test
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    outputs:
      version: ${{ steps.v.outputs.version }}
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - id: v
        run: echo "version=$(git rev-parse --short HEAD)" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
      - run: make build-artifact VERSION=${{ steps.v.outputs.version }}
      - run: make publish-artifact VERSION=${{ steps.v.outputs.version }}

  deploy-prod:
    needs: release
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment: prod                    # required reviewers + branch rule
    permissions: { contents: read, id-token: write }
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials@v4
        with:
          role-to-assume: ${{ vars.CI_PROD_DEPLOY_ROLE_ARN }}
          aws-region: us-east-1
      - run: make deploy ENV=prod VERSION=${{ needs.release.outputs.version }}

What the YAML encodes: no stored cloud keys (OIDC via id-token: write, granted per job), a stale lockfile fails the build, the data diff runs only with a dev-scoped role, the artifact is built once and the prod job deploys that version, and prod requires a protected environment with reviewers.

13. Releasing Data Safely: Rollback, WAP, Blue/Green, Shadow

The sentence that separates data platform engineers from application engineers: you can roll back code; you cannot un-publish a table. Once visible, a bad table is cached in dashboards, pushed to the CRM, trained on, and pasted into a board deck. Redeploying yesterday's code fixes tomorrow's run, not today's damage. Data release strategy is therefore about not publishing bad data, and restoring state fast when you do.

Rollback vs roll-forward for data

SituationPreferHow
Bad run published wrong values; inputs still availableRoll back the table, then roll forwardRestore the table to the last good snapshot (time travel / restore — see Part 07 rollback), redeploy the previous artifact, re-run affected partitions once fixed.
Bad code deployed, table appended to over several runs, downstream consumers have read itRoll forwardFix code, recompute affected partitions idempotently (overwrite by partition), notify consumers with the affected range. Restoring a snapshot would also discard good concurrent writes.
Bad data went to external systems (CRM, partner feed, emails)Roll forward with compensationYou cannot restore someone else's system. Send corrections, and add a WAP gate before the external sync next time.

Time travel is your undo button only while snapshots exist. Snapshot expiration and retention settings (Part 07 §8) are therefore a recovery-point decision, not just a storage-cost decision. If you expire snapshots after 24 hours and a bad deploy is noticed after a weekend, the undo button is gone.

Write-audit-publish

Implementations of the same idea: in Iceberg, write to a branch or stage an uncommitted snapshot, validate, then fast-forward main (check your engine's syntax); in Delta or generically, write a staging table and atomically replace or merge into the published one; in a warehouse, build a new table and swap (ALTER TABLE … SWAP WITH in Snowflake) or repoint a view.

The trade-off to state out loud: WAP converts correctness incidents into freshness incidents. When the audit fails, the dashboard is stale instead of wrong. That is almost always the right trade — but only if consumers can see freshness (a "last updated" indicator, a freshness SLO) so stale doesn't silently become "wrong but looks current."

Blue/green tables and view swaps

For large rebuilds (re-keyed dimension, three-year backfill), build "green" beside "blue" while consumers read a stable view name. Cut-over is one view redefinition or table swap; rollback is pointing it back. Costs: double storage during the overlap, and incremental writes landing in blue during the build must be replayed into green. Keep blue for a defined window, then drop it deliberately.

Canary and shadow deployment for pipelines

Services canary by routing a percentage of traffic. Pipelines usually can't split one table's rows between two code versions, so the pipeline equivalent is the shadow run: the new version runs on the same inputs, on the same schedule, writing to a shadow table. A daily diff job compares shadow to prod — key-level for facts, distribution-level for metrics — and the cut-over happens after N clean days, or after every difference is explained and signed off. For streaming, run the new job as a separate consumer group writing to a shadow sink.

Interviewer pushes back

You: “If a deploy goes bad, we roll back to the previous version in CI.”

Interviewer: “The bad version ran at 2 a.m. and overwrote yesterday's revenue partition. Finance exported it at 8. Your rollback just finished. What's the state of the world?”

Strong answer: “The code is back; the data is still wrong and some of it has left the building. Restore the partition to the pre-2 a.m. snapshot or recompute it with the previous version, verify against source, and find every consumer of the bad snapshot from lineage and query history. Publish a correction with the affected range and the window in which exports were wrong. Then fix the process: WAP with a reconciliation check against billing, and snapshot retention longer than our detection time.”

Weak answer: Treating a code rollback as the end of the incident. It is the first ten percent.

14. Schema Migrations & Release Strategies

Expand / contract

A breaking schema change deployed in one step breaks every consumer that has not changed yet — and in data platforms you rarely control all of them. Expand/contract (also called parallel change) splits it into safe steps:

  1. Expand: add the new column/table alongside the old. Writers populate both. Nothing breaks, because nothing was removed.
  2. Backfill: populate the new column for history, idempotently, through the normal WAP path.
  3. Migrate readers: consumers move to the new column on their own schedule. Track who still reads the old one — query history and column-level lineage (Part 10) answer this.
  4. Contract: once usage of the old column reaches zero (measured, not assumed), stop writing it, then drop it — after a deprecation window announced in advance.

Renaming amount to amount_usd takes four deployments instead of one — the price of not paging twenty downstream teams. CI should fail a PR that removes or retypes a contracted column without an expand phase first (data contracts: Part 15).

Pipeline release strategies at a glance

StrategyUse whenCost
Direct deploy + WAP gateRoutine logic changes with a strong audit.Cheap; relies on audit coverage.
Shadow run then cut-overRewrites, engine migrations, metric definition changes.Double compute for the shadow window.
Blue/green table + view swapFull rebuilds, re-keying, large backfills.Double storage during overlap; catch-up replay.
Partition/tenant canaryPartitioned outputs where one slice can go first.Two code versions live at once; mixed-version table for a while.
Expand/contractAny breaking schema change with consumers you don't control.Multiple deploys; a deprecation window.

Streaming adds state compatibility: upgrading a stateful Flink or Structured Streaming job restores from a savepoint/checkpoint, and changed operator ids, key types or state schemas can make it unreadable. Test a restore from a production savepoint in staging first; keep the old savepoint as the rollback point.

15. Failure-First: The Production Platform

Failure-first: what can fail?
FailureDetectRecoverPrevent recurrence
Credentials expire or are revoked (cert, rotated password, changed trust policy)Auth errors spike across jobs sharing an identity; synthetic auth check fails.Issue a new credential through the normal path; re-run failed tasks (idempotent writes make this safe).Eliminate static credentials; dual-validity rotation; expiry alarms at 30/7/1 days with an owner; one identity per workload.
Region failureProvider health events; cross-region canary jobs fail; control-plane API errors.Fail over orchestrator and compute to the secondary region on replicated storage; accept the declared RPO.RPO/RTO per dataset; replicate storage and catalog metadata; IaC that can stand up the region; scheduled failover tests — an untested DR plan is a hypothesis.
Object storage or warehouse degraded5xx/throttling rates, latency percentiles, retries climbing.Jittered backoff; pause non-critical workloads; WAP keeps prod at last good.Retry budgets, circuit breakers, prioritised queues; SLOs that separate "late" from "wrong."
Bad deployment publishes wrong dataAudit gate fails (best case); reconciliation alert; consumer complaint (worst case).Restore last good snapshot or swap view back; redeploy previous artifact; recompute; notify with affected range.WAP on every published table; data diff in CI; shadow runs; snapshot retention ≥ detection time.
Incompatible schema change (upstream or ours)Contract check fails in CI; registry rejects; cast errors or null-rate jump in prod.Pin to last compatible schema or add a compatibility view; dead-letter bad records.Expand/contract; enforced registry compatibility; data contracts; consumers in lineage.
Access policy regression (mask dropped, grant widened)Policy diff in CI; nightly "who can read PII" report changes; unexpected-role alert.Revert; review access logs for the exposure window; incident process.Grants and policies in code only; tests that query as a restricted role and assert masking.
Drill · Release engineering

Tuesday 09:40. A deploy at 01:00 changed the currency-conversion join in fct_revenue. The 02:00 run published. The executive dashboard shows EMEA revenue up 38% day over day. Reverse-ETL pushed account-level revenue into the CRM at 06:00. Recover.

STOP. Answer before revealing.

Reveal the recovery
  1. Observe A 38% jump in one region the morning after a currency-logic deploy is a deploy problem until proven otherwise. Declare an incident, and put a "known issue since 02:00" banner on the dashboard before debugging — stopping people acting on the number beats fixing it.
  2. Hypothesize Join fan-out (duplicate FX rates for a date) or inverted rate direction. Both fit +38%.
  3. Measure Key-level diff of today's snapshot against the previous one: rows per region (fan-out adds rows), amount by currency, sampled changed rows. Check the FX table for duplicate keys.
  4. Isolate Lineage and query history give the blast radius: downstream tables, the CRM sync, exports, and the time window. Pause downstream builds and syncs.
  5. Fix Restore fct_revenue to the pre-deploy snapshot so the dashboard is right in minutes; redeploy the previous artifact; rebuild downstream; re-run the reverse-ETL sync to overwrite the CRM and tell its owners which records were wrong and for how long. Then fix the join, prove it with a data diff, and release it normally.
  6. Prevent WAP gate on fct_revenue with per-region reconciliation against billing and a day-over-day threshold; uniqueness test on the FX key; data diff required for finance facts; reverse-ETL reads only published snapshots; blameless postmortem.
L5 Interview CardProduction Data Platform — Cloud, Security & Release Engineering
Must know
  • Workload identity federation: short-lived credentials minted per run; the security is in the trust-policy conditions.
  • RBAC for coarse entitlements, ABAC (tags) for sensitive columns and rows; untagged fails closed.
  • Envelope encryption: the KMS decrypt call is an independent, audited authorization check; crypto-shredding via per-tenant/subject keys.
  • Data perimeter = trusted identity + trusted resource + expected network, all three.
  • Column/row policies are enforced per engine; any engine that can read the raw storage bypasses them.
  • Terraform state, locking, saved-plan apply, drift, blast radius; destroy-on-rename.
  • You can roll back code but not un-publish data: WAP, snapshot restore, blue/green view swap, shadow runs.
  • Expand/contract for schema changes you don't control consumers of.
Must be able to explain
  1. Why "encrypted at rest" is not an access control, and what is.
  2. How a GitHub Actions job deploys to prod without any stored cloud secret.
  3. Why WAP turns correctness incidents into freshness incidents, and why that trade is usually right.
Must be able to draw

The reference platform with its boundaries and the release path through it:

SSO/OIDC ─▶ roles ─▶ [ private network:
  Kafka ─▶ Spark ─▶ staging tbl ─▶ AUDIT ─▶ publish ]
  restricted zone (clear PII, own key) ─tokenize─▶ curated
  audit logs ─▶ separate account, append-only
Must be able to code
  • A tag-bound masking policy plus a mapping-table row access policy in one warehouse dialect.
  • A Terraform bucket with CMK encryption, public-access block, prevent_destroy, and an OIDC-trusted CI role.
  • A CI workflow: lint/test, data diff on PR, build once, promote the same artifact with an approval gate.
Must be able to debug
  • A deploy published wrong revenue and reverse-ETL pushed it to the CRM: banner, restore snapshot, redeploy, re-sync, notify, add WAP.
  • A service-account key leaked to a public repo: revoke first, scope the exposure from audit logs, replace with federation, block key creation org-wide.
Numbers that matter
  • Federated credentials live minutes to about an hour; a leaked static key lives until someone notices (days to years).
  • A 9-digit identifier has ~10⁹ values: a keyed hash is brute-forceable in seconds once the key leaks.
  • Snapshot retention must exceed time-to-detect; if detection takes a weekend, 24 h retention means no undo.
  • Blue/green costs ~2× storage for the overlap window; shadow runs cost ~2× compute for the shadow window.
  • Rename a column with expand/contract: ~4 deploys plus a deprecation window, instead of 1 deploy and N broken consumers.
Classic traps
  • “AES-256 at rest” offered as the answer to “who can see SSNs?”
  • Catalog policies on the warehouse while a Spark cluster role can read the same files directly.
  • “We'll roll back” — meaning the code, while the bad table has already been exported.
30-second answer

How do you safely change and secure a production data platform? Separate the control plane from the data plane and design both. Identities are federated and short-lived, scoped per workload; sensitive data is tokenized or policy-protected by tag, behind its own key and network boundary, with audit logs outside the blast radius. Every change — infrastructure, code, grants — goes through code review, a plan or data diff, and an immutable artifact promoted through environments, and every published table passes a write-audit-publish gate so a bad run costs freshness, not correctness.

2-minute answer

Identity first: humans via SSO groups, workloads via federated identities with no static keys, least privilege scoped to resources, break-glass for elevation. Data controls: tokenize regulated identifiers at ingest into a restricted zone with its own customer-managed key; tag-bound masking and row policies in every engine that can read the data, or deny that engine the storage. Network: private endpoints restricted to org-owned resources, no general egress, public access blocked org-wide, export limits. Audit reads, decrypts and grants to an append-only store in a security account. Change: Terraform with locked state, reviewed plans and guards on stateful resources; CI that tests code and diffs data against a production-shaped clone; one immutable artifact promoted through environments; WAP in prod; snapshot restore or view swap to roll back; shadow runs for rewrites; expand/contract for schema. Then name the failure modes — copies, free text, engines that bypass policy, expired snapshots — before the interviewer does.

Deep-dive follow-up

“Your masking policy lives in Snowflake, but the same Iceberg tables are read by Spark and Trino. How do you guarantee one policy is enforced everywhere, and how do you prove it to an auditor?”

Staff+ follow-up

“You're moving 50 teams onto this platform. Which controls do you centralise as non-negotiable guardrails, which do you give teams as paved-road defaults, and how do you measure whether the platform is becoming more or less secure each quarter?”
