Part 15

CDC, Data Contracts & Transformation Engineering

Quick refresh15 minInterview study55 minDeep practice90 min
Last technically reviewed September 2026
Covers log-based CDC, bootstrap, tombstones, ordering, LSN-versioned apply, transactions, replication slots, registry compatibility, contract enforcement, expand/contract, dbt at L5
Versions referenced PostgreSQL 16/17, Debezium 3.x, Kafka 4.x (KRaft), Confluent Schema Registry, Iceberg 1.x on Spark 3.5/4.x, dbt Core 1.8–1.12; dbt 2.0 (September 2026, Rust engine — check current docs for parity)
Primary references Debezium docs · PostgreSQL logical replication · Kafka log compaction · Schema Registry compatibility · Iceberg Spark writes · dbt docs
Known implementation differences CDC mechanics (slots, binlog, GTIDs, snapshot locking) and dbt adapter behavior (which incremental strategies and constraints are supported) differ per database and platform; treat every config name here as version-specific.

The interviewer is testing whether you know what happens between the boxes. Anyone can draw Postgres → Debezium → Kafka → lake. The L5 signal is knowing that the connector can fill the primary's disk, that a harmless enum value can break fourteen consumers, and that dbt fixes one class of problem while creating others. Basics live elsewhere: Part 02 §10 covers the three CDC patterns and a first-pass upsert, Part 01 §13 shows a contract file and the change-type table, Part 07 §9 covers Iceberg column-id evolution, and Part 12 §5 covers test layers. This chapter goes one level down on each.

1. CDC end to end: what each hop owns

Every hop has its own notion of position, and your correctness story is only as good as the weakest one.

HopOwnsAcknowledges byClassic failure
WAL / binlogDurable, ordered record of committed changesPostgres: slot's confirmed_flush_lsn. MySQL: binlog file+position or GTID setWAL retained forever by an abandoned slot; binlog purged before the connector reads it
ConnectorDecoding, envelope, snapshot, schema historyCommits source offsets to Kafka Connect after producingCrash between produce and offset commit → replay → duplicates
KafkaPer-partition order, retention, compactionConsumer-group offsetsPartition count changed → one key in two partitions
Stream processorParse, dedupe, order within batch, applyCheckpoint that pairs Kafka offsets with sink commitSink committed, checkpoint not → batch reapplied
Lake tableQueryable current state and/or historyTable commit (snapshot)Small files and delete-file buildup from frequent MERGE

The one sentence that makes this design safe: everything downstream of the WAL is at-least-once, so the final apply must be idempotent and version-aware. Kafka Connect gained exactly-once source support in KIP-618 (Kafka 3.3), but with a stream processor, a lake commit and backfill replays in the path, you design for duplicates anyway. Part 03 §7 proves why.

2026 Interview Note

Timeless: a database's transaction log is the only source that sees every committed change in commit order; everything else is a sample of state. Per-key ordering comes from partitioning by key; idempotency comes from versioned upserts. Version-specific: Debezium's config names, snapshot modes, incremental-snapshot signalling and envelope fields; Postgres failover-slot support (added in 17); Kafka Connect exactly-once source support. Say the concept first, then the product detail with a hedge.

2. Log-based vs polling vs timestamp CDC: what each one misses

Part 02 §10 lists the patterns. The interview is about their blind spots — the source of the wrong finance number six weeks later.

ApproachMechanismMissesUse when
Full snapshotRe-read the tableEvery intermediate state between reads; expensive past tens of GBSmall reference tables; reconciliation baseline
Polling diffRead all PKs + hash, diff against last copyIntermediate states; cost scales with table size, not change volumeNo log access and no trustworthy timestamp; deletes matter
Timestamp (updated_at)Query WHERE updated_at > hwmHard deletes; intermediate states; writes that forget to bump the column; long transactions; clock skew; equal-timestamp boundary rowsAppend-mostly tables; soft deletes enforced; minutes-to-hours latency fine
Log-basedDecode WAL / binlogOnly what bypasses the log: unlogged tables; MySQL binlog not in ROW format; TRUNCATE handling varies by connectorDeletes matter, history matters, low latency, high change rate

The long-transaction trap, step by step

The standard mitigation is a lookback window (updated_at > hwm − margin, then dedupe). It shrinks the hole to "transactions longer than the margin"; it doesn't close it. Clock skew across app hosts, coarse timestamps at the boundary, and replica lag are the same bug in different clothes.

Interviewer pushes back

You: “I'd use Debezium for log-based CDC.”

Interviewer: “That's a lot of infrastructure. Why not just poll updated_at every five minutes?”

Strong answer: “It depends on three answers. Do we need hard deletes? Do we need intermediate states — for example every status transition for SLA metrics — or just current state? Is updated_at set by the database or by application code? If deletes are soft, only current state matters and a trigger maintains the timestamp, polling with a lookback and a nightly reconciliation is cheaper and fine. Otherwise polling is silently wrong: zombie rows, pending→paid→refunded collapsing to 'refunded', long transactions committing behind the watermark. Log-based CDC buys correctness at the cost of a slot, a Kafka cluster and on-call.”

Weak answer: “Polling doesn't scale.” It often scales fine. The problem is correctness, not throughput — and a weak answer names the wrong problem.

3. Snapshots and bootstrap: joining the stream without a gap

The log holds recent changes; the table holds 2 billion rows written years ago. You need a consistent snapshot plus every later change, with no gap.

Initial snapshot + streaming handoff

The classic approach (Debezium's initial mode, per its docs): create the slot, which pins a starting LSN; read the tables in a transaction consistent with that LSN, emitting rows as op = 'r'; then stream from the pinned LSN. Snapshot and stream meet at one LSN, so nothing falls between; seam duplicates are harmless if the apply is version-aware (§5). The costs to name:

  • Duration. 2 B rows at a hypothetical 50k rows/s ≈ 11 hours of WAL pinned on the primary (§7).
  • Restartability. A snapshot that dies at hour 9 may restart from zero, depending on connector and version.
  • Vacuum. A multi-hour snapshot transaction holds back vacuum and bloats the busiest tables.

Incremental snapshots: watermarks in the log itself

Debezium's incremental snapshot (based on the watermark algorithm from Netflix's DBLog paper) removes the giant transaction. Behavior as documented at time of writing (check current docs for your connector): you send a signal — typically by inserting a row into a signalling table, or via a Kafka signal topic — and the connector snapshots the table in primary-key-ordered chunks while streaming continues.

It buys resumable snapshots, on-demand re-snapshot of one table, and no long transaction. It costs a writable signalling table (or signal topic), and r events interleaved with live events — a consumer that assumes "all snapshot rows come first" will break.

Lake-side alternative: bulk-export the big table at a recorded LSN, start the connector without its own snapshot, apply only events with LSN > export LSN. Faster and gentler on the source, but you own the proof that the export was consistent at that LSN.

4. Deletes, tombstones and log compaction

A missed delete produces no error — just a row that should not exist.

What a delete looks like on the wire

  1. Source. In Postgres a delete's before image holds only the replica identity — by default the PK. Need the full old row? REPLICA IDENTITY FULL, at the cost of larger WAL.
  2. Connector. Debezium emits a d event and, by default, a tombstone: same key, null value (tombstones.on.delete, check your version).
  3. Kafka. On a compacted topic, the tombstone tells the log cleaner it may eventually drop every record for that key. The tombstone itself survives for delete.retention.ms and is then removed too.

Compaction semantics the interviewer will probe

  • Compaction guarantees at least the latest value per key survives — not that only the latest survives. The active segment is never compacted, so a consumer can still see older values.
  • The zombie row: a consumer that was offline longer than delete.retention.ms resumes after the tombstone has been cleaned. It never sees the delete; its copy lives forever. A compacted topic bootstraps a new consumer correctly and a too-far-behind one incorrectly. Alert on consumer lag in time, well inside that window.
  • Null-value tombstones crash naive deserializers. Filter them at the edge; act on the d event.

Deletes in the lake: soft first, hard later

A physical delete in the lake also deletes the row's version (last LSN), so a replayed older event finds no match and gets inserted — resurrection. Soft-delete (is_deleted, _src_lsn kept), filter in a view, and purge only after a horizon longer than your maximum replay window. GDPR erasure is the exception: it must purge physically and also expire the table snapshots and old data files that still contain the row (see Part 10).

5. Ordering, idempotency and late events

Per-key ordering and what breaks it

Debezium keys events by primary key; the default partitioner hashes the key, so one row's changes land in one partition, in order. Per-key order, not global order — all a current-state table needs. What breaks it:

CauseWhat happensGuard
Adding partitions to the topicKey→partition mapping changes; old events for a key in partition 3, new ones in partition 7; consumers read them in any interleavingDon't repartition a CDC topic live; create a new topic and re-snapshot, or rely on version-aware apply
Primary-key updateDebezium (per its docs) emits a delete for the old key and a create for the new key — two keys, two partitions, no ordering between themTreat as delete+insert; don't correlate by PK across the change
Tables without a primary keyNo key (or a message key you chose badly) → no per-row orderingConfigure a message key column, or refuse the table
Producer retries without idempotenceWith multiple in-flight requests, a retried batch can land after a later oneIdempotent producer on the Connect workers (the default in modern Kafka clients — verify)
Parallel apply in the processorTwo tasks apply events for the same key concurrentlyPartition processing by the same key; dedupe to one event per key per batch

Idempotency: the source position is the version

The apply rule that survives replays: upsert by primary key, carry the source position as a version, and reject anything not newer than what you have. For Postgres that's the change's LSN, exposed in Debezium's source block (check your version's fields); for MySQL, binlog position or GTID plus the event's index in the transaction. LSN is safe as a per-key version because the log is totally ordered and writers to the same row are serialized by row locks, so a later committed change to a key always has a higher LSN.

Why not ts_ms, which Part 02's upsert uses as its guard? Two changes to a row in the same millisecond compare equal and > drops the second; and it's a wall-clock time, not a sequence. Fine for latency metrics, wrong as a version.

Interviewer pushes back

You: “The MERGE is idempotent because it upserts by primary key.”

Interviewer: “The connector crashed and replayed the last ten minutes. One of those replayed events is an update from before a delete you've already applied. What does your table look like?”

Strong answer: “Upsert-by-key is idempotent for one event, not for a replayed sequence: an old update replayed after a delete resurrects the row. So each row carries its source LSN, the MERGE applies only strictly newer LSNs, deletes are soft so the LSN survives, and each batch is deduped to the highest LSN per key. Replays then converge.”

Weak answer: “We use exactly-once, so there are no replays.” Backfills, connector restarts and manual re-snapshots are all replays. Design for them.

Late events in CDC

In a current-state table a late event is just an older version; the LSN guard discards it. Lateness matters for history tables — an older event must be slotted into the middle of the history, so rebuild affected keys' intervals from the ordered change log rather than patching — and for event-time aggregates on CDC, which need Part 03 §6's watermarks with commit time as event time.

6. Transaction boundaries: when one commit arrives as five messages

A checkout commits an orders row and three order_items rows in one transaction. CDC emits them to two independently partitioned topics; the processor may apply the order and one item, checkpoint, then the rest. "Order total = sum of items" at that checkpoint is a number that never existed in the source.

Options, in increasing cost:

  1. Tolerate it. The next micro-batch converges. Most analytics lives here; say so explicitly.
  2. Apply by commit. Debezium can emit transaction metadata (provide.transaction.metadata at time of writing): BEGIN/END markers with per-table event counts on a transaction topic, and a transaction block on each event. The consumer buffers by transaction id until all N events arrive. Costs checkpointed state and latency.
  3. Outbox. The service writes one denormalized event to an outbox table in the same transaction; CDC captures only that. One commit, one message. Needs app changes, and the event becomes a product the service owns (§9).
  4. Consistent cut. Commit lake snapshots only up to a commit LSN every table has fully applied. Multi-table consistency, paced by the slowest topic.

The L5 move is asking which consumers need it. Usually a small set (finance, inventory) justifies an outbox or buffered apply; the rest get eventual consistency with a lag SLO.

7. Postgres replication slots: the pipeline that fills the primary's disk

The most important operational fact about Postgres CDC. A logical slot tells Postgres "don't recycle WAL this consumer hasn't confirmed." If the connector stops — crashed, stuck on a poison message, or deleted without dropping the slot — WAL accumulates on the primary until the disk fills and writes stop. Your analytics pipeline has just taken down production.

Do the arithmetic first

Hypothetical: the primary generates 20 MB/s of WAL at peak (bulk jobs, index builds and vacuum all count, not only the tables you capture), 8 MB/s on average. Free space on the WAL volume: 1.5 TB.

  • Connector down for a weekend (60 h) at average rate: 8 MB/s × 216,000 s ≈ 1.7 TB. The disk fills before Monday.
  • At peak rate: 1.5 TB ÷ 20 MB/s ≈ 21 hours of headroom.
  • A 12-hour initial snapshot pins WAL from its start LSN: budget for it before you begin.

So the slot's lag is a primary database SLO, not a pipeline metric. It belongs on the DBA's dashboard and pages someone.

Monitor and cap

Engine: PostgreSQL 13+Dialect/Language: PostgreSQL SQLExecutable: Yes
-- Retained WAL per logical slot. Alert on bytes AND on "inactive for N minutes".
SELECT slot_name,
       active,
       wal_status,                          -- reserved / extended / unreserved / lost
       pg_size_pretty(pg_wal_lsn_diff(pg_current_wal_lsn(), restart_lsn))        AS retained_wal,
       pg_size_pretty(pg_wal_lsn_diff(pg_current_wal_lsn(), confirmed_flush_lsn)) AS unconfirmed
FROM pg_replication_slots
WHERE slot_type = 'logical';
  • max_slot_wal_keep_size (PostgreSQL 13+) caps retained WAL. Past it, the slot is invalidated (wal_status = 'lost') and the primary survives. You trade a disk-full outage for a pipeline that needs a re-snapshot. That is the right trade for almost every business; state it as a decision.
  • Quiet-database trap. If the captured database is idle while others on the cluster are busy, the slot may not advance while WAL piles up. Debezium's heartbeat settings (with an action query writing to a tiny table) exist for this.
  • Orphaned slots. A connector decommissioned without dropping its slot is a delayed-action outage. Slot lifecycle belongs in tooling.
  • Failover. Before PostgreSQL 17, logical slots existed only on the primary; after a failover the new primary had no slot, and the connector either re-snapshotted or silently skipped the changes in between. PostgreSQL 17 added synchronization of logical slots to physical standbys (slots created with the failover option, plus standby settings such as sync_replication_slots). Managed services expose this differently. Hedge it: “on 17+ with failover slots configured, the slot survives promotion — I'd verify that in a game day before trusting it.”
Drill · Postgres CDC

Saturday 03:10. The primary's WAL volume is at 91% and climbing 4% per hour. Write traffic is normal. The CDC pipeline's Kafka topics have had no new messages since Friday 18:40. The analytics on-call is asleep; you're the platform on-call.

STOP. Answer before revealing.

Reveal the diagnosis
  1. Observe WAL growth with normal writes plus a silent CDC topic points at a slot holding WAL, not at a write spike.
  2. Hypothesize The connector stopped consuming Friday 18:40 (task failed, deploy, poison message, credentials rotated) and its logical slot has pinned WAL since.
  3. Measure pg_replication_slots: one logical slot, inactive or not advancing, retained WAL ≈ 8.5 hours of generation. Connect task status and logs give the reason.
  4. Isolate Two clocks: disk full in ~2 hours, and pipeline correctness. Protect the primary first. If a restarted connector catches up faster than WAL grows, restart; otherwise drop the slot — a re-snapshot is recoverable, a primary outage is worse.
  5. Fix Fix the root cause (e.g., a row the converter rejected → dead-letter it instead of failing the task), recreate the slot, incremental-snapshot affected tables, reconcile counts.
  6. Prevent max_slot_wal_keep_size; slot-lag and "inactive 15 min" alerts to the database on-call; task failure pages; heartbeats; "drop the slot" pre-approved in the runbook so the 3 a.m. engineer doesn't decide alone.

8. Design walkthrough: CDC from Postgres into a lakehouse

A common interview prompt: “Design CDC from our Postgres order database into the lakehouse. Analysts want near-real-time current state and full change history.” A quality-gate question: can you run requirements → numbers → model → architecture → failure modes → trade-offs → ops → evolution without naming Kafka in sentence two? (Part 08's SCD2-from-CDC answer covers the dimension-modeling half; this is the platform half. Part 18 covers the framework itself.)

Requirements (ask, then write down)

  • Which tables? Assume 40 tables, three hot ones (orders, order_items, payments).
  • Freshness: "near real time" → pin it. Assume p95 ≤ 5 minutes source-commit to queryable.
  • Hard deletes in source? Assume yes (GDPR erasure and admin tools).
  • History: every intermediate state, or daily state? Assume every change (status-transition SLAs).
  • Cross-table consistency needed? Assume only finance reconciliation needs it, at daily granularity.
  • Source constraints: DBA allows one logical slot and forbids long transactions on the primary. Postgres 17 with a standby.

Numbers

  • Change rate: 3k row changes/s average, 15k/s peak (hypothetical). Per day: 3k × 86,400 ≈ 260 M events.
  • Event size: Avro-encoded envelope with before+after ≈ 0.5 KB → ~1.5 MB/s average, 7.5 MB/s peak. Kafka is bored. Six partitions per hot topic is plenty; more partitions buy nothing but repartitioning risk.
  • Bootstrap: orders 2 B rows. Connector snapshot at ~50k rows/s ≈ 11 h of pinned WAL. At 8 MB/s WAL that's ~320 GB retained — acceptable only if the volume has headroom; otherwise bulk-export at a known LSN.
  • Lake commits: 5-minute freshness → one MERGE per table per 1–2 minutes → ~1,000 commits/table/day. That number drives compaction and snapshot-expiry design, not throughput.
  • Change-log history: 260 M × ~300 B columnar ≈ 80 GB/day before compression gains; ~30 TB/year. Partition by day of commit time.

Model

Two tables per source table, because they answer different questions:

  • bronze.orders_changes — append-only change log: op, after.*, before key, _src_lsn, _src_commit_ts, _src_txid, _ingested_at. Never updated. This is your replay source and your history.
  • silver.orders — current state: one row per order_id, plus _src_lsn, is_deleted. Updated by MERGE. SCD2 dimensions are derived from the change log, not from this table.

Architecture

Debezium (Postgres connector, pgoutput, failover slot on 17) → Kafka topic per table keyed by PK, Avro with a schema registry → Spark Structured Streaming (or Flink) job per table group: write the micro-batch to the change log (append), then dedupe to latest-LSN-per-key and MERGE into current state. Checkpoints in object storage. Iceberg tables in merge-on-read mode for the hot current-state tables, because frequent MERGEs on copy-on-write rewrite whole files for a handful of changed rows (see Part 07 §10 on delete files).

Engine: Spark 3.5+ with Iceberg 1.xDialect/Language: Spark SQLExecutable: Illustrative — adapt to your catalog and envelope schema
-- Runs inside foreachBatch; the batch is registered as temp view `cdc_batch`
-- with columns: op, order_id, status, total_cents, updated_at,
--               _src_lsn BIGINT, _src_commit_ts TIMESTAMP
MERGE INTO lake.silver.orders AS t
USING (
  SELECT * FROM (
    SELECT b.*,
           ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY order_id ORDER BY _src_lsn DESC) AS rn
    FROM cdc_batch b
    WHERE op IN ('c', 'u', 'd', 'r')          -- tombstones filtered upstream
  ) WHERE rn = 1                              -- one source row per key, or MERGE fails
) AS s
ON t.order_id = s.order_id
-- stale or duplicate events (s._src_lsn <= t._src_lsn) match no clause: row untouched
WHEN MATCHED AND s.op = 'd' AND s._src_lsn > t._src_lsn THEN
  UPDATE SET t.is_deleted = true, t._src_lsn = s._src_lsn,
             t._src_commit_ts = s._src_commit_ts
WHEN MATCHED AND s._src_lsn > t._src_lsn THEN
  UPDATE SET t.status = s.status, t.total_cents = s.total_cents,
             t.updated_at = s.updated_at, t.is_deleted = false,
             t._src_lsn = s._src_lsn, t._src_commit_ts = s._src_commit_ts
WHEN NOT MATCHED AND s.op <> 'd' THEN
  INSERT (order_id, status, total_cents, updated_at, is_deleted, _src_lsn, _src_commit_ts)
  VALUES (s.order_id, s.status, s.total_cents, s.updated_at, false, s._src_lsn, s._src_commit_ts);

Notes worth saying aloud: MERGE clauses are evaluated in order and the first matching clause wins; a matched row that satisfies no clause is left alone, which is exactly what a stale or replayed event should do. The LSN guard must be on every MATCHED clause — forget it on the delete clause and a replayed old delete wipes a re-created row. A delete for a key never seen is dropped here; if the change log matters for audit, it's already in bronze. The ROW_NUMBER dedupe is not optional — Iceberg and Delta both reject a MERGE where multiple source rows match one target row.

Failure modes

Failure-first: what can fail in Postgres → lake CDC?
FailureDetectRecoverPrevent recurrence
Connector stops; slot pins WAL on primarySlot retained bytes; slot inactive > 15 min; topic silenceRestart and catch up, or drop slot to protect primary then re-snapshotmax_slot_wal_keep_size; page DB on-call; heartbeats
Primary failover, slot missing on new primaryConnector error on reconnect; LSN gapIncremental snapshot of all captured tables; reconcile countsPG17 failover slots; failover game day
Poison event (unserializable value, TOAST placeholder)Task FAILED; DLQ volumeRoute to DLQ, fix converter, replay DLQError tolerance + DLQ on converters; test with unchanged-TOAST updates
Replay after crash applies duplicatesChange log has repeated (key, LSN)None needed if apply is LSN-guardedLSN guard + dedupe; test by replaying a batch twice in CI
Consumer offline past tombstone retentionLag in time > thresholdRebuild current state from change log, or re-snapshotAlert on lag well under delete.retention.ms
Source DDL (column added / type changed)Registry rejects new schema, or connector errorEvolve lake schema (add column), resumeDDL review with contract check (§11); additive-only policy
Small files / delete-file buildupFiles per partition; MERGE and query latency trending upCompaction; rewrite position deletesScheduled compaction; snapshot expiry; right-sized commit interval
Silent data loss anywhereDaily count + checksum reconciliation vs source replicaTargeted re-snapshot of drifted key rangesReconciliation as a first-class job (Part 12 §4)

The TOAST row: an update that doesn't touch a large out-of-line column may omit its value from the logical stream, and Debezium emits a placeholder instead (check docs). A naive MERGE overwrites real text with the placeholder. Use REPLICA IDENTITY FULL on those tables or keep the existing value when the placeholder appears.

Trade-offs to name

  • Spark vs Flink. Flink gives second-level latency and native changelog upserts, but equality deletes make reads expensive until compacted. At a 5-minute SLO, Spark is enough.
  • MoR vs CoW. MoR for write-heavy current-state tables, with mandatory compaction; CoW for read-heavy, rarely updated ones.
  • Managed CDC vs Debezium. Managed removes the Connect cluster but check it exposes the source position; without it your apply can't be version-aware.
  • Commit interval. Halving it doubles commits and small files. Pick the slowest interval that meets the SLO.

Operations

SLOs on freshness (p95 commit → lake), completeness (daily reconciliation) and slot retained WAL. Runbooks for slot drop + re-snapshot, DLQ replay, single-table re-snapshot, compaction backlog. Ownership: service team owns the source schema (§9), platform owns the pipeline, DBA owns the slot budget.

Evolution

At 400 tables the per-table job becomes a config-driven apply service, and the busiest domains move to outbox events so the lake stops mirroring internal table layout. Which makes the schema a contract — the next section.

9. Data contracts at L5: an interface with an owner

Part 01 §13 shows what a contract file contains and Part 08 gives the checklist answer. At L5 the question is who can break it, who finds out, and where the change is stopped.

“Explain data contracts.”
30 sec

A data contract is an API for data: a versioned, producer-owned agreement on schema, meaning, and service levels, enforced by machines at the points where changes happen. Its purpose is to move breakage from the consumer's dashboard at 9 a.m. to the producer's pull request at 2 p.m.

2 min

Four parts. Structure: fields, types, nullability, keys — checkable by a schema registry. Semantics: units, enum meanings, what null means, time zone — mostly not machine-checkable, which is why most contract incidents are semantic. Service levels: freshness and completeness with an on-call owner. Change policy: compatibility mode, deprecation window, who must be notified. Enforced in producer CI, at the registry, and at runtime with a dead-letter path. Organizationally, the producer owns it: a breaking change is their incident, not the consumer's.

Deep dive

Contracts are only as good as their coverage of semantics and their consumer list. Registries check structure: an amount field that changes from cents to dollars stays a long and passes every compatibility check. Close that gap with consumer-driven contract tests — each consumer registers the assumptions it relies on (accepted enum values, value ranges, non-null keys) as executable checks that run in the producer's CI — and with a semantic changelog that ships with every schema version. Scope matters: contract interfaces that cross team boundaries, not every staging table. And raw CDC tables make poor contracts — they expose internal storage layout, so every refactor breaks someone; publish designed events (outbox) or curated views instead.

Where to stop: once you've said "semantics are the unchecked half" and "contract the boundary, not every table", let them pick the thread.

10. Compatibility, precisely

"Backward compatible means old stuff still works" loses points. Use registry vocabulary, where the words have exact meanings. Definitions below follow Confluent Schema Registry's docs; other registries differ in detail.

ModeGuaranteeWho upgrades firstAllowed (Avro)
BACKWARDConsumers using the new schema can read data written with the previous schemaConsumersDelete fields; add fields with defaults
FORWARDConsumers using the previous schema can read data written with the new schemaProducersAdd fields; delete fields that have defaults
FULLBoth of the aboveEither, in any orderAdd or delete only fields with defaults
*_TRANSITIVESame, checked against all previous versions, not just the latest—Same rules, stricter check
NONENo checkEveryone, simultaneously, good luckAnything

Two consequences. The registry default is BACKWARD (Confluent, at time of writing), which protects consumer-first upgrades — but on a shared topic the producer usually deploys first, so you often need FORWARD or FULL. And non-transitive checks compare only against the latest version; a topic replayed from the start needs a transitive mode.

“Backward vs forward compatibility — which do you want?”
30 sec

Backward: the new schema reads old data, so consumers can upgrade first. Forward: old schemas read new data, so producers can upgrade first. For a shared event stream where the producer ships independently of many consumers, I want forward at minimum, and full-transitive if data is replayed from the beginning.

2 min

Ask who deploys first and how far back readers go. A Kafka topic with one producer and fourteen consumers: the producer can't wait for fourteen teams, so new data must be readable by old consumers — forward. A lake table that gets reprocessed from history: new readers must read old files — backward. Both at once, or when you can't control deploy order: full. Then add transitive whenever old data stays readable, because "compatible with the last version" is not "compatible with version 1 files still in the topic".

Deep dive

Avro resolution does the work: a reader field missing from the writer takes the reader's default; a writer field unknown to the reader is skipped — hence defaults make additions and deletions safe. Protobuf identifies fields by number and preserves unknown fields, so additions are safe both ways, but reusing a field number for a new meaning is catastrophic and invisible to the registry. JSON Schema rules depend on open vs closed content models. None of it covers semantics.

Where to stop: name deploy order and replay depth as the deciding questions; go into Protobuf/JSON only if asked.

Change by change: what the registry sees vs what consumers feel

ChangeRegistry view (Avro)What actually breaks
Add optional field with defaultFull-compatibleConsumers doing SELECT * into a fixed-width sink; CSV exports with positional columns
Add required field (no default)Forward-only (old readers ignore it; new readers can't read old data)Any replay of historical data with the new reader
Make required field optional (add null to union)Backward, not forwardOld consumers that assumed non-null get nulls they can't handle — often a crash in the next system
Add enum symbolBackward, not forward unless the enum declares a default (Avro 1.9+)Old readers fail to deserialize; SQL consumers with exhaustive CASE silently bucket it as "other"
Rename fieldDelete + add; aliases help readers onlyEvery consumer that references the old name; lineage tools; dbt models
Widen type (int → long, float → double)Backward (reader promotion), not forwardOld readers with int; downstream warehouse columns typed INT
Narrow type / change type familyIncompatibleEverything
Change units or meaning, same typeFully compatibleEvery number downstream, silently. The worst row in this table.
Interviewer pushes back

You: “We enforce FULL_TRANSITIVE in the schema registry, so producers can't break consumers.”

Interviewer: “The payments team changes amount from cents to dollars. Still a long. What stops it?”

Strong answer: “Nothing in the registry. It checks structure, not meaning. Three layers catch it. Policy: a unit change is a new field — amount_cents stays, amount_usd_micros is added — and units live in field names so review catches it by eye. Producer CI: finance's registered check on value ranges fails on a staging sample. Runtime: distribution monitoring alerts on a 100× shift in the mean within minutes.”

Weak answer: “We'd add a test.” Which test, where, owned by whom, running before or after the data ships? The answer is the enforcement point, not the word test.

11. Enforcement points, consumer-driven contracts, ownership

  • [1] Producer CI. Check the proposed schema against the registry's compatibility API and run consumer-registered checks on a sample. The only point where a fix costs a review comment.
  • [2] Registry. Disable auto-registration in production (Confluent serializers auto-register by default at time of writing) and register through CI, or producers bypass the check.
  • [3] Runtime validation + DLQ. Catches schema-valid, contract-invalid data. A DLQ without an owner, an alert and a replay tool is a slower way to lose data.
  • [4] Consumer tests. dbt source tests and freshness. Last line of defence, and usually the one teams build first.

Consumer-driven contracts

The Pact idea applied to data (Part 12): consumers publish the assumptions they rely on, and those run in the producer's pipeline. The value is precision — the producer learns exactly which consumers depend on status being exhaustive. The cost: each check gates another team's deploy, so keep them few, owned and fast.

Ownership and on-call

A contract without an owner is a comment. Minimum: a named owning team, a pager that receives the dataset's freshness and validation alerts, a consumer registry built from lineage (OpenLineage, dbt exposures) rather than a wiki, and a deprecation window agreed in advance (30–90 days is policy, not physics). The producing team takes on new work; frame it as moving incidents from consumers' pagers to their own PR checks.

12. Incident narrative: one enum value, fourteen consumers

A representative scenario — all numbers hypothetical. The payments team adds PARTIALLY_REFUNDED to the status enum on the payments event topic. Previously, partial refunds stayed COMPLETED with a separate refund event. The registry runs BACKWARD, where adding a symbol is compatible; it accepts. Review sees a one-line change. Everyone is right, and fourteen consumers are about to disagree.

TimeEvent
Tue 14:05Producer deploys. Schema v8 auto-registered. First PARTIALLY_REFUNDED event at 14:07.
14:12Three JVM consumers with generated Avro classes (enum without default) fail deserialization and stop. Consumer-lag alerts page their on-calls, not payments.
14:20A Flink fraud job enters a restart loop on the same event. Fraud scoring for all payments is now stale.
15:10A consumer finds the unknown symbol in a stack trace. Payments replies "it's backward compatible". Forty minutes on what that means.
16:30Events can't be un-produced. Consumers upgrade to v8 one by one; Flink patched to skip-and-log unknown symbols.
Wed 02:00Finance's nightly dbt build fails an accepted_values test on status and blocks downstream models. Loud, correct, and 12 hours after the change.
Wed 09:40CFO asks why exec revenue is down 3.1% while the ops dashboard is flat. Six SQL consumers were silently wrong: status = 'COMPLETED' filters now drop partially refunded payments entirely; CASE mappings bucket the new value as "other".
FriAll reconciled; silent consumers backfilled from the retained topic and change log. Three never read status.

Blast radius: 3 crashed, 1 restart loop, 1 blocked build, 6 silently wrong, 3 unaffected. Detection gap: 7 minutes for loud failures, ~20 hours for silent ones — and the silent ones were the expensive ones. The crash was the good outcome.

What went wrong was not the enum: (a) a semantic change shipped as a "compatible" structural one, (b) the mode protected consumer-first upgrades on a producer-first topic, (c) nobody knew who the fourteen consumers were, (d) alerts went to victims, not the cause.

Prevention, mapped to enforcement points:

  • [Policy] Enum additions on contracted topics are treated as potentially breaking: announced, versioned, with a deprecation window. Enums declare a default symbol (e.g. UNKNOWN) so old readers degrade instead of crashing.
  • [1] Consumer-driven checks registered by the six SQL consumers ("status ∈ {…}") run in payments CI and fail the PR, forcing the conversation before deploy.
  • [2] FORWARD_TRANSITIVE or FULL_TRANSITIVE on the topic; auto-registration disabled in prod.
  • [3] New distinct values in low-cardinality columns alert the producer's on-call; a lineage-driven consumer registry makes "who reads this" a query; a daily revenue reconciliation across marts catches the next one before the CFO does.

13. Drill: handle an incompatible schema change

Drill · Contracts

The orders team must change customer_name (one string) into first_name and last_name, and change amount (integer cents) to amount_decimal (DECIMAL(18,4), currency-aware). Nine consumers read the topic; four dbt models and two dashboards read the lake table. Walk through the migration.

STOP. Answer before revealing.

Reveal the migration plan

Principle: never make an incompatible change in place. Use expand / migrate / contract (parallel change): add the new shape alongside the old, move every consumer, then remove the old.

  1. Expand. Producer emits both shapes: old fields stay, first_name, last_name, amount_decimal are added as optional with defaults, and the old fields get defaults too so they can be removed later — each step full-compatible. Lake: add columns (metadata-only in Iceberg, Part 07 §9). Document semantics; name splitting is lossy for some cultures.
  2. Backfill. Derive history where possible (amount / 100); where not (names), leave null and say so. Don't invent data.
  3. Migrate. The consumer registry is the checklist, with owners and dates. dbt consumers move to a new model version v2 while v1 stays live (§15).
  4. Verify. Runtime check that old and new fields agree on every event — proof the dual-write is correct.
  5. Deprecate. Announce the removal date; monitor reads of old columns via query logs. Remove only at zero reads or explicit sign-off.
  6. Contract. Remove old fields (allowed under FORWARD/FULL because they had defaults), drop lake columns, retire v1.

If the producer can't dual-write (e.g., a third-party source), put the translation in a thin adapter that publishes the old shape from the new, or publish a new topic orders.v2 and run both until consumers move. New topic is cleaner for semantic breaks; dual fields are cheaper for additive ones.

14. Why introduce dbt — and what new problems it creates

A common interview prompt: “You have 300 SQL transformations run by Airflow tasks and stored procedures. Why would you introduce dbt into this architecture, and what new problems does that create?” It tests whether you evaluate a tool by the problems it moves, not the features it lists. Elsewhere: snapshot syntax in Part 01, test YAML in Part 12, and a behavioral story about adoption in Part 09.

“Why would you introduce dbt, and what new problems does it create?”
30 sec

dbt turns a pile of SQL into a dependency graph with tests, documentation and environments, so transformations get the same engineering loop as application code: review, CI, deploy, lineage. The new problems: Jinja-heavy SQL that's harder to read, a DAG that grows past what one team can reason about, CI cost that scales with the project, and a false sense that "dbt tests pass" means the data is right.

2 min

What it fixes: dependency order is derived from ref() instead of hand-maintained in Airflow; every model is a SELECT, so logic is reviewable; the same code deploys to dev, CI and prod via targets; tests and freshness checks sit next to the code; docs and lineage come free; and with state comparison you can build and test only what a PR changed. What it creates: a second orchestrator inside the first (two places to look when something is late); macro sprawl; incremental models whose correctness hangs on untested filter logic; unclear ownership at 800 models; and warehouse cost from CI and full refreshes. So: conventions from day one — layers, groups with owners, contracts on public models, slim CI — and streaming and procedural work stay out.

Deep dive

At scale: incremental strategy and late data, deferral so CI doesn't rebuild the world, versions and access so public models can evolve, multi-project splits, and where metrics live. Each is below.

Where to stop: the 2-minute answer is the answer. Go deeper only on the axis they probe.

15. dbt mechanics that matter at L5

2026 Interview Note

Timeless: declarative dependency graphs, idempotent rebuilds, tests as code, environments, and state-based CI apply to any transformation framework (SQLMesh, Dataform, Spark jobs). Version-specific: dbt config names, which strategies an adapter supports, unit tests (dbt Core 1.8+), microbatch (1.9+), snapshot YAML config and hard_deletes (1.9+). The examples here use dbt Core 1.x syntax. dbt Labs' Rust-based engine (previewed in 2025 as "Fusion") shipped as dbt 2.0 in September 2026, with the open-source edition now called "dbt OSS"; configuration largely carries over, but adapter coverage and edge-case behaviour differ — check current docs before claiming parity. The concepts in this section don't change.

The DAG and ref()

ref('model') resolves to the right relation per environment and declares a DAG edge — so dependency order is a property of the code and can't drift from it. The failure mode: hard-coded names (analytics.prod.orders) that read prod from CI and hide lineage edges. Make it a lint rule.

Incremental models: strategy is a correctness decision

StrategyMechanismGood forTrap
appendInsert new rows onlyImmutable event logsAny replay duplicates rows
mergeMERGE on unique_keyMutable entities, CDC-fed current stateFull scan of target without partition pruning predicates; non-unique key → error or duplicates depending on platform
delete+insertDelete matching keys, insert batchPlatforms where MERGE is slow or absentTwo statements; atomicity depends on the platform's transactions
insert_overwriteReplace whole partitionsDate-partitioned facts, reprocessing a window (BigQuery, Spark)Partitions you didn't select in this run are untouched; partitions you did are replaced entirely — select wrong and you delete data
microbatch (1.9+)dbt splits by event_time into batches (e.g. day), runs each independently, retries failed batchesLarge time-series models with late data, targeted backfillsUpstream models need event_time configured for filtering; adapter support varies — check docs

Support is adapter-specific at time of writing. The universal trap is the incremental filter:

Engine: dbt Core 1.8+Dialect/Language: Jinja + SQLExecutable: Illustrative — adapt to your adapter
{{ config(materialized='incremental', unique_key='order_id',
          incremental_strategy='merge', on_schema_change='append_new_columns') }}

SELECT order_id, status, total_cents, updated_at, _src_lsn, _loaded_at
FROM {{ ref('stg_orders') }}
{% if is_incremental() %}
  -- Lookback window: re-read 3 days so late-arriving rows are not skipped.
  -- "max(updated_at) from this" alone has the long-transaction hole from §2.
  WHERE _loaded_at > (SELECT max(_loaded_at) FROM {{ this }}) - INTERVAL '3 days'
{% endif %}

Filter on load time (when the row reached the warehouse), not business time, with a lookback, and let the unique key absorb re-reads. on_schema_change decides what happens when upstream adds a column: ignore (the default, silently drops it), fail, append_new_columns, sync_all_columns. Pick deliberately; the default hides upstream changes.

Drill · dbt incremental

Finance reports daily revenue from an incremental dbt model. Every day, the previous three days are 0.2–0.6% lower than the same days after a monthly --full-refresh. No test fails.

STOP. Answer before revealing.

Reveal the diagnosis
  1. Observe The full refresh is correct, the incremental is short, and only recent days are affected: rows exist upstream that the incremental run never selected.
  2. Hypothesize The incremental filter uses business time — WHERE order_ts > (SELECT max(order_ts) FROM {{ this }}) — so rows that arrive late (CDC lag, mobile retries, long transactions) with an older order_ts fall behind the high-water mark.
  3. Measure For one short day, anti-join upstream vs model on key; check the missing rows' _loaded_at − order_ts. Expect a tail of minutes to days.
  4. Isolate Confirm the filter, confirm no dedupe/unique-key issue (a duplicate problem would overstate, not understate).
  5. Fix Filter on load time with a lookback sized to the observed lateness tail (p99.9 plus margin), use merge or insert_overwrite of the last N days, or move to microbatch with a lookback. Backfill the affected window.
  6. Prevent A scheduled reconciliation test comparing incremental totals against a recomputation for a trailing window; alert on lateness distribution changes. "Tests pass" meant nobody tested completeness.

Snapshots: SCD2 by polling, with polling's blind spots

A dbt snapshot compares the current state of a source to the last snapshot on each run and writes SCD2 rows with dbt_valid_from / dbt_valid_to, using either a timestamp strategy (trust an updated_at) or a check strategy (compare listed columns). It is §2's polling pattern with a nicer interface — so it inherits polling's limits:

  • It only sees state at run time. Three changes between two hourly runs become one version. Status-transition history is gone.
  • Validity times are approximate. With the check strategy, dbt_valid_from is the snapshot run time, not when the change happened.
  • Deletes need configuration (hard_deletes in 1.9+, previously invalidate_hard_deletes) and are detected only as "missing at run time".
  • Not reproducible. The source no longer holds the past, so treat snapshot tables as source data: back them up.
Interviewer pushes back

You: “For the customer dimension history I'd stream CDC into a change log and derive SCD2 from it.”

Interviewer: “Why not just a dbt snapshot? It's one file and no Kafka.”

Strong answer: “If the business question is 'what was the customer's segment on the first of each month' and changes are rare, a daily snapshot is the right, cheap answer — and I'd pick it. It fails when intermediate states or deletes matter: two changes between runs become one version, validity times are run times, and a hard delete is only an absence. So the question picks the tool: state at run granularity → snapshot; every transition with exact times → CDC. Or combine: CDC change log in the lake, SCD2 built from it by a dbt model.”

Weak answer: “Snapshots don't scale.” They scale fine for most dimensions. Name the semantic difference, not a performance myth.

Tests: generic, singular, unit

  • Generic (unique, not_null, accepted_values, relationships): assertions on built data. They test data, not logic.
  • Singular: SQL returning failing rows, for business rules ("refunds never exceed payment").
  • Unit (dbt Core 1.8+): mocked input rows → expected output for one model. The only kind that tests your CASE and window logic, and runs before data exists. Use on non-trivial models.
  • Cost. Use where to test recent partitions; a unique test on 10 B rows every hour is a warehouse bill.
Engine: dbt Core 1.8+Dialect/Language: YAMLExecutable: Illustrative
unit_tests:
  - name: partial_refund_is_net_revenue
    model: fct_payments
    given:
      - input: ref('stg_payments')
        rows:
          - {payment_id: 1, status: COMPLETED,          amount_cents: 1000, refunded_cents: 0}
          - {payment_id: 2, status: PARTIALLY_REFUNDED, amount_cents: 1000, refunded_cents: 300}
    expect:
      rows:
        - {payment_id: 1, net_revenue_cents: 1000}
        - {payment_id: 2, net_revenue_cents: 700}

That test would have caught half of §12's silent consumers, because it forces someone to write down what a new status means.

Sources and freshness

sources give lineage a root and enable dbt source freshness (loaded_at_field, warn_after/error_after). Gate the build on it: 400 models built on stale inputs are stale data with today's _built_at.

Model contracts, versions, access, exposures

Engine: dbt Core 1.8+Dialect/Language: YAMLExecutable: Illustrative
groups:
  - name: finance
    owner: {name: Finance Data, email: finance-data@example.com}

models:
  - name: fct_payments
    group: finance
    access: public            # other groups/projects may ref() it
    latest_version: 2
    config:
      contract: {enforced: true}
    columns:
      - name: payment_id
        data_type: bigint
        constraints: [{type: not_null}]
      - name: net_revenue_cents
        data_type: bigint
    versions:
      - v: 2
      - v: 1
        deprecation_date: 2026-12-31
  • Contracts (contract: {enforced: true}) fail the build if the SQL doesn't return exactly the declared columns and types. Constraints are enforced on some platforms and informational on others (PK/FK usually informational on cloud warehouses) — check your adapter. §9, applied inside the warehouse.
  • Versions let a public model do expand/contract (§13): v2 ships beside v1, consumers migrate by ref('fct_payments', v=2), v1 gets a deprecation date.
  • Groups and access (private, protected, public) turn "please don't depend on our staging models" from a wiki plea into a build error, and give each model an owner.
  • Exposures declare downstream dashboards, ML jobs and apps as DAG nodes. They're how you answer "what breaks if this model changes" — and how state:modified+ in CI can tell you which dashboards a PR touches.

16. dbt in CI and at scale

Slim CI: state comparison and deferral

Building all 800 models on every PR costs hours and real money. The pattern: keep the production run's artifacts (manifest.json), compare the PR against them, build only what changed plus its descendants, and defer every unchanged upstream reference to the production relation.

Engine: dbt Core 1.8+Dialect/Language: ShellExecutable: Illustrative — paths and target names are yours
# In CI, after fetching the latest prod manifest into ./prod-artifacts
dbt build --select state:modified+ --defer --state ./prod-artifacts --target ci
# Optional: zero-copy clone prod relations into the CI schema (dbt 1.6+, platform-dependent)
dbt clone --select state:modified+,config.materialized:incremental --state ./prod-artifacts

The traps: macro and vars changes can modify many nodes at once or, depending on configuration, be missed; a stale prod manifest makes everything look modified; CI reading prod data is a PII access decision (Part 14); and tests alone miss value regressions — add a data diff against prod for models with exposures.

Monorepo scaling, Mesh and ownership

One project works until parse times hit minutes, 20 teams share one CODEOWNERS file, and nobody knows whether a model can change. Responses, in order:

  1. Groups, access and owners inside one project. Cheap, and solves most "who owns this" problems.
  2. Layered conventions: staging (1:1 with sources, private) → intermediate (private) → marts (public, contracted, versioned).
  3. Multiple projects ("dbt Mesh"): domains depend on each other's public models via cross-project ref. At time of writing that resolution is a dbt Cloud / dbt platform capability, with packages as the Core alternative — check current docs. A project boundary is an API boundary: you inherit §9–§13 between projects.

Semantic / metrics layer

"Revenue" defined six ways in six dashboards (§12) is the problem. A semantic layer defines metrics once — measures, dimensions, entities, joins — and serves them to BI and APIs. dbt's is built on MetricFlow, whose licensing and packaging have changed more than once — check current docs. L5 point: it is a contract on meaning, the part registries can't check. Cost: another serving layer with its own latency and BI compatibility matrix.

17. When dbt is the wrong tool

WorkloadWhy dbt fits badlyBetter fit
Streaming, sub-minute latencydbt runs batch SQL invocations; scheduling every minute means paying startup, compile and warehouse overhead per runFlink / Spark Structured Streaming; warehouse-native streaming objects (dynamic tables, materialized views) where freshness targets allow
Heavy procedural logic (loops, external API calls, stateful retries)SQL + Jinja is a template language, not a control-flow language; macros become an untestable programPython/Spark jobs orchestrated alongside dbt
ML feature engineering beyond SQL (embeddings, custom UDF-heavy transforms)Python models exist on some adapters but are second-class for testing and cost visibilitySpark / Ray / feature-store pipelines (Part 17)
Massive per-row PythonRow-by-row UDFs on a warehouse are the slowest, most expensive pathVectorized batch compute in Spark or dedicated services
CDC apply with ordering guaranteesCan be done with a merge model, but you're rebuilding §8's LSN logic in JinjaStreaming apply job; dbt downstream of the current-state table

The architecture that holds up: CDC and streaming land bronze; dbt owns SQL from bronze to contracted marts; Python/Spark handles what SQL can't. Each tool at the layer where its failure modes are cheap.

L5 Interview CardCDC, Data Contracts & Transformation Engineering
Must know
  • Log-based CDC sees every committed change; updated_at polling misses hard deletes, intermediate states and long transactions.
  • Snapshot + stream must meet at one log position; incremental snapshots interleave chunks with live events using watermarks.
  • Per-key order comes from keying by PK; repartitioning, PK updates and parallel apply break it.
  • Apply rule: upsert by PK, source LSN as version, reject not-newer, dedupe per key per batch, soft-delete.
  • An inactive Postgres logical slot pins WAL on the primary; cap with max_slot_wal_keep_size and page on slot lag.
  • BACKWARD = new schema reads old data (consumers first); FORWARD = old schema reads new data (producers first); FULL = both; transitive = all versions.
  • Registries check structure, not meaning; incompatible changes go through expand/migrate/contract.
  • dbt: ref DAG, incremental strategies, snapshots ≠ CDC, unit tests (1.8+), contracts/versions/access, slim CI with state:modified+ --defer.
Must be able to explain
  1. Why does updated_at CDC lose rows even when every writer sets it?
  2. How can a stopped CDC connector take down the source database?
  3. Why does adding an enum value pass the registry and still break consumers?
Must be able to draw

Postgres WAL → slot → Debezium → Kafka (keyed by PK) → stream processor → change log (append) + current state (LSN-guarded MERGE), with the position each hop acknowledges.

WAL ─▶ slot ─▶ connector ─▶ topic(pk)
                              │
                     ┌────────┴───────┐
                     ▼                ▼
               changes (append)  current (MERGE
                                  by LSN, soft del)
Must be able to code
  • A MERGE that dedupes to latest LSN per key, soft-deletes, and ignores stale replays.
  • A slot-lag monitoring query against pg_replication_slots.
  • An incremental dbt model with a load-time lookback filter and a unit test for its logic.
Must be able to debug
  • Primary WAL disk climbing on a weekend while CDC topics are silent.
  • Incremental model 0.4% short for recent days until a full refresh.
Numbers that matter
  • WAL rate × connector downtime = retained WAL: 8 MB/s × 60 h ≈ 1.7 TB (hypothetical rates — measure yours).
  • Snapshot time = rows ÷ read rate: 2 B ÷ 50k/s ≈ 11 h of pinned WAL.
  • Change events/day = rate × 86,400: 3k/s ≈ 260 M/day.
  • Commit interval sets commits/day: 1–2 min → ~1,000/table/day → compaction is required.
  • Detection gap: loud failures in minutes, silent semantic failures in hours to days.
Classic traps
  • Using ts_ms as the version, or hard-deleting in the lake so old replays resurrect rows.
  • Saying "BACKWARD compatible, so producers are safe" on a producer-first topic.
  • Treating a dbt snapshot as a substitute for CDC history.
30-second answer

“How do you get correct, low-latency change data from an OLTP database into the lakehouse and keep it safe to change?” Log-based CDC keyed by primary key, applied with a MERGE that treats the source LSN as a version and soft-deletes, so replays converge. Protect the source by capping slot WAL retention and paging on slot lag. Put a producer-owned contract with a transitive compatibility mode on the interface, and ship incompatible changes through expand/contract.

2-minute answer

Requirements first: deletes, intermediate states, freshness, cross-table consistency. If deletes or intermediate states matter, polling is wrong. Bootstrap with a snapshot that meets the stream at one LSN. Key topics by PK; never repartition them. Everything after the WAL is at-least-once, so dedupe to latest LSN per key, MERGE only newer LSNs, soft-delete, and keep an append-only change log for history and replay. Operate the slot as a primary-database risk. Contracts: producer-owned structure, semantics, SLO and change policy, enforced in CI, at the registry and at runtime — knowing the registry can't see meaning. dbt then owns batch SQL with tests, contracts and slim CI.

Deep-dive follow-up

“An order and its items commit in one transaction but reach the lake in different micro-batches. Which consumers care, and how do you give them a consistent view without slowing everyone?”

Staff+ follow-up

“Forty service teams expose their tables via CDC and every refactor breaks analytics. What do you change in ownership, interfaces and incentives over the next year — and what do you stop doing?”
