Part 16

Serving Systems & Warehouse Architecture

Quick refresh10 minInterview study55 minDeep practice75 min
Last technically reviewed September 2026
Covers access-pattern-first storage selection, key design, hot keys, secondary indexes, consistency levels, TTL, LSM vs B-tree, capacity estimation, caching and eviction, tail latency, sub-100-ms serving design, Snowflake / BigQuery / Databricks / Redshift / open Iceberg architecture comparison, platform selection
Versions referenced DynamoDB, Cassandra 5.x, Redis / Valkey 8.x, OpenSearch 2.x/3.x, PostgreSQL 17/18, Snowflake, BigQuery (editions), Databricks (Unity Catalog, Delta), Redshift (RA3 & Serverless), Apache Iceberg format v2/v3
Primary references DynamoDB docs · Cassandra docs · Redis docs · OpenSearch docs · PostgreSQL docs · Snowflake docs · BigQuery docs · Databricks docs · Redshift docs · Iceberg docs
Known implementation differences Every vendor number in this part (item size limits, partition throughput, cache lifetimes, billing minimums, price per unit) is a 2026 snapshot that changes without notice; the shapes and trade-offs are what you are examined on.

This chapter tests whether you pick storage from the access pattern or from your CV. Two question families live here. The first is serving: "the model needs features in under 100 ms" or "the app needs a user's stats on every page load" — a point-lookup problem that a warehouse cannot solve and a key-value store solves only if the key is right. The second is platform: "why does this model cost 10x more on platform B?" and "pick a warehouse for this workload". The interviewer is not checking whether you know DynamoDB's API. They are checking whether you ask for the read pattern, the QPS, the item size and the freshness before you say a product name — and whether you can do the memory math out loud.

2026 Interview Note

Timeless: partition key plus sort key, the write/read/space amplification triangle of LSM vs B-tree, quorum arithmetic, cache-aside and its stampede, tail-latency amplification under fan-out, compute/storage separation, metadata-driven pruning, and "the cost model shapes the behavior". Version-specific: DynamoDB's per-partition throughput and item size limit, Cassandra's default compaction strategy, Redis vs Valkey licensing, BigQuery on-demand price per TiB, Snowflake's cache lifetimes and per-second billing minimums, Databricks' data-skipping column defaults, Redshift Serverless RPU billing. Say which kind of fact you are stating. A candidate who says "at time of writing BigQuery on-demand bills per byte scanned — check current pricing" sounds senior; one who recites a price as a law of nature does not.

1. Access pattern first: choosing a storage shape

If your answer starts with a technology name before you have asked how the data is read, you have already skipped a step. Serving stores are not general-purpose. Each family is a bet on one access shape, and it is fast precisely because it refuses the others.

Ask four questions before naming anything:

  1. How is it read? By exact key? By key plus a range (latest N events for a user)? By arbitrary predicates? By text relevance? By aggregation over millions of rows?
  2. How much, how often? Read QPS, write QPS, item size, total keys, p99 target.
  3. How fresh, how correct? Can a read return a value 5 seconds stale? Must a read see its own write? Is a missing value worse than a stale one?
  4. What changes? Will new query patterns appear monthly (favor flexible query engines) or is the pattern fixed for years (favor precomputed key-shaped storage)?

The six families, conceptually

FamilyMental modelFast atBad atExamples
Key-valueA distributed hash map: key → opaque blob or small itemPoint get/put at any scale, predictable latencyAnything not by key; ad-hoc filters; joinsDynamoDB (as KV), Redis, RocksDB-backed stores
Wide-columnPartition key → sorted map of rows (clustering key → columns)"All rows for X, ordered by Y, in range"; very high write ratesQueries that do not name the partition; cross-partition aggregationCassandra, ScyllaDB, HBase, Bigtable; DynamoDB with a sort key behaves this way
DocumentKey → nested JSON document, some secondary indexesFetch/update a whole aggregate (an order with its lines)Cross-document joins, large fan-in analyticsMongoDB, DynamoDB (as document), Postgres JSONB
Relational (OLTP)Normalized rows, B-tree indexes, transactionsCorrectness, multi-row transactions, flexible queries at moderate scaleHorizontal write scale without sharding effort; huge scansPostgres, MySQL; distributed SQL (CockroachDB, Spanner) at the far end
SearchInverted index: term → posting list of document idsFull-text, faceting, fuzzy match, filter + relevance ranking; vector kNNBeing the source of truth; strong consistency; heavy updatesOpenSearch, Elasticsearch, Solr
CacheBounded, lossy, in-memory copy of something elseSub-millisecond reads of hot keys; absorbing read skewDurability, completeness — it is allowed to forgetRedis / Valkey, Memcached, in-process LRU

DynamoDB appears three times on purpose: the data model you design on it decides which family you are using. Families are shapes, not brands. And a cache is not a database. If losing every key would lose data, it is not a cache, and you now need persistence, replication and a recovery story.

Decision table: access pattern → storage shape

Access patternStorage shape that fitsWhyCommon wrong answer
Get features/profile for one user_id, p99 < 10 ms, 20K QPSKey-value (PK = user_id), optional cache in frontOne hop, one partition, O(1)"Query the warehouse" — seconds, and billed per query or per running warehouse
Last 50 events for a user, newest firstWide-column: PK = user_id, clustering key = event_ts DESCRows for a partition are stored sorted; a range read is a contiguous scanKV with the whole list in one blob — rewrites the blob on every event
Time-series per device, retained 30 daysWide-column with time bucket in PK + TTLBounded partitions; expiry is free-ish; time-window compactionPK = device_id alone — unbounded partition that grows forever
Transfer money between two accountsRelational / distributed SQL with transactionsMulti-row atomicity and constraints are the requirementKV with application-level "compensations" you will get wrong
"Products matching 'red running shoe' under $80, ranked"Search index (fed from the source of truth)Inverted index + filters + scoringLIKE '%red%' in Postgres at scale
Arbitrary slice-and-dice by analysts over billions of rowsColumnar warehouse / lakehouse (Section B)Scan-oriented; pruning; vectorized executionA KV store with a secondary index per filter column
Dashboard tile read by 5,000 users, refreshed every minutePrecomputed result in KV/cache, or a warehouse result cacheCompute once, read many5,000 identical warehouse queries per minute

For the analytics side of this boundary — why columnar wins scans and where row stores still win — see Trade-offs: Row-store for analytics?. For the online/offline split of a feature store, see Design: a feature store for ML serving; this part zooms into the online half.

2. Primary key design and hot keys

In every partitioned store, the primary key does two jobs at once: it distributes data across nodes (the partition key, hashed) and it orders data within a partition (the sort or clustering key). Get the first wrong and you have a hot node. Get the second wrong and you cannot answer the query without scanning.

Partition key + sort key

The rule: the partition key is whatever every query names with equality; the sort key is what the query ranges or orders over. Design the key from the list of queries, not from the entity diagram. That is the inversion that trips people coming from relational modeling: in Postgres you normalize and let indexes serve queries; in a wide-column or KV store you denormalize so each query is one partition read.

Engine: Apache CassandraDialect/Language: CQLExecutable: Illustrative — adapt to your dialect
-- Query: "last N sessions for a user, newest first"
CREATE TABLE sessions_by_user (
  user_id     bigint,
  day_bucket  date,          -- bounds partition size
  session_ts  timestamp,
  session_id  uuid,
  device      text,
  duration_s  int,
  PRIMARY KEY ((user_id, day_bucket), session_ts, session_id)
) WITH CLUSTERING ORDER BY (session_ts DESC, session_id ASC)
  AND default_time_to_live = 2592000;   -- 30 days

-- One partition, contiguous read:
SELECT * FROM sessions_by_user
WHERE user_id = 42 AND day_bucket = '2026-09-24'
LIMIT 50;

Notice three decisions. The composite partition key (user_id, day_bucket) caps partition size — a partition that grows forever eventually becomes the slowest thing in the cluster. session_id in the clustering key makes the primary key unique when two sessions share a timestamp. The TTL encodes retention in the table instead of in a cleanup job someone forgets to run.

Hot keys and hot partitions

A hashed partition key spreads keys evenly. It does nothing for traffic. If one key receives 20% of requests, one partition (and its replicas) receives 20% of the load, no matter how many nodes you add. Adding nodes is the classic wrong fix: it lowers average utilization while the hot partition stays pinned.

Typical sources: a celebrity user, a default or null value, a time-based key where "now" is always the hot bucket, a global counter, one giant tenant.

TechniqueHowCost
Write sharding (salting)Key becomes item#N with N in 0..k-1; writes pick N randomly or by hash of a secondary fieldReads must fan out to k keys and merge; k is a capacity decision
Pre-aggregate before writingBuffer increments in the stream processor and write one sum per second instead of 50,000 incrementsFreshness bounded by the flush interval
Cache hot readsHot read keys served from cache (in-process for the very hottest)Staleness; invalidation
Change the keyIf time is the hot dimension, lead with something else and put time in the sort keySome query becomes harder; that is the trade
Engine: Any KV / wide-column storeDialect/Language: PythonExecutable: Pseudocode
SHARDS = 16   # sized from: peak writes/s on hottest key ÷ safe per-partition write rate

def write_like(post_id, user_id):
    shard = hash(user_id) % SHARDS            # deterministic: idempotent retries land on same shard
    kv.increment(f"likes#{post_id}#{shard}", 1)

def read_likes(post_id):
    keys = [f"likes#{post_id}#{s}" for s in range(SHARDS)]
    return sum(v or 0 for v in kv.batch_get(keys))   # read fan-out is the price

Vendor-specific, hedge it: DynamoDB at time of writing (2026) has adaptive capacity and "split for heat", which rebalance throughput toward busy partitions and can split a partition whose sort-key range is hot. That helps; it does not rescue a single hot item, because one item cannot be split. Per-partition throughput ceilings exist in the order of a few thousand reads and around a thousand writes per second per partition — check the current DynamoDB docs for exact numbers before quoting them. Cassandra has no equivalent auto-splitting; a hot partition is your problem.

Interviewer pushes back

You: “I'd partition the counters table by post_id. It's high-cardinality, so load spreads evenly.”

Interviewer: “A post goes viral and takes 60,000 likes per second. What happens?”

Strong answer: “Cardinality spreads keys, not traffic. One post means one partition, so writes on it are bounded by what a single partition and its replicas can absorb — throttling or rising latency, and neighbouring keys on those nodes suffer too. I'd fix it at two layers. First, don't send 60K writes: the stream processor aggregates per post per second and writes one delta, so the store sees one write per second per post regardless of popularity. Second, if we genuinely need per-event writes, salt the key into k shards for posts detected as hot, and read by fanning out k keys. k is sized from peak rate ÷ safe per-partition rate with headroom. I'd also check whether readers even need exact live counts — '60K likes' displayed with 5-second staleness is fine for a UI.”

Weak answer: “Add more nodes” or “the database auto-scales.” Neither moves load off a single key.

3. Secondary indexes, consistency levels and TTL

Local vs global secondary indexes

A secondary index answers a query that does not name the primary partition key. There are two ways to build one in a partitioned store, and they have opposite trade-offs:

Local indexGlobal index
Partitioned bySame partition key as the base table; alternate sort keyIts own partition key (the indexed attribute)
Write pathUpdated with the base row, same partitionUpdated asynchronously, possibly on other nodes
ConsistencyCan be read consistently with the baseTypically eventually consistent
Query must nameThe base partition keyOnly the index key
Hot-key riskInherits base partitioningNew risk: a low-cardinality index key (status) is a hot partition by construction

In DynamoDB terms at time of writing (2026): local secondary indexes (LSIs) must be declared at table creation, support strongly consistent reads, and impose a size cap per partition-key value; global secondary indexes (GSIs) can be added later, have their own capacity, and support only eventually consistent reads. Check the docs for current limits. The interview-grade consequence: "write then immediately query by a GSI" is a read-your-writes bug waiting to happen. If the flow requires it, read the base table by primary key, or design the key so the query is a primary-key query.

Cassandra's secondary indexes (including the storage-attached indexes in 5.0) are local per node, so a query that does not restrict the partition key asks many nodes — fine for low-QPS lookups, dangerous on a hot path. The durable wide-column answer is a second denormalized "query table" keyed by the other access pattern, written together with the first.

Consistency levels: tunable, and what it buys

With replication factor N, a write acknowledged by W replicas and a read that consults R replicas is guaranteed to overlap at least one up-to-date replica when R + W > N. With N = 3: QUORUM/QUORUM (2 + 2 > 3) gives read-your-writes in steady state; ONE/ONE (1 + 1) is fast and may return stale data. Cassandra lets you choose per query (ONE, QUORUM, LOCAL_QUORUM, ALL, …); LOCAL_QUORUM is the usual multi-region compromise because it avoids cross-region round-trips on the hot path. DynamoDB reads are eventually consistent by default with an option for strongly consistent reads on the base table (at time of writing, typically at higher read-capacity cost and not available on GSIs).

Quorum overlap is a steady-state guarantee; hinted handoff and last-write-wins clocks can still surprise you (Part 13). And the right question is not "strong or eventual?" but "what is the cost of a stale read here?" A feature vector 3 seconds stale costs nothing. A balance check 3 seconds stale can cost money.

TTL and deletes

TTL turns retention into data. It is not free, and its semantics are loose:

  • Expiry is lazy. In DynamoDB (at time of writing) expired items are deleted by a background process, and the docs describe the delay in days, not seconds; expired-but-not-yet-deleted items can still be returned, so filter on the expiry attribute if it matters. Redis expires lazily on access plus a sampling sweep.
  • In LSM stores, a delete is a write. Cassandra writes a tombstone; data is really removed only at compaction after a grace period. A queue-like access pattern ("insert, read, delete") piles up tombstones and makes range reads scan thousands of dead cells. Model queues as time-bucketed partitions that expire as a whole, or use a real queue.
  • Mixed TTLs in one partition defeat time-window compaction. Put data with the same lifetime together.

4. Storage engines: LSM tree vs B-tree

You will not be asked to implement either. You will be asked why Cassandra swallows writes that make Postgres sweat, why a "read-heavy" table on an LSM store got slow after a bulk load, or why a write-heavy workload chews through SSD endurance. All three answers come from one triangle: write amplification, read amplification, space amplification. You can optimize two; the third pays.

B-treeLSM tree
Write pathRandom I/O: find page, modify, write back (plus WAL)Sequential: WAL append + memory insert; files written in bulk
Write amplificationA page rewritten for a small change; full-page writes after checkpointsEach byte rewritten once per compaction level it passes through
Read amplificationLow and predictable: tree heightHigher: memtable + multiple sorted runs; Bloom filters rescue point reads, not range reads
Space amplificationFragmentation, half-full pages; MVCC bloat in Postgres until vacuumObsolete versions and tombstones until compaction
Background workVacuum / page splitsCompaction — competes with foreground I/O and is the usual cause of latency spikes
Best atRead-heavy, update-in-place, range scans on indexes, transactionsWrite-heavy, append-mostly, time-series, high ingest
ExamplesPostgres, MySQL InnoDBCassandra, ScyllaDB, RocksDB (and stores built on it), HBase
“LSM tree or B-tree — which is better?”
30 sec

Neither; they spend different budgets. A B-tree updates pages in place, so reads are cheap and predictable but writes are random I/O. An LSM tree turns writes into sequential appends and pays later with compaction and with reads that may check several files. Write-heavy and append-mostly favors LSM; read-heavy with in-place updates and transactions favors B-tree.

2 min

Frame it as the amplification triangle. B-tree: low read amplification (tree height), moderate space overhead from partially filled pages, and write amplification because a 100-byte change rewrites an 8 KB page. LSM: low write cost on the foreground path, but every byte is rewritten as it moves through compaction levels, reads consult the memtable plus multiple sorted runs (Bloom filters make point lookups cheap, range scans still touch several files), and deleted or overwritten data costs space until compaction. The operational consequence is that LSM latency is bursty: when compaction falls behind, reads fan across more files, p99 climbs, and disks fill with dead data. So I size LSM clusters with compaction headroom — not just for the ingest rate.

Deep dive

Compaction strategy chooses a point on the triangle (defaults vary by version — Cassandra 5.0 adds a unified strategy; check before asserting): size-tiered minimizes write amplification at the cost of transient 2x space during big merges; leveled bounds read and space amplification at the cost of rewriting data roughly once per level; time-window suits data that expires by time, but mixed TTLs in one partition break its promise. Tombstones are the classic LSM failure: a delete-heavy partition makes range reads scan dead cells until the grace period passes and compaction removes them. On the B-tree side, Postgres MVCC makes updates append new tuple versions, so an update-heavy table needs vacuum to keep space and index bloat in check — a B-tree engine with LSM-like space behavior.

Where to stop: once you have named the triangle, the compaction trade-off and one operational failure (tombstones or compaction lag), stop unless asked about a specific engine.

The same intuition carries to analytics: warehouse micro-partitions and lakehouse data files are immutable, so every update is "write new, retire old, compact later" — LSM thinking at file granularity. See copy-on-write vs merge-on-read and indexes, zone maps and Bloom filters.

5. Capacity estimation: do the math before the diagram

Five lines of arithmetic usually decide whether you need a cache, whether the data fits in memory, and whether the nightly load or the daytime reads is the real peak.

A reusable template (all numbers hypothetical):

Engine: Back-of-envelopeDialect/Language: ArithmeticExecutable: Pseudocode
Keys (users)            200 M
Item size               ~1 KB  (60 features × ~12 B + key + overhead)
Raw data                200 M × 1 KB            = 200 GB
Store overhead          ×1.5–2 (indexes, fragmentation, versions)
                        ≈ 300–400 GB per replica
Replication             ×3                       ≈ 1–1.2 TB on disk

Read peak               20 K QPS × 1 KB          = 20 MB/s   (tiny)
Daily active users      40 M → hot set 40 GB     (fits in RAM)

Daily full refresh      200 M writes in a 2 h window
                        200 M ÷ 7,200 s          ≈ 28 K writes/s
                        → the batch LOAD is the peak, not the reads

Vendor-neutral rules: cache the hot set, not the dataset; per-partition rates are the real limits, so divide load by the partitions that actually receive it; and always compute the write side — refreshes, backfills, replays — because it arrives all at once.

6. Caching: patterns, stampedes and eviction

A cache is a bet that reads are skewed and some staleness is acceptable. Uniform reads over a dataset far larger than memory get a hop and a failure mode, not a hit rate. Ask for the distribution first.

Write and read patterns

PatternHowStalenessFailure mode
Cache-aside (lazy)App reads cache; on miss reads store, then populates cache with TTLUp to TTL, unless writers invalidateStampede on popular miss; cold start after deploy/flush
Write-throughWriter updates store and cache synchronouslyLowWrite latency rises; caches data nobody reads; partial failure leaves them diverged
Write-behindWriter updates cache; cache flushes to store laterStore lagsData loss if the cache dies before flush — now it is a database
Refresh-ahead / precomputePipeline pushes new values before they are asked forBounded by pipeline cadencePipeline lag silently serves old values

The invalidation race to know: "update store, then delete key" can interleave with a reader that fetched the old value and re-populates the cache after the delete. Short TTLs bound it; version-checked writes remove it. For data produced by pipelines rather than user writes, the cleaner answer is usually to put a version in the key (feat:v20260924:user:42) and never invalidate at all — flip readers to the new version.

Stampede, thundering herd and negative caching

  • Single-flight / request coalescing: one caller per key recomputes; others wait on the same future or serve the previous value.
  • Stale-while-revalidate: keep a soft expiry and a hard expiry; after soft expiry, serve stale and refresh in the background.
  • Probabilistic early refresh: each reader near expiry refreshes with a small, rising probability, so refresh happens before the cliff.
  • TTL jitter: ttl = base × (1 ± 10%). Without it, a bulk load that set 10 million keys with the same TTL schedules 10 million simultaneous expiries.
  • Negative caching: cache "not found" (with a shorter TTL). Otherwise a request stream for non-existent keys — new users with no features yet, or an enumeration attack — passes straight through the cache to the store every time.
Engine: Any cache clientDialect/Language: PythonExecutable: Illustrative — adapt to your client library
import random

MISSING = b"__none__"
BASE_TTL = 3600

def ttl(base=BASE_TTL):
    return int(base * random.uniform(0.9, 1.1))       # jitter

def get_features(user_id):
    key = f"feat:{CURRENT_VERSION}:{user_id}"          # versioned key
    val = cache.get(key)
    if val == MISSING:
        return None                                     # negative hit
    if val is not None:
        return decode(val)

    with single_flight(key):                            # one loader per key per process
        val = cache.get(key)                            # re-check after acquiring
        if val is None:
            row = store.get(user_id)
            if row is None:
                cache.set(key, MISSING, ttl(300))       # short negative TTL
                return None
            cache.set(key, encode(row), ttl())
            return row
        return None if val == MISSING else decode(val)

Eviction

LRU is fooled by scans (one batch job touching every key once flushes the hot set). LFU resists scans but adapts slowly when popularity shifts, so implementations decay counts. Redis/Valkey implement approximated versions of both, selectable by policy at time of writing — check the maxmemory-policy docs; the important decision is whether eviction applies to all keys or only keys with a TTL, because the second can leave you with an out-of-memory error instead of eviction. TTL is an eviction policy for correctness (bounded staleness); LRU/LFU are eviction policies for capacity. You usually need both.

Interviewer pushes back

You: “We'll put Redis in front of the database to hit the latency target.”

Interviewer: “Your store already returns in 5 ms at p99. Why the cache? And what happens the first minute after you flush it?”

Strong answer: “Fair — if the store meets the p99 at peak with headroom, a cache adds a hop, an invalidation problem and a cold-start risk for no latency win. I'd add it only for a stated reason: read skew that creates hot partitions, store cost per read at our QPS, or protection for a store that can't take peak. If we do add it, the flush case is the design point: with a 95% hit rate, the store sees 5% of traffic in steady state and 100% after a flush — a 20x step. So either the store is sized for full load and the cache is a cost optimization, or we warm the cache before shifting traffic and roll deploys gradually so the whole fleet never starts cold together.”

Weak answer: “Caching always makes it faster.” It makes the average faster and the failure mode worse unless the store can survive a cold cache.

7. Serving latency: tails, fan-out and precompute

Averages hide the users who are angry. p50 tells you the typical request; p99 tells you what one in a hundred requests experiences — and for a page that makes many calls, that is most page loads.

Fan-out amplifies the tail

If one backend call exceeds its p99 with probability 1%, a request that waits on N independent parallel calls is slow whenever any of them is slow:

Engine: Back-of-envelopeDialect/Language: ArithmeticExecutable: Pseudocode
P(request slow) = 1 − (1 − p)^N         p = 0.01

N =   1   →  1%
N =  10   →  ~10%
N =  50   →  ~39%
N = 100   →  ~63%

So "every call is fast at p99" + fan-out of 100
      = the request's MEDIAN sees a tail event.

Mitigations, in order: reduce N (batch-get, co-locate data read together); tighten the component tail (GC pauses, compaction storms, noisy neighbours); hedged requests (after the p95 time, ask another replica, take the first answer — a few percent more load); timeouts with graceful degradation; and budget the tail explicitly across hops.

Precompute vs compute-on-read

Precompute (write-time)Compute-on-read
Read latencyOne lookup, predictableDepends on data volume touched; tail grows with it
FreshnessAs of the last pipeline run or stream updateAs of now
CostPay for every key, even those never readPay only for keys read, but at every read
FlexibilityNew question = new pipeline + backfillNew question = new query
FitsHigh QPS, fixed questions, bounded key spaceLow QPS, open-ended questions, huge key space with sparse reads

The usual answer is a hybrid: heavy aggregates in batch, short windows in a stream processor, cheap combinations on read. The senior move is to state the read/write ratio: a value written once a day and read 50,000 times a day wants precompute; a value read twice a month for a support tool does not.

8. Design: a serving layer with sub-100-ms latency

A common interview prompt: “The mobile app shows each user personalized stats and the ranking service needs user-level features on every request. Design the serving layer. p99 under 100 ms, about 20K QPS at peak.” Here is a full walkthrough in the order you should say it.

Step 1 — Requirements, asked not assumed

  • Read pattern: by user_id, whole feature vector (or a named subset). No range or ad-hoc queries on the hot path. Ranking may request features for one user plus up to 50 candidate items — ask.
  • Latency: 100 ms p99 is end-to-end for the caller. Carve a budget: say 15 ms for the feature service including the store, leaving the rest for the model and network.
  • Freshness: batch features daily (30-day aggregates) and a few streaming features at seconds to minutes (last-session activity). Ask which features have which SLA.
  • Correctness: stale is acceptable within the SLA; missing should fall back to defaults and be counted; wrong-user data is a severity-1 incident.
  • Scale: 200M users, ~40M daily active, ~1 KB per user, 20K QPS reads peak, availability target e.g. 99.9%.

Step 2 — Numbers

From Section 5: ~200 GB raw, ~1 TB replicated on disk; hot set ~40 GB; reads 20K QPS × 1 KB = 20 MB/s; the daily batch refresh at ~28K writes/s for two hours exceeds the read peak. Conclusion stated out loud: the store must be sized for concurrent refresh plus peak reads, or the refresh must be throttled, or it must not go through the online write path at all. That one sentence is the difference between an L4 and an L5 answer to this question.

Step 3 — Storage shape and key design

Point lookup by one key → key-value shape: a managed KV, a self-run wide-column cluster, or in-memory with persistence. Choose by operations capacity and cost model. Managed removes cluster operations; self-run gives cheaper sustained writes and bulk-load control; all-in-memory at ~400 GB pays RAM for 160M users who will not visit today.

  • Partition key: user_id (hashed). High cardinality, even traffic except for a handful of test/bot accounts — detect and rate-limit those rather than salt everyone.
  • Item layout: one item per user per feature group (user_id + group as sort key), so the daily batch group and the streaming group are written independently and never overwrite each other.
  • Values: compact encoding (a small binary or protobuf blob per group), with feature_version and computed_at fields. Readers need computed_at to detect staleness.
  • Item features for ranking: item-level features live in a separate table keyed by item_id; the 50-candidate lookup is one batch-get, not 50 calls.

Step 4 — Write path from lakehouse and stream

Batch features. Two options, and you should name both:

  • Streaming upserts from Spark. Simple, but 200M writes compete with live reads, readers see a yesterday/today mix mid-run, and a bug overwrites good values with no instant rollback.
  • Versioned bulk load + pointer swap (preferred at this scale). Build the snapshot as a new version (new table, key prefix, or pre-built store files), validate it (row count vs yesterday, null rates, key-feature distributions, a diffed sample of known users), then flip active_version. Rollback is flipping back; old versions expire. Cost: 2x storage during overlap.

Vendor note, hedged: some managed stores can import from object storage only into a new table (DynamoDB's S3 import at time of writing works that way), which conveniently matches the versioned-table pattern; wide-column stores can often stream pre-sorted files to skip the normal write path. Check your store's current import mechanics before promising either.

Streaming features. Flink computes windowed aggregates and upserts the streaming group. Writes must be idempotent — key by (user_id, group) and include the event-time watermark or a sequence number so a replay after restart does not regress a value (conditional write: only if incoming as_of > stored as_of). Exactly-once to an external KV is usually "at-least-once + idempotent upsert"; see Part 03.

Step 5 — Read path

  1. Feature service resolves active_version (cached locally, refreshed every few seconds).
  2. Checks an in-process LRU for the very hottest keys (seconds of TTL) — cheap protection against a single bot or celebrity account.
  3. Batch-gets batch group + streaming group (+ item features) from the store with a per-call timeout of a few ms and one hedged retry to another replica after the p95 time.
  4. On timeout or missing key: return documented defaults, flag features_degraded=true in the response so the model and dashboards can see it, and increment a metric. Never block the caller past its budget.
  5. Checks computed_at; if the batch group is older than its SLA, still serve but emit a staleness metric — a silent stale feature store is the failure that costs weeks of model quality before anyone notices.

Is a shared cache tier (Redis-style) needed? Only if the store cannot meet p99 at 20K QPS within budget, or if the cost per read favors it. With a KV store serving single-digit-millisecond p99 for 1 KB items, many teams skip it. Say that — then say what would make you add it.

Failure-first: what can fail in the serving layer?
FailureDetectRecoverPrevent recurrence
Hot key (bot account, load test user, celebrity)Per-key request metrics / store hot-partition metrics; throttling on one partition while table-level capacity is unused (bulk loaders writing in key order cause the same pattern)Rate-limit the offending caller; in-process cache for top keysTop-K key tracking with alerts; salting for known heavy keys; bot filtering upstream
Cache cold start after deploy or flushHit rate drops, store QPS steps up 10–20x, p99 climbsShift traffic back / slow the rollout; shed low-priority callersRolling deploys; pre-warm from the hot-key list; size the store for full miss traffic or document that it cannot survive it
Stale features (pipeline late or failed, pointer never flipped)computed_at age metric per group; version-age alertKeep serving last good version (it is still valid data); rerun pipelineFreshness SLO with paging; publish pipeline completion as an event, not an assumption
Bad batch version (bug writes zeros)Pre-flip validation; post-flip model score distribution shiftFlip pointer back — seconds, not a rebuildValidation gates in the load job; canary flip for a slice of traffic
Backfill or refresh overwhelms the storeWrite throttling; read p99 rises during the load windowPause/throttle the job; it is resumable if keyed by versionWrite-rate limiter in the loader; bulk-import path; schedule off-peak; separate capacity for the load
Stream replay regresses valuesFeature values move backwards in time; as_of decreasingReplay from a checkpoint with conditional writesConditional upsert on as_of; test replays in staging

Step 6 — Trade-offs and operations

Managed vs self-run store trades money for people-time and compaction tuning. Versioned snapshots trade 2x storage for instant rollback and consistent reads — worth it at this size. Defaults vs errors is decided per caller: ranking degrades, billing fails. Operate it with p50/p99 per hop, hit rate, degraded-response rate, version age and per-key heat on one dashboard, runbooks for pointer rollback and load throttling, and a staging game day that flushes the cache.

Drill · Serving latency

The feature service's p99 jumped from 40 ms to 900 ms the day a new "similar items" feature launched. p50 barely moved (6 ms → 8 ms). Store-side p99 per request looks unchanged. CPU on the feature service is fine.

STOP. Answer before revealing.

Reveal the diagnosis
  1. Observe Tail exploded, median did not, and each individual store call looks healthy. That pattern points at the number of calls per request, not the speed of each call.
  2. Hypothesize The new feature fetches features for ~80 similar items per request, issued as 80 separate parallel gets. With a per-call 1% tail, 1 − 0.99^80 ≈ 55% of requests now contain at least one slow call; with client retries on timeout, the slow ones get slower. A second candidate: connection pool exhaustion queuing calls in the client.
  3. Measure Trace one slow request: count store calls per request (before vs after launch), per-call latency distribution, and time spent waiting for a pooled connection. Compare calls-per-request histogram to the launch timestamp.
  4. Isolate Turn the feature flag off for 5% of traffic; if that cohort's p99 returns to ~40 ms, the fan-out is confirmed.
  5. Fix Replace 80 gets with one or two batch-gets; hedge the stragglers; cap candidates; set a per-request deadline so a slow item fetch drops that item instead of stalling the response; size the connection pool for the new concurrency.
  6. Prevent Track "store calls per request" as a first-class metric with an alert; require a latency budget review (calls × per-call tail) for features that add fan-out; load-test with the production p99 of dependencies, not their average.

9. Warehouse and lakehouse architecture compared

Section B shifts from point lookups to scans. Five architectures dominate interview conversations in 2026: Snowflake, BigQuery, Databricks (Delta, with Iceberg interoperability), Redshift, and an open stack such as Iceberg on object storage + a REST catalog + Trino and Spark. Treat them as five answers to three questions: where does data live, where does metadata live, and what do you pay for?

The comparison table (at time of writing, 2026 — verify against current docs)

DimensionSnowflakeBigQueryDatabricks / lakehouseRedshiftOpen Iceberg stack
Compute / storageSeparated; virtual warehouses (clusters) read shared storageSeparated; shared slot pool reads distributed storageSeparated; clusters / SQL warehouses read files in your cloud storageRA3 and Serverless separate them via managed storage; older node types coupledSeparated by construction; any engine, your buckets
Metadata: where / whoVendor's cloud services layer; not directly visibleVendor-managedDelta transaction log next to the data + Unity Catalog for governanceVendor-managed in the cluster / serviceMetadata and manifest files in your storage; catalog holds the current-pointer (REST, Glue, Polaris, Unity, Nessie…)
PruningMicro-partition min/max and other metadataPartitions (date/integer/ingestion) + clustering on up to a few columnsDelta file stats (min/max on a default set of leading columns) + partitions + clusteringZone maps on blocks + sort keysPartition transforms + manifest-level and file-level column stats
CachingResult cache (cloud services), local SSD cache on warehouses (lost on suspend)Query result cache; optional in-memory BI accelerationDisk cache on worker SSDs; result cache on SQL warehousesResult cache; local cache of hot managed-storage dataEngine-dependent (e.g. Trino filesystem cache); nothing by default
ClusteringNatural load order; optional clustering keys with automatic (billed) reclusteringClustered tables, reclustered in the backgroundLiquid clustering (newer) or Z-order via OPTIMIZESort keys (compound/interleaved/AUTO); vacuum re-sortsTable sort order; rewrite / compaction jobs you run
ConcurrencyMulti-cluster warehouses add clusters under queueingSlots shared across queries; reservations and autoscaling in editionsSQL warehouse autoscaling (clusters); job clusters per workloadWLM queues; concurrency scaling adds transient capacity; Serverless scales RPUsEngine-level (Trino coordinator/workers, Spark clusters); you scale them
TransactionsACID in the service; multi-statement transactionsACID per statement; multi-statement transactions supported; DML concurrency limits existDelta: optimistic concurrency with conflict detection at commitACID; serializable by default, snapshot isolation optionOptimistic concurrency: writer commits by atomic pointer swap in the catalog; losers retry
Serving patternBI via warehouses; result cache for repeated dashboards; not a point-lookup store (hybrid tables exist — check scope)BI and ad-hoc; BI acceleration for dashboardsSQL warehouses for BI; separate online stores for low-latency servingBI on provisioned capacity; predictable fixed workloadsTrino/Spark for BI and batch; export to KV or warehouse for serving
Cost behaviorCredits per warehouse-second while running (minimum on resume); size × timeOn-demand: bytes scanned; editions: slot capacity × timeDBUs + cloud VM cost (classic) or serverless DBUsNode-hours (provisioned) or RPU-hours (Serverless)Your compute + object storage + request costs + your people

Deep links for cost mechanics: Snowflake cost, result cache, clustering keys, Databricks cost, Delta caching, Redshift tuning, distribution and sort keys. For how open formats keep metadata and how catalogs arbitrate commits, see why open table formats exist and catalog architectures. For why columnar files prune at all, file format internals.

How to read the table in an interview

Do not recite it. Pull out the rows that change the answer. Three change behavior, not just price: the cost model (bytes scanned, running compute time and reserved capacity reward opposite habits), metadata ownership (vendor-owned means tight optimization and one engine; a catalog you control means many engines and you own compaction, snapshot expiry and conflicts), and clustering responsibility (who reclusters, and who pays, decides what the table performs like in six months).

2026 Interview Note

The platforms are converging on each other's features: Snowflake and BigQuery read and write Iceberg tables, Databricks' Unity Catalog serves Iceberg clients, Redshift queries open formats, and serverless options exist almost everywhere. So "Snowflake is closed, Databricks is open" is a 2021 answer. The 2026 answer asks which copy is authoritative, which catalog commits to it, and which engines are writers. Feature parity claims age fast; the architecture questions do not. Check the vendor docs for current support levels before claiming a specific Iceberg feature (v3 deletion vectors, row lineage) works on a specific engine.

10. Why the same data model behaves differently across platforms

A common interview prompt: “We're migrating the same star schema from platform A to platform B. Same tables, same SQL. Why might cost and performance change dramatically?” The answer is that a logical model does not specify physical layout, pruning metadata, caching, concurrency or billing — and those are exactly what differ.

Same logical thingWhere it behaves one wayWhere it behaves anotherMechanism
Analyst runs wide SELECT * with LIMIT 100On a running Snowflake warehouse: seconds of compute that was already paid forOn on-demand BigQuery: billed for every column's bytes in the scanned partitions; LIMIT does not reduce bytes on a non-clustered tableCompute-time vs bytes-scanned billing
Filter on customer_id = 123 (high cardinality)Clustered by customer_id: touches a handful of files/micro-partitionsLoaded in event-time order: min/max per file spans nearly all customers, so nothing prunes; full scanPruning works only if values are physically co-located
Stream of small updates (1,000 rows every minute)Warehouse with managed storage: the service merges behind the scenes (you still pay for it)Iceberg/Delta with copy-on-write: each commit rewrites files → thousands of small files and snapshots per day unless you compactFile immutability + who runs compaction
Dashboard benchmark: 200 msSecond run hits the result cache: no compute at allUnderlying data changed or a non-deterministic function (CURRENT_TIMESTAMP) is in the query: cache bypassed, true latency is 9 sResult caching; benchmarks that do not disable it lie
50 concurrent dashboard users at 9 a.m.Multi-cluster warehouse or concurrency scaling adds capacity (and cost)Fixed slot reservation: queries queue; or a single Trino cluster saturates its coordinatorConcurrency model
Nightly MERGE into a 5 TB tableEngine with row-level deletes / deletion vectors: touches few filesCopy-on-write without them: rewrites every file containing any matched rowDelete/update representation (delete files)
Join fact to dimension on customer_keyRedshift with both distributed on that key: co-located joinDifferent distribution style: data redistributed across nodes on every runPhysical distribution choices
“Why does the same model behave differently across warehouses?”
30 sec

Because a data model is logical and performance is physical. Platforms differ in how data is laid out and pruned, what is cached, how concurrency is added, and — above all — what is billed. The same query can be free on one platform and expensive on another, or fast only where the table happens to be clustered on the filter column.

2 min

Walk four mechanisms. Billing: bytes-scanned models punish wide selects and unpruned scans directly; compute-time models punish idle warehouses and long queries; reserved capacity makes marginal queries free until they queue. Pruning: all these engines skip files using min/max metadata, but that only helps if the filtered column is physically clustered — so a high-cardinality filter prunes on a clustered table and scans everything on one loaded in arrival order. Mutation: immutable files mean small updates either get merged by the service (billed, invisible) or create small files you must compact. Caching: result caches and local SSD caches make repeated queries look instant; a cold warehouse or changed data shows the true cost. Then give one concrete example from each.

Deep dive

Go into how each platform's metadata enables pruning: micro-partition metadata held by the service, partition and cluster metadata in BigQuery, Delta file stats collected for a default set of columns (so a filter on column 40 of a wide table may not prune unless stats are configured), Iceberg's two-level manifest list → manifest → file stats, Redshift zone maps per block ordered by sort key. Then the migration consequences: re-choose clustering keys for the new mechanism, rewrite queries that relied on caches or free wide scans, add compaction if moving to an open format, retune concurrency, and cost-model each query class before cutover.

Where to stop: billing, pruning, mutation, caching — one example each. Go deeper only on the platform the interviewer's company runs.

Drill · Warehouse cost

After migrating a BI dashboard from a Snowflake warehouse to on-demand BigQuery with the same tables and SQL, the monthly bill for that dashboard is 8x the estimate. Query latency is fine. The estimate was made by running each tile's query once.

STOP. Answer before revealing.

Reveal the diagnosis
  1. Observe Latency fine, cost high: the problem is bytes scanned × number of executions, not speed.
  2. Hypothesize (a) Tiles use SELECT * or wide column lists that were harmless under compute-time billing; (b) tables are not partitioned/clustered on the dashboard's filters, so each run scans the full date range; (c) the one-off estimate hit a cache or a small date range, while production runs with auto-refresh every few minutes per viewer; (d) a filter wraps the partition column in a function, defeating partition pruning.
  3. Measure Job history: bytes billed per query, executions per day, cache-hit ratio, top queries by bytes; compare with a dry-run estimate per tile.
  4. Isolate Rank tiles by bytes × executions — typically one or two tiles account for most of the cost.
  5. Fix Select needed columns; partition by date and cluster by the common filter columns; rewrite predicates to hit the partition column directly; precompute an aggregate table the dashboard reads; reduce refresh frequency or rely on result caching; evaluate capacity-based pricing if the workload is steady.
  6. Prevent Per-query byte limits (maximum bytes billed) on dashboard service accounts; cost-per-tile review in the migration checklist; cost estimates that multiply by real execution frequency, not a single run.

11. Choosing between Snowflake, BigQuery and a lakehouse

A common interview prompt: “Choose between Snowflake, BigQuery and a lakehouse for this workload.” The interviewer is not waiting for your favourite. They are waiting to see which requirements you extract and how you weigh them. Use the same six axes every time:

  1. Workload shape: ad-hoc interactive BI, scheduled batch ELT, streaming ingest, ML feature engineering, point serving? Spiky or steady?
  2. Concurrency: how many simultaneous queries at peak, and how much queueing is acceptable?
  3. Open formats / multi-engine: must Spark, Trino, Flink, Python and a warehouse read (or write) the same tables? Is avoiding a proprietary storage format a hard requirement or a preference?
  4. Team skills: SQL-only analytics engineers, or a platform team comfortable operating Spark, catalogs and compaction?
  5. Governance: row/column security, lineage, data residency, sharing with partners; which catalog is the policy enforcement point?
  6. Cost model fit: spiky and sparse favors pay-per-use; steady and heavy favors reserved capacity; huge scans with few users favor cheap compute you control.

Workload A — 40 analysts, SQL-first, spiky BI on a single cloud

Stated: ~5 TB of data, dbt-managed models, 40 analysts and a few dashboards, usage concentrated in business hours with heavy Monday mornings, no Spark skills on the team, no requirement for other engines to write the data.

Reasoning: a managed SQL warehouse fits — the team's skill is SQL, the workload is BI/ELT, and nobody needs multi-engine writes. Between Snowflake-style and BigQuery-style, both meet the governance needs; the deciding axis is the cost model against the team's habits. Spiky usage with idle nights suits both auto-suspending warehouses and on-demand billing — but wide exploratory queries over unpartitioned data are punished by bytes-scanned billing, and oversized never-suspending warehouses by compute-time billing. Weigh the existing cloud (egress, identity), then run a two-week proof of concept on the ten most expensive real queries, caches disabled. Answer shape: "Managed warehouse; which one is a cost-model and ecosystem decision I'd make from a PoC, not a capability gap."

Workload B — multi-engine platform, ML and streaming, open-format mandate

Stated: 800 TB, Flink writes streaming events, Spark runs feature engineering and training data prep, analysts want SQL, a second business unit uses a different warehouse and must read the same tables, and leadership mandates no lock-in to one vendor's storage format.

Reasoning: several writers across engines is the defining requirement. That makes the table format and the catalog the centre of the architecture: Iceberg (or Delta with Iceberg-compatible reads) on object storage, a single catalog that arbitrates commits and enforces access policy, and engines chosen per workload — Flink for ingest, Spark for heavy transforms, a SQL engine (Trino, Databricks SQL, or a warehouse reading Iceberg) for BI. The cost is operational: someone owns small-file compaction, snapshot expiry, concurrent-writer conflicts (conflict spiral) and catalog availability — or you buy a managed lakehouse platform that does. Answer shape: "Lakehouse on an open table format with one authoritative catalog; the warehouse becomes a reader. I'm buying engine freedom and paying in table maintenance."

Workload C — steady heavy batch plus high-concurrency embedded analytics

Stated: a SaaS product embeds customer-facing analytics: 2,000 tenants, 300 concurrent queries at peak, each filtering by tenant_id and a date range, p95 under 2 seconds; plus a nightly 3-hour batch. Traffic is steady 18 hours a day. Finance wants predictable monthly spend.

Reasoning: steady, heavy, predictable load plus a budget-predictability requirement favors reserved capacity (slot reservations, provisioned clusters, or committed spend) over per-query or per-byte billing. Concurrency is the hard requirement: workload isolation so one tenant's heavy query cannot starve others (multi-cluster warehouses, per-workload reservations, WLM queues), and a layout where every query prunes by tenant_id then date. Honest additional answer: 2-second p95 at 300 concurrent queries is at the edge of what warehouses are designed for; the tiles customers load most should be precomputed per tenant into aggregate tables or a serving store (Section 8), and the warehouse handles drill-downs. Answer shape: "Reserved-capacity warehouse with workload isolation and tenant-clustered tables, plus a precomputed serving layer for the hottest tiles — the platform matters less than not asking a scan engine to be a point-lookup engine."

Interviewer pushes back

You: “For Workload A, I'd use Snowflake.”

Interviewer: “Why not BigQuery?”

Strong answer: “On capability, BigQuery would work — both are managed, SQL-first, separate compute from storage, and meet the governance needs. The difference is the cost model against this team's habits and the ecosystem we already run. If they're on GCP already, identity, networking and egress tip toward BigQuery. If analysts write many wide exploratory queries over large tables, bytes-scanned billing makes every one visible on the bill unless we partition, cluster and set per-query byte limits; a compute-time model with aggressive auto-suspend caps that behaviour by warehouse size instead. I said Snowflake assuming AWS and exploratory habits — I'd validate with a PoC on our ten most expensive queries with caches off, and I'd change my answer if the data says so.”

Weak answer: “Snowflake is faster” or “I've used it before.” Brand preference and anecdotal speed claims are not requirements, and the next question will be about a benchmark you cannot cite.

Cross-cutting traps: benchmarks with result caches on (disable them, run cold and warm, use the real query mix); choosing on read speed and then failing on small updates, MERGE or streaming ingest; putting a warehouse behind a customer-facing API at thousands of QPS; and treating governance as an afterthought — in a multi-engine lakehouse, policy must live in the catalog every engine honours (Part 10). Every choice locks something in; name which lock-in you accept.

L5 Interview CardServing Systems & Warehouse Architecture
Must know
  • Storage families are access shapes: key-value, wide-column, document, relational, search, cache — pick from the read pattern.
  • Partition key = what every query names with equality; sort/clustering key = what it ranges over.
  • Cardinality spreads keys, not traffic; hot keys need salting, pre-aggregation or caching.
  • Global secondary indexes are usually eventually consistent; R + W > N for quorum overlap.
  • LSM vs B-tree: write vs read vs space amplification; compaction and tombstones are the LSM tax.
  • Cache-aside needs stampede protection, TTL jitter and negative caching; a cache must be survivable when cold.
  • Fan-out amplifies the tail: 1 − (1 − p)^N.
  • Warehouses differ in metadata ownership, pruning mechanism, caching, concurrency and billing — hedge every vendor detail.
Must be able to explain
  1. Given an access pattern, which storage shape fits and what is the key?
  2. Why does p99 explode when a feature adds fan-out, even if each call is fast?
  3. Why might the same logical model cost 8x more on another platform?
Must be able to draw

The versioned serving path:

lakehouse ─▶ Spark ─▶ bulk load v=N ─┐
Kafka ─▶ Flink ─▶ upsert stream grp ─┤
                                    KV store
app ─▶ feature svc (LRU, timeout) ──┘
        active_version pointer ↺ rollback
Must be able to code
  • Cache-aside with single-flight, TTL jitter and negative caching.
  • A salted counter: sharded write, fan-out read and merge.
  • A wide-column table definition for "last N events per user" with a bounded partition and TTL.
Must be able to debug
  • p99 40 ms → 900 ms after a launch, p50 flat: fan-out, not slow calls.
  • Throttling at 30% table utilization during a nightly load: hot partition from ordered writes.
Numbers that matter
  • 200M keys × 1 KB = 200 GB raw; ×2 overhead ×3 replicas ≈ 1.2 TB.
  • 200M writes in 2 h ≈ 28K writes/s — often more than read peak.
  • 1% per-call tail, 50-way fan-out → ~39% of requests slow; 100-way → ~63%.
  • 95% hit rate → a cache flush is a ~20x step in store load.
  • Memory is roughly an order of magnitude or more pricier per GB than SSD, which is pricier than object storage: cache the hot set, not the dataset.
Classic traps
  • Naming a product before asking for the read pattern, QPS and item size.
  • "Add nodes" as the fix for a hot key.
  • Benchmarking warehouses with result caches on, or estimating cost from a single run.
30-second answer

“How do you choose where data is served from?” From the access pattern. Point lookups by key at high QPS go to a key-value store keyed on what the caller always knows, with a cache only if skew or cost justifies it. Scans and ad-hoc analytics go to a columnar warehouse or lakehouse, chosen by workload shape, multi-engine needs, team skills and cost model — never by brand.

2-minute answer

I start with four questions: how is it read, how much and how often, how fresh, and how stable is the query pattern. Fixed high-QPS lookups want precomputed data in a partitioned KV or wide-column store, keyed so each request hits one partition; I check for hot keys and size the store for the bulk refresh as well as reads, preferring versioned loads with a pointer flip for rollback. I budget the p99 per hop and minimize fan-out because tails multiply. Open-ended analytics want a scan engine; there the decision is about who writes the tables (several engines → open format and one catalog), how concurrency is added, and whether the billing model — bytes scanned, compute time or reserved capacity — matches the workload's shape. Then I name the failure modes: hot key, cold cache, stale features, backfill overload, lost pruning.

Deep-dive follow-up

“Your versioned bulk load doubles storage and the new version takes 3 hours to build. The streaming group keeps updating the old version's users meanwhile. How do you guarantee no streaming update is lost at flip time?”

Staff+ follow-up

“Three teams run three warehouses and a lakehouse, each with its own copy of customer data. Design the target state: which copy is authoritative, which catalog commits, how serving stores are fed, and how you migrate without a big-bang cutover.”
