Part 17

Data Engineering for AI Systems

Quick refresh10 minInterview study45 minDeep practice70 min
Last technically reviewed September 2026
Covers unstructured ingestion, ACL propagation, chunking, embedding pipelines, vector indexes (HNSW, IVF, PQ), metadata filtering, re-embedding cutovers, RAG data quality, training/serving skew, feature freshness SLAs, answer-level lineage, erasure propagation, AI pipeline cost
Versions referenced PostgreSQL 16/17 with pgvector 0.8.x, OpenSearch k-NN, FAISS, Feast (all at time of writing, 2026)
Primary references pgvector · FAISS wiki · OpenSearch k-NN · Feast docs · OpenLineage
Known implementation differences Vector stores differ most in how they combine metadata filters with ANN search and how they handle deletes; never assume one product's behaviour transfers to another.

This chapter is not about prompts, agents or model choice. It is about the pipelines underneath them. The interviewer is testing whether you can treat documents, chunks and vectors as data with keys, versions, owners, freshness and lineage, and whether you notice that an AI system fails in exactly the places a data pipeline fails: stale inputs, duplicate rows, broken joins, missing access control and costs nobody modelled.

1. What actually changes for a data engineer

The discipline barely changes: idempotency, incremental processing, contracts, backfills, lineage and cost still decide survival. The shape of the data and the meaning of "correct" change.

Classic pipelineAI data pipelineWhy it matters
Unit is a row with a primary keyUnit is a document, split into chunks, each carrying a vectorYou now own three keys (document, version, chunk) and a derived artifact (the embedding) whose identity depends on a model
Quality = completeness, validity, freshness of rowsQuality = retrieval quality: did the right chunk come back for the question?A pipeline can be green on every row-level check and still return the wrong answer
Lineage stops at a table or dashboardLineage has to reach an individual answer"Which documents produced this answer?" is an audit, legal and debugging question
Access control lives in the warehouseAccess control must travel with every chunk into retrievalIf it does not, the model will summarise a document the user was never allowed to open
Recompute is cheap relative to storageRecompute (OCR, embeddings) is often the dominant costChange detection and "don't redo work" become first-class design goals
Transformations are deterministic SQLSome steps are model calls: versioned, rate-limited, non-free, occasionally non-deterministicThe model version becomes part of the data's key

The model is a consumer. Your job is to make what it consumes current, permitted, de-duplicated, versioned and traceable. Opening an AI design answer with a vector database name skips the same step as opening a batch design with "Spark".

“How does RAG change data pipelines?”
30 sec

Retrieval-augmented generation turns documents into a serving dataset. The pipeline now extracts, chunks and embeds documents, and loads them into an index the model queries at answer time. The data problems are familiar ones: freshness, duplicates, deletes, access control and lineage. But they now surface as wrong or leaked answers, not as wrong numbers on a dashboard.

2 min

Three things change. First, the key: a chunk is identified by document, document version and position, and its vector is also keyed by embedding model version, because vectors from different models are not comparable. Second, quality: row checks are necessary but not sufficient. You need a golden question set that asserts the right chunks are retrieved, and you run it like a regression suite on every chunking, model or index change. Third, obligations: ACLs and deletions have to propagate from source to index to caches, and every answer should log the chunk ids and versions it used so you can explain it later. Operationally it is an incremental ELT pipeline with an expensive transform in the middle, so change detection by content hash is what keeps the cost sane.

Deep dive

Name the failure at each stage. Extraction: scanned PDFs silently yield empty text. Chunking: boundary changes re-key everything. Embedding: retries demand idempotent upserts. Index: deletes are tombstones, and filtered ANN can return fewer than k. Retrieval: log chunk ids, versions, scores, model and prompt versions. Then the quality gate: no index is promoted unless golden-set recall@k matches production, checked automatically, not by someone eyeballing ten answers.

Where to stop: when you have named keys, freshness, ACLs, lineage and the golden-set gate. Don't drift into prompt engineering unless asked.

2. Unstructured ingestion

Most AI data work is ingestion work, from sources that were never designed to be extracted from.

2.1 Formats and what breaks

Source typeExtraction concernSilent failure to guard against
Digital PDF (text layer)Reading order across columns, headers/footers repeated on every page, hyphenation, tables flattened into word soupTwo-column layout interleaved line by line; footer text ("Confidential — page 3") repeated in every chunk
Scanned PDF / imageNeeds OCR; quality depends on scan resolution, skew and languageNo text layer, so the parser returns an empty string and the pipeline "succeeds" with zero chunks
Tables (in PDFs, HTML, spreadsheets)Structure matters more than text; row/column headers carry the meaningA cell value like "30" retrieved without its header ("days notice") is useless or misleading
Audio / video transcriptsSpeech-to-text quality, speaker diarization, timestampsSpeaker labels lost, so "we will not refund" cannot be attributed; no timestamps, so a citation cannot point to the moment

Classify before you parse (digital vs scanned per page, not per file), then measure what came out: characters per page, OCR confidence, tables, language. Extraction without output metrics gets debugged from user complaints.

2.2 The metadata that must travel with every document

Metadata makes the system correct, filterable, auditable and deletable. Capture it at ingest; you cannot reconstruct it later.

FieldPurpose
source_uri + source_systemCitation, re-fetch, deletion lookup
doc_id (stable, derived from source identity, not from content)Joins across versions; the key that erasure requests resolve to
version / etag / source_modified_atChange detection and "which version did we answer from?"
content_hash (of normalised extracted text)Skip re-embedding when content is unchanged even if the etag moved
owner, acl (principals or groups allowed to read)Retrieval-time filtering; the security boundary
language, mime_type, page/timestamp offsetsRouting to the right extractor and embedder, precise citations
effective_from / effective_to / status (draft, active, retired)Excluding superseded policies; the fix for the most common RAG incident
ingested_at, extractor_versionFreshness monitoring and targeted re-extraction after a parser bug

2.3 Change detection by content hash

Etags and modified_at lie a little: a permissions change or a re-save bumps them with no change to the text. With an expensive transform downstream, detect change at three levels.

  1. Cheap signal: etag or modified_at tells you what to re-fetch.
  2. Authoritative signal: a hash of the normalised extracted text (whitespace collapsed, boilerplate stripped) tells you what to re-chunk and re-embed. If the hash is unchanged, update metadata (ACL, status) in place and stop.
  3. Per-chunk hash: after re-chunking a changed document, hash each chunk. Chunks whose hash already exists under the same embedding model reuse the stored vector. An edit to page 40 of a 60-page manual should re-embed a handful of chunks, not all of them.

Note the asymmetry: an ACL-only change must still propagate immediately, even though it costs no embedding work. Metadata updates and content updates are separate paths with separate SLAs.

2.4 Access control must travel with the document

This is where AI systems leak data. The source enforces permissions when a human opens a file. Copy the text into an index and that enforcement is gone unless you carry it. An unfiltered shared index will hand the model an HR investigation file to answer an intern's question, and the model will summarise it well.

  • Propagate ACLs onto every chunk as filterable metadata (allowed groups), and filter at retrieval using the caller's identity resolved server-side, never a group list from the client.
  • Store groups, resolve membership at query time. Denormalising user ids onto chunks means every membership change rewrites chunks.
  • Revocation is a security fix. Give ACL changes their own lane and a tighter, monitored SLA than content freshness.
  • Caches are part of the boundary. An answer cache keyed only by question text will serve a director's answer to a contractor. Key caches by permission scope, or don't share them across users.
  • Too complex to mirror? (per-item sharing, inherited folders) Check the final top-k against the source system's authorisation API. It's slower, and it's the only thing that is exactly right.

Governance background is in Part 10 PII handling and auditability. The point here is narrower: ACL propagation is a pipeline requirement with a freshness SLA, not a policy document.

3. Chunking is a data transformation

Chunking splits a document into the units you embed and retrieve. Treat it like any other transformation: it has inputs, a deterministic output, a version, tests and a blast radius when it changes.

3.1 Strategies

StrategyHow it worksGood forBreaks when
Fixed-size with overlapSplit every N tokens, overlapping by M so a sentence cut at a boundary appears in both chunksUniform prose, fast baseline, easy to reason about costHeadings get separated from their content; a table is split mid-row
Structure-awareSplit on document structure (headings, sections, list items, slides, transcript turns), then cap sizeManuals, policies, wikis, anything with headingsExtraction lost the structure (flat PDFs), or sections are wildly uneven
SemanticSplit where adjacent sentence embeddings diverge (topic shifts)Long unstructured text like transcripts and essaysCosts an embedding pass just to chunk; output is less predictable and harder to keep stable across versions
Parent–childRetrieve on small chunks, return the enclosing larger section as contextPrecise matching with enough surrounding contextTwo levels of ids to keep consistent

A sensible default: structure-aware splitting with a size cap and modest overlap, each chunk prefixed with its heading path ("Travel Policy › Reimbursement › International"). The prefix is cheap and fixes many "right paragraph, missing context" misses. The right size is measured against the golden set, not asserted.

3.2 Tables are not prose

A flattened table embeds badly and chunks worse. Serialise each row with its headers ("Region: EMEA | Notice period: 30 days"), keep small tables whole, or load structured tables into a real table and answer numeric questions with SQL. "What is the notice period for EMEA contractors?" may be a lookup, not a similarity search. Saying so is an L5 signal.

3.3 Stable, deterministic chunk ids

The chunk id is the primary key of the vector upsert, the retrieval log, the citation and the deletion. It must be deterministic. Random UUIDs make every re-run a duplicate insert. A workable scheme: chunk_id = hash(doc_id, doc_version, chunker_version, ordinal_or_offset), plus a separate content_hash of the text. The id says where a chunk came from; the content hash says whether you already have a vector for this text.

The consequence people miss: re-chunking invalidates embeddings. Change size, overlap or the split rule and every boundary moves, every id and content hash changes, and the whole corpus must be re-embedded. A chunker change is a costed backfill with schema-migration controls: version it, build a new index, evaluate, cut over (5.4).

Engine: any (library-agnostic)Language: Python 3.11+Executable: Illustrative — adapt to your embedder and store
import hashlib
from dataclasses import dataclass

CHUNKER_VERSION = "struct-v3"      # bump on ANY rule change: it re-keys everything
EMBED_MODEL = "embed-m2@1024"      # model id + dims; part of the vector key

def h(*parts: str) -> str:
    return hashlib.sha256("\x1f".join(parts).encode()).hexdigest()[:32]

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Chunk:
    chunk_id: str        # WHERE it came from (deterministic)
    content_hash: str    # WHAT it says (for vector reuse)
    doc_id: str
    doc_version: str
    ordinal: int
    text: str
    acl_groups: tuple[str, ...]

def chunk_document(doc_id: str, doc_version: str, sections: list[tuple[str, str]],
                   acl_groups: tuple[str, ...], max_chars: int = 2000) -> list[Chunk]:
    """Structure-aware: split by section, cap size, prefix the heading path."""
    out, ordinal = [], 0
    for heading_path, body in sections:
        for start in range(0, max(len(body), 1), max_chars):
            text = f"{heading_path}\n{body[start:start + max_chars]}"
            out.append(Chunk(
                chunk_id=h(doc_id, doc_version, CHUNKER_VERSION, str(ordinal)),
                content_hash=h(text),
                doc_id=doc_id, doc_version=doc_version, ordinal=ordinal,
                text=text, acl_groups=acl_groups))
            ordinal += 1
    return out

def sync_document(store, embedder, chunks: list[Chunk],
                  doc_id: str, doc_version: str) -> None:
    """Idempotent: safe to re-run after a crash or a retry storm."""
    # 1. Reuse vectors for text we have already embedded with THIS model.
    known = store.vectors_by_content_hash(
        [c.content_hash for c in chunks], EMBED_MODEL)
    todo = [c for c in chunks if c.content_hash not in known]
    new_vecs = embedder.embed_batch([c.text for c in todo])   # retries/backoff live here
    vectors = {**known, **{c.content_hash: v for c, v in zip(todo, new_vecs)}}

    # 2. Upsert by (chunk_id, embed_model): a re-run overwrites, never duplicates.
    store.upsert([(c.chunk_id, EMBED_MODEL, vectors[c.content_hash], c)
                  for c in chunks])

    # 3. Retire chunks from older versions of this doc AFTER the new ones are live,
    #    so a reader never sees the document missing.
    store.delete_where(doc_id=doc_id, doc_version_not=doc_version,
                       embed_model=EMBED_MODEL)

What to point at: version constants in the key, vector reuse by content hash, upsert by (chunk_id, embed_model), and old versions retired only after new ones land, so a document is never missing. The price is a moment where both versions are retrievable. If that matters (legal text), filter on a current_version pointer at query time.

4. Embedding pipelines

4.1 Batch vs incremental

Same trade-off as any ELT pipeline (Part 02, Part 03), with a far more expensive transform. Backfill is batch and throughput-bound by rate limits, so plan it in days for large corpora (section 9). Steady state is incremental from a change feed or etag poll, so work scales with churn, not corpus size. Priority lanes let deletes and ACL revocations jump the queue: an edit can wait an hour, a revoked permission cannot.

4.2 Idempotency and retries

  • Upsert by deterministic key, never append. A retried batch overwrites itself.
  • Batch and throttle: token bucket plus exponential backoff with jitter, budgeted in tokens per minute as well as requests (providers typically limit both; check current limits).
  • Checkpoint per document ("doc_id at version V embedded with model M", the key you already have) so a crashed backfill resumes rather than restarts.
  • Dead-letter, don't drop. Extraction and embedding failures go to a DLQ with error, extractor version and source URI. Alert on DLQ growth: nobody reports a missing document they never knew existed.
  • Re-split oversized chunks; never truncate silently.

4.3 The embedding model version is part of the key

Vectors from different embedding models, or different versions or dimension settings of "the same" model, live in different spaces. Cosine similarity across them is a number that means nothing. So: store embed_model (id, version, dims, normalisation) in the key; never mix vector spaces in one index; assert at query time that the query was embedded with the index's model; treat a model upgrade as a full backfill with a migration plan; and pin hosted model versions explicitly, because an alias the provider moves forward is a silent vector-space change.

4.4 Backfills and re-embedding cost

A new model, a new chunker or a cleaning change that alters chunk text each forces a full re-embed. Before approving one, ask what it buys, measured on the golden set. "The new model is better" is a hypothesis until evaluated. Scope backfills where you can: an extractor bug affecting only scanned PDFs re-processes extractor_version = X AND scanned = true, which is only possible because you recorded those fields at ingest.

Interviewer pushes back

You: “To keep it fresh, we re-embed everything nightly.”

Interviewer: “The corpus is 50 million chunks. Walk me through that night.”

Strong answer: “Then I withdraw it. At a few hundred tokens a chunk that's ten to twenty billion tokens a night. It won't fit a night at any plausible rate limit, it pays full cost daily to pick up roughly 1% churn, and an edit at 9am still isn't visible until tomorrow. Incremental is right: a change feed finds changed documents, content hashes skip false changes, per-chunk hashes reuse vectors, and deletes and ACL changes take a priority lane. Full re-embeds happen only for a model or chunker change, into a new index, gated by the golden set. Freshness becomes a measured per-source SLA: source edit to retrievable.”

Weak answer: “We'll parallelise it across more workers.” That scales the bill and still hits the provider's rate limit, and the freshness is still wrong.

5. Vector data: indexes, filtering, freshness, placement

5.1 ANN intuition

Exact search is O(N·d) per query: fine at hundreds of thousands of vectors, ruinous at hundreds of millions. ANN indexes trade a little recall for orders of magnitude less work. You need the intuition for three families, not the papers.

TechniqueIntuitionCostsTuning knob (conceptually)
HNSW (graph)A layered "small world" graph: start at a coarse top layer, greedily walk toward the query, and descend layers to refineHigh memory (full vectors plus graph links, usually RAM-resident); slow, memory-hungry builds; deletes are awkwardNeighbours per node and search breadth: more means higher recall, more memory and latency
IVF (clustering)k-means partitions the space into lists; a query searches only the nearest few listsNeeds training on representative data; recall drops if the data distribution drifts from the training sampleNumber of lists and number probed per query
PQ (compression)Split each vector into sub-vectors and replace each with a codebook id: a 4 KB vector becomes tens of bytesLossy distances lower recall; usually paired with a re-rank on full vectorsCode size: smaller means cheaper and less accurate

The triangle is recall vs latency vs memory; every knob moves along it. Don't quote one library's starting parameters as a law. Tune by measuring recall@k against exact search on a sample of your own data at your latency budget. That sentence is the whole L5 answer to "how do you tune HNSW?"

5.2 Metadata filtering: pre-filter vs post-filter

Real queries are "nearest vectors the user may read, from active documents, in EMEA". How a store combines filters with ANN is the most important, least documented difference between products.

  • Post-filter: ANN returns the top k, then the filter drops non-matching results. If the user can read 0.1% of the corpus, you get zero or two results instead of ten, and nothing errors.
  • Pre-filter: restrict candidates first, then search among them. Correct, but excluding most nodes disconnects an HNSW graph, degrading toward brute force.
  • Filter-aware / iterative search: the engine keeps expanding until it finds k matches (pgvector 0.8 added iterative index scans, for example; check current docs for your engine).
  • Partitioning: a separate index per tenant for hard boundaries. Structural, unforgettable, and per-tenant deletion is trivial.

An ACL filter that returns zero results is a quality bug; one that is skipped is a security bug. Test both, with narrow-permission users in the golden set.

5.3 Freshness, deletes and tombstones

ANN structures are append-friendly and delete-hostile: removing a graph node leaves neighbours pointing at it. So most engines tombstone deletes, filter them at query time and physically remove them at compaction or rebuild. Three consequences follow. Heavy churn degrades latency and recall until compaction, so periodic rebuilds are routine operations. "Deleted" in the API is not "gone from disk", which matters for erasure (section 8). And freshness is end-to-end, source edit → detected → embedded → indexed → visible, including any engine refresh interval. Measure it with a canary: edit a known test document on a schedule and time until retrieval returns the new version.

5.4 Re-embedding strategy: dual-write, shadow eval, cutover

A model or chunker change is a blue/green migration of a derived dataset (release mechanics in Part 14):

  1. Build new: backfill a new index keyed by the new versions; the old one keeps serving.
  2. Dual-write: incremental changes go to both, so the new index isn't stale on arrival.
  3. Shadow eval: golden set against both (recall@k, MRR), plus replayed real queries with retrieval diffs.
  4. Cutover: flip the read alias and the query embedder in the same deploy.
  5. Keep the old index for a rollback window, then delete it (an erasure-relevant event).

5.5 Where vectors live

Decide on scale, filtering needs and operations, in that order. Product names come last.

OptionFits whenWatch out for
Postgres + pgvectorUp to tens of millions of vectors; Postgres already in place; transactional joins with ACLs and statusSingle-node HNSW memory, build times, vacuum under churn
Search engine (OpenSearch, Elasticsearch, Solr and similar)Hybrid lexical + vector search, facets; a search cluster already runRefresh and segment merges govern freshness and delete cost
Dedicated vector databaseHundreds of millions of vectors, high QPS, built-in quantisation and tieringOne more stateful system to secure, back up and keep consistent
Lakehouse table (Iceberg/Delta) + batch similarity or an attached indexOffline dedup, clustering, evaluation; the durable system of recordNot a low-latency serving path by itself

A pattern that ages well: the lakehouse is the system of record for documents, chunks, metadata and vectors, and the serving index is a rebuildable projection. A rebuild, engine migration or new model becomes a re-projection, not archaeology. Broader serving-store choices: Part 16.

Engine: PostgreSQL 16/17 + pgvector 0.8.xDialect: PostgreSQL SQLExecutable: Illustrative — adapt to your dialect
CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS vector;

-- One table per embedding model/dimension: vector spaces never share an index.
CREATE TABLE chunk_vec_m2_1024 (
  chunk_id      text        NOT NULL,
  doc_id        text        NOT NULL,
  doc_version   text        NOT NULL,
  content_hash  text        NOT NULL,
  acl_groups    text[]      NOT NULL,
  status        text        NOT NULL,          -- active | retired
  effective_to  timestamptz,
  embedding     vector(1024) NOT NULL,
  PRIMARY KEY (chunk_id)
);

CREATE INDEX ON chunk_vec_m2_1024 USING hnsw (embedding vector_cosine_ops);
CREATE INDEX ON chunk_vec_m2_1024 USING gin (acl_groups);

-- Idempotent write: a retry overwrites, never duplicates.
INSERT INTO chunk_vec_m2_1024 AS t
  (chunk_id, doc_id, doc_version, content_hash, acl_groups, status, effective_to, embedding)
VALUES ($1, $2, $3, $4, $5, $6, $7, $8)
ON CONFLICT (chunk_id) DO UPDATE
  SET acl_groups = EXCLUDED.acl_groups, status = EXCLUDED.status,
      effective_to = EXCLUDED.effective_to, embedding = EXCLUDED.embedding
  WHERE t.content_hash IS DISTINCT FROM EXCLUDED.content_hash
     OR t.acl_groups   IS DISTINCT FROM EXCLUDED.acl_groups
     OR t.status       IS DISTINCT FROM EXCLUDED.status
     OR t.effective_to IS DISTINCT FROM EXCLUDED.effective_to;

-- Retrieval: ACL + lifecycle filter, cosine distance. Groups come from the
-- server-side identity lookup, never from the client.
-- $query_vec / $caller_groups stand for driver bind parameters.
SET hnsw.iterative_scan = relaxed_order;   -- keep scanning until LIMIT is met
SELECT chunk_id, doc_id, doc_version, embedding <=> $query_vec AS distance
FROM   chunk_vec_m2_1024
WHERE  acl_groups && $caller_groups
  AND  status = 'active'
  AND  (effective_to IS NULL OR effective_to > now())
ORDER  BY embedding <=> $query_vec
LIMIT  10;

Version-specific: hnsw.iterative_scan exists from pgvector 0.8; without it a selective WHERE behaves like a post-filter and can return fewer than 10 rows. The distance operator must match the index's operator class or the index isn't used. Check current pgvector docs.

Interviewer pushes back

You: “Simplest thing: put every document from every team into one vector index.”

Interviewer: “Legal wants their privileged documents in there too. And ML wants to trial a new embedding model next month.”

Strong answer: “Then 'one index' has two problems. Security: a shared index is only safe if every query carries a mandatory ACL filter and the filter is correct under ANN, which means no post-filter that returns empty results and no code path that forgets it. For privileged material I'd make the boundary structural, a separate index or partition that the general retrieval path cannot reach, so a missing WHERE clause can't leak it. Model versions: the new model's vectors live in a different space, so they can't share the index. We build a parallel index, dual-write, evaluate on the golden set, then flip an alias. So the real answer is one logical corpus with one system-of-record table, projected into as many physical indexes as the security boundaries and model versions require.”

Weak answer: “We'll add a team field and filter on it.” That's right for convenience filtering and wrong as the only line between a privileged memo and an intern's chat window. It also says nothing about the model change.

6. RAG data quality

Row-level checks from Part 12 still apply, but users feel failures at the retrieval level. Name each, and give it a detector.

FailureWhat it looks likeHow to detectFix at the data layer
Stale documentAnswer cites last year's policyPer-source lag monitor; canary edits; chunks whose source has a newer versionIncremental sync; lifecycle metadata (status, effective_to) filtered at retrieval
Incorrect chunk (boundary cut)Answer quotes half a rule; a number without its unit or headerGolden-set failures clustered on tables and long sections; chunks ending mid-sentenceStructure-aware chunking, heading-path prefixes, table serialisation, parent–child retrieval
Duplicate / near-duplicate chunksTop-k filled with copies from mirrors or old versionsExact: content hash. Near-dup: MinHash/LSH on shingles, or vector similarity above a threshold. Share of top-k from one clusterCanonicalise mirrors to one doc_id; only current versions retrievable; query-time collapse as backstop
Missing provenanceAnswer cannot cite a source, or cites a URI that 404sNot-null constraints on source_uri, doc_version, chunk_id; link checksReject at load time: a contract, not a hope
Conflicting sourcesWiki says 30 days, signed policy PDF says 45Golden questions with authoritative answers; high-scoring chunks from different sources disagreeingSource authority in metadata (policy system beats wiki); surface conflicts with both citations
Extraction holeSome documents never appear in any answerZero-chunk docs; chars-per-page anomalies; DLQ size; docs never retrieved in 90 daysOCR fallback; re-extraction by extractor_version

6.1 Golden question sets are regression tests

A golden set is a curated list of questions with the documents that should be retrieved. It is the retrieval pipeline's test suite, and it turns "the answers feel worse" into a number.

  • Build it from reality: anonymised real questions and owner-written ones, including hard cases: tables, narrow-ACL users, recent edits, retired policies that must not be retrieved.
  • Measure retrieval separately from generation: recall@k and MRR for retrieval, answer correctness end to end. Right retrieval with a wrong answer isn't your pipeline; wrong retrieval is.
  • Gate on it: a drop beyond tolerance blocks any chunker, model or index cutover, like a failing data contract (Part 15).
  • Key it to stable ids, and version it: reference doc_id or content anchors, not chunk ids, which change on re-chunking.
Drill · RAG freshness

An internal assistant answers an expense question by citing a travel policy that was retired three months ago. The new policy is in the index too.

STOP. Answer before revealing.

Reveal the diagnosis
  1. Observe The retrieval log shows old and new policy chunks in the top-k, old one first.
  2. Hypothesize (a) The old policy lives at a different URI (mirror, export), so the new version never superseded its doc_id. (b) It is retired at the source but lifecycle metadata isn't ingested or filtered. (c) A cache still serves it.
  3. Measure Check the old chunk's source_uri, status, effective_to, and the answer cache.
  4. Isolate Typically: it was moved to an "Archive" folder, not deleted. The connector still sees it and nothing marks it retired.
  5. Fix Ingest lifecycle state and filter on it at retrieval; link superseding documents to one doc_id; purge cached answers that cited it (the retrieval log says which).
  6. Prevent "Must NOT retrieve" golden questions for retired policies; a conflicting-active-documents monitor.
Drill · Chunking regression

A team changed chunk size from ~500 to ~1,500 tokens "for more context". The deploy went fine. Two days later, golden-set recall@5 has dropped from 0.86 to 0.71 and some answers cite chunks that don't contain the answer.

STOP. Answer before revealing.

Reveal the diagnosis
  1. Observe The drop concentrates in precise-fact questions (numbers, thresholds, table cells); broad questions improved slightly.
  2. Hypothesize (a) Bigger chunks dilute the embedding: one vector averages several topics. (b) An unclean rollout left old and new chunks mixed in one index. (c) Golden expectations reference old chunk ids, so the metric itself is broken.
  3. Measure Count distinct chunker_version values in the serving index; recompute recall keyed by doc_id and content anchors.
  4. Isolate Index clean, metric valid: it's (a).
  5. Fix Flip the alias back to the old index (you kept it, right?). For more context, use parent–child retrieval instead.
  6. Prevent Chunker changes go through the re-embedding playbook with a gated cutover, never in place.

7. Feature pipelines: skew, freshness, point-in-time

The feature-store design is already covered in Part 08: a feature store for ML serving (offline + online tiers, dual materialisation from batch and streaming, a single feature definition), with point-in-time correct training data and the SQL mechanics in Part 05 §10 as-of joins. More scenarios are in ML & Feature Store Scenarios. This section adds the two things interviewers probe next: a precise taxonomy of skew, and freshness as a contract.

7.1 A taxonomy of training/serving skew

"Skew" gets used for four different problems with four different fixes. Separating them is the answer.

TypeCauseExampleDetectPrevent
Logic skewFeature computed by different code offline and onlineTraining SQL counts sessions in UTC days; the serving service counts in local timeLog served feature values; recompute them offline for the same entity and timestamp; diffOne definition compiled to both paths; shared tests on fixtures
Data skewSame logic, different inputs: an upstream source differs between environments, or the population differsOffline reads a cleaned, de-duplicated table; online reads the raw stream with duplicatesDistribution comparison of served vs training features (per feature, per day)Same sources, or an explicit contract on the difference
Time skew / leakageTraining uses values that weren't available at prediction timeJoining the current customer tier onto last year's labels; including late-arriving correctionsFeatures whose training importance is suspiciously high; offline/online metric gap; backtests with strict as-of joinsPoint-in-time as-of joins keyed on availability time, not just event time
Freshness skewOnline value lags what training assumedModel trained on "purchases in last 1h" computed exactly; online value is 40 minutes stale because the stream job is laggingFeature age at serve time (served_ts minus value_ts) as a metricFreshness SLA per feature; fallback or refuse when a feature is too stale

One subtlety carries the time-skew row: event time is not availability time. A transaction that happened at 10:00 but landed in the warehouse at 14:00 was not knowable at 11:00. A strict point-in-time join uses the time the value became available to the serving system. Otherwise training quietly sees the future, offline metrics look great, and production underperforms. This is the same bitemporal idea as in Part 01, applied to features.

7.2 Freshness SLAs per feature

Not every feature needs to be real-time; pretending otherwise is how feature platforms get expensive. Make freshness part of the definition:

  • Declare it: "p99 age at serve ≤ 5 min" for fraud velocity, "≤ 26 h" for a 30-day average. The SLA decides batch vs streaming, not the other way round.
  • Measure it at serve time, not at write time. A healthy writer feeding a lagging replica still serves stale values.
  • Define the stale behaviour: default, last value with a staleness flag, or fail closed. A product decision, written down before the incident.
  • Train with the same staleness: if production serves values 10 minutes old, training on perfectly fresh ones is freshness skew by design.

Monitor lag, age and drift in the Part 12 observability stack, with SLOs per Part 12 SLA/SLO.

“What is training/serving skew?”
30 sec

It's when the features a model sees in production differ from the ones it was trained on, for the same entity at the same moment. The model's offline metrics then don't hold in production. It usually comes from different code paths, different inputs, or training data that leaked information from the future.

2 min

I split it into four types. Logic skew: two implementations of one feature. Data skew: the same logic reading different inputs. Time skew or leakage: training joins values that weren't available at prediction time. Freshness skew: online values lag what training assumed. The fixes differ. Logic skew needs a single feature definition compiled to both paths. Leakage needs point-in-time as-of joins keyed on availability time. Freshness skew needs a per-feature SLA measured at serve time. The detector common to all of them is logging the features actually served, recomputing them offline for the same key and timestamp, and diffing.

Deep dive

Go into availability time vs event time and late data. With a CDC-sourced offline store, a row's commit time in the lakehouse can be hours after its event time, and the as-of join must use the former or it leaks. Then the diff at scale: sample served requests, as-of join to the offline store at request time, report per-feature mismatch rates with tolerances, and alert on rates, not single mismatches.

Where to stop: four types, one detector (log served features and diff). Go into modelling only if asked.

8. AI data lineage: which documents produced this answer?

Table- and column-level lineage (Part 10 §5, with OpenLineage in Part 10) tells you the support_chunks index is built from kb_documents. Necessary, nowhere near sufficient. Users, auditors and on-call ask: for this answer, which documents, at which versions, contributed? You can only answer by logging it at retrieval time; afterwards the index has moved on.

8.1 The retrieval event log

Treat every answer as an event with a schema. Minimum fields:

FieldWhy
request_id, ts, caller principal (or pseudonymous id), resolved permission scopeReplay and audit; proving the ACL filter was applied
Query text (or a hash, where retention rules forbid storing it) and query embedding model versionReproduce retrieval; detect model mismatch
Index name / version (alias target at that moment)Which projection answered; essential during cutovers
Retrieved chunk_ids with doc_id, doc_version, score and rank; which ones were passed to the model after re-rankingThe lineage itself, at chunk and version grain
Generation model id/version, prompt template version, parametersSeparating a data regression from a model or prompt regression
Citations shown to the user; feedback if anyClosing the loop into the golden set

Land it in the lakehouse. "How many answers last month used the retired policy?" becomes a join of the log with document versions where status = 'retired', and never-retrieved documents become a coverage metric. The log inherits the classification of the most sensitive thing it references; set retention accordingly.

8.2 Deletion and right-to-erasure propagation

An erasure request (see Part 10 GDPR and erasure mechanics) that removes a record from the source and the warehouse but not from the AI stack is not complete. Personal data now has more copies than it used to:

  • Deletion is by key, so the key has to exist. Without doc_id and a subject mapping on chunks, deletion is a full scan and a guess.
  • Tombstones aren't erasure. Know when your engine physically removes data and whether snapshots retain it; lakehouse snapshots need expiry too (Part 07).
  • Embeddings are derived personal data. Text can be partially reconstructed from embeddings; give them the source text's obligations. "It's just numbers" is not a defence.
  • Models are the hard case. Deleting documents from the index doesn't remove their influence on fine-tuned weights. What may be used for training is an upstream governance decision, not a pipeline fix. Say so.

9. AI pipeline cost

Numbers first, then architecture (the full method is in Part 18; general cost levers in Part 11). The cost lines are:

Cost lineDriverMain lever
Parsing / OCRPages processed × per-page cost (API or compute)Content-hash skip; OCR only pages with no text layer
EmbeddingTokens × chunks × (1 + re-embeds)Per-chunk hash reuse; fewer, deliberate model changes
Vector storage / memoryVectors × dims × bytes per dim × replicas + index overheadQuantisation, smaller dimensions, tiering cold tenants to disk
Vector queriesQPS × candidates per query × filter selectivityRight-sized recall targets; caching (permission-scoped)
Refresh cadenceHow often you re-scan sources and rebuild or compact indexesChange feeds over full scans; compaction on thresholds
Model inferenceQueries × (prompt tokens incl. retrieved context + output tokens)Fewer, better chunks; top-k is a cost knob as well as a quality knob

9.1 Worked capacity example

A representative scenario, with deliberately hypothetical numbers: an enterprise knowledge assistant over 5 million documents, averaging 10 chunks each, so 50 million chunks of roughly 400 tokens, embedded at 1,024 dimensions in float32.

Raw vector storage: 50,000,000 × 1,024 dims × 4 bytes = 204.8 × 109 bytes ≈ 205 GB. HNSW links add tens to a few hundred bytes per vector, engines add their own overhead, and two replicas put you around 450–600 GB. RAM-resident, that is a memory-bound cluster.

Levers on storage: float16 halves it (~102 GB raw); int8 scalar quantisation quarters it (~51 GB); product quantisation to, say, 128 bytes per vector gives 50M × 128 B ≈ 6.4 GB, a 32× reduction, recovering recall by re-ranking top candidates against full vectors on disk. 512 dimensions halves everything again, if the golden set agrees.

Metadata and text: 50M chunks × ~1.6 KB of text (400 tokens × ~4 chars) ≈ 80 GB, plus metadata. Small next to the vectors.

Initial embedding: 50M × 400 = 20 billion tokens. At a hypothetical price of $0.02–$0.10 per million tokens (check your provider's current pricing), that's roughly $400–$2,000. Cheap. The binding constraint is throughput: at a hypothetical 5M tokens/minute, 20B tokens take 4,000 minutes, about 2.8 days. A multi-day, checkpointed job, not an overnight one.

Steady state: with 1% daily churn, and per-chunk hashing re-embedding only the changed chunks, that's ~500K chunks and ~200M tokens a day. Minutes of rate-limit budget. Nightly full re-embeds would be 100× that and wouldn't finish.

Each re-embed event (new model or chunker) costs another 20B tokens, another multi-day backfill and, during dual-write, double the vector storage. Budget 2× memory for migrations.

OCR: if 20% of 5M documents are scanned at ~20 pages each, that's 20M pages. At a hypothetical $1–$2 per thousand pages, $20K–$40K. The biggest line here, and a re-OCR bug repeats it. Key extracted text by content hash and extractor_version so you never pay twice.

Inference: at 20 QPS peak and top-5 chunks of 400 tokens, each query sends ~2,000 context tokens plus the prompt. Context usually dominates, so chunk size and k are cost decisions too.

Present it as: "vectors are a memory problem, embeddings are a throughput problem, OCR is a don't-do-it-twice problem, and inference scales with how much context retrieval hands the model."

10. Operating it: failure-first

Failure-first: what can fail?
FailureDetectRecoverPrevent recurrence
Scanned PDFs extracted as empty textChars-per-page near zero; docs with zero chunksRe-run with OCR for affected extractor_version + scanned flagPer-page digital/scanned classification; extraction output gates
ACL revocation not propagated; user retrieves a doc they lost access toPermission-propagation lag metric; periodic audit comparing index ACLs to sourcePriority re-sync of affected docs; purge caches; review retrieval log for exposureSeparate ACL event lane with tight SLA; query-time group resolution; permission-scoped caches
Query embedded with a different model than the indexRetrieval scores shift abruptly; golden-set recall collapsesRoll back the query-side model or the aliasAssert model version match at query time; deploy query embedder and index alias together
Selective filter returns fewer than k results (post-filter)Result-count distribution by caller; recall on narrow-ACL golden sliceEnable iterative/filter-aware search, or partition by tenantTests for narrow-permission users in the golden set
Embedding backfill stalls on rate limitsThroughput vs plan; 429 rate; DLQ growthResume from checkpoint; backoff with jitterToken-budgeted scheduler; multi-day plan; checkpoint per doc/version/model
Erasure incomplete (vector/caches still hold data)Post-erasure verification query by subject identifiersPurge remaining copies; force compaction; expire snapshotsErasure fan-out runbook driven by lineage keys; automated verification step
Training/serving skew after a feature logic changeServed-vs-recomputed mismatch rate per featureRoll back the feature version; retrain if the offline path changedSingle definition for both paths; shared fixture tests
2026 Interview Note

Timeless: deterministic keys and idempotent upserts; versioning derived data by the code and model that produced it; incremental processing driven by change detection; point-in-time correctness; access control as data that must propagate; lineage at the grain of the question you'll be asked; evaluation sets as regression tests; the recall–latency–memory triangle. Fast-moving: which vector database is fashionable; specific ANN parameter defaults; embedding model names, dimensions and prices; how a given engine combines filters with ANN search (this changed materially across pgvector, OpenSearch and dedicated stores in recent releases); framework APIs for chunking and orchestration. Reason from the timeless list; name tools as dated examples. "At time of writing pgvector 0.8 added iterative scans, but I'd verify" sounds senior. Reciting one framework's defaults sounds like one tutorial.

L5 Interview CardData Engineering for AI Systems
Must know
  • Chunk ids are deterministic: hash(doc_id, doc_version, chunker_version, ordinal). Upserts, never appends.
  • The embedding model version is part of the vector's key. One index per vector space; never mix.
  • Re-chunking or changing the model means re-embedding everything: a backfill with a cutover plan.
  • ACLs travel with every chunk and are enforced at retrieval, with caches permission-scoped.
  • Pre- vs post-filter: post-filter plus a selective ACL returns fewer than k results, silently.
  • Deletes are tombstones until compaction; erasure fans out to indexes, caches, logs and snapshots.
  • Skew has four types (logic, data, time/leakage, freshness), each with a different fix.
  • Golden question sets gate every chunker, model and index change.
Must be able to explain
  1. How does RAG change the data pipeline, and where does quality get measured?
  2. Why can't you compare vectors from two embedding models, and how do you migrate between them?
  3. What is training/serving skew, and why is event time not availability time?
Must be able to draw

The RAG pipeline with keys and DLQs, plus the retrieval log:

SRC → EXTRACT → CLEAN → CHUNK → EMBED → INDEX
       │DLQ            (id)    │DLQ    (acl)
                                 ▼
             QUERY → ACL filter → top-k → MODEL
                      └─ log chunk ids+versions
Must be able to code
  • A deterministic chunker with stable ids and content hashes (Python).
  • An idempotent upsert that reuses vectors by content hash and retires old versions after the new ones land.
  • A point-in-time as-of join of features onto labels (SQL, see Part 05 §10).
Must be able to debug
  • Answers cite a policy retired three months ago (lifecycle metadata, mirrors, caches).
  • Recall dropped after a chunk-size change (embedding dilution, mixed index, broken golden keys).
Numbers that matter
  • Raw vector bytes = vectors × dims × 4 (float32): 50M × 1,024 × 4 ≈ 205 GB before index overhead and replicas.
  • float16 is ½, int8 is ¼, PQ is often 16–64× smaller; recover recall by re-ranking.
  • Embedding a 50M × 400-token corpus is ~20B tokens: cheap in dollars, days in rate-limit throughput (hypothetical limits).
  • Incremental vs nightly full: proportional to churn (often ~1%/day) vs 100% every day.
  • Re-embed migrations need ~2× vector memory during dual-write.
Classic traps
  • Leading with a vector DB product before sizing, filtering and ACL requirements.
  • One shared index with a team filter as the only security boundary.
  • Quoting HNSW parameter defaults as universal instead of tuning recall@k against exact search on your data.
30-second answer

How do you build the data pipeline behind a RAG system? As an incremental ELT pipeline whose unit is a versioned chunk. Extract with metadata and ACLs, detect changes by content hash, chunk deterministically, and embed with the model version in the key. Then upsert idempotently into an index that is a rebuildable projection of the lakehouse, enforce ACLs at retrieval, log which chunks answered, and gate every change on a golden question set.

2-minute answer

Start with scale and obligations: corpus size, churn, per-source freshness SLA, permission model, erasure. Ingest from change feeds with source URI, version, ACL, lifecycle status and a content hash; unchanged text updates only metadata. Chunk by structure with deterministic ids and treat tables separately. Embed in rate-limited, checkpointed batches with a DLQ, reusing vectors by chunk hash. Keep the lakehouse as system of record and project a serving index per model version, sized from vectors × dims × bytes. Enforce ACL and lifecycle filters with filter-aware search; scope caches by permission. Log chunk ids, versions, scores, model and prompt versions for lineage and erasure. Model or chunker changes go through new index, dual-write, shadow eval and alias cutover.

Deep-dive follow-up

A user with access to 0.1% of the corpus gets two results where others get ten. Walk through how your vector store applies the ACL filter, and what you'd change.

Staff+ follow-up

Legal requires that any answer can be reproduced and explained for seven years, and that erasure requests complete within 30 days across every copy. What do you retain, what do you refuse to retain, and how do those two requirements constrain each other?
