Part 18

System Design Framework & Capacity Planning

Quick refresh10 minInterview study60 minDeep practice90 min
Last technically reviewed September 2026
Covers 8-step design framework, capacity planning, Kafka partition sizing, worker sizing, storage and network estimation, backfill duration, cost method, multi-region data platforms, failure-first design, idempotent batch design, defending trade-offs under pushback
Versions referenced Kafka 4.x (KRaft), Flink 2.x / 1.20 LTS, Spark 4.x, Iceberg 1.x (format v2/v3)
Primary references Kafka docs · Flink docs · Spark Structured Streaming · Iceberg docs
Known implementation differences Cross-region Kafka replication differs by product: Apache MirrorMaker 2 translates offsets, while vendor features such as Confluent Cluster Linking mirror them; per-partition throughput and partition-count ceilings are hardware- and version-specific, so measure them.

This chapter is not another list of design questions. It is the method underneath all of them. The interviewer is testing whether you can turn an ambiguous prompt into requirements, turn requirements into numbers, and turn numbers into an architecture you can defend when it is attacked. Scenarios live elsewhere: the bad/average/strong transcripts in Part 09 §5, the decision forks in Part 09 §7, the scenario skeletons in Part 08. This part is the engine you run on every one of them. If your answer starts with a technology name before you have asked about scale, you have already skipped a step.

1. The Senior/L5 System Design Framework

Mid-level candidates design by recall: they have seen a clickstream architecture, so they draw it. Senior candidates design by derivation: every box traces back to a requirement or a number. Eight steps, always in the same order — the order is what stops you drawing Kafka before you know the data arrives once a day in a CSV. They map onto the handbook’s progression: steps 1–2 Explain and Calculate, 3–4 Design, 5 Debug in advance, 6 Defend, 7–8 Operate.

The 45-minute budget

#StepMinutesCumulativeOutput on the whiteboard
1Requirements55Functional list + non-functional table
2Numbers49A column of back-of-envelope figures
3Data model413Grain, key, schema sketch, partition spec
4Architecture1023Sources → Ingestion → Processing → Storage → Serving → Consumers
5Failure modes730“What breaks first?” list with detect/recover
6Trade-offs535Two or three “X over Y because…” statements
7Operations540Monitoring, retries, backfill, reconciliation, ownership
8Evolution343“At 10× this changes…”
—Buffer / interviewer’s deep dive245—

The budget is a guide. When the interviewer hijacks step 4 for a deep dive, follow them — they found something worth probing — then say “let me come back to failure modes.” A candidate who never reaches step 5 usually scores below one who reached it with a thinner architecture.

Step 1 — Requirements

What to say. Split functional from non-functional out loud. Functional: what questions will the data answer, for whom, at what grain. Non-functional, one line each:

  • Latency / freshness — end-to-end from event creation to consumer, and whether that is p50 or p99. “Real-time” is not a number.
  • Correctness — can the dashboard be 0.1% off for an hour if the nightly number is exact? Is this finance (reconcile to the cent) or product analytics (directionally right)?
  • Retention — hot replay window, queryable history, legal minimum and maximum.
  • Access — who queries, how (BI, SQL ad hoc, API, ML training), with what concurrency.
  • Compliance — PII present? Erasure obligations? Data residency? (See Part 10.)

What the interviewer is checking. Whether you can tell which requirement is load-bearing. Usually one dominates — freshness, exactness, or residency — and the strong candidate names it: “the hard part is the 100% accuracy requirement, not the volume.”

Time. 5 minutes. Three to five questions, then state assumptions and move.

Typical mid-level failure. Asking about volume but not correctness, then building an at-least-once pipeline for revenue.

Step 2 — Numbers

What to say. “Before I draw anything, let me size it.” Then run the chain: events/sec (average and peak) → record size → MB/s → GB/day → retention → partitions → worker count → backfill size → SLA → rough cost. Section 2 is the toolkit.

What the interviewer is checking. Physical intuition. 100K events/sec is moderate — one well-run Kafka cluster. 10M events/day is small — about 116/sec. Numbers are how you avoid over-building.

Time. 4 minutes. Round aggressively while choosing; be exact when writing down.

Typical mid-level failure. Doing the numbers and never using them. If the partition count on the whiteboard is not derived from your MB/s, the numbers were theatre.

Step 3 — Data model

What to say. Grain (“one row per order line per day”), key (what makes a row unique — also your dedup key), schema (the columns that matter, and how it evolves), partition (layout matching the dominant predicate). Partition sizing math is in Part 02 §8; key choice examples are in Part 02 §17.

What the interviewer is checking. Whether you separate the message key (ordering in Kafka) from the table partition (pruning in the lake).

Time. 4 minutes.

Typical mid-level failure. Never stating the grain. Every duplicate-counting bug in an interview answer traces back to an unstated grain.

Step 4 — Architecture

What to say. Six layers, always the same: Sources → Ingestion → Processing → Storage → Serving → Consumers. Name each box’s job before its technology: “I need a durable, replayable buffer for three consumer groups — Kafka or Kinesis; I’ll pick Kafka because…”.

What the interviewer is checking. Coherence. A box you cannot justify is a box they will ask you to remove.

Time. 10 minutes, including one pass of “follow one event through”.

Typical mid-level failure. A reference architecture from memory with boxes no requirement asked for — a feature store for a reporting pipeline.

Step 5 — Failure modes

What to say. “What breaks first?” Walk the diagram: what happens when each box is slow, down, wrong, or duplicated; one line each on detect and recover. Section 6 is the catalogue.

What the interviewer is checking. Production scar tissue — volunteering the failure they were about to ask about.

Time. 7 minutes. The step most worth protecting.

Typical mid-level failure. “Kafka is fault tolerant, Flink has checkpoints, so we’re fine.” That describes components. Failures live in the seams: between the producer retry and the dedup key, between the Flink commit and the Iceberg snapshot.

Step 6 — Trade-offs

What to say. Two or three explicit sentences in the form “I chose X over Y because [requirement], at the cost of [what I gave up]. If [condition] changed, I’d switch.” Section 8 is the technique; Part 09 §7 has the common forks.

What the interviewer is checking. Whether you know the cost of your own choices. If you cannot name it, you repeated a default.

Time. 5 minutes.

Typical mid-level failure. “X is better than Y.” Better along which axis, for which requirement?

Step 7 — Operations

What to say. Six words, each with one concrete line: monitoring (freshness, volume, lag, error rate per stage — see Part 12 §2), retries (where, with what backoff, what is idempotent), backfills (how you reprocess a month without touching live traffic — Part 02 §6), reconciliation (the independent count that proves the pipeline is right — Part 12 §4), deployment (how a job upgrade preserves state), ownership (who is paged, and for what).

What the interviewer is checking. Whether you have ever run the thing you are designing.

Time. 5 minutes.

Typical mid-level failure. “We’d add monitoring.” Monitoring of what, alerting whom, at what threshold?

Step 8 — Evolution

What to say. “What changes at 10×?” Name the first component to hit a wall, using your step 2 numbers, plus one sentence on organisational growth.

What the interviewer is checking. Whether the design grows or has to be rebuilt.

Time. 3 minutes.

Typical mid-level failure. “We’d add more nodes.” At 10×, cross-AZ network, small files and metadata tend to bite before CPU does.

The printable card

2. Capacity Planning Toolkit

One toolkit, reused in every design round. The instinct: numbers before architecture. Most architecture choices are threshold decisions — below some MB/s one node is fine, above it you partition — and you cannot make a threshold decision without the number. One running example throughout: 100K events/sec at 800 bytes/event, a representative clickstream. Derived figures are hypothetical and exist to show the method.

The base chain

QuantityArithmeticResult
Throughput (average)100,000 ev/s × 800 B80,000,000 B/s = 80 MB/s
Daily raw volume80 MB/s × 86,400 s6,912,000 MB = 6.912 TB/day (decimal) ≈ 6.9 TB
Events per day100,000 × 86,4008.64 B events/day
Peak (assume 3× average; measure yours)300,000 ev/s × 800 B240 MB/s
Yearly raw6.912 TB × 365≈ 2.52 PB/year uncompressed

Say whether the headline is average or peak — systems are sized for peak and billed on average. Say which units: 6.912 TB decimal is 6.29 TiB; the 9% gap changes no architecture, but naming it shows you know it exists.

Compression — ranges to measure, not constants

Ratios depend on the data more than the codec. Present ranges; measure on a day of real traffic.

  • JSON on the wire, batch-compressed by the producer (lz4/zstd on Kafka record batches): typically ~3–5×. Tiny batches barely compress.
  • Columnar at rest (Parquet/ORC, dictionary + RLE + codec) vs raw JSON: ~5–10× for event data with low-cardinality columns. UUID-heavy or free-text payloads land at the low end or below.
  • Binary serialisation (Avro/Protobuf) before any codec: often 2–3× smaller than JSON, since field names are not repeated.

The running example plans on 4× on the wire and 8× in the lake, labelled so results can be rescaled.

LayerRawRatio (assumed)Stored
Kafka (per replica)6.912 TB/day4×1.728 TB/day
Lake, Parquet bronze6.912 TB/day8× (range 5–10×)0.864 TB/day (range 0.69–1.38)

Replication and retention

Kafka with replication factor 3 stores every byte three times and ships it twice across the network (leader → two followers). With replicas spread across three availability zones, both follower copies cross an AZ boundary. RF=3 therefore means 3× broker disk and 2× the produce rate in cross-AZ replication traffic.

QuestionArithmeticResult
7 days hot, uncompressed, one copy6.912 TB × 748.384 TB
… compressed at 4×48.384 / 412.096 TB
… × RF=312.096 × 336.288 TB broker disk
… provisioned at ~65% fill36.288 / 0.65≈ 56 TB

The 65% fill is a planning choice: room for reassignment and for the day traffic doubles. If 56 TB of local disk is expensive, tiered storage enters (production-ready in Apache Kafka 3.9+/4.x at time of writing — check current docs): hours local, days on object storage.

Kafka partitions

The formula:

partitions = max( T / pproduce , T / pconsume ) × headroom

  • T — target throughput at peak, in the same units you measured p in (compressed or uncompressed; do not mix).
  • pproduce — what one partition sustains on the produce side on your brokers, with your acks, batch size and compression. A measured number, typically single-digit to tens of MB/s per partition.
  • pconsume — what one consumer instance sustains on one partition, including the processing it does. This is usually the smaller number, because deserialisation, enrichment and sink writes are slower than the broker.
  • headroom — 1.5–2× for growth, key skew, and the fact that you cannot shrink a topic’s partition count later.
StepRunning example (hypothetical measurements)
T (peak, uncompressed)240 MB/s
pproduce (measured)10 MB/s → 240 / 10 = 24
pconsume (measured: Flink parse + enrich)5 MB/s → 240 / 5 = 48
max48
× 2 headroom96

Why 96, not 100? 96 divides by 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12, 16, 24, 32 and 48; 32 consumers get exactly three partitions each. With 100, some tasks get four and become stragglers. A small detail that reads as experience.

Partitions are not free: open segment files, replica fetchers, controller metadata, longer failover. KRaft (the only mode in Kafka 4.x) raised the practical ceiling, but it remains version- and hardware-specific. “Thousands per cluster is routine; hundreds of thousands needs evidence” is a safe statement.

Worker count

Workers come from a per-core processing rate, which you measure by running the job on one core against a replayed hour of traffic.

StepArithmeticResult
Measured rate (hypothetical)parse + enrich + serialise20,000 ev/s per core
Cores at peak, 100% busy300,000 / 20,00015 cores
Target 60% utilisation15 / 0.625 cores
Round to a divisor of 96 partitions—32 task slots

The 60% target is catch-up capacity. Catch-up time ≈ backlog / spare capacity. At 60% busy at peak, capacity is 300K / 0.6 = 500K ev/s, so spare is 200K ev/s; a 10-minute outage at peak builds 300K × 600 = 180M events; draining takes 180M / 200K = 900 s = 15 minutes. A job at 95% has almost nothing to drain with. Put that number next to your freshness SLA.

Parallelism does not rescue skew; Part 02 §15 quantifies the skew tax.

Lake storage per year

CompressionPer dayPer year (× 365)
5× (pessimistic)1.3824 TB≈ 505 TB
8× (planning)0.864 TB≈ 315 TB
10× (optimistic)0.6912 TB≈ 252 TB

Then add layers: silver is typically comparable to bronze, gold is small, so ~1.5–2× bronze for the medallion is a reasonable planning figure to verify. Snapshot retention adds files that compaction and MERGE have replaced until expiry runs. In-region durability replication is priced into the per-GB rate; cross-region copies are yours.

Network

The term candidates forget, and often the one that dominates a streaming bill. Three flows, in compressed bytes (4× turns 80 MB/s into 20 MB/s):

FlowArithmeticAverage
Ingress (producers → leaders)80 / 420 MB/s
Replication (leader → 2 followers)20 × 240 MB/s
Consumer fan-out (3 consumer groups)20 × 360 MB/s
Broker egress total40 + 60100 MB/s

Cross-AZ, with three AZs and clients spread evenly: all 40 MB/s of replication crosses; about two-thirds of producer traffic (≈ 13.3 MB/s) and of consumer traffic (40 MB/s) does too, unless consumers fetch from a same-AZ follower (rack-aware follower fetching, KIP-392, in Apache Kafka since 2.4). Replication alone is 40 MB/s × 86,400 = 3.456 TB/day across AZs. Consumer fan-out is the lever you control.

Backfill duration

Duration = work / throughput you are allowed to use. The constraints are the interview: where the history lives (Kafka holds 7 days, so a 30-day backfill reads bronze — say it first), how much capacity you may take (starving the live job is an outage you caused), and the bottleneck (CPU, read bandwidth, or sink commits). Drill 2 below works it.

Cost — a method, not a price list

Never quote vendor prices from memory; they change by region and contract. Show the method with symbolic unit prices and use illustrative numbers only to find the dominant term. Monthly cost ≈ Σ (quantity × unit price) over storage (TB-month), compute (core-hours), network (TB across billable boundaries) and requests (object-store and catalog calls). Part 02 §14 has the batch version; Part 11 the platform levers.

TermQuantity (running example)Unit price (ILLUSTRATIVE placeholder, not a quote)Monthly
Lake storage (steady state, 1-yr retention, 8×)≈ 315 TBS = $20 / TB-month≈ $6,300
Kafka broker disk56 TB provisionedB = $80 / TB-month$4,480
Stream compute32 cores × 730 h = 23,360 core-hC = $0.05 / core-hour$1,168
Cross-AZ replication3.456 TB/day × 30 = 103.68 TBN = $10 / TB≈ $1,037
Cross-AZ consumer reads (no follower fetching)40 MB/s → 103.68 TBN = $10 / TB≈ $1,037

The value is the ranking, not the total. With these placeholders, storage and broker disk dominate, so lifecycle policies and tiered storage are the first levers and follower fetching a cheap second. Real prices may flip the ranking — cross-AZ transfer surprises most, because it scales with fan-out, not volume. Name the dominant term and your lever; that is the senior answer.

Handy numbers

FactValue
Seconds per day86,400 (≈ 105)
Seconds per 30-day month2,592,000 (≈ 2.6M)
Seconds per year31,536,000 (≈ 3.15 × 107)
1M events/day≈ 11.6 /s
1B events/day≈ 11.6K /s
1K events/s86.4M /day
100K events/s8.64B /day
1 KB × 1B1 TB
1 MB/s sustained86.4 GB/day ≈ 31.5 TB/year
1 GB/s sustained86.4 TB/day
10 Gbit/s link1.25 GB/s line rate; plan on ~60–70% usable
210 vs 1031,024 vs 1,000 (≈ 2.4% gap; ~10% by TB/TiB)
Peak-to-averageoften 2–5× for consumer traffic; measure
Parquet file target~128 MB – 1 GB

Latency orders of magnitude

Orders of magnitude only — exact figures depend on hardware and configuration. What matters is which operations can sit in a per-event hot path.

OperationOrder of magnitude
Main memory reference~100 ns
Local NVMe random read~10–100 µs
Round trip within one AZsub-millisecond
Round trip across AZs in one region~1–2 ms
Round trip across regions on one continent~10s of ms
Round trip across continents~100–200 ms
Object store GET, time to first byte~10–100 ms
Kafka produce with acks=all, p99 on a healthy cluster~ms to tens of ms
Lakehouse table commit (Iceberg/Delta)~hundreds of ms to seconds
Warehouse query on a warm cluster, small result~100 ms to seconds
Streaming checkpoint interval (configured)typically ~10 s to minutes

The consequence: a synchronous object-store call per event at 100K events/sec is 100K × ~50 ms = 5,000 seconds of waiting per second — it needs async I/O, batching or a cache. A table commit is seconds-scale, so commit per checkpoint, never per event.

2026 Interview Note

Timeless: the capacity chain itself (rate × size × time, replication multiplies disk and network, consumer parallelism is capped by partitions, catch-up time = backlog / spare capacity). Version-specific: per-partition throughput, practical partition ceilings (raised by KRaft, which is the only mode in Kafka 4.x), tiered-storage availability, follower fetching, and every unit price. Say the first category with confidence and the second with “at time of writing, on this version — I’d measure.” Interviewers reward the distinction; they penalise a memorised constant stated as law.

“Estimate storage and compute for 2 billion events a day at about 1 KB each.”
30 sec

2B a day is ~23K events/sec average (2 × 109 / 86,400 ≈ 23,150); at 1 KB, ~23 MB/s and 2 TB/day raw. At ~8× columnar, ~250 GB/day in the lake, ~90 TB/year. Peak at 3× is ~70K/s; at ~20K/s per core, four cores busy, six to eight with headroom. One moderate streaming job, not a platform.

2 min

Add multipliers. Kafka, RF=3, 7 days, 4× wire: 2 TB × 7 / 4 × 3 = 10.5 TB, ~16 TB provisioned at 65% fill. Lake: 0.25 TB × 365 ≈ 91 TB/year bronze, ~150–180 TB with silver and gold. Compute: 70K / 20K = 3.5 cores busy; ÷ 0.6 ≈ 6; round to 8 to divide a 24-partition topic. Partitions: 70 MB/s ÷ 5 MB/s measured consumer rate = 14, × 1.5–2 → 24. It all fits comfortably; the interesting questions will be correctness and late data, not scale.

Deep dive

Challenge each assumption. Is 1 KB the mean or the median? A tail of 50 KB events shifts storage and per-core rate. Does a push campaign create 20× spikes for ten minutes? Then size Kafka for the spike and let consumers lag and catch up rather than sizing compute for it. Files: 250 GB/day over 1-minute commits is ~170 MB per commit — fine from a few writers, small files from 64. Retention: if legal requires seven years, bronze is 7 × 91 ≈ 640 TB and lifecycle tiering becomes the main cost lever.

Where to stop: once you have named the dominant cost term and the first resource that runs out, stop computing and return to design.

Drill · Capacity — Kafka

Estimate Kafka partitions and cluster shape for 250 MB/s (bytes as stored on the broker, i.e. after producer compression) with 3 consumer groups. Measured: one partition sustains 10 MB/s produce; the slowest consumer group sustains 5 MB/s per partition; RF=3; 3-day retention.

STOP. Answer before revealing.

Reveal the estimate
  1. Partitions max(250 / 10, 250 / 5) = max(25, 50) = 50. With 2× headroom, ~100; pick 96 or 120 for divisibility. Note what does not happen: three consumer groups do not triple the partition count. Each group reads every partition independently; the slowest group sets pconsume.
  2. Where the groups do cost you Broker egress = replication (250 × 2 = 500 MB/s) + consumers (250 × 3 = 750 MB/s) = 1,250 MB/s ≈ 10 Gbit/s across the cluster. Ingress = 250 + 500 = 750 MB/s.
  3. Broker count from network If one broker can sustainably push, say, 400 MB/s of egress (measure it — depends on instance type), 1,250 / 400 ≈ 3.1 → at least 4. Then size for losing one broker: its load moves to the rest, so 6 is a more honest answer than 4.
  4. Disk 250 MB/s × 86,400 = 21.6 TB/day per copy; × 3 RF = 64.8 TB/day; × 3 days = 194.4 TB; at 65% fill ≈ 300 TB provisioned (194.4 / 0.65 = 299). Across 6 brokers that is ~50 TB each — likely a signal to use tiered storage and keep hours, not days, local.
  5. Caveat worth saying Caught-up consumers read from page cache; a lagging group reads cold segments from disk and competes with producers. One slow group can hurt the other two.
Drill · Capacity — Backfill

A bug in sessionisation corrupted 30 days of silver. Reprocess it. Running example volumes (100K ev/s average, 800 B, 8× Parquet). Measured batch rate: 20K events/sec per core. You may use 200 cores without affecting the live pipeline. How long, and what else constrains it?

STOP. Answer before revealing.

Reveal the estimate
  1. Source Kafka keeps 7 days, so the backfill reads bronze from the lake. Saying this first is half the answer.
  2. Work 30 × 8.64B = 259.2B events; 30 × 6.912 TB = 207.36 TB logical; 30 × 0.864 TB = 25.92 TB of Parquet to scan.
  3. Duration 200 cores × 20K = 4M ev/s. 259.2 × 109 / 4 × 106 = 64,800 s = 18 hours. With 400 cores, 9 hours — if the budget allows.
  4. Read bandwidth 25.92 TB over 64,800 s = 25,920,000 MB / 64,800 s = 400 MB/s from object storage. Comfortably within what an object store serves to a parallel reader; not the bottleneck.
  5. Sessionisation specifics Sessions cross midnight, so each day reads a margin of the previous day’s tail. Overwrite each day’s partition atomically; gold is rebuilt after silver, so the critical path is 18 h plus the gold rebuild. Publish via write-audit-publish (§5).
  6. Communicate “About a day of wall clock, most of it compute-bound; I’d run it in three 10-day chunks so a failure costs a chunk, not the lot.”

3. Reference Architectures

Two diagrams to draw from memory — not because every design looks like them, but because they give you a vocabulary of layers. Start from the reference and delete boxes your requirements do not justify. Deleting a box with a reason is a stronger signal than adding one.

The system-design reference

How to use it:

  • Ingestion enforces contracts (Part 15) and attaches the idempotency key. Quarantine here, not in gold.
  • The durable log needs a reason: replay, multiple consumers, or decoupled availability. One nightly consumer of a daily file? Delete it.
  • Processing splits by freshness, not fashion (Part 09 §7).
  • Serving is per access pattern: warehouse for SQL/BI concurrency, OLAP for sub-second slicing, key-value for point lookups (Part 16).

Multi-region data platform

Multi-region questions are RPO/RTO questions in an architecture costume. Ask RPO (how much data can we lose?), RTO (how long until consumers are served?), and why multi-region: disaster recovery, user latency, or residency — three different designs. Part 08’s multi-region scenario has the prompt skeleton; this is the mechanism.

Active-passive vs active-active, for data specifically.

DimensionActive-passiveActive-active
Who ingestsPrimary region onlyBoth, each for its local producers
DuplicatesOnly across a failover boundaryNormal state; global event_id dedup required
Append-only factsEasyEasy — union of both regions, dedup by event_id
Mutable state (dimensions, counters)Easy — one writerHard — conflict resolution, or partition ownership by key
Global aggregatesComputed in one placePre-aggregate per region, merge; exact distinct counts need mergeable sketches or a global pass
CostStandby capacity mostly idleBoth regions fully provisioned, plus cross-region transfer
ResidencyEverything flows to primary — may violate residencyData can stay in its region; only aggregates cross

Kafka cross-region replication. Apache MirrorMaker 2 (on Kafka Connect) copies topics, by default prefixing them with the source cluster alias; the target assigns its own offsets, so consumer offsets are translated via MM2 checkpoints, not copied. Vendor features such as Confluent Cluster Linking mirror topics with offsets preserved, which simplifies failover; managed services have their own equivalents (check current docs). The timeless point: after failover, consumers resume from a position that is approximate at the tail, so downstream must tolerate replaying seconds to minutes of events. Another reason sinks must be idempotent.

Object storage and table formats. Cross-region object replication is asynchronous and per-object, with no ordering across objects, so an Iceberg metadata file can reach region B before the data files it references.

  • Advance region B’s catalog pointer only to a snapshot whose every referenced file has replicated.
  • Iceberg metadata records absolute paths; if region B’s bucket name differs, replicated metadata points back at region A. Use path-agnostic aliases, or rewrite paths — recent Iceberg releases include a procedure for this (check your version).
  • Delta logs usually use table-relative paths, which avoids the path problem but not the ordering problem.

Catalog failover. The catalog is the pointer that makes files into a table. If it is region-scoped and region A is gone, region B has files but no tables. Replicate the catalog consistently with the object store, or keep a DR catalog you re-register tables into from the last complete metadata file. An untested DR catalog is a hypothesis.

RPO/RTO as arithmetic. Mirror lag of seconds, object replication of minutes at the tail, DR catalog pointer advanced every 15 minutes: lakehouse RPO ~15 minutes, raw-stream RPO seconds — and the lakehouse gap refills from the mirrored topic if retention covers it. RTO is dominated by human decision time unless failover is automated; say so.

2026 Interview Note

Timeless: RPO is bounded by the slowest asynchronous replication path; offsets are cluster-local, so cross-cluster consumer positions are always translated or mirrored; a table is files plus a pointer, and both must be replicated consistently. Version-specific: MirrorMaker 2 behaviours and replication policies, Cluster Linking and managed-service equivalents, object-store replication SLAs, Iceberg path-rewrite tooling, and catalog replication features. Name the product and version when you rely on one.

4. Worked Example — Design a Pipeline Ingesting 100K Events/sec

A common interview prompt: “Design a pipeline that ingests 100K events a second from our apps and makes them available for analytics.” All eight steps, at the depth a strong candidate reaches in 40 minutes. The 1M events/sec variant is Part 08’s clickstream scenario; this section shows the method rather than repeating it.

Step 1 — Requirements

Questions asked, and the assumed answers:

QuestionAssumed answerDesign consequence
Who consumes?Product dashboards, analysts (SQL), one ML team (daily features)Three consumer groups; warehouse-grade SQL serving
Freshness?Operational dashboard: 1 min p95. Analytics tables: 15 min. Daily reports: by 06:00Two tiers: streaming aggregates + minute-scale lake commits
Correctness?Dashboard may be approximate; daily reported metrics must be exact and reproducibleDedup by event_id in silver; daily recompute from bronze
Is 100K average or peak?Average; peak 3× during evening + campaignsSize for 300K/s
Retention?Replay 7 days; raw 1 year; aggregates 5 yearsKafka 7 d; bronze lifecycle to cold tier; gold long-lived
Compliance?Contains user_id and device ids; erasure requests applyPseudonymise at ingest; erasure path on silver/gold (Part 10 §1)

The hard requirement, stated out loud: exact, reproducible daily metrics from a source that retries and duplicates. Volume is moderate; correctness is the design driver.

Step 2 — Numbers

From section 2, compressed into what goes on the whiteboard:

FigureValue
Average / peak80 MB/s / 240 MB/s (800 B events)
Raw per day6.912 TB; 8.64B events
Kafka, 7 d, RF=3, 4× wire36.3 TB stored, ~56 TB provisioned
Partitions96 (from max(24, 48) × 2)
Stream workers32 slots (15 cores busy at peak, 60% target)
Lake, bronze, 8×0.864 TB/day, ~315 TB/year
Commit sizing0.864 TB/day ÷ 24 = 36 GB/hour; 1-min commits → ~600 MB/commit; ÷ 32 writers ≈ 19 MB/file
Commits per day1,440 snapshots/day per table
30-day backfill~18 h on 200 cores (Drill 2)

Two numbers change the design. 19 MB files: 1-minute commits create small files by construction, so compaction is part of the design (Part 02 §9). 1,440 snapshots a day: expiry and manifest rewriting must be scheduled (Part 07 §8).

Step 3 — Data model

  • Grain: one row per client-emitted event.
  • Key: event_id, a UUID generated by the client SDK at creation time and reused on every retry. Without a client-generated id, dedup is guesswork.
  • Schema (silver): event_id, event_ts (client clock), received_ts (server clock), user_id (pseudonymised), anonymous_id, session_id, event_type, platform, app_version, schema_version, properties (typed where known, map/variant for the long tail), plus lineage columns kafka_partition, kafka_offset, ingest_run_id.
  • Schema evolution: Avro or Protobuf with a registry; backward-compatible changes only on the main topic; breaking changes get a new topic version.
  • Partitioning: bronze by hour(received_ts); silver by day(event_ts) with sort/cluster on event_type, user_id.
“Choose a partition strategy for this pipeline.”
30 sec

There are two partitioning decisions, and they are different. The Kafka message key decides ordering and co-location: I key by user_id only if a consumer needs per-user order, otherwise by event_id for even spread. The lake partition decides pruning: bronze by ingest hour so it is append-only, silver by event day because every query filters on event date. Never partition the lake by user_id.

2 min

Bronze by received_ts hour is immutable once the hour closes, so incremental jobs process “the next closed hour” without late arrivals rewriting old partitions. Silver by event_ts day matches how analysts filter; late events land in old partitions, so I bound lateness (say 3 days) and route anything later to a late table the daily job folds in. At ~0.86 TB/day, day partitions are well sized. Within a partition, sort by event_type, user_id so min/max stats skip files. Iceberg hidden partitioning prunes on an event_ts predicate without users knowing the partition column (Part 02 §8).

Deep dive

Keying by user_id exposes you to hot keys (the second attack in §7), and changing the partition count later remaps keys and breaks ordering across the change — so if ordering is required, overprovision up front (96, not 48) and plan salting for known heavy keys. In the lake, partitioning on a high-cardinality column gives millions of kilobyte partitions, which Part 02 §8 rules out. Iceberg can evolve partitioning, but old data keeps its old layout until rewritten, so record the reason for the choice.

Where to stop: two decisions named, each tied to a query or ordering requirement, one failure mode each. Stop there unless asked about evolution.

Step 4 — Architecture

Follow one event: the SDK assigns event_id; the collector validates and produces idempotently; the bronze writer lands it at the next checkpoint (~1 min); the live aggregator counts it into a 1-minute window in the OLAP store; the 15-minute silver job reads new bronze snapshots, dedups on event_id, types the payload and merges into the event-day partition; at 02:00 gold recomputes yesterday from silver and publishes atomically.

Step 5 — What breaks first

FailureFirst symptomBlast radiusResponse built into the design
SDK retries after a timeout that actually succeededDuplicate event_ids in bronzeInflated counts if not dedupedDedup on event_id in silver; bronze keeps everything for audit
Hot key (bot or tenant)One partition lagging; watermark stallsAll event-time windows latePer-partition lag alert; key by event_id unless ordering needed; idle-source/skew handling
Bronze writer crash mid-checkpointRestart from last checkpointNone if sink commits on checkpointIceberg sink commits files only on checkpoint completion; orphan files cleaned later
Producer ships incompatible schemaRegistry rejects, or quarantine rate spikesThat producer’s events onlyCompatibility check at registry; quarantine + alert the producing team
Small files accumulateQuery planning time rising week over weekAnalyst query latency, costScheduled compaction on closed partitions; alert on files per partition
Late mobile events (offline devices)Late-table row countYesterday’s numbers shift3-day lateness bound for silver; daily gold recompute; publish restatement policy

The one to say first: duplicates from client retries, because the hard requirement is exact daily metrics and this is the most common way to miss it. The generic catalogue is in section 6.

Step 6 — Trade-offs

  • I chose Kafka over a managed stream such as Kinesis because we have three consumer groups, a 7-day replay window, and a team that already operates Kafka. With no streaming operators on the team, I would take the managed service and its limits.
  • I chose Flink over Spark Structured Streaming for the live tier because the dashboard needs event-time windows at 1-minute freshness with checkpoint-aligned Iceberg commits. If only the 15-minute tier existed, Spark for everything would be simpler — one engine beats two.
  • I chose to dedup in silver rather than in the stream because exact dedup over a multi-day retry window means hundreds of GB of keyed state in streaming but a bounded join in batch (§8 works the numbers). The cost: the dashboard over-counts by the retry rate, acceptable because it is labelled approximate.
  • I chose 1-minute over 15-minute bronze commits to leave headroom inside the 15-minute analytics SLA, paying with small files and 1,440 snapshots a day.

Step 7 — Operations

  • Monitoring: per-stage freshness, consumer lag per partition (the group average hides the hot one), quarantine rate, dedup ratio (a jump means an SDK bug), files per partition, snapshot count.
  • Retries: SDK backoff with jitter reusing event_id; idempotent producer; batch retries whole partitions because every write is an overwrite or keyed MERGE.
  • Backfills: from bronze, separate compute pool, write-audit-publish (§5).
  • Reconciliation: collector counts per hour vs bronze rows per received_ts hour vs silver distinct event_ids. Collector–bronze gap is loss; bronze–silver gap beyond the dedup ratio is a bug.
  • Deployment: Flink upgrades via savepoint with stable operator UIDs; schema compatibility checked in CI.
  • Ownership: platform owns collector → bronze (paged on freshness); analytics engineering owns silver → gold (paged on the 06:00 SLA); producer teams own schemas and receive quarantine alerts.

Step 8 — What changes at 10×

At 1M events/sec: 800 MB/s average, 2.4 GB/s peak, 69.12 TB/day raw (0.8 GB/s × 86,400 s). What hits a wall first:

  • Cross-AZ network cost, before CPU: replication and fan-out scale with volume × consumers; follower fetching becomes necessary.
  • Kafka local disk: 7 days at RF=3 becomes ~363 TB; tiered storage becomes required.
  • Lake metadata: commit latency and manifest size grow; fewer, larger commits, or tables split by event class.
  • One topic for everything: split a small critical topic (purchases, sign-ups) from a firehose (impressions) where sampling is an acceptable product decision.
  • Organisation: many producing teams make collector-enforced contracts mandatory (Part 15).

Part 08’s 1M events/sec scenario picks up from here.

5. Designing Idempotent Batch Processing

A common interview prompt: “Design a daily batch job that can be safely re-run.” The mechanics — partition overwrite, MERGE by key, hash-upsert, and the anti-patterns — are in Part 02 §3; restart semantics in Part 02 §16. Here is the framework applied in five minutes of interview time.

Requirements. Re-running any day, any number of times, produces the same output. A failed run leaves consumers seeing the previous good state. A backfill of a range is just N re-runs.

Numbers. How big is one logical day? That decides whether overwrite (rewrite the whole day) is cheap or whether you need a keyed MERGE on a much larger table.

Data model. Grain and natural key stated explicitly; the key is what MERGE matches on and what dedup keeps unique.

The design checklist

CheckWhat it meansWhat goes wrong without it
Deterministic inputsThe run reads a fixed input set derived from logical_date, or pinned snapshot ids recorded at startRe-run at 14:00 reads late data the 02:00 run did not; outputs differ
Deterministic transformNo now(), no random ids, no unordered “first” without a tiebreakEvery run produces different surrogate keys and different winners
Idempotent writeOverwrite the target partition, or MERGE on the natural keyINSERT appends a second copy on every retry
Run idsEach run has an id stamped on output rows or in the commit summary, and a run ledgerYou cannot tell which run produced a bad number
Write-audit-publishWrite to a branch/staging, validate, then atomically publishConsumers read a half-written or unvalidated day
Side effects after publishNotifications, exports and downstream triggers fire after the commit, keyed by run idA retried run emails the CFO twice
Bounded scopeA run touches only its logical partition(s)A re-run of Tuesday silently rewrites Monday
Engine: Spark 3.5+/4.x with Iceberg 1.xDialect/Language: Spark SQL + Iceberg proceduresExecutable: Illustrative — adapt to your catalog and Iceberg version
-- 1. Write to an audit branch, not main
ALTER TABLE lake.gold.daily_metrics SET TBLPROPERTIES ('write.wap.enabled' = 'true');
ALTER TABLE lake.gold.daily_metrics CREATE BRANCH IF NOT EXISTS audit_r8841;
SET spark.wap.branch = audit_r8841;

-- 2. Idempotent write: overwrite exactly one logical day
INSERT OVERWRITE lake.gold.daily_metrics
SELECT metric_date, product_id, SUM(revenue) AS revenue, 'r-8841' AS run_id
FROM lake.silver.orders
WHERE metric_date = DATE '2026-09-23'
GROUP BY metric_date, product_id;

-- 3. Audit on the branch (fail the task if any check fails)
SELECT COUNT(*) AS rows, COUNT(DISTINCT product_id) AS keys
FROM lake.gold.daily_metrics VERSION AS OF 'audit_r8841'
WHERE metric_date = DATE '2026-09-23';

-- 4. Publish atomically
CALL lake.system.fast_forward('gold.daily_metrics', 'main', 'audit_r8841');

The overwrite here relies on dynamic partition overwrite mode with the table partitioned by metric_date; check how your engine and version interpret INSERT OVERWRITE before trusting it. Delta has no branches; the equivalent is writing to a staging table, validating, then a single replaceWhere overwrite or MERGE into the target.

Failure modes to volunteer: publish fails after a good write (safe — re-run publishes the same result); two runs for one day race (orchestrator lock or optimistic-concurrency retry); the source is restated after the run (trigger re-runs on upstream snapshot change, not only on a clock).

6. Failure-First Architecture

Design the failure path before the happy path. Every box fails in one of four ways — down, slow, wrong, duplicated — and every seam is where one box’s failure becomes another’s corruption. This is the handbook’s canonical catalogue.

Failure-first: what can fail?
FailureDetectRecoverPrevent recurrence
Source unavailable (API down, DB replica lagging, file not delivered)Freshness SLO on the landing table; sensor timeout; source-side heartbeatRetry with backoff; downstream waits rather than processing an empty input as “zero”Distinguish “no data” from “data is zero” in contracts; alert the source owner, not only the consumer
Partial write (job dies mid-write)Row count vs expected; orphan files in storage; missing commit for run idRe-run: atomic table commits mean readers never saw the partial files; clean orphansOnly write through transactional table formats or temp-then-rename; never write directly to a live path
Duplicate event (retries, replay, failover)Dedup ratio metric; distinct-key count vs row countDedup on the idempotency key; recompute affected aggregatesClient-generated event_id; idempotent producer; MERGE/overwrite sinks (Part 03 §7)
Poison message (unparseable, violates schema)Deserialisation error rate; one partition stuck at one offsetRoute to dead-letter topic with error and offset; continueSchema validation at ingestion; DLQ alert to producer team; replay tooling from DLQ
Checkpoint corrupt or incompatibleJob fails to restore; restart loopRestore from an older retained checkpoint or savepoint; else rebuild state from source replayRetain several checkpoints; savepoint before every upgrade; stable operator UIDs; test restore in staging
Schema incompatible (field removed, type changed)Registry compatibility failure; quarantine spike; null-rate jump on a columnPin consumers to last compatible version; quarantine and replay after fixCompatibility checks in producer CI; contracts with owners (Part 15)
Storage unavailable or throttled (object store errors, rate limits)Write latency and 5xx/503 rate from the sinkBackpressure: upstream buffers (Kafka retention is the buffer); retries with jitterSpread object key prefixes; fewer, larger files; retention sized to cover the outage you are willing to absorb
Downstream slow (warehouse, OLAP store, API sink)Backpressure metrics; rising consumer lag; sink latency p99Let lag absorb it; scale the sink; shed non-critical consumersDecouple via the log; async I/O with bounded concurrency; SLO per consumer (Part 03 §12)
Region failureHealth checks across regions; replication lag alarmsExecute DR runbook: repoint producers, promote catalog, start jobs from mirrored offsetsDefined RPO/RTO; tested failover drills; idempotent sinks to absorb replay (§3)
Credentials expire (tokens, certificates, keys)Auth error rate; certificate-expiry monitor ahead of expiryRotate and restart; replay the gap from the logShort-lived credentials with automatic refresh; expiry alerts days ahead; no long-lived keys in jobs (Part 14)

Two patterns cut across the table. The log is your shock absorber: most recoveries work because the log retains enough to replay the gap, so Kafka retention is a failure-recovery parameter — size it to the longest outage you intend to survive. And idempotent sinks turn replay from a risk into a routine; otherwise every recovery is its own incident.

7. Interviewer Attack Mode

Interviewers push back to see whether your choices were choices. The strong answer has one shape: back to the requirement, name the axis, give the condition for switching. The weak answer defends the brand.

Interviewer pushes back

You: “I’d use Kafka for ingestion.”

Interviewer: “Why not Kinesis? We’re already on AWS.”

Strong answer: “Both are durable, partitioned, replayable logs; the concepts transfer. Kinesis wins on operational burden — no brokers. The costs are per-shard throughput and fan-out limits I’d check in current AWS docs, and a smaller ecosystem than Kafka Connect. At 240 MB/s peak with three consumer groups, both work. If nobody here operates Kafka, I’d take Kinesis or managed Kafka and spend the saved effort on data quality. Needing the connector ecosystem or cross-cloud portability would push me to Kafka.”

Weak answer: “Kafka is the industry standard and Kinesis doesn’t scale.” It does scale; the question was about trade-offs, and you just told the interviewer you don’t know them.

Interviewer pushes back

You: “I would partition the topic by user_id.”

Interviewer: “What happens when one user generates 20% of traffic?”

Strong answer: “At peak that user is 20% × 300K × 800 B = 48 MB/s into one partition, against a consumer that handles 5 MB/s. It lags without bound, and since the watermark is the minimum across partitions, every event-time window closes late. More partitions won’t help — the hash still sends that user to one place. So: why did I key by user_id? If sessionisation needs per-user order, I salt only the hot keys into N buckets and merge partial sessions downstream, with runtime hot-key detection. If not, I key by event_id and do per-user work after an even shuffle.”

Weak answer: “We’ll add more partitions.” Hash partitioning maps one key to one partition regardless of partition count.

Interviewer pushes back

You: “I’d use Flink for the streaming layer.”

Interviewer: “Why not Spark Structured Streaming? The team already runs Spark.”

Strong answer: “That’s a strong argument for Spark — one engine, one skill set. The axis is latency and state. Flink treats per-record processing, timers and large keyed state as first-class; Spark micro-batches trade seconds of latency for simplicity and a unified batch API, and recent releases narrowed the gap with new stateful APIs and a lower-latency mode whose status I’d check for our version. If our tightest requirement is 1-minute freshness, Spark meets it and I’d choose Spark. Sub-second per-event decisions or very large timer-heavy state would justify a second engine.”

Weak answer: “Flink is true streaming and Spark is only micro-batching.” That’s a slogan, not a requirement.

Interviewer pushes back

You: “The dashboard is refreshed nightly.”

Interviewer: “Product says it has to be real-time.”

Strong answer: “What does real-time mean in seconds, and what does someone do differently when the number updates? If support reacts to outages, one minute matters and a streaming tier is worth it. If an executive checks at 9am, hourly incremental is enough at a fraction of the cost. And do they need it fresh or correct? Streaming numbers are provisional until late data settles. Usually: a small streaming tier for a few operational metrics, batch for the rest.” (See Part 08.)

Weak answer: Redesigning everything as streaming on the spot. You multiplied operational cost without learning whether anyone needed it.

Interviewer pushes back

You: “A streaming path for fresh numbers and a batch path for corrected ones.”

Interviewer: “So, Lambda architecture. Isn’t that dead?”

Strong answer: “Classic Lambda failed because business logic was written twice in two frameworks and drifted. I’m describing one set of logic, run in streaming for freshness and re-run in batch over bronze for authoritative numbers — the pragmatic middle in Part 03 §13. Pure Kappa needs log retention as long as the correction window; with 7 days of Kafka and 30-day restatements, it doesn’t fit here.”

Weak answer: Either defending two independent codebases, or abandoning the batch correction path because the label sounds dated.

Interviewer pushes back

You: “The pipeline is exactly-once.”

Interviewer: “Exactly-once from where to where?”

Strong answer: “Exactly-once is a property of a pipeline, not a product, so let me name the boundaries. Kafka to Iceberg bronze: effectively once — replayable source, checkpointed offsets and state, a sink that commits on checkpoint completion. Phone to Kafka: no. The SDK retries on timeout, so duplicates arrive by design and silver dedups on event_id. Side effects — an email, an external call — sit outside the boundary and need their own idempotency key.” (Mechanics in Part 03 §7.)

Weak answer: “Kafka supports exactly-once, so we’re exactly-once.” Transactions cover Kafka-to-Kafka; they say nothing about the phone or the warehouse.

Interviewer pushes back

You: “Consumer lag is growing, so we’ll add more partitions.”

Interviewer: “Will that help?”

Strong answer: “Only if consumers are partition-bound. First, where does the time go? One lagging partition is a hot key; more partitions won’t move it. A slow sink gets more parallel pressure on the thing already slow. On a keyed topic, more partitions remap keys, breaking per-key order across the change and misaligning co-partitioned topics and state stores — and the count can’t be reduced later. A real lever, but the last one I’d reach for.”

Weak answer: “Yes, more partitions means more parallelism.” True only when partitions are the constraint, which is exactly what you didn’t check.

Interviewer pushes back

You: “The nightly job is missing SLA; we’ll use a bigger cluster.”

Interviewer: “How much bigger, and will it work?”

Strong answer: “I’d look before I spent. One 20-minute task among 40-second ones is skew, and more executors sit idle around the same straggler — the skew tax in Part 02 §15. Long planning on a million small files is layout. A collecting driver is code. Evenly slow, CPU-bound stages: then scale out, expecting runtime roughly ∝ 1/cores until shuffle or I/O saturates. Bigger clusters fix throughput, not skew, layout or serial work.”

Weak answer: “Double the executors.” The bill doubles; the runtime may not move.

Interviewer pushes back

You: “Long term, we’ll move to a data mesh.”

Interviewer: “What does that change in this design?”

Strong answer: “Mostly ownership, not boxes. Data mesh is an organisational model: domains publish data as products on a self-serve platform under federated governance. It fits when there are many producing domains with engineers willing to own data products and a platform mature enough to make that cheap. For one product team and one analytics team it is pure coordination cost. For thirty teams bottlenecked on a central team, I’d adopt the concrete parts: contracts at domain boundaries, per-domain on-call, shared quality checks (Part 15, Part 10).”

Weak answer: Treating “data mesh” as an architecture diagram or a product you install.

8. How to Explain a Trade-off Under Pushback

A common interview prompt: “Your design uses X. I think Y is better. Convince me.” It tests whether you can hold a technical position under social pressure without folding or digging in. Four moves.

  1. Restate the constraint. “We said the daily number must be exact and reproducible.” This moves the argument from taste to requirements.
  2. Name the axis. “This is a trade between operational simplicity and per-event latency.”
  3. Quantify. “Flink gets us seconds; Spark micro-batches get about a minute. The requirement is one minute. A second engine buys ~50 seconds nobody asked for, at the cost of another deployment path and on-call surface.”
  4. State what would change your mind. “If this becomes sub-second fraud decisions, I switch.” The move most candidates skip, and the one that makes the rest credible: the choice is conditional on requirements, not identity.
Common axisThe question that decides it
Latency vs costWhat action does fresher data enable, and what is it worth?
Freshness vs correctnessCan the consumer tolerate a provisional number that is later revised?
Operational burden vs controlWho is on call, and what do we need to tune that a managed service won’t let us?
Consistency vs availabilityDuring a partition or outage, is a stale answer better than no answer?
Flexibility vs performanceAre the query patterns known (model for them) or exploratory (keep it general)?
Build vs buyIs this a core competency, and what is the exit cost? (Part 09 §7)

A worked exchange.

Interviewer: “Why dedup in batch? Do it in the stream so the dashboard is exact too.”

You: “The dashboard is 1-minute fresh and labelled approximate; daily metrics are exact. [restate] The trade is state size and operational risk against dashboard accuracy. [axis] Retries arrive up to three days late, so exact streaming dedup holds three days of event_ids: 25.92B keys at 16–24 bytes is ~400–600 GB before state-backend overhead, to remove a duplicate rate we measured at about 0.5%. [quantify] If the dashboard drove billing, or duplicates were 10%, I’d pay — probably with a one-hour dedup window in the stream, which catches most retries for a fraction of the state. [what changes my mind]”

Arithmetic: 3 × 8.64B = 25.92B keys; × 16 B = 414.72 GB; × 24 B = 622.08 GB. The duplicate rate is hypothetical, and you would say so.

Three failure modes under pushback.

  • Folding. “Good point, let’s use Y.” Interviewers push on correct choices specifically to see this.
  • Digging in. Repeating the reason louder. If they added a constraint, the answer may legitimately change: “With that constraint, I’d switch, because…”
  • Brand arguing. “Everyone uses X.” Popularity is not a requirement.

The posture is conditional confidence: firm on the reasoning, open on the inputs.

L5 Interview CardSystem Design Framework & Capacity Planning
Must know
  • The eight steps in order: requirements, numbers, data model, architecture, failure modes, trade-offs, operations, evolution.
  • The capacity chain: ev/s × bytes → MB/s → TB/day, then × retention ÷ compression × replication.
  • Partitions = max(T / pproduce, T / pconsume) × headroom, with per-partition rates measured.
  • Workers = peak ÷ per-core rate ÷ target utilisation; catch-up = backlog ÷ spare capacity.
  • Compression ratios are ranges to measure (wire ~3–5×, columnar ~5–10× for event data).
  • RPO is bounded by the slowest asynchronous replication path; offsets are cluster-local.
  • Kafka message key and lake partition are two different decisions.
Must be able to explain
  1. Why sizing comes before choosing technologies.
  2. Why more partitions do not fix a hot key.
  3. Where exactly-once starts and stops in your pipeline.
Must be able to draw

The six-layer flow with a replay path and a correction path:

SDK → collector → Kafka ─┬→ stream → OLAP (fresh)
                         └→ bronze → silver → gold
                                (exact, WAP)
Must be able to code
  • An idempotent daily job: overwrite one logical partition, with write-audit-publish.
  • Dedup by event_id keeping the earliest received row (window function with deterministic tiebreak).
  • A reconciliation query comparing source counts to target distinct keys per hour.
Must be able to debug
  • Consumer lag rising on one partition only; watermark stalled; every window late (hot key).
  • Query planning time doubling weekly on a streaming-written table (small files, snapshot build-up).
Numbers that matter
  • 86,400 s/day; 1M/day ≈ 11.6/s; 1B/day ≈ 11.6K/s.
  • 100K ev/s × 800 B = 80 MB/s = 6.912 TB/day raw.
  • 1 MB/s sustained ≈ 86.4 GB/day ≈ 31.5 TB/year.
  • RF=3 → 3× disk, 2× produce rate in replication traffic.
  • Target ~60% utilisation to leave catch-up capacity.
Classic traps
  • Naming Kafka before asking the volume.
  • Backfilling 30 days from a topic that keeps 7.
  • Quoting a vendor limit or price from memory as a constant.
30-second answer

How do you approach a data system design question? I clarify requirements and name the hardest one, then size it — events per second, bytes, MB/s, TB a day, retention — before I pick anything. Then grain and key, then a six-layer architecture where every box traces to a requirement. Then I spend real time on what breaks first, state my trade-offs as “X over Y because”, and finish with operations and what changes at 10×.

2-minute answer

How do you approach a data system design question? Requirements first, functional split from non-functional — freshness, correctness, retention, access, compliance — because one usually drives the design, often correctness rather than scale. Then numbers: 100K events/sec at 800 bytes is 80 MB/s, ~6.9 TB/day raw, which gives Kafka disk with replication, partitions from measured per-partition rates, workers at 60% utilisation, lake growth and backfill time. Then grain, idempotency key, schema evolution and partitioning — separately for log and lake. Then sources-to-consumers architecture, then failure modes box by box, because pipelines break at the seams: retries duplicate, commits half-fail, keys run hot. Finally trade-offs with the condition that reverses each, operations with named owners, and the first wall at 10×.

Deep-dive follow-up

“Your consumers run at 60% utilisation at peak. A 10-minute outage happens at peak. How long until you’re caught up, and does that meet your freshness SLA?”

Staff+ follow-up

“Three teams each want their own streaming copy of this data with different latency and retention needs. How do you decide what the platform provides centrally and what each team owns, and how do you keep cross-AZ and storage costs from scaling with the number of consumers?”
