Part 19

Debugging Lab

Quick refresh10 minInterview study45 minDeep practice180 min
Last technically reviewed September 2026
Covers debugging method, Spark stragglers and skew, Kafka consumer lag, Airflow date semantics, warehouse plan regressions, streaming duplicates, lakehouse file explosion, revenue reconciliation, Flink checkpoints, dbt enum drift, CDC replication slots, cost spikes, SCD2 overlaps
Versions referenced Spark 3.5 / 4.x, Kafka 4.x (KRaft), Flink 2.x / 1.20 LTS, Airflow 2.x and 3.x, Iceberg 1.x (format v2/v3), Delta Lake 3.x/4.x, PostgreSQL 15–17, dbt Core 1.x
Primary references Spark Web UI · Kafka docs · Flink checkpoint monitoring · Airflow docs · Iceberg maintenance · PostgreSQL logical decoding
Known implementation differences The method is timeless; the metric names, UI tabs and defaults you cite are version-specific, so name the engine and version when you quote one.

This chapter tests one thing: whether you diagnose before you prescribe. Every drill below has a tempting one-line fix, and every one of those fixes is wrong at least some of the time. The interviewer is not grading whether you land on the right root cause in minute two. They are grading whether you can name three hypotheses, say which measurement separates them, and stop the bleeding while you find out.

1. The method: observe before you fix

Senior debugging is a loop, not a guess. Six steps, always in this order, even when you are fairly sure of the answer — because saying the steps out loud is what the interviewer is scoring.

1.1 What the interviewer listens for at each step

Observe. Before any hypothesis, pin down the symptom precisely. Which job, partition or dashboard? Since when — a step change at 02:00 Tuesday or a drift over three weeks? A step points to a deploy, config flip, schema change or data event; a drift points to growth in volume, files or state. The interviewer is listening for you asking "what changed?" and "what is the blast radius?" in the first thirty seconds. If you start with a fix, you have told them you debug by pattern-matching.

Hypothesize. Produce two to four candidate causes, not one. Rank them out loud by prior probability and by cost to check. "Skew is the most common cause of one slow task, and the Spark UI tells me in a minute, so I check that first" is a complete, senior sentence. One hypothesis defended to the death is how strong engineers fail these rounds.

Measure. This is the L5 move. For each pair of hypotheses, name the observation that would distinguish them. "If it's skew, the slow task's shuffle-read bytes will be far above the median. If it's a bad node, its bytes will be normal but its duration abnormal, and other tasks on that executor will also be slow." A measurement that doesn't discriminate is just activity.

Isolate. Narrow the search space mechanically: reproduce on one partition, one day, one key; bisect by time (last good run vs first bad run) or by change (config diff, code diff, input diff). "Diff the last good run against the first bad one" is the cheapest isolation technique there is.

Fix. Two fixes, in order. First the mitigation that stops the bleeding: pause the downstream publish, roll back the deploy, route to a DLQ, scale out, serve the last good snapshot. Then the root-cause fix. Blast radius first: stop the bleeding, then root-cause.

Prevent. Name what would have caught this earlier and what stops it recurring: an alert on the leading signal (not the symptom), a test, a contract, a guardrail in CI, a runbook entry. The Staff+ answer also asks why this class of bug was possible at all.

1.2 How to talk while debugging in an interview

The interviewer cannot see your head. Narrate it, and narrate it in a shape they can score.

  • Restate and scope. "So the job is green, the row count is normal, but the partition for 2026-09-23 is absent. Is anything else missing, or just that day?"
  • Rank hypotheses on two axes. "Most likely is a date-semantics bug — it's the most common cause and I can check it by reading the rendered template. Less likely but worse is an overwrite that deleted it; I'd check the table history." Probability and cost-to-check, stated together.
  • Ask for the data, don't invent it. "What does the task-duration distribution look like?" If they say "you tell me", state what each answer would mean.
  • Say what would change your mind. "If shuffle read on that task is normal, I drop skew and look at the node."
  • Mitigate out loud. "Before I root-cause, I'd stop the downstream publish so nobody consumes a partial table." One sentence, then continue.
  • Close with prevention. Without it, the answer is a war story, not engineering.
Interviewer pushes back

You: “I'd look at the logs to see what went wrong.”

Interviewer: “Which logs, looking for what? There are 4,000 executor logs.”

Strong answer: “I wouldn't start in logs. I'd start with aggregated metrics that tell me where to look — the stage's task-duration distribution, then the one outlier task's executor and input size. Logs are for confirming a hypothesis on one executor, not for generating one across 4,000.”

Weak answer: “I'd grep for ERROR.” — Most performance and correctness bugs log nothing at ERROR. That is why they reach production.

2026 Interview Note

The loop above is timeless — it predates every tool named in this chapter. What ages quickly is the vocabulary: UI tab names, metric names, config keys and defaults move between releases. Say "in Spark 3.x the Stages tab shows…" rather than "Spark shows…". Tying a signal to a version is itself a seniority signal: it tells the interviewer you have operated the thing, not read about it.

1.3 How to use the drills

Each drill gives you the symptom as an interviewer would phrase it. Say your answer out loud — all six steps — before opening anything. Open the hint only if you have no idea where to look. Then compare your answer with the reveal, paying most attention to the Measure step and the wrong turns: those are the answers the interviewer has heard a hundred times. Longer incident walk-throughs live in Part 08 (for example missed SLA and Monday OOMs); this chapter deliberately covers different ground.

2. Core drills

2.1 Spark: the 21-minute task

Drill · Spark

999 tasks finish in 40 seconds. One runs for 21 minutes.

STOP. Answer before revealing.

Hint: what would you look at first?

Open the stage in the Spark UI and compare the slow task's input or shuffle-read bytes against the median. Same bytes or 50× the bytes? That one number splits the hypotheses in half.

Reveal the diagnosis
  1. Observe One task out of 1,000 takes ~30× the median. Which stage — a scan stage, a shuffle stage after a join, or an aggregation? Same task index every run? A scan-stage straggler and a post-shuffle straggler have different suspect lists.
  2. Hypothesize Four candidates, ranked by prior: (1) key skew — one join or group key holds a huge share of rows; (2) one huge non-splittable input file — a 12 GB .csv.gz is read by exactly one task because gzip is not splittable; (3) spill — the task's partition doesn't fit in execution memory, so it spills to disk and GC thrashes; (4) straggler node — a bad disk, noisy neighbour or throttled instance slows whatever lands there.
  3. Measure In the Stages tab, open task-level metrics sorted by duration. For the slow task compare against the median: shuffle read size / records (skew: 20–100× the median), input size on a scan stage (non-splittable file: one task reads one giant file, others read ~128 MB splits), spill (memory) / spill (disk) and GC time (spill: large spill, GC a big fraction of duration), and executor ID / host (straggler: normal bytes, abnormal duration, and other tasks on the same host are also slow). Skew often causes spill, so look at bytes first; spill without outsized bytes means too few partitions for the memory.
  4. Isolate For skew, find the key: df.groupBy("customer_id").count().orderBy(desc("count")).limit(20) on the join input. One key with 40% of rows (null, "UNKNOWN", a bot account) is the classic finding. For the file hypothesis, list input files by size; a single multi-GB .gz is conclusive. For the node, check whether re-running moves the slowness with the host or stays with the task index. Moves with the host means node; stays with the index means data.
  5. Fix Skew in a sort-merge join: confirm AQE skew-join handling is enabled and its thresholds would actually classify this partition as skewed; otherwise isolate the heavy keys (broadcast-join the hot keys, sort-merge the rest) or salt. Skew in GROUP BY: two-stage aggregation (partial aggregate on a salted key, then final). Null keys: filter before the join and union back — they never match anyway. Non-splittable file: fix it upstream (splittable compression such as zstd-compressed Parquet, or many smaller gzip files); as a one-off, read and repartition immediately. Spill without skew: more shuffle partitions. Bad node: speculative execution (spark.speculation) mitigates; decommission the node.
  6. Prevent Alert on the ratio max/median task duration per stage (not wall-clock alone). Add an upstream contract that files land splittable and bounded in size. Track top-key share for critical join keys as a data-quality metric so the next "one customer is 40% of traffic" is a dashboard, not an incident.

Plausible wrong turns

  • "Add more executors." More executors do nothing for one task — the stage is serial on its slowest partition.
  • "Turn on speculation." It re-launches the same skewed partition on another node, which is equally slow, and doubles the cost of the slowest task. Speculation fixes nodes, not data.

Where this is taught: Part 04 §7 — skew detection, salting, AQE, verifying AQE fired, memory model and spill, Part 02 §9 — file sizing.

2026 Interview Note

AQE skew-join splitting arrived in Spark 3.0 and AQE has been on by default since Spark 3.2. It splits skewed partitions of sort-merge joins when a partition exceeds both a size threshold and a multiple of the median (keys under spark.sql.adaptive.skewJoin.*). It does not rescue every skew shape — a skewed GROUP BY, or a join type where the skewed side cannot be split, still needs your hand. Check the current docs for your version, and confirm in the SQL tab that the plan shows the skew handling actually fired rather than assuming it did.

2.2 Kafka: lag climbs, CPU idles

Drill · Kafka

Consumer lag keeps growing, but CPU is only 35%.

STOP. Answer before revealing.

Hint: what would you look at first?

Low CPU means the consumer is waiting, not working. Look at lag per partition, not the group total, and at where time goes in the poll–process–commit loop.

Reveal the diagnosis
  1. Observe Group lag grows steadily; consumers are far from CPU-bound. "More compute" is not the first answer. Did producer rate rise or consumer throughput fall? Uniform or concentrated? What deployed first?
  2. Hypothesize Ranked: (1) IO-bound sink — each record or batch waits on a database write, HTTP call or object-store PUT; (2) hot partition — one key dominates one partition and the single consumer that owns it can't keep up while the rest idle; (3) parallelism ceiling — fewer partitions than consumers, so extra consumers sit idle, or more partitions than consumers can each drain; (4) blocking processing loop — synchronous per-record work, a large max.poll.records batch processed serially, or synchronous commits after every record; (5) rebalance storms — processing exceeds max.poll.interval.ms, the consumer is kicked, the group rebalances, work pauses and restarts; (6) downstream throttling — the sink returns 429s or throttles and the client retries with backoff.
  3. Measure Per-partition lag (kafka-consumer-groups.sh --describe --group … gives LAG per partition and the owning consumer): one partition with most of the lag means hot key, uniform lag means capacity. Compare partition count against active consumers in that output — idle members with no assignment mean a parallelism ceiling. Consumer metrics: records-consumed-rate, commit-latency-avg, rebalance counts and the group state history (frequent PreparingRebalance). Application timing: split each batch into poll time, processing time and sink time; if sink time is 80% of the loop, you've found it. Sink side: write latency p99, throttling or 429 counts, connection-pool saturation.
  4. Isolate Replay a fixed slice of one partition into a no-op sink. If throughput jumps 10×, the sink is the bottleneck. If one partition stays hot even with a no-op sink, the problem is data distribution. Correlate lag inflection points with rebalance events in the log — a sawtooth that resets every few minutes is a rebalance storm.
  5. Fix IO-bound sink: batch writes, make them async with bounded in-flight requests, raise sink-side concurrency, and commit offsets only after the batch is durable. Hot partition: fix the key (compound key or bounded salt, if per-key order permits) — consumers can't split one partition. Parallelism ceiling: add partitions, knowing it remaps keys and cannot be undone. Rebalance storms: shrink batch size or move slow work off the poll thread so the consumer polls within the interval; use cooperative or the newer server-side rebalance protocol where available. Per-record sync commits: commit per batch, async, with a final sync commit on shutdown.
  6. Prevent Alert on lag in time (seconds behind) per partition, not total messages. Dashboard the poll / process / sink / commit breakdown. Load-test the sink at 2× peak. Size partitions up front, not during an incident.

Plausible wrong turns

  • "Scale consumers." Useless past partition count and useless if the sink is the bottleneck — it can even make throttling worse.
  • "Increase max.poll.records." Bigger batches processed serially make each loop longer and can trigger the very rebalance storm you're fighting.

Where this is taught: Part 03 §9 — Kafka internals, Part 03 §12 — backpressure. Further practice: Part 08 — lag won't drain (the generic version of this drill) and Part 13 for partitioning theory.

2.3 Airflow: green run, missing partition

Drill · Airflow

Job succeeded, but yesterday's partition is missing.

STOP. Answer before revealing.

Hint: what would you look at first?

Open the task instance's rendered template and read the actual path and date it wrote. Then ask where the data went, not whether the job ran.

Reveal the diagnosis
  1. Observe Status green, downstream sees no dt=2026-09-23. First scope it: only this day or a pattern (every Monday, every day since a deploy, only on DST boundaries)? Did the partition never exist or exist and then vanish? Those two branches split the whole diagnosis.
  2. Hypothesize Never existed: (1) logical date vs run date confusion — the task wrote the partition for the run's logical date, which is a different day than the author assumed; (2) timezone — UTC scheduler, local-time business day, or a naive datetime.now() in the code; (3) templating bug — {{ ds }} in a field that isn't templated, so the literal string or a stale value went through; (4) wrote to the wrong path — a staging bucket, a typo, an environment variable pointing at dev; (5) success on zero rows — upstream wasn't ready, the query returned nothing, and nothing fails on empty; (6) sensor soft-fail — a sensor with soft_fail=True timed out, was marked skipped, and a downstream trigger rule let the run end green. Existed then vanished: (7) dynamic partition overwrite gone wrong — a static overwrite mode replaced the whole table with only today's partitions; (8) idempotent overwrite with empty input — a rerun of yesterday found no source rows and "correctly" overwrote the partition with nothing.
  3. Measure Rendered template for the task instance: the literal date and path it used. Task log: rows read, rows written — a successful write of 0 rows is a finding. Task-instance states for the whole run: any skipped sensors? Table history (DESCRIBE HISTORY in Delta, the snapshots metadata table in Iceberg, or object-store listing with timestamps): was there ever a commit adding that partition, and did a later commit remove it? The run's data_interval_start/data_interval_end versus the partition the business expected.
  4. Isolate Compare what the run thinks it processed (its data interval) with what the author thinks it processed ("yesterday"). If the partition exists under a neighbouring date or path, it's semantics or path. If history shows an overwrite commit removing it, find which run issued that commit and what its input count was. If nothing was ever written, look at upstream readiness at run time.
  5. Fix Mitigate: block downstream consumers of that date (or publish a known-incomplete flag), then re-run the backfill for the correct interval with a non-zero row check. Root cause: derive partitions from data_interval_start, never from wall-clock; make timezones explicit in the DAG; set partition overwrite to dynamic mode for partitioned writes; make empty input a failure unless the source genuinely publishes empty days.
  6. Prevent A post-write assertion task: the expected partition exists and its row count is within a band of the trailing median. Fail on zero rows by default. Ban soft_fail sensors on critical paths, or route skipped runs to an alert. Freshness checks downstream so a missing partition pages before a human notices.

Plausible wrong turns

  • "Just clear and re-run the task." If the bug is date semantics, the re-run writes the same wrong partition again, green again.
  • "The scheduler must have skipped it." The run is in the UI as green; the scheduler did its job. The question is what the task did.

Where this is taught: Part 02 §12 — orchestration, Part 02 §3 — idempotency, Part 02 §6 — backfills, Part 12 §4 — reconciliation.

2026 Interview Note

Timeless: a scheduled run processes an interval, and the partition you write should be derived from that interval, not from when the task happened to execute. Version-specific: Airflow 2.2 renamed execution_date to logical_date and introduced data intervals; in classic cron scheduling the run for a day's interval fires after that interval ends, which is why "the 23rd's run executes on the 24th" confuses people. Airflow 3 removed the deprecated execution_date context names and, at time of writing (2026), changed the default cron behaviour so a cron schedule's logical date is the trigger time rather than the interval start — the same DAG can write a different partition after an upgrade. Manually triggered and asset-triggered runs may also have no meaningful logical date. Check the current Airflow upgrade notes before quoting any of this as fixed.

2.4 Warehouse: 20 seconds to 11 minutes

Drill · Warehouse

Query went from 20 seconds to 11 minutes without code changes.

STOP. Answer before revealing.

Hint: what would you look at first?

Pull the query profile for a fast run and a slow run and put them side by side. Is the time in queueing or execution? If execution, did the plan change or did the same plan get more work?

Reveal the diagnosis
  1. Observe 33× slower, same SQL text. "No code changes" is a claim to verify, not a fact — check the view definitions and UDFs underneath too. Step change or drift? One query or everything on that warehouse?
  2. Hypothesize Split into three families. Not running: (1) concurrency queueing — the warehouse is saturated and the query waits; (2) warehouse was resized down or moved to a different compute pool. Same plan, more work: (3) data growth — the table grew or a partition exploded; (4) clustering or sort order degraded, so pruning reads far more micro-partitions or files; (5) result cache miss — it was never 20 seconds of compute, it was a cache hit, and something invalidated the cache; (6) spilling to local or remote disk because the working set now exceeds memory. Different plan: (7) plan flip — a dimension grew past the broadcast threshold and the join became a shuffle join, or the join order inverted; (8) stale statistics fed the optimiser a wrong cardinality; (9) partition pruning lost — an upstream column changed type (DATE to STRING or TIMESTAMP), so the filter now wraps the column in a cast and can no longer prune.
  3. Measure From the query history / profile (every major warehouse has one): queued time vs execution time; partitions or bytes scanned vs total (pruning ratio); bytes spilled local and remote; whether the result came from cache; the join operators and their order (EXPLAIN or the graphical profile) for both runs. Table-level: row count and size over time, clustering depth or file-level min/max overlap, last stats refresh. Warehouse-level: size history and concurrent query count at the slow run's timestamp.
  4. Isolate Diff the two profiles operator by operator. Queued time dominates → capacity. Same operators but 30× bytes scanned with a similar table size → pruning lost (look for an implicit cast in the filter) or clustering degraded. Different join strategy → plan flip; check the size of the smaller side now. Remote spill appears → memory. Re-run with the result cache disabled to learn the true baseline.
  5. Fix Queueing: scale out (multi-cluster / more slots) or move the workload to its own warehouse. Pruning lost: fix the type upstream, or rewrite the predicate so the column stays bare (col >= '2026-09-01' on a correctly typed column, not CAST(col AS DATE)). Clustering: recluster and schedule it. Plan flip: refresh stats; if the dimension genuinely grew, pre-filter it or size for the shuffle join. Spill: filter earlier, project fewer columns.
  6. Prevent Track p50/p95 duration and bytes-scanned per recurring query fingerprint; alert on a step change in bytes scanned, which precedes the latency complaint. Contracts forbidding type changes on partition and cluster keys. Workload isolation for anything with an SLA.

Plausible wrong turns

  • "Double the warehouse size." It might hide it for a month at twice the cost. If pruning is lost, you are paying to scan 30× the data faster.
  • "Nothing changed, so it's the vendor." Something always changed: data, stats, schema, concurrency or the cache.

Where this is taught: Part 05 §13 — query tuning workflow, Part 05 §5 — what prunes and when, Part 04 §11 — broadcast thresholds, Part 11 — warehouse cost, and Part 16 for engine-by-engine architecture.

2.5 Streaming: duplicates after restart

Drill · Streaming

Duplicates appear after a restart.

STOP. Answer before revealing.

Hint: what would you look at first?

Characterise the duplicates: how many, over what time window relative to the restart, and are they byte-identical or do they differ (different processing time, different computed values)? Then draw the offset-commit and sink-commit points on one timeline.

Reveal the diagnosis
  1. Observe After a restart (deploy, crash, rebalance), some records appear twice in the sink. Do duplicates cluster just before the restart (replay)? Identical, or different values (state loss or non-determinism)? Which sink: append-only table, keyed store, or a topic read by another consumer?
  2. Hypothesize (1) At-least-once source + non-idempotent sink — the pipeline replays from the last committed position, and an append sink writes the replayed records again; this is the default outcome and the most likely. (2) Offsets committed on a different schedule than the sink — auto-commit, or commits that aren't tied to sink durability. Commit after the sink write gives duplicates on crash; commit before gives loss, which people often don't notice. (3) Checkpoint not aligned with sink commit — in Flink or Spark Structured Streaming, the sink writes outside the checkpoint/transaction protocol, so on restore the engine replays records the sink already has. (4) Transactional producer, but consumers read with read_uncommitted — downstream consumers see records from aborted transactions. (5) Changed operator uid or query plan — the job restarted with state it couldn't map, dropped dedup state, and re-emitted keys it had already emitted.
  3. Measure Count duplicates by the record's natural key and by event time; plot against the restart timestamp. The window of duplicated records should be about one checkpoint or commit interval wide for replay causes. Check consumer config: enable.auto.commit, commit placement in code, and downstream consumers' isolation.level. In Flink, check the restore log — did it restore from a checkpoint or savepoint, and did it report operators whose state couldn't be mapped (and was --allowNonRestoredState passed)? In Spark, check whether the checkpoint location changed or was deleted.
  4. Isolate Duplicates width ≈ commit interval and identical payloads → replay into a non-idempotent sink. Duplicates only visible to one downstream consumer → isolation level. Duplicates spanning far longer than a checkpoint interval, or all keys re-emitted since some date → state lost on restore (changed uid, new checkpoint path, or allowNonRestoredState).
  5. Fix Mitigate: deduplicate downstream on the natural key plus event identity for the affected window, and tell consumers. Root cause, pick one per boundary: make the sink idempotent (upsert/MERGE on a deterministic key), or make it transactional and tied to the checkpoint (two-phase commit sinks in Flink; Structured Streaming's file sink or foreachBatch writing idempotently keyed by batch id). Set consumers of transactional topics to read_committed. Pin explicit operator uids in Flink and never change them casually; stop-with-savepoint for deploys.
  6. Prevent A duplicate-rate metric on the natural key in the sink, alerting at a tiny non-zero threshold. A restart test in CI or staging: kill the job mid-stream, restart, assert zero duplicates and zero gaps. A lint that fails the build if a stateful Flink operator lacks a uid.

Plausible wrong turns

  • "Enable Kafka exactly-once." Idempotent/transactional producers cover Kafka-to-Kafka. They say nothing about your Postgres or S3 sink.
  • "Turn off retries." Trades duplicates for data loss.

Where this is taught: Part 03 §7 — delivery semantics, Flink 2PC and checkpoints, idempotent sinks, Part 03 §16 — idempotent producers and EOS, savepoints vs checkpoints.

2.6 Lakehouse: 20K files to 8 million

Drill · Lakehouse

File count increased from 20K to 8 million.

STOP. Answer before revealing.

Hint: what would you look at first?

Separate live files (referenced by the current snapshot) from all files in storage. Then group live files by partition and by the commit that added them.

Reveal the diagnosis
  1. Observe 400× more files. Which count — object-store listing or table metadata? When did the curve bend? Are queries slower, is storage cost up, are commits slower, or all three? That tells you whether the files are live (hurting reads) or dead (hurting cost).
  2. Hypothesize Live-file causes: (1) streaming micro-batches committing into high-cardinality partitions — each commit writes at least one file per touched partition, so a 1-minute trigger × 500 partitions touched is 720K files a day; (2) over-partitioning by a high-cardinality column (user_id, device_id, hour × country × event type); (3) merge-on-read delete files — every MERGE/UPDATE/DELETE adds position or equality delete files (or deletion vectors) that accumulate until compacted; (4) no compaction job, or one that has silently failed for weeks. Dead-file causes: (5) snapshot expiration not running, so every rewritten file is still referenced by some old snapshot; (6) orphan files from failed or aborted writes that no snapshot references.
  3. Measure Iceberg: SELECT partition, COUNT(*), AVG(file_size_in_bytes) FROM db.t.files GROUP BY partition ORDER BY 2 DESC; db.t.snapshots for commit frequency and operation; db.t.delete_files (or content in the files table) for delete-file count; count snapshots and the oldest one's age. Delta: DESCRIBE DETAIL for numFiles, DESCRIBE HISTORY for commit cadence and operations. Compare live file count with an object-store listing count: a big gap means expiration or orphan cleanup isn't running. Compare distinct partitions over time: a jump means a partition-spec change.
  4. Isolate If live files per partition are high and average size is kilobytes → commit cadence × partition fan-out. If partitions count jumped → someone partitioned by a high-cardinality column. If delete files dominate → MOR without compaction. If live files are sane but storage listing is huge → expiration/orphans. Identify the writer from the snapshot summary (application id, operation).
  5. Fix Mitigate: run bin-pack compaction on the hottest partitions first, rewrite manifests, then expire snapshots and remove orphans (with an age threshold longer than any in-flight write). Root cause: lengthen the trigger; distribute the write by the partition columns so each partition gets one writer; move the high-cardinality column from partitioning to sort order; make maintenance a monitored job, not a cron nobody watches.
  6. Prevent Alert on files-per-partition and average file size per table, and on snapshot count. Budget commits per hour × partitions touched per commit before launch.

Plausible wrong turns

  • "Run remove_orphan_files." Orphans are rarely the 8 million; and with too short a threshold it deletes files an in-flight write is about to commit.
  • "Just compact." Without fixing the writer, compaction is a treadmill — and on a table that is being streamed into, it fights the writer for commits.

Where this is taught: Part 07 §7 — compaction, delete compaction, the small-files killer, the expiration trap, Part 02 §9. Further practice: Part 08 — Iceberg reads 10× slower, which starts from the read symptom rather than the file count.

2.7 Data quality: revenue 3.7% above Finance

Drill · Data Quality

Revenue is 3.7% higher than Finance.

STOP. Answer before revealing.

Hint: what would you look at first?

Before any SQL: get Finance's exact definition of revenue in writing. Then slice both numbers by the same dimensions until the gap concentrates somewhere.

Reveal the diagnosis
  1. Observe A stable 3.7% gap, or new? Every period, or one month? Stable gaps are usually definitional; new gaps are a pipeline change. Higher everywhere, or higher in some slices and lower in others? The netting case is common and hides two bugs.
  2. Hypothesize Definitional: (1) gross vs net — we sum order value, Finance nets discounts, refunds, chargebacks; (2) tax and shipping included in ours, excluded in theirs; (3) FX conversion date — we convert at order date, Finance at settlement or month-end rate; (4) timezone cutoffs — our day ends at UTC midnight, Finance closes the day in the company's reporting timezone; (5) late cancellations — Finance recognises a cancellation that arrived after our snapshot. Pipeline: (6) duplicate events from replay or a join fan-out; (7) test or internal accounts not excluded; (8) currency rounding — rounding per line vs per order vs per total, which compounds on high-volume, low-value items.
  3. Measure Reconcile at the grain Finance uses, usually order or invoice. Slice the gap by: day (a spike vs a constant), currency (FX hypothesis concentrates the gap in non-home currencies), country/timezone (cutoff hypothesis puts the gap at day boundaries), channel/product, order status (refunded, cancelled), and account type (test accounts). Count duplicates on the natural key. Compute the gap with tax and shipping stripped. Each slice either absorbs a chunk of the 3.7% or it doesn't.
  4. Isolate Take the slice with the largest share of the gap, pull ten orders that exist in one system and not the other or differ in amount, and trace each end to end. Build a gap bridge: 3.7% = 1.9% refunds + 0.8% FX + 0.6% timezone + 0.3% test accounts + 0.1% unexplained.
  5. Fix Mitigate: label the dashboard with its definition and the known gap so nobody makes decisions on an unexplained number. Root cause: align the definition with Finance (or deliberately publish two named metrics — "gross bookings" and "net revenue" — never one ambiguous "revenue"); fix any pipeline bugs found (duplicates, test accounts) as defects, not definitions.
  6. Prevent Daily automated reconciliation against the ledger with a tolerance band and an owner. One metric definition in a semantic layer. Track the "unexplained" residual — if it grows, something new broke.

Plausible wrong turns

  • "Finance is wrong." Finance's number is audited. Yours isn't. Start by assuming you are the one who has to explain.
  • "Apply a 0.963 correction factor." You've now hidden three bugs behind one constant, and it will be wrong next month.

Where this is taught: Part 12 §4 — reconciliation frameworks, Part 12 §6 — data incident management, Part 01 §5 — grain, late-arriving facts. Further practice: Part 08 — half the revenue (a step change, not a definitional gap).

3. Extended drills

Five more, covering failure shapes the core set doesn't: slow degradation, silent row loss, infrastructure damage caused by a pipeline, cost, and a modelling bug. The "Lakehouse reads 10× slower after a MERGE-heavy week" scenario is intentionally left out — it is the same diagnosis as drill 2.6 entered from the read side, and Part 08 already covers it.

3.1 Flink: checkpoint durations creeping up

Drill · Flink

Checkpoint duration went from 20 seconds to 9 minutes over three weeks. Now some checkpoints time out.

STOP. Answer before revealing.

Hint: what would you look at first?

In the checkpoint history, split duration into alignment / start delay versus sync and async upload per subtask. One tells you about backpressure, the other about state size.

Reveal the diagnosis
  1. Observe A drift over weeks, not a step — so growth, not a deploy. Is the job also lagging? Did checkpointed state size grow alongside? Are all subtasks slow or one?
  2. Hypothesize (1) State growth — a window or join with no TTL, keyed on something with unbounded cardinality, grows forever, so each checkpoint uploads more; (2) backpressure delaying barriers — barriers queue behind buffered records, so alignment time (or start delay) dominates; (3) one skewed subtask — a hot key makes one subtask's state and throughput the outlier and every checkpoint waits for it; (4) slow checkpoint storage — object-store throttling or a network change; (5) full rather than incremental checkpoints with RocksDB, so every checkpoint uploads everything.
  3. Measure Checkpoint UI per subtask: end-to-end duration, checkpointed data size, sync duration, async duration, alignment duration, start delay. Big start delay/alignment with small state → backpressure. Big async duration with large and growing checkpointed size → state. One subtask far worse than the others → skew. Per-operator backPressuredTimeMsPerSecond and busyTimeMsPerSecond locate the bottleneck; storage-side latency and throttle errors cover hypothesis 4.
  4. Isolate Plot state size per operator over the three weeks. A straight line up on one operator is almost always missing TTL or an unbounded key. If state is flat but alignment grew, walk backpressure to the first operator that is busy while its downstream is idle — that operator or its sink is the bottleneck.
  5. Fix Mitigate: raise the checkpoint timeout and set a minimum pause between checkpoints so the job isn't in permanent checkpointing; consider unaligned checkpoints if the cause is backpressure (they trade larger checkpoint size for not waiting on alignment). Root cause: add state TTL or window cleanup; bound the key space; fix the bottleneck operator or sink; ensure incremental checkpoints are on for large RocksDB state; rescale if throughput genuinely outgrew parallelism.
  6. Prevent Alert on checkpoint duration as a fraction of interval and on state size growth rate, not just failures. A design review rule: every keyed state declares its TTL or its bound.

Plausible wrong turns

  • "Increase the checkpoint timeout." It stops failures today and hides a curve that keeps rising.
  • "Checkpoint less often." Longer intervals mean more replay on failure and bigger duplicates windows for non-transactional sinks — and the state is still growing.

Where this is taught: Part 03 §8 — Flink barriers and state, backpressure and checkpoints, incremental checkpoints, Part 03 §11 — state at scale.

3.2 dbt: rows silently dropped after an upstream enum change

Drill · dbt

Since last Tuesday, fct_orders has 6% fewer rows than stg_orders. All dbt tests pass.

STOP. Answer before revealing.

Hint: what would you look at first?

Which rows are missing? Anti-join staging to the fact and group the missing rows by every low-cardinality column. Then read every WHERE, JOIN and CASE between the two models.

Reveal the diagnosis
  1. Observe A step change on a specific day with no failing tests. That says the models run and the data is "valid" by every rule we wrote — the rule we didn't write is the bug.
  2. Hypothesize (1) Upstream enum change — the source added or renamed a status ('completed' became 'COMPLETED', or a new 'partially_refunded' appeared), and a WHERE status IN (…) or an inner join to a status mapping table silently excludes it; (2) inner join to a dimension that lacks new keys; (3) incremental model filter — the is_incremental() predicate uses a column whose semantics changed; (4) a CASE without ELSE producing NULL, then filtered.
  3. Measure SELECT s.status, COUNT(*) FROM stg_orders s LEFT JOIN fct_orders f USING (order_id) WHERE f.order_id IS NULL GROUP BY 1. If one value accounts for all of the gap, you have it. Compare distinct status values before and after Tuesday. Check the source's changelog or contract.
  4. Isolate Run each CTE of the fact model with a row count; the CTE where the count drops is where the rows die. dbt compile and read the compiled SQL rather than the Jinja.
  5. Fix Mitigate: add the new value to the mapping and backfill since Tuesday (full refresh or a targeted incremental rebuild for the affected window). Root cause: make the mapping total — a default branch that routes unknown values to 'unknown' instead of dropping them, and a left join to mapping tables.
  6. Prevent accepted_values tests on enum columns in staging so a new value fails loudly. A row-count reconciliation test between staging and fact (equal, or within a documented filter). A data contract with the source team that treats enum additions as a change requiring notice.

Plausible wrong turns

  • "Tests passed, so the data is fine." Tests check what you thought of. Row loss between layers needs a reconciliation test.
  • "Full-refresh the model." Rebuilds the same filter on the same data; still 6% short.

Where this is taught: Part 01 §13 — contracts and schema evolution, Part 12 §5 — testing, dbt tests, and Part 15 on contracts and transformation engineering.

3.3 CDC: the Postgres primary's disk is filling up

Drill · CDC

The production Postgres primary is at 91% disk and climbing. Application traffic hasn't changed. The CDC pipeline has been down since the weekend.

STOP. Answer before revealing.

Hint: what would you look at first?

pg_replication_slots. How much WAL is each slot holding back, and is it active?

Reveal the diagnosis
  1. Observe This is a production OLTP incident caused by the data platform, and it outranks every analytics concern. If the primary's disk fills, writes stop. Blast radius first: how long until full at the current rate?
  2. Hypothesize (1) Inactive logical replication slot — the CDC connector (Debezium or similar) stopped consuming, the slot's confirmed position froze, and Postgres retains all WAL since then; (2) slot active but lagging on a low-traffic captured table while the rest of the database generates WAL — the slot's position only advances when the connector confirms, and with nothing to emit it may not; (3) unrelated growth: table bloat, logs, a long-running transaction pinning old rows. The CDC-down timing makes (1) the strong prior.
  3. Measure SELECT slot_name, active, pg_size_pretty(pg_wal_lsn_diff(pg_current_wal_lsn(), confirmed_flush_lsn)) AS retained FROM pg_replication_slots; — a slot retaining hundreds of GB with active = false is conclusive. Check the WAL directory size directly and compare. Check max_slot_wal_keep_size. Check connector status and its last committed offset.
  4. Isolate If WAL retained ≈ disk growth since the weekend → the slot. If the slot is active and still lagging, check whether the connector's captured tables are idle while others write — the heartbeat case.
  5. Fix Mitigate, with the DBA and in order of reversibility: restart the connector so the slot advances (best — no data loss); if it can't catch up before the disk fills, grow the disk; as a last resort drop the slot, which frees WAL immediately and guarantees the CDC pipeline has lost changes and needs a fresh snapshot. Root cause: why the connector was down for two days with nobody paged; configure a heartbeat (a periodic write the connector emits) so idle-table slots advance.
  6. Prevent Alert on retained WAL per slot and on slot active = false for more than minutes. Set max_slot_wal_keep_size so a dead consumer invalidates its slot rather than killing the primary — explicitly choosing "CDC needs a resnapshot" over "production goes down". Runbook for resnapshot.

Plausible wrong turns

  • "Drop the slot" as the first move. It works, and silently forces a full resnapshot of every captured table. Restart first.
  • "Vacuum the database." Vacuum reclaims dead tuples, not WAL retained by a slot.

Where this is taught: Part 02 §10 — CDC patterns, log-based CDC, Part 12 §6 — incident management, and Part 15 for CDC in depth.

2026 Interview Note

Timeless: a replication slot is a promise by the database to keep WAL until the consumer confirms it, and an abandoned promise costs disk. Version-specific: max_slot_wal_keep_size exists since PostgreSQL 13; logical decoding from a standby arrived in 16 and failover of logical slots in 17. Managed Postgres services add their own limits and metrics. Connector heartbeat options differ by connector and version — check current docs.

3.4 Cost: the warehouse bill doubled overnight

Drill · Cost

Yesterday's warehouse spend was 2.1× the trailing 30-day average. Nobody announced a launch.

STOP. Answer before revealing.

Hint: what would you look at first?

Break the spend down by warehouse / project, then by user or service account, then by query fingerprint. Cost incidents almost always concentrate.

Reveal the diagnosis
  1. Observe A one-day step change. Still running today? Then it is burning money now and the first job is to find and contain it.
  2. Hypothesize (1) Runaway or looping job — a retry loop, an orchestrator backfill launched with the wrong date range, or catchup enabled on a DAG with a start date two years ago; (2) compute never suspends — auto-suspend disabled or a monitoring/BI tool pinging every minute keeps a warehouse awake; (3) resized compute — someone scaled a warehouse up for a one-off and didn't scale back; (4) a query that lost pruning or a new dashboard running a full scan on every refresh (on bytes-scanned pricing, this is the classic); (5) background services — automatic clustering, materialized-view refresh or search-optimisation maintenance triggered by a large rewrite.
  3. Measure The platform's usage/metering views: credits or slot-hours by warehouse per hour; query history grouped by user, role or service account and by query hash, ordered by cost or bytes scanned; warehouse size change events; serverless/background feature spend separately. On bytes-billed engines, top queries by bytes billed.
  4. Isolate If one warehouse accounts for the delta and its active hours went from 8 to 24 → suspend problem. If one service account accounts for it → runaway job; read its run history. If a single query fingerprint dominates → pruning or a dashboard refresh. If background services dominate → find the rewrite that triggered them.
  5. Fix Contain: pause the job, set a resource monitor or quota to cap spend, restore the warehouse size, re-enable auto-suspend. Root cause per branch: bound backfills, disable catchup by default, fix the pruning, change the dashboard refresh cadence or materialise it.
  6. Prevent Daily spend anomaly detection per warehouse and per service account with an owner. Hard quotas on non-production and ad-hoc compute. Tag every workload with a team. Treat warehouse resizes as reviewed config changes.

Plausible wrong turns

  • "Reduce every warehouse a size." Punishes every workload for one runaway and may push others into spill.
  • "Buy a larger commitment." Negotiates the price of the bug instead of fixing it.

Where this is taught: Part 11 — Snowflake cost, Part 11 §6 — FinOps, cost anomaly detection, cost-aware backfills, and Part 16 for pricing-model differences between engines.

3.5 Modelling: SCD2 rows with overlapping validity

Drill · Data Modeling

A point-in-time join to dim_customer returns two rows for some customers, inflating historical revenue.

STOP. Answer before revealing.

Hint: what would you look at first?

For one affected customer, list every version ordered by valid_from. Look at the boundaries: overlaps, gaps, and more than one row flagged current.

Reveal the diagnosis
  1. Observe Fan-out in a point-in-time join means some instant matches two versions. Which customers, since when, and do the overlapping rows share a load batch?
  2. Hypothesize (1) Non-idempotent SCD2 load — a rerun or retry inserted a new version without closing the previous one; (2) two changes in one batch — the merge handled one change per key per run, so multiple same-batch changes produced versions with the same valid_from; (3) late-arriving change — an update with an event time earlier than the current version was appended as "newest" without re-splitting history; (4) boundary convention mismatch — some rows use inclusive valid_to, others exclusive, so the boundary instant matches both; (5) timestamp precision or timezone — valid_from truncated to the day on one path, full timestamp on another.
  3. Measure Overlap detector: SELECT customer_id, valid_from, valid_to, LEAD(valid_from) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY valid_from) AS next_from FROM dim_customer and flag rows where next_from < valid_to. Count keys with more than one is_current. Join overlapping rows to load metadata (batch id, load timestamp).
  4. Isolate Overlapping pairs sharing one batch id → multiple changes per batch. Pairs from different batches where the older version was never closed → rerun non-idempotency. The newer row has an earlier event time → late arrival. Overlap only at the exact boundary instant → convention mismatch.
  5. Fix Mitigate: rebuild the affected keys' history from the change log with a window function (valid_to = LEAD(valid_from)), which is deterministic and idempotent; downstream facts that joined during the bad window need a backfill. Root cause: dedupe and order changes per key within a batch before merging; make the merge idempotent on (key, change timestamp); pick one boundary convention (half-open [valid_from, valid_to)) and enforce it.
  6. Prevent Tests after every load: no overlaps, no gaps (if the dimension should be contiguous), exactly one current row per key. A fact-level row-count check on point-in-time joins: output rows must equal input fact rows.

Plausible wrong turns

  • "Add QUALIFY ROW_NUMBER() = 1 to the join." Picks one version arbitrarily; you have hidden the corruption and possibly attributed revenue to the wrong segment.
  • "Delete the duplicate rows." Which one? Without the change log, you may delete the true version.

Where this is taught: Part 01 §7 — SCD types, late-arriving dimensions, CDC to SCD2, Part 05 §10 — point-in-time joins.

4. The debugging interview scorecard

How a debugging answer tends to be read at each level. Use it to grade your own recorded mock answers honestly.

DimensionWeakL4L5Staff+
First moveProposes a fix immediatelyAsks for logs or metrics generallyScopes the symptom: what, since when, who is affectedScopes and states business impact and who needs to know now
HypothesesOne, defended regardless of evidenceSeveral, unranked2–4, ranked by prior probability and cost to checkRanked, plus names which ones would be worst if true and checks those early
Measurement"Look at the dashboard"Names the right toolNames the metric that distinguishes hypothesis A from BAlso notes when the needed metric doesn't exist and how to get it
IsolationNoneReproduces the failureBisects: last good vs first bad, one slice, one keyBisects and identifies which change process let it through
FixA config change that hides the symptomFixes the root causeMitigates first, then fixes root cause, names the trade-offFixes the class of bug across the platform, not the instance
PreventionAbsent"Add monitoring"Specific alert on a leading signal, a test, a runbookGuardrail that makes the mistake hard to make: contract, lint, default change
CommunicationSilent thinking, then an answerNarrates actionsNarrates reasoning and what would change its mindAlso narrates stakeholder updates and decision points
Version awarenessTreats one product's default as a lawKnows the defaults of one versionSeparates concept from version-specific behaviourKnows where the behaviour changed and why it matters for upgrades

5. Further practice

Once the drills here feel automatic, run the Part 08 incidents under the same six-step discipline: incident response at 3am, missed SLA, half the revenue, lag won't drain, Iceberg reads 10× slower, Monday OOMs and late data corrupted a report. For each, write down the measurement that distinguishes your top two hypotheses before you read the skeleton. Part 20 has the self-assessment rubric to score yourself.

L5 Interview CardDebugging Lab
Must know
  • The loop: observe → hypothesize → measure → isolate → fix → prevent.
  • Step change means something changed; drift means something grew.
  • Outlier vs uniform: one slow task or partition points at data; everything slow points at capacity or a shared dependency.
  • Green is not correct: zero-row success, passing tests and silent filters are how data goes missing.
  • Duplicates and loss come from source offset, checkpoint and sink commit moving separately.
  • Mitigate first, root-cause second, prevent third — and say which is which.
  • Metric names, defaults and UI tabs are version-specific; the reasoning isn't.
Must be able to explain
  1. How do you tell key skew from a straggler node from a non-splittable file when one Spark task is 20× slower?
  2. Why can consumer lag grow while CPU is low, and what per-partition evidence separates the causes?
  3. How do you reconcile a metric that disagrees with Finance by a few percent?
Must be able to draw

The commit timeline for a streaming job on one axis — source offset, checkpoint barrier, sink write — marking where a crash causes duplicates and where it causes loss.

offset  ──●─────────●────────▶
ckpt    ────■───────────■────▶
sink    ──────▲──────▲───────▶
             crash here ⇒ replay
Must be able to code
  • Top-N key share on a join input to prove skew.
  • Anti-join between two layers grouped by low-cardinality columns to find silently dropped rows.
  • SCD2 overlap detector with LEAD() over validity ranges.
Must be able to debug
  • Airflow run green, yesterday's partition missing — logical date, timezone, empty-input overwrite.
  • Postgres primary disk filling from an inactive CDC replication slot — restart before you drop.
Numbers that matter
  • Max/median task duration above ~5–10× is worth investigating; 30× is an incident.
  • Files per day = commits per day × partitions touched per commit (1-minute trigger × 500 partitions ≈ 720K).
  • Consumer parallelism ≤ partition count, always.
  • Duplicate window after restart ≈ one checkpoint or commit interval; much wider means lost state.
  • Free disk ÷ WAL generation rate = time to disk-full; compute it before choosing a mitigation.
Classic traps
  • Scaling compute for a problem that is one partition, one key or one sink.
  • Raising a timeout or threshold and calling it fixed.
  • Destructive recovery (offset reset, slot drop, snapshot expiry) without stating the data-loss trade-off.
30-second answer

“How do you debug a production data problem?” I scope it first — what, since when, who is affected — and contain the blast radius. Then I list two to four hypotheses ranked by likelihood and cost to check, and pick the one measurement that separates them. I isolate by diffing the last good run against the first bad one, fix the root cause, and add the alert or test that would have caught it earlier.

2-minute answer

Same loop, with the reasoning shown. Step change or drift tells me whether to look for a change or for growth. Outlier or uniform tells me data distribution versus capacity. Then discriminating metrics — for a slow Spark task, shuffle-read bytes against the median separates skew from a bad node; for lagging consumers, per-partition lag separates a hot key from a slow sink; for duplicates, the width of the duplicate window separates replay from lost state. Mitigation comes before root cause whenever people are consuming wrong data: pause publishing, serve the last good snapshot, cap spend. Prevention means an alert on a leading signal, such as bytes scanned, files per partition, retained WAL or state growth, not on the symptom a user will report anyway.

Deep-dive follow-up

“You've mitigated the duplicates with a dedup view. Walk me through making the pipeline exactly-once end to end, naming each boundary and what happens if the sink transaction times out before the checkpoint completes.”

Staff+ follow-up

“Three of last quarter's incidents were 'job green, data wrong'. What would you change in the platform — defaults, contracts, tooling, ownership — so that class of incident becomes hard to cause, and how would you measure that it worked?”
