Part 20

Self-Assessment & Night-Before Cheat Sheets

Quick refresh5 minInterview study25 minDeep practice50 min
Last technically reviewed September 2026
Covers skills matrix across sixteen areas, readiness levels from Needs work to Staff+, ten one-page cheat sheets (SQL, Spark, Kafka, Flink, Modeling, Lakehouse, System Design, Data Quality, Debugging, Behavioral), last-hour checklist
Versions referenced Spark 3.5 / 4.x, Kafka 4.x (KRaft), Flink 2.x / 1.20 LTS, Iceberg 1.x (format v2/v3), Delta Lake 3.x/4.x
Primary references Spark performance tuning · Kafka docs · Flink docs · Iceberg docs · Delta Lake docs
Known implementation differences The concepts on these sheets are timeless; every number is a vendor default or a hypothetical and is labelled as such, so check current docs before quoting one.

This part tests nothing new. It tests you. The matrix tells you where you actually stand, area by area, in terms an interviewer would recognise. The cheat sheets compress nineteen parts into ten pages you can read the night before without learning anything new — because the night before is for retrieval, not acquisition.

1. How to use the self-assessment

“L5 ready” is not a feeling. Confidence is cheap the night before and expensive at minute twenty of a design round. Every cell in the matrix below is a thing you can demonstrate: out loud, on a whiteboard or in a blank editor, with no notes, in roughly the time an interview gives you.

The scoring rule is strict on purpose: you are at a level only if you can do everything in that cell and everything in the cell to its left. A candidate who can recite Iceberg’s manifest hierarchy (L5 knowledge) but cannot explain why a MERGE got slower after a week of streaming writes (L4 debugging) is not L5 in Lakehouse. They are L4 with a party trick. Interviewers find the gap; the matrix just finds it first.

  • Do it with a friend. They read a cell aloud and say “show me.” You perform it. If you hesitate for more than ten seconds, or reach for your phone, the cell is not yours yet.
  • Mark honestly. Three states per cell: can do it cold, can do it with a hint, cannot. Only “cold” counts.
  • Fix the lowest row first. One Needs-work row sinks a loop faster than one Staff+ row lifts it. Interview panels average down.
  • Re-run it weekly. Pair it with the four-week plan in Part 09’s roadmap and the mock interview loop.
2026 Interview Note

The levels describe behaviour, not titles. Companies calibrate “Senior” and “L5” differently, and some loops probe Staff+ behaviours in a Senior interview to see how much headroom you have. Treat the Staff+ column as “what earns a strong hire,” not as a separate exam.

2. The skills matrix

Read across a row, not down a column. Each L5 cell ends with where to go if you cannot do it yet. On a phone, the table scrolls sideways.

AreaNeeds workL4L5 readyStaff+
SQL Writes joins and GROUP BY; reaches for a self-join or cursor where a window function belongs; cannot say what NULL does in NOT IN. Writes top-N-per-group, running totals and dedup with window functions; explains ROWS vs RANGE frames; reads an EXPLAIN at a glance. Write a sessionization query and a point-in-time join from memory; explain the plan, why it’s slow, and which rewrite prunes it. Card · Sessionization · As-of joins Sets SQL standards for a team: review rules, anti-pattern linting, cost guardrails; explains the same query’s different behaviour across two engines and why.
Python Loads a whole file into a list; no tests; cannot say what the GIL blocks. Writes a generator-based chunked reader, a dataclass or Pydantic record, and a pytest for a pure transform. Explain when to use threads, processes, async or a vectorised engine for a given job; stream a 50 GB file in bounded memory; test a transformation with fixtures. Card · Chunked I/O · Testing Designs the team’s pipeline library: packaging, typed contracts, test harness, and when to stop writing Python and push work into the engine.
Data Modeling Starts drawing tables before stating the grain; treats SCD2 as “add a timestamp.” Builds a star schema from a prompt; chooses SCD1 vs SCD2 per attribute; knows conformed dimensions exist. State the fact grain in one sentence first; model SCD2 with late-arriving dimensions and defend star vs OBT vs Data Vault for this workload. Card · Grain · SCD Owns cross-domain conformance: a shared customer and date dimension across teams, versioned contracts, and a migration path for a model everybody already depends on.
Batch Pipelines append on rerun; “we just delete and reload” with no partition boundary. Writes an idempotent daily job with partition overwrite; knows why small files hurt. Prove a job is idempotent under retry and partial failure; design a throttled backfill that doesn’t starve production; do the partition-size math. Card · Idempotency · Backfills Designs the orchestration standard: dependency contracts, critical-path SLAs, backfill policy and who is allowed to run one against shared tables.
Streaming Uses “real-time” without a latency number; confuses event time with processing time. Explains tumbling, sliding and session windows; knows what a watermark is for. Explain watermarks, late data and allowed lateness with a timeline; state exactly-once boundaries end to end; pick windowing for a stated correctness need. Card · Watermarks · Delivery semantics Argues when not to stream; designs a replay and correction strategy that makes streaming and batch agree on the same number.
Kafka Thinks more consumers always means more throughput; cannot say what a partition guarantees. Explains partitions, consumer groups, offsets and per-partition ordering; sizes partitions from throughput. Explain ISR, acks, idempotent and transactional producers; diagnose lag with idle CPU; choose a key that avoids hot partitions. Internals · EOS · Distributed card · Lag drill Designs a multi-tenant event platform: topic governance, quotas, schema compatibility policy, retention economics and cross-region replication trade-offs.
Spark Adds executors to fix every slow job; cannot read the stages tab. Explains narrow vs wide transformations and when a shuffle happens; uses broadcast joins deliberately. Diagnose a straggler from the UI; explain shuffle, AQE skew handling, BHJ vs SMJ with sizes; fix an executor OOM without just doubling memory. Card · Shuffle · Skew · Drill Sets cluster and job standards: sizing policy, cost per job, when Spark is the wrong engine and a single-node engine wins.
Lakehouse Thinks Iceberg is a file format; cannot say where ACID comes from on object storage. Explains snapshots, time travel and schema evolution; runs compaction. Walk an Iceberg or Delta commit end to end; choose copy-on-write vs merge-on-read for a write pattern; plan compaction, snapshot expiry and orphan cleanup. Card · Snapshot isolation · COW vs MOR · Serving card Chooses the catalog and multi-engine access model; owns table maintenance as a platform service with SLOs.
Cloud Knows service names; cannot draw how a job gets its credentials. Draws a reference platform on one cloud; uses IaC for resources they own. Draw the platform with identity, network and storage boundaries; explain environments, immutable artifacts and CI/CD for a pipeline. Card · Reference platform · CI/CD Designs multi-account or multi-project landing zones; decides what is shared platform and what each team owns.
Security Long-lived keys in config; “the bucket is private” is the whole answer. Uses roles instead of keys; knows encryption at rest and in transit are separate controls. Design “analysts see transactions, never SSNs” across storage, compute and BI; explain envelope encryption, masking vs tokenization, and exfiltration paths. Identity · Data-layer controls · SSN scenario Threat-models the platform; designs the break-glass path and audit trail, and says what they deliberately left out and why.
Governance Treats GDPR as a legal team problem. Tags PII columns; knows retention and lineage exist. Design right-to-erasure through bronze, silver, gold, backups and derived tables; explain column-level lineage and a data contract with an owner. Card · GDPR · Lineage · Contracts Sets governance that engineers follow because it is cheaper than avoiding it: defaults, automation, and exception handling with an expiry date.
Cost “It’s in the cloud, it scales.” Cannot name the top cost driver. Knows compute usually dominates storage; right-sizes a cluster or warehouse. Estimate the monthly cost of a design from first principles; attribute spend to a team or pipeline; cut a bill by fixing the query, not the invoice. Card · FinOps · Cost method Builds unit economics (cost per event, per dashboard, per model) and makes cost a design review criterion.
Data Quality Tests are “the job didn’t fail.” Adds not-null, unique and range checks; knows freshness is a check. Design reconciliation against a source of truth; define SLIs and SLOs for a dataset; decide which checks block publish and which only alert. Card · Reconciliation · SLA/SLO Owns the quality programme: incident severity for data, error budgets, and consumer-facing trust signals.
System Design Draws Kafka in the first minute; no numbers; no failure modes. Gets to a coherent architecture; sizes throughput when asked. Run all eight steps in 45 minutes: requirements, numbers, model, architecture, failure modes, trade-offs, operations, evolution — unprompted. Card · Framework · Capacity Reframes the prompt when it is the wrong problem; designs for the organisation that will run it, not just the load.
Debugging Proposes a fix in the first sentence. Finds the cause with hints; fixes the symptom. Observe, hypothesise, measure, isolate, fix, prevent — out loud, on an unseen incident, naming the metric that would disprove each hypothesis. Card · Method · Scorecard Turns incidents into systemic fixes: runbooks, alerts that fire before users notice, and a blameless review someone reads.
Behavioral Stories are “we”; no numbers; no conflict. Has STAR stories for most prompts; results are vague. Tell eight stories in two minutes each, with “I,” a number, a trade-off and what you’d do differently; survive two follow-ups on each. STAR frames · Tricky questions Stories show influence without authority: cross-team decisions, saying no, and raising the bar for people who don’t report to you.

If your honest scores show five or more rows below L5, do not spend the next week on cheat sheets. Go back to the chapters. Cheat sheets compress understanding you already have; they do not create it.

3. Night-before cheat sheets

Ten sheets, one printable page each. Every sheet has the same five boxes: Know (facts you retrieve), Explain (questions you answer in two minutes), Draw (the one picture), Debug (the symptom-to-cause pairs), Avoid (what costs you the round). Read them; do not study them. If a bullet surprises you, that is a finding — note it and read the linked section after the interview, not before bed.

SQL

Know
  • Logical order: FROM → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → window → SELECT → ORDER BY → LIMIT.
  • ROW_NUMBER vs RANK vs DENSE_RANK: ties decide which one.
  • Default frame with ORDER BY is RANGE to current row — ties included.
  • NOT IN with one NULL returns nothing; use NOT EXISTS.
  • COUNT(col) skips NULLs; COUNT(*) doesn’t.
  • Pruning needs a predicate on the partition or cluster column, un-wrapped by functions.
Explain
  • Gaps and islands: row number minus sequence gives the group key.
  • Sessionization: LAG, flag gaps over the timeout, running SUM of flags.
  • Point-in-time join: latest row with effective time ≤ event time.
  • Why a correlated subquery may be rewritten as a join, or may not.
  • Hash vs sort-merge vs nested-loop: which inputs each suits.
Draw
  • The plan tree for a join + aggregate: scan → filter → exchange → join → aggregate.
  • A window partition with its frame boundaries sliding over ordered rows.
  • A timeline of SCD2 validity intervals and where an event lands.
Debug
  • Row count exploded after a join: duplicate keys on the “one” side.
  • Query 20 s → 11 min: stats stale, plan flipped, or pruning lost.
  • Totals off by a few percent: timezone boundary or late rows.
  • LEFT JOIN behaving like INNER: filter on the right table in WHERE.
Avoid
  • SELECT DISTINCT to hide a fan-out you don’t understand.
  • Functions on partition columns in WHERE.
  • Assuming your dialect’s syntax (QUALIFY, ASOF JOIN) exists elsewhere — say which engine.
  • Writing before stating the grain of the output.

Full material: Part 05 card · Window functions · Gaps and islands · Tuning workflow · SQL bank

Spark

Know
  • Job → stages (split at shuffles) → tasks (one per partition).
  • Catalyst: parsed → analysed → optimised logical → physical plan.
  • AQE re-plans at stage boundaries using real shuffle sizes.
  • Broadcast threshold is a config (Spark’s default is 10 MB at time of writing — check docs).
  • Executor memory splits into execution, storage, user and reserved.
  • Python UDFs cross the JVM boundary; Arrow-based pandas UDFs cut the cost.
Explain
  • What happens on disk and network during a shuffle.
  • BHJ vs SMJ vs SHJ, with the sizes that tip the choice.
  • Skew: detect it, then AQE split, salting, or isolating the hot key.
  • coalesce vs repartition and when each is wrong.
  • Why a filter did not push down.
Draw
  • Driver, cluster manager, executors with task slots.
  • Two stages joined by a shuffle: map output files → fetch → reduce.
  • The skewed-partition picture: 999 short bars, one long one.
Debug
  • One task runs 30× the median: skew — check task input sizes.
  • Executor OOM: huge partition, collect, or broadcast too big.
  • Heavy spill: too few shuffle partitions for the data.
  • Job slower on Mondays: weekend volume, not code.
  • Thousands of tiny output files: partition count × write partitions.
Avoid
  • “Add more executors” before reading the stages tab.
  • collect() on anything unbounded.
  • Quoting config defaults as universal — name the version.
  • Treating caching as a fix instead of a trade-off.

Full material: Part 04 card · AQE · Join algorithms · Memory model · Straggler drill

Kafka

Know
  • Order is per partition, never per topic.
  • Consumer parallelism is capped by partition count in a group.
  • Durability = replication factor + acks=all + min.insync.replicas.
  • Idempotent producer dedups retries per partition per session.
  • Transactions + read_committed give exactly-once inside Kafka only.
  • Kafka 4.x runs on KRaft; ZooKeeper mode is gone — version-specific.
Explain
  • What ISR is and what happens when it shrinks below the minimum.
  • Consumer group rebalance, and why cooperative protocols hurt less.
  • Log compaction: latest value per key, tombstones, retention of deletes.
  • Where exactly-once ends: the sink must be idempotent or transactional.
  • Choosing a key for ordering without creating a hot partition.
Draw
  • Producer → leader → followers (ISR) → consumer group with offsets.
  • A topic’s partitions mapped to consumers, with one idle consumer.
  • Read-process-write loop committing offsets inside the transaction.
Debug
  • Lag climbs, CPU idle: blocked on a slow sink or external call.
  • Lag on one partition only: hot key.
  • Duplicates after restart: offsets committed after the side effect, not with it.
  • Rebalance storms: processing exceeds poll interval.
  • Consumers can’t keep up: partitions, not consumers, are the ceiling.
Avoid
  • “Kafka gives exactly-once” with no boundaries named.
  • Adding partitions to a keyed topic without mentioning remapping.
  • Using Kafka as the system of record without a retention plan.
  • Quoting default retention or batch sizes as constants.

Full material: Kafka internals · Idempotent producers & EOS · Delivery semantics · Part 13 card · Lag drill

Flink

Know
  • Checkpoints are barrier-based consistent snapshots of operator state + source offsets.
  • Aligned checkpoints wait for barriers; unaligned ones store in-flight data.
  • Savepoints are user-triggered, portable; checkpoints are for recovery.
  • Watermark = min across input partitions; one idle partition stalls it.
  • Keyed state lives in a state backend (heap or RocksDB); RocksDB supports incremental checkpoints.
  • Flink 2.x introduces disaggregated state — version-specific, check docs.
Explain
  • How a checkpoint gives exactly-once state, and why the sink still needs two-phase commit or idempotence.
  • Event time, watermarks, allowed lateness, side outputs for late data.
  • State TTL and why unbounded keyed state is a slow leak.
  • Backpressure propagation through bounded network buffers.
Draw
  • Source → keyBy → window → sink, with barriers flowing through.
  • Two-phase commit sink: pre-commit on checkpoint, commit on completion.
  • Watermark per partition, merged as the minimum.
Debug
  • Checkpoint duration creeping up: state growth or backpressure delaying barriers.
  • Windows never fire: idle partition holding the watermark.
  • Output stalls downstream of a busy operator: backpressure — find the first red task.
  • Restore fails after deploy: operator UIDs changed.
Avoid
  • Processing-time windows for business metrics.
  • Deploying without stable operator UIDs.
  • Growing checkpoint timeouts instead of finding why barriers are slow.
  • Claiming end-to-end exactly-once without naming the sink protocol.

Full material: Flink internals · Watermarks · State at scale · Backpressure · Checkpoint drill · Part 03 card

Modeling

Know
  • Grain first: “one row per X per Y.” Everything else follows.
  • Facts: transaction, periodic snapshot, accumulating snapshot.
  • SCD1 overwrites, SCD2 versions with valid_from/valid_to/is_current.
  • Surrogate keys decouple the warehouse from source key changes.
  • Conformed dimensions make cross-process metrics joinable.
  • Medallion is a staging convention, not a data model.
Explain
  • Star vs OBT vs Data Vault — which workload each fits.
  • Late-arriving dimension: inferred member now, backfill later.
  • Many-to-many via bridge table with weighting factor.
  • Why a soft delete in a fact table breaks naïve aggregates.
  • Additive, semi-additive (balances), non-additive (ratios).
Draw
  • A star: one fact, four dimensions, grain written above the fact.
  • SCD2 rows for one customer across three address changes.
  • Bronze → silver → gold with what changes at each hop.
Debug
  • Revenue doubled: join to SCD2 without the validity predicate.
  • Overlapping SCD2 intervals: non-idempotent merge on rerun.
  • Metric differs between dashboards: non-conformed dimension.
  • Averages of averages: non-additive measure summed.
Avoid
  • Drawing tables before stating the grain.
  • Mixing grains in one fact table.
  • SCD2 on every column “just in case.”
  • Natural keys as warehouse keys when the source can reuse them.

Full material: Part 01 card · Grain · SCD types · Late arrivals · SCD2 overlap drill

Lakehouse

Know
  • Table format = metadata that turns files into a table with snapshots.
  • ACID via optimistic concurrency and an atomic commit (catalog pointer swap in Iceberg, log entry in Delta).
  • Iceberg: metadata.json → manifest list → manifests → data files.
  • Copy-on-write rewrites files; merge-on-read writes delete files.
  • Hidden partitioning and partition evolution are Iceberg features.
  • Maintenance is not optional: compaction, snapshot expiry, orphan cleanup.
Explain
  • An Iceberg or Delta commit end to end, including a conflict.
  • COW vs MOR for a given read/write ratio.
  • Position vs equality deletes, and why readers slow down.
  • Schema evolution by column id, not name.
  • What the catalog does, and what breaks with two catalogs.
Draw
  • The metadata tree with two snapshots sharing manifests.
  • A writer commit racing another: read base, write, validate, retry.
  • Stream → table (small files) → compaction → readers.
Debug
  • Reads 10× slower this week: small files or piled-up delete files.
  • File count exploded: streaming commits with no compaction.
  • Commit conflicts under concurrency: overlapping partitions in writers.
  • Storage keeps growing: snapshots never expired, orphans left behind.
Avoid
  • Calling Iceberg or Delta a file format.
  • Expiring snapshots shorter than your time-travel or replay needs.
  • Quoting feature support without the format and engine version.
  • Assuming every engine supports every table feature.

Full material: Part 07 card · Iceberg on disk · Compaction · Operating · Architectures compared · File explosion drill

System Design

Know
  • Eight steps: requirements, numbers, model, architecture, failure modes, trade-offs, operations, evolution.
  • Rough budget: 5 / 4 / 4 / 10 / 7 / 5 / 5 / 3 minutes.
  • 86,400 seconds a day; ~2.6 million a month.
  • 1K events/s × 1 KB ≈ 1 MB/s ≈ 86 GB/day raw (hypothetical sizes).
  • Name the load-bearing requirement: freshness, exactness or residency.
Explain
  • Why every box traces to a requirement or a number.
  • Batch vs streaming for this latency, with the cost difference.
  • Where exactly-once ends and how you reconcile past it.
  • How you backfill without breaking consumers.
  • What changes at 10×.
Draw
  • Sources → ingestion → processing → storage → serving → consumers.
  • The same picture with a failure list beside it.
  • A column of back-of-envelope figures to the side of the diagram.
Debug
  • “What breaks first?” — answer with the bottleneck from your numbers.
  • Region loss: what is lost, what replays, what is stale.
  • Upstream schema change: where it’s caught, who is paged.
  • Late data: what the dashboard shows, when it corrects.
Avoid
  • Naming a technology before asking about scale.
  • Never reaching failure modes.
  • “Real-time” with no number.
  • Defending a choice by brand instead of requirement.

Full material: Part 18 card · Framework · Capacity toolkit · 100K events/sec · Attack mode · Transcripts

Data Quality

Know
  • Dimensions: freshness, volume, schema, distribution, validity, uniqueness.
  • Reconciliation compares to an independent source of truth; tests compare to rules.
  • SLI is measured, SLO is the target, SLA is the promise with consequences.
  • Write-audit-publish: stage, check, then swap.
  • A contract has a schema, semantics, an owner and a change process.
Explain
  • Which checks block publish and which only alert — and why.
  • How you test a transformation vs how you monitor a dataset.
  • How to reconcile revenue with Finance to the cent.
  • Data incident severity: who is paged, what is rolled back.
Draw
  • Pipeline with check gates between stage and publish.
  • Reconciliation loop: source totals ↔ warehouse totals ↔ diff table.
  • Freshness timeline: event → landed → published → SLO line.
Debug
  • Revenue a few percent above Finance: duplicates, currency, refunds, or cutoff time.
  • Green run, missing partition: wrong logical date or empty upstream.
  • Rows silently dropped: new enum value filtered by an inner join or CASE.
  • Alert fatigue: thresholds with no owner or action.
Avoid
  • “The job succeeded” as a quality signal.
  • Hundreds of checks with no severity.
  • Fixing the number without finding the cause.
  • Publishing before checks run.

Full material: Part 12 card · Reconciliation · SLA/SLO · Releasing data safely · Contracts · Revenue drill

Debugging

Know
  • Six steps: observe, hypothesise, measure, isolate, fix, prevent.
  • First question: what changed — code, data, config, volume, dependency?
  • Compare to a known-good run before theorising.
  • Every hypothesis needs a metric that could disprove it.
  • Mitigate first, root-cause second, when users are affected.
Explain
  • How you narrate while debugging so the interviewer can score you.
  • Symptom vs cause, with one example from your own work.
  • What “prevent” means: a test, an alert, or a design change.
  • When to roll back data vs roll forward.
Draw
  • The pipeline as a chain; mark where the symptom appears and bisect.
  • A timeline: last good run, change, first bad run, detection.
Debug
  • Slow: skew, spill, small files, plan flip, contention.
  • Wrong: fan-out join, timezone, late data, filter on outer join.
  • Missing: logical date, empty upstream, dropped enum.
  • Duplicated: retry without idempotency, offsets vs side effects.
  • Expensive: full scans, runaway retries, forgotten schedules.
Avoid
  • A fix in your first sentence.
  • Restarting the job as a diagnosis.
  • Stopping at the fix — say how it never recurs.
  • Silence while you think.

Full material: Part 19 card · The method · Core drills · Scorecard · Missed-SLA incident

Behavioral

Know
  • STAR, weighted: Situation and Task short, Action long, Result with a number.
  • Eight stories cover most prompts: conflict, failure, influence, ambiguity, saying no, mentoring, trade-off, ownership.
  • Say “I.” The team did things; the interviewer is hiring you.
  • Two minutes per story, then stop and let them dig.
Explain
  • A time you were wrong and what changed afterwards.
  • A time you said no to a stakeholder, and what you offered instead.
  • A pipeline you owned that produced a bad metric.
  • How you decide what not to build.
Draw
  • A one-line index of your eight stories, mapped to the prompts each answers.
  • For your biggest project: before/after architecture in five boxes.
Debug
  • Story runs long: cut Situation to two sentences.
  • No number: find one — latency, cost, hours saved, incidents avoided.
  • No conflict: the story isn’t Senior yet; pick another.
  • Follow-up stumps you: you’re telling someone else’s story.
Avoid
  • Blaming a former colleague or employer.
  • Stories with no trade-off or no cost.
  • Memorised scripts that break on the first follow-up.
  • Reusing the same story for every prompt.

Full material: STAR frames · Tricky behavioral questions · Saying no · Bad metric · Staff and Principal

4. The last hour before the interview

The last hour is for loading, not learning. If you open a new chapter now, you will carry its half-understood edges into the room. Run this list and stop.

  1. The eight steps, in order. Requirements, numbers, model, architecture, failure modes, trade-offs, operations, evolution. Say them out loud once. See the Senior/L5 framework.
  2. Five numbers in your head. 86,400 seconds a day. 1 MB/s ≈ 86 GB/day. Memory ~100 ns, SSD ~100 µs, same-region network ~1 ms, cross-region ~tens of ms (orders of magnitude). One compression ratio you have measured yourself — not one you read.
  3. The debugging chain. Observe, hypothesise, measure, isolate, fix, prevent. First question: what changed?
  4. Three stories, rehearsed to two minutes. Your biggest technical win, a failure you owned, a disagreement you resolved. Each with “I” and a number.
  5. One grain sentence. Practise: “One row per order line per day.” You will need this reflex in any modeling prompt.
  6. One exactly-once sentence. “Exactly-once is a property of a pipeline, not a product; here are the boundaries.”
  7. Three questions to ask them. How is data quality owned here? What broke last quarter and how was it found? What would make this hire a success in six months? Pick the one that fits each round.
  8. Environment check. Editor, whiteboard tool, camera, water, phone silent. Know which SQL dialect you will write and say so up front.
  9. Stop reading ten minutes before. Stand up. The day-of routine in Part 09’s day-of playbook takes it from here.

You will not remember everything on these pages in the room. You don’t need to. Interviewers are not checking recall; they are checking whether you reason from requirements, name what breaks, and change your mind when the numbers say so. That is the whole handbook in one sentence. Go do it.
